Father Doctor Antonio Rubio prays for happiness of both kinds.

ince I saw that our Commentaries on Logic,

S       lately published, were so welcome to you, most

worthy Rector, most grave and most wise Doctors

and Masters, of an Academy famed and illustrious on many accounts, that by common counsel, approved by the vote and judgment of all, you prescribed that they be expounded to their pupils by the professors and Masters of Dialectic for the instruction of youth; since, finally, your decree was confirmed and established by royal authority, inasmuch as it would be useful to all Schoolmen, who might imbibe in these Commentaries a doctrine, approved by your judgment, genuine and consonant with that of this Academy and of the Aristotelian discipline: this, indeed, long since made my whole mind entirely devoted to this University, and not undeservedly; and it has bound me by so close a bond of attachment and love that I thought there was nothing I should not undertake, nothing I should not attempt, which I judged would be useful, or at least welcome, to this Academy. But when the most grave men of this same Academy,

ã ij

[PDF 8]

as well as most learned, to whom I confess myself bound by many titles, saw that our Commentaries had been drawn out more fully than long-established usage in that same University would bear, they judged that it would be welcome and likewise useful if I were to bring out the same Commentaries again, reduced to a compendium— not without the acclaim of many who had long been asking for it. Since, therefore, they were fired with zeal for the common good, and asked this of me again and more often, I had to obey their precepts altogether: their authority, which weighs very much with me, at once turned my mind, hastening to other things, to undertaking this labor. I undertook it indeed, and completed it with what diligence I could. You now have, most grave men, this compendium—hardly more ours than wholly yours: small indeed in substance, very great in the desire to please. This, certainly, was to be kept in view above all, that the minds of those approaching the threshold of the liberal arts should be helped, lest, overwhelmed by the multitude of matters, or at least deterred, they should abandon what they had begun, or despair of being able to master the subject perfectly. This labor, then, undertaken with a truly willing mind, a monument of a mind grateful toward you, I submit to your more mature and prudent judgment, and I wish it dedicated to your dignity. But if I perceive that our efforts are approved by you, endowed as you are with such kindness, I shall pursue all that remains with equal and (if it can be done) greater diligence.

## QUESTIONS

ON DIALECTIC,

B Y WA Y O F I N T R O D U C T I O N .

## QUESTION ONE

Whether Dialectic is necessary.

o explain the title of the question, some divide

T          Dialectic into Natural and Acquired: calling Natural those discur‐

sive reasonings which even rustic men are accustomed to carry

out by the natural light alone; and Acquired, that which we obtain by study and labor. If, however, we are to speak properly, what we have from nature is not Dialectic but a certain beginning of it, namely the natural light of the intellect, from which those disordered reasonings proceed that are quite improperly called Dialectic: properly, however, it is taken only for the acquired faculty, about which we are inquiring whether it is necessary. But “necessary” is customarily taken in the schools in two ways: either simply, that is, without qualification, or in a certain respect, that is, on a supposition. That is called necessary simply which has its necessity not through an order to something else but from its own nature: in which acceptation God alone is called a necessary being, because He has it without order to or dependence on another that He cannot not be. We call necessary on a supposition, on the other hand, that which is such on the supposition of some end to be attained, as we say that taking food is necessary for sustaining life. Therefore, when the title of the question asks whether the faculty of Dialectic is necessary, it is understood not of the former mode of necessity but of the latter, so that the sense is: whether it is necessary for acquiring the other sciences. The first opinion holds that Dialectic is not necessary for the other sciences, but that they can be acquired without it, although

A

[p. 2]

not without great labor nor without an admixture of errors; but that it is useful, so that they may be obtained more conveniently and easily and without danger of erring. So holds Javelli in the Compendium of his Logic, tract. 1, ch. 2, whom few follow; and it is proved by a twofold argument. First, because it is necessary neither for its own sake nor for the sake of the other sciences; therefore in no way. The antecedent is proved: that it is not necessary for its own sake, because, since Logic is at once a science and a mode of knowing, if it were necessary for itself, the science and the mode of knowing would have to be acquired at the same time, against that saying of Aristotle, Metaph. 2, text 1: It is absurd to seek at the same time a science and the mode of knowing. That it is not necessary for the sake of the other sciences is proved because every science has its own definitions and demonstrations, and is therefore its own mode of knowing, so that it does not need Dialectic as a mode of knowing. Second, because two things are necessary for someone to attain science: first, that he know the principles; second, that he know with certainty that he is using apt reasonings, and not fallacious ones, in drawing conclusions from them. But a man can do both without Dialectic, by the natural light of the intellect, as is plain in rustics, who evidently infer one thing from another in this or that matter; and it is related of others that they obtained sciences without Dialectic, as Hippocrates did medicine, and others the mathematical disciplines: therefore Dialectic will not be necessary for acquiring the other sciences.

The second opinion is the opposite one, which affirms that no science can in any way be acquired without Logic. It is held by many, whom the same Javelli cites in the place above, and they prove it by a single argument: because in order to acquire science one must know with certainty how to reduce the conclusion back to the first principles, as Aristotle teaches in Posterior Analytics 1, ch. 2, through evident consequences; but it is impossible to effect such a reduction without Dialectic, since one cannot know with certainty that the whole multitude of conclusions is derived from the principles except by art; therefore one cannot do so except by Dialectic.

The common opinion seems to lie midway between these extremes. It is held by Soto and Cardinal Toledo, proem. q. 1, whom others follow: namely, that Dialectic is necessary for acquiring the remaining sciences perfectly, but that for obtaining them in an imperfect manner it is not necessary but useful, so that without it they can be obtained imperfectly.

2 For the solution of the question three things should briefly be noted. The first is that two things are necessary for obtaining science: first, that the conclusion be deduced through an evident consequence from an evident principle; second, that both be evidently

[p. 3]

evident to the one who acquires the science: for if he does not know the principle evidently, it will be only believed or opined; and if he does not know the consequence to be evident, it will be only probable with respect to him; and from both the first and the second it follows that the conclusion he gathers is not evident but probable, since it cannot be more certain than the premises or the consequence; wherefore it will not be scientific. Second, it should be noted that a man can indeed, by the natural light of the intellect, reason discursively in a certain imperfect manner and deduce one thing from another, though in a disordered way, that is, without knowing the order and dependence that the conclusion has on the principles. This Aristotle taught in Rhetoric to Theodectes 1, ch. 1, in these words: Many do these things at random, and some by practice and habit, etc., because that order cannot be known without art. Third, it should be noted that the habit of science generated through one demonstration, on account of the efficacy of the demonstration, while it is being generated through one act, has the ratio of a habit, or of science, imperfectly, because it is not yet rooted in the subject; wherefore it does not denominate its subject such simply: for a man is not said to have acquired such a science because he has acquired one or another conclusion of it, except in a certain respect, that is, according to that one conclusion.

From these I gather two conclusions, by which I explain my view. The first is: For acquiring one or another conclusion of another science Logic is not necessary, but it can be acquired by the natural light alone. This is proved: because just as the natural light extends itself to knowing the principles, so it can also extend itself, by a man’s own industry and labor, to one or another conclusion proximate to the principles, since it is very well known; and since through one conclusion science is acquired, at least imperfect science, it is true in this sense that Dialectic is not necessary for obtaining the other sciences imperfectly. Second conclusion: An entire science cannot be acquired without Dialectic, that is, according to all its conclusions; which I prove thus. No one can gather all the conclusions from the principles through evident demonstrations unless he knows evidently the order according to which one is derived from another, down to the last, which is gathered proximately from the principles. But the order of all the conclusions among themselves and with the principles cannot be known without the art of reducing or resolving them into the principles; therefore an entire science cannot be acquired without Dialectic: and this is what it means that it cannot be acquired perfectly without it. And in accordance with these two conclusions of ours the third, common, opinion is to be understood, which, understood thus, we say is true.

A ij

[p. 4]

## 4 To the first argument of the first opinion Cardinal Toledo replies that

Logic is necessary for itself according to its different parts, which are presup‐

posed by the others: as the part on the categories by the part on enunciation,

and this latter by the syllogism. But since the first part does not presuppose an‐

other, this solution does not explain how Logic according to its first part can

be necessary for itself. Therefore I reply in another way: Logic has two aspects,

namely that it is a science, inasmuch as it demonstrates its conclusions, and

that it is a mode of knowing, inasmuch as it produces the instruments by

which we are able to know; and this latter ratio is prior to the former according

to our way of considering, because we understand the instruments of knowing,

such as definition and demonstration, before we understand the conclusions

demonstrated in logic. We say, therefore, that Logic as a mode of knowing is

necessary for itself as a science, not only according to its different parts but

also according to its whole self; for which it is enough that as a science it pre‐

supposes itself as a mode of knowing. And when Aristotle taught that it is ab‐

surd to seek at the same time a science and the mode of knowing, by the mode of know‐

ing he meant Dialectic, but by science not Dialectic itself but any other sci‐

ence whatever, as St. Thomas taught in his exposition of that same passage,

which it is absurd to seek together with Dialectic: as if to say that Dialectic

must be learned first, as necessary for the others. To the second I reply that the

natural light, unless it is perfected by the art of Dialectic, cannot know the or‐

der of all the conclusions among themselves and with the principles, and there‐

fore cannot acquire the other sciences perfectly either, as we have already

taught. The argument of the second opinion proves only that without Dialectic

science cannot be obtained in a perfect manner. From what has been said it is

gathered what place Dialectic ought to hold in the acquisition of the sciences:

for it is the first, with which one must begin; because, since it is the mode of

knowing, the others cannot be obtained without it, nor, consequently, be ac‐

quired together with it, unless that absurdity follow, that we seek at the same

time a science and the mode of knowing.

## QUESTION II

Whether Dialectic is a science.

3

S    cience is taken here in its proper sense, for certain cognition obtained

through demonstration, as Aristotle taught in Posterior Analytics 1, ch. 2; but

it is divided into Actual

[p. 5]

and Habitual. Actual science is said to be the assent to a conclusion that is proved through demonstration, as the assent to this conclusion, Man is risible; habitual science, on the other hand, is that which is generated in the intellect from many demonstrated conclusions. And although each is properly science, yet in the common manner of speaking it is taken for the habitual. Of this the title of the question speaks when we ask whether Logic is a science.

And the first opinion denies that Dialectic is a science, but asserts that it is a certain faculty or art inferior to science. This was held by Ammonius in the prologue to the Categories, Alexander at the beginning of the Topics, Giles of Rome on the Posterior Analytics 1, q. 1, Magnesius on On Interpretation 1, at the beginning, Peter Nigri in q. 11 of his Clypeus, and others, whom Villalpando followed in proemial q. 16. It is proved, first, by a twofold testimony of Aristotle, who in Rhetoric to Theodectes 1, ch. 2, teaches that Rhetoric is a certain part of Dialectic, and that neither is a science, but a certain faculty of finding arguments; and in Topics 1, ch. 1, he says that the office of the Dialectician is to discourse from probable premises. Second, it is proved by reason: because every science must have a particular and determinate matter about which it is concerned, as about its proper object, and through which it is distinguished from the others; but Logic does not have a determinate matter, but is concerned with the matter of all the sciences, because in every matter it produces definitions and syllogisms; therefore it will not be a science. Whence Aristotle, Metaph. 2, ch. 2, text 5, and Posterior Analytics 1, ch. 8, text 27, taught that it does not have a definite genus of subject, that is, a definite matter about which it is concerned.

The second opinion is the common one, and to be held: that Logic is a true science. It is followed by St. Thomas, Metaph. 2, 2, lect. 4; Scotus, on the Sophistical Refutations 1, q. 1, and on the Predicables, also q. 1; Nifo, Metaph. 4, text 5, at the end; Soto and Cardinal Toledo, proemial q. 2; Fonseca, Metaph. 2, 3, q. 1, sect. 9; and all the others. It is proved by a single argument, from the definition of science handed down by Aristotle in Posterior Analytics 1, ch. 2: Science is a habit acquired through demonstration; but Dialectic has many demonstrations proceeding from evident principles; therefore science will be generated from them. The minor is proved: for that a syllogism of the first figure concludes evidently is demonstrated from those principles, Said of all and Said of none; and in the individual parts of Dialectic other similar demonstrations are made.

4 To the first argument we say that Aristotle taught that Rhetoric is a part of Dialectic because under the Topical part it is in a certain way

A iij

[p. 6]

contained, inasmuch as it teaches how to find the places from which probable arguments are drawn; and as regards this, neither is a science. But Dialectic not only teaches how to find the places, but proves them through demonstration; and further, that probable arguments generate opinion; and from this it has the true ratio of science. Rhetoric, however, does none of these things, and therefore it is not a science but a certain art inferior to science. The second testimony of Aristotle is explained in almost the same way: because the office of the Dialectician is to discourse probably, not in just any way, but by teaching through true demonstration from what premises a probable syllogism is to be constructed, and that it generates only a probable assent; and this is to be a true science.

For the solution of the second argument a twofold matter of Logic must be distinguished, Remote and Proximate. The remote matter is the things of the whole world, for it produces syllogisms and definitions about all of them. The proximate matter, on the other hand, is the operations of the intellect, which it directs and orders, constructing instruments out of them. The argument, therefore, proves concerning the remote matter, of which Aristotle also speaks in that passage; but a science must have a proximate matter about which it is concerned and through which it is distinguished from the others, and this suffices for it to be a determinate science. That its remote matter is not determinate is no difficulty, because the ratio of a science is taken not from the remote matter but from the proximate.

## QUESTION III

Whether logica utens is a science.

T     he title of the question presupposes that Logic is divided into docens and

utens: a division handed down by St. Thomas, Metaph. 4, lect. 4, and by Scotus, q. 1 on the Sophistical Refutations and also the first question on the Predicables, from whom the schools took it. But before we set out the different opinions, it must be explained whether, just as logica docens is taken for the whole science itself, so too logica utens is taken for the whole, or only for the Topical part. For some say that only the Topical part is utens, and not the demonstrative part nor the rest. Their foundation is the authority of St. Thomas, who seems to assert this in Metaph. 4, lect. 4, and they prove it by this argument: because Logic, as it is the use of defining, dividing and demonstrating in the other sciences, is to be called not so much Dialectic as Philosophy, or whatever other science it is about whose matter such use is concerned.

The common manner, however, of speaking and thinking of the Dialectical

[p. 7]

school divides Logic, taken for the whole science, into docens and utens, so that, just as the whole of it is docens inasmuch as it hands down through demonstration the precepts for producing the enunciation and the syllogism and the remaining instruments, so, inasmuch as it uses all the instruments in the other sciences, it is called utens. And this we must hold as true and necessary. And it is proved, first: because logica utens extends as far as the use of logica docens; but logica docens is said of the whole science and of its individual parts, and not of the Topical part alone; therefore logica utens will also be said of the whole and of the individual parts. Second, the Topical part is called logica utens because it uses probable arguments in the other sciences; but Logic also uses definitions and demonstrations in the other sciences; therefore it will be called utens as regards the remaining parts besides the Topical.

To St. Thomas I reply that his mind is this: that Logic as regards the demonstrative part and the rest (besides the Topical) is truly utens; but because the form of demonstrating which it uses in the other sciences is universal and as it were generic, and is determined by their matter as by a difference and species, it is called not so much Dialectic as Philosophy, in the way in which the genus of any thing is comprehended under the name of the species: for example, the animal that is in man we do not call animal but man. But with the Topical part the ratio is different: because, since probable arguments generate not science but opinion, the use of this part retains the name of Dialectic rather than of the other sciences; because it is a part of Dialectic, which is a true science, and because it is the proper office of the Dialectician to dispute probably in any science whatever. And this difference between the Topical part and the remaining parts of Logic St. Thomas indicated in the same place; from which I gather that this was his mind, and that he does not exclude any part of Logic from the true ratio of utens.

5 Supposing, then, that logica utens ought to be taken for the whole science itself and all its parts, we ask whether it is a science, or at least a habit distinct from logica docens. And the first opinion asserts that it is a true science, but not a habit distinct from docens, rather the same one, so that it is science both inasmuch as it is docens and inasmuch as it is utens. Nifo seems to follow this, Metaph. 4, text 5, and it is proved by this argument. When someone uses Logic in the other sciences by producing demonstrations, he acquires a facility of the intellect for producing those and others again; and he acquires this facility through acts proceeding from logica docens, which they presuppose; therefore it perfects the same logica docens; and therefore it will be true science, because science is not perfected except by science

A iiij

[p. 8]

yet not a distinct science, nor a distinct habit, but the same one, as it were perfecting itself.

The second opinion, which certain moderns follow, asserts that logica utens is a true science and distinct from docens. And in order to prove both, they distinguish two offices or acts of Logic. The first, by which it teaches how to construct instruments, such as a syllogism or a definition; the second, by which it uses the precepts handed down, producing those same instruments in the other sciences. And since through the multiplication of acts a facility is generated in the powers, which facility we call a habit, it is necessary that from different acts different habits too are generated in the intellect: so that first the intellect is made apt for handing down precepts, and then it acquires another, different faculty through the exercise of the same precepts, by producing syllogisms. An example can be given in music, in which a twofold facility is acquired: the first in the intellect, which hands down the rules of consonances; the second in the hands; and the first they are accustomed to call Theoretical, the latter Practical. Whence it follows that a twofold facility must also be posited in Logic, one which is Theoretical, or speculative, the other which is Practical; and the former will be the habit of logica docens, the latter that of logica utens. They prove, first, that they are distinct habits: because a syllogism made in natural Philosophy does not proceed from the habit of that Philosophy, since it does not teach how a syllogism is to be composed; but neither does it proceed from logica docens, for this has only to hand down in general the precepts for producing instruments, not to produce them in particular; therefore it must proceed from another habit, which is that of logica utens. Next they prove, second, that each habit is a science. Of docens it is manifest; but of utens it is proved: because in order that the act of producing a syllogism be perfect and proceed without error, it must presuppose the habit of logica docens, through which we are taught how it is to be produced; but if it presupposes it, it cannot proceed from the same; therefore from another, distinct habit, which is also a science, since it presupposes the habit of docens, which is truly a science, and proceeds in a scientific manner in composing a syllogism.

Our view is that Dialectic utens, as utens, is not a science, nor a habit distinct from logica docens, but the same habit as it is an art producing singular syllogisms. And so the very same habit of Logic, as it hands down through demonstration the precepts in general for composing a syllogism and the other instruments, is logica docens; but inasmuch as it produces singular syllogisms it is an art, and is called logica utens. This

[p. 9]

view St. Thomas follows, Metaph. lect. 4. But because it contains two parts, the first, that logica utens is not a science, the second, that it is an art, each must be proved. It is proved first, then, that it is not a science: because a scientific conclusion is an act which we gather through demonstration from principles known per se; but the act of logica utens is not the assent to a conclusion which we gather through demonstration, but a work that we produce, namely a syllogism or a definition; therefore logica utens is not a science.

Second, science is proximately concerned with universals, and is not of singulars; but logica utens is not concerned with universals but with the singular acts which it exercises in composing syllogisms according to the precepts handed down by docens; therefore it is not a science, but presupposes science.

6 The second part of our view, that logica utens as such is not a habit distinct from docens but the same as it is an art, presupposes that Logic is an art: not a mechanical one, which is concerned with external works, as the smith’s art is, but a liberal one, which is concerned with the works of the intellect, directing them. This St. Thomas teaches expressly, 1-2, q. 57, a. 3, ad 4, and Posterior Analytics 1, lect. 1; and it is gathered evidently from the doctrine of Aristotle, Ethics 6, ch. 4, where he defines art: That it is a habit, with reason, productive or active; by productive understanding the mechanical arts, by which external works are produced, but by active the liberal ones, by which no external work is produced, but the internal works of the soul are directed. This supposed, it is proved first: because it is evident that the habit of Logic is a science, since it proceeds through demonstration; but it is also an art, because it is a habit active with reason, for it directs the works of the intellect and produces singular syllogisms out of them; therefore it is at once a science and an art under different rationes, so that inasmuch as it hands down through demonstration the precepts for producing a syllogism and the other instruments, it is logica docens and a true science; but utens inasmuch as it is an art producing singular syllogisms according to the precepts handed down by itself as docens.

It is proved, second: for the habit of logica docens, acquired through the first demonstration, has for its object the mode of knowing, whose nature it contemplates, and the works of reason, out of which it teaches how to construct syllogisms; but by the very fact that it teaches how to produce syllogisms, it has the power of producing them, since it does not need another instrument through which to produce them, but produces them through the same intellect; therefore, by the very fact that it is logica docens, it is also a habit active with reason, which is to be a liberal art. Wherefore it follows that both rationes are possessed by

[p. 10]

the same habit of Logic, namely of science and of art; but the ratio of science is primary and principal in it, whereas the ratio of art is as it were secondary and presupposes the ratio of science. For we first understand that it delivers precepts through demonstration, and then that, according to the precepts delivered, it produces singular syllogisms.

To the argument of the first opinion I reply that Logic is perfected by the exercise of producing syllogisms not as a science but as an art, just as it is perfected in the ratio of science by the demonstrations by which it proves its conclusions. Wherefore what follows is not that, as using, it is a science, but that it is an art.

7 For the solution of the arguments of the second opinion, note the difference between the arts that are exercised in some way through the members of the body, such as house-building and music, on the one hand, and the others, which are concerned with purely internal acts, such as Logic: namely, that the former require a twofold facility. One in the intellect, in which they exist as in a subject; the other in the external member through which they are exercised: as music, besides the facility of the intellect, requires another in the hand, or in the tongue and palate. And since a facility is a habit, they include two habits, although the facility that is in the external members is not properly a habit. But the other arts, which only direct the operations of the intellect, such as Dialectic, just as they are not exercised through external members but through the intellect alone, so they require only a facility of the intellect: because this is the habit by which they produce and direct singular operations; and this is one and the same in Logic, as has been proved, by which it delivers precepts in general and through demonstration, as a science, and by which it produces singular syllogisms, as an art. And therefore the habit of the science and of the art is one and the same. From which it follows that the distinction of a twofold facility must be denied in those arts which are not exercised through external members.

Now, then, to the first argument of the same opinion I reply that a syllogism made in natural Philosophy proceeds from a twofold habit, namely from the habit of that Philosophy and at the same time from the habit of Logic: from the former according to the particular ratio of such a science, but from the habit of Logic according to the common ratio of the syllogistic form, that is, of mood and figure; moreover from the former as a science, but from the habit of Logic as an art. Such a syllogism therefore requires a twofold facility and a twofold habit, not of Logic, but one of Logic, the other of Philosophy.

To the second, I grant that the act of producing a syllogism presupposes the habit of logica docens; but from this it does not follow that it generates another habit, but that it generates the same habit under

[p. 11]

the ratio of art. It is false, therefore, that it does not proceed from the same

habit of logica docens.

Q U E S T I O N I V.

Whether Logic is one simple habit, and one simple quality.

8

W        e can consider a threefold unity in science, as in other things: numer‐

ical, specific, and as it were generic. But the question does not pro‐

ceed concerning numerical unity, because it is certainly established that

Dialectic is not one in number, but that there are as many as there are differ‐

ent intellects: as the Dialectic that Peter has is other in number from that

which John has. In this sense, then, it is manifest that it is not one simple

quality but manifold. It is asked, then, concerning specific or generic unity,

which of these it has. For if it has only generic unity, it will not be one simple

quality nor one habit, but will contain several under itself, just as animal con‐

tains several species, which have generic unity under it. But if it has specific

unity, it will be one according to species, like whiteness; wherefore it will not

be composed of many habits or qualities, but will be called a simple quality

and a simple habit.

In accordance with these two unities, generic and specific, there are two

opinions. The first asserts that Dialectic is not one habit nor a simple quality,

but composed of many habits and qualities: so that there are as many dis‐

tinct habits of Logic as there are different conclusions, namely one habit of

the predicables, another of the categories, and that distinct habits are like‐

wise to be posited for the other parts; indeed, even for the individual conclu‐

sions of the same part, if they are different; out of which one total and as it

were generic habit is composed, and also one science, inasmuch as the ob‐

jects of all the parts are contained under the most common ratio of being of

reason, or of mode of knowing. This opinion is held by Scotus, q. 3 of the

prologue, doubt 2; Ockham in the same place, doubt 8; Marsilius, q. 2, a. 4;

Gregory, in the same q. 3, a. 3; Gabriel, q. 8; Cardinal Toledo, proemial q. 3;

Fonseca, Metaph. 5, ch. 7, q. 5, sect. 2; and Soto, proemial q. 3, considers it

probable. And it is proved by a twofold reason. First, habits and sciences

take their specific unity and distinction from their objects, and also from the

principles through which they prove their conclusions; but the parts of

Dialectic have different objects and principles; therefore they require dis‐

tinct habits. The minor is proved

[p. 12]

because the predicable, the category, the enunciation and the syllogism, which are the objects of the different parts, are different in species. They also have different principles, because the definitions of these objects are the principles through which the conclusions in the individual parts are demonstrated; and they are very different; therefore they will have different principles and different conclusions, through which different habits of Logic will be generated.

The second reason. We often see that the intellect is more facile with one part of Logic, on account of more frequent use of it, than with another: as with producing probable syllogisms than with demonstrations; therefore it has different habits of them. The consequence is proved: because one habit cannot at the same time be more facile and less facile, just as the same man cannot run swiftly and slowly at the same time.

The second opinion posits a greater unity in Logic, affirming that it is one in species: so that it does not have several habits, either concerning the different conclusions of the same part or concerning the different parts, but the same habit extends itself to all the parts and to all their conclusions. This is the express opinion of St. Thomas, Posterior Analytics 1, ch. 22, and 1-2, q. 54, a. 1. It is followed by Cajetan in the same place; Ferrara, Contra Gentiles 2, ch. 4; Soto, proemial q. 3; and many of the moderns; and to us it seems more probable. But whence, or from what, it receives this unity is not certain among all who follow it. Some assert that it has its unity from the matter, or material object: not in such a way that the material object is one in species, because this is not required; but it is enough that it be one in some way or other, that is, univocal or analogous, a genus or a species, or even most universal, like being, which is the object of Metaphysics; from which, even if it is analogous and most universal, Metaphysics takes its specific unity. Thus, then, Logic has its specific unity from being of reason, or from the most universal mode of knowing.

Others say that habits take their unity from the object too, but from the formal, not the material, object. For they distinguish a twofold unity in the object of any science, Power or Habit: so that one is its unity in its being as a thing, which they call Material; the other in its being as knowable, which they call Formal. Thus in color, which is the object of sight, the unity in its being as a thing is to be a quality, which is a genus with respect to whiteness and blackness; the unity in its being as visible is that which it has inasmuch as it can move sight. They say, therefore, that a science has its unity from its object, not in its being as a thing, because it would follow that there are as many sciences as there are things different in species or genus, which no one has said; but from the same object in its being

[p. 13]

as knowable, that is, inasmuch as it is knowable through science. This distinction of the object, however, is reputed false by certain moderns, which they prove by the testimony of Aristotle and by reason. For Aristotle, Metaph. 4, ch. 15, teaches that neither is the knowable to be defined through science nor science through the knowable, because a vicious circle would be committed, explaining each in turn through the other, and consequently the same thing through itself: as if you were to define sight through the visible, saying, The visible is that with which sight is concerned, and again, Sight is that which is concerned with the visible, this is nothing other than to define sight through itself. This is proved: for if the visible is defined through sight, then sight defines the visible; and if the visible is in turn defined through sight, then it is defined through its own definition; which is the same as to define it through itself, for the definition and the defined are the same. Their reason is that the object in its being as knowable is posterior to the science, since it is called knowable from it; therefore the science does not take its specific unity from it. The consequence is proved: because if the science is prior, then it is one before the object is understood; therefore it must take its unity from something else, which is prior to the object in its being as knowable.

9 To us, however, the distinction of the object in its being as a thing or in its being as knowable seems true and necessary, and so too that science takes its specific unity from the object in its being as knowable; because both are gathered from the doctrine of St. Thomas, 1 p., q. 1, a. 4, and 2-2, q. 1, a. 1; and it is the common opinion of almost all. Which I prove first: because the same conclusion in its being as a thing pertains to two sciences, which cannot be true unless we consider a different ratio of knowability in it; but this different ratio of knowability is taken from the different middle through which it is proved, namely from different principles and a different demonstration; therefore such a distinction and specific unity of a science must necessarily be taken from the unity of the object in its being as knowable and not in its being as a thing. We can take an example in this conclusion, The earth is round, which pertains to Astrology inasmuch as it is demonstrated by it through a Mathematical middle, and to natural Philosophy inasmuch as it is demonstrated through a Philosophical middle. Second, it is proved in the visual power, which perceives color and light, things so different, and which cannot agree in constituting one object of sight under the ratio of quality, for it would follow that sight perceives every quality; nor yet under the ratio of passible quality, because it would follow that it perceives every passible quality; and both are false. It is necessary, therefore, that they agree under another, more particular ratio, so that both may be perceived by the same power; and this ratio

[p. 14]

can be no other than that both can move sight; and this is the ratio of the visible. By the same reasoning, then, all the material objects of any science, which are indeed different in their being as things, since they are different things, must agree under some particular ratio, inasmuch as they can be perceived by the same science; and this Cajetan calls the ratio of knowability, through which the object confers unity on the science.

10 To the argument of the moderns one must reply with this distinction: the denomination “knowable” is twofold, Actual and Relative, and virtual and absolute. And the first is taken from the science itself, and therefore it is posterior; the second, on the other hand, from the nature and essence of the object itself: just as is also the denomination “intelligible.” For example, man is called intelligible by an actual and relative denomination from the intellect and the intellection through which he is understood or can be understood; and therefore in his being as intelligible he is posterior to the intellect and the intellection. But the virtual and as it were radical denomination he takes not from the intellect but from his own nature, because by its own nature and entity anything whatever is intelligible; wherefore according to this denomination it does not depend on the intellect, but is prior to it. The testimony of Aristotle, on the other hand, touches on the manner of defining one relative through the other; wherefore it cannot be conveniently explained before we reach the category of relation.

But although the distinction of the object in its being as a thing and in its being as knowable, handed down by Cajetan, is necessary, it is not, however, sufficient to explain the specific unity that we posit in Logic, unless it is explained further and it is shown from what the unity of the object in its being as knowable is to be taken; for that alone will be the formal ratio from which the science will receive the same unity. It is to be explained, then, by another distinction, which runs thus. In any object of a science, power or habit we find two things: namely the thing which we perceive through the science or power, and this is called the ratio Quae, that is, the ratio Which is perceived; and there is also found the ratio Sub qua, under which the power is concerned with it or perceives it; and this is called the ratio Sub qua of the object, by which it is determined. And from both rationes, the Quae and the Sub qua, one complete and total object is constituted: from the ratio Quae as from the material, and from the ratio Sub qua as from the formal. Whence it can happen that the same ratio Quae is the object of different habits or powers, on account of the different rationes under which it is perceived; and therefore it is true that powers, habits and sciences take their unity from the ratio Sub qua, as from the formal and ultimate one. By this example the matter will become manifest. In the object of sight we find that which is seen, and this is color or light, and it is called

[p. 15]

the objective ratio Quae; we also find visibility, which is nothing other than that color or light can, from its own nature, move the visual power and be seen by it; and from both rationes, namely color and visibility, the complete object of the visual power is constituted: from color, as matter, and from visibility, as form, from which the same power receives its unity. And in the same way this distinction is to be applied to the objects of the sciences; and it is to be said that the ratio Sub qua is the ratio of knowability, from which their specific unity is to be taken.

But it remains to explain what is most difficult in this matter, namely the ratio Sub qua in the objects of the sciences; for the ratio Quae is quite manifest: for it is the matter about which the science is concerned, as being of reason in Logic, and real being in Metaphysics. Cajetan and Ferrara, in the places cited above, teach that the ratio of knowability in the object of any science is to be taken from such and such a mode of abstracting from matter: so that the ratio Sub qua in the object of Metaphysics is its total abstraction from matter, that is, abstraction from matter not only sensible but also intelligible; in natural Philosophy, abstraction from singular matter, but not from sensible matter.

This opinion, however, I consider false, because abstraction from matter is too universal; and therefore it cannot be the ratio Sub qua conferring specific unity or distinction on a science: for under the same abstraction several and different sciences are contained: as under abstraction from singular matter and not from sensible matter, both Philosophies, Natural and Moral; under abstraction from sensible matter, both Mathematical sciences, namely Geometry and Arithmetic.

The true opinion, then, I gather from the doctrine of St. Thomas: namely that the ratio Sub qua in the objects of the sciences is to be taken from such and such a middle for assenting to the conclusions, just as in faith it is taken from the testimony of the one speaking. Now the middle for assenting to the conclusions is the principles disposed in a demonstration, from which the conclusion is gathered: for example, the middle for assenting to this conclusion, Man is risible, is those principles, Every rational animal is risible, Every man is a rational animal, so disposed that from them it is gathered that man is risible: for on account of them we assent to the conclusion. The matter, therefore, about which a science is concerned, inasmuch as it is taken under such principles of the same science disposed in a demonstration, on account of which the intellect assents to the conclusions demonstrated of it, is the complete object; but the principles so disposed are the formal objective ratio Sub qua, from which the science takes its specific unity. And it is gathered also from the doctrine that Aristotle hands down

[p. 16]

on the unity and distinction of the sciences, Posterior Analytics 1, ch. 23, where he teaches that the principles of the sciences stand in two ways: for either they are so different that they neither come from others nor from one another, that is, they neither depend on other, common principles, nor have a necessary dependence among themselves; and these constitute different sciences: thus stand the principles of Philosophy and of Mathematics, and therefore such sciences are different. But the principles of natural Philosophy come from the common principles of Physics, pertaining to matter and form, and have an intrinsic dependence among themselves, inasmuch as the principles of the books On the Heavens and the World are necessarily presupposed to the principles of the books On Generation and Corruption, and these to the books On the Soul; therefore all these parts constitute the same science according to species. And so too stand the principles of Logic: because the particular principles of all the parts presuppose the common principles of being of reason, or of mode of knowing, from which they are said to come; and the same principles of the parts of Logic presuppose one another, and the posterior ones have a necessary connection with and dependence on the prior ones: as the principle of the enunciation, which is its definition, necessarily presupposes the principles of the predicables and categories, which are their definitions; and finally the principles of the syllogistic art presuppose and depend on the principles of the enunciation; and this is to come from one another, that is, the posterior from the prior, on account of the necessary dependence they have on them. And principles that stand thus are called the same formally, on account of their intrinsic connection and dependence, and different only materially, because they contain different matter, simple or composite, and composite matter of different kinds too. Whence it follows that the ratio Sub qua in the object of Dialectic, taken from those same principles, is the same, and therefore confers specific unity on the science.

11 To the first argument of the first opinion the reply is that the parts of Logic are indeed different materially, or in their being as things, but formally, or in their being as knowable, they have specific unity. Just as colors differ in species, as whiteness and blackness, in their being as things, since they are things or qualities of different species; but under the formal ratio of the visible they are of the same species: which is efficaciously proved, because they have the same mode of moving sight; whence the vision of white and of black are not of different species but of the same. By the same reasoning, then, the parts of Logic, such as the predicables, the categories, the enunciation and the syllogism, as they are certain things and different instruments, are distinguished in species; but under the ratio of the knowable,

namely

[p. 17]

namely as their conclusions are proved under the same principles and through the same demonstrations, they are of the same ratio, because Logic has the same mode of knowing them, that is, through the same principles. And what is added in the argument, that the principles are different, is to be resolved in the same way: that they are indeed different truths; but on account of the intrinsic connection and dependence that they have on the common principles of being of reason, and among themselves, inasmuch as the posterior necessarily presuppose the prior (as the principles of the syllogism and the principles of the enunciation presuppose the principles of the simple terms of which the enunciation is composed, that is, of the predicables and categories), they are reputed formally the same principles, as Aristotle taught in the place above; and on account of the formal identity of the principles, the demonstrations of any part of Logic are also of the same ratio, and so too are all the conclusions, and the object is likewise the same, on account of the formal identity of the principles.

To the second I reply that when the intellect has acquired the habit of Logic through the demonstration of one part, and afterwards exercises itself about other parts through new demonstrations, it acquires certain other facilities, yet not other habits: because these facilities are of the same ratio, on account of the specific unity of the principles and conclusions through which they are acquired, and are distinguished only materially, as integral parts of the same habit. And although this habit is a spiritual quality, and therefore does not have quantitative and bodily integral parts, as bodies have, it has nevertheless spiritual ones, according to its own nature, which are called parts of extension; just as it is certain that it has parts of intension, as will be explained in its place. Nor on account of such parts does it cease to be a simple quality, as it would cease to be if there were distinct habits, as the opposite opinion asserts: because to be a simple quality signifies only that it is not composed of many qualities or habits formally or specifically different; for such a composition would take away its specific unity, which it is certain integral parts, different only materially, do not take away: just as the fact that Peter’s whiteness has integral parts in the head and in the foot does not prevent it from being a simple quality. And this composition of integral and material parts St. Thomas attributes to science, 17, q. 12, a. 2, even though he expressly teaches that it is a simple habit and quality, as we have seen; wherefore he does not believe that it is repugnant to its simplicity.

B

[p. 18]

Q U E S T I O N V.

Whether Dialectic is a practical or a speculative science.

12

T      he title of the question presupposes that some sciences are practical

and others speculative: which Aristotle teaches expressly, Metaph. 2, and

it is the common opinion of the whole school; and it is proved by this argu‐

ment. That is practical which by its own nature is ordered to a work; but

some sciences are about things operable by us, and order their cognition to

the end of operating, as moral Philosophy, which treats of the virtues, and

medicine, of the human body as able to be healed; others, however, are con‐

cerned with purely speculative things; therefore it is necessary to admit prac‐

tical and speculative sciences. This supposed, we ask whether Dialectic be‐

longs to the practical or to the speculative sciences. But in order that the

question may be better understood, it should be noted what praxis is, and

what the practical is. Praxis is the same as operation, and the practical the

same as the operative, or the principle of the operation, or what is directive

of the same operation. But the principle of an operation is twofold, proxi‐

mate and remote. The proximate is that from which the operation proceeds

or by which it is directed; the remote, on the other hand, is that which con‐

siders the operation in general, handing down precepts for making or direct‐

ing it; from which it follows that it makes or directs it in the singular. We

have an example of the first in the arts: for the smith’s art is the proximate

principle of the operation. An example of the second in the practical sci‐

ences: for since science is not of singulars but of universals, and an operation

does not take place except in the singular, the sciences cannot be the proxi‐

mate principle of operation, but only the remote one, from the fact that they

hand down precepts in general, teaching in what way things are to be made

or directed in the singular. Whence it follows that “practical” is said first and

more principally of the arts than of the sciences; but for the true ratio of a

practical science it is enough to be the remote principle of an operation in

the manner explained, because it is impossible for it to be the proximate

principle of an operation, since it considers it not in the singular but in gen‐

eral. Both acceptations of “practical” are contained in the doctrine of

Aristotle: the first and proper one in Ethics 6, ch. 5 through 8, where he enu‐

merates only two practical habits, namely prudence and art, because only

these are proximate principles, productive or directive, of an operation; the

second and less proper one in Metaph. 2, ch. 1, text 1; bk. 6, ch. 1, text 2 and 3;

and bk. 11, ch. 1, in which places he attributes “practical” to the sciences, di‐

viding them into speculative and practical

[p. 19]

but it cannot belong to the sciences taken in the first and most proper mode, but only in the second and less proper mode, which is nevertheless sufficient for them to be truly and properly called practical sciences. From which it is understood that when we ask whether Logic is a speculative or a practical science, we are not speaking of the most proper “practical,” but of the less proper, which can belong to the sciences.

13 On the question so explained, then, there are four opinions. The first holds that Logic is a speculative science and not a practical one. It is followed by Scotus, q. 1 of the prologue; Durandus, q. 6; Soto and Toledo, proemial q. 5; Soncinas, Metaph. 6, q. 6; Capreolus, q. 1 of the prologue, a. 2; Nifo, Metaph. 1, q. 1; Canariensis in his writings on the first part, q. 5, a. 1; and of the same opinion St. Thomas seems to be, opusculum 10, fol. 128, p. 1, and 1-2, q. 57, a. 1, ad 2. And it is proved by two arguments. First, because whether a science is practical or speculative is gathered from its end, as Aristotle teaches, Metaph. 2, text 3; but the end of Logic is not to compose a syllogism or any other instrument whatever, but to inquire into and speculate on its nature and properties; therefore it is not a practical science but a speculative one. The antecedent is proved: because someone will not be said to have acquired Logic from the fact that he produces syllogisms, but because he knows its nature through demonstration; therefore Logic is not productive of the syllogism but speculates on its nature; wherefore it will not be practical but speculative.

Second, it is proved from the mode of proceeding: for a practical science proceeds in the compositive mode, because composition is a certain operation; but a speculative one in the resolutive mode, resolving or reducing its own conclusions back to the first principles; but Logic does not proceed in the compositive mode but in the resolutive, inquiring into the nature and properties of syllogisms and of the other instruments; therefore it will be speculative. The minor is proved: because even if someone composed no syllogism, he would truly be called a logician from the fact that he knew its nature and properties through demonstration; therefore Logic does not proceed in the compositive mode but in the resolutive.

The second opinion affirms that Logic is a practical science. It is held by Gabriel, q. 13 of the prologue; Ockham on bk. 3, d. 2, q. 6; Paul of Venice at the beginning of his Logic; Albert the Great, On the Soul 2, ch. 1, 2; Jandun, Metaph. 6, q. 1 and 5; Fonseca, Metaph., ch. 3, q. 2, sect. 4. And it is proved, first: for that science is practical which is operative or directive of operations; but Logic is directive of the operations of the intellect; therefore it is practical. The minor is proved, first, from Aristotle, Rhetoric 1, ch. 1, where he teaches that Dialectic

B ij

[p. 20]

was invented to direct operations which could be done well and badly. Next, by reason: because the operations of the intellect, considered according to their own nature, do not pertain to Logic but to natural Philosophy; therefore they are considered in Logic only insofar as they are directed and ordered, so that they may take place without error and a syllogism or another instrument may be constructed out of them; therefore Logic is directive of them, which is to be practical. We have an example of this truth in the art of the carpenter, which is perfectly practical, and which is concerned with pieces of wood: not according to their nature (for considered in this way they pertain rather to Philosophy), but by disposing and preparing them so that a chair may be made out of them; therefore Logic, which is concerned with the works of the intellect by so ordering them that a syllogism can be made out of them, will be a practical science.

Second, speculative sciences are sought for their own sake, so that through them we may attain the cognition of their objects; practical ones, however, not for their own sake but for the sake of directing operations; but we seek Logic not for its own sake but for the sake of the other sciences, to the attaining of which it is ordered as their instrument; therefore it is not speculative but practical.

The third opinion, seeing that Dialectic has both rationes, namely the practical and the speculative, and that both rationes cannot belong to the same habit, distinguishes a twofold habit in it: one speculative, by which we consider the nature of syllogisms and of the other instruments; the other practical, by which we compose them. And the first habit it calls Theoretical Dialectic, that is, cognitive of the object; the second, practical Dialectic, that is, directive. And it uses the example of medicine, in which a twofold habit must also be posited: one by which the nature of the healable body and of medicines is considered, and it is called Theoretical medicine; the other by which medicines are applied to curing the body, and it is called practical medicine.

The last opinion asserts that Dialectic is neither speculative nor practical per se, but rather an instrument ordered to attaining the speculative and the practical sciences; and that on account of this both rationes, the speculative and the practical, belong to it in a certain accidental manner. So holds Peter Nigri, q. 14 of his Clypeus, and all the Greeks, who assert that Dialectic is not a part of Philosophy taken universally, but an instrument. This opinion is proved by a certain testimony of Aristotle, Topics 1, ch. 9, where he divides problems, which are propositions probable on either side, into contemplative, active and instrumental

[p. 21]

and these last he calls dialectical problems: therefore he holds that Dialectic is neither speculative nor practical, but instrumental. Next, by reason: because Logic directs the works of the intellect; but the intellect is neither speculative nor practical, but a certain more universal power, to which each ratio belongs accidentally: the same, therefore, must be said of Dialectic.

14 For the solution of the question, it should be noted, first, that Logic performs two things. For first it delivers the precepts for constructing syllogisms and the other instruments, explaining the parts of which they ought to be composed. This is proved from the definition of the syllogism, which asserts that it is an expression in which, certain things being posited, something else follows of necessity because these are posited, that is, by virtue of the premises. The premises, therefore, which are the major and the minor, disposed in mood and figure, are as it were the material parts of the syllogism; while the disposition in mood and figure is as it were its form. Aristotle also, in the books Posterior Analytics, especially bk. 1, ch. 2, defines demonstration, saying that it is a syllogism consisting of first things, that is, of principles, and of true ones indeed, for from the false a true conclusion does not follow, and of the causes of the conclusion: because the premises are the causes of the conclusion. These, then, are the precepts for making a syllogism and a demonstration. The second thing it performs is to prove these same precepts through demonstration, resolving the conclusions all the way to the first principles, which Aristotle did in the same place, teaching that one cannot have science of any conclusion unless one knows how to demonstrate the premises and to reduce them all the way to the first principles, known per se and indemonstrable.

It should be noted, second, that to deliver the precepts for composing a syllogism and a demonstration is the same as to teach the mode in which it ought to be composed so that it can be an instrument for acquiring science; and this is also to proceed in the compositive mode: just as the art of house-building is said to proceed in the compositive mode because it teaches that a house is to be composed of stones and timbers disposed in this or that way. To teach through demonstration how to compose a syllogism, resolving or reducing the conclusions all the way to the first principles, is likewise the same as to proceed in the resolutive mode: whence it follows that it is evident that Logic has each mode of proceeding, and intrinsically indeed: because it could not deliver a perfect cognition of the mode of knowing unless it proceeded in both modes.

It should be noted, third, that Logic has not only each mode of proceeding but also each end, namely of operating and of speculating, and of composing a syllogism, which I prove thus. The compositive mode is by its nature ordered to correctly

B iij

[p. 22]

composing a syllogism; and to compose a syllogism well is to order or direct the operations of the intellect of which it is composed: therefore Logic has for its end to direct operations, which is a practical end. As for the end of speculation, it is plain: for the resolutive mode of proceeding is of itself ordered to speculating the nature of the object, of which attributes are proved through demonstrations whose conclusions are reduced to the first principles; therefore from the resolutive mode the end of speculating the nature of the object is evidently gathered.

15 Finally it should be noted that these modes of proceeding, the resolutive and the compositive, and also these ends of directing the operations of the intellect and of speculating the nature of the mode of knowing, are as it were partial and inadequate with respect to Logic, and are contained under the adequate and total end of the same science, which is to know perfectly the nature of the mode of knowing. This is proved by this argument: for a perfect cognition of the mode of knowing it is not enough to know the mode of composing a syllogism and the other instruments, but it is required that it be known through demonstration; and demonstration, in order to be perfect, demands the resolution of the premises all the way to the first principles, which is to speculate the nature of that same mode: therefore the perfect cognition of the mode of knowing, which is the object of Logic and its adequate and total end, contains each end as a partial one, as it were, and is superior with respect to both. But under it the partial and inadequate ends, and the modes of proceeding, correspond mutually to each other, and one is ordered to the other and conversely: because Logic teaches how to compose a syllogism so that through it, as through an instrument, it may speculate its nature; and it speculates its nature so that it may know perfectly how to compose it, because perfect composition demands perfect cognition of the whole composite and of its parts; and thus mode corresponds to mode, and end corresponds to end, and from both there results the perfect cognition of the mode of knowing, which is the adequate end of Logic, higher than both and containing both eminently.

These things supposed, our view is that Logic is at once a practical and a speculative science; which, besides others, Father Suárez follows, vol. 1 of his Metaph., disp. 44, near the end, and Father Gabriel Vázquez on 1 p. of St. Thomas, disp. 9, ch. 1, no. 1, who proves it effectively by this argument, gathering it thus from the doctrine delivered. A practical science is one that is not only about a thing that is operable or directible, but proceeds in an operable mode and is ordered to the end of operating or of directing operations: but Logic has these three conditions; therefore it is truly practical. The minor is proved: for in the first place it deals with a thing that is operable or directible, namely with the operations

[p. 23]

of the intellect; and indeed in an operable mode, that is, the compositive; and finally it is ordered to the end of directing those same operations, which it also does when it orders them into a syllogism or another instrument. That it is also speculative I prove. For a speculative science is one that deals with a speculable thing, proceeds in the resolutive mode, and is ordered to the end of speculating its nature; but such is Logic; therefore it is speculative. The minor is proved thus. The mode of knowing, or being of reason, which is the object of Logic, is a speculable thing having attributes which can be demonstrated of it, and are truly demonstrated in logica docens, which resolves those demonstrations all the way to the first principles: which is to proceed in the resolutive mode; and that resolutive mode is of itself ordered to speculating the nature of the thing; therefore it also has for its end the speculation of its object. And this argument shows clearly enough how false is what certain of those who follow the first opinion assert, namely, that Dialectic proceeds in a practical mode, but that this mode of proceeding is ordered to speculation, and therefore does not make a practical science but a speculative one. For the resolutive mode of proceeding is no less ordered to praxis, since it is ordered to composing a syllogism perfectly, and nonetheless it constitutes Dialectic speculative: therefore, even if the compositive mode is ordered to speculation, it will constitute a practical science. Moreover, since the compositive mode is of the essence of practical science, it cannot be found in any science without constituting it practical, whether it is ordered to speculation or not. For the ordering rather shows that such a science has each ratio, the practical and the speculative.

This is proved, second, because Logic is the gate through which we enter the other sciences, and as it were the organ and instrument for acquiring them, and it furnishes the mode of knowing to all of them; but among the other sciences some are speculative, others practical: therefore Dialectic must have each condition: because if it is not practical, it cannot be the gate through which we enter the practical sciences, nor will it be able to give them the mode of knowing and of proceeding practically; and by the same reasoning it could not give this to the speculative ones unless it were speculative. It is necessary, therefore, to grant it each condition.

But there remains a certain argument against our view, which must be solved before we proceed to solve the arguments of the other opinions; and it is of this kind. Practical and speculative are differences by which sciences are distinguished in species; therefore they cannot belong to the same science. The consequence is proved

B iiij

[p. 24]

because from two species a third cannot be composed: therefore neither can Dialectic be composed of the practical and the speculative. For it would follow that it is placed in two species, and is as it were a monster.

For the solution of this argument it should be noted that, just as in universal efficient causes virtues of diverse species can exist in unity, so that one simple virtue of the superior cause contains both eminently, and with respect to it each is as it were inadequate; and as in formal causes the essential rationes of inferior forms can be contained under one superior form, so that, since the superior form is one and simple, it can give the one and the other being that is given by each of the inferior forms: in the same way one superior science, which has the mode of a form, can contain diverse essential rationes or modes of inferior sciences. We can have sufficiently manifest examples of these three. For the sun, by one simple virtue, can produce several effects diverse in species, which cannot proceed except from particular causes diverse in species: because in that one form the inferior virtues diverse in species are contained eminently. In forms, too, the rational soul gives the body vegetative and sensitive being, which grades of being are given by inferior forms diverse in species, such as the form of a plant and that of a horse: so that it is true that the rational soul is at once vegetative and sensitive, and that there is found in it, in unity, the perfections of forms diverse in species, which it is said to contain not only eminently but also formally, under a certain superior grade. And finally, in the sciences, St. Thomas teaches, 1 p., q. 1, a. 4, that sacred Theology is at once practical and speculative, so that it embraces each perfection under a superior grade, on account of the eminence of its object, which is God, as speculable truth and as the ultimate end of our operations. The same, therefore, we grant to Dialectic, not on account of the eminence of its object, but on account of its universality: because the mode of knowing bears on all the sciences, and it gives the mode of knowing to the practical and to the speculative ones; and therefore it must contain each mode, eminently indeed, because as to this it is superior to the other sciences, and also formally, because it formally contains each mode of proceeding, the resolutive and the compositive, and it is ordered to each end, that of directing the operations of the intellect and that of speculating the nature of the mode of knowing. But the practical and speculative rationes are inadequate with respect to it, being contained under the adequate and superior ratio of knowing perfectly the nature of the mode of knowing.

From these things I reply to the form of the argument: for when it is said that the practical and the speculative are rationes diverse in species, it must be granted

[p. 25]

and therefore they cannot belong to the same particular science, but they can well

belong to a universal one, having a certain superior ratio that contains each perfec‐

tion eminently and formally. Just as vegetative and sensitive cannot belong to the

same particular form, but can well belong to a universal one, such as the rational

soul is; nor on that account will such a universal science be in a twofold species,

but it will have one more eminent species, containing each ratio, with respect to

which each is as it were partial and inadequate.

The arguments of the first and second opinions do indeed prove that Dialectic

is practical and that it is speculative, but not that it has only one ratio, so that it is

either only practical or only speculative.

The last opinion, however, is false, because Dialectic’s being the instrument of

all the sciences does not take away from it the true ratio of science, and therefore

not the true ratio of practical and speculative either; but it proves that it is a uni‐

versal science, from which it has it that it embraces both rationes at once, emi‐

nently and at the same time formally: because it does so under a superior and

more eminent formal ratio.

The testimony of Aristotle about the instrumental problem, which he attribut‐

es to Dialectic, is free of difficulty; for its sense is that it is not only active, or only

contemplative, but contains both under a superior ratio. With the intellect, how‐

ever, the case is different from that of the sciences: because, since it is a universal

power, it abstracts from each ratio, the practical and the speculative, which with

respect to the sciences are as it were essential modes by which they are distin‐

guished in species.

## QUESTION VI

What the object of Dialectic is: whether the real mode of knowing, or a being of reason.

17

O      bject, subject, and matter are the names customarily given to the thing

about which a science is concerned: for these three names have almost the

same signification. It is called object by order to the habit, because it is as it were

the target at which the habit aims; subject, by order to the attributes which are

proved of it in the science; matter, by relation to the formal ratio under which it is

considered by the science itself. It is the same, therefore, to ask what the object of

Logic is, and what the matter is about which it is concerned, or what the subject is

of which it demonstrates attributes and whose cognition it intends to attain: and

with this the title of the question is explained.

But the conditions which the object ought to have must be proposed, so that it

may be understood that this is the object of this science rather than something

else, to which they belong better. Now the first condition

[p. 26]

is that it exist in the nature of things, or at least be possible: for its actual existence is not required; for of the rose in winter, when it does not exist, there is science, because it is at least possible; but of an impossible thing, such as a chimera, there cannot be science. The second condition is that its cognition be intended in the science. The third, that it comprehend under itself all the things that are treated in the science. The last, that it be one in some way, so that it can give unity to the science.

These things set out, the points on which all agree must be presupposed as certain, so that we may arrive at the difficulty of the question. Now it is certain, first, that Dialectic has some determinate matter about which it is proximately concerned, as about its proper object. The reason for this is that every determinate science must intend the determinate cognition of some thing; but Logic is a determinate science, and distinct from the others: therefore it will have a determinate matter, or object, whose cognition it intends, and by which it is distinguished from the other sciences: because just as a power takes its specific unity from its object, so also does a science, as Aristotle teaches, On the Soul 2, ch. 4. And although this seems contrary to the doctrine of Aristotle, who asserts that Dialectic is not of an object of one genus, or that it is concerned with all the objects of the sciences, Posterior Analytics 1, ch. 12, and text 24, and Metaph. 4, text 5, yet in truth it is not contrary, because he speaks of the remote matter of Dialectic, and this is not determinate, since it makes enunciations and syllogisms about all the things in the world; but its proximate matter is determinate, and about it the present question inquires whether it is this or that.

It is certain, second, that this proximate matter of Dialectic is not words or names, as the ancient Dialecticians asserted, from which they came to be called Nominalists in the school: because, although it uses words to signify things, it nevertheless disputes principally about the things, as Aristotle expressly taught, Metaph. 4, text 5, and as experience proves: because it constitutes syllogisms and the other instruments in things.

It is certain, third, that the proximate matter, or object, of Dialectic is a being of reason: for from this it is called Rational. But being of reason is twofold: one is made directly and per se by reason or the intellect, such as are its operations, like the apprehension of simples, composition and division, and the syllogism; the other is a being of reason not made directly by the intellect, but as it were indirectly and per accidens; and it is a property following those same operations as ordered by it, that is, as constituted in a proposition or a syllogism; and this property is not real, because it does not belong to those operations from their own nature, but is attributed to them

[p. 27]

by the intellect while they are thus ordered by it: as when it orders three propositions, the major, the minor, and the conclusion, according to the syllogistic rules, there follows on such an ordering of them the property or denomination of syllogism, which the intellect attributes to them; and this property is called a being of reason made not directly but indirectly by the intellect, and one which has no other being than to be known by it.

18 Corresponding to these two beings of reason, there are in the first place two opinions about the object of Dialectic. The first, which several moderns defend, holds that the first being of reason is its object, namely the real operations of the intellect themselves, as directible by the intellect, or as they are actually directed, that is, as they can be constituted in a syllogism, or as they are actually constituted; and they say that each of these is something real, that is, both the operations themselves and their directibility (so to speak), that is, the aptitude for a syllogism to be made from them, and also their actual ordering. For this opinion is defended in two ways by the moderns: some say that the real operations are the object, not as they are actually ordered, because the actual ordering can posit nothing intrinsic in them, but only an extrinsic denomination from an as it were reflex operation of the intellect ordering them, but according to the aptitude they have to be capable of being ordered; and this aptitude they call ordinability or directibility, and a real one indeed, since it belongs to them from their own nature, even before they are ordered. Others say that those same operations as actually ordered are the object, so that the actual ordering is some real mode in them: for since they are ordered through a true and real judgment of the intellect, or at least the operations themselves are nothing other than certain ordered judgments of the intellect, the ordering cannot fail to be something in them. Those holding either view agree, however, in this, that these operations are the object according to some real mode or property; and therefore all of them say that the formal object of Dialectic is the real mode of knowing.

The authors of this opinion prove that the second being of reason is not the object by this argument. The object of a science must have two things: first, attributes which are demonstrated of it in the science; second, that it be considered per se by the science itself; but a being of reason has neither: therefore it cannot be the object. Not the first, for a being of reason is nothing in things, but has only objective being in the intellect, as something fashioned by it; therefore it neither has a nature whose cognition the science might intend, nor attributes which might be proved of it: for if it had attributes, they would be either real, and this is not so; or beings of reason, and then they would be predicated of them formally, which is repugnant; just as it is repugnant for man to be predicated formally

[p. 28]

of risibility or of the risible. Second, it is proved: because, since it is not made directly by the intellect, neither is it known directly or per se by it, but indirectly and per accidens: therefore neither will it be known directly or per se by science, which is an intellectual habit.
