Next they prove, second, that the first being of reason, or the real mode of knowing, is the object of Logic, by another argument. A syllogism or demonstration contains ordered operations of the intellect, and is a real instrument: therefore it is a real mode of knowing; wherefore it is considered in Dialectic as something real; and the same reasoning holds of the other instruments: therefore the real mode of knowing, as something common to all of them, will be the object of Logic. The antecedent they prove thus: Demonstration has a real effect, namely the science which it generates: therefore it is its real cause; wherefore it cannot be a being of reason, but is real. And they confirm it: because Dialectic is a practical science, as we have seen; therefore it has a praxis, that is, an operation made or ordered by it, for its object; but an operation, as made or ordered, is something real: because nothing can be per se made or per se ordered unless it is real: therefore the object of Logic must be real.

Second. The operations of the intellect, insofar as they are directible by that same intellect, pertain to some science or art by which they can be directed, and to no other than Dialectic, because they are not directed by any other: therefore, as directible, they are the object of this science; and directibility is a real property of them, just as intelligibility is a real property of real being, and numerability of number, and visibility of color: therefore under a real ratio they are the object of Dialectic, which consequently will be something real.

19 The second opinion asserts that the being of reason which is made indirectly by the intellect is the object of Dialectic. It is followed by St. Thomas, Metaph. 4, lect. 4, and opusc. 4, On the Nature of Genus, ch. 4; Cajetan on the chapter on genus; Dominic of Flanders, Metaph. 4, q. 5, a. 2; Soto, proem. q. 5; and among the more ancient, the Commentator in the Epitome of the Predicables, last ch., and Metaph. 4, text, comment 2; Avicenna, Metaph. 1, ch. 2; and not a few of the moderns; and it has foundations in the doctrine of Aristotle, Metaph. 4, text 5, where he asserts that Dialectic, like Philosophy, deals with universal being; but it does not deal with real universal being, with which the Metaphysician and the Philosopher deal: therefore Aristotle means that it deals with another universal being, which has no real being in the nature of things, but only objectively in the intellect, and this is a being of reason.

20 It is then proved by this single argument. Logic deals per se with genus and species insofar as they are predicables, and also with subject and predicate, as they are such and compose a proposition; but all these are beings of reason: for on the side of the thing, or before the operation of the intellect, there is neither genus nor species, nor subject and

[p. 29]

predicate: therefore the being of reason, as it comprehends these and other things, will be the object of Logic. And it can be confirmed: because the things that are treated in Logic, the category, the proposition, and the syllogism, are real beings according to their material ratio, but formally they are beings of reason, as are the forms from which they are denominated, which are relations of reason or second intentions: therefore the formal object of this science is the being of reason, although the material object is real being.

The third opinion, considering that all the things that are treated in Logic are ordered to composing argumentation as to an end, holds that this is its object; so Albert the Great in the prologue to the Predicables, whom Lemosius follows, bk. 1 On the Errors of the Dialecticians, ch. 6. And because among the species of argumentation the principal one is the syllogism, to the composing of which the other things this science deals with are ordered, Scotus, q. 3 of his Logic, held that its object is the syllogism; and finally, because among the species of syllogism the chief is demonstration, to which the others are ordered, others taught that demonstration is the object, as Ammonius and Simplicius in the prologue to the Predicables, and Alexander and Philoponus at the beginning of the Prior Analytics.

Before we propose our view, we refute these three opinions as insufficient by a single argument. The adequate object must contain proximately and adequately all the things that are treated in the science; but neither argumentation, nor syllogism, nor demonstration contains proximately and adequately the simples about which Dialectic disputes, but only remotely, insofar as they are parts of the enunciations of which they are proximately composed; and division or definition they contain in no way: therefore they cannot be adequate objects of Logic, though they can well be objects of some part of it; and perhaps one of them could be called the principal object, such as demonstration, which is the chief instrument for attaining science. Hence if they spoke of the principal object, at least the last could be admitted; but as for the adequate object, none of them is to be admitted.

21 There remain the first and the second, concerning which it must be judged which of them is the more probable; and for this to be done better, it must be supposed as certain that the proper matter of Dialectic is the operations of the intellect, and that therefore they pertain to its object not according to their own nature (for in this way they pertain rather to Philosophy, like the soul and the intellect, from which they proceed as from efficient principles), but insofar as they are directed by it.

22 Second, it must be supposed what it is for these operations to be directed by the intellect: for it is nothing other than for a syllogism, a definition, or another instrument to be made: as for three propositions to be ordered is nothing other than to take one for the major, another for the minor, and the third for the conclusion, so that in mood and figure there is constituted

[p. 30]

from them a syllogism; and what results in them is the passive ordering, that is, their being ordered and constituting a syllogism. We can therefore consider three things in these operations insofar as they pertain to Dialectic: ordinability or directibility, the active direction of the intellect, and the passive direction resulting in them from the active.

And concerning directibility, it is proved either that the operations do not pertain to Logic according to it, or that it is not real but a being of reason, by this argument. The operations’ being directible is either a natural potency or aptitude, belonging to them from their own nature, or else only an obediential one, consisting in this: that just as wood is subject to the craftsman, and as it were obeys him, so that he can make a chair from it, so these operations are subject to the intellect, so that it can make a syllogism from them. And if it is a natural potency, it is evident that it pertains not to Dialectic but to natural Philosophy: just as whatever the operations themselves have from nature pertains to the science that deals with their nature, and this is natural Philosophy. But if it is obediential, it cannot be real. For the obediential potency of wood is real for this reason, that through it the wood is subject to the craftsman for receiving the real form of a chair; wherefore if the form of the chair were not real but a being of reason, neither would that potency be real; but the operations are subject to the intellect for receiving the form of syllogism, which is not real but a being of reason: therefore such a potency is not real. The minor is proved. The ordering by which it makes a syllogism is a relation of one to another, and not a real one, because they are not ordered from the nature of the thing but by the intellect: therefore it is a relation of reason.

23 The second thing that we can consider in the operations is the active ordering, which the intellect makes by a reflex act by which it reflects upon them and orders them, constituting a syllogism; and this active ordering is real, since it is a real act of the intellect that orders; and by it alone the operations are called ordered by a real extrinsic denomination, e.g., syllogism or demonstration; but they have their being a syllogism or a demonstration formally through the relation of ordering that results between them from the operation of the ordering intellect; and the relation of ordering between them cannot be real, because they are not ordered from their own nature but by the intellect, which can posit nothing real in things through its ordering: therefore the direction through which they are formally a syllogism or another instrument, and pertain to Logic, is not some real mode, but only a relation of reason.

These things explained, the first conclusion of this question is: The object of Logic signifies something as material and something as formal: as material, indeed, the real operations of the intellect;

[p. 31]

and as formal, the relation of reason which is called their formal ordering, through which they make a syllogism or another instrument. This is proved effectively from the doctrine delivered, by this argument. Logic has for its object the operations of the intellect which it directs, so that through direction it may constitute from them a syllogism or another instrument: therefore the material object is the real operations, while the formal object is their direction or ordering, through which they constitute such instruments; but the ordering is a relation of reason: therefore the formal object is a being of reason.

Second conclusion. The adequate object of Logic is the mode of knowing common to all the instruments, which consists of real being as material and of being of reason as formal. This follows from the first; wherefore it needs no new proof. In these two conclusions is contained and explained the second opinion, that of St. Thomas and others, which has always been the common one in the school and is to be embraced as the more probable.

25 It remains only to solve the arguments of the first opinion; and to the first, granting the major, the minor must be denied, namely that the logical being of reason has neither a nature nor properties, nor is considered per se in Dialectic: for although it does not have a real nature, nor inhere in a subject, but only exists objectively in the intellect actually considering it, it is nevertheless a certain denomination attributed to things by the intellect after the mode and likeness of an inhering form, as being a genus or a species is attributed to a nature by the intellect, just as whiteness or another inhering form is attributed to a body. Hence it is not altogether a fictitious being, like a chimera, but has a foundation in the very natures to which it is attributed, according as they are conceived by the intellect in this or that way; and this diminished being can be considered by some science.

26 As regards its properties, the matter must be explained by this distinction: a being of reason can be considered in two ways: first, in the abstract, that is, as a certain form without order to the subject to which it is attributed, as whiteness is considered without order to the body in which it inheres. In another way it can be considered in the concrete, that is, as a form applied to the nature which it denominates. And considered in the first way, it has universal attributes after the likeness of real being, such as true, good, etc.; but considered in the second way, it does not have attributes so universal, because it is not applied or attributed to natures considered in common, but in particular, according to its species: for a nature is not denominated by the most universal being of reason, but by particular ones, as by genus, species, subject, or predicate. Wherefore, taken thus, it has no attributes except in its species: as the universal in common has predicability as

[p. 32]

its attribute, and the predicables have particular attributes, as genus has that of being predicable of the species; and so of the rest. And just as the being of reason considered in the abstract does not pertain to Logic but to Metaphysics, as falling short of the perfection of real being, which is considered per se by that science, so to prove universal attributes of it pertains not to the logician but to the Metaphysician; but the attributes which it has as applied to natures, or as denominating them, are proved in Logic; and this suffices for it to be its object. Of these attributes, however, the species of being of reason to which they are attributed are not predicated by formal predication: because it is not formally true that the predicable is the universal, just as neither is the risible formally man.

To the second I reply that a being of reason, while it is being made by the intellect, is not known directly or per se, but indirectly and as it were per accidens; but after it has been made, the intellect can well take it for its object, as it were by reflection, and intend its cognition per se and primarily; and it is taken in this way when it is said to be the object of Logic.

To the first of the other arguments, by which the real operations are proved to be the object of Dialectic, one must reply with this distinction. Demonstration is considered in two ways: materially, for the ordered operations, or formally, for the ordering from which they have it that they are a syllogism or a demonstration; and in the first consideration it must be admitted that it is a real instrument, but not in the second: rather it is a relation of reason. And what is said, that it has a real effect, namely the science which it generates, must also be admitted, by reason of the operations which it includes as material; not by reason of the formal significate, which consists in a relation of reason. Finally, that Logic is a practical science, as is said in the same argument, is true, and that it has as its object a praxis, or operation, directed by the intellect; from which it does not follow that the direction is real, nor is that necessary for Logic to be a practical science; but it is enough that it direct operation in some way, whether the passive direction be real or only a relation of reason.

To the second, it must be granted that the operations as directible can be considered by some science, and are truly considered by Dialectic; but it must be denied that directibility is real: for it is nothing but a being of reason, just as the direction through which they constitute a syllogism, and to which directibility is ordered, is only a relation of reason, as has been proved. With intelligibility and numerability, however, the case is different: because these belong to things or qualities from their own nature, whereas directibility is nothing but an obediential potency with respect to the syllogistic form, which is only a relation of reason; and therefore it is not something real, but a being of reason.

C H A P T E R I O F P O R P H Y R Y. Since it is necessary, Chrysaorius, both for the doctrine of the Categories which is found

in Aristotle, etc.

B R I E F E X P O S I T I O N O F T H E T E X T.

his first chapter is as it were the proem of the whole book of

T          the Predicables, and in it Porphyry does three things. For first, he

teaches that knowledge of the predicables is necessary for under‐

standing Aristotle’s categories: because, since a category is an ordering of predicables according to due subjection and predication, the categorial ordering cannot be known without knowledge of the predicables. Second, he proposes the matter to be treated in the whole book, which is the five universals or predicables, namely genus, species, difference, property, and accident. And finally he asserts that the questions which can be treated concerning these predicables are of two kinds: for some are easy, because they concern matters judged to lie close to the nature of these same predicables, and therefore, once their nature is known, they admit of an easy solution, as: Whether universals are predicated of their inferiors in this or that way, and the like. Others are difficult, because they inquire into certain higher matters, as: Whether universals exist in things, or only objectively in our cognition. The former, he asserts, are to be proposed and disputed; the latter are to be left to Philosophy, because they cannot easily be understood by Dialecticians. In these words the letter of Porphyry is contained.

C

[p. 34]

## QUESTION I ON UNIVERSALS

Whether universals exist in things.

his question is as it were the foundation of all the others that can be 29

T          disputed concerning universals. But in order that its title may be un‐

derstood, it should be noted that the universal is twofold, Complex

and Incomplex. The complex universal is a universal proposition, known per se,

which is the principle of some science, from which many conclusions are in‐

ferred: as in the science of man the universal principle is that he is rational, from

which it is gathered that he is capable of wonder and risible. The incomplex uni‐

versal is a certain simple word signifying something common to many, as man and

animal. Now the present question does not proceed concerning the complex uni‐

versal, but only concerning the incomplex, which is fourfold: in causing, in signi‐

fying, in being, and in predicating. The universal in Causing is said of a cause

that can produce several effects, as the heavens. The universal in signifying is a

common word or concept signifying a common thing, as the word man and the

concept of man which we form in the mind. The universal in Being would be a

thing separated from singulars and existing in them, if such a thing were given,

such as would be that idea which some say Plato posited, namely a man separat‐

ed from Peter and John, from which these would proceed. Finally, the universal

in predicating is said of the common nature which can be predicated of many

and which common words signify: as the nature of man, signified by this word

man, which is predicated of Peter and John.

And the universal in Causing pertains to the Physicist or the Metaphysician,

who treats of the nature of causes; therefore we do not dispute of it now. Nor of

the universal in Signifying, because the Dialectician does not deal principally

with words but with the things signified by them. Nor of the universal in Being,

because it is judged impossible, as we shall see below. Only the question of the

universal in Predicating, therefore, is proposed: whether in these propositions,

Peter is a man, John is a man, that which is predicated of Peter and John is truly

something besides the word, which exists in them.

On this the first opinion was that of Heraclitus of Ephesus and Cratylus, an‐

cient Philosophers, as Aristotle relates in On the Heavens 3, text 3; Metaph. 1, ch. 5,

text; and also 4, text 22: who altogether denied that anything universal exists in things,

on account of this argument: All things that are in the world are singular; there‐

fore nothing is universal. They proved the antecedent in two ways:

[p. 35]

First, from the senses: because whatever we know through the senses, as through sight, hearing, and the rest, is singular, and nothing is common to many; therefore there is no universal in things. Second, all things that come to be in the nature of things are singular, since they come to be through the actions of causes, which are only of singulars: therefore nothing that comes to be is universal; but there is nothing in things that has not been made: therefore all things are singular, and nothing is universal. And since the sciences are not of singulars, which perish on every side, those who denied universals consequently denied the sciences. And Aristotle seems to hold the same, On the Soul, text 8, where he speaks thus: The universal animal either is nothing, or is posterior; and similarly if anything else common is predicated.

The second opinion was that of Plato, as Aristotle affirms, Metaph. 1, ch. 3, text 12, and ch. 5, text 5 and 6, who posited certain universal natures separated from singulars, from which those same singulars proceeded: as for men, a human nature separated from Peter and John and the rest, from which singular men came to be; although St. Augustine, book of 83 Questions, q. 46, and Seneca, Letters bk. 8, letter 66, affirm that this was not Plato’s mind, but that by ideas he understood certain likenesses of all things, which God has within himself and through which he produces them. I omit the opinion of the Nominalists, who seem to have posited universals only in words, of which, they said, the sciences are, and not of things.

31 The true opinion of Aristotle, now common in the school and to be held by all, must be explained in three conclusions. First conclusion. There are not only universal words but also universal things, of which the sciences are. This is proved against the Nominalists by the authority of Aristotle, On Interpretation, ch. 5, where he says that some things are universal, others singular: therefore he holds that the universal is found not only in words but in things. Next, by reason: because universal names, such as man or horse, are not imposed to signify singular things, such as Peter and John, nor do they signify any of them distinctly; rather these are signified by proper names: therefore something is given besides singulars, to signify which proximately and distinctly they are imposed; and since this is not singular, it will be universal. Second, these propositions are true and necessary, Peter is a man and Man is an animal; and yet, if nothing besides words is predicated, they will be false, since neither is one word the other, nor is it included in it: therefore it is necessary to posit universal things besides words.

Second conclusion. There is no universal really separated from singulars. This is against Plato (if the opinion

C ij

[p. 36]

he held about ideas, which Aristotle attributes to him); and it is proved from

Aristotle, Posterior Analytics 1, ch. 35, text 38; Metaph. 3, text 10; Metaph. 7, text 51

and 57; and Metaph. 10, text 6; in which places he shows that universals cannot be

separated from singulars. Next it is proved by reason: because whatever is truly

and really predicated of something must be in it; but universals are truly predi‐

cated of singulars in these propositions, Peter is a man and Man is an animal:

therefore they are truly and really in them. The major is proved: because a

proposition is called true or false from the fact that the thing is or is not; but in

these propositions universals are predicated of singulars: therefore either they

are in them, or the propositions are false.

Third conclusion. Although all the things of the world are singular, in the sin‐

gulars themselves there are universal natures, which are predicated of them.

This is against Heraclitus, and it is proved and at the same time declared by this

argument. The singulars of human nature, such as Peter and John, are more like

each other than the singulars of another nature; for they have a definition and

essential predicates common to them: for each is a man and a rational animal:

therefore the intellect conceives the human nature existing in both and com‐

mon to both; and therefore it will be one and in many, which is to be universal.

32 To the argument of the first opinion, granting the antecedent, that all the

things of the world are singular, the consequence must be denied, that nothing

is universal: for although there is nothing universal really separated from those

singulars (as perhaps Plato asserted), nor anything in the singulars themselves

really distinct from them, yet the nature in which they all agree is universal, be‐

ing distinct from them only through the intellect, which conceives it without

conceiving the singulars; and of this there is science, even if there is none of sin‐

gulars. To the testimony of Aristotle, St. Thomas replies in his commentary on

that work that by those words he wished to exclude Plato’s error about separat‐

ed ideas, and at the same time to teach in what way the universal is found in

things: therefore the sense of his words is this: The universal animal is nothing

separated from the species of man and horse, as Plato imagined; but it is in

them as something posterior, because it is founded in them and is taken from

their agreement.

## QUESTION II

What the essence and nature of universals is. 33

T    he nature and essence of any thing whatever is explained by its definition:

therefore the solution of this question from the definition

[p. 37]

of the universal depends; once it has been adduced and explained, the question too will be solved. Aristotle gives a twofold definition of the universal in different places of his doctrine: the first in Metaph. 7, text 45, in these words: For that is called universal which is apt by nature to be in several. The second in On Interpretation 1, ch. 5, where he speaks thus: Now I call universal that which is apt by nature to be predicated of several, as man is one of the universals. And he posited both together in Posterior Analytics 1, ch. 10, text 25, saying: It is necessary, then, that there be one thing truly said of many: for there will not be a universal unless this is so. There must, therefore, be something one and the same in several, not equivocally: by which words he teaches that the universal has two things. That it be one, that is, univocal: wherefore equivocals and analogues are excluded from the ratio of the universal: because either they have no unity, like equivocals, or only a unity in a certain respect, that is, according to proportion or attribution, like analogues. Next, that it be in many, and that it be predicated of them; which, although they are not really distinguished in the universal (because, taken formally, it is not something real), are nevertheless two rationes, related as if they were really distinguished; of which the prior is that it be in many, the posterior that it be predicated of many. This I prove thus. The cause of the truth of predications is that the thing is outside just as it is signified and enunciated through them, as Aristotle teaches, On Interpretation 1, saying: From the fact that the thing is or is not, a proposition is called true or false: therefore this causal proposition is true: Because the universal is in many, it is predicated of many; but a cause is prior in nature to its effect: therefore its being in many is prior to its being predicated of many. Now, although the ratio of being in them is prior to that of predicating, they are nevertheless convertible: because it is true that what is in many is predicated of many; and conversely, that whatever is predicated of many is in them, since nothing is predicated of something unless it is in it.

34 From which it follows, first, that the essence of the universal is to be in many, and as it were its proper attribute, to be predicated of many. This is proved by this argument. That which we first understand of something we call its essence; but the first thing that we understand of the universal is that it is in many; therefore this will be of its essence. That, too, which we understand posteriorly, if it is convertible with the prior, we call its proper attribute; but to be predicated of many is something posterior to being in many, and is convertible with it, as we have proved; therefore it will be its proper attribute.

But when we say that being in many pertains to the essence of the universal, and that being predicated of many is its attribute, neither is to be understood

C iij

[p. 38]

according to act, but each according to aptitude, as the words of Aristotle teach and as experience proves: since we see that the nature of the Sun and of the Moon is universal, and that it neither is actually in many nor is actually predicated of them, but has each in potency. And this is what is commonly said: Words in definitions do not signify act, but aptitude: wherefore the sense of the first definition is: The universal is that which is apt to be in many; and the sense of the second: The universal is one thing predicable of many.

It follows, second, that the first definition is quidditative or essential, because it contains the essence of the universal; but the second is descriptive, because it is given through an attribute.

35 It follows, third, that what is said by certain moderns is false, namely that being in many and being predicated of many are not distinct rationes of the universal, but altogether the same: because by the very fact that we understand a nature to be in many, we also understand it to be predicable. For this is not true: for if being in many is the prior ratio and the cause of predicability of many, as we have proved, it evidently follows that it can be understood without predicability of many being understood; since it is evident that what is prior can be understood without what is posterior.

The essence of the universal having been explained, we must answer three questions which Porphyry omitted on account of their difficulty: because from their solutions that same essence of the universal will be better understood. The first question was: Whether universals are in things. The second: Whether they are substances or accidents. The third: Whether they are eternal or temporal. For their solution, the distinction of the universal which St. Thomas gives, Metaph. 7, lect. 13, must be noted: for it can be taken in two ways, namely for the nature which is denominated universal, such as man or animal, and in this way it is taken materially or fundamentally; or for universality, which is the form from which the universal is denominated; and this form is called second intention, or relation of reason, through which the nature is referred to the individuals. And if universals are taken in the first way, they are said to be in things, and not separated from them: because man and animal are in the things themselves; man in singular men, animal in its species, horse and lion. But if they are taken in the second way, they are not in things, but only objectively in the intellect: because the second intention, or relation of reason, has no other being than to be known by the intellect, which attributes it to the nature that it compares with the individuals.

36 And in the same way the second question is solved: because universals, considered materially, or for the foundation, either are

[p. 39]

real beings, such as horse or lion, or beings of reason, such as genus or species; or they are substances, such as man or animal, or accidents, such as whiteness and color. But if they are taken in the second way, they are not substances but accidents: not real ones, but of reason: because they are only certain denominations which the intellect attributes to natures, calling them universal. To the third question, finally, one must reply thus: if universals are taken formally, for universality, they are not eternal but temporal: because universality exists only while it is actually considered by the intellect; but the intellect is not always in actual consideration: therefore neither is universality always. But if it is taken for the foundations, another distinction must be added. For universal things can be taken in two ways, namely according to the actual existence which they have in their inferiors, that is, in individuals or species; and in this way they are not eternal, but when these are corrupted, they too are corrupted. E.g., flowers of diverse species are universal; and if they are taken according to their actual existence in individuals, they do not exist in winter: therefore they neither always are nor are eternal, but temporal, like the individuals themselves. But if they are considered according to essence, that is, according to their essential predicates, they are eternal: because, although they do not actually exist in singulars, those same essential predicates are owed to them no less than if they actually existed in them; as man and animal are eternal according to essence: because, even if there were no man or animal in the nature of things, it is true that man is a rational animal, and animal a living sentient thing: because these essential predicates are owed to them.

37 And if you ask where universals would be if there were no singular (for if they are perpetual, they would have to remain somewhere), I reply that they would be nowhere in act, but only objectively in the divine intellect, which actually knows that the essential predicates are owed to them, and also virtually in the divine omnipotence, by which they can be produced in their singulars: and behold how, taken essentially, they are eternal.

## QUESTION III

Whether there is in things, before the operation of the intellect, a formal unity less than

numerical.

A    ristotle, treating of the unity of things, Metaph. 5, ch. 6, posited a threefold

unity: Generic, Specific, and Numerical. Generic is that which species have in the genus, as horse and lion in animal. Specific, that which individuals have in the species, as Peter and John in man. Numerical, that which any individual whatever has in itself, insofar as it is not

C iiij

[p. 40]

distinct from itself, but from anything else whatever: as Peter is called one in number because he is this individual, that is, not distinct from himself, but from John and the rest.

38 Of these three unities, the greatest is the numerical, the lesser the specific, and the least the generic: the reason for which is manifest: because that unity is lesser which is compatible with greater diversity; but generic unity is compatible with greater diversity, specific unity with lesser, and numerical with none: therefore the latter can be called the greatest unity, the specific lesser, and the generic least. The minor is proved: because things that are one in genus differ by essential and specific differences, as man and lion; things that are one in species differ not by essential differences but by individual ones, which are much less; but what is one in number has in itself neither specific nor individual diversity, but is one in itself in both ways. And concerning numerical unity there can be no doubt that it is both real and given before the operation of the intellect: wherefore the question does not proceed concerning it, but concerning the specific or the generic, which is called formal: because it is a unity in essence and in the essential predicates proceeding from the substantial form of things, and it is less than numerical; and of it, therefore, the title of the question asks whether it is given before the operation of the intellect.

39 And the first opinion is that of Scotus, Metaph. 7, q. 16, and on 2, d. 3, q. 2, who asserts that there is a formal unity, generic and specific, before the operation of the intellect, and that it is essential to the natures themselves, or at least belongs to them as a proper attribute. And it is proved, first, from Aristotle in the category of relatives, where he teaches that the first genus of relation is founded on specific or generic unity; which, if it is between substances, will be a relation of identity, as specific identity between Peter and Paul in the unity of human nature; if it is between qualities, it will be a relation of similarity, as between two white things; if between quantities, a relation of equality or of inequality, as between two bodies of the same length. From which such an argument is gathered. A relation of this genus is real and is given before the operation of the intellect: for two white things, even if they are not known by the intellect, will be similar: therefore its foundation, which is formal unity, will also be real and will be given before the operation of the intellect. It is also proved by reason: because unity is an attribute of real being; therefore to every grade of real being there corresponds its real unity: as to the grade of real entity there corresponds its real unity, as to the grade of numerical entity a real numerical unity, and to the grade of specific entity a real specific unity, and this is formal; therefore it will be real, just as the grade of specific entity is real, and it will be given before the operation of the intellect.

[p. 41]

The second opinion altogether denies that there is any formal unity less than numerical before the operation of the intellect. It is followed by St. Thomas, opusc. 55, not far from the beginning, and 1 p., q. 85, a. 2, ad 2; Albert the Great in the book of the Predicables, q. 6; Themistius in his paraphrase on the proem of Aristotle’s On the Soul, ch. 4; Alexander of Aphrodisias on Metaph. 7, after the middle, fol. 131, p. 1 and 2; Javelli, tract. 4, on the five universals, in his Dialectic; St. John Damascene in his book on Dialectic, ch. 64; Capreolus in 2, d. 8, q. 2; Venetus, bk. 2 of his Dialectic, tract. 4, part 4, ch. 4. And it is proved: because whatever belongs to the specific nature essentially, or as a proper attribute, must also belong to any individual of it: as, if rationality and risibility belong to human nature, they must belong to Peter and John; therefore, if specific formal unity belongs to it essentially, or as a proper attribute, it must belong to any individual whatever, and so Peter will be one by a specific formal unity common to many, which is evidently false.

The third opinion distinguishes formal unity into Actual and Potential. It calls actual that by which the nature is actually and formally one common to many; potential, that which it can have. And it says that both are real, but that the potential belongs to the nature before the operation of the intellect only in that property of the nature by which it is prior to its individuals; which (it says) it would have as actual if it were really separated from them, although this is impossible; but that this unity is not communicated to the individuals, because it belongs to the nature inasmuch as it is prior in nature to them. This opinion is held by Soncinas, Metaph. 7, q. 40; Fonseca, Metaph. 5, ch. 18, q. 3, sect. 2, 3 and 4; and they prove it by this argument. The specific nature is signified by a common and univocal name, as human nature by this name man; but a univocal name signifies something one; therefore there is some formal unity in the nature before the operation of the intellect, by reason of which it is signified by a common name. If you deny this, it follows that the name man, and any other signifying a common nature, is equivocal, since it does not signify something one, which is false.

The last opinion is that of Cajetan in the opusculum On Being and Essence, ch. 4, q. 6, where he distinguishes formal unity in another way, into positive and negative. Positive unity is that which some things have in a form or positive predicate: as Peter and John have positive formal unity in humanity abstracted by the intellect from the individuals, or compared with them. Negative unity, however, is nothing other than the negation of division, and if

[p. 42]

it is the negation of material division, it will be numerical unity, which Peter has through this matter undivided in itself; but if it is the negation of formal division, it will be negative formal unity. Supposing this distinction, he asserts that the nature does not have positive formal unity before the operation of the intellect, because it is divided by the numerical differences in the singulars: wherefore no common positive form is given in which men agree singly, until the same human nature is abstracted by the intellect from those same singulars and is cognized without their being cognized; for then it will be conceived as a positive form common to them. But it has, he says, negative formal unity on the part of the thing; because although it is divided by material and numerical differences, it is not, however, divided by formal and specific ones: hence Peter and John agree in humanity before the operation of the intellect negatively, solely from the fact that they are not distinguished in it formally or essentially, although they are distinguished individually by this and that singular humanity. This opinion of Cajetan is followed by many moderns, and they prove it by this argument.

41 Numerical unity is the lack of material division; therefore formal and specific unity is the lack of formal and specific division; but Peter and John before the operation of the intellect lack formal and specific division, since they are not distinguished by formal or essential differences, but only by numerical and as it were material ones; therefore they have formal unity in humanity, at least negative.

And it can be confirmed: because whatever things are not distinct in something are said to agree in it and to be one, at least negatively; but Peter and John before the operation of the intellect are not distinguished formally or in species in humanity; therefore they agree in it and are one: wherefore there will be a negative unity common to both.

43 For the solution of this question it should be noted first that formal unity is twofold. For one is that by which something is said to be formally one in itself: which Peter has through his form and essence, from which he is said to be formally one. The other is that by which something is said to be formally one, common to many, as the formal unity which human nature has while it is considered by the intellect as abstracted from the conditions of the singulars, by which it is divided in them. And concerning the first formal unity two things are certain among all. First, that it belongs to any nature of itself, really and essentially, and therefore the nature has it before the operation of the intellect in its individuals: so that each thing is said to be formally and essentially one through the same nature that is in it; so hold St. Thomas, Scotus and others in the places cited above.

[p. 43]

44 Second, it is certain that this formal unity is in some way distinguished from the numerical, since it arises from a different root. For the numerical arises from matter, or also from form, inasmuch as from their union there results this entity of this individual; but the formal arises from the form alone, not as the cause of this entity, but as the root of all the essential predicates that can belong to it. For example, the formal unity by which Peter is one man proceeds from his soul inasmuch as it is the principle of reasoning, from which the same Peter has it that he is rational; and in the same way in other natures. But whether this formal and numerical unity are distinguished in the same individual from the nature of the thing and before the operation of the intellect, or by reason alone and through the intellect: on this Scotus does not agree with St. Thomas. For he asserts that they are distinct from the nature of the thing; but St. Thomas, whom almost all follow, holds that they are not distinguished from the nature of the thing, but by reason alone through the intellect, a foundation in the thing being presupposed, however, inasmuch as they proceed from a different root, as has been explained. And this seems to us not only more probable but altogether true and to be held, which is efficaciously proved by this argument. To be a man and to be this man are the same from the nature of the thing in Peter, because he is not a man except inasmuch as this humanity has the true essence of humanity, but through this humanity he is formally one man; therefore both unities, the formal and the numerical, are the same thing. But they are distinguished by the intellect, inasmuch as they come from a different root.

45 It is certain, third, that the formal unity of any thing whatever is determined by the individual difference, and becomes this in number through it: which I prove first. Peter is formally one through the one form and one essence that he has, that is, through one humanity; but his humanity is one in number by reason of the individual difference; therefore the formal unity which he has through it is one in number by reason of the same individual difference. Which is so true and necessary that all the grades of his nature, all the essential predicates that can belong to him by reason of them, are this, on account of the individual difference: for Peter is this substance, this body, this living thing, this animal, this rational thing, and this man; indeed, it is impossible that there be anything in Peter that is not this in number, by reason of the individual difference by which his nature and essence are this, distinct from any other whatever. Hence it follows that, just as there are in Peter as many formal unities, distinct in reason, as there are grades of his nature, so all are individual, because they are all joined to the individual difference, determined by it, and it makes them these in number.

[p. 44]

These things being supposed, our view is contained in three conclusions. First: There is not given, before the operation of the intellect, any positive and actual formal unity which belongs to the nature really and essentially, or as a proper attribute, through which it is said to be common to many. This is against Scotus.

46 Second conclusion: There is not given before the operation of the intellect a formal unity in potency which belongs to the nature in that priority which it has with respect to the individuals, to which it is not communicated. This is against the second opinion, that of Soncinas.

Third conclusion: There is not given a negative formal unity before the operation of the intellect. This is against Cajetan. And all are proved together from the doctrine delivered, by this argument. One and undivided are the same; therefore division is opposed to unity, and takes it away and dissolves it: as, if the parts of a man are divided, namely the arm from the head and the head from the feet, by that very fact the unity of the composite and of those same parts is taken away; but every nature, according to all the grades which it has on the part of the thing, is divided by the individual differences; therefore it has no formal unity common to many. The minor is proved. The human nature that is in Peter and John is divided by their individual differences: so that whatever Peter has is this, and distinct from the others that John has, namely this substance, this body, this living thing, this animal, this man; and Paul has another this substance, another this body, another this living thing, another this animal, another this man: therefore they can have neither a nature or essence, nor any grade of the nature, that is one or common; but every formal unity must belong to them by reason of the nature, or of some grade of it, which is one in them; therefore they have no common formal unity.

This argument concludes against Scotus that they have no positive and actual real unity. But it seems that Soncinas and Cajetan can reply that the former does not posit an actual unity but a potential one, and Cajetan does not posit a positive unity but a negative one. But in truth it concludes no less against these same than against Scotus. That it concludes against Soncinas is proved: because if the human nature in Peter before the operation of the intellect is this according to all its formal and essential grades, and diverse from the nature of Paul and its grades, then it is impossible that on the part of the thing it can have any unity in them; wherefore neither will they have formal unity in potency, for potency cannot belong to things to which the act is repugnant. But the same second opinion is proved false, because it asserts two impossible things. First, that the nature, as it is prior

[p. 45]

to the individuals, has real formal unity: but this is impossible, because the nature is not prior to the individuals by any real priority, but only through the intellect, which considers it without considering the individuals; therefore, if according to this priority it is formally one, such unity does not belong to it on the part of the thing, but through the intellect.

The second thing it asserts is that the nature does not communicate that formal unity to the individuals, which is proved impossible by this argument. The nature is communicated to the individuals according to all the formal and essential grades which it has; but it cannot have actual or potential formal unity on the part of the thing except by reason of some formal and essential grade; therefore neither can it have a unity that is not communicated to the individuals.

48 That our argument concludes against Cajetan is proved: because he could only reply that the nature is divided according to all its grades by the individual differences, not by the essential or formal ones; wherefore with such a division there can well be a non-distinction in form, which is called negative formal unity. But this does not remove the difficulty of our argument. For although human nature is not divided by formal differences in Peter and John, it is enough that it is divided by individual ones, so that it is true that its formal unity in them is diverse; therefore it cannot have any formal unity, even negative, or a non-distinction common to them. The consequence is proved: because, since the forms and essences are diverse, the formal unities, even the negative ones, or the non-distinctions, must be diverse: wherefore, just as they cannot have anything positive in common before the operation of the intellect, so they cannot have anything negative in common; therefore the negative unity on the part of the thing which Cajetan posits will not be given.

49 The arguments of the other opinions must be solved. And for the solution of that testimony from Aristotle, in the category of relatives, which we adduced for the opinion of Scotus, it should be noted that, although the formal unity by which something is one in itself is really conjoined and really the same with the numerical unity, it is nevertheless distinguished from it as it were virtually before the operation of the intellect, because it comes from a different root, as we have seen; and by reason of this virtual distinction the intellect can distinguish them, conceiving the formal unity without conceiving the numerical unity; and while it conceives it thus, it is said to abstract it from the individuals and to make it common to many and universal. From which it is understood that the whole foundation of the formal unity,

[p. 46]

specific or generic, through which something is common to many and universal,

is the formal unity by which something is formally one in itself, inasmuch as it is

virtually distinct from the numerical unity, to which on the part of the thing it

is conjoined: therefore such formal unity can be called universal, specific or

generic unity, at least in its remote foundation; and also the remote foundation

of the universal, sufficient, however, for the relations of the first kind, of identi‐

ty, similarity and equality; and it is in this, not in another, that Aristotle under‐

stands them to be founded.

50 To the argument of Scotus I reply that to the single grades of entity there

correspond their unities, which are not, however, distinct except through the

intellect, just as the grades of the nature are not distinguished except by the in‐

tellect; and therefore they do not belong to the nature on the part of the thing

either, but only through the intellect.

To the argument of Cajetan the major must be denied, namely that numeri‐

cal unity is the lack of material division, or specific unity the lack of formal divi‐

sion. For a lack is a negation, whereas unity does not express a negation alone,

but also an entity as its foundation; and since the specific entities are diverse,

and the formal unities diverse, before the operation of the intellect, even if they

lack formal division, they cannot have formal unity.

And in the same way I reply to the confirmation that the antecedent is false,

namely that whatever things are not distinct in something are said to agree in it:

because non-distinction expresses a negation alone, whereas one expresses a pos‐

itive entity with a negation adjoined. The argument therefore proceeds from a

pure negation to a positive having a negation adjoined, and therefore it is not

good.

Finally, to the argument of the third opinion it must be replied that names

signify things by means of the concepts which we form of them; hence they do

not signify them as they are on the part of the thing, but as they are cognized by

us; and since univocal names are common, they signify the thing as conceived by

us by a common concept: wherefore it does not follow from their signification

that there is something one common to many on the part of the thing, but only

objectively in the intellect; nor, consequently, a formal unity among many, but

that this is made by the intellect cognizing the nature without the inferiors be‐

ing cognized, whether that unity be positive or negative.

Q U E S T I O N I V.

Whether the universal exists in things before the operation of the intellect.

51

S   ince the universal is one in many, authors speak in almost the same way of it

and of unity; and therefore Sco-

[p. 47]

tus, who taught in the preceding question that formal unity less than numerical belongs to the nature of itself, and that it therefore has it before the operation of the intellect, consistently teaches that the universal exists on the part of the thing. And this is the first opinion on this question, which he held in 2, d. 3, q. 1, and Metaph. 7, q. 18, where it is defended by Antonius Andreas, and also by Juan Monllor in a certain disputation on the universal, ch. 5 and 6. And it is proved by a twofold argument. First, because universals are the objects of the sciences, and they are also said to be ingenerable and incorruptible; but these conditions are real; therefore they belong to the natures before the operation of the intellect: wherefore before it they will really be universals. The minor is proved: because the sciences are about real natures, which are neither generated nor corrupted except according to the real being that they have.

52 Second, human nature of itself is not incommunicable to several; therefore of itself it is communicable, and before the operation of the intellect it is communicated to many singulars; but to be universal is the same as to be communicable to many; therefore of itself and before the operation of the intellect it will be universal. The major I prove thus. If the nature of itself is not communicable to many, then of itself it is incommunicable; but to be incommunicable is to be singular; therefore of itself it will be singular, wherefore it could in no way become universal: which is false.

The second opinion is that of St. Thomas, Metaph. 7, lect. 13; in the opusculum On Being and Essence, ch. 4; 1 p., q. 85, a. 1 and 12, q. 29, a. 6; in which places he asserts that the nature of itself, that is, from its own essence, is neither universal nor singular, but becomes singular through the individuating conditions, and universal through the intellect; and therefore that before the operation of the intellect the universal is not given. St. Thomas is followed by Capreolus in 3, a. 3, d. 5, q. 3; Soncinas, Metaph. 7, q. 40; Cajetan in the opusculum On Being and Essence, ch. 4; Soto, q. 2 on universals; Durandus in 1, q. 2 of the prologue, and d. 14, part 2; Toledo in his questions on universals; Fr. Francisco Suárez, tom. 1, disp. 6, lect. 5. And it is the common opinion of the school, to be held by us.

53 But in order to prove it, it should be noted that, since the universal is one apt to be predicated of many, according to the definition delivered by Aristotle, two things are necessarily required for something to be universal. First, that it be one, not only by the formal unity by which something is one in itself, but by the formal unity by which something is common to many. For that the first formal unity is required was proved by us in the preceding question: because, since the universal communicates its essence to the singulars, and through

[p. 48]

its essence is something formally one in itself, it is necessary that the universal have the formal unity through which it is formally one in itself; and this unity we call the first and remote foundation of the universal. But that this unity does not suffice for the ratio of the universal is proved: because, as we also said in the preceding question, the formal unity by which something is one in itself is the same in reality with the numerical unity, and therefore always conjoined with it on the part of the thing; from which it follows that it is divided in the singulars, so that there are as many formal unities as there are individuals. It does not suffice, therefore, for the nature to be called universal; but it is required that the same formal unity be considered by the intellect without considering the singularities by which it is divided on the part of the thing; and so considered it is called the formal unity through which the nature is formally one common to many, which is to be universal.

54 Second, it is required that it be apt to be in many. And this aptitude, according to Scotus and the others who follow his opinion, is real in the nature and before the operation of the intellect; but according to St. Thomas the nature has neither, but they belong to it through the operation of the intellect. The nature, then, must have two conditions in order to be said to be apt to be in many. The first is as it were remote, namely, that from its real principles it can be multiplied in many individuals: which all material and corruptible natures have; but if it can be in one only, so that it is altogether impossible for it to have many, as many hold of the natures of the angels, it will not be universal, as we shall see in the chapter on species. The other is required as proximate, namely, that it be not determined by singular conditions but as it were indifferent, so that it does not regard one singular more than another; and since on the part of the thing it is determined by singular conditions, it does not have the aptitude to be in many, because the singular, since it is incommunicable, cannot be communicated to many. It is necessary, therefore, in order that it be indifferent, that it be considered by the intellect without the singular conditions; and so considered it will not be determined to any singular, but will be able to be determined equally to all: and this is to be indifferent and apt to be communicated to many. And so the aptitude of the nature presupposes three things, two as it were remote. First, that it can be multiplied from its real principles; second, that it be one by the formal unity by which something is one in itself; and besides these, a third, as it were proximate, that it be one by the formal unity by which something is common to many. And besides these three it adds that it be indifferent to many; and although it has this indifference by the very fact that it is one by universal unity,

nevertheless

[p. 49]

nevertheless this unity is understood in it before the indifference or aptitude, just

as we said in q. 1 that it is understood in the nature that it is universal before it is

understood that it is predicable.

From this whole doctrine is gathered an efficacious argument for proving our

view, that the universal is not given on the part of the thing but only through the

operation of the intellect, against Scotus. The universal is one in many and apt to

be predicated of many; but the nature before the operation of the intellect is nei‐

ther one nor has the aptitude of being predicated of many; therefore it is not uni‐

versal. The minor is proved. The nature on the part of the thing is divided by the

individual differences, so that it is one in Peter and another in John; therefore it is

many and not one. But if it is not one, it cannot have the aptitude of being predi‐

cated, because aptitude presupposes unity, as has been proved; therefore it will be

neither one nor in many until it is abstracted by the intellect from the conditions

by which it is divided, and becomes one.

To the first argument of Scotus, the major must be granted and the minor de‐

nied: because, just as the sciences are had through operations of the intellect and

are not given before them, by the same reasoning the objects of the sciences are

not given except through the intellect abstracting the nature and making it in

some way universal; and as so abstracted it is ingenerable and incorruptible, and

not as it is in the individuals, which are corrupted everywhere. Wherefore what is

said in the minor is false, that the nature has such conditions on the part of the

thing: for it has neither except on the presupposition of the operation of the

intellect.

To the second, granting the antecedent, the consequence must be denied, and

it must be said that the nature is of itself neither proximately communicable to

many, but only remotely, nor of itself incommunicable, as St. Thomas taught in the

place cited above; but that it has the first through the intellect, the second on the

part of the thing, through the individual differences with which it is conjoined;

while of itself only the essential predicates belong to it, as rationality to human na‐

ture, and so of the rest.

Q U E S T I O N V.

Through which operation of the intellect the universal is made.

57

T     hat the question may be understood, the mode must be explained in which

the intellect proceeds when it understands, so that from it we may come to

know in what way it makes the universal. It should be noted, therefore, that since

all our understanding begins from the senses, it is necessary that what is to be un‐

derstood be first perceived by sight or some other sense: which happens through a

certain likeness of itself which, to

D

[p. 50]

it sends to the eye, and which is called the intentional species of the thing by which it is represented. Through this species, then, the object is united to the visual power, and the vision of the thing takes place. By virtue of this vision another species of the same thing seen is produced in another, interior sense, which is called the common sense, from the fact that the species of all the things that are sensed by the external senses reach it; and it discerns among them all, cognizing that they are diverse. Then from this sense another species of the same object is emitted into another, which is customarily called the phantasy, and is like a kind of memory: not only sensing the things that are perceived through the other senses, but preserving the species of all sensibles; and the species preserved in it are customarily called phantasms.

58 It should be noted second that, once the object has been cognized through the senses as far as the phantasy, the operation of the intellect begins. The intellect is twofold: one which is called Agent, and the other Possible; between which there is this difference, that the agent intellect is not a cognitive power, nor does it understand anything, whereas the possible is the one that cognizes. Moreover, the agent intellect, aided by the phantasm, that is, by the sensible species preserved in the phantasy, produces another species of the same thing represented through the same phantasm in the cognizing intellect, no longer sensible and corporeal, but spiritual, just as the agent intellect by which it is produced and the possible intellect in which it is received are spiritual powers. And the former is called agent because by its action it produces the species; the latter possible, as it were passible or passive, because it receives that same species, through which the same object which was cognized by the senses is united to it; and informed by this species, or likeness of the object, which is called intelligible (just as the species through which the senses cognize are called sensible), it understands the object. Through this intelligible species (as many assert) the nature is represented without the conditions of singularity, and therefore they call it abstraction, because the nature represented without the conditions is said to be as it were abstracted from them.

But it should be noted third that the possible intellect has a twofold operation: one through which it cognizes the object as represented in the species without the conditions; and this is most properly called abstraction, because it is the cognition of the nature without the individuals being cognized. The other is the operation of the intellect through which the same nature, cognized without the singulars being cognized, is cognized again with those same singulars cognized at the same time, and is compared to them; and therefore it is called comparison. And behold three operations: one of the agent intellect, called abstraction by some, and two others of the possible intellect, one which is called abstraction, and the other comparison.

[p. 51]

In accordance with these three operations, then, there are three different opinions. The first asserts that the universal is made through the abstraction of the agent intellect. It is followed by Cajetan in the opusculum On Being and Essence, ch. 4, q. 6, toward the end; Soto, q. 3 on universals; Zumel, 1 p., q. 13, a. 7, concl. 3. And it is proved by the testimony of Aristotle, On the Soul 3, text 18, where, comparing the office of the agent intellect with corporeal light, he teaches that just as corporeal light by its material illumination makes colors actually visible, which in the darkness were only potentially visible, so the agent intellect, through the action by which it produces the intelligible species in the possible intellect, makes the nature actually intelligible. From which they gather as follows. The object of the possible intellect is the universal; but through the agent intellect the nature becomes actually intelligible, while it is represented in the intelligible species without the conditions; therefore it becomes actually universal.

Then by a twofold argument. The first is taken from the definition of the universal, which is one in many; but the nature through the abstraction of the agent intellect is one in many; therefore it is universal. The minor is proved: because in the intelligible species it is represented without the conditions; therefore, as so represented, it is one, since it is many on the part of the thing only through the conditions; and it is also in the many from which it is abstracted; therefore it is universal.

Second, for the nature to be one by universal unity expresses two things: one as foundation, namely the formal unity by which it is one in itself; and the other as it were as the formal element, namely the lack of the division which it has on the part of the thing through the individual differences; but represented in the intelligible species it is formally one, and it lacks division, since it is represented without the conditions; therefore it is one by universal unity; and it has the aptitude of being predicated of many, because, represented without the conditions, it is not determined to any individual, but is indifferent to all; therefore it is universal.

The second opinion holds that through the abstraction of the agent intellect the nature is not yet universal, but that the abstraction of the possible intellect is required, through which the nature is cognized without the conditions, and that through it it becomes universal. This is the opinion of Durandus in 1, d. 2, q. 5, ad 2, and in 2, d. 3, q. 7, no. 12, and of Cardinal Toledo, q. 2 on universals. There is a single argument for this opinion. The nature is not universal on the part of the thing; therefore its universality is not real, but must be attributed by the intellect; but the intellect can attribute nothing to the nature unless it cognizes it; therefore, since the agent intellect does not cognize, it cannot attribute universality to it; but when it is first cognized by the intellect, it is denominated universal.

D ij

[p. 52]

61 The third opinion teaches that neither the one nor the other abstraction suffices for the nature to become universal, but that it is necessary that it be compared to the individuals; and since this is done through the second operation of the possible intellect, which is called comparison, that the universal is made through this. It is followed by Soncinas, Metaph., q. 17, concl. 2, and Metaph. 10, q. 15; Niphus, Metaph., q. 17, concl. 1; Deza of Seville in 1, d., q. 1, a. 4, ad 1; Canar., 1 part, q. 28, a. 1, fol. 2. It is proved first: because the intellect cannot attribute to the nature the denomination of universal unless it cognizes it as universal. The universal expresses a respect to many, as is gathered from its definition, in which it is said to be one in many; therefore the nature is not cognized as universal unless it is cognized through its respect to many; but it cannot be cognized through its respect to many unless they are cognized, because a respect is not cognizable unless its term is cognized. But through the abstraction of the agent intellect it is in no way cognized, and through the abstraction of the possible intellect it is cognized without the individuals being cognized; therefore it is not cognized as universal, nor can such a denomination be attributed to it, except through comparison alone, through which it is cognized in order to many.

Second, universality is a relation of one to many, not real, since it does not belong to the nature on the part of the thing; therefore of reason; but a relation of reason cannot be made except through comparative cognition; therefore the universal is made through this alone. The minor is proved: because a relation is a comparison between two extremes; therefore it cannot be made except by the intellect cognizing and comparing both; therefore it becomes universal through comparison alone.

62 Besides these three different opinions, I find a fourth, through which certain moderns seem to bring the second and third into agreement, by this distinction. The universal can be taken in two ways. First, after the manner of an absolute, not expressing a respect to another but able to found such a respect, as white or quantity, which are absolute and can found a relation of similarity or equality. In another way, as a relative. For they think that universality can be understood in both ways, namely as a relative form, and also as an absolute one, upon which, however, there follows a certain respect through which it is explained: for the unity by which something is common, and the aptitude of being predicated of many, are absolute forms, just as numerical unity and the aptitude for laughing, which we nevertheless explain through a respect to the act of laughing and to the object. And they illustrate this by the example of the Platonic universal, separated from singulars: which would truly be a substance, since it would exist per se, and therefore its universality would be an absolute form, because substance is an absolute thing, not expressing a respect

[p. 53]

essential to another, and yet it would be explained by us through a respect to the many by which it would be participated; therefore the universal made by the intellect can also be taken after the manner of an absolute. In another way it is taken as a relative, essentially regarding the individuals. The universal taken in the first way, then, they say is made through the first cognition of the possible intellect, because it has unity with the aptitude of regarding the many from which it has been abstracted. But if it is taken in the second way, it is not made except through comparison: because a relative cannot be cognized except through comparison to its term; and therefore neither can the universal as a relative, except through comparison to the many. And they affirm that the second opinion is to be understood of the universal as absolute, and that so understood it is true; but the third, of the universal as relative.

63 In order to propose our view, certain things must be noted. First, that universal is a concrete name, having a material significate, which is the nature, and a formal one, which is universality, from which it is denominated. Now a concrete is twofold, absolute and relative, just as the denominating form is also absolute or relative. An absolute concrete is white; a relative one, similar, or father. And this is the difference between the one and the other, that the absolute concrete has for its material significate only the bare subject, as white the bare body. But the relative concrete has not the bare subject, but something else by reason of which it is made the proximate foundation of the relation: as similar, besides white, must have some unity or commensuration with another, by reason of which it is capable of the relation, namely unity in whiteness and commensuration in the same grade of it. For in order that some things may properly be called similar, they must agree in whiteness, and also in its grade, so that it is in both as three, or as four.

Second, it should be noted that there are three foundations of a relation: the Most Remote, the Remote, and the Proximate; as in similarity, the most remote foundation is the body; the remote is the white; but the proximate is the white having unity and commensuration with another. And the foundation is called most remote and remote because the relation does not follow upon them: for the body, unless it has whiteness or some other quality, will not be called similar; nor even if it has whiteness, until it has unity and commensuration with another. But then it will be called the proximate foundation, because, once it is posited, the relation follows at once and necessarily. So, then, must it be understood of the universal, if it is a relative. For the most remote foundation of the relation of universality will be the nature on

D iij

[p. 54]

the part of the thing, through the formal unity by which it is formally one in itself. The remote foundation, however, is the nature while it is represented in the intelligible species without the conditions, or while it is cognized without them through the first cognition of the intellect, if the relation of universality, from which it is denominated, does not follow at once. And finally it will be the proximate foundation while it is compared to the inferiors, because the relation of universality to them follows at once.

These things being supposed, our view is contained in these conclusions. First: The universal is not an absolute name but a relative one. This is against the last opinion, and it is proved by a twofold argument. First: A concrete name is absolute if the form signified by it is absolute, and relative if it is relative; but the form of universality is not absolute but relative; therefore the name universal will not be absolute but relative. The minor is proved from the definition of the universal: One in many, and apt to be predicated of many. In which the universal is explained through a relation to many; and not only is it explained so, but universality is a relation, not an absolute form, as the last opinion asserts: which I prove thus. Universality is not a form belonging to the nature of itself or essentially, nor on the part of the thing, but through the intellect, as the same opinion grants; therefore it is not a substantial form but an accidental one; it is not a real accident, but one of reason; but every accident of reason which the intellect attributes to things is a relation of reason: for it does not attribute to them an absolute accident of reason after the manner of quality, or quantity, or of another category, having its foundation in those same things understood by it, as will be proved; therefore universality is a relation of reason and not an absolute form. Second: The nature is not called universal solely from the fact that it is one or common in itself, but because it is one of many and common to many, or one in which many agree: as Porphyry taught in the chapter on species, saying: By participation in the species many men are one man. Therefore through universality it is essentially ordered to the inferiors, of which it is the one nature; and therefore universality is a relation and not an absolute form, and universal is a relative name, not an absolute one. Understanding which, Porphyry taught that the predicable names (which are certain universals) are to be defined through their inferiors, as genus, that it is predicable of several things differing in species, and so of the rest.

65 Second conclusion: Through the operation of the agent intellect the universal is given only as in its remote foundation, or in remote potency; not as in its proximate foundation, nor actually and formally universal. This follows from the preceding and from the doctrine noted, and it is proved by this argument. The univer-

[p. 55]

sal is a relative; therefore the nature is not called actually and formally universal unless it is denominated from universality, which is a relation; but through the operation of the agent intellect it only has being represented in the intelligible species, the singulars not being represented; therefore it neither regards them nor can it be denominated from universality, which is a respect to them: and this is not to be actually and formally universal. Therefore it can only be universal in potency, or in its foundation, not the proximate one, because the relation follows at once upon the proximate foundation, and yet the relation to the individuals does not follow upon the nature so represented until it is understood in order to them; but in potency and in its remote foundation, although less remote than while it is outside its causes.

66 Third conclusion: The universal actually and formally, or in proximate potency, is not made through the first cognition of the possible intellect, which is called abstraction. This is against the last opinion. And it is proved first: Nothing is denominated actually and formally such except from its proper form; but the proper form of the universal is universality, which is a relation of reason to the individuals; therefore the nature is not denominated actually and formally universal except from a relation of reason to the individuals; but no such relation of reason follows upon the nature cognized through the first operation of the intellect; therefore through it it is not actually and formally universal. The minor is proved: Through that cognition it is not cognized in order to the individuals; indeed, the individuals are not even cognized; therefore neither is the relation of reason of the nature to them cognized; but a relation of reason has no other being than to be actually cognized; therefore, if it is not cognized through that cognition, it does not exist, nor does it denominate the nature actually and formally universal.
