Second, the nature through the first cognition has nothing other than to be cognized as represented in the intelligible species without the conditions; therefore only a new real extrinsic denomination follows upon it through that cognition, that of being cognized without the conditions: which it is certain is not the denomination of the universal; for this is neither real nor merely an extrinsic denomination, but one of reason, having the mode and likeness of an inherent form, like the denomination of predicate or subject. Therefore through such a cognition the nature will only be universal in potency, not proximate but remote, in the same way as through the operation of the agent intellect already explained.

67 Last conclusion: The nature becomes universal, not only in proximate potency but actually and formally, through the cognition of the intellect

D iiij

[p. 65]

which is called comparison. This is proved first from the three preceding: because, if it is not made through the operation of the agent intellect, nor through the first cognition of the possible intellect, there remains no other operation through which it can be made besides comparison.

But it is proved second that it is made through it: because universality is a relation of reason of the nature to the individuals, and a relation is a comparison of two extremes; therefore the relation of reason of the nature to the individuals is a comparison of the nature to them: wherefore universality, and the universal formally, will be made through comparison.

68 But in order that these conclusions may be better understood, and that from them we may come to know how the universal is in some way made through those three operations of the agent and the possible intellect, that distinction of the universal, sufficiently well known in the school of the Dialecticians, should be noted. The universal is twofold, Logical and Metaphysical. The Metaphysical universal is the real nature taken in common, that is, without the individuating conditions, and not as denominated by second intention or by the relation of universality. And it is called the Metaphysical universal because it is taken only according to its real essence, as it were abstracted from material conditions, which is the proper mode according to which things are considered in Metaphysics; and it can also be called the universal fundamentally, and also the universal in potency, at least remote, as has been explained. The other is the Logical universal, namely the nature denominated by second intention or by the relation of universality, which is also called the universal in proximate potency, actually and formally; because while the nature is actually denominated by the relation, it is said proximately to found that same relation; and it is called the Logical universal because second intention, or the relation of universality, properly pertains to logical consideration. This distinction supposed, we say that the Metaphysical universal is made through the operation of the agent intellect, since the nature is represented without the conditions in the intelligible species produced by it: which is to be the Metaphysical universal. But through the first cognition of the possible intellect the same Metaphysical universal is made, or rather, already made by the agent intellect, it is cognized; but the Logical universal is made through comparison alone.

69 The arguments of the other opinions must be answered, and the testimony of Aristotle for the first opinion in two ways. First, that its sense is that light makes colors actually visible not because they were not actually visible in the darkness, but because they could not be seen through an obscure medium; but that light, illuminating

[p. 57]

it, makes them actually seen. Or second, I reply by granting that light makes

colors actually visible, since in the darkness they were only potentially visible;

and so the agent intellect, as a kind of spiritual light, makes the nature actually

intelligible: from which it does not follow that it makes it actually universal,

because for it to be actually intelligible it suffices that it be universal in poten‐

cy, which it has while it is represented through the intelligible species without

the conditions, etc.

To the first argument of the same opinion, granting the major, the minor

must be distinguished: for the nature is one in two ways. First, by negative uni‐

ty, and this it has as represented in the intelligible species, because it is repre‐

sented without the individuating conditions; but through this unity it is only

the Metaphysical universal, or the universal in potency. In another way it is

one positively, which it does not have except while it is compared to the indi‐

viduals; and because this is required for it to be actually and formally universal,

it is not universal in this way except through comparison.

To the second the reply is by the same distinction: because the nature rep‐

resented in the intelligible species has the negative unity of the Metaphysical

universal, and in potency, not that of the Logical universal, except through

comparison.

To the argument of the second opinion, I grant that the nature is not uni‐

versal on the part of the thing, but becomes universal through the cognition of

the intellect; I deny, however, that through the first cognition of the intellect

the form of universality is attributed to it: rather, it is attributed to it only

through comparison.

To the third opinion it must be denied that the universal can be divided

into absolute and relative, because by its proper nature and essence it is rela‐

tive, as we have proved. It is false, therefore, that an absolute universal is giv‐

en, and no less false that this absolute universal is made through the first cog‐

nition of the intellect.

## QUESTION VI

Whether the Logical universal is made through a simple comparison of the nature with

the individuals, or only through the composite comparison which is called actual

predication. 70

T    hat the title of the question may be explained, it should be noted that al‐

most all posit a twofold comparison of the intellect, one Simple, the oth‐

er Composite.

Simple comparison is that through which the intellect cognizes one thing

in another, or in order to another, without composition: as when by a simple

cognition we cognize a father in order to

[p. 58]

the son, without affirming that he has a son; or whiteness in a wall, without affirming that it is in it. The other is the comparison through which the intellect cognizes two extremes and attributes one to the other, affirming that it is in it; and therefore this comparison is called actual predication. We ask, therefore, whether, supposing that the universal is made through comparison, as we proved in the preceding question, it is made through simple or through composite comparison. And there are two opinions. The first does not admit simple comparison, but only composite, and asserts that the universal is made through it; and since this comparison is the actual predication of one thing of another, it teaches that it is made through actual predication, and that before it the universal is not given actually and formally, but that actual predication is the universality from which the nature is denominated universal; and so it does not admit an aptitude or potency of being predicated in the nature, but holds that it is the same for it to be universal and for it to be an actual predicate. This opinion is followed by certain moderns, and they prove it by this argument.

71 The intellect cannot compare the nature to the individuals unless it cognizes that it is in them; but it cannot cognize that it is in them except by judging that it belongs to them. But to judge that it is in them and belongs to them is to predicate it of the individuals; therefore there is no simple comparison of the nature to the individuals, but only composite, which is actual predication: wherefore, if it is true that the universal is made through comparison, it necessarily follows that it is made through actual predication, so that it is not given before it.

72 This opinion is, in the first place, against Aristotle and St. Thomas, which is proved by a single testimony of each. For Aristotle, treating of the universal in On Interpretation 1, ch. 5, defines it in these words: And I call universal that which is apt to be predicated of several. From which it is evidently gathered that the nature is universal through the aptitude of being predicated of the individuals; but the aptitude of being predicated, since it is a potency, is prior to actual predication, which is the act of that same potency; therefore the nature is universal before it is actually predicated, according to the mind of Aristotle. Wherefore it does not become universal through composite comparison, which is actual predication, but through another, prior comparison, which is called simple.

And St. Thomas, in the same place, explaining the same definition of Aristotle, says: He defined the universal well through the aptitude of being predicated and not through actual predication, because there are some natures, such as the Sun and the Moon, which are not actually predicated of many, since they have only one individual, and yet they are truly universal through the aptitude and potency of being predicated of many. St. Thomas therefore posits the aptitude of being predicated in the universal nature, and asserts that through it

[p. 59]

it is universal, with Aristotle. Therefore the opinion which takes away the aptitude, and affirms that the universal is made only through actual predication, is expressly against Aristotle and St. Thomas.

Next, it is against reason, which I prove thus. If the nature is universal through actual predication, it follows that it is not universal unless it is predicated of many at once, so that we say that Peter and John are men, not man, and that man and horse are animals; and not while it is predicated of single ones: wherefore neither will there be a universal predication when the species is predicated of the individual, or the genus of the species, as in these predications: Peter is a man, and Man is an animal; but the consequent is false; therefore the antecedent also. That the nature is universal through actual predication, the consequence is proved: because universality is actual predication; but universality is the respect of the nature to many; therefore the nature is not universal except actually, while it is predicated of many, and not of one only. But that the consequent is false I prove: because this is a predication of the genus, Man is an animal; therefore it is a predication of a superior, because the genus is superior to the species; but a superior predicate is universal; therefore it is a universal predication, and yet of one alone; therefore the nature will be universal while it is predicated of one inferior, because it is predicable of many: wherefore not through actual predication, but through predicability, as all assert.

73 The common opinion, therefore, of Aristotle, St. Thomas and all, is true and to be held: That the nature is universal before it is actually predicated, through the potency of being predicated of many; and that it becomes universal through the simple comparison of the intellect, through which it is cognized in order to the individuals, and not through the composite comparison, which is actual predication. Which I prove by this argument. The intellect can cognize one thing in another, or in order to another, without affirmation and negation and without actual predication; therefore it can cognize the nature in order to the individuals through simple comparison, without actually predicating it of them; but, cognized in order to the individuals, it is cognized as universal; therefore it becomes universal through simple comparison, not through composite. The antecedent is proved in two ways: first in the intellect, then in the senses. In the intellect indeed: because through a simple cognition we cognize a father ordered to his son, and two walls similar in whiteness, both being cognized at once; and in such a cognition we neither compose nor judge anything; therefore without composition and judgment we can compare one thing with another. Then in the senses, of which it is most certain that they do not judge, nor compose or divide; and it is no less

[p. 60]

certain that they cognize one thing in order to another, or by comparing it to another; therefore the intellect will be able to do the same through a simple comparison of the nature to the individuals. The minor is proved. The common sense cognizes that the sensible of one external sense, such as sight, is not the sensible of another sense, namely hearing: which cannot in any way be done without comparison of the one with the other. And the sheep cognizes the wolf as an enemy, and therefore flees from it, and the lamb as a friend, from which it does not flee; and between two lambs it cognizes that this one is its offspring, and the other another’s. Does it not, then, cognize one thing in order to another, and through comparison with it, without formal judgment and without composition or actual predication? Therefore the intellect will be all the better able to cognize the nature in order to the individuals and to compare it with them, without composition or actual predication.

For the solution of the argument of the other opinion it should be noted that one thing can be cognized in order to another, or compared to it, in two ways. First, by cognizing each extreme per se, as agreeing with the other, attributing the one to the other: and this cannot be done except through a formal and express judgment and composite comparison, which consists in the actual predication of one thing of another. Second, by not cognizing each extreme per se, nor attributing the one to the other, but only the one with an order to the other, as agreeing or disagreeing, but not after the manner of attribution, or by affirming anything about the agreement or disagreement: and this is done through simple comparison by the intellect, and also by the senses, as I have proved; and in this way the nature is compared to the individuals and becomes universal and predicable before it is actually predicated of them. To the form of the argument, then, the minor must be distinguished, namely that the intellect cannot cognize that the nature is in the individuals except by judging: for judgment is twofold. One formal and express, through which the intellect judges that one thing belongs to another after the manner of attribution; the other as it were virtual, through which by a simple cognition it cognizes one thing in another, or in order to another, as agreeing or disagreeing with it, but not after the manner of attribution. We deny, therefore, that the intellect cannot cognize that the nature is in many except through express and formal judgment; and we grant that it cannot do so without the virtual judgment included in simple comparison, which we therefore call virtual judgment, because to cognize one thing through comparison to another is the foundation of the formal and express judgment through which it is attributed to it.

[p. 61]

## QUESTION VII

Whether the universal is univocal with respect to the predicables, and their true genus.

75

T     he title of the question presupposes what a univocal name is, and also

what an analogous one is, which is known from the Summulae. It asks,

however, in what manner the universal stands with respect to the predica‐

bles: as analogous, or rather as univocal, so that it is their genus.

The first opinion holds that it is analogous. Different authors defend it in

different ways, but they agree in this, that it is said primarily of one, or of

several, and secondarily of the rest. So teaches Albert the Great, tract. 2 on

the Predicables, ch. 9, affirming that it belongs first to genus, then to species,

and by reason of the latter to difference; but secondarily, and as it were per

accidens, to property and accident, as to accidental predicates. And Canterus

explains the analogy in almost the same way, ch. 4 of the Categories. The chief

argument of this opinion is that real being is analogous to substance and ac‐

cidents; but three predicables, namely genus, species and difference, are sub‐

stances, while the other two, namely property and accident, are accidents;

therefore the universal, which is said of all, since all the predicables are uni‐

versals, cannot be univocal.

Secondly, it can be proved in this way. The universal and the predicable

are convertible and stand as essence and proper attribute; but the predicable

is analogous with respect to all; therefore the universal too will be analogous.

The minor is proved: predication is said analogically of predication per se

and per accidens, since the former is such simply, the latter only in a quali‐

fied sense; therefore the predicable too will be analogous, since they stand as

act and potency with respect to the predicable per se and per accidens; but

three predicables, genus, species and difference, are predicated per se, since

they are predicated essentially; and the two others are predicated per acci‐

dens, since they are predicated accidentally; therefore the predicable is anal‐

ogous with respect to all.

The second opinion asserts that the universal is univocal with respect to

the predicables, and their true genus, as animal is with respect to man and

horse; and it is that of St. Thomas in the questions on universals, q. 2; Scotus,

q. 8; Javelli, tract. 4 on the Predicables, ch. 1 and 6; Soto, q. 4 on universals,

and the chapter on genus, the only one; and Cardinal Toledo, q. 2 on univer‐

sals; and it is now almost common, true, and to be held.

76 But in order that we may prove it effectively, it should be noted that

the universal

[p. 62]

since it is a concrete and accidental name, can be taken in two ways: Materially, for the subject or nature denominated; and Formally, for the universality that denominates it; just as white is taken for the body and for the whiteness. But further, the subject denominated is considered in two ways: according to its proper essence and nature, or inasmuch as it is denominated by universality; just as body is taken according as it is corporeal substance, or inasmuch as it is denominated by whiteness, in which way it is visible and is reduced to the category of quality. And of the natures that are denominated universal, if they are taken according to their proper essence or entity, some are substances and some accidents; indeed some are real accidents and some accidents of reason; and since nothing univocal can be common to substance and accidents, nor to real accidents and accidents of reason, neither can anything univocal be common to the diverse natures which are denominated universal, taken in this way. But if they are taken in the second way, they will be able to have a univocal ratio, if the form that denominates them is univocal. We can give an example in genus, which is the first of the five universals, and consider the universal natures which are denominated by the second intention of genus as by a form, such as substance, quantity and quality. First, indeed, according to their proper essences; and in this way they can have nothing univocal in common. Then, inasmuch as they are denominated genera; and since the ratio of genus is univocal, explained by Porphyry through one definition, that it is predicable of many differing in species in quid, substance, quantity and quality agree univocally under the ratio of genus, because they are denominated by such a form in the same way, so that substance is not more, nor prior, predicable of many differing in species than quantity or quality, but altogether equally.

77 From this distinction an argument is gathered to prove our view, which is also the common one: The univocal is that which signifies many things under the same ratio; but universal signifies all universals or predicables under the same ratio; therefore it is univocal with respect to them. The minor is proved: that ratio is one and the same which is explained through one definition; but the ratio of the universal is explained by Aristotle through one definition, namely, that it is one in many, apt to be predicated of many; therefore it is one with respect to all universals, and under it they agree univocally.

To the first argument one must reply, from the doctrine delivered, by distinguishing the major in this way: if substance and accidents are taken according to their proper entity and essence, nothing

[p. 63]

univocal can they have in common; but if they are taken as they are univer‐

sals, they agree univocally, because they are denominated in the same way by

universality; and therefore the universal is univocal with respect to them.

For the solution of the second, it should be noted that, just as animal sig‐

nifies only the sentient nature, not the rational or the irrational, because the

differences, as Porphyry teaches in the Predicables, are outside the signification of

the genus, in the same way universal expresses only one in many, and apt to be

predicated of many; but that it is predicated essentially or accidentally, per se

or per accidens, is outside its signification, and belongs to the different uni‐

versals not under the ratio of universals, or as they are signified by such a

name, but according to other particular rationes not signified by the name

universal. Hence, although those rationes are so related that one is prior to

another, or one is such simply and another in a qualified sense, the common

name by which they are signified does not on that account cease to be

univocal.

Now, then, to the form of the argument the minor must be denied, name‐

ly that the predicable, or predication, is analogous with respect to the five

predicables: for although some of them are predicated essentially, or per se,

and others accidentally and per accidens, these particular rationes do not

pertain to the signification of predicable, but only the potency of predicating

in common; and since this is the same in all, all the predicables are signified

univocally by the name predicable, common to all; nor is the univocation tak‐

en away by particular rationes not signified by the same name.

## QUESTION VIII

Whether the universal is the adequate object of the book of the Predicables, or rather

the predicable. 79

T     he book of the Predicables is a certain part of the whole of Logic, and

therefore some partial object ought to correspond to it, which is as it

were a part of the total and adequate object of the same science; concerning

which we inquire whether it is the universal or the predicable, since it is cer‐

tain that nothing else besides these can be the object; and of them that one

will be the object to which the general conditions of an object, delivered by

us in the last proemial question, belong rather than to the other.

The first opinion defends that the predicable is the object rather than the

universal. It is usually attributed to Scotus, and is defended by many mod‐

erns. And it has two arguments. The first: that is the object of any

[p. 64]

part or science which contains all the things it treats of; but the universal does not contain all the things treated of in this book; therefore it is not its object. The minor is proved: Porphyry, in the chapter on species, treats of the individual, and also of the subjicible species, which are not universals: because the individual is not in many, nor does the subjicible species, inasmuch as it is such, regard individuals.

The second: that is the formal object of a science under whose formal ratio it considers all things; but all the things treated in this book are considered under the ratio of the predicable, and not under the ratio of the universal; therefore the universal is not the object, but the predicable. I prove the minor from the definitions of the predicables, which Porphyry delivers through the predicable, as the definition of genus, that it is predicable of many differing in species in quid; and so of the others: whence he also calls this work the book of the Predicables.

The second opinion asserts that the universal is rather the object. St. Thomas holds it, q. 9, on the object of this book; Soto, q. 4 on universals; Toledo, q. 1; and it seems to us the more probable and to be held. For its explanation it should be noted, from the doctrine of St. Thomas, opusc. 48, ch. 6, that the intellect attributes universality to the nature as the foundation of the other denominations: because the first thing it understands in it is being in many, and therefore it calls it universal; and because from the ratio of being in many there follows being able to be predicated of many, it immediately attributes to it the denomination of predicable; and then other special denominations, of genus and of species. From which it follows that, just as the first thing that is in a thing, as the foundation of the others, is its essence, so universality, which is the first denomination of the nature, is as it were its essence in the logical order, while predicability is an attribute common to all universals.

From this doctrine of St. Thomas, true and necessary, this argument is gathered to prove his view and ours: The universal and the predicable are considered per se in this book, and the former stands as essence, the latter as proper attribute; therefore the universal is the object rather than the predicable. The consequence is proved: because the office of a science is to prove attributes of the subject; but in this book it is proved of the universal that it is predicable, as the posterior of the prior, therefore as a proper attribute of the subject; which cannot belong to the predicable, since it has no attribute that can be proved of it; therefore neither can it be the object.

81. To the first argument of the other opinion the minor must be denied, because the subjicible species and the individual, in their own way, are contained

under

[p. 65]

under the universal: not because they are formally universals, but because they are

the terms of the relation of universality of the genus and of the species. For the

genus is universal because it is in many species, of which it is apt to be predicated;

and from this relation of the genus to the species there results in them another re‐

lation, of subjicibility, through which they are said to terminate it, as will be ex‐

plained in the chapter on species. And for the same reason the individual is the

term of the relation of the species, by which it is denominated universal and predi‐

cable, because it is in many individuals and is apt to be predicated of them; and

therefore individuals and subjicible species are reduced to the genus and the

species, and to their treatment.

To the second I reply by distinguishing the minor: for that the universal is con‐

sidered by Porphyry in this book under the ratio of the predicable can be under‐

stood in two ways. First, so that predicability is the objective ratio which is consid‐

ered; and in this sense it must be denied, because, since universality is the essential

ratio and foundation of predicability and of the other denominations which the

intellect attributes to the nature, it is the objective ratio under which all things are

considered. In the second way it can be understood that all things are considered

under the ratio of predicability as under a common attribute which is demonstrat‐

ed of the five universals in this work; and in this sense the minor must be granted;

but from this it is not rightly inferred that the predicable is the object, but only

that it is an attribute which is demonstrated of the object. And it is demonstrated

in this way: Whatever is one in many is predicable of many; but genus is in many

species; therefore it is predicable of them; and so of the other predicables, which

are defined by Porphyry through predicability as through a proper attribute more

manifest to us; and therefore by definitions that are not quidditative but descrip‐

tive, as will be explained in the chapter on genus. And in the same way it must be

understood that this work is called the Book of the Five Predicables, the denomi‐

nation being taken from the common attribute, better known, which is demon‐

strated of them, rather than from the universal, which is its object.

## QUESTION IX

Whether the predicables are five, or more, or fewer.

82

J  ust as Aristotle invented the art of the categories in order to reduce the modes

of being of all things to certain heads, so that we might easily recognize their

nature once the category in which it is placed is known, so Porphyry invented the

art of the predicables in order to reduce all predications

E

[p. 66]

to certain heads, and so that we might easily know of what kind any predication whatever is, Essential or Accidental; and, if essential, generic or specific; and in the same way, if accidental, of a proper or of a common accident; from the knowledge of which we may know the natures of things. But in order that we may better understand this art of the predicables, it is necessary to know their determinate number; and therefore the last question on universals inquires about their number, whether they are five, so that they are neither more nor fewer. And although there are no differing opinions about the number, but all follow Porphyry, the author of this book, who posits only five,

we nevertheless propose certain arguments to the contrary, which seem to prove, on the one side, that they are fewer, and on the other, that they are more, so that from their solutions the truth may become manifest. That they are fewer than five, then, is proved by two arguments. First, predicables and predicates are distinguished only as potency and act: because the predicable is that which can be predicated of another, and the predicate that which is actually predicated; but the predicates are four, and not more, as Aristotle teaches in Topics 1, ch. 2, 3 and 4, namely Genus, Definition, Property and Accident; therefore there will be only four predicables.

83 Second, Porphyry distinguishes two predicables, of genus and of difference, because genus is predicated in quid and difference in quale quid; but definition contains both; therefore it will suffice for two predicables. The consequence is proved: because definition is predicated of the same things of which genus and difference are predicated; and moreover it contains the mode of predicating of both, in quid and in quale quid, by way of one predicable. For if it is the definition of a subalternate species, as living sentient, it is predicated of many differing in species, namely of man and of lion, like a genus; but if it is of a lowest species, as rational animal, it will be predicated of many differing in number, as the difference is predicated of Peter and John; therefore two predicables, of genus and of difference, are not to be distinguished, but definition will suffice for both; and so they will be only four and not five.

The other part, however, that the predicables are more than five, can be proved. First, because Porphyry, in the chapter on genus, distinguishes the predicables by the things of which they are predicated, as genus from species: because the former is predicated of many differing in species, the latter of many differing in number; and so of the rest. But if they are distinguished in this way, it follows that at least seven must be posited, so that there are two predicables of difference and two others of property. The consequence is proved: because the subalternate difference,

[p. 67]

as corporeal, is predicated of many differing in species, namely of living and non-living body; but if it is a lowest one, as rational, it is predicated only of many differing in number, namely of Peter and John; therefore they will make distinct predicables. Property too, if it is subalternate, as sensible, which follows the nature of the subalternate species animal, is predicated of many differing in species, namely of horse and lion; but if it is a lowest one, as risible, it is predicated only of things differing in number, as of Peter and John; therefore there will be seven predicables.

4 Second, the vague individual, as a certain man, is predicated of many differing in number, as of Peter and John; and yet it is not a species, because it is not predicated in quid. And actual existence too has the same character; therefore another predicable, distinct from species, must be posited for them. The minor is proved: because, just as a certain man does not express the essence or quiddity of individuals, but the common ratio of individual, which either is accidental or at least is outside their essence, so actual existence does not pertain to the essence of any creature, which easily loses it through corruption, or can lose it through annihilation. Wherefore it is not predicated in quid, since to be predicated in quid is the same as to predicate the quiddity or essence of a thing.

Yet the opinion of Porphyry, which is also the common one in the schools, is true. But the whole difficulty of it consists in assigning the reason by which it may be sufficiently proved that the predicables are neither more nor fewer than five; and different reasons are assigned by different authors. For some distinguish the predicables by the things of which they are predicated; others by the things that can be known about a thing, which seem to be five. But these reasons seem to me insufficient: the sufficient one, by which it is effectively proved that the predicables are neither more nor fewer than five, must be taken from the formal mode of predicating, or of standing in order to the subject; which is proved thus. The mode of predicating, which is taken from the mode in which the predicate stands to the subject, is the formal ratio of predication; therefore it will also be the formal ratio of the predicables; but the essential distinction of things is taken from their diverse formal rationes; therefore the predicables ought to be distinguished by the diverse modes of predicating.

By this discourse, then, it must be proved that they are neither more nor fewer than five. The things that constitute the predicables must, in the first place, be universals, because the predicable, as the proper attribute of the universal, is convertible with it; but the universal is one in many; therefore nothing will be predicable

E ij

[p. 68]

unless it is one. And in order to be one, it must be simple, that is, not complex: because the complex is not one but many, as white man, or rational animal. Moreover, if it is one, it will be univocal, not equivocal or analogous. By the first condition, then, complex predicates, such as definition, are excluded from the ratio of the predicable; by the second, equivocal and analogous ones, as dog, being, accident, and the like. Next, that which is one, that is, incomplex and univocal, can stand in only five ways in order to the subject; therefore it can be predicated of it in only five ways; wherefore there will be only five predicables. The antecedent is proved: for it is predicated either essentially or accidentally; and if essentially, either by way of an actual whole, because it actually contains the whole essence of the subject, as man is predicated of Peter and John, and this is the predicable of species; or by way of a potential whole, which is truly the material part of the same species, and therefore contractible by differences as by forms, and this is genus; or by way of a formal, actual and contracting part, and this is difference. But if it is predicated accidentally, either by way of that which proceeds from the essence and is convertible with it, and this is property; or, if by way of an extrinsic or common accident, it is called the predicable of accident. And since no other modes of predicating besides these are possible, and all predications can be reduced to them, it follows that there are only five predicables, so that they are neither more nor fewer. For the solution of the first argument, the difference between predicable, predicate and category should be noted: namely, that a category is a certain essential ordering of the predicables, according to due subjection and predication, from the supreme genus down to the last species and the individual; as the category of substance is this ordering: substance, body, living, animal, man, Peter.

86 But Aristotle took the predicates, in Topics 1, ch. 2, 3 and 4, in order to the dialectical or probable proposition from which a dialectical or probable syllogism is made; and because the syllogistic form requires propositions about a common subject (for from singular propositions only expository syllogisms are made, which have no mood or figure except in order to universal propositions), he therefore takes the ratio of predicates from their order to a common subject.

From which it follows that there are only four predicates, which is proved thus. Species is not a predicate but the common subject, in order to which the distinction of the predicates is taken; which is so true that there is no other common subject

[p. 69]

besides it. This supposed, the predicate either is convertible with the species or is more universal. If it is convertible with it, either it is within its essence, and it will be a definition, as rational animal; or it follows naturally from it, and it will be a property, as risible with respect to man. But if it is more universal than the species, either it pertains to its quiddity, and it is a genus; or it is outside it, and it will be a common accident. Difference, however, Aristotle teaches is to be numbered with genus, in that ch. 3, in these words: Difference, since it is generic, is to be ranked with genus. And he is speaking of subalternate difference, because this is generic, since it is convertible with the genus, as corporeal with body; but if it is a lowest one, it is reduced to the definition. In distinguishing the predicates, however, nothing is said of the modes of predicating in quid or in quale quid, of genus and difference: because in order to the dialectical proposition and syllogism they make no distinction, since the mode of disputing probably is the same in those propositions in which the predicate is more universal than the subject and is within its essence, whether it is genus or difference. Nor are complex predicates different from incomplex ones, if they stand in the same way in order to the common subject: because one disputes in the same way about dialectical propositions made from either; and therefore definition is numbered among the predicates, though it is excluded from the predicables on account of its complexity.

87 The predicables, finally, are taken in order to the categories; and therefore definition is excluded, because a category is made of simple things alone, while genus, species and difference are placed in it. The number of the categories, however, is taken from the diverse modes of being, the first of which is the mode of being per se. But the modes of being in another, which belong to accidents, are nine; and therefore it follows that there are ten categories, four predicates, and five predicables.

And to the form of the argument, the antecedent must be denied, namely that predicate and predicable are distinguished only as act and potency: for if predicate is taken most commonly, it is not the act of the predicable; nor even if it is taken in a special way, for the topical predicate; but it stands to the predicable as act only if it is taken in such a way, namely as the nature of the same predicable requires. The second argument of this part, however, has been solved from the doctrine delivered.

To the first argument of the other part I reply that Porphyry does not distinguish genus from species by the things of which they are predicated, except with such a mode of predicating joined to them, from which the essential distinction of the predicables is to be taken.

E iij

[p. 70]

To the second argument some reply that the vague individual is not predicated univocally of Peter and John, but equivocally: because, since such individuals exist through altogether diverse individual differences, they can have nothing in common except the name. I, however, hold it more probable that a common modal concept can be abstracted from the individual differences, because they all agree in this, that they are particular and substantial modes determining the species; whence the ratio of particular mode, considered in common, which the vague individual signifies, is univocal with respect to the individuals. Therefore I reply in another way, granting that the vague individual is not properly predicated in quid, as species is, but is predicated in a similar way, since it signifies a substantial mode; and by reason of this similarity it is reduced to the predicable of species: because, since it is not a predicate of the nature but of a mode of the same nature, a distinct predicable ought not to be posited for it, but it ought to be reduced to the predicable of the nature. And one must think in the same way of actual existence.

But two very brief doubts remain which pertain in some way to the number of the predicables, and therefore they are to be solved at the end of this question. The first is whether, supposing that the five predicables are universal species, the universal is their immediate genus or a remote one, so that between it and the predicables there is given another immediate genus, as living is called the remote genus of man and horse, because animal mediates between it and these species. To which I reply that it is not the immediate genus but a remote one, which is proved by this argument: from any essential agreement a concept common to the things that agree essentially can be abstracted; but the predicables agree essentially in some ratio inferior to the universal; therefore a concept of that ratio inferior to the universal can be given, which will be predicated of the same things differing in species; and therefore it will be their immediate genus, and the universal a remote one. The minor is proved, because three predicables, namely genus, species and difference, agree in an intrinsic or essential mode of predicating, and two others, namely property and accident, in an accidental mode of predicating; therefore essentially predicable will be common to the former, and accidental predicate will be common to the latter, and nearer than the universal; and each is predicated of several species, the former of three, the latter of two; therefore they will be nearer genera than the universal, and consequently the universal will not be their proximate genus, but a remote one.

The second doubt is whether the five predicables are species

[p. 71]

that are subalternate, having other species under them, as animal or living, or

lowest ones, not having other species under them but only individuals, as man or

horse, and the other lowest species of the other genera. For if they are said to be

subalternate species, it follows that the predicables are more than five, because

the species they have under them will have to be counted together with them;

but if they are lowest, the number of the predicables will not be greater. I reply

that they are lowest species, which I prove thus: the predicables are distin‐

guished in species by the diverse modes of predicating; but these modes are not

divisible into others; therefore the predicables do not have other species. The

minor is proved: because the mode of predicating of genus is that it is predicated

as the material part of the species and by way of a potential whole, contractible

by differences; but it is impossible that there be a genus which is not predicated

in the same way; therefore this mode is not divisible into others; and this is for

genus to be a lowest species of the universal. And the same argument is made

about the other predicables; wherefore none of them can be a subalternate

species.

## TREATISE ON THE NATURE

## OF THE BEING OF REASON, AND OF SEC-

## OND INTENTIONS

even things are to be disputed in this order concerning the being of

S       reason. First, whether it exists. Second, what it is. Third, how manifold

it is. Fourth, whether it is made by the intellect or reason alone, or also

by other powers. Fifth, whether by our intellect alone, or also by the angelic and

divine. Sixth, to which science it pertains to treat of it. Last, in what manner it is

reduced to the categorial order.

1

S   ome few, and without foundation, deny that there is a being of reason, as

Vallés, controversy 9, ad Tyron., and others; and therefore it is not to be

called an opinion, nor to be held; but it is the common view of the whole school

that there is a being of reason. But in order that we may understand it, it should be

noted that the being of reason is twofold. The first, that which is made directly

and per se by reason or the intellect, and inheres in it,

E iiij

[p. 72]

as in a subject; and this is the operation of the intellect itself, and therefore it is a

real being, like the operation of sight; and it is called a being of reason only be‐

cause it is made by reason. The other is the being of reason which is not made di‐

rectly by the intellect, nor per se, but follows its operation as it were per accidens:

as, if the intellect composes this proposition, Man is an animal, the composition it‐

self, which is a real operation of the intellect, is followed by the denomination of

proposition, and of predicate and subject; and these denominations are nothing

other than certain relations of reason, of the whole proposition compared to the

predicate and the subject as to its parts, and of the same predicate and subject

among themselves: for by the very fact that one is attributed to the other, the for‐

mer is called the predicate and the latter the subject. And the first being of reason

is not properly called such, since it is a real being; and therefore we do not treat of

it, but only of the second, which is not in anything as in a subject, but only has be‐

ing while it is known by the intellect; and therefore it is said only to be objectively

in the intellect. Of this being of reason, then, is our conclusion, that it exists in the

nature of things, which is gathered from Aristotle, Metaph. 4, text 3; bk. 4, 13 and 4;

and bk. 6, text 8; in which places he teaches that the most universal being is divided

into that which is in things, and that which is said to be not in things but only in the mind,

which is only to be objectively in the intellect; and the whole school follows the

same conclusion.

It is proved by reason, because the intellect composes a proposition out of two

extremes which are not distinguished on the part of the thing, as out of man and

Peter; and out of Peter alone it makes an identical proposition, making him the

predicate and the subject; but the distinction and attribution of one to the other

is an ordering to it, and the ordering is a relation between them, not a real one, be‐

cause on the part of the thing Peter is neither distinguished from himself nor or‐

dered to himself; therefore it is a relation of reason, or a being of reason. It fol‐

lows, then, that a being of reason is given and exists.

What the being of reason is. 2

C     oncerning the essence of the being of reason, the first opinion is that of

those who assert that every extrinsic denomination is a being of reason: as

the denomination by which a wall is called right, because it is at the right hand of

a man, or a stone is called seen, because it is seen by us. Which they prove, first,

because denomination is a work of reason; therefore it is not given before the op‐

eration of the intellect; but extrinsic denominations posit nothing in the things

denominated besides the denomination itself, which the intellect effects; there‐

fore they are beings of reason. The minor is proved, because the stone acquires

nothing by being at my right, except the denomination

[p. 73]

of right; and so of the rest.

Second, extrinsic denominations are relative, and are not made by real relations; therefore by relations of reason, which is to be beings of reason. I prove the major thus: because through extrinsic denominations the things denominated are referred to others, as the wall that is right to the man at whose right it is. And the minor: because through such denominations the things denominated acquire no real relation, as the wall, from the fact that it is seen, does not acquire a real relation to the man seeing it.

But this opinion is false. It is proved by two arguments. First, the being of reason has no other being than to be known by the intellect, and therefore it is not given before the operation of the intellect; but extrinsic denominations are given before the operation of the intellect; therefore they are not beings of reason. The minor is proved: God is called creator, and a wall that is seen by some animal is called seen, not only before they are known by the intellect, but even if there were no intellect in the nature of things; therefore extrinsic denominations are given before the operation of the intellect, and therefore they cannot be beings of reason.

Second: these denominations (although they are not made by any form inhering in the things denominated, and are therefore called extrinsic) are real; therefore they are not beings of reason. The consequence is evident, because the being of reason has nothing real, but only to be known by the intellect. The antecedent is proved, because God is really called creator, and the wall really seen. Therefore these denominations are real.

To the argument of this opinion, the antecedent must be distinguished, that denomination is a work of reason. For denomination is twofold. One, which is made by some real form, whether it inheres in the thing denominated, such as intrinsic denominations are, or in another thing diverse from it, as extrinsic denominations; and these are not a work of reason, nor do they depend on the intellect, just as the real form by which they are made does not depend on it; because if they did depend on it, just as the wall is not denominated seen before the operation of the intellect, so neither would a man be denominated white by whiteness, which is plainly false. The other is the denomination which is not made by a real form but is only attributed by the intellect to things understood, as the denomination of subject or of predicate; and of this denomination it is true that it is a work of reason, as is the form by which it is made, which is a relation of reason and is said to be made by the intellect.

The second opinion asserts that not all extrinsic denominations are beings of reason, but only those which things known receive from the act of the intellect by which they are known, and from which

[p. 74]

they are denominated understood and known. And so that the sense of this opinion may be declared in one word, it asserts that the being of reason is that being-known which a thing acquires when it is known by the intellect, which is plainly an extrinsic denomination.

But this opinion is proved false by the same reasons by which the falsity of the other was proved: because the denomination of known (although it is extrinsic) is no less real than the denomination of seen in the wall, or the denomination of creator in God; therefore it cannot be a being of reason, because the being of reason has nothing real.

The common view is explained in two conclusions. The first: the being of reason is not something inhering in the things denominated, nor an extrinsic denomination from some real form existing in another, but solely a denomination which the intellect attributes to them. This is proved by this argument: to be a genus, or to be a species, does not belong to man or to animal on the part of the thing, but the intellect attributes these denominations to them through comparison to their inferiors; therefore they are neither something inhering, nor are they made by some real form existing in another. The consequence is proved, because that which inheres in something, or is made by a form inhering in another, belongs to it on the part of the thing.

Second conclusion: although the being of reason is not something inhering, and can therefore be called an extrinsic denomination, it nevertheless has a likeness to an inhering form, and on account of this likeness it can be called an intrinsic denomination. The first part of this conclusion follows evidently from the preceding conclusion, already proved; the second part, that it can be called an intrinsic denomination on account of the likeness, is proved because the denominations of genus, species, predicate and subject are like real denominations proceeding from inhering forms, such as the denominations of white and black; therefore, just as the latter are truly intrinsic denominations, so the former can be called intrinsic by likeness.

How manifold the being of reason is.

B     y the first division the being of reason is divided into that which has a

foundation in the thing, and that which has no foundation but is truly impossible. The being of reason having a foundation is that denomination which is attributed by the intellect to things known by it in such a way that their nature, as known in such a way, requires that denomination. For example, when the intellect knows human nature abstracted from individuals and compares it with them, it requires, as so known, the denomination of species; and therefore such a denomination is a being of reason having a foundation in the thing.

[p. 75]

But this foundation is understood in two ways by different moderns. First, so that it consists only in our mode of understanding, which distinguishes things that are not truly distinct, and separates or abstracts things that are not truly separated from their inferiors, but not in the things themselves. By others, however, it is affirmed that beings of reason have a foundation not only in our mode of understanding but in the known things themselves.

But for the understanding of this it should be noted, first, that for producing beings of reason and attributing them to known things it is necessary that the things be known imperfectly, that is, through several concepts, although they could be known through one by an intellect that knows perfectly. For example, in order that the intellect may attribute to man the denomination of species, and of predicate of this proposition, Peter is a man, it must know it as it were abstracted, or separated and distinct from him, although on the part of the thing it is neither distinguished nor separated. But it does this without falsehood, because it does it without affirmation or negation, but only through knowing one thing without another; and this proceeds from an imperfect mode of knowing, because it knows not the whole at once but as it were by parts, or by diverse grades: as when it distinguishes in the rational soul the grade of vegetating, of sensing and of understanding, although the soul itself is a certain simple substance.

It should be noted, second, that in the known things themselves there is also given a foundation for their being known as distinct, or for such a denomination, which is called a being of reason, being attributed to them: as in things composed of matter and form there is found the formal unity which the form gives it, and also the numerical unity, which is taken from this matter and form, or, if from the form alone, it is taken as numerical under a different ratio: because the Formal unity is taken from the form as it is the principle and root of the essential predicates, but the Numerical unity from the same form as it is the principal component part. From this, then, there is found a foundation in human nature for the formal unity in it to be understood without the numerical unity being understood, which is to be abstracted from the individuals; and also for it to be compared with many of them and denominated species, or with only one, by way of attribution, and denominated predicate.

These things supposed, our view is explained in two conclusions. The first is: the being of reason sometimes has a foundation not only in our imperfect mode of understanding, but in the things themselves, which from their own nature have a foundation for such a denomination being attributed to them. It is proved by a single argument from the doctrine delivered: not only in our imperfect mode of knowing,

[p. 76]

but in the things we conceive, there is sometimes given a foundation for one thing in them being able to be known without another; therefore there is given a foundation for denominations which are beings of reason being able to be attributed to them. The antecedent is proved. First: in human nature, in which there is given a foundation for knowing the formal unity without the numerical unity being known; therefore there is given a foundation for abstracting it from the individuals, and for comparing it with many by a simple comparison and attributing to it the denomination of species, or with only one by a composite comparison, by way of attribution, and attributing to it the denomination of predicate. Second: in the rational soul, in which there is given a foundation for distinguishing the vegetative, sensitive and rational grade; and this foundation is nothing other than its eminence or perfection, by reason of which, under the grade of a superior form not depending on matter, it contains the other grades which are found in diverse inferior forms.

7 Second conclusion: beings of reason sometimes have no foundation in the things to which they are attributed, but in other things, or in our imperfect mode of understanding alone. In this conclusion all agree, and it is proved by a twofold example. First, in God, in whom we distinguish justice from mercy, not on account of a foundation existing in them, but in creatures, in which these virtues are distinct. Second, in propositions which are called Identical, because the same thing is predicated of itself, as in this one, Peter is Peter, in which the intellect distinguishes Peter from himself, making him as it were two, and attributes to him the denomination of predicate and of subject; of which distinction there is no foundation in him, but only in the imperfect mode of knowing, which distinguishes as it were into two extremes that which in itself is neither distinct nor has a foundation for being distinguished from itself.

From these conclusions it follows that the distinction of reason is twofold, as the common consensus of the school asserts. One is that which has a foundation in the things themselves, and this is called the distinction of Reasoned Reason, which we posit between the universal and the singulars, and between the diverse grades of vegetating, sensing and understanding of the rational soul. The other is the distinction having no foundation in the known thing itself, but in other things, or only in our imperfect mode of knowing, as that which we posit between Peter and himself when he is predicated in an identical proposition. And so much concerning beings of reason having a foundation in things.

8 There are other beings of reason which have no foundation in things, but are feigned by the intellect out of certain impossible things joined together, as the Chimera and the Sphinx. Out of impossible

[p. 77]

joined together we say they are made: not because they are impossible in themselves, for this is necessary, but because, although they are possible, their conjunction is judged impossible. And in this way the Chimera is called impossible, because it is feigned as it were composed of things of different species, as of some part of a man and of another part of a lion or of some other animal. And beings of reason of this kind can be multiplied to infinity by the intellect, just as it can join things of different species in infinite ways.

9 The second division of the being of reason is as it were a subdivision of the first member. For the being of reason having a foundation in things is divided into three members, namely into Negation, Privation and Relation; which division Aristotle intimated in Metaph. bk. 4, text 2, and bk. 5, ch. 7, text 14, asserting that privation and negation are non-beings, so as to signify that they are not true real beings, but made by the intellect after their likeness. And in the second place he teaches that besides true beings there are certain others, true not so much according to entity as according to the truth of predication, affirmative as well as negative; which cannot be anything but beings of reason, which are called privations and negations. Of the relation of reason, however, he treated in ch. 15 of the same book, explaining the relations of the third kind, of the measurable and the measure, and teaching that the measure is referred to the measurable not by an intrinsic relation but by an extrinsic one, of the measurable to it; although it is certain that nothing can be ordered to another except by a relation existing in itself, which it is also certain that the measure does not have in itself, since it is rather an absolute thing. Aristotle therefore means it to be inferred that, through a relation made by the intellect, the same measure is ordered to the measurable as if it were ordered from its own nature. St. Thomas seems to gather the same division from these places: q. 21 On Truth, a. 1; d. 1, q. 2, a. 3; and d. 13, q. 1, a. 1; and it is also common in the school.

But concerning Negation and Privation two things are to be noted, so that their nature and distinction may be understood. The first is that both can be considered in two ways. First, according to themselves, or according to their essences, namely as they are negations of some real form; and in this signification they are called by Aristotle not real beings: because, since real being has being from some real form, negation or privation, which deny the real form, are consequently said to deny real being, and therefore not to be real beings, but rather non-beings, as Aristotle taught in Phys. 1 and 5. Which is to be understood of being simply; for negations of a real form are called real beings in a qualified sense, that is, not positive but negative ones. In this signification too Aristotle taught in Phys. 1, concerning privation, that

[p. 78]

it is a principle of a natural thing. And of negations St. Thomas teaches, in the opusculum On Being and Essence, that they belong to the essence of a real nature: as it is of the essence of man to be not a horse, or not capable of neighing. Taken, finally, in this signification, it is true and necessary that they are given before the operation of the intellect and do not depend on it. This is proved evidently: because privation cannot be a principle of natural generation if it depends on the intellect, before whose operation it is certain that that same generation is given. Negation cannot belong to the essence of a real nature if it is not given before the operation of the intellect, taken in this way.

In another way Privation and Negation can be taken as they are attributed to things in a proposition; and in this way they are not taken according to the ratio of negation and privation, but after the likeness of a positive form, because what is attributed to another must be a positive form or have its likeness; and since they do not have of themselves to be taken by way of a positive form, but only from the intellect, therefore, taken in this way, they depend on it: they are not given before its operation, nor can they in any way be real beings, but they are beings of reason. Which we can explain by this example: when we say that a man is blind, we do not take blindness as a negation but as a privation of sight; because, taken in this way, it is not properly said to be in another, but rather to take away a form from it; therefore neither is it attributed to another in a proposition as it is a privation, but inasmuch as it is conceived after the likeness of a positive form; and since it has this from the intellect alone, it is also said necessarily to depend on it and not to be given before its operation; which are the proper conditions of a being of reason.

It should be noted, second, for understanding the distinction of privation from negation, that they agree in one thing and are distinguished in another. They agree in this, that each is a negation of a real form in a subject. But they differ, because Negation only denies the form of the subject, whether it is apt to have it or not; whereas Privation expresses the negation of a form not in any subject whatever, but in one apt to have it. Whence a stone is not called blind, even if it does not have sight, because it does not have the aptitude for having it; but a man or an animal is rightly so called, in which, if it is not present, there is nevertheless the aptitude for having sight.

From which it is understood in what manner Privation and Negation are distinguished: for they are distinguished by a formal distinction, which is usually called that of the Including and the included; because privation includes negation and adds over it an order to a determinate subject apt to have the form which it lacks, whereas negation

[p. 79]

does not express an order except to a subject without it, whether it is apt to have it or not.

From what has been said about the diversity of beings of reason, it follows that it is not to be asserted absolutely that a being of reason is a being feigned by the intellect, but that this way of speaking is true only of the being of reason having no foundation in the things to which it is attributed, as the Chimera or the Sphinx, but not of those which have a foundation. And the reason for this is manifest: because only he is said to feign who speaks without any foundation; but speech in some way founded in the truth or nature of things is not properly called feigned; but, speaking properly of these beings of reason, it must be said that they are made by the intellect, a foundation in things being presupposed.

By what power and operation the being of reason is made.

T     o this doubt some reply that not only the intellect produces beings of

reason, but also the interior senses, especially the imagination or phantasy, of which we know that it feigns a golden mountain, which, since it is not given in the nature of things, will be called a being feigned by the imagination, which is a being of reason.

We, however, assert that one must reply with a distinction: for beings of reason that are feigned, that is, that have no foundation in the thing, can be made not only by the intellect but also by the phantasy; but those which have a foundation, only by the intellect. And of the first it is plain that they are made by the phantasy, as it were composing some one thing not existing in the nature of things out of two truly existing ones: as out of the species of mountain and of gold it composes a golden mountain; which cannot be done by any other sense, nor by the will or appetite, because they do not have such a power of composing. But beings of reason which have a foundation in things cannot be made by any other power except by the intellect alone. And the reason for this is that these beings of reason are certain denominations or relations which the intellect attributes to natures already known by it, through another cognition; whence they are said to be made as it were by a reflex cognition; but no other power besides the intellect has this reflexive power, by which it can take as object a thing as known by itself through another cognition; therefore neither does it have the power of producing beings of reason. The major is manifest from what we said in q. 5 on Universals, about the mode in which the universal is made by the intellect through simple comparison. For we said that Comparison is a cognition by which the intellect as it were reflects upon the nature already known through simple abstraction, and compares the nature so known to

[p. 80]

its inferiors. The minor, however, is manifest, because this reflection cannot belong to the will, which knows nothing but tends to the object known by the intellect; nor can it be attributed to the senses, whose cognition is most imperfect; and therefore they cannot operate about a thing as already known by themselves; although it may happen that they know again the same thing already known, yet not by a reflex cognition, but by several cognitions that are as it were direct.

But now, granted that beings of reason are made by the intellect alone, someone could doubt by which of its operations they are made: whether by the first, which is the apprehension of simples, or by the second, which is composition and division, or by discursive reasoning, which is the third. Some reply that they cannot be made by the first, and they prove it by this reason: beings of reason are made through the comparison of the nature with its inferiors, or of the predicate with the subject; but every comparison is a composition or division, and an actual predication; therefore they cannot be made through simple apprehension.

The common view, however, to be followed by us, holds (as we saw in q. 5 on universals) that some beings of reason are made through the first operation of the intellect, others through the second, and some others through the third. Which is proved by this argument. Some beings of reason belong to simples before a composition is made out of them; others belong to the same simples as they already are in a composition, or to the composition itself; others, finally, to compositions as they are in a syllogism; therefore different beings of reason are made through each of these operations. The antecedent is proved, because through the simple comparison of the nature with its inferiors there is made the being of reason which is the universal; there are made also genus and species, all of which belong to the predicables before they are actually predicated, therefore before a proposition is made out of them. Wherefore it is necessary that they be made through simple apprehension, through which we know one thing in order to another; for this simple cognition is prior to composition. Of the beings of reason which belong to composition and to discursive reasoning, it is manifest that they are made through the second and third operation of the intellect; and such are the denominations of predicate and subject, and also of proposition; and moreover the denominations of argumentation and syllogism.

To the argument of the other opinion, however, it must be denied that every comparison is a composition or division, since it was proved in q. 5 on universals that there is given a comparison which is an apprehension of simples, through which we know one thing in order to another, or to many.

Whether

[p. 81]

Whether beings of reason are made by the divine or the angelic intellect.

T      he first opinion affirms that the divine and the angelic intellect produce

beings of reason; it is held by certain moderns. And it is proved, first, by the testimony of St. Thomas, 3 p., q. 15, a. 2, ad 3, where these words are found: Respects of this kind, by which the ideas are multiplied, are not caused by things but by the divine intellect, comparing its essence to things, etc. From which this argument is gathered: The distinction of the ideas in God is not real, since the ideas agree with the divine essence, in which there can be no real distinction; therefore it is only a distinction of reason. But a distinction of reason is a relation of reason; therefore a being of reason is made by the divine intellect, according to the mind of St. Thomas. The consequence is proved, because he says that the distinction of the ideas is caused by the divine intellect.

It is proved also by a twofold argument. First, the divine intellect knows beings of reason most perfectly; but beings of reason have no other being than to be known; therefore they have being from the divine intellect, which is to be made by it.

Second, the divine intellect distinguishes things which are not distinct on the part of the thing; but this cannot be done except by producing a being of reason; therefore the divine intellect produces beings of reason. The major is manifest, because it distinguishes its justice and mercy, and also the ideas existing in itself, which are not distinguished on the part of the thing. The minor is proved, because distinguishing things which are not distinct is done through a relation of reason, which is a being of reason.

The second opinion asserts that the divine intellect does not produce beings of reason; and this is the more probable and is to be held. I explain it by two conclusions. The first: the divine intellect most perfectly knows the beings of reason which are made by our intellect. All grant this, and it is proved by an evident argument. Beings of reason are made by our intellect; therefore they are known by it. But whatever is known by the intellect is contained under its object; therefore beings of reason are contained under the object of our intellect. But the object of the divine intellect is not less universal than ours, since it comprehends things diminished and most imperfect; therefore it no less contains beings of reason, nor knows them less.

The second conclusion: the divine intellect makes no being of reason, nor can it make one. In order to prove this, it must be supposed that two imperfections are necessarily required for producing a being of reason, in the mode of understanding. The first, that things which are not distinct on the part of the thing, but one, be distinguished

F

[p. 82]

by the intellect and conceived through several concepts. The second, that the object be represented to the intellect and understood by it, not as it is in itself or on the part of the thing, but in another mode. Both conditions are made manifest by this example. In order that the intellect may make the universal nature genus or species, it is necessary that it distinguish it from the inferiors from which it is not distinct, and abstract it from them, since it is not abstracted of itself but is joined to them on the part of the thing; and this is to understand it in another mode than it is on the part of the thing, that is, to understand by several and distinct concepts what on the part of the thing is one. But the intellect does both without falsehood, because without affirmation and negation. And what we say of these beings of reason is evident in the rest.

From these things an argument is gathered to prove our view effectively. Beings of reason cannot be made by the intellect except by distinguishing things which on the part of the thing, or according to themselves, are not distinct, and by conceiving through several concepts things which in themselves are one, and also by understanding them in another mode than they are on the part of the thing. But such a mode of understanding is most imperfect, and one that cannot belong to the divine intellect; therefore neither will it be able to produce beings of reason. The minor is proved: for the divine intellect understands all things by a single cognition and a single and most simple concept, and according to the same mode which they have on the part of the thing: so that if they are one, it knows them in the mode of one; but if they are distinct, as distinct. Therefore such an imperfect mode of understanding, through which a being of reason must necessarily be made, cannot belong to it; and therefore neither will it be able to produce one.

To the arguments of the other opinion I reply, and to the first, the testimony of St. Thomas, that his sense is gathered from another place, namely from De potentia, q. 17, a. 6, where he teaches that the distinction of reason which is found among the divine attributes, as between justice and mercy, or among the ideas, is found in a different way in the divine intellect and in ours: because in the former it is found as in its root and as it were virtually, but in ours formally. Which is to be explained in this way. An idea is nothing other than the divine essence as it can be participated by creatures. And since there are several creatures distinct according to essence, we distinguish in it several ideas, so that by the ratio by which it can be participated by man, it is the idea of man and not of lion; and as it can be participated by the lion, it is the idea of lion and not of elephant; and so of the rest. But although the divine intellect understands the divine essence as imitable by all creatures by a single and most simple concept,

[p. 83]

and therefore does not distinguish several ideas in it, yet through that single concept it understands that, by our intellect conceiving it in an imperfect mode, that is, through several and distinct concepts, it is distinguished into several ideas, of man, of lion, and of other things. For by one concept we understand the divine essence as it can be participated by man, and by another, distinct concept as it can be participated by the lion; and this is to distinguish several ideas in the divine essence by a distinction of reason, and therefore to produce beings of reason by understanding the divine ideas.

From which is understood the difference between the divine intellect and ours: that the former does not distinguish the ideas in the divine essence by an actual or formal distinction, but by a fundamental or virtual one, inasmuch as it knows that they can be distinguished by ours; whereas our intellect makes an actual distinction of reason among the ideas. And because all our understanding is caused and regulated by the divine, St. Thomas taught that the divine intellect causes the distinction of the ideas, not by producing it actually, but only virtually, inasmuch as it understands the divine essence as it can be understood by our intellect through several concepts, and that therefore several ideas can be distinguished by us; which distinction, made by us, the divine intellect itself causes through its understanding. And this is the sense of that testimony.

To the first argument, the antecedent is to be granted, that the divine intellect knows beings of reason by a most perfect cognition; but the consequence is to be denied, that it makes them. And the reason is that it does not know things with those two imperfections necessarily required for producing beings of reason. And to declare the solution in one word, it must be said that the divine intellect does not know beings of reason by a cognition productive of them, but by a cognition through which it understands them as made by us.

To the second, the major is to be distinguished: because “to distinguish things which are not distinct” can be understood in two ways. First, by producing an actual distinction among them; and in this sense it is to be denied. In another way, by producing the distinction only as it were virtually or fundamentally; and in this way it can be granted.
