For since the divine intellect understands things which are not distinct as able to be distinguished by us, who know imperfectly through several concepts, it is said virtually to produce the distinction which our intellect makes actually, inasmuch as our understanding is caused and regulated by the divine. And what we say of the divine intellect must also be understood, in its own way, of the angelic: which, since it understands perfectly, is not said to make beings of reason, but to know them as made by us.

E ij

[p. 84]

To which science it pertains to treat of being of reason.

T      his doubt must be answered with two distinctions presupposed. The

first is the one we adduced above, of being of reason having a foundation in things and not having such a foundation. And concerning the second it is certain that it pertains per se to no science. Which is proved by two arguments. First, because the things of which a science treats per se must be determinate; but beings of reason which have no foundation can be multiplied to infinity by the intellect; therefore no science can treat of them per se. Second, that of which a science treats must have determinate principles, through which determinate attributes are proved of it; but these beings of reason do not have determinate principles; therefore no science can treat of them per se. I prove the minor, because they are composed of disparate things, or things diverse in species; therefore no determinate principle can be taken from them, nor can such an impossible composite have determinate attributes.

The other distinction is of being of reason having a foundation in the thing. If it is a relation of reason, it can be considered in two ways. First, according to itself, or according to its proper entity; and in this way it pertains to Metaphysics, not per se, because the per se object of this science is real being, but as it were per accidens, inasmuch as it has a certain likeness to real relation, of which this science treats per se. Second, it can be considered as it is a denomination of the nature to which it is attributed, as the denomination of genus, species, predicate and subject. And according to this consideration it is called logical being of reason, of which Logic treats per se as of its proper object. But if it is a privation or a negation, it must be reduced to that science which treats per se of the form or essence which it denies or of which it deprives: as the privation of a natural form pertains to Philosophy, as one of the three principles of natural generation, as Aristotle teaches in Phys. 1; and a negation which is of the essence of this or that nature is reduced to the science which treats per se of such a nature, as not to be a horse to the science of man; and so of the rest.

In what way being of reason is reduced to the categorial order.

C    oncerning being of reason not having a foundation in things, it is cer‐

tain that it cannot be reduced to the categorial order, because it is composed of things diverse according to essence,

[p. 85]

and therefore it does not have some one determinate nature according to which it could be ordered in a category. But concerning being of reason having a foundation, as regards privation and negation, it is also certain that it has a certain likeness to qualities. Which I prove thus. Privation and negation are beings of reason as they are considered by the intellect as positive forms and are attributed to some subject in a proposition, as when we say that a man is blind; but so considered they have a likeness to qualities; therefore they are reduced to their category. The minor is proved: because blindness is predicated of a man just as whiteness or color is; therefore it has a likeness to these and to other qualities.

There remains only relation of reason, which could be ordered in a special category. This, however, will not be proper, because a category can properly be made only of real beings; but it will have the greatest likeness to the true category of relation, ordered out of real relations. The category of relation of reason, therefore, is to be ordered thus: that the supreme genus be relation of reason (for being of reason, the most universal, must be excluded from this category on account of its transcendence, just as real being is excluded from all the real categories), which can be divided into three genera, or subalternate species, according to its diverse foundations, which are the diverse operations of the intellect, namely simple apprehension, composition and division, and discursive reasoning. Just as Aristotle divided the supreme genus of the category of relation, which is the relative, or real relation, through its diverse foundations, so that the first genus is of relations which are founded on unity, as the relations of identity, likeness and equality; the second, of relations which are founded on action and passion, as paternity and filiation; the third, of those which are founded on measure, as are the relations of science to the knowable and of a power to its object: so relation of reason is to be divided into that which is founded on the cognition of simples and is attributed to the simples themselves, and this is the first genus, having under it diverse species, as the relation of universal, genus, species and the other predicables; next, into that which is founded on composition and division, to which genus the various species of propositions pertain; and finally into that which is founded on the third operation, which is discursive reasoning, under which genus are contained the diverse species of argumentations and syllogisms. And so these three genera have others under them, down to the lowest species, from all of which, so ordered, the proper category of being of reason results.

F iij

[p. 86]

TREATISE ON THE WAY I N W H I C H P R E D I C AT I O N S A R E M A D E IN CONCRETES AND ABSTRACTS

## OF FIRST AND SECOND INTENTIONS

t the end of the preceding treatise we said that Dialectic treats of

A          being of reason as it is a certain relation, or a denomination at‐

tributed to natures by the intellect; in which acceptation it is

called logical being of reason. Therefore in this second treatise we must treat of the mode and order which it has with respect to the predications of concretes and abstracts, in which are exercised the denominations which natures receive from it. And since predications can be made in first intentions, which are real natures, and also in second intentions, which are beings of reason, we shall divide the present treatise into two parts: so that in the first we treat of the predications of concretes and abstracts of first intention, and in the second of the same abstracts and concretes of second intentions.

And in first intentions they can be exercised in four ways. First, so that a concrete is predicated of a concrete, as man is animal. Second, an abstract of an abstract, as humanity is animality. Third, an abstract of a concrete, as man is humanity. Fourth, a concrete of an abstract, as humanity is man. And so that we may suppose what is certain as regards the truth and falsity of propositions, we must speak only of those propositions in which the predicate and subject are in some way ordered, so that they are related as superior and inferior, or as equals, one of which pertains to the other because it is included in it, or is its proper attribute, or a common accident.

These things explained, it is certain, first, that a proposition is true in which a concrete is predicated of a concrete inferior or superior, or also equal, whether it be of its essence, or a proper attribute, or a common accident: such are these, man is animal, man is rational, man is risible, man is white. True also are the others into which these are converted, but indirectly and improperly.

Second, it is certain that propositions in which an abstract is predicated of a concrete, or a concrete of an abstract, are false, whether they be related as superior and inferior, or be equals;

[p. 87]

as man is humanity, man is rationality, or risibility, or whiteness. And the reason

for this is manifest. First, on account of the diverse mode of signifying of the

terms: because the abstract is signified by way of a part, but the concrete by way of

a whole; but a part is not predicated of the whole, as foot or hands of a man.

Second, because the subject in these propositions includes something which the

predicate in no way includes, as white includes body, which whiteness does not in‐

clude; or, conversely, the predicate includes something which the subject does not

include, as in the indirect propositions made from the same terms. Which suffices

for it not to be true that the one is the other, as is signified by the proposition.

From which it follows, first, that the opinion of Soto, q. 3 on Universals, is false,

who asserts that a proposition in which an abstract is predicated of a concrete, as

man is humanity, is false only on account of the diverse mode of signifying of the

terms; for they are false also on account of the inclusion of something in the one

and not in the other: because, as we shall see in its place, no proposition can be

true unless the whole that is included in the subject in some way includes the

predicate.

It follows, second, that the opinion of Durandus, in 1, d. 24, last q., is even

more false, where he laid down a universal rule, saying that in creatures all propo‐

sitions are true in which a substantial abstract is predicated of a substantial con‐

crete, as man is humanity; although they are false in accidental concretes and ab‐

stracts, as man is whiteness, and others like it.

It is certain, third, that propositions in which the abstract of a genus is predi‐

cated of the abstract of a difference, or conversely the abstract of a difference of

the abstract of a genus, as rationality is animality, or animality is rationality, are

false. And the reason for this is that the generic and the differential grade are for‐

mally diverse, and, signified in the abstract, they do not include each other, be‐

cause neither does animality include rationality nor rationality animality; therefore

neither is predicated formally of the other. The consequence is proved, for in or‐

der that a proposition be true, the predicate must be included in the subject.

Whether a superior abstract is predicated of an inferior abstract.

14

T    he question can only be about propositions in which a superior abstract is

predicated of an inferior, or equal, abstract; but these can be taken in two

ways, namely in terms

F iiij

[p. 88]

that are accidental or essential. And if they are made in accidental terms, it is certain that all are false, as humanity is risibility, or humanity is whiteness. And the reason for this is that the predicate and the subject of these propositions are often distinguished really, and the one is never included in the other: for although man includes whiteness as its subject, yet humanity, since it is signified as a form, is not the subject of accidents, nor does it include them, as signified in the abstract. The question can therefore only be about the propositions of abstracts which are made in substantial terms, such as these, humanity is animality, humanity is rationality: whether they are true or false.

And the first opinion asserts that they are true; it is followed by Soto, q. 3 on Universals, Canterus, chapter on difference, and many of the moderns. And it is proved by two arguments. First, that proposition in which a superior concrete is predicated of an inferior, as man is animal, is true, because the predicate is included in the subject, as animal in man; but the superior abstract is also included in the inferior abstract, as animality in humanity; therefore this will be true, humanity is animality. The minor is proved, because humanity is composed of animality and rationality, just as man of animal and rational; therefore it includes both.

It is proved, second, in substantial and accidental forms. And first in substantial ones, such as are the rational and the sensitive soul, of which the latter is superior and the former inferior; and both are signified by an abstract name; and yet this is true, the rational soul is sensitive; therefore this too will be true, humanity is animality. The consequence is proved, because a superior form is predicated of an inferior precisely because it is included in it; but animality is a superior form with respect to humanity; therefore it is included in it, and consequently it will be truly predicated. In accidental forms too, such as whiteness and color, it is manifest: for this is true among all, whiteness is color; and in it a superior abstract is predicated of an inferior abstract, just as in the other, humanity is animality; therefore this too is true and to be granted.

The second opinion holds that such propositions are false. It is followed by Scotus, in 1, d. 5, q. 1, a. 1; Nifo, Metaph. 3, q. 2, concl. 5, ad 3; Canariensis, 1 p., q. 28, a. 2, disp. 2; Ferrara, Contra Gentiles 1, ch. 18, 2, 3, § Considerandum, and bk. 4, ch. 81; Cajetan, in the opuscule On Being and Essence, ch. 3 and 4. But Scotus maintains that they are false because he thinks that the predicate and the subject are distinguished from the nature of the thing, or formally, before the operation of the intellect; but the others, who posit only a distinction of reason between them,

[p. 89]

do so on account of the mode of signifying of abstracts, by which animality is signified as a principle or part of animal, and humanity as a principle of man; and the principle of one is not predicated of the principle of another. And this opinion is gathered evidently from St. Thomas in the two places cited, and it seems to us more probable and to be followed.

15 But in order that we may prove it more effectively, two things are to be noted. The first is that the concrete and the abstract signify the same thing, but by a different ratio: for the concrete signifies it by way of the haver, but the abstract by way of the principle or form of that same haver. For example, man and humanity signify the same human nature; but man signifies it by way of an actual and complete whole, and therefore by way of the haver; humanity, on the other hand, only by way of the principle and form of that same complete whole, or haver. Which is manifest from the common way of speaking and understanding: for we say that a man is the same as one having humanity, and that humanity is as it were the principle and form of man.

From which it is gathered, first, that the concrete signifies the nature not as altogether prescinded from the singular conditions, but as containing them, at least confusedly and in potency. For although it is abstracted from singulars by an abstraction through which it becomes in some way universal, and therefore does not signify or contain the same singulars in act, yet it contains them in potency: because from its proper mode of signifying it can be determined through singular conditions to this and that individual, or to Peter or John. But the abstract signifies the same nature as altogether prescinded from singulars, and not as determinable through their singular conditions: because, since it does not signify it by way of the haver but of the principle or form, and a principle or form does not have the mode of what is determinable through another, but rather of what determines another, namely that whose principle or form it is, the nature signified in the abstract cannot be understood by way of the haver; and therefore, so signified, it can contain neither in act nor in potency the singular conditions through which it would be contracted to this or that singular. And what we say of the specific nature with respect to the singulars is to be understood in the same way of the generic nature signified in the concrete or in the abstract, as of animal or animality: so that animal signifies the sensitive nature as contractible or perfectible through the differences rational and irrational, which it contains in potency; but animality in no way, or rather as the form or principle of that same animal and of its species.

[p. 90]

It is gathered, second, that abstracts signify the nature by way of a part, just as concretes do by way of a whole. Which is proved by a twofold evident argument. First, because abstracts signify the nature by way of the principle and form of that same thing as it is signified by the concrete name: as animality signifies the sensitive nature as it is the principle and as it were the form of animal; but that which is the principle and form of another is related as a part of it; therefore the abstract signifies the nature by way of a part. Second, animality does not signify the sensitive nature by way of a whole; therefore by way of a part. The antecedent is proved: because if it signified it by way of a whole, it would be either of an actual or of a potential whole; but it signifies it in neither way; therefore not by way of a whole. I prove the minor: because a potential or actual whole signifies the thing by way of the haver, but the abstract only by way of the form of that which has it; therefore not by way of a whole but of a part. And hence it comes about that neither is animality predicated of animal, nor humanity of man: because a part cannot be predicated of the whole.

It follows, third, that abstracts are not genera or species, but principles of genera and species; which Avicenna asserted, Metaph. 5, ch. 7, as Cajetan testifies in the opuscule On Being and Essence, ch. 4; and St. Thomas proved it in the same place by this argument. A genus by its proper nature has the mode of a potential whole, and a species the mode of an actual whole; but abstracts do not signify the nature by way of a potential or of an actual whole, but by way of a part; therefore they are not genera or species, and for that reason they are not denominated by the second intentions of genus or species, or of the other predicables. All this doctrine that has been noted is found in St. Thomas, opuscule On Being and Essence, ch. 4.

From it two arguments are gathered for proving our view, that this predication, humanity is animality, and similar ones, are false. The first is: for any predication to be true, it is necessarily required that whatever the subject contains, the predicate contain in act or in potency; but animality does not contain, in act or in potency, whatever humanity contains; therefore it cannot be truly predicated of it. The major is most certain, because it cannot be true that this is that, as is affirmed through the proposition, unless the whole that this contains that also contains; and this is the reason why a part is not predicated of the whole, nor could a genus be predicated of a species unless it contained in potency the difference which the species contains in act, as St. Thomas says well in the place above. But the minor is proved: because humanity contains animality and rationality, of which it is composed; but it is evident

[p. 91]

that animality does not contain rationality in act or in potency, since it does not have the mode of an actual or a potential whole, but of a part or form; therefore it cannot be truly predicated of humanity.

The second. An actual part is not predicated of the whole, as all grant; but animality is an actual part of humanity; therefore it is not truly predicated of it. The minor is proved: because just as man is composed of animal and rational, so humanity is composed of animality and rationality. And if you say that this argument also proves that this proposition is not true, man is animal, because animal is an actual part of man: I reply that animal is indeed a part, yet it is not signified by way of a part, but by way of a potential whole, and therefore it is truly predicated of man; animality, on the other hand, is not only a part but is signified by way of a part, which cannot be predicated of the whole. And this is the reason why this is true, Man is animal, and this false, Humanity is animality.

To the first argument it is replied that it is not enough for the truth of a proposition that the predicate be included in the subject: because if that sufficed, it would follow that a proposition in which a part is predicated of the whole is true, since it is certain that the part is included in the whole. It is required, therefore, not only that it be included in it, but that the whole that the subject contains the predicate contain in act or in potency, as has been explained. And since animality does not contain the whole that humanity contains, because it does not contain rationality in act or in potency, it follows that it is not truly predicated of it.

The second argument has two parts. The first proceeds about substantial forms, the second about accidental ones. To the first, therefore, I reply by denying the antecedent: that that predication, the rational soul is sensitive, is of an abstract of an abstract. And concerning the predicate, namely sensitive, it is evident that it is not an abstract name but a concrete one. Which is also true of soul: for although it is a form, yet it is signified by way of what has the grade of sensing; not indeed as man has it, who is composed of it, but as the form, which gives that grade to the composite, yet signified as it were by way of a whole, and therefore by way of a concrete. Which is made manifest from this: because unless soul were signified by way of a concrete, sensitive, which is a concrete name, could not be truly predicated of it; and by the very fact that it is truly predicated, signifying the same as what has the grade of sensing, it cannot be denied that soul too is signified by way of a concrete. Hence it is not well inferred that this too is true, Humanity is animality, in which it is certain that an abstract

[p. 92]

is predicated of an abstract; and therefore it has a different ratio.

For the solution of the second part, a threefold difference is to be noted between the abstracts of substances and those of accidents. The first: that the former are abstracted by metaphysical abstraction from genera, species or differences, as animality from animal and humanity from man; but the abstracts of accidents are abstracted by physical abstraction from the subject in which the accidental form signified really inheres. Hence, by the very fact that it is signified as abstracted from it, it is not signified as inhering in it or dependent on it, but after the manner of a complete nature subsisting per se. The second: because the abstracts of substances always have the mode of the form or principle of that from which they are abstracted, whereas the abstracts of accidents rather have the complete mode of a total nature, subsisting per se; which comes from the proper mode of physical abstraction. The last difference is that the abstracts of substances, because they are abstracted metaphysically, are ultimate abstracts, because metaphysical abstraction is ultimate; hence no other abstraction can be made from them: for nothing further can be abstracted from humanity or animality. But the abstracts of accidents are not ultimate, because neither is physical abstraction ultimate, but metaphysical abstraction can still follow upon it: so that from whiteness, which is abstracted by physical abstraction, another, metaphysical abstract can be taken, which will be the ratio of whiteness, or albedineitas [whitenessness] (a barbarous word, but one that signifies by explaining the nature of the thing). From which it is understood that the abstracts of accidents are called abstracts only in the physical order, but in the metaphysical order are rather concretes.

From these differences we can reply to the form of the argument, granting the major, that this is true, whiteness is color, but denying the minor, that in it a superior abstract is predicated of an inferior abstract; rather it is a predication of concretes in the metaphysical order, like this, man is animal. Hence neither is the predicate signified by way of a part, but by way of a complete whole, subsisting per se and containing whatever the subject contains, which is related as genus to species, as in this, man is animal. But that one, humanity is animality, is a predication of abstracts in the same metaphysical order, and therefore it is false. And in the same way a predication of abstracts in accidents will be false if they are abstracted by metaphysical abstraction: as if from whiteness and color we metaphysically abstract albedineitas and coloreitas, or the ratio of whiteness and the ratio of color, this will be false, albedineitas is coloreitas: because metaphysical abstracts are signified by way of principle and form, and therefore cannot make a true predication.

[p. 93]

S E C O N D PA RT O F T H I S

T R E AT I S E , O N T H E P R E D I C A-

tions of Second Intentions.

econd intentions are certain relations of reason which the intellect

S        attributes to first intentions, that is, to real natures, which are denomi‐

nated by them: as the second intention of species is a relation of reason of the specific nature, which the intellect attributes to it when it compares it to the individuals; and all the predicables are certain relations of reason, diverse because they are attributed to diverse natures, and in order to diverse inferiors, or to inferiors of which they are predicated in diverse ways. Thus the predicable of genus is a second intention, or a relation of reason in order to several species, of which it is predicated in quid as a potential whole. The predicable of difference is a second intention, or a relation of reason in order to several species or individuals, of which it is predicated in quale quid. The predicable of property is a second intention, or a relation of reason of a proper attribute to species or individuals: as of sensible to man and horse, or of risible to man, and to Peter and John. And the predicable of accident is a second intention, or a relation of reason of an accident to several subjects distinct in species or in number: as the relation of reason of white to man and horse, or to Peter and John. And finally the universal, which is common to all the predicables, is a second intention, or a relation of reason to all and each of the predicables, of which it is predicated in quid as a genus.

These things supposed, second intentions can be compared in two ways. First, among themselves, inasmuch as one is predicated of another; and if they are compared in this way, whether in the concrete or in the abstract, they behave in the same way as first intentions: so that if one pertains in some way to another, concretes are predicated of concretes essentially or accidentally, as a proper or a common accident. Therefore all of these are true: Genus is universal, Species is universal; and also this: Universal is genus; but the former are essential, the latter accidental. This one, however, The universal is predicable, is a predication of a property, or of the fourth predicable. But concretes of abstracts, or abstracts of concretes, always make false propositions: as Genus is genericity, or Specificity is species, or Genus is universality. Only

[p. 94]

in the predications of abstracts is there a difference: because in second intentions the predication of a superior abstract of an inferior abstract is true, as genericity is universality; which, however, in first intentions we said is false, as humanity is animality. And the reason for this difference is that second intentions are relations of reason, and therefore accidents of reason. Wherefore, just as real accidents signified in the abstract do not have the mode of parts but of a whole subsisting per se, because they are not abstracted by metaphysical abstraction from genera or species, but by physical abstraction from their subjects, in the same way second intentions have a likeness to accidental forms, and therefore are not signified through abstract names as forms or principles of genera or species, but by way of a whole subsisting per se. And this is the reason why they constitute a true predication, although in first intentions it is false.

Second, with first intentions. If second intentions are compared to first ones, they are always compared accidentally, since they are relations and accidents attributed to them; and they also behave in the same way in all things as we said first intentions behave among themselves when they are compared accidentally. In this alone they differ: that real accidents which are truly predicated of inferiors are truly predicated also of superiors; and if they are truly predicated of superiors, they are truly predicated also of some inferior: as if white is predicated of Peter, it must be truly predicated of man; and if it is predicated of man, it must be truly predicated of some singular man. Which is not found in second intentions, but the contrary: because neither can the second intentions which are predicated of inferiors be truly predicated of superiors, nor are those which are predicated of superiors truly predicated of inferiors, as is made manifest by these examples. Species is predicated of man, and not of animal, nor of Peter; and genus is predicated of animal, and not of man; and the second intention of individual is truly predicated of Peter when we say Peter is an individual, and yet it is not predicated of man, but this is false, man is an individual. And the reason for this difference is that real accidents belong to their subjects absolutely and as they are on the part of the thing; but second intentions, which are relations and accidents of reason, do not belong to natures absolutely, nor on the part of the thing, but as they are conceived in such a mode by the intellect, namely in common, in order to species or individuals, or also in the singular; and therefore those which belong to the inferior, namely to the individual, cannot belong to the species, nor can that which belongs to the species belong to the genus: because the second intention

[p. 95]

of individual belongs to Peter as he is conceived as indivisible into other individuals, and to be conceived in this way is repugnant to the species; and the second intention of genus belongs to the nature as it is conceived in order to species, but it is conceived in order to individuals.

## CHAPTER II

On Genus.

But it seems that neither genus nor species is said simply, etc.

B R I E F E X P O S I T I O N O F T H E T E X T.

T      he intent of Porphyry in the present chapter is to explain the nature of

genus, which is the first predicable. And it is divided into three parts. In the first he lays down two real acceptations of genus and compares them with each other; from their likeness, in the second part, he gathers its third, logical acceptation. And in the third he hands down the definition of genus and at the same time expounds it.

The first real acceptation of genus is that in which it is taken for some collection of men having an order among themselves and to one first, from whom all are derived: in which signification we are accustomed to call the Roman people the genus of the Romans, because they are ordered among themselves by such laws, and descend from Romulus as from their first principle.

Second, genus is taken for the very principle of generation from which others are derived, whether it be the father or the fatherland: in which signification the poet speaks when he says: Mantua begot me, etc., calling his fatherland his genus, or principle of generation. But properly speaking, it is not so much the father or the fatherland as the origin through which men are derived from them that is called genus: for we do not so much call him their genus as say that the Romans draw their genus from him. And of these two acceptations Porphyry teaches that the second is more proper than the first. First, because we use it more frequently. Second, because a collection of men is called a genus precisely because the men of it draw their origin from one first; therefore the origin through which they are derived from him is more properly called genus than the collection itself.

In the second part, from both real acceptations, Porphyry gathers the logical one, which he intends per se, saying: The logical genus is taken for that under which the species are placed, that is, under which they are set, as animal is a genus, because under it are placed man,

[p. 96]

and lion: which species have an order and a certain likeness among themselves by reason of the same nature, which they participate from the genus itself, from which they are also said in their own way to draw their origin.

In the third part of the chapter he defines the logical genus, taken according to the last acceptation; and the definition is this: Genus is what is predicated of many differing in species, in quid. Which he explains thus: Things that are predicated are predicated either of one, as the individual, or of many, as universals. By the particle of many, therefore, genus is separated from the individual, which is predicated of one alone. By the particle differing in species, it is separated from species, which is the second predicable and is predicated only of things differing in number. By the last particle, in quid, it is separated from the three other predicables, difference, property and accident: for difference is predicated in quale quid, property and accident in quale, genus only in quid; because to a question put through what we do not answer well through those, but through genus: as if you ask what man is, I answer well that he is an animal. Thus far Porphyry.

## QUESTION I

What the defined of the definition of genus is.

T      hat the definition of genus assigned by Porphyry has no defined, I prove by

two arguments. First: if it had any, it would above all be genus; but genus is not definable; therefore it has none. The minor is proved: A good definition must consist of genus and difference, or of something in place of the genus and something else in place of the difference; but there is no genus of genus: for if there were, there would be another genus of that genus, and so we should proceed to infinity. It follows, therefore, that genus is not definable, and therefore that the aforesaid definition has no defined.

Second: a definition must be given through genus and difference; therefore nothing can be defined except species, because this alone is composed of genus and difference; indeed, nothing can be defined except inasmuch as it is a species, because to have genus and difference belongs to the species inasmuch as it is a species; therefore genus cannot be defined. The consequence is proved, because it is not a species but another predicable distinct from species; and therefore the present definition will have no defined.

It must be held, however, that the definition of genus is good and has a definite defined, whose nature it explains. And that the definition is good is proved, first, from Aristotle, Topics 1, ch. 4, where Aristotle laid it down; and it was from him that

Porphyry

[p. 97]

Porphyry took it. Second, by argument: because a good definition is one that so explains the nature of the defined that it distinguishes it from any other things with which it could agree; but through this definition it is explained what genus is, namely a predicable of many differing in species, in quid, and it is distinguished from the individual and from the remaining predicables, as we saw in the explanation of the text. It is therefore good.

And the second point, that it has a definite and determinate defined, I prove thus.

3 To be predicated of many differing in species, in quid, is a common ratio, belonging in the same way and equally to all genera; therefore it is one and can be explained through one definition; wherefore this will be the determinate defined of that definition.

But in order that this truth may be better understood and the arguments solved, it should be noted that the second intention of genus, which is the first predicable, is a certain relation of reason, and a most universal ratio of denominating all generic natures, even if they are the supreme genera of the categories, as substance, quantity and quality; and at the same time it is a certain species of universal. Hence, since every species is composed of genus and difference, this second intention too is composed of universal, which is the common genus of the predicables, and of a difference, which is to be relative to several species of which it can be predicated in quid. And so genus agrees with the other predicables in the common ratio of universal, which is to be one in many; and it is distinguished from them because it is in many species, of which it can be predicated in quid. And therefore, although it is a most universal ratio of denominating, because the natures which it denominates as genera are also for the most part most universal, since they are the supreme genera of the categories, nevertheless according to its essence it is a particular and determinate species of a certain genus, which is universal. From which it is understood that it can be defined through a determinate definition, and that its definition handed down by Porphyry has a determinate defined.

To the form of the first argument it must be replied by denying the minor of the first syllogism; and when it is said in the minor of the second syllogism that there is no genus of genus, by distinguishing: because the second intention of genus can be taken in two ways, in the ratio of denominating or in the ratio of being. And in the first way it has no other genus by which it is denominated, because it is not a genus denominatively or accidentally, but essentially; but in the ratio of being it is a determinate species, and has a superior genus, which

G

[p. 98]

is universal, of which, together with the difference, it is composed.

And if it is said that universal too is denominated genus by this second inten‐

tion of genus, which is the first predicable, like the remaining genera, and there‐

fore is inferior with respect to it: it is replied that the antecedent is true, but the

consequent must be distinguished. For in the ratio of denominating it is superior

to universal, but in the ratio of being inferior; and because denomination is acci‐

dental with respect to that which is denominated, as the denomination of white

with respect to body, while the ratio of being is essential, therefore the second

intention of genus explained by this definition is accidentally superior to univer‐

sal, but essentially inferior, as its true species.

To the form of the second argument I reply: nothing is defined by a proper

definition except a species; but genus, which is the first predicable, is a species of

another genus, namely of universal, which it denominates accidentally; and

therefore it can properly be defined. But to what is added in the argument, that

everything which is defined is defined inasmuch as it is a species, it must be

replied with this distinction. “Something is defined inasmuch as it is a species”

can have a twofold sense. The first, that the ratio of species is explained through

the definition; and this is false: because although man is a species, when he is de‐

fined as rational animal, yet it is not explained through such a definition that he

is a species. The second sense is “to be defined inasmuch as it is a species” in

such a way that to be a species is a necessary condition for a proper definition;

and this is true. But nothing is explained through the definition except the prop‐

er and essential ratio of the defined, which nevertheless is accidentally denomi‐

nated species by the second predicable.

## QUESTION II

Whether the proper defined of the same definition is the real nature which is denominated

genus, or the second intention of genus by which it is denominated.

6

G     enus considered in common can be taken in four ways. First, for the nature

which is denominated genus, considered according to its essence: as if we

take animal for the sensitive nature. Second, it is taken for the aggregate of the

nature denominated and the second intention denominating, just as white can be

taken for the aggregate of body and whiteness. Third, it is taken for the generic

nature, not according to its essence, but inasmuch as it is denominated genus by

the second intention of genus. Fourth, for that same second intention denomi‐

nating the same nature genus. And of these four,

[p. 99]

it is certain that the aggregate is not the defined, because it is a being per accidens, composed of two beings in act, namely of the nature and of the second intention. But a being per accidens does not have one essence but a twofold one, and therefore it cannot be explained through one definition, as Aristotle expressly teaches, Metaph. 7, text 21.

The question therefore proceeds about the three others. And there are three opinions concerning it. The first asserts that the defined of this definition is the generic nature according to its essentials, so that animal is a genus and a predicable of many differing in species, in quid, as it is a sensible living thing; and so of the other genera. This is attributed to Scotus, who, since he affirms that the nature is universal according to itself and before the operation of the intellect, seems consequently to assert that it is a genus or a species essentially. And it is proved by argument: because that is the defined to which the definition belongs; but to be predicated of many differing in species belongs to the nature according to its essence, and not as it is denominated by the second intention; therefore that is the defined. The minor is proved, because animal, according as it is a sensible living thing, is predicated of man and lion, and not as it is denominated by the second intention: for if it were predicated in this way, when we say man is animal, then the sense would be, man is a genus. The consequence is proved: because animal, as it is denominated by the second intention, is a genus.

This opinion is neither Scotus’s, nor true, but false. The first is proved: because although Scotus asserts that there is a formal unity on the part of the thing which is the foundation of genus and species, yet he teaches that genera and species are denominations attributed to natures by the intellect; wherefore he does not hold that the real nature according to its essence is the defined. But that this opinion is false is proved by this argument. If the generic nature according to its proper essence is the defined, then according to its proper essence it is a genus, or at least to be a genus will be its proper attribute; but whatever things are essential to the generic nature, or are its proper attributes, necessarily belong to its species, as whatever things are essential to animal, or belong to it as proper attributes, are essential to horse and lion, or are their proper attributes; therefore to be a genus, or to be predicated of many differing in species, will belong to the species; which is plainly false.

The second opinion is that of Cajetan in the opuscule On Being and Essence, ch. 4, where he holds that neither the generic nature according to its essentials, nor as it is denominated by the second intention, is the defined, but the second intention. Which, however, he says can be considered in two ways. First, as That by which, that is, as the ratio of denominating the generic nature, just as whiteness is the ratio of denominating

G ij

[p. 100]

a white body; and this is to consider it in the abstract. Second, it can be considered inasmuch as it is referred to the species: for since it is a relation of reason, it essentially regards its term; but the term of the relation of genus is the species; and therefore it can be considered in order to them; and in this way it is taken as That which, and in the concrete, and it is the proper defined of this definition, but not when taken in the first way.

Cajetan proves it by this argument. A definition must belong to the defined essentially, if it is quidditative, or as a proper attribute, if it is descriptive; but to be predicated of many differing in species belongs to the generic nature, as to animal or to color, accidentally, even considered in common; and to the second intention in the concrete essentially, because the second intention of genus essentially regards the species, since it is a relation to them; therefore this, and not that, will be the defined.

8 This opinion too is false, which I prove. First, to be predicated of many belongs to genus in the concrete, because what is predicated of many is a concrete, just as to disperse sight belongs to white in the concrete; but this opinion does not hold that genus in the concrete is defined; therefore it is false. The minor is proved: because an accidental concrete, such as genus is, signifies the form, namely the second intention, and connotes the subject, namely the generic nature, to which it belongs to be predicated of many. If, therefore, the generic nature is not the defined, but the second intention, then genus is not defined in the concrete but in the abstract, which contradicts the words of the definition.

Second, even if the second intention of genus is considered inasmuch as it is a relation to the species, it is not a concrete but an abstract; therefore Cajetan falsely calls it a concrete. The antecedent is proved, because the concrete of relation is the relative, just as the concrete of whiteness is white; but the second intention of genus, even in order to the species, is not the relative, because it is not that which is referred but the ratio of referring; therefore it is not a concrete but an abstract.

9 The third opinion is that of St. Thomas in the opuscule On Being and Essence, ch. 4, where he asserts that the adequate defined consists of the generic nature and the second intention, considered in this way: namely the generic nature not according to itself but as it is denominated by the second intention, and the second intention as denominating; so that the nature considered in this way is the material defined, and as That which, because it is that which is predicated of many differing in number; and the second intention is the formal defined, and as That by which, because it is not that which is predicated but the ratio of predicating; and from both

[p. 101]

there results one adequate and per se defined, because it is not considered as an aggregate of them, but as including the one in order to the other; and things that are ordered per se do not make something one per accidens. We have an example in this definition, Dispersive of sight. Its material defined, and as That which, is body as denominated from whiteness, because to disperse sight belongs to it; its formal defined, and as That by which, is whiteness, which is rather the ratio of dispersing sight; but from both, as ordered to each other, there results one adequate and per se defined. This opinion is followed by Javelli in his Logic, tit. 4, ch. 2, Paul of Venice in the chapter on genus, Soto in the same place, the single question, Toledo q. 1. And it seems to us more probable, and to be followed.

And it is proved by this argument. That is the defined of a definition to which the definition belongs per se; but to be predicated in quid of many differing in species belongs per se to the generic nature as denominated by the second intention of genus, and is convertible with it per se, and it cannot belong to anything else; therefore this alone can be the defined. The minor is proved: because just as it belongs per se to body, as denominated or informed by whiteness, to be dispersive of sight, so the generic nature, as denominated by the second intention, is per se predicable of many differing in species; and whatever is predicable in quid of many differing in species is the generic nature as denominated by the second intention. That it belongs per se to it alone is proved because it does not belong essentially to the same nature, as was proved against the first opinion, but can only belong to it accidentally; and it can belong to the second intention only as That by which, since this is not predicated of many differing in species, but is only the ratio of predicating. Therefore it can belong per se only to the same nature as denominated by the second intention.

For the solution of the argument of the first opinion it should be noted that two things are to be considered in the predication of any predicable on the part of the predicate.

First, the formal ratio which it predicates of the subject. Second, the condition under which it is predicated of it: as when species is predicated of the individual in this predication, Peter is a man, the formal ratio which it predicates of him is the essence of man, but the condition under which it is predicated is being a species, which is to be denominated by the second intention of species, which is the relation of the species to the individuals.

From this distinction I reply to the form of the argument by distinguishing the minor in this way: if in the predication of genus of species, when we say Man is an animal, the formal ratio is considered which

G iij

[p. 102]

animal predicates of man, it is true that it is predicated according to essence, inasmuch as it is sensible living thing; but if the condition under which it is predicated is considered, it is the second intention of genus, by which it is denominated; and therefore by reason of such a condition it belongs to it to be predicated in quid of many differing in species, and not according to essence or essential predicates, although it predicates these of the same species. And from this the sense of this proposition, Man is an animal, is understood, and of the others in which genus is predicated of species: which is not that man is a genus, but that he is a sensible living thing; for this is the formal ratio which it predicates of him, from which the sense of the proposition is to be taken, and not from the condition under which it is predicated, which is the second intention.

For the solution of Cajetan’s argument something else should be noted, namely that the material significate of genus, in the concrete signified, is twofold, as of other accidental concretes: one proximate, adequate, and per se; the other remote, inadequate, and per accidens. As the material significate of white, adequate and per se, is body; inadequate and per accidens, a wall or any other particular body: so the material significate of genus, per se, adequate, and proximate, is the generic nature in common, which is denominated genus from the second predicable; the remote, or inadequate and per accidens, is animal or color. And from this one replies to the form of the argument by distinguishing the minor: for although the definition of genus belongs accidentally to animal or to color, because they are remote and per accidens material significates, yet to the generic nature, as denominated by the second intention of genus, it belongs per se and not accidentally. Just as to be dispersive of sight belongs per se to body as having whiteness; but to the second intention, even in order to several species, the definition does not belong except as That by which, as was proved by us against Cajetan.

## QUESTION III

Whether the definition of genus is quidditative or descriptive.

T      wo things are to be explained in order that the present question may be

solved. First, of what kind the definition of genus is, quidditative or descriptive. Second, what is placed in it for its genus: universal, or predicable, or something else; and so the question is to be divided into two parts. Concerning the first there are two opinions, as it were extreme, and another in the middle.

The first extreme opinion asserts that the definition of genus is not only not quidditative or essential, but that genus can in no way

[p. 103]

be defined by a quidditative definition. It is followed by Albert the Great, tract. 1 of the Predicables, ch. 5; Villalpando on the present chapter, who also cites Ammonius for the same view; Toledo, q. 1 on this chapter. And it is proved by this argument. Genus is an accidental concrete, including as its material the generic nature, which can be a substance or a real accident, and as its formal the second intention, which is a being of reason; but these have diverse essences; therefore they cannot be explained by one definition; wherefore genus cannot be defined by a quidditative definition.

The second extreme opinion asserts not only that genus can be defined by a quidditative definition, but that this definition of it assigned by Porphyry is quidditative. So Scotus, q. 14 and 15 on Universals, whom Cajetan follows, q. 1 on this chapter, in the solution to the first. Scotus proves it by this reasoning. Genus is considered by Porphyry in this work under the ratio of predicable, as are the other predicables too; but it is defined by being predicated of many differing in species; therefore the definition is quidditative. The consequence is proved: because predicable means the potency of predicating, and to predicate is the proper act of such a potency; but a potency is defined quidditatively through its proper act, from which it takes its essence or species; therefore genus, as predicable, is defined quidditatively.

The third opinion is the common one, which affirms two things. First, that genus can be defined quidditatively. Second, that the definition of Porphyry is not quidditative but descriptive. And as regards this second point it is held by St. Thomas, opusc. 84, tract. 1, ch. 2 and 3; Albert the Great, tract. 3 of the Predicables, ch. 34; Ammonius and Villalpando in the places above; Scotus, the single question on this chapter, the last §; Toledo, q. 2; Mercado, chapter on species, fol. 16, col. 2. And this is more probable and to be followed.

The first thing it affirms, that genus can be defined quidditatively, is proved by this argument. Universal is a genus to the five predicables, as we proved in q. 8 on Universals; therefore the first predicable, which is genus, is a species of universal; but every species is composed of genus and difference as of essential parts; therefore it can be defined through them; and a definition delivered through genus and difference is quidditative; therefore genus can be defined by a quidditative definition.

It is proved second that the definition of Porphyry is not quidditative: first, from his words in the present chapter, which run thus: Which those describing it also assigned, saying that genus is that which is predicated of many, and differing in species, in what it is. Next, by reason, because the predicables have two things, as we proved above. First, that they are universals, that is, one in

G iiij

[p. 104]

many; next, that they can be predicated of the same; and the first stands as

their essence, the second as a proper attribute. But genus is defined by being

predicated of many; therefore it is defined through a proper attribute; and a

definition that is given through a proper attribute is descriptive, as if man were

defined through risibility; therefore the definition of genus is descriptive.

To the argument of the first opinion the reply is that the things which genus

includes are diverse, but ordered among themselves: for it includes the nature

as ordered to the second intention, as to a denominating form, and the second

intention as ordered to the nature, as to a denominated subject; and by this

they make one order, so that it can be explained by one definition.

To Scotus’s argument I reply by distinguishing the antecedent: for if it is un‐

derstood that genus and the remaining predicables are considered by Porphyry

as predicables in the sense that predicability is their essential ratio, it is false,

for the essential ratio is rather universality. But if it is understood that they are

considered as predicables in such a way that predicability is a common at‐

tribute which is proved of them, it is true; and therefore they are all defined

through it as through a common attribute, which is to be defined by descrip‐

tive definitions; and all are to be reckoned such.

S E C O N D PA R T O F T H E Q U E S T I O N . 13

B     ut supposing that the definition is descriptive, it is asked in the second

part of the question: What is placed in it for its genus? And the first opin‐

ion asserts that the genus of this definition is universal, because although it is

not placed there in an express word, it is nevertheless referred to by that rela‐

tive, which is predicated of many: for it is the same to say, Genus is that which is

predicated of many, as to say, Genus is universal. This opinion, however, cannot

in the first place be defended in Porphyry, which I prove thus. Porphyry, ex‐

pounding the same definition, says that by the particle predicated of many the in‐

dividual is excluded; which cannot be true if universal is the genus, for it would

already be excluded by that, since the individual is not universal. Next, it can‐

not be defended that the definition is descriptive: for if you take away the par‐

ticles predicated of many and put universal in their place, the sense of the defini‐

tion will be: Genus is universal in many differing in species in quid; and thus

the proper attribute will be taken away; and once it is taken away, the defini‐

tion will not be descriptive, against the common opinion, proved from

Porphyry and by reason.

The second opinion asserts that the genus in this definition is predi

[p. 105]

cable, which is expressed by the words which is predicated of many: for a verb in a definition does not express act but aptitude; it is the same, therefore, to say Genus is that which is predicated of many, as if one said, that which is apt to be predicated of many; but to be apt to be predicated of many is the same as to be predicable of many; therefore predicable is placed for the genus in this definition.

14 The third opinion is the common one and to be held: that in place of the genus the generic nature is put, not indeed taken in the same way as when it is said to be the defined, but in another: for when it is the defined, it is taken together with the second intention by which it is denominated, and with which it makes one per se defined, by a unity of order; but for the genus it is put only as it is taken in common, not as ordered to the second intention. This we can explain by the example of white: when it is defined in this way, White is dispersive of sight, the defined is body as denominated from whiteness, so that from both, namely from body and whiteness, as ordered, one complete and per se defined is made; but in place of the genus body is put, taken absolutely, that is, not considered under the denomination of whiteness, nor together with it. This opinion, so explained, is followed by Ammonius, Albert the Great, and Canterus, in the places cited above. And it seems to us more probable.

15 For in the first place it is gathered from the doctrine of St. Thomas, On Interpretation 1, ch. 1, lect. 4, and the opusc. On Being and Essence, ch. 7, where he teaches the mode of defining accidents: in the concrete, through the subject in place of the genus; and in the abstract, through a true genus, and the subject in place of the difference: as risible, that it is man apt to laugh; but risibility, that it is the aptitude of man to laugh. And that the reason of both is this: because to be able to inhere in a subject is of the essence of an accident; but inherence in a subject is properly expressed through the same subject placed in the definition; therefore accidents are properly defined through the subject, in place of the genus if they are defined in the concrete, and in place of the difference if in the abstract.

16 Next, from this doctrine this argument is constructed to prove that opinion. Genus is defined by Porphyry in the concrete, as the words of the definition signify: That which is predicated of many differing in species in quid. For what is predicated is the concrete, not the abstract; but genus is an accidental concrete, like white; therefore it is defined through the subject in place of the genus; and the subject is the generic nature, just as the subject of whiteness is white; therefore it is defined through this nature placed in the definition in place of the genus, and the sense of the definition is: Genus is a nature which is predicated of many differing in species in quid.

[p. 106]

To the argument of the first opinion the reply is that accidents are better

defined in the concrete through the subject than through the genus, because

through it the aptitudinal inherence, which is of their essence, is better ex‐

pressed. Hence the subject of genus, which is the nature, is more properly re‐

ferred to by the relative which is predicated than universal is. And in the same

way one replies to the argument of the second opinion.

Q U E S T I O N I V.

Whether genus includes the differences and species in act, or only in potency.

17

T     his question is very useful for understanding the nature of genus; but for a

briefer resolution of it, it should be noted that one thing can be under‐

stood to contain another in act in three ways. First, in distinct act, as a defini‐

tion contains each of its parts, namely genus and difference. Second, in deter‐

minate act, but not expressed: as the species contains genus and difference, as

man contains animal and rational. Third, confusedly and indeterminately: as

being contains the intrinsic modes of substance and of accident, which are per

se and in another; not only confusedly, but determining neither one rather than

the other.

Of these three modes, first, it is certain that genus does not contain the dif‐

ferences in distinct act, as a definition contains genus and difference. This is

proved evidently: because if animal contained rational in distinct act, we could

define man through it alone, saying that man is an animal, because in animal ra‐

tional too would be included in act and distinctly; and therefore such a defini‐

tion would consist of genus and difference, and would therefore be sufficient,

which is plainly false.

Second, it is certain that genus does not contain the differences in determi‐

nate act, even if it contains them confusedly, as animal does not contain ratio‐

nal as man does. This is proved because if animal contained rational and irra‐

tional in act, all the predications in which it is predicated of its species would

be false, as Man is an animal, A lion is an animal: because the sense would be, man

is rational and irrational, and likewise the lion, which is absurd.

The only doubt, then, can be whether genus contains the differences in in‐

determinate and confused act, so that it expresses no particular one rather than

another, but is said to contain them all indeterminately, in a different way from

that in which any species contains its difference: for man, although he does not

contain rational expressly, yet contains it determinately, so that this difference

[p. 107]

and not another is contained in it; but animal cannot contain rational and irrational in that way, because it expresses the one no more than the other, but both under the same confusion. Nevertheless it could be understood to contain them in confused and indeterminate act, according to the third mode. And it is of this mode of containing the differences in act that the question proceeds; its sense is: whether genus contains the differences in confused and indeterminate act, or only in potency, as matter contains forms only in potency.

18 And the first opinion asserts that genus contains the differences in act in this third mode. It is proved by two testimonies of Aristotle. The first is found in Phys. 1, text 4, where he speaks thus: But the universal is a certain whole, for it comprehends many things as parts. The second in Phys. 7, text 31, where he speaks of genus thus: Genus is not some one thing, but in it many things lie hidden. From which I argue thus. Genus contains many things as parts; therefore it contains them in act, because every whole contains its parts in act, since it is composed of them; but the things that genus contains in this way cannot be other than the differences and species, as is known; therefore it contains them in act, and not in potency, according to the mind of Aristotle.

Next it is proved by this reasoning. For a predication to be true, it is necessary that the whole which contains the subject contain the predicate, not only in potency but also in act; but genus is predicated of species; therefore it must contain in act whatever the species contains, namely the difference, of which together with the genus it is composed. The major is proved: because when animal is predicated of man, the sense of the predication is that man is an animal in act; which will not be true if animal expresses in act only sensitive nature: for since this is a part of man, the part will be predicated of the whole; in order, then, that it be true, animal must also contain rationality in act, and in potency is not enough, since it is predicated in act and not in potency.

The second opinion holds that genus contains the species and differences not in act but only in potency, as animal contains rational and irrational. Posterior Analytics, text 17, where he speaks thus: For let genus be supposed to be such that it is in more according to potency. But to be in more than the species is to be more universal and to contain more than the single species, that is, other species and their differences; if, then, it is in more according to potency, it will contain the species and differences only in potency. This is also the express opinion of Porphyry in the chapter on difference, where, speaking of genus, he says thus: In potency indeed it has all the differences that are under it, but in act none. And St. Thomas on the words of Aristotle cited, and opusc. 42, ch. 9, whom follow

[p. 108]

Albert the Great, tract. 5 of the Predicables, ch. 4; Javelli, tract. 4 of the Predicables, ch. 4, before the middle; Cajetan, Soto, Banterus, Toledo, on the chapter on difference, in the exposition of the text; Mercado, the single question on this chapter. And it is true and to be held. But in order to prove it, two things should be noted. First, that genus signifies a superior grade of the nature, and difference an inferior grade, by which it is determined to constitute the species: as animal signifies the grade of sensitive nature, which is superior to the grade of rationality, which the difference rational signifies; by this it is contracted to constitute the species of man.

Second, it should be noted that genus is considered in two ways. First, as an actual part composing the species together with the difference. Second, as a potential whole, contractible by the differences: as animal is an actual part of the human species, which it composes together with the difference rational; and as a potential whole it is that which is determined by the same difference to constitute man, and by the difference of horse to constitute horse.

19 From these two notes two arguments are gathered to prove our opinion. The first is: genus signifies a grade of nature diverse from and superior to the grade which the difference signifies, and it is abstracted from the species and differences, as animal from man and horse, and consequently from rational and irrational; but that which is abstracted from its inferiors, as so abstracted, does not include them, since to be abstracted from them is to be known without them; therefore genus cannot include in act the species and differences from which it is abstracted, but only in potency.

The second argument. Genus can be considered only as an actual part of the species, or as a potential whole contractible by the differences; but in neither way does it include them in act; therefore only in potency. The minor is proved: because it does not include them in act as it is a part of the species, for one actual part does not include another, since by the very fact that it included it in act it could not compose the whole with it, as the components must be distinct and therefore not including each other; but neither as it is a potential whole can it include them except only in potency, because they are only its potestative parts, of which it is composed as such a potestative whole.

And it can be confirmed: because if genus contained the differences in act, since these are altogether diverse, as rational and irrational, it would contain in act many diverse things, and would therefore be equivocal with respect to the species of which it is predicated, or at least analogous, like being with respect to substance and accident, which it contains in confused and indeterminate act, as genus contains the differences,

[p. 109]

according to the opposite opinion; but the consequent is false, since genus is univocal; therefore it will also be false that genus contains the differences in act.

To the testimonies of Aristotle adduced for the other opinion I reply: genus contains many things in potency, that is, species and differences, not as actual parts but as potestative ones; for just as among wholes one is actual and another potential, so among parts some are actual and others potential. The actual are those which compose an actual essence; the potential or potestative, those through which, or to constitute which, the whole is contracted or determined: for it is the same to be the parts to constitute which in act the whole is determined, and to be the parts of its potency.

20 To the argument, the major is to be denied: because it is not required for the truth of a proposition that the predicate contain in act whatever the species contains, but it is enough that it contain something in act and something in potency; for thus it will predicate a part of the species, included in the species, yet not by way of a part but of a whole; and therefore it will make true the proposition in which it is said that man is an animal, whose sense is that man includes animal, which is determined by rational to constitute him. For this is to include rational and the other differences in potency. Which is to be explained thus. Contractible or determinable means potency, and the contracting means act; but genus is contractible by the difference as by an act; therefore it is a potency with respect to the difference and to the species which it can constitute with it; wherefore it cannot contain the species and differences in act, but only in potency.

Q U E S T I O N V.

Whether genus is predicated of species as a whole, or also as a part of it.

G      enus can be considered in three ways. First, as it expresses the generic na‐

ture abstracted from the species, as animal inasmuch as it expresses sensitive nature abstracted from man and horse; and taken in this way it is not a part but a whole, because it is signified by way of something having the nature; yet it is not an actual whole but a potential one, because it is signified as having a nature perfectible by the differences; and what is perfectible is signified as in potency to further perfection, which is to be signified as potential. In another way genus is taken as the other part of the species, composing it together with the difference; and then it is not taken as abstracted from the species,

[p. 110]

but only as it expresses in act their partial nature. But further, signified by way of a part, it can be taken either as an actual part, inasmuch as it is joined in act with the difference in composing the species, or as a potential part, if we consider it not as composing in act but as able to compose.

And according to these three acceptations there are three opinions. The first holds that it is predicated of the species even as an actual part. It is followed by Cajetan on the present chapter, Paul of Venice on the following chapter toward the end, and others. And they prove it first from Aristotle, Posterior Analytics 1, ch. 4, where he teaches that the whole definition and each of its parts are predicated per se of the defined; but the parts of the definition are actual, of which one is the genus; therefore it is predicated of the species as an actual part.

21 They prove it next by reason. First, because this is the difference between the predication of genus and of species, granted by all: that the predication of species is complete, but the predication of genus incomplete; genus is therefore predicated of the species as something incomplete; but the incomplete is a part; therefore it is predicated as a part.

Second, physical parts, such as matter and form, are more distinguished among themselves and from the whole than metaphysical parts, which are genus and difference, since the former are distinct things, but the latter only distinct concepts of the same thing; but physical parts, signified in the concrete, are truly predicated of the whole, when we say Man is corporeal, or is animate; therefore the metaphysical parts, which are genus and difference, signified in the concrete, will all the better be predicated of the species which they compose; and so this will be true, Man is an animal, even if the genus is taken as a part; just as this too is true, Man is rational, although rational is not a potential whole but an actual part.

The second opinion affirms that genus is predicated of the species not as an actual part but as a potential part, that is, not as composing in act but as able to compose together with the difference. Canterus holds this, on the present chapter, doubt 3, and proves it by this argument. For a predication to be true, the predicate must contain the whole that the subject contains; but genus as an actual part does not contain the other part of the species, which is the difference, either in act or in potency, but it does so well as potential: because as able to compose the species it is not considered as joined in act with some difference, but as able to be joined; wherefore it will contain all of them in potency; which is enough for it to be said to contain the whole that the species contains, namely one part in act and the other in potency; it will therefore be predicated as a potential part

[p. 111]

, not as an actual part.

22 The third opinion is that of St. Thomas, in 1, d. 15, and the opusc. On Being and Essence, ch. 3, who asserts that genus is predicated of the species not as a part but as a whole. His words are: If animal were not the whole that man is, it would not be predicated of him, since no part is predicated of its whole. It is followed by Boethius, in the book On Division, near the beginning; Cajetan too, although he is cited for the opposite opinion, expressly asserts in the same ch. 3 of the opusc. On Being and Essence that genus is predicated of the species not as a part but as a potential whole. Likewise Soto, the single question on this chapter, and Father Francisco Suárez, vol. 1 of his Metaph., disp. 15, sect. 11, no. 16. And it seems to us more probable.

23 But in order to explain its foundation, it should be noted first that both genus and difference are taken from the whole specific nature, or from its whole entity, considered under diverse grades, and not from a part alone, as will be explained in the chapter on difference; yet by a diverse ratio: for genus is taken from the whole nature of the thing under a more universal and imperfect ratio, which is nevertheless perfectible through the same nature considered under the specific grade; but difference, also from the whole nature, as determined and perfect. For example: animal, as it is the genus of man, is taken from his whole nature according to the superior and imperfect grade, that is, as sensitive, determinable by the same nature of man as rational; and rational, which is the difference, is also taken from the whole nature of man, as perfect and determinate. Whence it follows that both genus and difference signify the whole nature of the species: the former under the ratio of the contractible, the latter under the ratio of the contracting.

Second, it should be noted that genus taken as a potential whole is very diverse from itself taken as an actual or potential part: for as a potential whole it expresses not only a part of the species but its whole nature, considered under a superior and more imperfect grade, and contractible through the inferior and specific grades of the differences; but as it is a part of the species, it in no way expresses the entire nature of the species, but only a part. And the reason for this difference is that genus as a potential whole is abstracted from the species by universal abstraction, because the common is abstracted from the particulars, as animal is abstracted from man and lion, as a universal from particulars; and therefore it expresses their whole nature, but under the superior sensitive grade, signifying the same as that which has a sensitive nature determinable by rational. But if the same genus is taken as a part of the species, it is not abstracted by the abstraction of the universal from particulars, but rather by the abstraction

[p. 112]

of precision, by which a part is prescinded from the whole, as the arm from man.

24 From this doctrine a twofold argument is gathered to prove that genus is predicated of the species as a potential whole and not as a part. First: genus is predicated of the species as a universal and superior predicate abstracted from them; but the universal which is abstracted from particulars contains their whole nature, considered under a superior ratio, the inferior rationes from which it is abstracted not being considered, as is plain in the species abstracted from the individuals; therefore it is predicated of them as a potential whole, contractible by the differences, and not as a part. The consequence is proved: because a part cannot be abstracted from the whole by the abstraction of the universal from the particular, but only prescinded from it, as the arm from man; which plainly is not predicated of the whole.

Second, for any predication to be true, it is not enough that the predicate be included in the subject, for if this were enough any part would be predicated of the whole; therefore it is required that it contain whatever the subject contains. The consequence is proved from the sense of the proposition itself, by which it is signified that this is that; which cannot be true unless the predicate contains the whole that the subject contains: for if it does not contain something of the subject, it will not be true on the part of that something that this is that. And this is the reason why no part can be predicated of the whole: because by reason of the other part, which the whole expresses, it cannot be true that the whole is the part, as that man is a head. And this argument proves in the same way of physical parts, such as matter and form: because although these are not really distinguished from the whole, it is enough that they are distinguished by formal ratio, on account of the diverse mode of being and of signifying of the whole and of the part as conceived by the intellect, for them to make a false proposition.
