To the testimony of Aristotle for the first opinion I reply that the parts of the definition are predicated per se of the defined, the due mode of predicating being observed, namely taken by way of a potential or an actual whole: for under the form of a part it is impossible. But for Aristotle’s intent in that passage it is enough that they are predicated in this or that way.

To the first argument of the same opinion one replies by distinguishing the antecedent. For a predicate can be incomplete on two counts: on the part of what it predicates of the subject, and from the mode in which it predicates it; and in the first sense genus is predicated incompletely of the species, because it predicates only sensitive nature, which is a part of the species; but on the part of the mode it is rather predicated completely, because it predicates the same sensitive nature

not

[p. 113]

not by way of a part but by way of a whole, because by way of something hav‐

ing it; not indeed of an actual whole, but of a potential one, because by way

of something perfectible and determinable by the differential grades.

25 To the second one replies by granting the antecedent, that a physical

part signified in the concrete is predicated of the whole: because it is not sig‐

nified as a part but under the ratio of a whole, since it is signified by an ad‐

jectival name; which, since it signifies by way of something adjacent, also sig‐

nifies the thing by way of something having: as when we say that man is ma‐

terial, it is the same as if we said that he is having matter; and to be material,

signified by an adjectival name, is signified by way of something adjacent, as

if it were an accident of man, although it is truly a substantial part. But

genus, even signified in the concrete, can be taken as a part, because it is sig‐

nified by a substantive name; and taken thus it cannot be predicated of the

whole according to the true sense of the proposition, by which it is said that

this is that. Which cannot be true on the side on which the whole imports

something else, diverse from any part per se.

To the argument of the second opinion one replies that the difference be‐

tween genus as an actual part and as a potential part does not consist in this,

that as an actual part it is joined to one difference only, while as potential it

can be joined to all: for in both ways it regards only one determinate differ‐

ence; but only in this, that as an actual part it is distinguished from itself as a

potential part, because as joined in act it is considered with such a determi‐

nate difference, but as a potential part it is considered as able to be joined,

not to all, but only to the same determinate difference. Hence it is false that

as a potential part it contains some difference in potency, and consequently

it is false that as a potential part it can be predicated of the species.

## QUESTION VI

Whether genus is separated from difference by the mode of predicating in quid.

25

T      he negative part, that it is not distinguished by the mode of predicating

in Quid and in Quale quid, is proved from Aristotle, Posterior Analytics 1,

text 12, where he teaches that both parts of the definition, namely genus and differ‐

ence, are predicated of the species in quid; and more expressly in Topics 7, ch. 2,

place 31, in these words: Of those things which are in the assigned expression, this

one is genus, that one difference; and genus and difference are predicated in what it is.

H

[p. 114]

It is proved also by reason: because the mode of predicating follows the mode of being; but difference has a more perfect mode of being in the composition of the species than genus, since it stands as form, and genus as matter; therefore it will have a more perfect mode of predicating. But the more perfect mode of predicating is to be predicated in Quid; therefore it will be predicated in this mode rather than in Quale. I prove the minor: because the mode of predicating in quid is proper to substance, and the mode of predicating in quale is the mode of an accident; which it seems cannot be denied, since it is an essential predicate. Nevertheless the common opinion of Porphyry and of all his interpreters, that genus is distinguished from difference in that the former is predicated in quid, the latter in quale quid, is true and to be held. It is proved by an express testimony of Aristotle, Topics 4, ch. 6, place 81, where he speaks thus: Since difference always signifies a quality of the genus, but genus does not of the difference: for he who says gressible says a certain animal; but he who says animal does not say a certain gressible thing; difference, therefore, is to be separated from genus in this way. And this mode of distinguishing these two predicables, genus and difference, by the mode of predicating in quid and in quale quid, is followed by St. Thomas, opusc. 58, tract. 1, ch. 4. It is proved next by reason: because genus is predicated of the species by way of a substance, that is, of something standing per se, of which an evident sign is that it is signified by a substantive name; but the mode of predicating in quid is proper to substance, which is the quiddity of the thing; therefore it is predicated in quid. But difference is predicated by way of a form, which is not the mode of a thing standing per se, but of one inhering in matter and determining and modifying it, after the likeness of a quality; therefore it is not predicated in quid but in quale; not, however, as a true quality, because it pertains to the essence of the thing; and therefore it is not predicated in quale simply, but in a certain respect and with an addition, that is, in quale quid; and in this it is distinguished from genus. For the explanation of the testimony of Aristotle adduced to prove the negative part, it should be noted that two things are to be considered in the predicate of any predication. First, the thing itself that is predicated. Second, the mode in which it is conceived and signified, according to which it is attributed to the subject; and the first is as it were the material element in the predication, from which the mode of predicating that distinguishes the predicables is not taken, but from the second, in which the formal ratio of predication consists. Aristotle, then, considered both in different places: in the one whose words we adduced for the negative part he considered the first; but the mode of conceiving the predicate and of attributing it to the subject he considered in the second place, which we adduced for our opinion

[p. 115]

; and therefore he distinguished genus from difference by the modes of predi‐

cating in quid and in quale; but in the other he taught that they are predicat‐

ed in the same mode, which is true on the part of the thing that is predicated,

considered in itself: for both difference and genus are a part of the quiddity of

the species.

To the argument I reply by distinguishing the major: for the mode of being

can be taken in two ways, according to itself, or as it is conceived by us; and

the mode of predicating is taken from it taken in this latter way, because

things are not predicated as they are on the part of the thing, but as they are

known in such a way; and although according to the first consideration differ‐

ence is more perfect than genus, yet in the latter way the latter has a more

perfect mode of predicating than the former, by which it constitutes a dis‐

tinct predicable.

## CHAPTER III

On Species.

1

P     orphyry’s intent in this chapter is to explain the nature of the second

predicable, which is Species. It is divided into four parts. In the first he

proposes two acceptations of species: the first physical and real, from whose

likeness he gathers the second, the logical. In the second he defines species

by a twofold definition. In the third he sets out the categorial ordering of the

category of substance, so that through it the twofold relation of species may

be understood: one which it has to the genus under which it is placed, the

other to the individuals of which it is predicated. In the last he defines the in‐

dividual by two definitions. The first, real acceptation of species is that in

which it is taken for the form and beauty of a thing. In this acceptation it is

customarily said: Praestantissimam speciem dignam esse imperio [the most excellent

species is worthy of rule]; that is, that the most beautiful man is worthy of rule,

because beauty of body is a sign of virtue existing in the soul. And similar to

this real acceptation is the logical acceptation, for species is taken for that which

is placed under the assigned genus, says Porphyry, that is, under the genus already

defined and explained in the preceding chapter. And the likeness of the two

acceptations consists in this: that just as the form of a thing, in which beauty

usually consists, includes and shows in an accidental way the essential perfec‐

tion of the thing, so the species, which is placed under the genus and consti‐

tuted by it together with the difference, includes in a substantial way the

whole essential perfection of the thing: as the human species the whole es‐

sential perfection of man. And this is in the first part of the chapter.

H ij

[p. 116]

In the second part Porphyry defines species, according to this logical acceptation, by a twofold definition. The first definition is this: Species is that which is subjected to the genus, and of which the genus is predicated in quid. By it species is explained according to the relation which it has to the genus, from which it is called subjicible species.

The second definition of species is: Species is that which is predicated of many differing in species in what it is. By it species is explained according to the relation which it has to the individuals, and as it is the second predicable; and this Porphyry does in the 2nd part. In the third he proposes the categorial order in the category of substance, which consists of these five predicates: Substance, Body, Living thing, Animal, Man. But in order that it may be understood, he says three things are to be considered in it. The first is that three things are found in it, namely: the supreme genus, which is a genus in such a way that it is not a species, as substance; the lowest species, which is a species in such a way that it is not a genus, as man or lion; and the intermediate genera, which are at once genera with respect to the inferior species and species with respect to the superior genus. The individuals, however, are not placed in the category as its parts, but as the foundation of all the essential predicates, of which, as of parts, the category is composed. For example: Substance is the supreme genus; Man, the lowest species. And these are as it were the extremes of the category. Animal, Living thing, and Body are called intermediate, because they are genera in such a way that they are at once species: for animal is the genus of man, the species of living thing; and therefore these are called subalternate genera, because they are genera in such a way that they are placed under another genus, with respect to which they are called species; and this is to be at once genera and species with respect to different things.

Second, it is to be considered that the supreme genera are ten, namely Substance, Quantity, Relation, Quality, Action, Passion, Where, Position, When, Having; and since these are as it were the heads of the categories, there are also ten categories; but the lowest species are finite, and in the same way the intermediate genera; but the individuals proceed to infinity, because, whatever ones are given, others and others multiply to infinity; and so they fall outside the science of the categories.

3 Third, it is to be considered that the difference between categorial ascent and descent is this: that descent takes place by the division of one into many, namely of the genus into several species through the differences; but ascent by the gathering of many into one: as when we descend from the supreme genus of substance down to the lowest species of man, we predicate by dividing it into corporeal and incorporeal substance, and this into

[p. 117]

living and non-living, down to man. But when we ascend, we gather several

species into one genus, as man, lion, and the other species of animal into one

genus of animal; and so on up to the supreme genus of substance. And this

Porphyry does in the 3rd part. In the last, since he defined species as predica‐

ble through the individuals, as through the term of its relation, he explains

the nature of the individual by two definitions, of which the first is: The indi‐

vidual is that which is predicated of one alone: as Peter of himself, in this identical

predication, Peter is Peter.

The second definition: The individual is that whose collection of properties,

which is in one, cannot be found in another. Which is explained thus. The specific

properties, such as risibility and wonder, are common to all the individuals of

the human species; and even many individual properties of any individual can

belong to others; but the collection of all that are found in one cannot be

found in another. For example: any individual property of Peter can belong

to John, but all of them taken together cannot belong to him. Porphyry, in

the whole chapter.

## QUESTION I

Whether species was defined by Porphyry with two definitions or three. 4

C     oncerning the number of definitions by which species was defined by

Porphyry, it is certain among all his interpreters that it was defined by

at least two definitions, according to the two relations or respects which it

has: one to the genus, from which it is called subjicible species, the other to

the individuals, from which it is called predicable species. But whether it was

defined by two only, or by three, there are different opinions.

The first is that of Soto, who asserts that it was defined by two only, so

that the first, which asserts that species is that which is placed under the as‐

signed genus, is not a definition but only the logical acceptation of species,

or a bare explanation of the word. But the other, in which it is said that

species is that which is subjected to the genus and of which the genus is

predicated in quid, is a definition; not, however, a twofold one, but one only,

because it explains the same respect: for it is the same to be subjected to the

genus and for the genus to be predicated of it. And since besides this there is

only another, by which species is explained as predicable, there will be only

two. He proves it by this argument. Species has only two respects, one to the

genus, as it is subjicible, the other to the individuals, as it is predicable;

therefore it has only two formal rationes explicable by definition; and there‐

fore it can be explained by two definitions only.

G iij

[p. 118]

But all the others assert that it was defined by three definitions, yet they do not enumerate them in the same way. For Toledo says that only the first is an explanation of the word, but he divides the second into two, so that one is: Species is that which is subjected to the genus; and the other: Species is that of which the genus is predicated in quid; and that therefore, with the other, by which species is explained as predicable, there are three. He proves it because each explains the same respect to the genus in a different way: for it is one thing for the species to regard the genus, another for the genus to regard the species when it is predicated of it.

But Cajetan and Canterus assert that there are three definitions in such a way that the first is not only an acceptation or explanation of the word but at the same time a definition, while the second is only one, because all those words explain only one relation to the genus. And this seems to me the more probable opinion, and more in accordance with the mind of Porphyry.

5 And the first point is proved, that the words Species is that which is placed under the assigned genus are not only an acceptation but also a definition: because Porphyry, when he proposed the other definition, asserted thus: They assign species thus too: Species is that which is placed under the genus, and of which the genus is predicated in quid. By which words he teaches that he is assigning another definition after the first one already delivered. Moreover, before proposing the second definition, he gives the reason why, since he defined genus through species in the preceding chapter, he has now explained species through genus: because, since they are relatives, one had to be defined through the other; therefore he admits that he had already defined species before proposing the second definition; which would not be true if the first were only an acceptation and not a definition.

The second point is proved, that the first and second, by which species is defined as subjicible, are distinct definitions, by this argument. Species, as it is subjected to the genus, has two diverse formal rationes; therefore it had to be explained not by one but by two definitions. The consequence is evident, because one definition can explain only one formal ratio. The antecedent is proved: because in genus there are diverse formal rationes, to be universal, that is, one in many species, and to be predicable of them; and the ratio of universal is prior and essential to it, while the ratio of predicable is posterior, and its proper attribute; and under each ratio it regards the species; therefore in the species too diverse formal rationes must correspond, namely to be the subject in which the genus is, and to be the subject of which it is predicated; so that the former is prior and as it were essential to the species as subjicible, the latter posterior and as it were a proper

[p. 119]

attribute of it; but those diverse formal rationes in genus are explained by diverse definitions, namely one in many species, and predicable of them; therefore the diverse rationes on the part of the species too must be explained by diverse definitions. And so it was done by Porphyry, who by the words Species is that which is placed under the assigned genus explained the subjicible species as it is the subject in which the genus is, but by the second as it is the subject of which it is predicated.

But that the second definition is not twofold but one is proved because the words Species is that which is subjected to the genus explain altogether the same ratio of species that had been explained by the first definition, namely to be the subject in which the genus is; wherefore they seem to be only a repetition of the first definition. But the other words, namely Of which the genus is predicated in quid, explain another formal ratio of the same subjicible species, namely to be the subject of which the genus is predicated. Porphyry therefore delivers two definitions of subjicible species, according to its two formal rationes, and a third of the same species as predicable.

6 To the argument of Soto and Toledo one replies with the same solution: for when it is said that species has only respects to the genus and to the individuals, this is to be granted; it must be said, however, that the respect to the genus has a twofold diverse formal ratio, by which it regards the genus in a diverse way, namely as the subject In which and as the subject Of which; just as the genus regards the same species by a diverse ratio, namely as the subject in which it is and of which it is predicated; therefore it had to be explained by diverse definitions.

But two very brief doubts remain. The first: for what reason Porphyry treats of subjicible species: for since this is a work on the predicables, species does not pertain to it except as predicable; but it is not predicable as it regards the genus, but the individuals; therefore it should not have been defined except with respect to them, and therefore by a single definition, and not by several. The reply is that Porphyry treats of subjicible species, first, because it is the subject of the genus, and the subject pertains to the same consideration as the predicate, because it is the term of its relation, without which it cannot be known. Second, because the subject is opposed to the predicate, and of opposites the science is the same; and therefore species had to be defined by two definitions as subjicible, because it is the subject of the genus in two formally diverse ways.

7 But concerning each of its definitions there is the second doubt: because it seems to belong to individuals, since they are placed under the assigned genus, as this or that animal under animal, and also

H iij

[p. 120]

Peter and John, and they are subjected to the same genus, which is predicated of them in quid, as of the species. I reply that to be placed under the genus, or to be its subject, can be understood in two ways: per se, by reason of itself and immediately; and through another, by reason of something else and remotely. And in the first way it belongs to the species alone, but to the individuals only in the second way. And the reason for this is that genus descends per se and immediately to the species through the differences, but to the individuals only by reason of the species; therefore the species alone is what is placed per se and first under the genus, but the individuals only through the species. The definitions of subjicible species, then, are understood by Porphyry according to the first way, so that the sense of the first is: Species is that which is placed per se, first, and immediately under the assigned genus. And the sense of the second: Species is that which is per se, first, and immediately subjected to the genus, and of which the genus is per se, first, and immediately predicated in quid; and so the individuals are excluded, which are not so placed under the genus, nor subjected to it.

## QUESTION II

Whether subjicible species, as subjicible, is universal, or in what way these relations of

species are related among themselves: universality, predicability, and subjicibility.

T    o understand the question, two things are to be presupposed as certain

among all. First, that these two respects of species, namely predicability and subjicibility, are as it were opposed, since they belong to it with respect to diverse and as it were opposed terms: for the respect of subjicibility belongs to species in order to the superior genus, the respect of predicability in order to the inferior individuals.

Second, it is certain that the respect of predicability belongs to species as universal. This is proved because, as was proved above, universality stands as the essence of the universal, and predicability as its proper attribute; therefore it is true that species, as universal, is predicable, just as it is true that man is risible as he is rational. The question, then, is whether the respect of subjicibility also belongs to species inasmuch as it is universal.

On this there are two opinions. The first is Cajetan’s, on the present chapter, where he says that these two rationes of species, namely universality and predicability, are so connected with the third, which is subjicibility, that this stands as the essence from which those two proceed as

[p. 121]

proper attributes. Whence it follows that species, as subjicible, is universal, just as it is true that man is risible inasmuch as he is man: because risibility proceeds from rationality, as a proper attribute always does from the essence.

The second opinion is that of Cardinal Toledo, q. 1 of this chapter, where he asserts: Universality is the essence of species, and from it proceed two attributes: one is predicability of many, with respect to the individuals; the other, subjicibility, with respect to the genus. From which it follows that species, as it regards the genus, is a subjicible universal, and as it regards the individuals, a predicable universal; and, to explain this opinion in a word, he says that species, as subjicible, is universal, just as it is universal inasmuch as it is predicable.

This is proved by a twofold argument. First: The universal (he says) is a genus to the five predicables, as animal to man and lion; therefore each predicable regards it as its proper genus, whose ratio it participates. But the species are subjicible with respect to the genus; therefore the predicables, as subjicible species, participate the generic ratio of the universal, as man and lion that of animal; wherefore, as subjicible, they are universal.

9 Second: Subjicible species, as subjicible, is not singular; therefore it is universal. The consequence is necessary, because between universal and singular there is no middle. And the antecedent is proved: because subjicible species is not a nature contracted by singular conditions, as is the nature of Peter, but abstracted from them; but an abstracted nature is common to many; therefore it is universal; and therefore inasmuch as it is subjicible it will be universal.

And this is confirmed: because subjicible species, inasmuch as it is subjicible, is common to this and that subjicible species, of which it is predicated in these predications: This subjicible species is a subjicible species, and That subjicible species is a subjicible species; therefore it is universal. The consequence is proved: because the predicable follows from the universal, as a proper attribute from the essence.

Each of these opinions is false. This is proved by this argument. Universality and predicability are respects of the nature to its inferiors, whereas subjicibility is a respect of the same to its superiors; therefore this respect is opposed to those. But one of two opposites cannot proceed from the other, as a proper attribute from the essence; therefore universality and predicability do not proceed from subjicibility, as from an essence, as Cajetan affirms, nor does subjicibility proceed from universality, as from an essence, as Toledo affirms.

[p. 122]

The true opinion, then, affirms three things. First, that universality and predicability are not opposed respects, but are related as essence and proper attribute. This is proved because each respect has the inferiors for its term, although considered in a different way, as was explained in the preceding question.

Second, that these respects are as it were opposed to subjicibility, and therefore neither can they proceed from it, as a proper attribute from the essence, nor subjicibility from them. Both have been proved against Cajetan and Toledo.

Third, that subjicible species, as it is subjicible, is not universal but the common and proximate subject of the genus. This follows evidently from the first two, and is proved by this argument: Opposed respects cannot belong to the same thing under the same formal ratio; but universality and subjicibility are opposed respects, as has been proved; therefore they cannot belong to species under the same ratio; and therefore neither is it subjicible as universal, nor universal as subjicible.

To the first argument of the second opinion, the antecedent must be granted, that the universal is a genus to the five predicables, and also the first consequence, that they participate its nature; but it must be denied that they participate it as they are subjicible species. Rather, they participate it according to their proper essence; and from the participation there results in them accidentally the respect of subjicibility, according to which they are not universal but subjects of the genus. This is made clear by this example. Animal is the genus of man and of lion according to their proper sensitive natures, and in this way they participate its nature and are formally animals. But from this there results in them the denomination of subjicible species: an accidental one, indeed, since it is attributed to them by the intellect; and therefore, as they are subjicible species, they are not animals but subjects. By the same reasoning the predicables, according to their proper natures, participate the essence of the universal, which is their genus. But the proper nature of the predicables is to be second intentions denominating universal natures: that of the first predicable, to denominate a universal nature in many species; that of the second predicable, in many things differing in number, in quid; and so of the rest. Whence in this way they participate the nature of the universal, and are essentially universals; but the denomination of subjicible species follows on them accidentally; and therefore according to it they cannot be universal, just as neither are man and lion animals as they are subjicible species.

To the second, the antecedent must be granted, namely that

[p. 123]

species, as subjicible, is not singular; but the consequence must be denied, that

it is universal: for between universal and singular there is a middle, which is

the common subject, that is, the abstracted nature, common negatively, be‐

cause it is appropriated to no singular, nor does it regard them, but only the

genus to which it is compared and under which it is placed; whereas for it to

be formally universal it is necessary that it be compared and referred to the

individuals.

To the confirmation I reply that subjicible species, compared to this and

that subjicible species, is not subjicible in reality but in name only, because it

is not compared to the genus nor does it regard it; but it is truly predicable

and universal, since it is one in many and of many. Wherefore it is not proved

that, as subjicible, it is in reality universal.

From what has been said in this question three things are understood. First,

that of the twofold respect of predicability and subjicibility, the second be‐

longs to species first. The reason for this is that the first thing species has is to

be composed of genus and difference; and after it has been composed of them,

it is participated by the individuals; therefore it follows on its nature with re‐

spect to the genus before it does with respect to the individuals.

The second thing understood is that the respect of predicability is nobler

in it than the respect of subjicibility, and therefore a nobler denomination of

species follows from it. I prove this thus. The predicate is nobler than the sub‐

ject, since it is its form; therefore the respect of the predicable is nobler than

the respect of the subjicible. Finally, it is understood third that species, with

respect to the subjicible and the predicable, is an equivocal name. This is

proved: because the respects of subjicibility and predicability are opposed and

altogether diverse, so that under the name of species they agree in nothing;

therefore they have only a common name, which is proper to equivocals.

## QUESTION III

Whether a species can be preserved in a single individual, and a genus in a single species.

12

T    hat the question may be more easily understood and solved, it should be

noted that genus and species can be considered in three ways. First, ac‐

cording to their physical and real entity. Second, logically, inasmuch as genus is

predicable in quid of many things differing in species, and species of several

things differing in number. Third, metaphysically, inasmuch as genus is a po‐

tential whole,

[p. 124]

contractible by opposed differences, or a part of the species, composing it with the difference. And according to the physical consideration it is certain among all that the genus can be preserved in one species, indeed in one single individual, and the species as well; and the reason for this is manifest: because the whole entity of the genus and of the species, as of animal and of man, is found in any individual whatever, as in Peter or John.

According to the logical consideration, too, it is certain that the genus is not preserved in one species, nor the species in one individual. This is proved from the definitions of each: for genus is predicable of many species, and species of many individuals; therefore each requires several for its preservation, in which they are equal. But whether the genus requires several actually existing species, and the species several individuals, or whether one in act suffices them for their preservation, provided there are several in potency: concerning species no one doubts that it can be preserved in one individual if several are possible. This is proved by evident experience: because the Sun and the Moon are logical species, and they have only one actually existing individual, yet several possible ones; therefore this will suffice for the preservation of a logical species.

13 But concerning the logical genus, Toledo asserts, in the single question of this chapter, that it cannot be preserved in one actually existing species, although several are possible, but requires several actually existing ones for its preservation. He proves it first by the testimony of Aristotle, Topics 4, ch. 3, where he speaks thus: But since several species are to be placed under every genus, see whether it is not possible for there to be another species of the said genus: for if it is not manifest, then it will not be a genus at all. Then by reason: because the genus is contracted to the species by the difference; but the difference does not constitute the species except by distinguishing it from others; therefore the genus requires several actually existing species. The consequence is proved: because the difference does not distinguish the species from others that do not exist, but only from those that actually are.

This opinion, however, is false. This is proved by this argument. The logical genus is predicable of several things differing in species, even if it is not actually predicated, as its definition shows; but even if it is in only one actually existing species, it suffices that others be possible for it to be predicable of several; therefore it will be preserved in one if several are possible, and it does not require several actually existing. But as regards the logical consideration, the reasoning is equal concerning genus and species, so that each requires several for its preservation, not actually existing, but one in act and several in potency. Concerning the third, metaphysical, consideration, it is first certain among all concerning the genus, as it is a whole

[p. 125]

potential, that it cannot be preserved in a single species unless others are possible. And the reason is manifest: because as it is a potential whole it is essentially contractible by opposed differences for the constitution of diverse species; therefore it requires several, at least possible ones, for its preservation.

Second, it is certain concerning the same genus, as it is an actual part of the species, that it can be preserved in one species even if several are not possible. This is proved: because as it is an actual part of the species it requires only one difference, to which it is actually conjoined; therefore for its preservation it requires only one species, which it composes with it.

But concerning the metaphysical species it is not so certain whether it can be preserved in one individual, or requires several, at least possible ones. On this there are two contrary opinions. The first is held by Oña, q. 2 of this chapter, a. 2, who affirms that genus and metaphysical species are equal: so that, just as the genus requires several species, one in act and another at least in potency, so the species cannot be preserved in one individual if several are not possible.

14 He proves this by an argument. The genus cannot be preserved in one species for this reason, that it is contractible by opposed specific differences, that is, such as cannot be in the same species, as animal by rational and irrational; but the species too is contractible by opposed individual differences, that is, ones not able to belong to the same individual, as man by the differences of Peter and of John; therefore, just as the genus cannot be preserved in one species, so the species will not be able to be preserved in one individual. But this opinion too is proved false by this argument. The metaphysical species, according to its essence, signifies only something composed of genus and difference, and is defined by genus and difference alone; but in one single individual, even if others are not possible, the composition of genus and difference can be saved; therefore the metaphysical species too will be saved, or preserved. The minor is proved: because the individual differences are outside the genus and the difference; therefore the composition of the species from genus and difference does not depend essentially on them; and therefore it will be preserved no less in one individual than in many, and consequently the species too. And this is confirmed: because it is probable that the species of the angels neither have nor can have more than a single individual; and yet no one denies that they are true species, composed of genus and difference.

Our view, then, asserts two things. First, that genus and species according to the logical consideration are equal, so that neither can the genus be preserved in one species unless others at least

[p. 126]

are possible, nor the species in one individual unless at least another is possible; yet that neither requires several actually existing ones for its preservation.

The second thing it asserts is that genus and species according to the metaphysical consideration are not equal; but that the genus, as it is a potential whole, cannot be preserved in one species unless at least another is possible, although as it is a part of the species it can be preserved in one; whereas the species can be preserved in one individual even if no other is possible. Both of these have already been proved from the refutation of the other opinions.

15 But that the truth of the second may become more manifest, and the opposing argument be more easily solved, it should be noted that there is this difference between genus and species considered metaphysically: that the genus is a potential whole, and essentially imperfect, yet perfectible by the specific differences as by other grades of perfection, essentially distinct. As animal signifies a sensitive nature, essentially imperfect, but perfectible by rational and irrational as by diverse grades of essential perfection. Whence it follows, first, that the genus is essentially contractible by opposed differences for the constitution of diverse species. But the species is an actual and perfect whole, so that it cannot receive a further essential perfection (we are speaking of the lowest species, which is a species in such a way that it is not a genus); wherefore it is not contractible by essential differences which are grades of essential perfection, but is only multiplied in individuals by individual differences, which are not essential but altogether outside its essence: for they are accidental, or at most certain substantial modes. It follows, second, that the species is not essentially contractible by individual differences, but without such contraction is essentially perfect and complete; and therefore, whether it is determined by several to several individuals or by one only to one, and whether others are possible or not, it will be a species essentially perfect and complete in one no less than in many; and therefore it will be preserved in that one alone, because determination by such differences is not essential to it, but either accidental or modal, and altogether outside the essence.

16 To the testimony of Aristotle which Toledo adduced, I reply that the sense of Aristotle is that the logical genus cannot be preserved unless it is cognized by the intellect in order to several species, because it is made by the intellect only through comparison to several, nor has it any other being than to be cognized by it; yet it does not require

[p. 127]

several existing on the part of the thing, but it is preserved in one, if others are

possible.

To the argument of the same opinion the reply is that the difference consti‐

tutes the species and distinguishes it from others, whether existing or possible:

for since specific distinction through differences is essential, it does not neces‐

sarily depend on the actual existence of the species. This is proved evidently: be‐

cause the diverse species of flowers are no less distinguished in species in winter,

when they do not actually exist, than while they actually are. The difference,

then, can well constitute the species and distinguish it from others, even ones

not actually existing but only possible.

To the argument of the second opinion, which proceeded concerning the

metaphysical species, the reply has been given from the doctrine noted above. It

is to be applied to its form thus: when it is said that the genus cannot be pre‐

served in one species because it is contractible by opposed differences, the an‐

tecedent must be granted; but the minor must be distinguished: for the species

is not essentially contractible by individual differences, as the genus is by specific

ones; rather, the determination to individuals is outside its essence; and there‐

fore it can be essentially preserved no less in one than in many.

Q U E S T I O N I V.

Whether the last definition of species belongs to those species which can have only one

individual.

17

N      o specific nature is found of which it is certain that it cannot have several

individuals; but concerning the angels and the heavenly bodies many are of

the opinion that they are so constituted that each species neither has nor can in

any way have several, but that all the angels are distinct in species and cannot be

distinguished in number alone, as Peter and John. This question, then, is condi‐

tional and not absolute, and its sense is: Whether, supposing that there are some

species to which it is repugnant to have several individuals, the last definition of

Porphyry belongs to them, namely that they are predicable in quid of several

things differing in number.

But before we propose the probable opinions concerning it, we must refute

what certain people assert without any foundation in reason: namely, that

Porphyry’s definition belongs to these species by non-repugnance. They explain

this thus: although it does not belong to them to be predicable of several inas‐

much as they are such species, not multipliable through several individuals, yet if

they are considered under the common ratio of species, it is not repugnant to

them to be predicated of many: because species, as species,

[p. 128]

is predicable of many. That this is false is openly proved. First, because definitions ought to belong to things positively, since they explain their positive nature; but non-repugnance is only a certain negation; therefore it does not suffice for the definition to belong to them. Second, because if such non-repugnance sufficed for it to be said to belong to these species, it follows that it also belongs to any individual whatever, as to Peter or John. The consequence is proved: because although it is repugnant to him to be predicated of many inasmuch as he is a singular thing, yet if he is considered under the common ratio of man, it will not be repugnant, since man is predicable of many; therefore any individual whatever will be a predicable species, which is absurd.

18 This, then, being refuted: the first opinion is Cajetan’s, 1 p., q. 13, a. 9, in the opuscule On Being and Essence, ch. 5, and on the present chapter, doubt 3, concerning the last definition of species, who asserts that it truly belongs to these species. To explain this, he distinguishes a twofold potency in a nature toward several individuals, physical and logical. He calls physical potency the real one, which it has on the part of the thing, inasmuch as from its own principles it can be multiplied in several individuals, as human nature; but logical the one which it has only as it is understood by us. And because we understand the spiritual natures of the angels through the likeness of material species having several individuals, and we abstract them from that one individual which they have, as we abstract material natures from many, as man from Peter and John, hence it is that we attribute to them the denomination of predicable of several individuals no less than to those which have several individuals.

This opinion, so explained, is proved by the authority of Aristotle, who in the chapter on substance asserts two things. First, that second substances are genera and species, as man and animal, but first substances individuals, as Peter and John. Second, that these same second substances are predicable of the first. But the natures of the angels are genera and species: as spirit is a genus, Michael and Gabriel are species; therefore they are second substances, and consequently they will be predicable of several.

It is proved also by reason: because if the species of Michael cannot have more than that single individual of Michael, it follows that its specific and its individual difference are the same in reality, yet distinct in reason: as specific, it is distinct from itself as individual; because as specific it composes the species together with the genus, but as individual it determines the species already composed to such an individual. This supposed, the intellect will be able to consider the nature of Michael as composed of genus and difference

[p. 129]

as specific, without considering the same difference as individual; and this will be to abstract the nature from that one individual. And so abstracted it will be able to be predicated of it, not by an identical predication, by which it is distinguished from the individual by a formal ratio, nor by an equal predication, because the individual is inferior with respect to the species; therefore by the predication of a superior of an inferior. But the predication of a superior is a universal predication; therefore it will be predicated by a universal predication of the singular, and it will be truly predicable of many, so that the definition of species belongs to it. The consequence is proved: because the universal and the predicable are convertible. This opinion is followed by Canterus, on part 2 of this chapter, doubt 2, and Mercado, single question, arg. 2.

19 The second opinion is that of many moderns: that Porphyry’s definition in no way belongs to these species. And it seems to me more probable and to be held.

But in order to prove it efficaciously, one thing should be noted: namely, that we understand God and the angels through the species or likenesses of material things in such a way that from them we do not form concepts repugnant to them, but proper ones, that is, ones that belong to them alone and are convertible with them. For example, through the likeness of a bodily thing we understand God by removing imperfection from him, and therefore conceiving of him that he lacks a body and is pure spirit; and through a nature composed of genus and difference, removing from him the imperfection of composition, we understand that he is most simple. And in the same way we understand the angelic nature through the species of bodily things, forming a proper concept of it: namely, that it is incorporeal and spiritual; and through the species of material natures, which are multiplied in several individuals, we understand that the angels cannot be multiplied, according to the probable opinion of many. And this doctrine is true: because if we did not form proper and true concepts of spiritual things, although imperfect and through the alien species of bodily things, we would not truly understand them; indeed we would attribute to them many things false and repugnant to their nature.

20 From this same doctrine, then, our view is proved first against Cajetan. Because although we understand spiritual natures through the species of bodies, yet we do not attribute to them the properties of bodies that are repugnant to them; rather, removing these from them, we understand that they are incorporeal. Therefore, supposing that we understand that they cannot have several individuals, as the bodily natures through whose species we understand them have, it is impossible that the intellect should attribute to them the denominations of universals or predicables,

I

[p. 130]

And in this Cajetan is deceived, first, because he thinks that from the fact that they are understood by us through the species of material things, they are denominated by the intellect universal and predicable of several; which is not true, just as it is not true that we understand them to be bodily. Second, he is deceived in that division of his into physical and logical potency: for logical potency, in order to be true and not fictitious, must have at least a remote foundation in the nature, even as it is understood by us; but the multiplication of individuals has no foundation in the angelic nature, even as it is understood by us, since rather we understand it to be repugnant to it; therefore it has neither a physical nor a logical potency according to which it could be denominated predicable of many.

It is proved second: because we understand God through the species of material things, just as we do the angels; therefore, if the angelic nature is universal as so abstracted and understood by us, God too will be universal and predicable of many, which is plainly false. And if you reply that the reasoning is still different concerning God and the angels, because the angelic species is composed of genus and difference, and therefore the intention of universality can be attributed to it, whereas it cannot be attributed to God, because he lacks such composition: this solution is worth nothing, because the denomination of universal or predicable is not attributed to the species from the fact that it is composed of genus and difference, but because it is compared to several individuals. This is proved in the subalternate species, which, although they are composed of genus and difference, are not predicable species but only subjicible; therefore, although the angelic species is composed of genus and difference, it is not on that account capable of the denomination of universal or predicable; rather, that is repugnant to it, as is the multiplicity of individuals.

21 From which it follows that not every subjicible species is predicable (even if it is lowest), but that it can be subjicible and not predicable. This is evident in the subalternate species, which are not predicable but only subjicible; and in the lowest too it will be true, if plurality of individuals is repugnant to them. And the reason for it is that for a subjicible species it is enough that it be composed of genus and difference, but for one predicable of many there is necessarily required a multitude of individuals, actually existing or possible.

To the testimony of Aristotle adduced for Cajetan’s opinion, some reply by denying that the natures of the angels are second substances; but this is contrary to the words of the same Aristotle, which I prove thus: because Aristotle asserts expressly that genera and species are second substances; but the natures of the angels are species composed of genus and difference; therefore they are second substances

[p. 131]

They also contain the superior predicates and sustain spiritual accidents, and therefore they are said to stand under them, no less than the material species; and not only as they are singular, or first substances, but also as they are species; therefore it cannot be denied in Aristotle’s doctrine that they are second substances.

It must be granted, then, that such species are second substances; but it must be denied that the universal property assigned by Aristotle does not belong to them, namely that they are predicated of the first: for this property is to be applied to the single species according to their nature, so that if they have several first substances they are predicated of all of them, and if only one, then of that one alone; which is enough for the truth of the universal statement, namely: It is proper to second substances to be predicated of the first.

22 To the argument, it must be granted that any one of these species can be abstracted from its individual; but it must be denied that, so abstracted, a relation of reason can be attributed to it through which it would be predicable of many: for the very intellect that abstracts it presupposes that several individuals are repugnant to it. Nor does it follow: The intellect abstracts it through the species of material things by which it abstracts other natures having several individuals; therefore, just as it denominates those universal, so too these. For from the fact that it understands them through such species of material things, it does not form the same concept of them as of material things, but a different one, according to the nature of each: so that it understands the former to be multipliable in several individuals, but the latter to be determined to a single one. Of which we grant that it can be predicated, not by an identical predication, nor by the predication of a superior, but by an equal one, in the way in which the last difference is predicated of its species. And the reason for this is that, supposing that the nature of Michael cannot have several individuals, it signifies an order only to one individual difference, even if it is abstracted from it; and therefore it is not further narrowed by it, but in whatever way it is taken it is convertible with it. Such a predication, however, of the same species of its individual, although it is similar to the predication of the last difference of its species by reason of equality, yet, because it is predicated in quid as an actual and complete whole, is rather to be reduced to the second predicable. The species, then, to which plurality of individuals is repugnant are only subjicible; and to them belong the two definitions assigned by Porphyry: for the species of Michael is subjected to its proximate genus, which is spirit, and also to its remote one, which is substance, corporeal or spiritual; but they are not predicable species; therefore the last definition does not belong to them.

I ij

[p. 132]

Q U E S T I O N V.

Whether species is distinguished from genus by those particles of its definition, “to be

predicated of several things differing in number.” 23

T     his question took its occasion from Porphyry, who in the chapter on

genus taught that species is distinguished from genus, because genus is predi‐

cated of several things differing in species, but species of several things dif‐

fering in number. But in the present chapter, and also in the last of this

book, he grants that genus too is predicated of several things differing in number:

because, since it is a superior predicate with respect to the species, as animal

with respect to man, it must be predicated of whatever things the species is

predicated of. Wherefore it does not seem that it can be excluded from the

last definition of species by those particles, to be predicated of several things dif‐

fering in number; nor is there any other by which it is excluded. And therefore

it will not be a good definition, because it does not distinguish the second

predicable from the first.

The first opinion, then, is that of Albert the Great, in the treatise on the

Predicables, ch. 1, who asserts that species is distinguished from genus by

those particles (to be predicated of several things differing in number), because they

are understood by Porphyry in this sense: that species is predicated of the in‐

dividuals through itself and immediately, but genus not through itself or im‐

mediately, but by means of the species. And the reason for this opinion is

that species is per se composed of genus and difference, and therefore

through itself participates the nature of the genus; but the individuals are

not per se composed of genus and difference, but only participate the nature

of the genus because they participate the nature of the species in which they

are contained: for Peter is an animal for this reason, that he is an individual

of the human species, composed of sensitive and rational nature.

This exposition is proved false by two arguments. First: Genus is predicat‐

ed of the individuals through itself, or immediately; therefore species is not

distinguished from it by this. The antecedent is proved: in these predica‐

tions, This animal is an animal, This living thing is a living thing, which are truly

immediate, and not in name only: for the predicate signifies the sensitive na‐

ture in common, and the subject the same nature singularized; but between

the nature taken in common and in the singular there can be no middle;

therefore the genus is predicated immediately of the individuals.

24 Second, because individuals can be considered in two ways. First, as

they are on the part of the thing; and thus there is none that is not contained

under some species and by means of it participates the generic nature; and

therefore they are called individuals of a species, as Peter

[p. 133]

and John, under these names. In another way, inasmuch as they are conceived by the intellect under the grade of the superior nature, without considering the specific grade which they really participate: as if Peter is considered under the grade of sensitive nature, without considering the rational grade which he participates from the human species; in which acceptation he is signified by the name this animal. And individuals considered in this way are called generic, because they formally and immediately signify and participate the generic nature. Whence it follows that, although the genus is predicated of the specific individuals by means of the species, yet of the generic ones it is predicated through itself and immediately; wherefore, when it is predicated of individuals considered in this way, it will not be distinguished from the species.

Therefore the second opinion, that of Avicenna, granting that genus is predicated through itself and immediately of the individuals, asserts that those words of the definition (which is predicated of several things differing in number) are to be understood with a twofold limitation, so that by them species may be distinguished from genus: namely, of those which are distinct in number alone, and of those only, and not of others which are distinguished by more than number. Whence, since genus is predicated not of individuals only but also of species, it is excluded from the definition of species by those words so expounded.

But this opinion too is insufficient. This is proved first: because, just as a definition must belong to the thing defined positively, and not only through negation, so too it must distinguish it from others by a positive difference, and not by negation alone; because negation alone cannot be a difference distinguishing species; but to be predicated of individuals, and not of others more diverse, is a pure negation; therefore it cannot distinguish the second predicable from the first.

25 Second: if it is once granted that genus is predicated immediately of individuals, as species is, even if it is predicated of species, it does not follow that it is not a species, but that it is not only a species but also a genus, since the definition of each belongs to it; therefore it is not distinguished from species by those particles.

For this reason a third opinion holds that it is not distinguished by them considered materially, but formally, that is, under such a mode of predicating as is proper to species: because species is predicated of the individuals completely, that is, as an actual and complete whole, predicating of them the whole essence; but genus is predicated incompletely, because, although it is predicated by way of a potential whole, yet it predicates only a part: as animal does not predicate the whole nature of Peter, but only the sensitive nature, which is a part of it. And in this way Porphyry is to be understood when he distinguishes species

I iij

[p. 134]

from genus by to be predicated of several things differing in number.

This opinion too is proved false by an argument ad hominem, taken from what it grants: namely, that genus is predicated through itself and immediately of the individuals of the genus, as animal of this and that animal. This supposed, I argue thus: Animal is predicated per se and immediately of this and that animal; therefore the sensitive nature is taken in these predications as immediately participated by them, and not by means of some species. But genus is not taken as a potential and incomplete whole, contractible by differences, except inasmuch as it descends through them to the species; therefore neither is it predicated incompletely except of the species, or of individuals with the species as means. Therefore it is impossible for it to be predicated immediately of the individuals and to be predicated incompletely. Wherefore neither can it be distinguished from species by an incomplete mode of predicating of the individuals.

27 These opinions being refuted, ours is explained in two conclusions. The first is: Genus is not predicated of the individuals through itself and immediately as genus, but by way of species; and therefore such predications pertain not to the first predicable but to the second. This conclusion is first to be explained, then proved. It is explained in this way: Genus is not predicated through itself or immediately except of generic individuals, as animal of this and that animal; and in these predications the generic nature is signified as immediately participated by the individuals, and not by means of some species; wherefore it is not considered as contractible by essential differences, and therefore not as imperfect and incomplete, but as complete from genus and difference, immediately determined to the individuals by individual differences proper to it and not to another inferior nature, which are proper to the lowest species. Whence in these same immediate predications it is formally taken by way of a lowest species, and not as a genus; nor is it predicated with the predication of a genus, but as a species and with the predication of a species.

28 The conclusion so explained is proved by a twofold argument. First: When genus is predicated immediately of the individuals of the genus, the generic nature is conceived as immediately participated by those same individuals; therefore as immediately contracted by individual differences proper to it. But to be immediately contracted by individual differences belongs to species, and not to genus as it is genus; therefore in these predications it does not have the mode of a genus, but of a species. The minor is proved: because genus, as genus, is not contracted immediately by individual

[p. 135]

differences, but by specific ones; therefore, when in these same predications it is formally conceived as contracted immediately by individual differences of its proper nature, it is not conceived as a genus, but by way of a species.

Second: That which is conceived as immediately contracted by individual differences is conceived as something already complete in its nature; but animal in this predication, This animal is an animal, is considered as immediately contracted by individual differences of the same sensitive nature; therefore it is signified as something complete in its nature, composed of genus and differences, namely of living and sensible; and therefore not as incomplete, nor as a genus, but by way of a species.

The second conclusion: Genus as genus is not predicated of the individuals through itself, but through the species. This is manifest enough, supposing the preceding one: for if genus is not predicated immediately of the individuals as genus, but by way of species, it follows that when it is predicated of them as genus it is not predicated through itself and immediately, but through the species, and also in a different mode from the species: because by way of a potential and contractible whole they predicate only a part of the essence, whereas species is predicated as a complete and perfect whole. And from these things it is understood that genus was well excluded by Porphyry from the definition of species by those particles, which is predicated of several things differing in number, understood by him in such a way that species is predicated of the individuals per se and not through another, and also completely, whereas neither can belong to genus as it is genus.

29 To the form of the argument of the first opinion I reply that species alone is per se composed of genus and difference, and therefore species alone per se participates the nature of the genus as it is genus, but the individuals by means of the species; but the same generic nature, as it is considered immediately contracted to its proper individuals, is also immediately participated by them, yet not under the ratio of genus but of species, to which it belongs to be immediately contracted by individual differences. Such individuals, however, so considered, do not exist on the part of the thing, but are formally taken by the intellect under the grade of the superior and generic nature.

QUESTION VI. Whether there is one common and real ratio of individuals which is defined by the sec‐

ond definition of the individual.

O     f the individual Porphyry treats in the present chapter because it is the

term of the relation of species, through which species

I iiij

[p. 136]

is defined in the last definition; and therefore knowledge of species depends on knowledge of it. And he defined the individual by a twofold definition. The first, inasmuch as it is predicable of one, through terms of second intention; and for this reason such a definition is understood by the expositors in the manner of second intention. The second he delivered through real properties, saying that the individual is that whose collection of properties, which are in one, cannot be found in another. Wherefore this is as it were the foundation of the first, and therefore it is to be examined by us before that one. And because any definition whatever ought to explain some ratio common to all things contained under the thing defined, as the definition of man explains the ratio of man common to all men, the title of the question asks whether by this definition of the individual some real ratio common to all individuals is defined.

30 And the first opinion is Soto’s, in the single question of this chapter, in the solution to the second, who asserts that nothing real is given which is common to all individuals and is explained by this definition; but that the formal thing defined, and as that by which, is the second intention of the individual, while the material, and as that which, is the real individual, not according as it is common to all, but as it is denominated by the second intention; just as we said in the definition of genus that the generic nature is defined as it is denominated by the second intention.

This opinion has two arguments by which it is proved that nothing real is given common to all individuals that can be defined. First: because individuals have two things. One is the participation of the specific nature, under which they agree univocally, as Peter and John in that each is a man; but this common ratio is specific and not individual; wherefore it cannot be the thing defined by this definition, but is rather explained by the definition of species. The other thing they have is the individual difference, proper and distinct, by which the specific nature is contracted and becomes singular; and through this difference they are constituted in the ratio of singulars, or individuals, and are distinguished among themselves. For example, Peter has the human nature, through which he is a man and agrees with John, and the individual difference, through which he is such a singular man and is distinguished from John; and under the first ratio it is certain that he is not defined, because considered under it he is not singular, but under the second. But under the ratio of singulars individuals cannot agree; therefore nothing real is given common to them which is defined. I prove the minor thus: the individual differences are primarily diverse, and are those by which individuals are ultimately distinguished; therefore by reason of them

[p. 137]

they cannot agree; wherefore they can have nothing real in common which is defined, just as, inasmuch as they are diverse, they cannot agree.

31 Second: Singulars, as they are distinct, are signified by proper and diverse names, as Peter and John; therefore under the proper and ultimate ratio of singularity they do not agree. The consequence is proved: because if they agreed under it, they would have to be distinguished by other individual differences, by reason of which they could also agree, if they agree by reason of those which they now have; and then they would be distinguished by other differences, and there would be a process to infinity.

And the argument can be confirmed in this way: if individuals, as individuals, are real and have a univocal agreement, as abstracted from Peter and John and the rest, it follows that the real atomic species too, as distinct, have a real univocal agreement: so that from man and horse, not only as they agree in animal but also as they are species distinct by rational and irrational, one real concept common to them and univocal could be abstracted; which is plainly false.

32 The second opinion affirms that something real is given, common and univocal to individuals, which is defined by this definition of Porphyry. This is the opinion of St. Thomas, 1 p., q. 30, a. 4; of Cajetan, on the present chapter and on 1 p., q. 29, a. 1; and of Canterus, in the exposition of this definition and in the chapter on substance, in the exposition of the definition of first substance; and many moderns follow it. And it seems to me more probable.

But two things are to be proved against the first opinion, so that the greater probability of the second may be established. The first is that what is defined is not the second intention, or the nature of the individual as it is denominated by it. The second, that something real is defined.

The first is proved: because all the words placed in the definition signify real properties of the individual, through whose collection one is distinguished from another: for although they can agree in many, yet each has some property proper to itself, diverse from the proper ones of the others; whence the collection, which consists of common properties and a proper one, is distinct in each, and by it they are distinguished. Therefore the collection by which the individual is defined consists of real properties, as they are real, and not as they are denominated by second intention. The consequence is proved: because the individual is constituted by real properties before the operation of the intellect; therefore without any order to second intention.

The second is proved by a twofold argument. First: This definition,

[p. 138]

is common to all the individuals of substance, which are defined by it; therefore something common is defined by it, not the word alone: because what was defined would be equivocal, as canis [dog], which, it is agreed, cannot be defined; therefore something common is defined, signified by the word, as real: as has been proved, namely the ratio of real individuation in the concrete.

33 Second: From any real univocal agreement whatever a real univocal concept can be abstracted; but individuals agree univocally in a particular mode of being; therefore such a mode can be abstracted from them, and, as they agree equally in it, they can be defined. The minor is proved: because the particular mode of being, by which human nature is determined so as to be singular in each, belongs equally to Peter and to John. And this common thing is defined. And it can be confirmed in this way: this syllogism is constituted in Darii: Every individual is incommunicable; Peter is an individual; therefore he is incommunicable. But if nothing common is given to individuals, it follows that it is faulty; therefore it must be said that something real common to them is given. The minor is proved: because the middle, namely individual, will be equivocal, signifying nothing common to the individuals besides the word.

34 For the solution of the arguments it should be noted that individuals can be considered in three ways. First, inasmuch as they agree in the specific nature, as Peter and John in human nature; by reason of which agreement each is called a man; and this concept is not of the individuals as they are individuals, but the concept of the species. In the second way they are considered as they are particular and determinate men through their proper individual differences; and this concept is not of the nature but of individuation. This we consider further in two ways. First, as it is of such an individual, signified by a particular and proper name, of Peter or of John. Second, as it is of a singular and individual thing, not determining this individual difference of Peter or of John, but the individual difference as such, abstracting from the determinate ones of Peter and of John. And according to the first consideration they can have nothing in common; but in the second the concept of the individual as such is common to them, by which is signified the individual difference, and not some determinate one, and in the concrete the individual under the ratio of individual, not determining this or that one.

35 Whence it follows that the common concept which we say individuals have is not a concept of the thing or of the nature, but a concept of the mode determining the nature; and under such a concept the individual is defined in this definition.

To the first argument: the major being granted, the minor is denied, that

[p. 139]

individuals, as they are individuals, can have nothing in common. For although the individual differences are primarily diverse, and as such can have nothing in common by their proper rationes, yet they agree in function, namely in determining the specific nature to a particular mode of being, which is to constitute it in an individual; although each, according to its proper ratio, constitutes a determinate and diverse individual.

To the second the reply is by distinguishing the consequent, namely that singulars do not agree under the ultimate ratio of singularity. For the proper singularities of Peter and of John can be considered in two ways. First, as they are singularities. Second, as they are such singularities. And if they are considered in the first way, they agree, because the function of singularizing the nature is common to them; but if in the second way, they cannot agree. Nor is there a process to infinity: because individuals considered under that common ratio are not distinguished by other individual differences, but by the same ones considered under the ultimate particular and determinate ratio; and to these, taken in this way, nothing common is given; and therefore it is not necessary that they be distinguished by other differences.

36 And what we say of the individual differences is to be understood of the specific ones: which, although according to their proper rationes they do not agree in anything but are primarily diverse, as rational and able to neigh, yet agree in the function of dividing the genus and constituting the species. This agreement Porphyry defines in the chapter on difference, saying: Difference is that which divides the genus and constitutes the species. And this agreement of the species, as they are constituted by specific differences, is also modal: because it is not by reason of the nature of the differences, but only by reason of the function of constituting the species; and therefore it is not a middle between the proximate genus and the species, but the nature of the genus descends proximately to the species through the differences, although the differences themselves, and the species through them, agree modally, as has been expounded. But if you ask to which predicable the real individual belongs under this common ratio under which it is defined, Cajetan replies that a special predicable, distinct from the others, must be posited for it, because it has a distinct mode of predicating: for it is predicated neither in quid nor in quale quid, but in cuiusmodi; nor is it an accidental predicate, but a substantial one. It must be said, however, that it cannot constitute a special predicable, because it is not a predicate of the nature, or of any essential grade of it, but of a substantial mode of the same specific nature; and therefore it ought to be reduced to the predicable of species

[p. 140]

on account of its very great similarity with it: because it is predicated of several

things differing in number, substantially.

## QUESTION VII

Whether the second intention of the Individual, defined by the first definition of the

Individual, is one. 37

T    his question presupposes one thing and asks another. What it presupposes

is that the second intention of the Individual considered in common, that

is, abstracted from this and that second intention of the Individual denominat‐

ing Peter and John, predicable of one, is the thing defined by the first definition

of the Individual: namely, The Individual is that which is predicated of one. What it

asks is whether it is one, that is, whether it has one common and univocal ratio

with respect to the second intentions denominating the particular Individuals.

But what it presupposes seems false, as these arguments prove. First: The

second intention of the Individual, considered in common, is predicated of this

and that second intention of the Individual denominating Peter and John;

therefore it is predicable of many. But the definition asserts that the Individual

is predicable of one; therefore it cannot belong to it; rather, the definition of

species will belong to it, since it is predicated in quid of several things differing

in number.

Second, it is proved that it is not one, from which it is also gathered that it is

not the thing defined: because the thing defined must be one, that is, univocal

with respect to all to which the definition belongs; but not every individual is

predicated of one, but some of several; therefore the second intention of the

Individual, which is their ratio of predicating, will not have one common univo‐

cal ratio with respect to all. The consequence is evident: because from that

which is predicated of one, and from another which is predicated of several, a

common ratio of predicating of one, to which this definition belongs, cannot be

abstracted. The antecedent is likewise proved: because the vague Individual, as

some man, is predicated univocally of several, as of Peter and John; and the

Individual by demonstration, as this white thing, is predicated of the same; there‐

fore one second intention of the Individual will be the ratio of predicating of

one, but another the ratio of predicating of many.

38 For the solutions of this question it should be noted that, just as we said

in the definition of genus that the defined is twofold, That by which and That
