40 To the testimony of Aristotle the reply is made according to the exposition of St. Thomas in his commentary on him, and of Scotus, 4, d. 11, q. 3, § ad rationes: where they assert that its proper sense is this, that he taught that a thing to be defined is to be defined in two ways, namely through the supreme genus and all the differences, superior and inferior, down to the last, or through the proximate genus alone and the last difference, and that neither way is to

[p. 169]

be contrary to the other; but that the reason of the first is that the intermediate differences constitute the subalternate species, which are the intermediate genera; therefore, when the same differences are placed in the definition, their formal rationes are sufficiently explained. Which is plain if we define man thus: Man is a corporeal, animate, sensitive, rational substance. And the reason of the second, that the proximate genus formally contains the rationes of all the superior ones; therefore, when the last difference alone is added to it, the whole ratio of the defined is sufficiently explained; and therefore, if after it some one of the superior ones is added, the fault of nugation or of useless repetition is committed, because such a difference is sufficiently explained once the proximate genus is placed, in which it is formally included. For example, animal formally contains living, body, and substance, and all their differences; wherefore, when rational alone is added to it, it sufficiently explains the whole essential ratio of man; and if after rational you add sensible or corporeal, you commit a useless repetition, because such differences are sufficiently explained once animal is placed, in which they are formally included.

41 And from this explanation the reply is made to the first: that the way of defining through the supreme genus and all the intermediate differences down to the last, and through the last alone with the proximate genus, is the same: not because the last includes the superior ones, but because they are formally included in the proximate genus, and therefore, once it alone is placed, they are sufficiently explained.

But when Aristotle asserts that the last difference is the whole substance of the species, they teach that this is to be understood not totally but completively, so that, presupposing the proximate genus, which it contracts and upon which it falls in the definition, it completes the whole substance of the thing. And the third thing which Aristotle asserts, on the division of the superior difference into opposed inferior ones, they expound thus: that the difference is divided not by reason of itself but by reason of the genus which it constitutes as a subalternate species, and which it formally includes; and not, indeed, into differences, but into species through differences: hence neither is the superior genus included in the inferior differences, but in the species, and much less the superior differences in the inferior. And those words of Aristotle, The cleaving of the foot is footedness, are not to be understood as if he meant to predicate the one of the other formally; but his sense is that cleaving is a per se difference dividing footedness, and not a per accidens one.

To the first argument, the antecedent is to be distinguished, namely, Rational is a substance: for if it is taken for complete substance, which is the supreme genus of the category, it is false;

[p. 170]

since rational, and any difference whatever, is formally a part of the species,

and therefore an incomplete substance; but if substance is taken more uni‐

versally, as it abstracts from complete and incomplete, it is true that rational

is a substance, not the categorial one, but one analogous to complete and in‐

complete substances. Hence, to the form of the argument, it is to be denied

that it is a substance which is divided into corporeal and incorporeal, and

consequently that it includes the superior difference.

42 The syllogism which is adduced we grant to be in mood and figure,

and therefore to conclude evidently that the inferior difference includes the

superior; not, however, in the formal sense: nor is this necessary to the syllo‐

gistic form, by virtue of which it is indeed inferred that the conclusion

stands in truth with the premises, but not always in the same sense: as can be

proved by this altogether similar example: Every man is an animal; every man is

risible; therefore the risible is an animal; whose premises are true in the formal

sense, but the conclusion cannot be true formally, but only in the material

sense.

To the second, the major being granted, the minor is to be distinguished:

because genus is not as simple as difference; for since it is a subalternate

species, it is composed of genus and difference; but difference cannot have

such a composition, because, since by its proper ratio it is the last act of the

species, it cannot be composite in any way; nor yet is it pure act, because,

since it is a part, it includes potency for composing the whole, and an intrin‐

sic imperfection coming to it from the ratio of a part.

## QUESTION VI

Whether difference is always and necessarily more perfect than the genus which it

contracts.

ny genus whatever is contracted by several opposed differences of 43

A           diverse perfection, so that some are nobler than others; and of

them some elevate the genus itself to the grade of a higher na‐

ture, while others contract it within its proper grade. For exam‐

ple, animal is contracted by rational and irrational: and rational elevates it to

the higher grade of rational nature, whereas irrational does not elevate it, but

leaves it within its proper grade of sensitive nature. And of the elevating dif‐

ference it is certain that it is nobler than the genus itself: as of rational, that

it is nobler than animal; but concerning the non-elevating differences the

[p. 171]

question is whether they are nobler than the genus, or less noble, or equal in nobility.

And the first opinion holds that not all differences are nobler than the genus which they contract, but only those through which it is elevated to the grade of a more perfect nature; but that the others are less noble than it, or at most of the same nobility: as all the differences of animals, except rational, and all the differences of angels, through which their genus, which is spiritual or incorporeal substance, is not elevated to a higher grade of essential perfection. Certain moderns follow this.

And they prove it by a twofold argument. The first is: because a more perfect grade of nature is the root of perfection of operation; therefore that difference which does not elevate the nature of the genus to a more perfect operation, or at least to a more perfect mode of operating, cannot be more perfect than it; but there are many differences which elevate the genus in neither way; therefore none of them will be nobler than the genus. The minor is proved in the differences of animal, of which none constitutes a species having another operation more perfect than the sensitive, which is proper to the grade of the genus; and also in the species of angels, which have no other more perfect operation besides intellection, nor another more perfect mode of operating besides understanding without discursive reasoning.

44 The second: among the species of animal several are found so imperfect that they lack several senses, as is manifest of moles, oysters, and leeches, and of others always fixed to rocks, which seem to have no other sense besides touch; therefore in these a less perfect grade of sensing is found than in the genus animal, which signifies sensitive nature abstracted from these defects.

The second opinion is the opposite, affirming that any difference whatever is more perfect than the genus which it contracts. This is the express view of St. Thomas, and not only more probable but true. It is proved first by two testimonies of the same: for in 2, d. 13, q. 1, a. 6, ad 1, he speaks thus: Difference is not nobler than genus as one nature is nobler than another, or as one form is nobler than another: because difference implies no form which is not implicitly contained in the nature of the genus; but it is said to be nobler than genus as the determinate than the indeterminate; and in this way to have intellect thus is nobler than to have intellect simply, and to have sense thus than to have sense simply, etc. And 1 p., q. 75, a. 7, ad 2, he says: The last specific difference is most noble inasmuch as it is most determinate, in the way in which act is nobler than potency: but in this way the intellectual is not nobler

[p. 172]

than the sensitive, because it is indeterminate and common to many grades of intellectuality, as sensible is to many grades in sensible being, etc.

45 From these two arguments are gathered for proving the same opinion. The first is: every difference elevates the genus to a higher grade of being, or to a higher mode of being within the same grade of its nature; therefore every difference is nobler than its genus. The consequence is evident: because a thing is more perfect not only because it implies a more perfect grade of being, but because it participates the same grade in a more perfect mode. But the antecedent is proved: because difference has two things in which it exceeds the genus: namely, to be the act determining and perfecting it, whereas the genus is related as a determinable potency; and also to be a determinate and distinct grade of nature, and to imply it in a determinate and distinct mode, whereas the genus, although it includes a determinate grade, includes it indeterminately and as it were confusedly; but to include a determinate grade of nature, and determinately, is more perfect than to include it only confusedly; therefore difference, by its proper mode of being, is always more perfect.

Second: genus is related as matter in the composition of the species, and difference as form; but form always elevates matter to a more perfect being; therefore difference always elevates genus to a more perfect being. And form is always nobler than matter; therefore difference will always be nobler than genus. The minor of the first syllogism is proved: because form elevates matter in the physical order to the determinate and actual specific being which it bestows on it; and in the same way difference elevates the genus in the metaphysical order; but specific, determinate, and actual being is more perfect than the confused and potential being which the genus has; therefore difference is always nobler than genus.

46 To the first argument of the other opinion the reply is made by denying the consequence of the first enthymeme: because, besides elevation to a more perfect operation or a more perfect mode of operating, there is found a more perfect mode of being, actual and determinate, to which every difference elevates the genus; and therefore it is always more perfect than it.

To the second, the antecedent being granted, the consequence is to be denied: for although the grade of sensing is found imperfectly in those species, it is still found more perfectly than in the genus, because it is determinate and specific; but in the genus it is neither determinate nor more perfect, but confused, abstracting from the perfect and the imperfect. But what is determinate and distinct is more perfect than the indeterminate and confused. And therefore still

[p. 173]

the differences of these species are more perfect than the genus.

## QUESTION VII

Whether the second definition of difference can belong to the last differences.

he title of the question presupposes two things as certain. First,

T           that difference is twofold, subalternate and last. The subalternate

is that which constitutes a subalternate species, as corporeal and

sensible; the last, that which constitutes a last species, as rational. It presupposes second that the second definition belongs to subalternate differences, since it is known that they are predicated of many things differing in species: as sensible of man and lion. But it calls into doubt whether it can also belong to the last ones. And the reason for doubting is manifest: because they are not predicated of many species, but of one only and its individuals: as rational of man alone and of singular men; therefore the definition does not belong to them which asserts that difference is that which is predicated of many things differing in species in quale quid.

47 And there is a first opinion, which holds that it belongs also to the last differences; and in order to explain the way in which it belongs to them, it teaches that the definition is to be expounded thus: that when it is said, Difference is that which is predicated of many things differing in species, the sense is: of many things which are distinguished in species either among themselves or from others. In which sense it is manifest that it belongs to the subalternate differences and also to the last: for the former are predicated of many things differing in species among themselves, as sensible of horse and lion; but the last difference, as rational, is predicated of many things differing in species, not among themselves but from others: as of man, who differs in species from the horse, and of Peter and John, who are distinguished in species from the individuals of other species through the same rational. Some held this opinion, whom Avicenna brought forward in the present chapter.

But it is proved false by a twofold argument. First: this definition of difference is assigned by Porphyry in the same way and in the same sense in which the definitions of the other predicables were assigned; but the other definitions, as those of species and genus, are understood thus: that the former is to be predicated of many things differing in number among themselves, the latter of many things differing in species among themselves, as the examples adduced in them by Porphyry prove; therefore this definition of difference is to be understood in the same way; but, so understood, it is plain that it does not belong to the last differences; therefore they were not defined by Porphyry.

[p. 174]

Second: if that sense were to be admitted, so that it belonged to the last differences, it follows evidently that the definition of genus also belongs to species. The consequence is proved: because it is predicated of many things differing in species, not indeed among themselves, but certainly distinct from the individuals of other species.

48 The second opinion is that of Cajetan, in his exposition of this definition, in the single doubt, where he presupposes two things for explaining the sense of the definition in which it belongs to the last differences. The first is that by this definition difference is defined under the common ratio of difference, abstracting from subalternate and last, because under the common ratio it is denominated by the second intention of the third predicable. Second, that the words of any definition can be applied in two ways to those things which are contained under the defined: positively, that is, affirmatively, or else negatively, that is, by non-repugnance; and this definition is applied in each way to diverse differences: positively, indeed, to the subalternate ones, which are truly predicated of many things differing in species; but to the last ones by non-repugnance, because it is true that it is not repugnant to them, inasmuch as they are differences, to be predicated of many things differing in species. Thus the last differences are considered in two ways, namely under the common ratio of difference, and under the particular ratio of last ones; and in this latter way the definition is altogether repugnant to them, but not in the first. For if it were repugnant to them as they are differences, it could not belong to any differences, not even the subalternate ones; and since they are not defined as last, but as differences, it is to be said absolutely that the definition belongs to them negatively, or by non-repugnance.

This opinion of Cajetan is followed by Soto in the present chapter, in the single question, ad 6; for it are also cited Avicenna, in the last chapter of the Predicables, and Iamblichus, in the chapter on difference. And Toledo, in the single question of this chapter, teaches that it is probable, although not according to the mind of Porphyry. Cajetan proves it by this argument: the definition of quantity is that it is divisible into parts, and it does not belong positively to a celestial body, because, since it is incorruptible, it cannot be divided; otherwise it would be corrupted by division; but it belongs to it negatively, that is, by non-repugnance, as it is quantity, not as it is an incorruptible body: because as it is quantity it is not repugnant to it to be divided, although division is repugnant to it as such an incorruptible quantity. And yet it suffices for it to belong to it in this way for the definition to be said to belong to it absolutely; therefore it will suffice that it belong to the last differences by non-repugnance, as they are differences, although it is repugnant to them as last.

[p. 175]

49 But to me it seems to have almost no probability. Hence hardly anyone now defends it. It is proved first: the definition of a thing, if it is essential, contains the essence of all the things that are defined; and if it is descriptive, some proper attribute of them; but essence and proper attribute cannot belong to things negatively, or by non-repugnance, but it is necessary that they belong to them positively; therefore it is repugnant to a definition to belong to anything by non-repugnance.

Second: because, if the definition belongs to the last differences only from the fact that it is not repugnant to them, considered under the common ratio of difference, to be predicated of many things differing in species, although it is repugnant to them as they are last differences, it follows that the definition of man belongs to the lion; indeed, that the definition of any species whatever belongs to the other species of the same genus. The consequent is absurd; therefore the antecedent will also be false. The consequence is proved: because, although the definition of man is repugnant to the lion under the specific ratio of lion, it is nevertheless not repugnant to it considered under the common ratio of animal.

The third opinion, common and true, holds that by this definition Porphyry defined only the subalternate differences, and not the last. So the Commentator, Avicenna, and Alfarabi, whom Albert the Great cites and follows, tract. 5 on difference, ch. 6; Javelli, the Louvain commentators, Soto, Canterus, Mercado, Villalpando, Toledo, and Fonseca, in the present chapter, in the explanation of the same definition. And it is proved from the refutation of the other opinions: because in no way can it belong to the last differences.

But why did Porphyry not define these? Some reply: because he did not know them. But this is false, because it is certain that he knew the last species, of which he made mention in the chapter on species, in the categorial ordering; therefore he also knew the last differences, at least in the common ratio of last ones, although he was ignorant of the particular ones; and in this chapter, and in the last of this book, he said that the last difference of man is rational mortal: whence it follows that he also knew some in particular.

Therefore others assert that he did not define them because he thought they were not simple but composite or complex, as rational mortal is the difference of man; but complex ones do not pertain to the predicables, which must be simple, or incomplex, as we said in the last question on universals. This reason, however, is against the mind of Porphyry, in the last chapter of this book, where, comparing difference with species, he speaks thus: Difference indeed is often considered in many species; but species only in those things which are under the species

[p. 176]

of the individual, etc. If, then, difference is often in many species, not always ac‐

cording to the mind of Porphyry, there will be given with him a predicable last

difference, which is compared with the species.

It is to be said, therefore, that Porphyry defined only the subalternate ones

because, since they are better known to us, we use them more frequently in defi‐

nitions. Which can be proved from a like case: for since property is twofold, sub‐

alternate and lowest, he defined only the latter in the following chapter, because

we use it more frequently in demonstrations. And it suffices to have defined the

subalternate differences: because, since all are predicated in the same way, name‐

ly in quale quid, from the knowledge of these it is easy to know the lowest differ‐

ences, inasmuch as they pertain to the third predicable; it is also easy to assign a

definition common to the subalternate and the lowest, which will be this:

Difference is that which is predicated of many in quale quid.

To the argument of Cajetan the reply is that it is false that the definition of

quantity designated by Aristotle does not belong positively to a celestial body:

because, since it has true quantity, it is truly, per se, and positively divisible into

parts, although actual division is impeded per accidens on account of the sub‐

stantial incorruptibility of the same body.

C H A P T E R V.

On Property.

T E X T O F P O R P H Y R Y.

But property is divided in four ways, etc.

B R I E F E X P O S I T I O N O F T H E T E X T. 1

T    he intent of Porphyry in the present chapter is to explain the nature of

property, which is the fourth predicable. And it is divided into two parts. In

the first, Porphyry hands down four acceptations, or modes, of property. In the

second, he teaches that only its fourth acceptation is proper, but that the others

are common to other accidents.

Property in the first mode is taken for that which belongs to some one species

alone, yet not to all its individuals: as to be a physician or a philosopher is said to

be a property of man, because it belongs to man alone, although it does not be‐

long to every man. In the second mode it is taken, in the opposite way, for that

which belongs to every individual of some species, yet not to it alone, but also to

the individuals of others: as to be a biped, or to have two feet, belongs to all men

from their own nature, yet not

to

[p. 177]

to them alone, but also to certain other animals of other species. In the third

mode it is taken for that which belongs to some species, and to all its indi‐

viduals, yet not at every time, but at a certain determinate one: as to grow

gray belongs to all men and to men alone, but not always, only at the time of

old age. In the fourth mode property is taken for that which belongs to some

species, and to all its individuals, not for a determinate time but always: as

risible belongs to man, and to every man, and also always: because, although

a man does not always laugh, he nevertheless always has the aptitude for

laughing, and therefore he is always risible.

Of these four acceptations, only the fourth is proper (says Porphyry): be‐

cause property properly taken is only that which is convertible with that of

which it is the property; but only property taken in the fourth mode is con‐

vertible; therefore only in the fourth acceptation is it taken properly.

## QUESTION I

Whether property taken only in the fourth mode constitutes the fourth predicable, or

also according to the other three modes. 2

T      he title of the question presupposes as certain that property according

to the fourth mode pertains to the fourth predicable; but it doubts

whether this alone constitutes the fourth predicable, and the other three

modes rather pertain to the fifth, or whether the fourth is made up of all

four modes.

And the first opinion holds that property not only according to the fourth

mode but also according to the others constitutes the fourth predicable: that

is, either according to all, or at least according to the third mode. So Albert

the Great seems to think, tract. 6 on property, ch. 1, and tract. 7 on accident,

also ch. 1; the Louvain commentators, in the present chapter; and in the

same place Canter., whom some of the moderns follow, at least as regards

property in the third mode.

It is proved first: because, although the properties of the other modes,

taken for the act, are common accidents, yet if they are taken for the apti‐

tude or potency, they are proper attributes emanating from the essence;

therefore they do not pertain to the fifth predicable, but to the fourth. The

antecedent is proved in property of the first mode: for to be a physician or a

philosopher, that is, to have some science among these, is a common acci‐

dent; but the aptitude for having them, as for having the others, is a proper

attribute of man, which they are accustomed to call the capacity for learning.

M

[p. 178]

Second: because property in the third mode belongs to every and to only; therefore it is a proper attribute. The consequence is proved: because to be a proper attribute consists only in this, that it emanate from the essence; but emanation is not removed by the fact that it does not always belong, but at a time fixed by nature: because at that time, and not at another, a disposition for such emanation is found in the subject; therefore neither is the ratio of proper attribute, which consists in emanation, removed.

3 The second opinion is common and true. It denies that any acceptation of property besides the fourth constitutes the fourth predicable, but affirms that the three prior ones pertain to the fifth predicable, and that only property in the fourth mode constitutes the fourth predicable. It is held by St. Thomas, opusc. 48, ch. 7; Javelli, tract. 4 on the predicables, ch. 5; Cajetan, Soto, and Toledo, in the present chapter; and it is expressed in the doctrine of Aristotle, in which the definition of property is contained as belonging only to property in the fourth mode. And moreover property according to the other acceptations is said to pertain to the predicable of accident. Both are found in Topics 1, ch. 4: the definition of property in these words: Property is that which does not indicate what the being of the thing is, but belongs to it alone and is predicated convertibly. Of the other acceptations of property, too, he speaks thus: For no one will call property that which can belong to another, nor perhaps that which belongs to it alone for some time, etc. And at the end of the chapter he says: But it is manifest from these things that nothing prevents an accident from becoming a property both when and relative to something; but simply it will not be a property, etc. Property relative to something he calls property taken in the first and second mode, because it is called such in order to other things, that is: because it belongs to only and not to every, or to every and not to only. But property when is the same as property in the third mode: for when signifies time; and since property in the third mode belongs only for a determinate time, it is called by Aristotle property when.

4 No less express is the opinion of Porphyry, in the last chapter of this book, where he teaches that the fourth and the fifth predicable are distinguished in three things. In the first, indeed, because property belongs only to one species, whose essence it follows, and to its individuals; but an accident belongs to many others. In the second they differ because property is predicated convertibly of the subject, but not so a common accident. In the last, because property does not admit of more and less, but common accidents do admit of them. But this threefold difference with respect to accident belongs only to property in the fourth mode.

It is also proved by a reason drawn from the testimonies of Aristotle: Not in the common mode of conceiving and speaking, says Aristotle, is that

[p. 179]

alone called property which so belongs to all that it is not common to others; and moreover, which always belongs to those of which it is the property; but only property in the fourth mode has these two conditions; therefore this alone will be property, but the others common accidents; and therefore this alone will constitute the fourth predicable, while the others will rather pertain to the fifth. The minor is proved: for property in the first and second mode either does not belong to all, or is common to others as well; but property in the third mode never belongs to many individuals, and to all the others it does not belong at least for a long time; therefore it is to be understood that none of them ought to be called truly property, nor pertain to the fourth predicable.

5 And if you say: Why, then, are the properties of the other modes adduced by Porphyry in this chapter? I reply: they are adduced only because they have some likeness and analogy with true property in the fourth mode, from which likeness the nature and essence of true property is better known, and also from their unlikeness and impropriety. Wherefore, if property is taken in common, it is said of all not univocally but analogically: and of property in the fourth mode simply, but of the others only in a certain respect and by attribution to it.

To the first argument, the antecedent is to be distinguished: for aptitude for the sciences is twofold, universal and particular. The universal is called the capacity which man has through the intellect; the particular, that with respect to particular sciences. For one man has a particular inclination and aptitude for one science or art which others do not have, although they do not lack the universal aptitude of the intellect. To the form of the argument, then, the reply is that it is true that property in the first and second mode, taken for the universal aptitude, is a proper attribute; but in this way it is not property in the first or second mode but in the fourth, because it is a property flowing from the specific essence of man; but if it is taken for the particular aptitude, it is only a property of individuals, not belonging to all, although it belongs to them alone; and therefore it is not property simply, but a common accident pertaining to the fifth predicable.

6 For the solution of the second argument, a twofold property is to be distinguished, specific and individual. The former flows from the essential principles of the species, which are genus and difference, as risibility from the proper principles of man. The individual, on the other hand, from the individual complexion, to which the humors and other qualities and dispositions of matter concur. Hence it follows that the former always

M ij

[p. 180]

belongs, because the specific essence is always disposed in the same way; but the individual property need not always belong, because the humors are not in the same disposition: hence it is not called a proper attribute simply, but a common accident. Such is grayness of hair, even if it is taken for the aptitude: which, although it belongs properly to man alone, and to other animals only by likeness to man, as is gathered from its causes which Aristotle hands down in On the Generation of Animals 4, ch. 5, nevertheless does not flow from his specific essence, but from the particular complexion of men, and also from other extrinsic causes concurring in the same men, and in men alone, at the time of old age; therefore it pertains not to the fourth predicable but to the fifth.

7 To the form of the argument, then, the consequence is to be denied, that property in the third mode is a proper attribute simply; it only has a likeness with a proper attribute. And when it is said that it is not necessary for it always to belong in order to be a proper attribute, this too is to be denied: because a proper attribute simply follows from the bare essence; hence it does not vary, but is disposed in the same way as the essence itself; but the properties of individuals depend on other accidental and extrinsic causes, which are disposed in a different way at a different time; therefore such properties are not proper attributes simply, nor are they comprehended under the name of property constituting the fourth predicable.

QUESTION II. Whether property is a universal, or the fourth predicable, with respect to the species or to the

individuals.

F    or an easier understanding of the question it should be noted, first, that prop‐

erty is twofold. One, which follows the nature of a genus or of a subalternate species, and therefore is called subalternate property, and is predicated convertibly of the genus itself, but is not convertible with any species whatever; and therefore with respect to the genus it is adequate property, and with respect to any species inadequate: as sensible is a subalternate property, which follows the nature of animal, with which it is convertible, but with none of its species; therefore it is an adequate property with respect to animal, but inadequate with respect to the species; yet it is predicated of all of them in the same way as of the genus, although not proximately but remotely: that is, in quale as a property, according to the antepredicamental rule handed down by Aristotle in ch. 3 of the Antepredicaments: That when something is predicated of something,

[p. 181]

whatever things are predicated of such a predicate are predicated of its subject and of all things contained under it, and in the same kind of predication, according to all interpreters: as animal is predicated of man and of lion, and sensible of animal, with the predication of a property; and therefore it is necessary that the same sensible be predicated of man and of lion, contained under the same animal, also with the predication of a property. The other property is the one that follows the lowest species, and is predicated of it proximately, adequately, and convertibly; but of the individuals of that species inadequately, because it is convertible with none of them, and remotely, because by means of the species: yet with the predication of a property, because in quale proper.

8 It should be noted second that each property was defined by Aristotle, Topics 1, ch. 4, with this definition: A property is that which does not indicate what the being of a thing is, but belongs to it alone and is predicated convertibly. For a subaltern property is no less convertible with the subaltern species which it follows (as sensible with animal) than a lowest property with the lowest species (as risible with man); although the former is not convertible with the inferior species, nor the latter with the individuals, because with respect to inferiors neither is an adequate property. And when it is said that it does not indicate what the being of a thing is, this signifies only that it does not pertain to the essence but is an accident of it; although a posteriori we know the essence through it, and in this sense it might seem to indicate what the being of a thing is; but the sense of the definition is the former. Each is also defined by Porphyry, when he says that a property in the fourth mode (which alone is a property simply) is that which belongs to all, to it alone, and always.

Concerning each property too, the subaltern as well as the lowest, it is asked whether it is a universal and the fourth predicable with respect to the subaltern or lowest species which it follows, or only with respect to the inferior species or the individuals. And the reason for doubting is manifest: because nothing is universal except with respect to many; but the species which each property follows is only one, for it is convertible with it; therefore with respect to it the property will not be universal or predicable, but only with respect to the inferior species or the individuals, which are many.

9 The first opinion asserts that property is not a universal, nor the fourth predicable, with respect to the genus or species which it proximately follows, but with respect to the inferiors. So the Louvain commentators, on the present chapter; Fonseca, Metaph. 5, ch. 28, q. 19, sect. 2; and several moderns. They prove it, first, because the universal extends to more things than the subject of which it is predicated; therefore if it is convertible with it, it will not be universal with respect to it. This is proved

M iij

[p. 182]

the antecedent: for the universal, by the force of the name, signifies that which is not particular but extends to many particulars; therefore it is repugnant for it to be universal with respect to one particular subject; whence, since the species is one particular subject, the property will not be universal with respect to it.

Second, because the ratio of universal and the ratio of property are opposed; therefore they cannot belong to the same thing with respect to the same thing; but something is called a property with respect to the species which it follows; therefore it is repugnant for it to be called universal with respect to the same. The antecedent is proved: for the universal is so called with respect to many, as its definition proves, that which is one in many; but a property with respect to one only, as is also plain from its definition, in which it is said: but belongs to it alone; therefore they are opposed rationes.

The second opinion affirms that property is a universal and predicable with respect to the species which it follows, and not only with respect to the individuals. This is followed by Albert the Great, tract. 5, on property, ch. 1; Cajetan; and Soto, q. 1 on this chapter; Toledo, at the end of the same; and also several moderns.

10 It is proved from Aristotle and Porphyry. From Aristotle indeed, because the definition which he gives of property does not belong to it with respect to the inferiors, but only with respect to the species; for he says: but belongs to it alone and is predicated convertibly, that is, to the species alone, of which alone it is predicated convertibly, and not of the inferior species or individuals; therefore Aristotle holds that property, with respect to the species alone, is a property, and therefore a universal and the fourth predicable. Porphyry too says that property in the fourth mode is that which belongs to all, to it alone, and always: which conditions it does not seem to have except with respect to the species; and in the last chapter of this book, enumerating the things that belong to the fourth predicable, he says that it is predicable of the species which it follows.

Again, it is proved by reason. First, because the mode of predicating follows the mode of being which a thing has from its own nature, or from the mode in which it is conceived by the intellect; but property, from its natural mode of being, and also as it is conceived by the intellect, regards the species as the proximate principle from which it flows, but the inferior species or the individuals only remotely and through participation in the species; therefore property has the ratio of universal and of predicable in quale primarily with respect to the species, and as it were secondarily with respect to the individuals.

Second, the predicables are ordered to demonstration, as the categories are; therefore the necessary and per se propositions of which demonstration is composed pertain to the predicables; but such are those in which a property is predicated of the species, as

[p. 183]

“man is risible”: they will therefore pertain to the fourth predicable, since there is no other to which they could pertain; and therefore property will be universal and predicable with respect to the species.

11 Our view is explained in two conclusions. The first: Property is not universal with respect to the species alone, but with respect to the inferior species or individuals. This is proved from the definition of the universal, namely one in many and of many; but the species is not many simply, but one, although it is many according to a virtual ratio, by which it is participated by many; therefore with respect to it the property cannot be universal. The consequence is proved: because only those things are, and are called, many simply which are in act many and distinct; but in the species neither are the individuals many or distinct, but one, nor is the species itself many in them, but likewise one; therefore property with respect to the species alone is not universal.

Second conclusion. Property does not have its being such a universal, that is, a property or the fourth predicable, in relation to the species alone, nor in relation to the individuals alone, but in relation to the individuals as they participate the ratio of the species. In order that this conclusion and the preceding one may be better understood, it should be noted that in property, as in any other predicable, two things are to be considered: both the common ratio of universal, which all participate and in which they agree, and the special ratio, taken from such a mode of predicating, by which they are distinguished. The ratio of universal as such, then, requires several things for its term; and therefore property does not have it with respect to the species, as was proved in the first conclusion, because the species is not many simply, but one. But the special ratio of such a universal and predicable it does not have with respect to the individuals alone: because it does not flow from them, nor is it primarily and per se their property, but the species’, from which it flows primarily and per se, and of which it is predicated per se and primarily in quale proper; whence in relation to it, it has per se and primarily the special mode of predicating by which it is distinguished from the other predicables. But because for the ratio of such a universal such many are required, just as for the ratio of the universal in common many simply, property is still not such a universal with respect to the species alone except with an order to the individuals, by which its essential ratio, and consequently the property itself flowing from it, is participated.

12 From this doctrine not only is each conclusion explained, but this argument is gathered by which the second is proved. Property, as it is the fourth predicable, is to be defined thus: A property is that which is predicated of many in quale proper; but it does not have the first with respect to the species alone, namely to be predicable of many, nor

M iiij

[p. 184]

the second, namely in quale proper, with respect to the individuals, except with an

order to the species, by reason of which it is predicated of them in quale proper;

therefore it has the complete definition of the fourth predicable neither from the

species alone, except with an order to the individuals, nor from the individuals

alone, except with an order to the species.

The arguments of the first opinion prove only that property does not have the

ratio of universal as such with respect to the species, but with respect to the indi‐

viduals; not, however, that it does not have from the species, with an order to the

individuals, the special ratio of such a universal, taken from the mode of

predicating.

The argument of the second opinion proves only that it has the same special ra‐

tio of such a universal, or of the fourth predicable, from the species, yet not with‐

out an order to the individuals; and since our view contains both, it is not neces‐

sary to solve the arguments of the other opinions in particular, but from the doc‐

trine noted they will easily be solved by anyone.

It remains only to explain in one word what some are accustomed to doubt:

whether property, as it is the fourth predicable, is referred by one and the same re‐

lation, according to species, to the species and the individuals, or to the genus and

the inferior species, or by different ones, so that one is to the species and another

to the individuals. To which I reply that it is referred by one and the same. Which

I prove thus: A relation takes its specific unity from the formal term; but the

species and the individuals have the same ratio of terminating the relation of

property; therefore it will be one with respect to all. The minor is proved:

Property is referred to the species and the individuals as to the principle from

which it flows and as to the subject with which it is convertible; but the species

and the individuals have the same ratio of principle and of subject, since the indi‐

viduals have both by reason of the species; therefore they have the same formal ra‐

tio of terminating, and are to be taken for a single formal term, from which the re‐

lation of property has its specific unity.

## CHAPTER VI

On Accident.

T E X T O F P O R P H Y R Y.

But an accident is that which comes and goes without the corruption of the subject, etc.

B R I E F E X P L A N AT I O N O F T H E T E X T.

1

T    he intent of Porphyry in the present chapter is to explain the nature of

Accident, which is the fifth predicable. And he treats

[p. 185]

three things in the whole chapter. First, he defines accident by three definitions.

Second, he divides it by a certain division. Third, he replies to a certain tacit

objection.

The first definition of accident is: An accident is that which comes and goes without

the corruption of the subject. As whiteness inheres in a wall and can be separated from

it without its corruption. The second definition is almost the same: An accident is

that which can both belong and not belong to the same thing. The last definition: An acci‐

dent is that which is neither genus, nor difference, nor species, nor property, but inheres in a

subject. This definition is given by Porphyry through the negation of the other

predicables, so that the proper mode of predicating of accident may be explained.

2 The division of accident is: One accident is separable, as to sleep; another in‐

separable, as whiteness in a swan. But someone could object against Porphyry that

the first definition of accident is not good, or that this division is bad: because ac‐

cording to the first definition every accident can be separated from the subject;

therefore none will be inseparable; but the division asserts that one accident is

separable and another inseparable; therefore they contradict each other. Therefore

Porphyry replies in the 3rd part with this distinction: It happens in two ways that

something is separated from the subject: according to the thing, or according to the considera‐

tion of the intellect; and in the first way not every accident can be separated from the

subject, but it can in the second way; and the definition is understood in the first

or in the second way, but the division only in the second way; therefore they are

not contrary.

## QUESTION I

Whether accident is a universal, and with respect to which things it has this.

3

I   t is proved that accident is not a universal by two arguments. First, because the

universal does not have on the part of the thing an aptitude for being in many

or for being predicated of them, nor does it regard its inferiors by a real relation,

but it has such an aptitude only through the intellect abstracting it or comparing

it to the inferiors, to which alone it bears a relation of reason; but accident on the

part of the thing has an aptitude for being in a subject; therefore it will also have

an aptitude for being predicated of it; and since it is really distinguished from it, it

will regard it by a real relation, as whiteness regards man; therefore accident is not

a universal with respect to the subject; indeed, it cannot even be predicated of it,

because what is really distinguished from another cannot be predicated of it, since

a real distinction makes the predication false.

[p. 186]

Second: the universal is said to be in many and to be able to be predicated of many, even if those many do not exist in act in the nature of things but only in potency, as is plain of the Sun and the Moon; but accident cannot be predicated of subjects except of those actually existing; therefore it is not universal or predicable. The minor is proved: because if no man existed in the nature of things, it would be false to say: Man is white, or Peter is white.

For the solution of this question it should be noted first that accident is considered in two ways. First, in relation to its quidditative inferiors, as color with respect to whiteness and blackness, or whiteness with respect to this and that whiteness; and in this way it does not constitute the fifth predicable, but the first, second, or third, for it is either a genus, or a species, or a difference. Second, it is considered in relation to the subjects in which it inheres, as white in relation to man or a wall. And in this way it constitutes the fifth predicable, because it is predicated in quale accidental.

It should be noted second that accident is considered in two ways: in the abstract and in the concrete. Considered in the first way, it does not express the subject but the form alone, as whiteness and color; and since this is really distinguished from the subject, it is not predicated of it, for it is false to say: Man is whiteness. But considered in the concrete, it expresses the subject, as white; and abstracted by the intellect from diverse subjects, as from man and a wall, it is universal and predicable with respect to those from which it is distinguished only by reason; nor does it have an aptitude for being predicated of them on the part of the thing, but only through the intellect; nor, finally, is it referred to them by a real relation, but by one of reason, just as the other predicables are to their inferiors. But because accident regards the subject according to the mode of actual inherence in it, and in this way is predicated of it, it requires the actual existence of the subjects of which it is predicated; otherwise the predications would not be true. And in this it is distinguished from the other predicables, which, since they are essential, as genus, species, and difference, or proper attributes following upon the essence, as the fourth predicable, abstract from existence and are predicated of their inferiors according to the natural connection of the extremes; and therefore they do not require their actual existence.

5 These things supposed, the conclusion answering the question is: Accident taken in the concrete is the fifth predicable, not with respect to its quidditative inferiors but with respect to the subjects from which it is abstracted and of which it is predicated in quale accidental; and taken in this way it is defined by Porphyry by a twofold

[p. 187]

definition, to be explained below. This conclusion is proved: because accident taken in this way is one in many accidentally, and therefore predicable of many in quale accidental, and distinct from the other four predicables.

To the first argument, the minor is to be denied, namely that accident has a real aptitude for inhering or being in many on the part of the thing: for if it is taken in the abstract, this is true; but so taken it is not universal or predicable, but expresses an accidental form really distinct from the subjects and really inhering in them, which cannot really be predicated of them, on account of the real distinction; but if it is taken in the concrete, with respect to the subjects from which it is abstracted, it is universal and predicable, as has been explained.

To the second, the minor is to be distinguished: for in order that accident be universal and predicable, it is enough that it regard several subjects existing according to potency; but for the exercise of predications it requires the actual existence of the subjects; and in the first it agrees with the other predicables, from which it is distinguished in this second, on account of the distinct, accidental mode of predicating which it has; for accident regards the subject according to actual inherence in it, and actual inherence requires the actual existence of the subject, because nothing can inhere except in what actually exists; but of the other predicables the ratio is different as regards the exercise of predicating, as has already been explained.

## CHAPTER II

Whether the division of accident into separable and inseparable accident is good.

t seems to be proved by two arguments that it is not good. First, be‐

I       cause accident according to Porphyry can be separated from the subject

in two ways, according to the thing and through the intellect; therefore no accident is inseparable. The consequence is proved: because an accident inseparable according to the thing is separable through the intellect; whence accident is not well divided into two members.

Second: because if every accident is separable through the intellect, then this division comprehends the proper attribute, which although it cannot be separated according to the thing, can nevertheless be through the intellect, as risible can be separated from man: because, since it is not of his essence, man can be understood without it. And from this it follows that the fourth predicable and the fifth are not distinguished. The consequence is proved: because the proper attribute, which constitutes

[p. 188]

the fourth predicable, pertains to the fifth, since it is an inseparable accident.

For the solution of the question, the distinction is to be noted which St. Thomas gives in the single question On Spiritual Creatures, last article, ad 7, where he says that the operation of the intellect by which it separates one thing from another is twofold. One is simple abstraction, by which it knows that one thing without the other, without affirmation or negation: as when we understand the whiteness existing in a wall without understanding the wall, yet without denying that it is in it. The other is composite abstraction, by which we understand one thing without the other while denying it of it: as if, when we understand whiteness without the wall, we deny it of the wall, saying: The wall is not white.

8 It should be noted second that this is the difference between the inseparable accident and the proper attribute as regards the second mode of abstraction from the subject: that the subject of an inseparable accident can be understood not only without it but also with its opposite, its essence remaining intact; as a swan can be understood not only without whiteness but with blackness, which is not repugnant to its essence. But the subject of a proper attribute, although it can be understood without it, yet cannot be understood with the opposite one; the reason for which is that, since the proper attribute flows from the essence, and it is impossible that the opposite should flow from it, it is also impossible that it be understood with the opposite; but the inseparable accident does not flow from the essence of the subject, and therefore it is not repugnant that the same subject be understood with the opposite accident. For example, man can be understood without risibility, yet not with the capacity to neigh, because it is repugnant that the capacity to neigh should flow from his essence; but a swan can be understood not only without whiteness but also with blackness, because, since whiteness does not flow from its essence, it is not repugnant that it be understood with the opposite blackness.

Our conclusion is that the division is good. It is proved: because each member is truly found in things, is truly an accident, and together they contain as much as the thing divided; therefore it is an adequate and good division. But it is to be understood really, and not through the intellect, so that the sense is: one accident is really separable from the subject, and another really inseparable from the same; and by this the first argument is solved.

9 To the second, the consequence is to be denied: because a common accident can be separated through the intellect by both abstractions, simple and composite, so that not only can it be denied of the subject, but its opposite can also be attributed to it; which the attribute does not have, because, since it flows from the essence, it is repugnant that the opposite attribute should belong to the subject. And so every common accident

[p. 189]

can be separated from the subject through the intellect in all ways, but a prop‐

erty not in all ways; and this suffices for it not to pertain to the fifth predicable.

10 But in order that the nature of this predicable may be better understood,

a further threefold difference is to be noted which it has with respect to prop‐

erty. The first is that a property flows from the essential principles of the sub‐

ject; a common accident does not flow from them, but comes from other caus‐

es. The second: that an attribute belongs primarily to the species and secondar‐

ily to the individuals; a common accident, on the contrary, belongs primarily to

the individuals, and by reason of them to the species. And the reason for this

difference is that a property flows chiefly from the specific nature, but a com‐

mon accident follows from particular individual causes. The third difference is

that a property is predicated per se of the subject, but an accident, which is the

fifth predicable, per accidens.

## QUESTION III

Whether the definitions of accident are understood by Porphyry of the real inherence of

the accident in the subject, or in terms of second intention, of affirmation and negation.

11

I   t seems that they are understood in this second way and not in the first,

which is proved from the same Porphyry, who assigned the last definition

through the negation of the other predicables; therefore he defines accident as a

predicable, and consequently not through real inherence but through predica‐

tion. And moreover, because, in order to explain that the division is not con‐

trary to the first definition, he taught that accident can be separated from the

subject not only according to the thing but through the intellect; therefore

when he asserts in the first definition that it can come to and go from the sub‐

ject, he speaks not of real inherence but of predication.

And it is then proved by reason. First, because accident according to real in‐

herence does not pertain to the Dialectician but to the Philosopher; therefore

in Dialectic it ought not to be defined through it, but through predication,

which is proper to Dialectic.

Second, accidents of reason, such as second intentions are when they are

predicated of first ones, pertain to this predicable, and do not have real inher‐

ence in the subject, but are only objectively in the intellect; and yet the defini‐

tions of accident belong to them; therefore they are not understood of real in‐

herence, but of predication. This opinion is held by Cajetan on the present

chapter, doubt 1; Javelli, tract. 4, on the five predicables, ch. 6; Soto in the ex‐

position of the text; and Toledo, doubt 3, says that it is probable.

[p. 190]

12 The second opinion affirms that the same definitions are understood by

Porphyry of the real inherence of the accident; and this is more probable. It is

proved effectively from Porphyry, who, in order to explain that the first defini‐

tion is not contrary to the division, gives different modes of separation of the

accident from the subject, namely real and through the intellect; which would

not be necessary if the definition were understood of predication and not of

real inherence: for predication, if it is negative, expresses separation through

the intellect.

It is proved second: because accident is taken in the definitions in the same

way as in the division; but the division cannot be understood of predication,

but of real separation, for in the first sense no accident would be inseparable;

therefore the definitions are understood of real inherence.

To the first testimony it is replied that Porphyry defined accident not

through the negation of the other predicables alone, but through real inher‐

ence, which he placed in the last word of the definition. The second testimony

rather proves our view.

To the first argument it is replied that real inherence is the foundation of

the second intention, which it was necessary to explain through the defini‐

tions, so that the nature of this predicable might be better understood.

To the second we say that beings of reason do not have real inherence in a

subject, but are understood by us through likeness to real accidents, which

have it; and therefore we also speak of them as if they really inhered; where‐

fore the definitions of accident are applied to them through likeness.

Q U E S T I O N I V.

Whether the first definition of accident is good.

13

T    he reason for doubting is that there are many accidents which corrupt

the subject, as a lethal disease, burning, and death; therefore the defini‐

tion does not belong to them, because they cannot come and go without the

corruption of the subject.

The difficulty of this question consists in this: whether the things enumer‐

ated in the argument are accidents or not. And the first opinion denies that

they are accidents, but says rather that they are destructions of substance, or

substantial predicates taken privatively. It proves this: because corruption or

death is the dissolution of the principles of life; but the principles of life are

substantial; therefore corruption and death will be something substantial

rather than accidental.

[p. 191]

For the solution of the question it should be noted that death can be taken in two ways: first, for the corruption of a thing in its becoming, that is, while it is coming to be; or for the corruption in its having been made, or already made. And it is certain that, taken in either way, it has at least the mode of an accident, and consequently a subject; and since it is as it were a privative change, it has not only a subject but also a term, as it were the thing made through it. And its subject is the matter, which is changed from the form that is corrupted to the form newly supervening: as from the form of man, which ceases to be in the matter, to the form of the corpse, which newly supervenes. But the term of corruption is the not-being of the thing, as the not-being of the man. And corruption denominates the matter as its subject, inasmuch as it is its change, and also the term, namely the thing corrupted, at whose not-being it terminates; and so the matter is denominated privatively, changed through corruption, as the subject of this privative accident; and that which ceases to be through it is said not to be, or to be dead or corrupted. And just as it is an accident of the matter as of the subject in which it is understood to inhere, so with respect to it the definition of accident belongs to it, because it comes to and goes from the matter without the matter’s corruption; but it does not denominate the term as a subject, but as the term which it destroys, and therefore it is not an accident with respect to it, nor does the definition of accident belong to it.

14 Our view, then, is that all the things enumerated in the argument are accidents, or at least have the mode of accidents, to which the definition belongs in its own way. This is proved evidently of disease, even lethal disease, by this argument: Disease comes and goes without the corruption of the subject; therefore the definition of accident belongs to it. The antecedent is proved: because as long as the disease lasts the subject remains, and when it is absent it also remains; therefore it can come and go without its corruption.

Second, it is proved of burning and death: for these have the mode of a privative change; but the subject is one in many, as Aristotle teaches in Phys. 1 and 5; therefore it is an accident: wherefore they must have the mode of accidents, to which the definition may belong.

From these things the reply would be given to the argument: disease is an accident and can come to and go from the subject without its corruption, because as long as it lasts the subject is not corrupted but remains. But of burning and death we say that they are privative accidents of the matter, to which they come and from which they go without its corruption; yet they are not accidents of the man or of the house, but they denominate the one and the other as terms. As for the truth of the propositions, namely The man is dead, or The house

[p. 192]

is burned, we say that they are true, as the common mode of conceiving and speaking holds, because the sense is: The man has ceased to be, or the house; and it is true indeed, because they are denominated not as subjects but as terms of the corruption, as if it were said that the man and the house have perished through death or burning; for death is called the corruption of the man, because it is the privation of life; but burning is not the corruption of the house, but such a burning.

15 Finally, concerning the ratio of accident, two things are to be noted. The first: accident is taken in two ways, namely for the accident of the categories and for the predicable accident; and this acceptation is more universal, because it comprehends not only true accidents but also those which, although they are substances, yet relate to others in a certain accidental mode, and therefore, on the part of the mode of relating, seem to regard them as subjects: as difference, with respect to the genus, is called a predicable accident, although it is often a substance, because it can come to and go from the genus, its essence remaining intact. But categorial accident comprehends only true accidents; yet on the other side the same accident, as predicable, is less universal: because categorial accident comprehends all true accidents absolutely, but predicable accident does not comprehend them except under a limited consideration, that is, insofar as they can come to and go from the subject, or be predicated and not be predicated of it. For whiteness or blackness, and so of the other accidents, are considered in two ways. First, according to their own essences, as there are in them genera, species, and individuals; and so they pertain to the special categories, and not to the fifth predicable, but to the first, second, or third. In another way, in relation to the subject to which they can come and from which they can go; and so they pertain to the fifth predicable.

From these things a certain quite necessary distinction of accidental predication is understood: for one is accidental from a categorial accident, when what is predicated is a true accident inhering in the subject of which it is predicated. The other is accidental from a predicable and not categorial accident, whose predicate is not a true accident of the subject, but relates to it in an accidental mode, inasmuch as it can come to and go from it without its corruption: as this predication, Man is white, is accidental from a categorial accident and also from a predicable one; but this one, Animal is rational, not from a categorial accident, but only from a predicable accident.

16 It should be noted second that accident, as it is the fifth predicable, is not to be defined through several species or several individuals

[p. 193]

as through its subjects: because, although both the former and the latter are true

subjects of the accident, yet each is inadequate; and so it is to be defined through

that more universal thing which is as it were its adequate subject and, taken in the

plural, the adequate term of the relation of the same accident as predicable.

Whence its adequate definition will be this: An accident is that which is predicated of

many in quale accidental. By this definition, by reason of the last particle, it is

plain that it is distinguished from the other predicables. And let it suffice to have

noted these things concerning the predicables.

Q U E S T I O N V.

Whether aptitudinal inherence is of the essence of accident.

17

I   nherence is twofold, actual and aptitudinal. Actual inherence is a certain mode

through which the accident is united to the subject, so as to be sustained by it;

and it is proportioned to the per se mode of substance, through which it subsists

in itself and per se independently of another. Whence, just as the mode of subsis‐

tence is the ultimate term of a substantial nature existing per se, by which it is

completed and constituted in a supposit, so actual inherence is the ultimate term

of an accidental nature actually existing, completing it and constituting it in act

in the subject. And finally, just as subsistence, presupposing actual existence (not

really distinct from the substantial nature, but through which it is outside its

causes), is distinguished from the nature of the thing from the same substantial

nature existing per se, by the same reason the actual inherence of an accident,

presupposing, in our mode of understanding, the accidental nature actually exist‐

ing, is distinguished from it from the nature of the thing.

The other is aptitudinal inherence, which is nothing other than the aptitude of

the same accidental nature for actually inhering in the subject: as, if God should

separate an accident from the subject, the mode of its actual inherence, through

which it actually inhered in the subject, will perish; but it will still be apt to in‐

here in it; and this aptitude for inhering is called aptitudinal inherence.

And concerning actual inherence it is certain among all that it is not of the es‐

sence of accident, because without it there can be an accident, if not naturally, at

least by divine power; and indeed the quantity of the Eucharist remains without

the actual inherence which it had in the substance of the bread. From which an

evident argument is deduced proving that it does not pertain to its essence; and

since the same reason holds of the other accidents, it follows that actual inher‐

ence is essential to no accident; in which it is also likened to substantial subsis‐

tence, of which it is evident that it does not pertain to the essence

N

[p. 194]

of the substantial nature, since it is certain in faith that the human nature of Christ does not have its own subsistence, but is terminated by the subsistence of the divine Word. Therefore the title of the question asks only about aptitudinal inherence, whether it is of the essence of accident.

18 And the first opinion is that of Scotus, In 4, d. 12, single q., and of Antonius Andreas, Metaph. 7, q. 1, with the other disciples of Scotus, who assert that it does not pertain to its essence, but is outside it. They prove this, first, because inherence is a relation of the accident to the subject, or at least includes a relation; therefore it cannot be of the essence of any absolute accident; indeed, it must presuppose some accidental ratio in that to which it belongs, through which such a relation is founded, and consequently the essence of the accident founding it; wherefore it will be altogether outside it.

Second: if aptitudinal inherence is of the essence of accident, it must belong to all equally, because the things that are essential must belong equally to all of that order; but it neither belongs to all nor can belong equally; therefore it is not essential. The minor is proved: because the mode which the quantity of the Eucharist has, separated from the substance, is an accident, since it terminates an accidental nature; and the aptitude for inhering is repugnant to it, since it is a mode of being per se and independently of the subject; therefore it does not belong to all accidents; nor yet equally, because then it would belong to them univocally, which we shall see is false.

The second opinion is the common and true one: that aptitudinal inherence is of the essence of accident. So St. Thomas, In 4, d. 18, q. and a. 1, q. also 1; Capreolus, In 4, d. 2, q. 1, ad 1 against the 5th and 6th conclusions; Hervaeus, Quodlibet 4, q. 9; Javelli, Metaph. 7, q. 1; Cajetan, On Being and Essence, ch. 7, q. 15. And it is gathered evidently from the doctrine of Aristotle, Metaph. 7, text 2, where he asserts that accidents are not beings, but beings of a being, that is, of substance, to which in their entity they bear an attribution; but to be beings of substance is to be able to affect it according to their own intrinsic modes; therefore the aptitude for inhering in it is essential to them, according to the mind of Aristotle.

19 It is proved also by reason: because to be per se and to be in another are the intrinsic modes of substance and accident, dividing being per se; but to be per se according to aptitude, that is, to be apt to subsist per se, is of the essence of substance; therefore to be apt to inhere in the same substance will be of the essence of accident. The minor is proved: because for substance to be such an entity that subsistence per se is due to it is essential to it; and this is for it to be essential to it to be the root from which subsistence arises; therefore it is also essential to accidents to be such a nature that there is due to it

[p. 195]

actual inherence in a subject: that is, to be the root of actual inherence; and this root is aptitudinal inherence, which will therefore also be essential to it.

To the first argument, the major is to be denied, namely that actual inherence is a relation; rather it is an absolute mode including a certain transcendental respect, of which the minor is to be denied, namely that it cannot be of the essence of an absolute thing, just as the other transcendental predicates, as we shall see in the category of Relation; where we shall prove that, although categorial relation, which is called relation secundum esse, cannot pertain to the essence of an absolute thing, yet transcendental respects, or respects secundum dici, necessarily pertain to the essence of many absolute things.

To the second, the first consequence is to be denied, namely that aptitudinal inherence belongs equally to all accidents, or univocally: for since it belongs to them through attribution to substance, or is itself the attribution to substance, it cannot belong to them univocally, because attribution is repugnant to univocation. And moreover, it belongs to each according to its own mode of attribution to substance, which suffices to constitute analogy, as we shall show in the Antepredicaments, ch. 2. But as for the per se mode of the quantity of the Eucharist, it is not certain that it has it, but it is probable that it is sustained immediately by God; and even if it be said to have it, it is not an accidental nature to which actual inherence is due, but a mode to which it is not due per se; just as to actual inherence another inherence is not due, otherwise there would be a process to infinity; but since it is the ratio or mode of inhering, it is not properly said to inhere. Nor is inherence due to that mode of per se being of quantity, because it is not an accidental nature, but a certain modal entity supernaturally granted to the accident, so that it may be per se, that is, without actual dependence on substance; which entity is accidental, because it gives the accident a mode of being. And so aptitudinal inherence belongs per se only to the accidental nature, just as actual inherence is due to it alone; but it does not belong to the modes per se, but by reason of the nature whose modes they are; just as neither do they inhere per se, but by reason of the nature; and since that mode is neither an accidental nature nor a mode belonging per se to the accident from its own nature, actual inherence is in no way due to it, nor will aptitudinal inherence be essential to it.

N ij

[p. 196]

## COMMENTARIES ON THE BOOK

O F T H E C AT E G O R I E S O F A R I S T O T L E

the Stagirite, which they have been accustomed to call the Predicaments, to‐

gether with the Doubts and Questions customarily debated in our time.

B R I E F P RO E M .

On the title of this book.

lthough the Greek word Categoria, from its first imposition, is 1

A          so called from predication or from the predicate, yet by the com‐

mon consent of Dialecticians and Philosophers it is now taken

for the entire ordering of essential predicates; and the same is the significa‐

tion of predicament, which we can describe thus: A predicament is the arrange‐

ment of essential predicates, superior and inferior, under some one supreme genus, than

which nothing is higher, down to the individual, than which nothing is lower.

Whence this work is entitled the book of the Categories or Predicaments:

that is, the book of the orderings by which predicates are arranged according

to the different grades of being, from the supreme genus, which is as it were

the head of the whole ordering, down to the lowest species and individuals.

On the inventor of the categorial art.

T     he common consent of the school now holds that the first inventor of

this art was Aristotle. For he was the first who taught how to arrange all

the grades of being in such a way that all the things of the world might be re‐

duced to certain definite classes, and that we might easily find the nature and

essence of anything by recurring to its proper category or predicament.

On the end of this work.

S  ince the categories are made from simple or incomplex things, it is plain

that they pertain to the first operation of the intellect, which is the ap‐

prehension of simples, and that they are ordered, for specifying the second,

which is concerned with composition and division,

[p. 197]

proximately; but as to their ultimate end, to Demonstration, to which it is estab‐

lished that all the things treated in Dialectic are ordered.

Whether the categories treat of words or of things.

B   y all is refuted the opinion of the Nominalists, who said that this work, like

the whole science of Dialectic, treats principally of words. Which is proved

false from this: because words are only instruments which we use in place of

things, since we are unable to bring the things that are disputed about into the

schools, as Aristotle teaches in Sophistical Refutations 1. It is things, therefore,

from which the categorial ordering is constituted, signified by means of words;

and therefore the categorial art treats principally of things, and less principally

of words, as of necessary conditions.

On the object of this work.

T    he object of this part of Dialectic is the category or predicament consid‐

ered in common, as it comprehends under itself all the categorial orderings.

Which is proved from this: because under it are proximately contained all the

things treated in this art, and they proximately participate its ratio; which two

are the proper conditions of an object.

On the mode of proceeding, and on the ordering of this work with the other parts of

Dialectic.

2

T    he mode of proceeding which Aristotle observes in this work is simple, be‐

cause he proceeds by definition and division, through which he teaches in

what way simples are to be ordered in the categories.

As for the order of this work among the other parts of Dialectic, it must be

explained thus: that it holds the first place among them all, because the ordering

of simples, and the ordered cognition of them, is as it were the door through

which we enter the remaining parts of Dialectic and the whole science itself.

To which science it pertains to treat of the categories.
