A    lthough some assert that the categorial art pertains to no determinate sci‐

ence, but that the intellect

N iij

[p. 198]

through the natural light, without any intermediate science, can have cognition of

this art, and that it therefore pertains neither to Dialectic nor to Metaphysics;

nevertheless, since the orderings of predicates cannot be made without an art or

science, it must necessarily be said that it pertains to a science, and first of all to

Metaphysics. The reason for this is sufficiently manifest and known per se: be‐

cause Metaphysics treats of the most universal real being; therefore it pertains to

it to consider all the modes of real being according to its proper ratio of abstract‐

ing from matter; but the categories are nothing other than orderings of things,

from which we know the proper modes of being; therefore this art of ordering

things according to the different modes of being will pertain properly to

Metaphysics; and also to Dialectic, but under a different ratio: for to the former

according to their proper entities, but to Dialectic in relation to predications,

enunciations, and syllogisms.

## CHAPTER I

On Equivocals, Univocals, and Denominatives.

## TEXT OF ARISTOTLE

Those things are called equivocal whose name alone is common, but the ratio of substance ac‐

cording to the name is different.

E X P O S I T I O N O F T H E T E X T.

3

T    he intent of Aristotle in this first chapter is to explain the nature of

Equivocal, Univocal, and Denominative names: for since the categories are

made from things as they are signified by words, the distinction of the things that

are to be placed in a category depends chiefly on the mode of signifying of words;

and so, from the application of these three words, three other things will be estab‐

lished. First, which things are to be excluded from the categories. Second, from

which things the categories are to be constituted. Third, in what way the things of

one category can be predicated of the things of another.

And the chapter is divided into three parts, in the first of which Aristotle pro‐

poses the definition of Equivocals; in the second, the definition of Univocals; and

in the third, the definition of Denominatives.

The definition of Equivocals is this: Those things are called equivocal whose name is

common, but the ratio of substance accommodated to the name is different. Which contains

two parts. In the first it is said that equivocals must have a common name, so that

it may be signified

[p. 199]

that they are distinct from that same name and are the things signified by it: as

the barking dog, the heavenly constellation, and the sea fish, which are the things

signified by this name canis [dog]; these are indeed distinct from it, but they are

not called equivocals except as they are signified by the name, because things do

not pertain to Dialectic except as they are signified by words.

And from this is taken that common distinction by which equivocals are dis‐

tinguished into equivocated equivocals and equivocating equivocals: so that

equivocated equivocals are the things which, as they are signified by such a name,

are said to become equivocal in it; but equivocating equivocals are the words

themselves, which, from such a mode of signifying, make the things equivocal.

4 The second part of the definition is the one in which it is said that the ratio of

substance accommodated to the equivocal name is different. By ratio is understood the

definition, or the quidditative concept in those things which do not have a defini‐

tion. The definition, therefore, or the concept of equivocals, as they are signified

by the equivocal name, must be altogether different, so that they in no way agree

in it, but have only the name in common.

The definition of Univocals is this: Those things are called univocal whose name

is common, and the ratio of substance according to the name is the same. In which by the

ratio of substance is understood the definition or concept of univocals, which

must be the same and not different, as we said it is different in equivocals.

The definition of Denominatives runs thus: Those things are called denominative

which, differing only in case, have their appellation according to the name from something:

as from fortitudo [courage], fortis [courageous]. In which three things are contained,

because in denomination there are three: the denominating form, the thing de‐

nominated, and the denominative name; to be understood in such an order that

the thing denominated is called such from the denominative name, and this is

called denominative from the form; and so the form is as it were the origin of the

whole denomination. For example: courageous is a denominative name, in which

the thing denominated is Peter himself; but the form from which he is denomi‐

nated is courage. From which the denominative name itself must differ in case, so

that the derivation of that denomination which the thing denominated receives

from the form may be signified.

## SINGLE QUESTION

Whether the definition of univocals belongs to denominatives.

5

T    he first opinion holds that denominatives are at the same time univocals, but

under a different ratio: for insofar as they have their appellation

N4

[p. 200]

from another, they are called denominatives; but in relation to the things denominated, of which they are predicated, they are truly univocal: as white, with respect to whiteness, from which it is denominated, is called denominative; but with respect to this and that body, namely a wall and a man, of which it is predicated, it is univocal; wherefore the definition of univocals belongs to all denominatives. So Soto, in the single question on this chapter, ad 2. Which opinion Cajetan says is probable, in the exposition of the definition of denominatives. And it seems to be proved from the definition of univocals: because the denominative name is common to all the subjects of which it is said, as white to man and to a wall; and the ratio signified, which is the accidental form, is also the same in them, as whiteness in the same; therefore the whole definition belongs to them.

And it can be proved second: because every universal must be univocal, as we said in the last question on universals; but among the universals, the fourth and fifth predicables are denominatives, as risible and white prove; therefore denominatives are univocal, and the definition of univocals truly and properly belongs to them.

The second opinion is that of Toledo, who, although he seems altogether to deny that denominatives are univocal, nevertheless asserts one thing from which the contrary seems to be gathered: namely, that that particle of the definition of univocals (ratio of substance) is understood of the quidditative or of the descriptive definition, so that it suffices for the ratio of a univocal that the descriptive definition be the same in all the univocates. From which it is gathered that the names of proper attributes, as sensible or risible, are univocal with respect to the subjects of which they are predicated, as sensible with respect to man and horse.

6 Our view, however, is that the definition of univocals in no way belongs to denominatives. So holds Cajetan on the present chapter, and it is the express opinion of Aristotle in the chapter on substance, where he asserts that denominatives are not predicated of their subjects in name and in ratio: because the form signified by the name is not in them quidditatively, but accidentally.

And it is proved by reason: because in the definition of univocals it is said (whose name is common, and the ratio of substance the same); but by the ratio of substance all understand either the quidditative definition or the quidditative concept, which properly pertain to the substance of the thing; but this is not found in denominatives: because the thing signified by them is neither the quidditative definition with respect to the inferiors nor their quidditative concept, but an accidental form; therefore they are not univocal.

To the first argument, the minor is to be distinguished: for the ratio signified

[p. 201]

by the name can be common in two ways: either as the same in the inferiors

essentially, or accidentally. And in the first way it must be common for the

name to be univocal; for this is what Aristotle means by those words (the ratio

of substance accommodated to the name) in the definition of univocals, because

the ratio of substance is the same as the essential ratio. But the significate of

denominatives is common and one in the inferiors only accidentally; and

therefore the definition of univocals cannot belong to them.

7 The second argument is solved by another distinction. Univocal is taken

in two ways: properly, for that of which not only the name is common to the

univocates, but also the definition or quidditative concept; and only this did

Aristotle define in the present chapter. The other is improper univocal,

whose significate is common to the inferiors only accidentally; and in this

way, improperly, denominatives can be called univocal. And although this

does not suffice for the definition of univocals to belong to them, it does suf‐

fice for them to be universals and predicables: for to the ratio of universal it

suffices that something be univocal only as it is distinguished against the

equivocal and the analogous, which denominatives have through an improper

univocation.

T R E AT I S E O N T H E A N A L O G Y

## OF NAMES

he treatment of the nature and ratio of analogy pertains for the 8

T           most part to Metaphysics, since it is found chiefly in being taken

most universally, which is its proper object, and also in its attrib‐

utes, and in accident, a name common to the categories. But it

pertains properly to Logic in order that from it we may know that analogous

terms are to be excluded from the categories, and also from syllogisms and

other argumentations, which can conveniently be made only in univocal

terms. Aristotle, however, did not define analogous terms in the present

chapter, but only equivocal and univocal ones: because, since analogous

terms are as it were midway between these extremes, once univocals and

equivocals are known it is easy to know analogous ones. Concerning these

only five things are to be disputed. First, what analogy is. Second, how mani‐

fold it is. Third, whether the analogous term can be abstracted or prescinded

from the analogates. 4. Whether being is analogous with respect to God and

creatures, and to created beings, substantial and accidental; and by what

analogy it signifies all these. 5. Whether accident, with respect to the nine

categories of accidents, is analogous or univocal.

[p. 202]

It is explained what analogy is.

9

I   f we wish to define analogy from the very signification of the name, we

shall have to say that it is nothing other than a proportion, or agreement, or

comparison among many things signified by the same name. For it is a Greek name,

which Quintilian, rendering it in Latin, calls proportion; while Cicero in one

place calls it agreement, and in another comparison, or proportion. And all these

significations can belong to different analogous terms, or to the same ones

under different consideration, as will be able to appear when we enumerate

the different species of analogy.

But if we consider rather the thing signified by the name of analogy than

the etymology of the same name, we can easily gather the definition of anal‐

ogous terms from the definitions of equivocals and univocals assigned by

Aristotle in the present chapter. For analogous terms, according to the com‐

mon opinion of the school, are something midway between equivocals and

univocals. Now Aristotle defines equivocals thus: Those whose name is common,

but the ratio of substance accommodated to the name is altogether different: as dog,

with respect to the barking animal, the fish, and the heavenly star. Univocals: those

whose name is common, but the ratio of substance accommodated to the name is alto‐

gether the same. Analogous terms, therefore, will be those whose name is common,

but the ratio of substance accommodated to the name is neither altogether different nor

altogether the same. According to this, analogous terms participate in both ex‐

tremes: for they agree with equivocals and univocals in the name, which

must be common in all of them; but in the thing or concept signified by the

name they partly agree and partly differ. They agree with equivocals in this,

that it must be different simply; and in this they differ from univocals, in

which it must be the same simply. But they differ from the same equivocals

in this, that it is not altogether different, but in some way one or the same;

and in this they resemble univocals. From which it follows that they have

greater similarity with equivocals. And this is the reason why they are cus‐

tomarily enumerated with equivocals, and are even called equivocal: because

they are distinguished from them only a little.

10 Thus the concept of the analogous term, as regards the things signi‐

fied, is not one but several, because the analogates are different; yet by rea‐

son of proportion, or attribution, or proportionality, they have a certain sim‐

ilarity, and by reason of it some unity; and this is for the ratio of substance

accommodated to the name to be neither altogether different nor altogether

the same, but proportional or similar.

[p. 203]

How manifold analogy is.

11

C      ajetan, in the opuscule On the Analogy of Names, ch. 1, 2 and 3, distin‐

guishes a threefold analogy. The first, of Inequality, which is found in

genera with respect to their species, by which, by reason of the differences,

they are participated according to an inequality of perfection: as in animal

with respect to man and lion; for it is participated more perfectly by man, by

reason of the more perfect difference, and therefore unequally by the two.

But he says that this analogy is not such simply, nor does it make a name

analogous, because it is found in truly univocal genera; and it can only be

called physical analogy, because it proceeds from different physical forms of

greater and lesser perfection.

The second species of analogy is that of Proportion of one to another, or

of several to one; and this is also called analogy of Attribution, because the

proportion that one has to another, or many to one, is a certain relation to it,

which is also called attribution. Thus healthy is called an analogous term of

proportion and attribution, because it is said of urine and medicine accord‐

ing to the proportion they have with the health of the animal, inasmuch as

urine is a sign of health and medicine a cause; and this is to be said by attri‐

bution to it. Wherefore healthy, with respect to animal, urine, and medicine,

is called an analogous term of proportion or attribution.

12 The third species of analogy is that of Proportionality. Proportionality

is nothing other than the similarity or proportion of two proportions. For

example: between three and six there is found a double proportion, and the

same is found between four and eight; then between these two double pro‐

portions there is found another proportion or similarity, consisting in this,

that as three is to six, so four is to eight. This proportion and similarity of

two proportions, therefore, is called proportionality. And therefore the name

that signifies several things among which it is found is called an analogous

term of proportionality. Thus laughter signifies the true laughter of man and

the as it were metaphorical laughter of a meadow, which, when it flowers,

shows a certain cheerfulness similar to that which a man shows when he

laughs. Now the name laughter is said of both, namely of the laughing man

and of the flowering meadow, according to proportionality: because as the

laughter of a man is to the man, so the floweriness of the meadow is to the

meadow. Wherefore it is called an analogous term of proportionality.

Of these three species of analogy, the first is reputed by no one to be true,

nor sufficient to constitute an analogous name; but all say that it is not analo‐

gy simply, but only

[p. 204]

in a certain respect. And the reason of all is that it is found in genera and in many other univocals without prejudice to univocation.

13 But the analogy of proportion, or of attribution, all receive as true and sufficient to constitute an analogous name. And the reason is manifest: because attribution alone, of one to another or of many to one, brings it about that not all are signified in the same way or equally, but that the one is called such simply, while the others are not, except in a certain respect; therefore attribution alone makes a name analogous. The consequence is proved from the definition of analogous terms: Analogous terms are those whose name is common, but the ratio of substance is neither altogether the same nor altogether different; but by the very fact that the significates are so related that all are said by attribution to one, the ratio under which they are signified belongs to that one first, per se, and principally, and to the others by attribution to it; therefore it is not altogether the same in all: because if it were the same, it would belong to each one equally first and without dependence on the others, as is plain in univocals. Wherefore it is necessary to say that attribution alone produces analogy.

Second, attribution alone takes away univocation; therefore it alone makes a name analogous. The consequence is evident: because where there is attribution of the significates there is no equivocation of the name, since something is common to them besides the name, namely that similarity and correspondence which attribution produces. If, therefore, attribution takes away univocation, it must make the name analogous, because no middle is given between univocal and equivocal besides the analogous. Moreover, the first antecedent is proved from the definition of univocals: Univocals are those whose name is common, but the ratio of substance accommodated to the name is altogether the same; but attribution brings it about that the ratio is not altogether the same, nor equally participated by all, but first by one, and by the rest with dependence on it; therefore it takes away univocation.

14 But concerning the analogy of proportionality it is not certain that it is such simply, so that it alone suffices to make a name analogous. The first opinion holds that it is sufficient, no less than the analogy of attribution. So Cajetan in the place cited above; so also St. Thomas seems to think, On Truth, q. 2, a. 11; so, finally, many moderns.

The second opinion is that of other moderns, who use this distinction. Proportionality can be found among the significates of a name in two ways. First, such that it is not itself signified by that name, but another ratio common to them; and taken in this way it does not suffice to make a name analogous

[p. 205]

That it is not signified by the name seems manifest: because animal signifies only the sensitive nature common to the species, not the proportionality found among them.

15 Second, such that the analogy itself is signified by the name; and this will be sufficient to constitute that name analogous. And because no name has been imposed by which it is signified, no such analogy is given; it would be given, however, if a name were imposed to signify it. Of which they do not bring a reason or an example. But we can bring both: an example, indeed, in this name principle, which is said analogically of the foundation of a house, of the point, which is the principle of a line, and of the premises of a demonstration known per se; and among these there is no attribution, but all are signified equally and per se; only proportionality is found: because as the foundation of a house is to the house that begins from it, so the point is to the line, and the principles of a demonstration to the demonstration. And because it is signified by the name (since they seem to signify those three by reason of proportionality, and not by reason of another concept common to them), it suffices to constitute analogy.

It can also be proved by reason: because proportionality necessarily presupposes that the things among which it is found are different, but that they receive from it some similarity and unity; therefore it brings it about that the ratio signified by the name is not altogether different, but not altogether the same either, because there is some similarity and unity in it. Wherefore it alone will make a name analogous.

16 The third opinion holds that proportionality, found in whatever way among the significates of the same name, does not suffice to constitute an analogous name; but it is necessary that it be found in such a way that one of them is absolutely such through its form or through its being, while the other is not absolutely such through its being, but as it underlies such a proportion or comparison to another. An example can be in laughter, which signifies the laughter of man and the floweriness of the meadow in such a way that the former is absolutely such through its own being, but the latter not, except inasmuch as it has such a proportion or proportionality with it. For it is manifest that the floweriness of the meadow neither is nor is called laughter except through its order to the laughter of man. So thinks Father Francisco Suárez, vol. 2 of his Metaph., disp. 28, sect. 3, no. 11.

Our view is explained in three conclusions. The first is: Proportionality is not true analogy, nor does it suffice to make a name analogous, unless it is signified by it. This seems to me evident, as this argument proves. Things do not have analogy, or

[p. 206]

univocation except inasmuch as they are signified by words; therefore neither are they analogous terms of proportion or attribution except inasmuch as they are signified as having it. Of which there is an evident sign: that, because they are signified in different ways by different words, it can happen that they are signified equivocally by one and univocally by another. Thus dog, the barking beast, the fish, and the star are signified equivocally by the name dog, and the same are designated univocally by the name substance, because substance signifies their essential agreement, but dog none. Therefore, for a name to be univocal it is necessary that it signify the agreement of many; and in the same way, for it to be analogous it is necessary that it signify at once the diversity and the agreement of many. But analogates have agreement or similarity by reason of proportionality or attribution, since they are different simply; therefore they cannot be signified as analogates unless the proportionality itself, or the attribution, is signified.

17 Second, it is proved: because, although the significates of some name have a univocal agreement, yet if they are not signified as having it, they will not be univocates, nor will the name by which they are signified be univocal; but the agreement will stand only materially or concomitantly, and will be as if it were not, as regards the effect of making the name univocal. Therefore, although some things have an analogical agreement among themselves, if this is not signified it will stand materially and as it were concomitantly, and will be as if it were not, as regards the effect of constituting an analogous name. Wherefore it is necessary that it be signified by the name.

Second conclusion: Proportionality is sometimes signified by an analogous name; and therefore, if when signified it suffices to constitute a species distinct from the analogy of attribution, it will make it distinct; and so it will have to be admitted that there are in act, in the nature of things, different species of analogy. This is against the second opinion, which denies that there are different species of analogy and of analogous terms, namely of proportionality and of attribution, although it admits that they are possible, if a name is imposed to signify the proportionality of many.

It is proved effectively by the example of laughter, by which the floweriness of the meadow is signified together with the true laughter of man, solely because the meadow, when it flowers, displaying a certain cheerfulness, is related as a man is related when he laughs; but this is proportionality; therefore the floweriness of the meadow is signified inasmuch as it has proportionality with the laughter of man. Wherefore it will be false that proportionality is never signified by an analogous name; and consequently it will be necessary, according to the same opinion,

[p. 207]

that, signified in this way, it makes a distinct species of analogy, and an analogous term distinct in species from the analogy and analogous terms of attribution. And if it is said that by the name laughter the floweriness of the meadow is signified only as it has similarity with the laughter of man, not proportionality, and that therefore it is not the proportionality itself that is signified, but attribution: against this is the fact that the floweriness of the meadow is not signified as having a similarity in common, but in particular, that is, such that, as laughter is a vital act by which the cheerfulness of the heart is shown, in this the floweriness of the meadow is similar to it, because it shows a certain cheerfulness; that is, it is related just as a man declaring his cheerfulness; and this is the proportionality which is truly signified by the name laughter. And certainly no other name could be imposed by which this proportionality would be better signified than the name laughter.

18 Third conclusion: Proportionality, even when signified by an analogous name, and moreover found in those analogates of which one is such through its own being while the other is not, except by reason of proportionality, does not of itself or by itself alone make a true and distinct species of analogy, nor an analogous name, but by reason of the attribution with which it is joined; and therefore it is the same as the analogy of attribution. And so neither according to act nor according to possibility are different species of analogy to be distinguished, but the analogy of attribution alone is to be posited.

This conclusion is against the second and third opinions, and it must first be explained, then proved. It is explained thus: Proportionality of itself is indifferent, so that it can be found among significates to both of which the appellation and signification of the name belongs formally and intrinsically, and among those to only one of which it belongs formally, and to the others by extrinsic denomination; indeed, even among those which under such a name have no agreement, as equivocates. This is proved evidently: because it is found among species of the same genus, as between man and lion; and also among the barking dog, the fish, and the star; and finally between the laughter of man and the floweriness of the meadow: because it is true of all these that as one of them is related to its own being, so is the other to its own; and although they are signified by the same name, it can be found in the same things in the same way or in a different way.

Which is proved no less effectively thus: because the fact that any one thing is related to its own being as another to its own does not make them more or less different in the apprehension of the intellect than if they did not have this; therefore neither will it make them more or less different, nor more or less the same, even if they are signified by the same name or by another. The consequence is evident, because things are signified

[p. 208]

by words as they are apprehended by the intellect. Further, the antecedent is proved: because it is found equally, in the apprehension of the intellect, among things altogether different and among things of the same ratio. For the significates of dog are not apprehended as less different from the fact that they are understood each to be related to its own being as another to its own; nor are white and black less dissimilar from the fact that they are apprehended under the same proportionality than if that were not apprehended. The conclusion, thus explained, is now proved against the second opinion by this argument.

20 Analogous terms are midway between equivocals and univocals; therefore they cannot be found together with either of the extremes, so that the same name, with respect to the same significates, is at once analogous and equivocal, or analogous and univocal. But proportionality alone, even signified by the name, can be found together with the one extreme and with the other; therefore it does not make a middle, which is not to make a name analogous. The minor is proved: because even if the species of animal are apprehended by the intellect under proportionality, that is, as the lion is related to its being of animal, which it participates from animal, just as man to his own, which he participates from the same, the same nature of animal is understood in them; therefore they do not cease to be univocal, and consequently they are not apprehended as analogous. Nor would they be analogous if they were signified by the name under the same proportionality: because, as has been proved, they are signified by the name in the same way in which they are apprehended by the intellect.

21 It is proved next against the third: because proportionality, by reason of itself, does not make the floweriness of the meadow be or be called laughter, but under the ratio of the attribution which it causes in it to the laughter of man; therefore neither by reason of itself does it make it an analogate of laughter, or laughter to be analogous, but by reason of attribution. The minor is proved: because if by reason of itself it made it an analogate, it would make all the other things in which it is found analogates; but we have proved that it does not make them so; therefore neither does it make the floweriness of the meadow an analogate of laughter except by reason of the attribution which it causes in it: because attribution is true analogy and per se makes a name analogous.

From these conclusions it follows that proportionality is not true analogy except as joined per se to attribution, and by reason of this, not by reason of itself; and therefore that it does not in any way make a distinct species of analogous terms, but that all analogous terms are of attribution, as St. Thomas expressly taught, 1 p., q. 13, a. 6, where he says thus: In all names which are said analogically of many, it is necessary that all be said with respect to one; and therefore that one must be posited in the definition of all.

And

[p. 209]

22 And it is proved by this argument: inequality alone does not suffice to make an analogous term, nor proportionality alone, even signified by the name; but besides these there remains only attribution, of which it has been proved that it per se makes a name analogous; therefore only the analogy of attribution is given, and only analogous terms of attribution. By the name of attribution, however, we understand any relation of one to another, or of many to one, by order to which such things are said. And understood in this way the third opinion can be true, which asserts that proportionality does not make analogy unless one of the things among which it is found is said to be absolutely such through its own being, and the other not, except through a relation to it: for a relation of this kind is comprehended under the name of attribution; and the proportionality by which it is caused makes the name analogous by reason of that, and not by reason of itself.

To the example of the first opinion, some reply that principle is equivocal by design, because it was imposed by design to signify different things. Others say that it is an analogous term of proportionality. But both seem false. The first, because Aristotle, Metaph. bk. 5, ch. 1, enumerating all principles, of different ratio, asserts that they agree in the ratio of principle, in these words: It is common, then, to every principle to be the first thing from which something either is, or comes to be, or is known. Therefore principle is not equivocal. The consequence is proved: because equivocals cannot agree except in the name alone. That it is not an analogous term of proportionality follows from what has been said, because proportionality does not suffice to make a name analogous. It could be said, then, that principle is an analogous term of attribution: because first and per se it signifies the principle from which something else proceeds according to being by a true origin, and by attribution to this principle it is said of the rest. Or, whoever is not pleased that it is analogous in this way, let him rather say that it is univocal than equivocal, because this last is expressly against Aristotle.

To the argument, the antecedent is to be denied, namely that proportionality presupposes that the things among which it is found are different: for although it supposes that they are distinct, yet it can be found indifferently among those which agree univocally and among those which agree in name alone; and therefore it does not per se make a name analogous.

To the testimony of St. Thomas I reply that without doubt he retracted that view in the same place of the First Part cited by us, where he so expressly holds the opposite.

O

[p. 210]

Whether it is necessary that the thing or concept signified by the name of the analogous

term be found intrinsically only in the principal analogate, and in the others only by ex‐

trinsic denomination.

25

S   upposing that only analogous terms of proportion, or attribution, are giv‐

en, it is doubted whether it is necessary that their significate be found

formally only in the principal analogate, and in the others not formally, but

only by extrinsic denomination: as we see in this name healthy, which signi‐

fies health; and this is found formally only in the animal, which is the princi‐

pal analogate, but in urine and medicine only by extrinsic denomination: in

the former as in a sign, in the latter as in a cause.

And the first opinion, of some, asserts that it is necessary that it be found

formally and intrinsically in the principal one alone. Which can be proved,

because it is found in this way in it alone, per se and first, while the others

seem to be only as it were attributions to it. Hence Aristotle said of acci‐

dents that they are not beings, but of a being, that is, something of substance.

But attribution does not seem to be anything but a certain extrinsic denomi‐

nation; therefore it will be found in them only by extrinsic denomination.

The second opinion is the common one of all the moderns, denying that

this is necessary, but holding that it can indifferently be in all formally, or

only in the principal one, according to their different nature and condition.

And this is the express opinion of St. Thomas, In 1, d. 19, q. 5; and it is true,

and to be embraced by us. It is proved by reason and by examples. By reason,

indeed: because it is attribution that makes analogy; but this can be found

among things which formally participate the ratio or concept of the analo‐

gous term, just as it is found among things of which only one formally partic‐

ipates it; therefore analogous terms can stand in both ways, and not in one

only, as the first opinion asserts. The minor is proved: because it can well be

understood that one or several things participate the formal ratio signified,

which they do not have except with dependence on and attribution to one,

in which it is found per se and first.

24 It is proved second by examples. For being is said analogically of sub‐

stance and accident, and also of God and creatures, as is proved below; but

the entity which it signifies is found formally not only in substance but also

in accidents, and not only in God but also in creatures; therefore it is not

necessary that it be found formally only in the principal analogate

[p. 211]

The minor is proved: because a creature has an intrinsic and formal entity, produced in the nature of things by creation or by another action; therefore it is not found in God alone, although it is found per se in him alone, and by participation and attribution to him in the creature. And in accidents too there is found a proper, formal, and intrinsic entity, though not without an intrinsic dependence on substance, as is manifest in quantity and quality.

But some reply, for the first opinion, that accident is not a being but of a being, that is, that it is something of substance, as Aristotle often asserts; and this is to have no other entity than attribution to substance, consisting in a certain denomination extrinsic to substance but intrinsic and essential to itself. But this cannot be true, as is gathered first of all from the same solution. For if accident is of a being, then it is of the being of substance; it has, therefore, a true entity, through which it affects substance. Which seems to be evidently proved by these experiences. Quantity in the Eucharist does not inhere in substance, but is separated from it; and yet it is a true entity, which we see and touch. Whiteness too we perceive by sight, and heat by touch. Therefore it is evidently proved that these accidents and the like are not extrinsic attributions or denominations, but true real entities: because an extrinsic denomination alone is not perceived, nor can it be a per se object of sense.

25 And it can be confirmed: because these accidents have their formal effects in the subjects in which they are; and not only formal but real and physical ones: as whiteness makes the wall really and formally white, and heat makes water really and formally hot. But these effects cannot proceed from causes consisting in extrinsic denomination alone, but from those which have a true and intrinsic real entity, by whose real power they produce them; therefore accidents have a true and intrinsic entity. Otherwise the intellect and will, which are accidents superadded to the substance of the rational soul for operating, will be nothing but extrinsic denominations superadded to it. Which is plainly false, since they are real powers, through which, as through real powers, the soul elicits true and real operations.

To the argument, the consequence is to be denied: because, although the ratio signified by the analogous term is found first and per se only in the principal analogate, and in the others only by attribution to it, yet it can be found in them intrinsically and formally, because attribution does not take this away, as has been proved.

O ij

[p. 212]

Whether the formal concept of analogous terms is one and abstracted from the analo‐

gates, or manifold; and whether it can be abstracted from them.

26

T     he concept that the intellect forms of something is twofold, as we not‐

ed in the chapter on difference: formal and objective. The formal con‐

cept is a quality of the mind which the intellect produces when it makes the

object actually present to itself and understands it: for through this quality it

is perfectly represented to it. The objective concept is the object that is un‐

derstood, inasmuch as it is represented through the formal one. And the

question proceeds concerning both, and therefore it will have two parts. In

the first we shall dispute about the unity of the formal concept; in the sec‐

ond, about the unity of the objective concept.

But the formal concept is also twofold: one is the concept of the signify‐

ing word, the other the concept of the thing signified. And concerning the

first it is certain that it is one, because the analogous name is one simple

word; therefore it is understood by us through one simple concept. But con‐

cerning the formal concept of the thing signified by the analogous name, the

question proceeds whether it is one.

The first opinion holds that there is given one formal concept of the thing

signified by the analogous term. So Scotus, in the place to be cited below;

Hervaeus, Quodlibet 2, q. 7; Soto, on the present chapter; Fonseca, Metaph. 4,

ch. 2, q. 12, sect. 5; Father Francisco Suárez, vol. 1 of his Metaph., disp. 2, sect.

1. But they proceed in different ways. For Scotus posits one formal concept

because he holds that being is univocal, and univocals signify their univocates

by means of a single formal concept. Father Suárez posits one formal concept

because he also posits one objective concept abstracted from the analogates.

Hervaeus and Soto, although they do not posit the same objective concept,

nevertheless assert that the formal one is one. And finally Fonseca posits one

formal concept, not distinct but confused, because it represents the analo‐

gates not distinctly but confusedly.

27 It is proved by a twofold argument. First, because the analogous term

is not only one simple word, and not equivocal, but one having one significa‐

tion from its imposition; but words signify by means of concepts; therefore

it will signify by means of a single formal concept. Which seems to be proved

by experience: for when the name being, or of another analogous term, is

heard, the intellect does not conceive the analogates under a determinate

concept, as substance or accident, but one something, namely entity; there‐

fore it does not form several formal concepts of them, but one of that same

entity.

Second, because if the formal concept of the analogous term is not one,

[p. 213]

but several, then the intellect, on hearing the name, will form as many concepts as the analogates it has; hence if these are ten, as happens in being, which signifies all the categories, or even if they are twenty, the intellect will form that many concepts at once, which seems impossible. The consequence is proved: because if it forms several, there is no greater reason why it should form two only and not more; nor, again, why it should form a concept of these rather than of others; therefore either as many as there are analogates, or only one.

28 The second opinion denies that the formal concept of the analogous term is one. Ferrara follows it, on Contra Gentiles 1, ch. 34, and with him many moderns; and this seems to us more probable.

And it is proved, first: because the analogous term agrees with the equivocal in this, that it signifies many things simply different, yet not altogether different, but the same in a certain respect; and in this it is distinguished. But on hearing an equivocal name the intellect forms different formal concepts, on account of the diversity of the significates; therefore on hearing an analogous name it will also form several, simply, although not altogether different, but having some similarity.

Second: the unity of the formal concept is taken from the unity of the objective concept represented by it, as the unity of an image from the unity of the thing represented; but the objective concept of the analogous term is not one, as will be proved in the second part of the question; therefore neither will the formal one be one. For those err quite plainly who, positing not one objective concept of the analogates but several, nevertheless admit a unity of the formal concept: against whom this argument concludes evidently, ad hominem, because it can have no unity of the formal concept which it does not receive from the objective one.

To the first argument, the antecedent is to be granted in the part where it says that the analogous term is one simple word, and therefore there is given one concept of it; but it is to be denied that it has one signification: just as it does not have one thing signified, but several, and simply different, to signify which it was imposed by a single imposition: because, although the things are several, yet all have attribution to one; and therefore they can be designated by a single word and by a single imposition to signify them.

29 To the experience adduced in the same argument, we grant that on hearing an analogous name the intellect does not conceive the analogates under an express or distinct concept, but it does conceive them under a confused actual one, as will be said in the second part. Yet it does not conceive one something common to them, but several things simply

O iij

[p. 214]

different, yet under a common ratio, the same only in a certain respect, on ac‐

count of the attribution which they have to one.

To the second: everything it assumes is to be granted, and it is to be denied that

it is impossible that the intellect form ten concepts if there are ten significates of

the analogous term, as happens in being, or even more, if it has more significates.

For it is not impossible for the intellect to form so many concepts at once under

the unity of the same word signifying so many things, which is quite manifest in

the equivocal: on hearing which no one denies that the intellect forms as many

concepts as there are significates of it, more or fewer. And in the analogous term

there is another particular reason: because the several concepts have an order not

only to one word, but also to one thing principally signified, to whose concept all

the others are ordered.

And from this it is understood that there is given no formal concept common

to the analogous terms and distinct from the concepts of the analogates, but only

several concepts of them. Hence there is given no formal concept of being besides

the concepts of the categories.

Second part of the question, on the unity of the objective concept of analogous terms.

30

A    nalogous terms are of two kinds, as we intimated in the preceding doubt.

Some are those whose significate is not found formally and intrinsically ex‐

cept in the principal analogate, and in the others by extrinsic denomination: as

healthy, which signifies health as white signifies whiteness; and yet health is not

found formally except in the animal alone, but in urine and medicine only by the

extrinsic denomination of sign or of cause. Others are analogous terms whose sig‐

nificate is found formally in all the analogates, but per se first and principally in

one only, and in the rest through an intrinsic dependence on and attribution to it.

And concerning both the question proceeds whether they have one common con‐

cept, abstractable from the analogates. But we must speak first of the first, then of

the others.

The first opinion, then, is that of moderns: that these analogous terms signify

one objective concept, which the intellect abstracts from the analogates. It is

proved, first: because these analogous terms are not equivocal; therefore they have

not only a common word, but also something signified by it; but any common ra‐

tio can be abstracted from the particulars that agree in it; therefore there is given

a concept of these analogous terms abstractable from them

[p. 215]

Second: because on hearing the name healthy someone can conceive some common ratio of health, not considering the particular ratios, or distinguishing the different ones which it has in the animal, urine, and medicine; and this concept is common to them; therefore it is one, and abstracted from them considered according to their particular ratios.

The second opinion is the common and true one: that from these analogous terms a common concept cannot be abstracted, but that they proximately signify the particular ratios of the analogates, in some way similar or proportioned in order to one principal. So Cajetan, opusc. On the Analogy of Names, ch. 5; Soto, on the present chapter, q. 1, a. 2, corol. 3; Fonseca, Metaph. 4, ch. 2, q. 1, sect. 6, at the verse “3. Discrimen.”

31 And it is proved by reason: because these analogates signify one form, existing only in the principal analogate, not in the others, in which it is only by extrinsic denomination: as healthy signifies the form of health inhering in the animal alone, not in urine and medicine, which are called healthy only by an extrinsic respect of cause or sign to the health of the animal. But from a thing signified formally and by extrinsic denomination alone, one ratio or common concept is not abstractable, because the form and the sign or cause stand as cause and effect, whose ratios are different, although they have an order of dependence or attribution; and therefore there is not given a concept common to them. Therefore neither will there be given a common concept of these analogates.

Second: because one concept, common to many, must be found in them formally; but the concept of these analogates is found formally only in the principal analogate, as is plain of the concept of health; therefore it is not one, common to all of them.

But some reply, for the first opinion, that the concept of these analogates is not of the form alone, but abstracts from the inclusion of the form, or of the ratio of sign or of cause, so that it is more general, expressing only universally the ratio of health and not the particular ratio of formal health; and that this abstracted concept is found formally in all: for to be a cause of health is found formally and intrinsically in medicine, and to be a sign belongs formally to urine, just as actual health belongs formally to the animal.

32 This solution, however, supposes something false: because the name healthy was imposed to signify true and actual health; hence in the common manner of speaking and conceiving, that alone

O iiij

[p. 216]

is called healthy which has formal health; just as the name laughter was imposed to signify the true laughter of man, which alone we understand on hearing this name. Therefore analogous terms of this kind do not signify that more universal ratio, but from the fact that they signify it they signify the less principal analogates, because these have an intrinsic attribution to the form existing in the principal analogate, primarily signified by the name. Nor is that common, more universal ratio, abstracting from formal and intrinsic health, which the argument objects, a true one, but a fictitious one: because to the form, the sign, and the cause nothing common is given, but these are only called healthy by attribution to that form, on account of which they are in some way assimilated to it. But the similarity is not intelligible without their particular ratios, and therefore it is not abstractable from them; indeed, the particular significates are not even intelligible except when the particular ratios are actually understood, not distinctly and expressly, as they are signified by their proper names, but only confusedly; and in this way they are signified by the common and analogous name, of which, therefore, there cannot be given an objective concept that is common and abstracted from the analogates.

33 To the first argument, the antecedent is to be granted, with the first consequence; but the minor is to be distinguished. For a common ratio is twofold: common simply, or in a certain respect. The former is found in univocals, the latter in analogous terms; and the former alone is abstractable from the particular ratios of the univocates, whereas the latter can in no way be abstracted from the particular ratios of the analogates, but must necessarily include them by a confused act. The reason for this difference is that a ratio common simply is the ratio of a nature or mode existing in the inferiors, while one common in a certain respect is nothing besides the proportion or attribution among the particular ratios; and therefore it is not intelligible without an actual inclusion of the particulars, at least a confused one; and consequently not unless the particulars are understood by a confused act, that is, not distinctly nor expressly, as they are signified by their proper names. And this is for there not to be a common concept abstractable from them: because a concept that is abstracted from particulars does not include them in act, but only in potency.

34 To the second, the antecedent is to be distinguished: because it happens in two ways that a common ratio is conceived on hearing an analogous name without the particulars being conceived: distinctly and expressly, or only confusedly. By an express act, then, and in the first way, a ratio common in a certain respect cannot be conceived without the particulars being conceived; but in the second way it can: because that common ratio is nothing other than the proportioned particulars; and therefore they are necessarily

[p. 217]

conceived in act by the same concept: not by an express or explicit act, but by a confused and as it were implicit one.

The difficulty is greater concerning the other analogous terms, whose ratio or form signified is found formally and intrinsically in all the analogates, although first and per se in one, and in the others through an intrinsic dependence on and attribution to it. And such an analogous term is being, according to the common and true opinion; and therefore it is fitting to take the example in it. For since the form signified, which is entity, is found formally in substance and in accidents, it seems that a common ratio of entity can be abstracted from the particular ratios of the categories, which all will participate as an intrinsic form.

35 And the first opinion is that which asserts that the concept of the analogous term is simply one, and abstracted from the particular ratios of the analogous terms, and therefore distinct in ratio from them. So Javelli, Metaph. 4, q. 1; Soto in the place cited above. It is proved by testimonies of Aristotle and St. Thomas, then by arguments. Aristotle, Metaph. 4, text 7, asserts that Metaphysics considers being inasmuch as it is being: as if to say, not as substance or accident, but under the more universal ratio of real entity. There is given, therefore, a ratio more universal than substance and accident, which must be abstracted from them, one and common. The consequence is proved: because the universal is something abstracted from particulars and common to them.

36 And St. Thomas, 1 p., q. 5, a. 3, ad 1, says that substance, quantity, and quality contract being by applying it to some quiddity or nature; but contraction cannot be understood except with respect to something common which is determined to particulars. Therefore he thinks that being, and any one of these analogous terms, signifies a common concept abstracted from the analogates.

It is also proved by reason. First: because entity is formally and intrinsically in substance and in accident; therefore they agree, or are assimilated, in this, that each is formally a being. But from any agreement whatever a concept common to the things that have it can be abstracted; therefore a common concept of entity is abstractable, in which substance and accident are assimilated; and this will be one, and distinct in ratio from them.

Second: because we can conceive of some thing that it is a being, and doubt whether it is a substance or an accident; therefore in the concept of being neither is included according to its particular ratio or intrinsic mode. The consequence is proved: because if the special ratios were included, we would know with certainty which of them belonged to it by the very fact that we conceive it to be a being, and therefore doubt would have no place. But if the special

[p. 218]

ratios are not included in that concept, it will be abstracted and one, since it includes nothing of diversity, but only agreement; therefore there is given one concept of the analogous term abstracted from the analogates.

37 It is proved third: because if there is not given an abstracted and common concept of being, it will be as it were an aggregate of all the special ratios of the categories, so that whoever says being says substance, quantity, quality, and the other categories. But such a concept can be predicated of no analogate; therefore all these predications will be false: Substance is a being, Quantity is a being, Quality is a being; which is absurd. The consequence is proved: because their sense will be Substance is substance, quantity, and quality, and so of the rest, which is manifestly false.

This opinion is defended by Father Francisco Suárez, vol. 1 of his Metaph., disp. 2, sect. 1, and he adds three things. First, that this objective concept of being is so prescinded from the inferiors that their intrinsic modes, namely per se and in another, are not included in it by a distinct or confused act. Second, that being does not immediately signify substance and accident, but that common and abstracted concept, by means of which being descends to both. Third, that this common concept is one not only as abstracted from the inferiors, but also as it is compared to them. And he added this on account of a certain opinion of other moderns, who say that it is one as abstracted, yet not as compared to the inferiors, because in them, as expressly conceived, it is diversified; which opinion I do not think it necessary to report specially. In these three things, however, the most learned Father speaks quite consistently.

38 The second opinion is that of other moderns, who grant that the concept of being can be abstracted from the particulars of substance and accident, and that, thus abstracted from them, it is one simply; but that compared with them, or considered in them as expressly conceived, that is, as they are signified by their proper names, it is not one, but becomes diverse in them. Which can be proved: because the common ratio of entity, as it is in substance and accident, is not distinguished from them, although it is distinguished in abstraction; but their express concepts are diverse; therefore the ratio of being, as existing in them, cannot be one, but must be diverse.

39 The third opinion altogether denies that there is given one objective concept simply abstracted from the analogates. It is followed by Capreolus, In 2, d. 2, q. 1, and, as reported by him, Auriol; Ferrara, on Contra Gentiles 1, ch. 30; Deza of Seville, In 1, d. 2, q.; Cajetan in the opuscule On Being and Essence, ch. 1, q. 2, and in the treatise On the Analogy of Names, ch. 5 and 6; Soto, Metaph. 4, q. 2; Pereira, Phys. bk. 2, ch. 2, at the end; Dominic of Flanders, Metaph. 4, q. 5;

[p. 219]

a. 6; Fonseca, Metaph. 4, ch. 2, q. 2; Father Gabriel Vázquez, 1 p., d. 22, ch. 5, and d. 114, ch. 2; and many others. And this is the more probable opinion.

It is proved against the first and second by testimonies of Aristotle and St. Thomas. For Aristotle, Metaph. 4, ch. 2, asserts two things, namely that being is said in many ways, and that it is said with reference to one, or to one nature. And from both it is gathered that there is not given one concept of it abstracted from the analogates, which I prove thus. For if it is said in many ways, then not in one way, nor through one concept, but through several; and if it is said in order to one, then in its concept it includes many. The consequence is proved: because where there is given one, or many ordered to one, there is multiplicity; but if it includes many in its concept, such a concept cannot be one, because the many are different; therefore there is not given one objective concept of being. And in Metaph. 8, ch. 6, text 16, he asserts that being is straightway substance, quantity, and quality, that is, that it descends to them immediately, and not as a univocal term, which descends to the univocates only by means of a single concept common to them, as animal to man and horse. Therefore he thinks that it does not have a common concept: for by means of it, it would descend to substance and accident.

And St. Thomas, 1 p., q. 13, a. 5, says thus: For in those things which are said analogically there is neither one ratio, as in univocals, nor a totally different one, as in equivocals; but the name which is thus said in many ways signifies different proportions in order to one, etc.

From these words this argument is gathered. The concept of being, according to St. Thomas, signifies different proportions in order to one; but it cannot signify different proportions in order to one unless it signifies at once those different things which have such proportions, and these are the analogates; therefore its concept cannot be abstracted from the analogates, nor be one simply.

It is proved next by an argument against the first opinion, taken from the definition of analogous terms, which all admit. Analogous terms are those whose name is common, but the ratio of substance accommodated to the name is neither altogether the same nor altogether different; but the ratio of substance is the objective concept; therefore this is neither altogether the same nor altogether different, but different simply and the same in a certain respect, by reason of attribution. Wherefore it follows that it is not abstractable from the analogates, among which attribution and diversity are found, nor can it be one simply.

Second: if the concept of being is abstracted or prescinded from substance and accident, then it is distinguished in ratio from them; but things that are distinguished by some distinction, as thus distinct, do not include each other; therefore the concept of being, as thus prescinded from the modes

[p. 220]

intrinsic to substance and accident, can neither include them nor be included in them. The first has been proved false; but the second is also proved to be false, because the concept of being is transcendental; therefore it is included in any entity whatever, whether complete or incomplete, whether a nature or a mode; otherwise, if being were not included, it would be nothing.

41 It is proved third: because if the concept of being is simply abstracted from the intrinsic modes and does not include them in act, as the first opinion admits, it follows that it is one in such a way that it includes no diversity. The consequence is proved: because the whole diversity of substance and accident is through the intrinsic modes per se and in another; if, then, it does not include these in act, as genus does not include the differences in act, it will be one simply, and consequently univocal.

The first opinion replies that, although it does not include the modes in act, and in this agrees with the univocal, yet it differs from it in that a univocal concept is participable by the univocates in the same way, or equally, whereas the concept of the analogous term, such as that of being, is of its own nature participable in different ways by the analogates, according to the attribution of one, or of many, to one; and this is enough for it not to be univocal but analogous. But this solution is attacked thus: the concept of being cannot be participable in different ways, nor can it have any diversity, except through the different intrinsic modes per se and in another, by which it is determined to the being of substance and of accidents; therefore it is repugnant that it have any diversity, or be participable in different ways, except through those very modes; but while it is abstracted from them it does not include them; therefore it cannot be participable in different ways.

42 And it can be effectively confirmed in this way: for a common concept to be abstracted from particulars is nothing other than for the common ratio to be known without the particulars, or with them not known; therefore for the concept of being to be abstracted from the modes per se and in another is for the ratio of being to be known without the modes being considered, or the order to them: for by the very fact that the order to them were considered, it would not be an abstracted concept. But the ratio of being can have no diversity without the modes, or without the order to them; therefore if it is abstracted from them, it will be a concept altogether one and the same, no less than a univocal concept, and being itself will not be analogous but univocal.

It is proved next against the second opinion. First: because if once a concept of being abstracted from the particulars of substance and accident is admitted, and that it is one, it follows that being is univocal. The consequence is proved: because being signifies first that abstracted and one concept; therefore the ratio signified

[p. 221]

by the name is the same, and the name common, as is said in the definition of univocals. Second, because it is repugnant that the concept be one in abstraction and not one when the inferiors are expressed: therefore it is always one. The antecedent is proved: because if once it is abstracted from them, then, as abstracted, it is distinguished by reason from the same taken as expressed; but compared to them it is the same concept which is considered in abstraction, and not another: therefore it will also be distinguished by reason; and therefore it will have the same unity that they attribute to it in abstraction.

In what way the concept of the analogous term contains the analogates.

O      ur view, then, holds that the objective concept of being, and of any anal‐

ogous term whatever, is not simply abstractable from the analogates, but necessarily includes them. But concerning the way in which it includes them, not all who follow it agree. Two things, however, are received among them. The first, that it includes them in act, and not only in potency, because this last takes away neither the unity of the concept nor the univocation of the name. The second, that it does not include them in explicit, distinct, or express act, which is to say, that it does not include them as they are signified by their proper names, but inasmuch as they are signified under the common name, as under the name of entity, if we are speaking of being. And the reason for this is that being signifies substance and accident inasmuch as they have attribution; but under their proper names they do not have it, but signified under the common name of being, and confusedly contained: therefore only in this way are they signified by the analogous name and contained in its concept, and not under express concepts or names.

They differ, then, as to the way of including them. For Soncinas and Hervaeus, in the places cited above, assert that the concept which being immediately signifies is this disjunctive one, substance or accident. This, however, is rejected by almost all. First, because a concept signified by a determinate word must be determinate, whereas that disjunctive one says determinately neither substance nor accident. Second, because being signifies many things by attribution to one; therefore it signifies all of them simply, that is, without disjunction. The consequence is proved: because attribution does not hold among many things signified disjunctively, but absolutely.

Nor again does the analogous term signify its analogates copulatively, so that the concept of being is substance and accident: because from this it would follow that all propositions in which it is predicated of any one of them are false, as Substance is a being, Accident is a being, because their sense would be: Substance is substance and accident:

[p. 222]

Accident is substance and accident.

Therefore there is a second opinion, that of others: that being, in its primary signification, signifies being per se, which is substance and being simply; but secondarily accidents, as something of the same substance. But this too seems false: because the analogous term per se and primarily signifies many things with attribution; therefore it does not primarily signify only the principal analogate, but all of them, although the principal significate is first in dignity.

44 The third opinion is that of Ferrara and Cajetan, in the places cited above: that the analogous term signifies immediately and per se all the analogates, inasmuch as they have attribution among themselves; and that being signifies immediately the ten categories, inasmuch as the nine of accidents are so called by attribution to substance. And this is the more probable and is to be held.

But for its explanation it must be presupposed as certain that the analogous term is in some way superior to each analogate, as Cajetan rightly says in the opuscule On Analogy, ch. 5: not only according to the word, which is common to the analogates (for the equivocal term also has this), but in some way according to the ratio or concept signified; which, since it must also be in some way common, must consequently be superior; and if it is in some way common, it must be abstracted from them.

But in order that these things may be better understood, Cajetan rightly notes, in the place cited above, that there is a twofold abstraction by which one thing is abstracted from others. One is that by which one thing is known without another, or with the other not known. The other, by which the same thing is known in another way than it is in itself: as when, though in itself it has an express and distinct mode, it is known as it were implicitly and confusedly. And the first mode of abstraction constitutes abstraction simply, and pertains to univocals, which are thus abstracted from their univocates. The second makes only abstraction in a certain respect, and pertains to analogous terms, which cannot be abstracted in the first mode, nor in any other except the second. Thus substance can be considered in two ways: either according to the express concept signified by the proper name substance; or according to a confused and as it were implicit concept, which seems to be nothing other than the principal entity to which accidents are attributed. And in this way it is signified by the name being, whose proper concept is of the first and principal entity, and of the less principal ones, which are accidents, attributed according to their particular modes of inhering to it, which is substance. And this concept is in some way abstracted with respect to the express concepts, among which, as thus expressed, there is no attribution, no order, no dependence, or

[p. 223]

similarity is signified; and the ratio of the abstraction consists in this, that although through the concept of being we conceive all things in act, and likewise while we conceive all of them together through their proper names, yet through the concept of being we conceive them with attribution and similarity, whereas, represented through their proper concepts, they have no attribution, no order, no similarity. Whence it follows that the concept of being is so predicated of any one whatever that it is also, in its own way, predicated of the others; and this is to be in some way superior with respect to each, and consequently abstracted from them in the same way, and as such to be predicated of each.

45 But in order that the mode of predicating being of the individual categories may be understood, we note second that, although the concept of being includes substance and accident in confused act, as has been explained, yet in predication it is applied to each according to its proper nature: so that when it is predicated of substance, it is applied to it as to the first being, to which accidents are attributed; and when it is predicated of some accident, it is applied to it as attributed to substance. The sense, then, of this proposition, Substance is a being, is this: Substance is the first entity, to which accidents are attributed; and of Quantity is a being: that is, it has entity by way of extension, attributed to substance. And the reason for this is that all things are signified according to attribution to one: therefore it is predicated of that one as of that to which the others are attributed, and of the others as they are attributed to it; and this same attribution is the reason why, although the concept of being contains many and diverse things, it can truly be predicated of each: because, while it is predicated of any one whatever, by the proper mode of its application and attribution it says that one only in recto, but the others in obliquo, as the very attribution signified among them requires.

46 But if you say that, according to the sense of these predications, being is not predicated of the individual categories as superior, but as equal, indeed by an identical predication, contrary to what was said, that it is superior at least in a certain respect: both points are proved. The first, indeed, because the predicate of this proposition, Substance is a being, is nothing other than Substance is the first entity, to which accidents are proportioned; and this is plainly convertible with the subject, indeed altogether the same as it; and therefore the proposition is not only one of equality, but identical. I reply that it is predicated by a predication of equality simply, of a superior in a certain respect, but identical in no way. The first will be manifest if we consider the concept of being according to the different modes in which it is predicated of all: for of substance, as of the first, to which the others are attributed; but of the individual accidents

[p. 224]

according to the particular modes by which they are attributed to substance. The concept of being, therefore, considered with all these modes that belong to it as to the analogous term taken adequately, since they belong to it by reason of the analogy of attribution, will be formally superior with respect to the individual analogates, although only in a certain respect, while it is equal simply if this consideration is set aside. And that it is formally superior in a certain respect I prove: because while it is predicated of one according to the mode of application to it, it can be predicated of the others according to their proper modes, which the subject manifestly does not have: therefore according to the mode of predicating they are not convertible, although they are convertible as regards the thing signified.

47 And from this it follows that the same propositions are not identical, but formal propositions of the analogous term: because, although the same thing is predicate and subject, it has a different mode in the predicate than in the subject, consisting in two things. In the first, indeed: for in the predicate it has greater extension, since it is so predicated of one according to the proper mode of that one that it can also be predicated of the others according to their proper modes. In the second, however: because, although both the predicate and the subject of this predication, Substance is a being, signify the same thing, yet it is signified more expressly and distinctly through the subject, as through a proper name, than through the predicate, as through a common name. And this different mode of signifying makes the proposition formal, and therefore not identical; just as the predication in which a definition is predicated of the defined is not identical, although they are the same thing, from this alone, that it is signified more expressly through the predicate than through the subject.

48 And from these things it will not be difficult to solve the arguments of the contrary opinion. For the testimony of Aristotle contains the truth, that Metaphysics considers being inasmuch as it is being: that is, not according to some particular ratio of some category, nor according to the express and distinct rationes of all, but according to the ratio of attribution to one, namely to substance. For they do not have this as signified under their proper names, but under the name of being, common to all, under which they have a certain similarity in entity, and unity in a certain respect, under which they can be abstracted, again in a certain respect, from the proper rationes expressly signified. And thus being, abstracted, is considered inasmuch as it is being, and can be the object of Metaphysics: because, although it is analogous, yet, considered under such a mode of abstracting from matter as it is considered in metaphysics, it has one objective ratio, under which and from which the science itself takes its specific unity.

The

[p. 225]

49 The testimony of St. Thomas, however, asks for the mode by which being is contracted through the particular modes of substance and accident. And the difficulty consists in this: because, if there is not given a common concept of it abstracted from those modes, but one including them, it does not seem that it can be contracted through them, because the contracting must be outside the ratio of the contractible; for if it is included in it, it will already be contracted by it. I reply that being is contracted through the modes per se and in another in the same way in which it is abstracted from them; but it is abstracted from them only in a certain respect, that is, as the same thing from itself signified in a different mode; therefore it can be contracted only through itself, as signified in a different mode. For example, being in its concept includes the intrinsic modes per se and in another, in act indeed, yet not under an express concept but under an implicit and confused one, that is, not as they are signified by their proper names, but by the common name of being; and this different mode of including them suffices for it to be said to be abstracted from them in a certain respect. But a concept is not contracted except as it is abstracted: for contraction and abstraction correspond mutually to each other; therefore the concept of being is contracted in the same way through the intrinsic modes signified under an express concept, which, however, it does not include in this mode, but under a confused ratio; so that it is always true (even in the contraction of the analogous term, which is only in a certain respect, like the abstraction) that the contracting is outside the ratio of the contractible. St. Thomas explained this sense in another place, and so we explain one testimony by the other. The place is On Truth, q. 1, a. 1, where he speaks thus: That which the intellect first conceives as most known, and into which it resolves all conceptions, is being: whence all the other conceptions of the intellect must be taken by addition to being. But nothing can be added to being as a nature extraneous to it, in the way in which a difference is added to a genus, because every nature is essentially being; but according to this some things are said to add above being, inasmuch as they express a mode of it which is not expressed by the name of being itself. And below: Substance does not add above being some difference, but by the name of substance a special mode of being is expressed.

50 To the first argument: granting the first enthymeme, the minor of the syllogism is to be distinguished: because such as the agreement of many things is, such will be the concept abstractable from them. If they agree simply, the abstractable concept will be simply common and one, as in univocals; but if they agree only in a certain respect, the abstractable concept will be common and one only in a certain respect. And so it is in analogous terms, and also in being, since it is analogous. But what it is to be abstracted in a certain respect

P

[p. 226]

has already been explained.

To the second: granting the antecedent, the consequent is to be distinguished.
