For actual inclusion is twofold: confused or implicit, and distinct or express; and of the former it is to be granted, but of the latter denied; and it is to be said that from this the doubt can arise whether that which we certainly know to be a being is substance or accident: because the concept of being includes the particular rationes of substance and accident only confusedly, not distinctly; and by reason of the confusion the doubt occurs, consisting in this, that the intellect does not know distinctly to which significate being is determined.

51 To the last: what is assumed in the antecedent is to be denied, namely that the concept of being is an aggregate of the particular concepts of the categories: because it does not include them by way of aggregation, but by way of attribution, in which there is essentially included an order of many to one; whereas order is repugnant to an aggregate, since it is an aggregate precisely because it includes many things without order. But to include all things according to the order of attribution is to include one as it were in recto, and the others in obliquo. Whence it follows that, when being is predicated of any analogate whatever, as in this proposition, Substance is a being, the sense is not Substance is substance and accident, because in this sense attribution is not signified; but the sense is this: Substance has the first entity, or is the first entity, to which accidents are attributed; and this is most true. Nor does it take away its truth that in the concept of being, besides substance signified in recto, accidents are signified in obliquo: just as it does not take away the truth of the proposition in which it is predicated of an accident, that substance is signified in obliquo, so that the sense is: Accident has entity, or is a being attributed to substance, as something of it. And the reason why such senses make these predications is the very nature of the attribution under which the analogates are signified by the analogous name: for this is why the same analogous term is applied to each in predications, according to the requirement of the same attribution.

52 One thing is to be noted in this place: namely, that the unity in a certain respect of the concept of the analogous term suffices for it to be able to be divided into its analogates, and also for the analogates themselves to be able to be compared, as signified by it, so that we may say that substance is more perfectly a being than accident; and finally for it to be able to be the object of the intellect and of science. The reason for the first is that division proceeds from one to many: therefore something is capable of division insofar as it is one; for if it is manifold, it brings division along with itself. Whence, just as the division of the equivocal term into its equivocates is not

[p. 227]

a division of the thing, but only of the word, because only the word is com‐

mon, in a similar way the division of the analogous term is simply a division of

the word, and in a certain respect a division of the thing: because the word is

common simply, but the thing signified is not common, nor one simply, but

manifold, and one only in a certain respect; and therefore the division of the

analogous term, if we attend to the thing, is not a division simply, but only in

a certain respect, for which the unity in a certain respect of its concept suf‐

fices. But the univocal term, because it is one both on the side of the word

and of the thing signified, can be divided simply; and its division alone ought

to be called such simply.

And in the same way the reason for comparison is to be given: for compar‐

ison must be made in some one ratio; therefore simply it must be made in the

univocal term, and, if it is to be proper, in the lowest species, as Aristotle

teaches in Phys. 7; but comparison of any sort whatever can also be made in

the analogous term, for which unity in a certain respect suffices.

53 And for the analogous term to be able to be the object of the intellect

and of science, the same unity suffices: because a science or a power does not

take its specific unity from the material object, but from the formal objective

ratio under which the power tends to it, or under which it is considered by

the science; from which the analogous term receives a greater unity when it is

the object of a power or of a science.

Whether being is univocal with respect to substance and accident, or analogous, and by

what analogy.

T    his is the fourth thing which we proposed to treat. But for knowledge of

it, it should be noted that being can be taken in two ways: for created

being, which is divided into the ten categories; or more universally, for being

common with respect to the created and the uncreated, or to God and crea‐

tures. And concerning being taken in either way there can be a question,

which we therefore divide into two parts. In the first we shall treat of created

being, whether it is univocal with respect to the categories, or analogous, and

by what analogy. In the second we shall inquire into the same things concern‐

ing the same being with respect to God and creatures.

First Part of the Question. 54

C     oncerning the first part there are two extreme opinions and one inter‐

mediate. The first extreme opinion is that of Auriol, in Capreolus on 1,

d. 2, q. 1, who asserts that being is equivocal with respect to substance and ac‐

cident. It is proved by testimonies of Aristotle and Porphyry: for Aristotle,

Metaph. 8, ch. 6, text 16, says: that each category is straightway something, that is, is

such by itself and diverse from another; which is customarily said in other words, that

the categories are diverse by themselves,

P ij

[p. 228]

and not through differences, but are diverse by themselves; and if they are diverse with their whole selves, to be diverse with their whole selves is the same as to be altogether diverse, which is proper to equivocates. Being, therefore, is equivocal.

And Porphyry, in the chapter on Species, according to the mind of the same Aristotle, said that being is equivocal.

This opinion, however (if it speaks of proper equivocation, and not of common equivocation, as it comprehends analogy), is contrary to the doctrine of the same Aristotle and to reason. The first is proved from Metaph. 4, ch. 2, and text 2, where Aristotle says: But being is said in many ways, not equivocally, but with respect to one nature, as healthy; that is, by attribution of many to one.

The second, that it is against reason, is proved from the definition of equivocals. Equivocals are those whose name is common, but the ratio of substance accommodated to the name is altogether different; but substance and accident agree in some way in the ratio of being, since each is a being, although one is diverse from the other and attributed to it: therefore they are not altogether diverse; wherefore neither can being be equivocal.

55 The second extreme opinion holds that being is univocal. So Scotus, on 1, d. 3, q. 3, and on 3, d. 8, q. 2, and all his disciples; Antonius Andreas, Metaph. 4, ch. 2; and also all the Nominalists, as Gabriel attests on 1, d. 2, q. 4. And it is proved by a twofold argument. The first, taken from the definition of univocals: Univocals are those whose name is common, but the ratio of substance accommodated to the name is the same, that is, the concept signified by the name; but it is established that the name being is common to substance and accident, and the concept, both formal and objective, is one and the same in the inferiors: therefore the name will be univocal. The minor is proved: because substance and accident agree in the ratio of being, and are distinguished by the intrinsic modes per se and in another; but the modes are distinguished by reason from entity, since they determine and contract it to substance and accident: therefore the intellect can conceive entity without conceiving the modes in any way. This last consequence is proved: for things which are distinguished by reason the intellect can well separate, and, as thus separated, they will not include each other; wherefore it will be able to conceive the ratio of being common to substance and accident, in which the modes are not included. And such a concept, formal and objective, will be one simply, including no diversity.

Second: because, if anything stood in the way of the concept of being’s being one simply and common to substance and accident, it would above all be the diversity in the mode of being of each, because substance has the mode of being per se, but accident the mode

[p. 229]

of being in another; but these things do not stand in the way: therefore it will be one simply. The minor is proved: because this ratio of diversity is not in the entity except by reason of the modes; therefore it does not take away the one ratio of entity, and so not the univocal one either; just as the diversity through rational and irrational does not take away the unity of the concept of animal, because it is not by reason of the sensitive nature, but of the differences.

Third: the intellect can be certain of something that it is a being, and doubtful whether it is substance or accident: as, if someone doubts whether some Host is consecrated or not, he knows with certainty that it is a being, but doubts whether there is substance there, or only accident. But this could not happen unless the intellect conceived the ratio of being without conceiving the particular rationes of substance and accident; and this concept will be common to them, and one simply, since it does not include anything by reason of which it could have any diversity. And consequently the name being, signifying such a concept, will be univocal.

56 The third, intermediate opinion between these extremes asserts that being is neither equivocal nor univocal, but analogous. And it is common in the school, and true; it is followed by Averroes, Alexander, and St. Thomas in their commentaries on the places of Aristotle to be cited below; Porphyry, Albert, and Ammonius, in the chapter on Species in the Predicables; and all the others, except those cited for the opinion of Scotus.

It is gathered effectively from the doctrine of Aristotle, Metaph. 4, ch. 2; bk. 7, ch. 1 and 4; and Ethics 1, ch. 6, where he expressly teaches that being is said in many ways, and not equivocally, but as healthy is said of urine, medicine, and animal, with respect to one nature, that is, by attribution of many to one. By these words he excludes both extreme opinions: for when he says being is said in many ways, as healthy, he takes away univocation, against Scotus; but when he adds not equivocally, he takes away equivocation, against Auriol.

It is next proved by reason. First, from the definition of analogous terms. Analogous terms are those whose name is common, but the ratio of substance accommodated to the name is neither altogether the same nor altogether different; but being stands thus with respect to substance and accident: therefore it is analogous and not univocal. I prove the minor thus: substance is the first being, having entity per se, independent of another; but accident is the entity of another, namely of substance, and therefore Aristotle said in Metaph. 4, ch. 2, Accident is not a being, but a being of a being; therefore it does not have entity per se, but by attribution to substance; wherefore in the very ratio of entity there is found, first of all, the greatest diversity, and on that account also in the concept signified by the name being. Then there is found some agreement by reason of the same attribution: therefore the ratio of being by

P iij

[p. 230]

the name signified is neither altogether different nor altogether the same. And this is for being to be analogous, and therefore not univocal.

But if Scotus says that the diversity between substance and accident does not come from the side of the entity, but from the side of the modes per se and in another, from which the ratio of entity can be abstracted; and that thus, abstracted, it will be one, because thus it is abstracted from the diversity, and therefore, as abstracted, does not include it; wherefore it will be one simply, and the name being, signifying it immediately, will be univocal: is it not then proved that it is analogous, or that it is not univocal? This does not take away the force of the argument: because the intrinsic modes of substance and accident are not grades of perfection distinct from the entity, but the very entity, more expressly conceived and signified, which is signified by the name being; whence neither is being outside their ratio, nor are they outside the ratio of being. Whence it follows first that neither can the entity be conceived without them, included at least in confused act, nor they without the entity. Second, it follows that it is the same that the diversity of substance and accident, as they are signified by the name being, comes from the intrinsic modes per se and in another, and that it comes from the entity itself; it is likewise the same that they are diverse through these same modes and that they are diverse by themselves; and finally, that just as the entity cannot be abstracted from itself, so neither can it be abstracted from the same modes; and therefore neither can the concept of being, which necessarily includes them, be one simply, nor univocal. But whether being, taken not in its whole universality but only for complete being, can be abstracted from substance and accident, and is univocal with respect to them, we shall say presently.

58 To the testimony of Aristotle for the first opinion I reply that the categories’ being primarily diverse has this sense: that they do not differ as species do, through differences containing a different grade of perfection, from the genus in which they agree, but through the modes, which are the very entity of the categories conceived in a special way: whence it is true that they are diverse through their proper entities so conceived. And this is also to differ by themselves. And when it is inferred that they differ with their whole selves, a distinction is to be made: for if the sense is, One is diverse from the other through its whole entity, it is true; but if, Through its whole entity conceived in all ways, it is false: because their entities can be conceived as diverse simply, and also as similar and the same in a certain respect, by reason of attribution; and therefore they are not conceived as diverse in all ways. Nor, though in this sense it is true that they differ with their whole selves, is it necessary that being be equivocal: because equivocates, as they are conceived and signified under that name, agree in no way. And therefore it is not proved from that testimony that being is equivocal. Porphyry, however, speaks of the equivocal according to the common acceptation,

[p. 231]

under which he comprehends the analogous term: for for his purpose, which

was that being is not the genus of all things, it sufficed that it be analogous.

59 To the first argument of the second opinion: the minor is to be denied,

that the concept of being is one simply. And when it is said that the modes are

distinguished by reason from the entity, a distinction is to be made: for things

happen to be distinguished by reason in two ways. First, by a total distinction,

so that the concept of one is so distinguished from the other that it does not

include it; and in this way the difference is distinguished by reason from the

genus. Second, not by a total distinction, but by that of the including and the

included; and so it is true that the concept of being is distinguished from the

modes, which it includes and by which it is included, inasmuch as they add

above its concept the ratio of expression. And if the concept of being were

distinguished by reason from the modes in the first sense, it could be abstract‐

ed from them; but since it is not distinguished except in the second, it is to be

denied that it can be abstracted, or conceived without them.

To the second: the minor is to be denied, that the ratio of the diversity of

substance and accident is not in the entity, but by reason of the modes. For it

is impossible that it be by reason of the modes and not by reason of the entity,

since the modes are entities, and are therefore included in the concept of the

entity. It is therefore by reason of both; and therefore it is repugnant that it be

conceived without diversity, or be abstracted from it, so that its concept is one

simply.

To the last: granting the major, the minor is to be distinguished. For to con‐

ceive the ratio of being without conceiving the particular rationes of sub‐

stance and accident happens in two ways. First, without conceiving them dis‐

tinctly and expressly. Second, without conceiving them in implicit and con‐

fused act. And in the case of the argument it is to be granted that it is con‐

ceived without the modes in the first sense, but not in the second; and from

its being conceived without the modes being conceived in the first sense, it

comes about that the intellect can doubt whether the being which it conceives

is substance or accident. Wherefore such a doubt does not prove that there is

given a concept of being one simply, abstracted from substance and accident,

by reason of which it could be univocal.

Whether at least complete being is univocal with respect to complete substance and

accident. 60

T     he special reason for doubting in favor of the affirmative side concerns

complete being: because it does not seem that it can be included in the

differences, nor in the intrinsic modes, through which accident and substance

are diverse: because concerning the modes and differences it is manifest that

they are incomplete beings; therefore a concept of being including no diversity

could be abstracted from them. The consequence is proved: because the

modes cause the whole diversity.

P iiij

[p. 232]

The common opinion, however, is to be held as true: that complete being cannot be univocal to complete substance and complete accident, but is analogous in this way no less than if it is taken in its whole universality. The reason for this is not assigned in the same way by all who think so. But it seems to me that it must be proved in almost the same way that complete being is not univocal but analogous as it was proved that being taken universally is analogous. It is proved, therefore, by a twofold argument. The first: just as being taken universally includes in act any entity whatever, however minimal, whether it be the entity of a thing or a mode, and is also included in it formally and essentially, so complete being includes in act any complete entity whatever, accidental as well as substantial: because to be a substantial or an accidental entity are not grades of perfection distinct from the same entity, but are the very same entity conceived and signified in a certain more express way; therefore the whole diversity and the whole attribution which they have among themselves is included in the concept of complete being, and consequently the whole analogy. Wherefore it is repugnant that the concept of complete being be one simply, and univocal.

61 The second argument is taken from the definition of univocates. Univocals are those whose name is common, but the ratio of substance altogether the same; therefore univocates must participate the concept of the univocal term equally and simply; but complete substance and accident do not participate the ratio of complete being equally, nor simply: therefore being cannot be univocal with respect to them. The minor is proved: because those things participate a common ratio equally each of which participates it per se, that is, without essential dependence on another; and those participate it simply each of which is called such simply, as it participates it; but complete accident does not participate the ratio of complete being except with essential dependence on substance, nor is it called complete being simply, but only in a certain respect; indeed it is not called complete being, but a being of a being, as we adduced from Aristotle: therefore it cannot participate univocally the ratio of complete being, nor can complete being be univocal with respect to both. And what we have said of complete being must be said of perfect being in relation to perfect substance and perfect accident, because, as far as the present division of being is concerned, the ratio is the same for both; and therefore the same arguments prove the same thing in the same way of both.

To the argument put forward for the reason for doubting it is replied that, although complete being does not include the intrinsic modes

[p. 233]

per se and in another as concepts separate from substance and accident, and

in the same way neither the differences, nor again is it included in them as

thus conceived, it nevertheless includes them and is included in them as they

are conceived in the constitution of substance and accident, or of the

species. And the reason for this is manifest: because complete being, as we

have proved, includes complete substance and accident, and is included by

them formally and essentially; but there is no complete and incomplete sub‐

stance without the modes that constitute it: therefore, as thus conceived,

they are included in complete being and include it. Which inclusion suffices

for the concept of being to include a diversity sufficient to take away univo‐

cation and to produce analogy.

Whether being is univocal with respect to some things of the same category, or of differ‐

ent categories. 62

H       aving now explained the analogy of being taken most universally with

respect to substance and accident, and of complete being with respect

to complete substance and complete accident, there remain two other, more

particular comparisons of being. The first is whether, with respect to two

species of the same category, as man and horse, Peter and John, or whiteness

and blackness; the second, whether, with respect to two things of different

categories of accidents, as whiteness and quantity, being is univocal or analo‐

gous. And we are not speaking of being as complete, but taken according to

itself.

63 The first opinion holds that being is univocal with respect to two

things of the same category, of substance as well as of accident, and also of

different categories of accidents. Fonseca holds it as to the first, Metaph. 4,

ch. 1, q. 1, sect. 3, not denying the second; and as to both, Father F. Suárez, in

Metaph., disp. 32, sect. 2, no. 21. He proves both by this argument: two sub‐

stances, and two accidents of the same category or of different ones, partici‐

pate the ratio of being without any attribution of one to the other, indeed

without any order, but equally primarily: therefore it does not belong to

them analogically, but univocally.

The second opinion is that of others, who hold that being, compared in

either way, is analogous by analogy of proportionality. They prove it: because

being is analogous by analogy of attribution and of proportion at once; but in

these comparisons it does not signify those members according to the attri‐

bution of one to the other: therefore it cannot have any other analogy except

that of proportionality. That it has this, however, is manifest: because it is

true that any species

[p. 234]

of the same category, or of different categories of accidents, stands to its entity, which it participates from being, as the other does to its own; and this is proportionality: therefore being, with respect to them, will be analogous by analogy of proportionality.

64 For the solution of this doubt it should be noted that in these comparisons being can be taken in two ways. First, according to the limited concept of the same category; and compared in this way to two substances, it is the same as the supreme genus of substance. In the second way it can be taken in its whole universality, as it signifies substance and accident. I omit a third consideration of it, which others posit as it were midway between the two, so that it is taken for a concept less universal than the one it has in the second acceptation, but more universal than the supreme genus of the category, and so superior to it: because this concept coincides with the second as far as analogy or univocation is concerned. For it is repugnant for it to be taken more universally than for the things of one category, and not to be taken for something in some way common to many categories. But to be taken for two and as it is common to all is the same, as far as analogy or univocation is concerned, according to the common and more probable opinion: therefore this acceptation need not concern us.

This supposed, our view asserts two things. The first: being taken in the first way is univocal with respect to things of the same category. It is proved: because being so taken is the same as the supreme genus of the same category; but this is univocal with respect to things of the same category: therefore being is too.

The second is: if being is taken in the second way, in all these comparisons it is analogous and not univocal. I prove it thus: the analogous term, in its proper and integral signification, is predicated analogically of the individual analogates taken by themselves, as healthy of animal by itself, or of urine and medicine by themselves; but being in its proper and integral signification is analogous: therefore, as analogous, it is predicated of substance by itself and of any accident by itself, and consequently of things of the same category or of different categories of accidents; but it is so taken in the second acceptation: therefore it is predicated analogically of the individual analogates.

65 To the argument of the first opinion: the antecedent is to be distinguished according to the different considerations of being that have been explained. For if it is taken according to the first, it is true that it is participated without attribution or respect by two species of the same category, just as the supreme genus of the same category is participated

[p. 235]

with which it is convertible; but if it is taken according to the second, it is to

be denied: because, although those two species do not participate the ratio of

being with attribution between themselves, they nevertheless participate it

with the attribution of accidents to them; just as it is true, and necessary, that

their supreme genus participates the ratio of being with the attribution of ac‐

cidents to it in this predication, Substance is a being; otherwise it would not for‐

mally be a predication of the analogous term, which is plainly false.

To the argument of the other opinion it is replied, from the doctrine hand‐

ed down above, that proportionality in no way makes a name analogous per se:

whence, by the very fact that being is not predicated according to attribution,

it cannot be predicated as analogous. But of this we shall speak presently.

Second Part of the Question.

Whether being is analogous when compared to created and uncreated being, or to God

and creatures.

66

T     his comparison of being is different from the preceding ones, because be‐

ing is not taken in its universality with respect to substance and accident,

but with respect to God and creatures. And by creatures we do not under‐

stand accidents: for, since God is a substance, it is manifest from what was

said in the first part of the question that he cannot agree univocally with acci‐

dents under the name of being; therefore by the name of creatures only creat‐

ed substance is understood. Whence the sense of the question is whether cre‐

ated and uncreated substance agree univocally under the name of being.

And the first opinion asserts that being is not univocal to God and creatures, but

equivocal. St. Thomas made mention of this opinion, 1 p., q. 13, a. 5, and On

Power, q. 7, a. 7; and Auriol seems to hold it, on 1, d. 2, q. 1 (unless perhaps he

speaks of the equivocal in the common acceptation, as it comprehends the

analogous). And it can be proved: because created entity is of a far different ra‐

tio from the uncreated, and infinitely diverse from it: therefore it can have

nothing in common with the uncreated except the word alone. And this is for

the name signifying both to be equivocal.

The second opinion is that of Scotus, on 1, d. 3, q. 1 and 3, who asserts that

being, with respect to created and uncreated substance, has one common concept, distinct

from the nature of the thing from both, as he had said above of the concept of be‐

ing, and that it is therefore univocal. His disciples follow him.

67 It is proved by a sufficient division: being so compared is not equivocal,

nor is it analogous: therefore it will be univocal. It is proved

[p. 236]

the first part of the antecedent: for created substance is not altogether diverse from the uncreated, but similar to it: therefore it does not agree with it in the word alone, but in some way in the entity itself; wherefore being cannot be equivocal with respect to both. The second part is proved in this way: being is not analogous by analogy of proportionality, nor of attribution: therefore in no way. I prove the antecedent: because the name being, with respect to God and creatures, does not signify proportionality, which is necessary for it to be thus analogous: therefore it is not analogous by analogy of proportionality. But neither does it signify attribution: for the creature is a being simply, therefore not by attribution to God.

The third opinion is that of St. Thomas, 1 p., q. 13, a. 5: that being, with respect to God and creatures, is neither equivocal nor univocal, but analogous. Almost all now follow it, especially Ferrara, Contra Gentiles 1, ch. 32; Soto, q. 4 on the Antepredicaments; Father F. Suárez, in Metaph., disp. 28, sect. 3; Father Vázquez, 1 p., d. 22, ch. 5, at the end; and it is true and to be held. And that it is not equivocal, against the first opinion, has been effectively proved by the argument of the second opinion. But that it is not univocal, against the second, is proved by this argument: the analogous is that which is not participated equally nor simply by the analogates, but by one per se primarily and simply, and by another or others not per se primarily nor simply, but with essential attribution and dependence on that one; but being stands thus with respect to God and creature: therefore it is analogous and not univocal. The minor is proved: because entity belongs to God per se and from himself, and belongs to him simply; but to the creature, as it is a creature, not per se primarily nor from itself, but by participation, and therefore not simply, but in a certain respect.

68 To the argument of the first opinion: granting the antecedent, the consequence is to be denied. For although the distance between created and uncreated entity is infinite, there is nevertheless some similarity, signified through attribution, because created entity is a certain participation of the divine entity. And this suffices for them not to be altogether diverse, and for being not to be an equivocal name with respect to them.

To the argument of the second opinion: the antecedent is to be denied. And again, when it is proved that being does not signify God and creature according to attribution, because the creature is a being simply, a distinction is to be made. For the creature can be signified in two ways: first, by the name being; second, by the name created being, as it is signified in comparison with God through the name being, as common to created and uncreated being. And if it is taken in the first way, it is not signified with attribution to God, but absolutely, and therefore it is called a being simply; but signified in the second way,

[p. 237]

it says attribution, and by reason of it it is not called a being simply, but in a certain respect, that is, a being by participation. And from this it is had that the name being, as it signifies created and uncreated being, is analogous and not univocal.

By what analogy being is said with respect to substance and accident, and also with re‐

spect to God and creatures.

T     he first opinion is that of some moderns, who attribute both analogies,

of proportionality and of attribution, to being with respect to substance and accident, and also with respect to God and creatures. They prove this by this argument: that is analogous by analogy of proportionality and of attribution among whose analogates proportionality and attribution are found; but between substance and accident, and between created and uncreated being, both are found: therefore it will be called analogous by analogy of proportionality and of attribution. The minor is proved: for it is true, first of all, that as substance stands to its being, which it participates from being, so accident stands to its own, which it participates from the same: therefore they have proportionality among themselves. But concerning attribution it seems manifest: because accident is called a being by attribution to substance, and created being by participation and attribution to the uncreated.

69 The second opinion is that it is not analogous by analogy of attribution, but only of proportionality: because accident is called a being absolutely in the common way of speaking, and much more so created substance: therefore they are not beings by attribution. The consequence is proved: because what is such only by attribution to another is not called such simply, but in a certain respect, as is plain of urine and medicine.

The third opinion is that it is not analogous by analogy of proportionality, but only of attribution. This is in conformity with the doctrine of St. Thomas, and more probable; therefore the greater part of the moderns now follow it, but not all hold it in the same sense or for the same reason. For some grant that not only attribution is found among the analogates, but also proportionality, but that the latter does not make being analogous because it is not signified by it: for substance and accident are not signified by the name being inasmuch as each stands to its being as the other to its own, although they have this proportionality and can be conceived according to it by the intellect: therefore such proportionality does not make being analogous by analogy of proportionality. The consequence is proved: because things are not called analogates of some analogous name, nor is the name itself called analogous

[p. 238]

with respect to them unless it signifies them as they have such an analogy; but it cannot so signify them except by signifying the analogy: therefore, if it does not signify it, as it has been proved that being does not, it will not be called analogous by that analogy, although it is found among the things signified.

70 We, however, defend this opinion by another way (as we said above). For we grant that proportionality is found between both analogates of being; and we said that proportionality, whether it is signified by the analogous name or not, is not sufficient to make it analogous, as we proved above when treating of the species of analogy. Therefore there is not given an analogous term of proportionality, nor ought it to be called such, but an analogous term of attribution: because attribution alone is to be reputed true analogy, and it alone makes a name analogous, and it is always signified by the analogous name. For it is necessary that the analogy be signified by the name in order that it constitute it analogous. This was effectively proved by that argument for our view put forward by those who defend it by the other way.

But to the argument of the other opinion the antecedent is to be distinguished, when it is said that accident is called a being simply, and also created being. For that something is, or is called, a being simply can have a twofold sense. The first is that it is a being intrinsically and formally, and not by extrinsic denomination alone; and in this sense it is true that accident is a being simply, and also created being. The other sense is that something is a being without an addition; and in this way the analogous term is predicated simply of no less principal analogate, but of all of them with that addition (in a certain respect). And the reason for this is that, although it formally participates the ratio of the analogous term, it does so only through essential dependence and attribution to the principal analogate, and therefore only in a certain respect. To signify which, Aristotle asserted that accident is not a being, but a being of a being. And so one must speak of any other less principal analogate of any analogous term whatever, since it has been proved that every analogous term is of attribution. And this is also what that common saying signifies (The analogous term taken by itself stands for its more famous significate), whose sense is that, although it signifies all, it signifies only the principal one simply and without an addition. Wherefore, when an analogous term is uttered absolutely, it supposits for that one alone.

And if you say that from this it follows that this proposition is true, Every being is substance, and indeed that it is identical, which is proved thus: being taken absolutely supposits only for substance; therefore subject and predicate are the same: I reply that neither

[p. 239]

follows. Not the first, that the proposition is true: because the analogous term taken absolutely always signifies all its analogates, but is said to stand for the first alone if it is taken by itself, because the rest are not such without an addition; but in the subject of that proposition, Every being is substance, being is not taken absolutely or by itself, but with the addition of distribution, which is carried onto the analogous name according to the signification of the analogous term, and therefore onto all the analogates. Wherefore, just as it is not distributed for the principal one alone, so it does not supposit for that one alone; and therefore it is not a true proposition, because the predicate contains only one of the analogates, but the subject all of them distributively; and this is the reason why it cannot be verified of the subject. And that it is not identical is manifest from the same thing, since the subject signifies more than the predicate; and also from another: because, although the subject supposited only for substance, it does not signify it expressly and distinctly, but only confusedly, while in the predicate it is signified distinctly and expressly; and the different mode of signifying of predicate and subject suffices for the proposition not to be identical.

72 To the argument of the first opinion a twofold reply is given. First, by distinguishing the antecedent. For proportionality can be found among analogates in two ways. First, so that it is signified by the analogous name; and if it were found in this way, it would suffice to make it analogous. In another way it is found not signified, but such that the intellect can conceive it in them; and so it does not make a name analogous. And in this way it is found not only in analogous terms but in equivocals and univocals; but in the first way in none: but if some name were imposed by which the analogates were signified as they have proportionality, it would be analogous from that alone. But by the name being it is not signified; and therefore it is not proved that it is analogous by analogy of proportionality.

Second, it is replied by denying absolutely the antecedent, that proportionality of itself, whether signified or not signified, makes a name analogous: whence, although it is found among the significates of being, it does not follow that it is analogous by analogy of proportionality.

To the argument of the second: the antecedent is to be distinguished. For if being simply is the same as being intrinsically and formally, it is true; but if simply is taken as it is distinguished against in a certain respect, it is false, as we have proved; and since it comes from attribution that the less principal analogates are not called such except in a certain respect, it is not proved that being is not analogous by analogy of attribution.

[p. 240]

Whether accident is univocal to the nine categories of accidents, or analogous.

T      he greater difficulty concerns accident with respect to all accidents:

whether it is univocal or analogous. In which it must be presupposed, first, that the question does not proceed concerning accident taken most universally, as it is common to real accidents and accidents of reason: for so it is certain that it is analogous, since accidents of reason are not accidents except by similarity and attribution to real accidents; wherefore a common univocal concept cannot be abstracted from both. Second, it is certain that neither does it proceed concerning real accident as it signifies both intrinsic accidents, that is, those truly inhering in a subject, and real extrinsic denominations, such as rightness and the like, which are found here and there in the last six categories (although I, for my part, do not understand that a real category can be made from extrinsic denomination alone, as I shall prove in its place). For these denominations are not true accidents, but are so called only by attribution and similarity to those which inhere in a subject: whence, with respect to all of them, accident cannot be univocal. But we speak only of real accident, as it signifies only those things which inhere in subjects, concerning which we inquire whether it is univocal or analogous.

73 And the first opinion asserts that it is univocal. So Soto, q. 2 on the Antepredicaments, and many moderns; but they differ from Soto in this, that they assert it to be univocal in such a way that it is also a genus, constituting one category of all accidents, as substance constitutes one category of all substances; whereas Soto denies that it is a genus.

Two things can be proved for this opinion. The first, that accident is not analogous; the second, that it is univocal. And this second is customarily proved by exactly the same arguments by which it was proved above that being is univocal, and therefore they need not be repeated in this place; but only the first will be proved, from the definition of analogous terms. Analogous terms are those whose name is common, but the ratio of substance neither altogether the same nor altogether different; but the ratio of accident is altogether the same: therefore it is not analogous, but univocal. The minor is proved: the ratio of accident is to be in a subject; but to be in a subject belongs to all accidents not only formally and intrinsically, but also equally and simply: therefore it is not diverse in them, but the same.

74 To this argument it is customarily replied that, although accidents are not called such by attribution to one accident, yet

all

[p. 241]

all of them express attribution to substance and intrinsic dependence on it. And this suffices for them to be called analogically among themselves under the name of accident. But it is proved that this does not suffice, by a twofold argument. First, because in order that attribution constitute analogy, it must obtain among the analogated significates, just as analogy itself does; but substance is not an analogate of accident, since it is not signified by that name; therefore the attribution of accidents to it does not constitute accident as analogous, but only being, by which all of them are signified.

Second, attribution to substance belongs equally and primarily to all accidents, and also intrinsically and formally; therefore they agree univocally in it; but according to such attribution they are signified by the name of accident; therefore they are signified univocally, and not analogically.

The second opinion holds that accident is not univocal, but analogous. So Soncinas, Metaph. 4, q. 4, ad 1; Cajetan, On Being and Essence, ch. 7, q. 15, ad 4; Fr. Francisco Suárez in Metaph., disp. 59, q. 3; Father Vázquez, 1 p., d. 14, ch. 2; Fonseca, Metaph. 5, ch. 7, q. 1, sect. 4. And this is more probable and to be held.

But it is proved in different ways by different authors. The argument of some is the proportionality which is found among accidents: because just as one is related to its own being, which it participates from accident, so is the other related. And this suffices for accident to be analogous with respect to all. But this argument is insufficient: for, as we proved above, proportionality is not signified by the name, and therefore it does not suffice to make it analogous; and even if it were signified, it would not suffice.

75 Therefore others, who agree with us that attribution alone constitutes true analogy, say that attribution is found among accidents, because all are called such in order to quantity, by reason of which they inhere in the subject. But this is proved false: because no spiritual accident inheres by the mediation of quantity, for not all accidents are corporeal; for substantial generation inheres in prime matter before quantity, and so do the relation of the substantial whole to matter and form, and the relation of matter and form to each other; therefore it is false that they are so called through attribution to quantity.

Others, finally, prove that accident is not univocal because, at least with respect to absolute and relative accident, it cannot have a univocal ratio: for the concept abstracted from both is either absolute or relative. Not absolute, because it would not belong to the inferior relative accident. Nor can it be relative, because it would not belong to the inferior absolute accident; therefore neither can it be univocal. And if you say that it is neither relative nor absolute,

Q

[p. 242]

but that it abstracts from both rationes, as the other univocal terms abstract from the particular rationes of the univocates, this is proved to be false: because if such a concept abstracts from the relative and the absolute, by that very fact it must be absolute. For if it abstracts from the relative, then it no longer regards a term; but what does not regard a term is absolute; therefore such a concept will be absolute, and will not abstract from the absolute and the relative.

76 This argument, however, seems to me insufficient, because it does not prove that such a concept cannot abstract from the absolute and the relative, and therefore it does not prove that it cannot be univocal. For I shall say, then, that relation has a twofold concept. The first, by which it regards the subject, and this it has in common with absolute accidents. The second, by which it regards the term, and this is the special concept by which it is distinguished from the other categories; and through the first concept relation does not regard the term, but through the second it does. When, then, one argues thus: That concept does not regard a term; therefore it is absolute, the consequence must be denied, because a middle can be given between an absolute concept and one regarding a term; and such a middle is the concept abstracting from the absolute and the relative, which neither regards a term nor excludes respect to a term, but only expresses a common ratio, contractible through respect to a term and through an absolute ratio, which not only does not express respect to a term but excludes it, which the common concept abstracting from the relative and the absolute does not exclude. It is not proved, therefore, by that argument that accident cannot be univocal.

77 In order, then, that this may be proved efficaciously, the doctrine of St. Thomas, 1 p., q. 13, a. 5, must be noted, where, speaking of analogous terms, he says: An analogous name signifies in two ways: the attribution of one to another, or of many to one. And he gives an example of each in healthy, which is analogous by attribution with respect to medicine and animal through the attribution of one to the other: for medicine is called healthy because it is the cause of the animal’s health. But the same healthy is said analogically with respect to urine and medicine, not because one of these has attribution to the other, but because each is called such through attribution to a third, namely to the animal: urine as the sign of its health, medicine as the cause.

From this doctrine, applied to our purpose, an efficacious argument can be gathered for proving that accident is analogous. For each mode of attribution, namely of one to another or of many to one, makes a name analogous; but in accidents the second mode of attribution is found; therefore accident will be

[p. 243]

analogous by attribution with respect to them, just as healthy is with respect to urine and medicine. The consequence is proved: because all accidents are signified with an intrinsic attribution to substance. But against this one argues thus. For in the first place it seems that the argument is not well gathered from the doctrine of St. Thomas, nor to have any force for proving the analogy of accident: because St. Thomas assigns each of those modes of attribution among the significates of the same name, healthy, namely animal, urine, and medicine. And it is necessary that they be so signified, as this argument proves: analogy is found only among the significates of the same analogous name, and not among the significates of different names, as is clear from the definition: Analogous are those whose name is common, etc. But by the name of accident substance is not signified, but only accidents; therefore the attribution must obtain among these, in order that it make the name of accident analogous, so that the attribution be of one to another, or of many to one, signified by such a name; and it does not suffice that it be between them and substance, which is not signified by the same name.

78 This can be confirmed and declared at the same time: for the attribution of accidents to substance does indeed make an analogy of attribution of many to one in being, by which all are signified; but it cannot make an analogy in accident, by which not all are signified; just as it does not make an analogy in the name of substance, although substance is one analogate of being together with accidents; and for this reason accidents are attributed to it only because they are not signified by the name of substance. It does not seem, then, that it is efficaciously proved in this way that accident is analogous. The minor is proved: because from the fact that accidents are attributed to substance it follows only that they are not beings simply, but not that they are not accidents simply; therefore such attribution to substance makes an analogy in being, by which all are signified, not in accident. The consequence is proved: because it is necessary in all analogous terms that one be such simply, and the other or others in a certain respect.

These things notwithstanding, the express mind of St. Thomas is that such attribution suffices for analogy: because those two modes of attribution, of one to another and of many to one, cannot be distinguished as St. Thomas distinguishes them unless healthy, in which he affirms that both are contained, is also taken in two ways: first with respect to medicine and urine alone, then with respect to medicine and animal alone. For if it is taken with respect to all, it is necessary that several be attributed to the same thing; therefore the second attribution, which is of one to another, will have no place. The consequence is proved: because it is impossible to take being in order to the ten categories and to constitute in it the attribution of one to another; rather it is only of many to one: because

Q ij

[p. 244]

the attribution of one to another can be found only between two, not among many, unless all are taken for one; therefore it is impossible to constitute in healthy the attribution of one to another, that is, of medicine to animal, except by taking it as it signifies only these two; and consequently another, distinct mode of attribution is constituted, which is of many to one, by taking the same name as it signifies only those things which are attributed to a third.

79 But it is proved by argument that such attribution of many to one suffices, even if that one is not signified by the same name: because when the attribution of many to one is intrinsic to them, so that they are signified by such a name, the attribution is true and signified by the name, although that one to which the attribution is made is not signified by the name, no less than if it were signified by the name; therefore it no less suffices for an analogous name. The consequence is proved from the definition of analogous terms: because such a name signifies several things inasmuch as they have attribution; therefore it is analogous. Then because the attribution signified by the name is true analogy, and the things which are signified with such attribution are true analogates; it is irrelevant, therefore, that that with respect to which the attribution is made be signified by the name.

80 To the principal objection proposed, it is replied by denying, first, that this analogy is not according to the mind of St. Thomas; and then by denying also that St. Thomas places each mode of attribution, of one to another and of many to one, only among those things which are signified by the same name. For he expressly asserts that healthy, with respect to urine and medicine, is analogous by attribution of many to one; but with respect to medicine and animal, by attribution of one to another; therefore he does not take healthy as it signifies all. Nor does he consider this necessary, but takes it as it signifies the less principal things with attribution to the principal, even when the latter is not signified. The consequence is proved: because if he took it according to the entire signification of all, he could not distinguish each mode of attribution, since the attribution of one to another is only between two. Moreover, St. Thomas expressly teaches that any mode of attribution makes analogy per se; but the mode of attribution of many to one is found in the analogates even if that one is not signified by the name, as I have already proved; therefore it suffices to make an analogous name.

But to the argument, the antecedent must be distinguished: because the mode of attribution that makes a name analogous is twofold, as St. Thomas asserts: either of one to another, and according to this mode of attribution there cannot be analogy unless both are signified by the same name; or of many to one, and this mode is indeed found

[p. 245]

among the significates of the same name; but because it is in order to a third, it happens in either way, namely to a third signified by the same name or by a different one. And the reason for this is: because, since the things that are attributed to another are many, such attribution can be signified adequately and completely by the name common to all, or as it were inadequately and partially, which is as it were to be divided into total and partial. And so it is in healthy, and also in being and accident: for healthy can be taken in its entire signification, and then it makes a complete analogy; or it can be restricted to the less principal analogates alone, and it makes an analogy as it were incomplete or partial, but sufficient: because, since the attribution to the principal is intrinsic to them, they cannot be signified without it; and being signified with attribution, they cannot be signified except analogically. This is proved efficaciously: because it is repugnant to univocal terms to be signified with attribution to a principal analogate, with which they are apt to make an analogy; therefore they are analogates, whether the principal is signified by the same name or by a different one: an analogy indeed as it were inadequate and partial, but since, from the mode in which they are signified, they are apt to make a complete analogy under a more universal name by which all are signified. And in this way the analogy of accident is to be understood. Second, we could also reply that substance is in some way signified by the name of accident, not in recto but in obliquo, because accident is the same as being of a being, as Aristotle said, that is, being of substance; and it suffices that it be so signified in order that the attribution of accidents to substance may in some way be said to be among the significates of the same analogous name, and also in order that the name of accident may in some way be common to accidents and substance.

81 Nor is this contrary to the definition of analogy, which says that the analogous name is common to the analogates: for the name is common to those to which the attribution belongs, although it is not common to that to which they have attribution, because this is not an analogate of such a name, but those only.

To the confirmation, the antecedent must be denied, that the attribution of accidents to substance makes an analogy only in being and not in accident; rather it must be said that it makes it in both, because it is signified by both names; but in being it makes one as it were complete and total, in accident one incomplete and partial, because it intrinsically presupposes substance and intrinsically depends on it. But in the name of substance there is no analogy, because substance neither has attribution to accidents, nor, even if it had it, would it be signified by that name, as was proved above.

82 The other thing, finally, which is said in the same confirmation, that the attribution

Q iij

[p. 246]

of accidents to substance brings about only that they are beings in a certain re‐

spect, but not that they are accidents in a certain respect, must be granted; but

the consequence must be denied, that it does not make an analogy under the name

of accident. For analogy of attribution does not necessarily require that the analo‐

gates, or some one of them, be such in a certain respect under the particular name

by which they alone are signified; but it suffices that they be such in a certain re‐

spect with respect to that to which they are attributed: for from this it follows

that they are analogates together with it under a more universal name, with a com‐

plete and total analogy, and consequently with an incomplete and dependent anal‐

ogy under the particular name by which they are signified, under which it is not

necessary that they be called such in a certain respect. But that being in a certain

respect which they have from their own nature is said of them simply, as they are

signified by the particular name, and therefore under it they are called such in a

certain respect simply (if we may speak so). And this is plain in accidents: for to be

called accidents simply in a certain respect is nothing other than to be called sim‐

ply beings in a certain respect, which will also be said of healthy with respect to

medicine and urine alone. Indeed, from this it is quite clearly understood that they

are signified analogically by both names, since they are signified by both names

with attribution, and on account of that same attribution with which they are sig‐

nified it comes about that, signified under both names, they are called such in a

certain respect, formally or presuppositively, by a presupposition intrinsic to them;

all of which are repugnant to univocal terms. And if it is finally objected that all

powers are ordered to their object, and that this does not suffice for power in

common to be analogous to them, I reply that this does not express an order of at‐

tribution, as accidents have to substance, but only of specification, and therefore

they are not analogates.

Whether accident must be a genus, if it is univocal. 84

M      any of those who hold that accident is univocal deny that it is a genus, as

Javelli and Soto in the places cited above; but they do not assign the same

reason. For Javelli says that it is not a genus because it is not outside the ratio of

the differences and modes; but since it is transcendental, it is necessarily included

in them; and this is against the ratio of genus, which, as we proved above, must be

outside the ratio of the differences; otherwise it could not be contracted by them.

85 This argument, however, is insufficient, because, as we proved above, acci‐

dent cannot be included in the intrinsic modes and ultimate differences without

also including them in itself in act, although confusedly, since they are certain acci‐

dental entities; but including them it cannot have a concept abstracted from

them, as is clear:

[p. 247]

therefore neither is it univocal. The consequence is proved: because such a

concept does not abstract from diversity but includes it; therefore it is not

univocal, if it is not a genus.

The second opinion is that of Soto, who asserts that accident is not a genus,

although it is univocal, because genus pertains to the quiddity of the species; but accident

does not signify the quiddity of accidents, but their being in substance; therefore it is not

a genus. But this is proved false by a twofold argument. The first, because it

pertains no less to the ratio of the univocal than to the ratio of genus to be of

the quiddity of the inferiors; if, then, accident is not a genus because it does

not express the quiddity of accidents, it follows by the same argument that it

is not univocal. The major is proved from the definition of univocal terms: For

univocal are those whose name is common, and the ratio of substance the same. But by

the ratio of substance Aristotle and everyone understand the definition, or

the quidditative concept in those things that lack a definition; therefore it is

repugnant that something be univocal and not be of the quiddity of the

inferiors.

The second, because it is false that accident does not express the quiddity

of accidents, which I prove thus: being pertains to the quiddity of particular

beings, and is divided, as such, into substance and accident, as into opposed

members adequate to its ratio; but substance expresses the quiddity of the in‐

ferior substances; therefore accident expresses the quiddity of the inferior

accidents.

Our view, then, is that accident cannot be univocal without by that very fact be‐

ing the genus of all accidents; whence whoever asserts that it is univocal must

consequently say that it is a genus. This is proved: because no sufficient rea‐

son can be assigned for excluding the univocal from the ratio of genus, as has

been proved from the refutation of the other opinions.

Whether at least with respect to some accidents, or categories, accident can be univocal.

56

T     he first opinion holds that accident with respect to some accidents, such as

quantity and quality, and perhaps also the other intrinsic ones, is univocal. So

Father Francisco Suárez in Metaph., disp. 39, sect. 3, no. 15; and he proves it by

this argument: accident with respect to these is not analogous by proportion‐

ality nor by attribution; therefore it has no analogy, but is univocal. The con‐

sequence is evident, because no one posits more modes of analogy. But the

antecedent is proved: because analogous terms of proportionality have no in‐

trinsic agreement, as is plain in the laughter of a man and of a meadow; but

these accidents have an agreement

Q iiij

[p. 248]

that is intrinsic, since all of them really inhere in the subject; therefore accident cannot be analogous by proportionality with respect to them. And concerning analogy of attribution he proves it because none of these accidents is called such through attribution to another, as is quite manifest; therefore accident with respect to them is not analogous by attribution.

87 Our view, however, is the opposite: that not even with respect to these accidents can accident be univocal, but it is analogous. This is proved by a twofold argument. The first, because just as accident with respect to all accidents cannot be abstracted from their intrinsic modes, so neither with respect to the intrinsic accidents can it be abstracted from their modes; therefore, just as it is not univocal but analogous with respect to all, so too with respect to these. The antecedent is proved: because the reason why with respect to all it cannot be abstracted from the modes is that the modes are nothing other than certain accidental entities, signified more expressly, and therefore it is necessary that they be comprehended in act, although confusedly, under the universal signification of accident. This supposed, the concept of accident can be neither abstracted nor one, but is related in the same way to the intrinsic accidents, if it is compared with them alone, as is plain of itself; therefore neither with respect to them can it be univocal.

88 That it is analogous is proved by the same argument by which we proved that it is analogous with respect to all: because the intrinsic accidents are signified with attribution to substance, just as healthy is, if it is taken only with respect to the extrinsic healthy things, which are urine and medicine; therefore it contains the mode of attribution of many to one, sufficient to make a name analogous, as has been proved.

To the argument of the other opinion, the antecedent must be denied, that accident with respect to the intrinsic ones is not analogous by attribution. Because although it does not signify them with the mode of attribution of one to another, it does signify them with the attribution of many to one, namely to substance, of which they are something, and they are signified as something of it, as we said of accident with respect to all.

From which it follows by what analogy accident is analogous, both with respect to all accidents and with respect to the intrinsic ones alone: namely, by the analogy of attribution of many to one.

But whether with respect to complete accidents it can be univocal, or rather is analogous, must be answered in the same way, and it must be proved that it is not univocal but analogous by the same arguments by which it was proved of being in order to incomplete beings alone. And let these things suffice concerning the analogy of names.

[p. 249]

Are.

## CHAPTER II

On the division of the things that are said and that are.

## TEXT OF ARISTOTLE

Of the things that are, some are said of some subject, but are in no subject, etc.

E X P O S I T I O N O F T H E T E X T.

he intent of Aristotle is to hand down two divisions, one of the 1

T          things that are said, the other of the things that are; in this alone

he is occupied in the whole chapter, which therefore does not

need division.

The first division is not of things but of words, as they signify things, be‐

cause combination does not belong to things but to words, as they signify

them. Aristotle therefore asserts: Of the things that are said, some are said with

combination, others without combination; as if to say that of the words which sig‐

nify things, some are complex, as white man, others incomplex, as color or ani‐

mal. Which is the same as if it were said that some are simple, others

composite.

The second division is of things. But in order that it may be understood,

it should be noted that to be in a subject and to be said of a subject are taken by

Aristotle in this chapter in a particular way. For to be in a subject is taken for

true and real inherence in it; and to be said of a subject, as of a quidditatively

inferior thing, as animal of man and man of Peter.

This supposed, the division is as follows: Of the things that are, some are

said of a subject and are not in a subject, as man, which is said of Peter, yet is

not in him by real inherence but substantially, and therefore not as in a sub‐

ject. Others are in a subject, but are said of no subject, as singular accidents: for

this whiteness inheres in the wall, but is said of no subject, because it does

not have quidditatively inferior things of which it could be predicated, al‐

though it is said accidentally of the wall and of other bodies. Others are said of

a subject and are in a subject, as accidents abstracted from their inferiors, name‐

ly the genus from the species and the species from the individuals: for color is

said of whiteness and blackness, and inheres in the wall and in man. Others, fi‐

nally, are neither in a subject nor said of a subject, as singular substances, Peter and

John.

[p. 250]

## CHAPTER III

On the rules of essential predicates.

## TEXT OF ARISTOTLE

When one thing is predicated of another as of a subject, whatever things are said of that

which is predicated will all be said of the subject too.

E X P O S I T I O N O F T H E T E X T.

he intent of Aristotle is to hand down two rules of essential predicates, 1

T          and in this alone he is occupied in that whole chapter. The first rule is:

When something is predicated of something as of a subject, that is, as of a

quidditatively inferior thing, whatever things are said of the predicate must be predicated

of the subject. So it is with whatever predicates are placed in the categorial straight

line: as animal is predicated of man and lion, and therefore whatever things are

predicated of animal must be predicated of man.

The second rule is more obscure, and runs thus in the translation of Boethius:

Of diverse genera, and not placed subalternately, the differences are diverse in species, as of

animal and of science. But if they are placed subalternately, they can have the same

differences: as animal and living have the same difference, because the differences

of living are included in animal.

## SINGLE QUESTION

Whether genera not placed subalternately can have some common difference.

2

T     his question has two parts. The first asks what Aristotle understands by genera

placed subalternately, and not placed subalternately. The second, whether they can

have some common difference.

First Part of the Question.

O     n the first part there are two opinions. The first asserts that genera placed sub‐

alternately are only those of which one is placed under the other, as animal

and living; and not placed subalternately those of which one is not under the other,

but both are under a third, as animal and plant; or also those of which neither is

one under the other nor both under a third, as are those that are placed in differ‐

ent categories, such as animal and science. So Soto in his exposition of this rule.

He proves it by two testimonies of Aristotle. The first is in this chapter, where,

according to the translation of Argyropoulos, those are called genera subalternately

[p. 251]

placed of which one is under the other, and not placed subalternately those of which one is not under the other. The other testimony is found in Topics 1, ch. 15, where Aristotle calls subalternate genera genera placed subalternately; but subalternate genera are those of which one is under the other; therefore not placed subalternately were those of which one is not under the other, although both are under a third.

He proves it next by reason: because if by genera placed subalternately are understood not only those of which one is under the other, but also those which are under a third, it follows that genera not placed subalternately are only those which are in different categories, of which it is evident that they cannot have a common difference, since they are in a different grade of being; so that this rule would have no difficulty. Which nevertheless all the interpreters make difficult.

3 Our view is that by genera placed subalternately are understood not only those of which one is under the other, but also those which are under a third; and therefore that those not placed subalternately are only those which are in different categories.

This is proved by an express testimony of Aristotle, Topics 6, ch. 2, locus 41, where he asserts two things. The first: That not only are those called subalternate genera of which one is under the other, but also those which are under a third. The second: That those genera which are under a third have a common difference: as walking animal and flying animal have biped as a common difference. From which it follows that either they are not called not placed subalternately, or Aristotle’s rule is false, that genera not placed subalternately cannot have a common difference.

It is proved next by reason. First, because genera not placed subalternately, according to Aristotle, cannot have a common difference; but those of which one is not under the other, but both under a third, have a common difference; therefore they are not called not placed subalternately by Aristotle. The minor is proved: because quantity is divided into successive and permanent, as into two genera of which one is not under the other, and they have a common difference: for the difference of the continuous is common to both, and also the difference of the discrete, since both permanent and successive quantity are divided into continuous and discrete.

Second, because subalternate genera and genera placed subalternately are the same; but those of which each is under a third are subalternate with respect to it, since each is under it; therefore they will be placed subalternately.

To the first testimony it is replied that, since a different

[p. 252]

way it is found in different translations, it must be explained and understood

through that express passage cited by us, in which there can be no doubt that

our view is contained.

To the other testimony we say that subalternate genera, or genera placed subalter‐

nately, comprehend both: namely, those of which one is under the other, and

those of which both are under a third.

To the argument: the antecedent must be granted together with the conse‐

quence, and it must be said that Aristotle’s rule, as far as this part is concerned,

is very clear if it is understood through other express testimonies of the same au‐

thor; but those who did not see the aforesaid testimonies have made it difficult.

Second Part of the Question. 4

T     he second part of the question asks whether genera not placed subalternately can

have a common difference. In order that this may be better understood, it

should be noted that difference is twofold: Constitutive and Divisive; and also

Superior and Inferior. As sensible is constitutive of animal and divisive of living;

and corporeal is a superior difference with respect to living, but sensible an inferior

one with respect to the same. The question, then, is understood of the inferior

divisive difference: for concerning the superior ones there is no doubt that they

can be common. On this the first opinion is that of Scotus, who asserts that gen‐

era not placed subalternately, of which one is not under the other in the same category, but

each is under a third, cannot have a common difference, and much less the genera of differ‐

ent categories. Others also follow him, even if they say with us that these are

placed subalternately.

They prove it by a twofold testimony of Aristotle: Topics 1, ch. 2, locus 22,

where he affirms that the genus is predicated of more things than the difference. The sec‐

ond is found in On the Parts of Animals 1, ch. 3, where he says that there are as many

differences as there are species. But if the same difference is common to two genera

which are under a third, each will be false; therefore it is not to be admitted. The

minor is proved: for if the same divisive difference of living is common to two

subalternate species contained under it, since the genus is predicated of them,

this common difference will also be predicated of them, and therefore the differ‐

ence will not be predicated of fewer things than the genus. And moreover, the

differences will be fewer in number than the species, since one difference is com‐

mon to two species.

They prove it next by reason: because just as it is repugnant that the same in‐

dividual be under two species, so it is repugnant that the same species be under

two genera; but if the same Divisive difference is common to two genera, it fol‐

lows that the same species is contained under

[p. 253]

two genera; therefore it will be impossible. The minor is proved: because the Divisive difference of a genus constitutes a species under it, as rational, dividing animal, constitutes man under it; therefore if animal and plant have a common difference, such a difference will constitute a species under each genus, and the same species will be of animal and of plant, which is absurd.

The second opinion holds that genera not placed subalternately do not always or necessarily have a common difference, but that some can have one. And this is more probable and to be held. And it is explained by two conclusions. The first: Genera placed subalternately, of which one is under the other, have all the Constitutive differences of the superior genera in common, and some Divisive ones, though not all. For example: Animal and living have in common the Divisive difference of substance, such as corporeal, and also the Constitutive difference of body; but neither has the Constitutive difference of the other, which is the Divisive difference of the proximate genus. So Aristotle in the last words of this chapter. And it is evidently gathered from the first rule of this chapter: because if the superior genus is predicated of the inferior genera, which are subalternate species, it follows that the Constitutive difference of the same superior genus, which constitutes it and is predicated of it, is predicated of them.

The second conclusion: Genera not placed subalternately according to the first opinion, of which one is not under the other but each is under a third, have the same Constitutive differences of the superior genera in common; and they can have some Divisive difference of the superior genus in common, although they do not necessarily or always have it; but the genera of different categories, which alone are called not placed subalternately, have none. The first part of this conclusion is evident in animal and plant, which have the Divisive and Constitutive difference of body in common. The second is expressly found in Aristotle, Topics 6, ch. 2, locus 41, where he proves it by this argument: Animal is divided into walking and flying, as into diverse subalternate species, and therefore into diverse genera which have other species under them; and yet the difference biped is common to each genus; therefore two genera not placed subalternately have a common Divisive difference of the superior genus. Aristotle, however, uses these differences in place of the essential ones, which we do not know. And this is confirmed: because quantity is divided into successive and permanent as into diverse subalternate species, of which one is not under the other but each is under a third, and they have the common differences of continuous and discrete. But if it is asked what the reason is why such genera do not always or necessarily have a difference

[p. 254]

in common, but some have it and others do not: I reply that the reason is that some are more similar to others, and therefore can have a greater agreement.
