For the solution of the argument, it should be noted first that the common difference which those genera sometimes have, of which one is not under the other but each is under a third, by the very fact that it is common, is not ultimately Constitutive of them: because the ultimately Constitutive difference distinguishes the species which it constitutes from any other whatever; but the common difference does not distinguish among themselves those species to which it is common; therefore it is not ultimately constitutive of them. For example: the differences of continuous and discrete, common to permanent and successive quantity, do not distinguish these among themselves, but only continuous quantity from discrete; and therefore they are ultimately constitutive of these, not of those.

It should be noted second that some differences are universal, which divide the whole line of the category, as corporeal and incorporeal; others particular, dividing only one or another particular genus of some partial line, as the differences dividing animal. And therefore genera too are twofold: some universal, each of which contains an entire line, as body and spirit; others particular, of partial lines, as animal or plant. And universal differences cannot be common, nor can universal genera have any common difference. And the reason for this is manifest: because universal differences have a universal opposition; but particular ones are not opposed, formally opposed, but diverse; therefore it is repugnant that the former be common, not the latter. It should be noted third that when we say that universal genera which are contained under a third cannot have a common difference, and that particular ones can, we are not speaking of the Constitutive difference of the superior genus, which it is certain and necessary that they have in common: for body and spirit are universal genera, and they have the common intrinsic mode of substance, which, although it is not a difference, because substance is not a genus, is nevertheless similar to a superior difference, and would include it no less if it were a true difference. And the reason for this is evident: because whatever is included in the superior predicate must be included in the inferior; but the Constitutive difference of the superior genus is included in it; therefore it must necessarily be included in any inferior genus whatever. We are speaking, then, of the Divisive difference of the superior genus, of which we say that it can be common to the inferiors, although this is not necessary nor does it always happen, but sometimes, as the difference

[p. 255]

of continuous and discrete, which are divisive of quantity, are common to permanent and successive quantity.

6 It should be noted fourth that this Divisive difference of the superior genus, which we say can be common to two genera contained under it, is not adequate to either of them but inadequate, so that they are adequately constituted through other differences distinct from it. For example: biped is a common difference of walking and flying animal, but inadequate to each, because they are adequately constituted through the proper differences walking and flying.

From these things one would reply to each testimony of Aristotle by denying the minor, namely that from our view it follows that the genus is not predicated of more things than the difference, or that there are not as many differences as there are species. For neither follows. For since the difference which can be common to two genera that are contained under a third, superior genus is not Constitutive of that superior genus but Divisive, it is therefore necessary that the inferior be predicated of fewer things than the genus itself, as biped of fewer than animal. And it is of this that Aristotle speaks in the first testimony, not of the constitutive difference, of which it is manifest that it is predicated of altogether the same things of which the genus that it constitutes is predicated: for sensible is predicated of as many things as animal is predicated of. And what Aristotle said in the second testimony, that there are as many differences as there are species, is most true: for although one may be common to two subalternate species placed under a third, superior genus, it is nevertheless not ultimately constitutive of them, but they have others through which they are constituted and distinguished. But that which is common, although it does not constitute them adequately, nevertheless has its own proper species, which it constitutes adequately: as biped does not adequately constitute flying or walking animal, but adequately constitutes animal having two feet. Whence it is understood that, even if one inadequate difference is common to two species, there are nonetheless as many differences as species, since there is no species which does not have its proper adequately constitutive difference, nor any difference which does not adequately constitute its own species.

To the argument: the antecedent must be denied, that just as the same individual cannot be under two species, so one species cannot be under two genera; for the ratio of the individual and of the species is different. For the individual difference adequately and ultimately determines the species, and therefore it is repugnant that the same individual difference determine two different species; but the specific difference, since it is a common predicate, and

[p. 256]

can belong inadequately to two, and constitute neither adequately or ultimate‐

ly, it can consequently be common to them.

C H A P T E R I V.

Containing the division of incomplexes into ten categories.

## TEXT OF ARISTOTLE

Of the things that are said without any combination, each one signifies either substance,

or quantity, etc.

E X P O S I T I O N O F T H E T E X T.

he intent of Aristotle in the present chapter is to explain that those 1

T            things of which the categories are to be constituted must be simple.

And it is divided into two parts, in the first of which Aristotle sets

down the universal division of incomplexes into ten categories. In the second he as‐

serts and proves that the same incomplexes of which a category is made are not affirma‐

tions or negations, but that affirmations and negations can be made from them.

The division is as follows: Of incomplex or simple being, one is substance, as

man or horse; another quantity, as body or line; another quality, as white; an‐

other relation, as double, half; another where, as to be in the forum; another

when, as yesterday or today; another position, as to lie, to sit; another having,

as to be armed; another acting, as to cut; another being acted upon, as to be

cut.

But these simple things (says Aristotle in the second part), considered in them‐

selves, are not affirmations nor negations, although, if they are united by some verb or cop‐

ula, affirmations and negations can be made from them. Which he proves thus: Every

affirmation and negation is true or false; but simple things, as man, or whiteness, taken by

themselves, do not express truth or falsity, as is known; therefore they are not affirmations

or negations. But if you join them by some verb, you will at once make an affirmation or

negation: as, if you add the verb is to man and white, there will result this affirmation,

Man is white, in which truth or falsity is now found.

## QUESTION I

Of which things the category is composed per se.

1

T     here are five things concerning which it can be doubted whether and how

they pertain to the category, so that, once those things are excluded which

cannot

[p. 257]

cannot pertain to it, it may be understood of which things it is composed per se. The first is the being of reason, which seems to pertain primarily to the category from this: that a category, like a proposition or a syllogism, is a certain being of reason; therefore the being of reason will pertain to the category not in just any way, but formally.

Second, a category is made of genera and species; but genera and species are beings of reason; therefore a category will be made of beings of reason.

The true view, however, is that it is made of real beings alone, and therefore that beings of reason do not pertain to the category, except that, through a certain likeness in the ratio of being, we can devise a certain category, or rather a likeness of a category, as we said in our treatise on the nature of the being of reason. So hold St. Thomas, Metaph. 5, lect. 9, and On Power, q. 7, a. 9; Capreolus on 1, d. 8, q. 2, and d. 29, q. 1, ad 5; Soto, ch. 4 of the Antepredicaments, q. 2, ad 4; Fonseca, Metaph. 5, ch. 7, q. 6, sect. 1; and all the others.

This is proved by the testimony of Aristotle, Metaph. 5, ch. 7, text 14, where he teaches that beings per se are divided into ten categories; but being per se, in his usage (wherever he speaks of it), and real being are the same.

It is proved next by reason: because beings of reason have neither true entity nor true essence, but one devised by the intellect after the likeness of real entity and essence; but a true category must be made of true being, having both entity and essence; therefore it is not made of beings of reason, but only of real beings. Which will be clear if we run through the categories one by one: for we shall see that the category of substance, of quality, and of quantity is made of true real natures.

3 But for the solution of the argument it should be noted that a category is made of real predicates, yet not of predicates distinct really or from the nature of the thing: because, as we proved in the chapter on difference, genus and difference are real objective concepts of the same thing, signifying different essential grades, and distinguished only by the intellect. But the species is composed of them, not as a third thing distinct from them, but as a third objective concept, total and complete; and therefore the composition is not real but of reason, because, although the composing and the composite concepts are real, they are nevertheless not distinct except by reason; wherefore they cannot make a real composition. So, then, it must be understood of the category that it is made by the intellect distinguishing the essential predicates, so that, just as before its operation there are no distinct predicates, and therefore no plurality, so a category cannot be given,

R

[p. 258]

but it is the work of the same intellect, which, distinguishing the predicates,

orders and disposes them, and makes a category out of them.

4 It should be noted second that a category is considered in two ways.

First, as it were for its matter, namely for the natures of things and their predi‐

cates, which are ordered in the categorial line; and so taken it is real, because

both the essential predicates and the natures in which they are founded are

real, although not really distinct. In the second way it is considered as it were

for its formal element, that is, for the very ordering and disposition of the

predicates, which necessarily supposes their distinction; and taken in this way

it is not something real but of reason. Whence it follows that the category

taken formally is a being of reason, and for its foundation is a real being; and

in this second way it is considered by Metaphysics, but in the first way by

Dialectic.

These things explained, we reply to both arguments at once by granting

that genera, species, and the category, taken formally, are beings of reason; but

we deny that they pertain in any way to the category: because only those

things are said to pertain to the category of which the category is made; but

the category is made only of the predicates which are ordered in it, and not of

the ordering itself, just as other artificial beings are said to be made only of

their matter, as a statue of wood, a house of timbers and stones; therefore be‐

ings of reason do not pertain to the category, nor do genera and species taken

formally, but only taken for their real foundations.

On Complexes. 5

T    he second thing about which it can be doubted is complexes, which are

distinguished by some thus: some are complexes which signify only one

thing, and are equivalent to a simple word signifying it. And such are the defi‐

nitions of substances, as rational animal or sensible living thing. Others are com‐

plexes which signify not one thing but several. And such are the definitions of

accidents, in which, besides those things which pertain to the essence of the

accident, the subject is included, so that through it the intrinsic order of the

accident to it may be explained. And the former complexes pertain per se to

the category, but the latter must be excluded from it.

This is proved from Porphyry, in the chapter on species, where, constitut‐

ing the category of substance, he placed ensouled body as the genus of living

thing, and also rational animal as a certain genus in which he thought men

agree with demons; but these are substantial complexes; therefore according

to the mind of Porphyry they are to be placed in the categories.

[p. 259]

Next by reason: because in place of the thing defined it is permitted to put its definition, including nothing extrinsic, as rational animal in place of man, because such a definition is equivalent to the simple thing defined; therefore in the categorial straight line it will be permitted to put in place of any genus and species its proper definition, which, since it is something complex, it follows that a category is made per se of substantial complexes.

6 Our view is the opposite: that no complex pertains to the category. And it is expressly found in Aristotle, in the present chapter, where he speaks thus: Of the things that are said without any combination, each one signifies either substance, or quantity, or quality, or relation, etc. By which words he excludes all complexes from the category, whether they are substantial or accidental, and divides only incomplex being into ten categories.

But it is proved by reason: because the categorial straight line is made of genera and species alone, as in the category of substance, of substance, body, living thing, animal, and man; but complexes, whether they are definitions of substances or of accidents, are not genera or species; therefore a category is not made of them. Which is proved also from its definition: for a category is an ordering of predicables; but predicables are certain universals, of whose ratio it is to be simple, as we saw in the last question on universals; therefore a category is made of simple things alone, not of complexes.

7 To Porphyry it is replied that he placed complexes in place of simple things not because he understood that they pertain to the categories, but either for the sake of greater explanation, or because he did not know the simple genera. For the first reason he placed ensouled body for living thing; and for the second, rational animal as the genus of men and demons.

To the argument, however, we deny that it is always permitted to put the definition, even one including nothing extrinsic, in place of the thing defined; rather it is permitted only as regards the equivalence of truth, because of whatever things the thing defined is predicated, the definition must be predicated; but where the mode of signifying must be determinate, and is distinct in the definition and in the thing defined, it is not permitted to put it in place of the thing defined. And so it is in the case at hand, because a thing is not placed in a category as signified or conceived in just any way, but by way of a genus or species, and therefore by way of an incomplex. Since, then, the definition, by reason of its being complex, does not have the mode of a genus or species, it follows that it does not have the categorial mode either; wherefore it cannot be placed in the category in place of the thing defined. To the form of the argument, then: when it is said, Although the definition is

R ij

[p. 260]

complex, it is equivalent to the simple thing defined, the antecedent must be distinguished: it is as it were equivalent to the thing defined as regards the truth of the thing, but not as regards the simple mode of signifying, which is altogether necessary for the categorial line; and therefore it cannot be placed in its stead in the category, although it may be so placed in a proposition or in other cases.

On Physical and Metaphysical Parts.

T     he parts of a thing are twofold, Physical and Metaphysical. And the

Physical parts are again twofold: some are Essential, as matter and form, and others Integral, which again are of two kinds: for some are of the same ratio, as the parts of water or of wood, and therefore they are usually called homogeneous; others of a different ratio, as the head and the hands, and they are called heterogeneous; and the integral parts, which are not essential, can be called substantial or entitative. The Metaphysical parts are genus and difference: but concerning the genus it is certain that it pertains per se to the category, because it has the mode of a complete substance. The question therefore proceeds concerning the difference alone, as concerning the Metaphysical parts, and concerning matter and form and the integral parts, as the Physical ones: whether they are per se in the category. And first we must speak of these, then of the Metaphysical parts.

But first it must be explained what it is to pertain per se to the category. There are two things in a category. The first is the very series or categorial ordering of superiors and inferiors, from which is made as it were a certain straight line, through which we can ascend and descend from the individual, which is the foundation of the whole line, up to the supreme genus, which is as it were its head. So the line of the category of substance proceeds from the supreme genus, which is substance, through its division into species, which are body and spirit; and again through the division of body into living and non-living; then through the division of living into animal and plant; and finally through the division of animal into man, horse, and lion. And from these divisions of genera into species through differences there results this line, which is called the series or ordering: namely substance, body, living thing, animal, man, Peter. And it is for this straight line that the category stands whenever we speak of it. But besides this the category has as it were two sides, by which it is as it were surrounded, and these sides are made of the opposed differences through which the genus is divided into species. As one side of the same category of substance is best known to us from these four differences: corporeal, animate, sensitive, rational,

[p. 261]

From this it is now understood what it is to be per se in a category, or what things a category is made of per se: for it is the same as to be placed in the straight categorial line, or for the same straight line to be made out of something; for the sides of a category are outside it, and as it were its ornament. When, therefore, we ask concerning parts, both Physical and Metaphysical, whether they are per se in a category, or whether a category is made of them, the sense is: whether they are per se in the straight categorial line.

And concerning Physical parts the first opinion holds that they are placed per se in the category; so Villalpando and the Louvain commentators, ch. on substance, whom others follow. They prove it first: because a complete substance is composed essentially of matter and form, and is integrated substantially out of integral parts; therefore it is repugnant that a complete substance be placed per se in the category without the parts also being placed there, and indeed per se, since they compose it per se.

Second, because in the parts of substance we understand genera and species; therefore a category can be ordered out of these, just as it is ordered out of the genera and species of total substance. The antecedent is proved: because just as we divide complete substance into corporeal and incorporeal, and so on with the other genera, so we can divide partial substance.

10 And it can be confirmed concerning homogeneous parts: because they are of the same ratio as the whole substance, and by division they can become complete substances: as, if we divide water, we shall make as many complete substances as we separate parts; for after they have been separated they neither depend on the whole substance nor are parts of it, but each begins to be a complete substance; therefore it also pertains per se to the category.

The second opinion excludes the Physical parts of substance from the category; and it is that of St. Thomas, 1 p., q. 29, a. 4, ad 5, and On Truth, q. 27, a. 1, ad 8; of Scotus, q. 15 on the Categories; of Giles of Rome, on d. 2, q. 3; of Cajetan and Soto, ch. on substance; of Toledo, q. 5 on the same category; of Fonseca, Metaph. 5, ch. 7, q. 7, sect. 2, and ch. 8, q. 3. And this is true and to be held.

It is proved first: because a category is made per se only out of genera and species, as we have already shown; but the genera and species are complete substances; therefore the parts, which are incomplete substances, cannot constitute the category per se, or be placed in it per se.

11 Second, nothing univocal common to complete and incomplete substance is given; therefore neither will a genus common to both be given, under which the incomplete could be placed; wherefore they do not pertain

R iij

[p. 262]

per se to the category.

To the first: the antecedent is to be granted, but the consequence denied; because things do not pertain to the category according to the entity they have on the side of the thing, but according to the mode in which such an entity is conceived by the intellect; and this mode, necessary for the constitution of the category, must be that of a complete entity. Hence, since the parts are only incomplete beings, they cannot, as such, make up a category per se, although they compose per se the complete substance out of which it is made per se. The only thing that can be granted to the parts is that they are placed reductively, or as it were indirectly, in the straight categorial line, where the species or genus whose parts they are is placed.

To the second: it is to be denied that true genera and true species can be understood in the parts; only concepts in some way similar to genera and species can be formed out of them. And the reason is that the parts cannot be conceived except as incomplete, although in common they are conceived abstracted from the singular parts, in which some similarity consists; and since genera and species, by the proper mode in which they are conceived, are complete, it is repugnant to conceive true genera and true species in the parts, or that there be a true categorial ordering among them.

12 To the confirmation concerning homogeneous integral parts, we grant that they are of the same ratio as the whole as regards entity, and also that they can become complete substances; we deny, however, that they pertain per se to the category. And the reason is that as long as they are in the whole they depend on it and have an incomplete mode of being. That they can be separated from it proves only that, once they have been separated, they will pertain per se to the category, because they will then no longer be parts; but this is only to be able to pertain, not to pertain in act.

But concerning Metaphysical parts, such as the differences are, some, whom Fonseca cites, Metaph. 5, ch. 8, q. 2, have said that they pertain to the category of quality, since they are predicated of the species in quale quid. But this is plainly false: because although they have some similarity with qualities in their mode of predicating, they are truly essential concepts, and as such they are conceived by the intellect, which composes the species out of them together with the genera; therefore they are not truly qualities, nor are they conceived as truly quality, but through a certain likeness to them; and therefore they cannot pertain to the category of quality. The only thing that can be doubtful is whether each of the differences pertains per se to that category in which the genera they divide and the species they constitute are placed.

13 And the first opinion is that of Ammonius, ch. on substance, who asserts

[p. 263]

that any differences whatever pertain per se to their own category; which he proves by this argument. For either the differences are excluded from the category because they are simple concepts, or because they are incomplete; but both reasons concur in the genera; therefore either the genera must be excluded or the differences placed there; but the genera cannot be excluded, as is known; therefore neither must the differences be excluded. The minor is proved: because the concept of the genus as such is not composite, although, if it is a subalternate species, it is composed inasmuch as it is a species; therefore it is simple; and it is a true part of the species no less than the difference; therefore something incomplete.

Nor is the argument solved if it is said that the genus is a potential whole: because the difference too is an actual whole, as it is predicated of the species, containing the whole that the species contains; for as a part it could not be predicated of it; therefore it will pertain to the category just as the genus does.

The common opinion of all the expositors, in the present chapter and the following, excludes the differences from the straight categorial line, and only grants them that they constitute the sides of the category; which is to be simply outside the category.

14 And it is proved by a twofold argument. First: the difference, taken formally, signifies only a part of the species; therefore formally it is something incomplete; but the straight line of the category is constituted only out of complete predicates, which are the genera and species; therefore the differences do not pertain per se to it.

And if you say that it includes the whole that the species includes, since it includes the genus at least materially, and therefore has the mode of a complete whole, just as the genus, from this alone, that it includes the differences in potency, is said to have the mode of a complete whole and to pertain per se to the category: against these it is that the difference includes the genus in the same way as an accident in the concrete does, namely by way of a subject, and therefore it is signified by an adjectival name, as rational; wherefore it does not include per se the whole that the species includes, but as it were per accidens; hence neither does it have the mode of something one per se. But the genus is per se and formally a potential whole, per se and formally including the whole that the species includes, though one part in act, namely the grade of its proper nature, and the other in potency, namely the differential grade; and therefore it has the mode of a whole, and of something complete per se, and a category is made out of it per se.

15 It is proved second: the straight line of the category is constituted out of predicates ordered per se, formally and essentially; but the difference is not ordered per se and formally with the genus; therefore it does not pertain per se to the straight line of the category. The minor is proved: because the difference does not include the genus per se and formally, as rational does not include animal per se and formally, but outside

R iiij

[p. 264]

its ratio is animal; therefore it cannot constitute a categorial line with it, nor

pertain per se to the category.

To the argument of the other opinion a reply has already been given: be‐

cause the difference is formally and per se not a whole but a part, whereas

the genus formally and essentially has the ratio of a potential and complete

whole, and therefore it is placed per se and formally in the category, from

which the difference is excluded on account of its incomplete ratio.

Whether and how individuals are placed in the category.

16

T     he first opinion is that of Javelli in his Logic, tit. 5, ch. 1, who asserts

that the individual does not pertain per se to the category, but reductively, by rea‐

son of the species in which it participates. This can be proved from Porphyry, ch.

on species, where he asserts that the Terms by which the category is closed are the

supreme genus and the lowest species, beyond which it is not permitted to ascend to the

individuals, because they are infinite; therefore he holds that they do not pertain

per se to the category. And besides, if they are infinite, just as there is no sci‐

ence of them, so they will not pertain per se to the category: because this

part is a part of the science of Dialectic.

But the opposite opinion, that the individual is per se in the category as

its base and foundation, is true and to be held. Fonseca follows it, Metaph. 5,

ch. 7, q. 7, sect. 2, and q. 8, sect. 3.

And it is proved by reason: because the individual is a being complete per

se, and containing in itself all the predicates of the straight categorial line, to

which it is subjected per se, and of which Substance, Body, Living, Animal, and

Man are predicated per se and formally; therefore nothing is lacking to it for

it to be in the category as its foundation.

17 To the argument it is replied that Porphyry posited the supreme genus

and the lowest species as the extreme essential predicates of the category,

presupposing that the individual is an extreme, as the foundation of all the

categories. That the individuals are infinite, however, does not take away that

the individual pertains per se to the category, even if they were infinite in

act; because they do not pertain to the category as distinct, or as making up

a number, but as participating in the essential predicates and sustaining

them; and this ratio is the same in all, whether they are infinite or only finite.

From which it is also understood that the individual can pertain to the sci‐

ence of the categories, not indeed as its object, but as that out of which, as

from a foundation, the object is integrated, namely the category, which is

part of the total object of the science of Dialectic.

[p. 265]

In what way infinite things are placed in, or excluded from, the category.

18

O     nly in general need we speak in this place about infinite things; for we

shall deal with them in particular in their own places, namely in the

category of substance and of quantity. But now the following doubt is to be

explained by this distinction: a thing can be infinite in two ways, either ac‐

cording to essence, as God, or according to some accidental ratio of exten‐

sion or of intension, as a line, if an infinite one were given, or a whiteness

having infinite degrees of intension. And what is infinite according to es‐

sence does not pertain to the category, as will be proved in the following

chapter; but of the rest it will be proved in the chapter on quantity that they

pertain per se to their proper categories no less than finite quantities or

qualities.

## QUESTION II

Whether things are to be placed in the categories under abstract names or concrete ones.

19

C     oncerning the things that pertain to the category of substance, it is cer‐

tain that they are to be placed in the category under concrete names,

and not under abstract names: as the human species and the genus of animal

under the names man and animal, and not under the names animality and hu‐

manity; and so of the rest. And the reason for this is that a category is made

out of complete things; but by abstract names substances are not signified as

complete beings, but only by concrete ones; therefore they will pertain to

the category under concrete names, and not under abstract ones. The minor

is proved: because by abstract names they are signified not as species or gen‐

era, but as principles of the genus and of the species: as by the name animali‐

ty the sensitive nature is signified as the principle of animal, and by the name

humanity the rational nature as the principle of man; therefore they are signi‐

fied in an incomplete and non-categorial mode.

The question therefore proceeds concerning accidents alone: whether the

abstract ones, as whiteness and color, or rather the concrete ones, as white and

colored, are placed in the category of quality; and so of the other categories.

20 And before we propose the other opinions, that one is to be rejected

which Cajetan holds, in the opusculum On Being and Essence, ch. 7, where he

distinguishes two considerations of the categories, the Logical and the

Metaphysical; and in the categories logically considered, the abstract

[p. 266]

are to be placed, not the concrete: because they are ordered to predications, which are better exercised in abstract terms than in concrete ones; but under the Metaphysical consideration, the concrete and not the abstract. This, however, is refuted by all: because the categories are the same in Logic and in Metaphysics; therefore they are signified out of the same things, conceived in the same way. And that in relation to predications the abstract rather than the concrete are to be placed is also false: because, since the concrete terms, by which accidental forms are signified as they are in a subject, are better known to us, predications are better exercised in concrete terms. But this reason is not sufficient to vary the mode of signifying of the things of the categories; and therefore under both considerations, Logical and Metaphysical, they are to be arranged in the categories.

The first opinion therefore holds: that the abstract terms of accidents are not placed in the categories, but only the concrete. So Nifo, Metaph. 5, q. 3 and 7; Toledo, q. 2 on the Postpredicaments; and others among the moderns. And they prove it from Aristotle himself, in the present chapter, where he enumerated the categories in the concrete, according to the translation of Boethius (although Argyropoulos put them in the abstract), and in Topics bk. 1, ch. 7, and bk. 4, ch. 1, locus 4, also in the concrete according to both translations.

21 They prove it next by reason: first, that the abstract are not placed; second, that the concrete are placed. The reason for the first is that substance is more perfect than the accidents; but substances are not placed in the abstract, because they are signified as parts, and therefore in an incomplete mode; therefore much less will accidents be placed in the abstract.

The reason for the second is that if the concrete were not placed in this way, it would be chiefly because they are beings per accidens, since they signify a form and connote a subject, as white, and out of a form and a subject, as out of two beings in act, there is made not something one per se but something one per accidens; but this is false; therefore they are not to be excluded from the category. The minor is proved: because out of act and potency, according to Aristotle, On the Soul 2, text 2, something one per se is made; but the subject behaves as potency, and the form as act; therefore out of such a composition there will result something one per se, which is the concrete.

The second opinion is the opposite one, which says that only the abstract terms of accidents are to be placed in the category; so St. Thomas, opusculum On Being and Essence, ch. 7, toward the end; Scotus, q. 5 on Universals and q. 11 on the Categories; Avicenna, bk. 3 of his Metaph., ch. 3; Javelli, Metaph. 5, q. 16; Soto, ch. on quantity, q. 1; Paul of Venice, on the present chapter; Villalpando, ch. on genus, q. 4.

22 It is proved by the testimony of Aristotle, Topics bk. 4, ch. 1, loci 3 and 4, where he asserts that justice is in a genus, that is, in a category, not the just

[p. 267]

And also by reason: because the concrete signifies things of different categories, namely the subject, which is substance, and the form, which is accident; therefore it cannot pertain to one determinate category. Indeed it can pertain to none, because categories are made out of beings per se; but out of things of different categories, since they are primarily diverse and in act, something one per se cannot be made; therefore the concrete cannot be placed in the category. The minor is proved, as to this last point, from Aristotle, Metaph. 7, text 15, where he teaches expressly that the white and the musical do not have one determinate essence per se, and therefore cannot be explained by one essential definition, but are beings per accidens.

23 For the solution of this question two things are to be noted concerning the concrete and abstract terms of accidents. The first concerns the nature of the concrete, which is to be explained by likeness to the substantial concrete. Now a substantial nature has actual existence, through which it is in the nature of things, distinct from it by reason alone; and beyond this it has subsistence, which is a certain substantial mode through which it is ultimately terminated and completed, and constituted in a supposit if it is not rational, and, if it is rational, constituted at once in a supposit and a person: as the human nature of Peter has actual existence, through which it is in the nature of things, and subsistence, which is its ultimate act and through which it is constituted a person. Hence the person of Peter is composed of humanity actually existing and of subsistence, or personality. And since humanity behaves by way of potency, that is, as terminable by subsistence, and subsistence is as a substantial act terminating and completing it, it follows that the person is something one per se and substantial. And each person is also a singular concrete, and from many persons there is abstracted a common nature thus terminated and complete. And thus abstracted it is signified by a common concrete name: as the name man signifies the human nature subsisting and complete in common, which is the same as man in common.

24 In a like manner an accidental nature, such as whiteness, has actual existence, through which it is in the nature of things, distinct from itself by reason alone, and also another mode through which it is ultimately terminated and completed; which mode is not subsistence but actual inherence in a subject. Out of this accidental nature, then, actually existing in the nature of things, and out of the mode of actual inherence in a subject, there is composed this concrete, which is this white thing or that. And from these singular concretes there is abstracted the common concrete, as white, signifying the nature of whiteness actually inhering

[p. 268]

in a subject. And this composition is per se, because it is made out of the accidental nature, behaving as a quasi-substantial potency, that is, out of the nature as determinable, and out of the mode of actual inherence as out of a quasi-substantial act terminating it. Now out of a substantial potency and a substantial act something one per se is made; and therefore the accidental concrete resulting from such a composition is something one per se. But because this mode by which the accidental nature is terminated is actual inherence in a subject, this concrete per se, as white, connotes the subject in which the accidental nature, thus complete and terminated, inheres. Now to connote the subject is nothing other than to denote it at the same time, as something extrinsic to which the accidental nature is as it were affixed. And the reason for this connotation is that the mode by which this nature is terminated is imperfect, as the nature itself is, and therefore cannot sustain it by itself, but needs the support of an extrinsic subject to which it may be as it were affixed. And for this reason such a mode is not called subsistence, or existence per se, but actual inherence, or actual in-existence.

From which it is understood that the accidental concrete can be taken in two ways. First, as signifying only something composed of the accidental nature and its proper mode of actual inherence, while it connotes consequently the subject in which it inheres; and this concrete is something one per se, because it is not composed of the accidental nature and the subject, but of the nature alone and its term, or proper substantial act, which is actual inherence, in the way in which the substantial concrete is composed of the substantial nature and the proper mode of substance; but the subject does not pertain to this composition, but is connoted outside it, as something extrinsic to which the nature is affixed through actual inherence; yet it is connoted per se. In another way the accidental concrete is taken by way of an aggregate of both, namely of the accidental nature and the subject, so that it is signified as composed of both. And in this way it is not something one per se but per accidens: because although it is composed of the subject as of potency and of the accidental form as of act, yet that potency of the subject which it has for receiving the accidental form is accidental, because it is in every way outside its essence, already wholly complete through its substantial principles and parts. But out of an accidental potency and an act that is also accidental, something one per se cannot be made, but only per accidens, because it is made out of two beings already complete in their own substantial being and pertaining to different categories, namely out of the subject and the accidental nature, already complete through its proper mode of actual inherence.

[p. 269]

And this is to be made out of two beings in act, from which it is inferred that it is something one per accidens. And if it is said that just as out of a substantial potency and a substantial act there is made something one per se, a substance, so out of the accidental potency of the subject and the act of the accidental form there can be made something one per se and accidental: I reply that it is impossible that it be something one, accidental and per se, because the accidental potency of the subject cannot be per se with respect to it, since it is of another genus than substance; therefore with respect to the subject it is a potency per accidens; but the subject concurs through such a potency to compose the concrete, together with the accidental form; therefore it concurs through a potency not per se but per accidens; wherefore it cannot through it make something one per se in composing together with another, but by the very fact that it makes something accidental one, since it is itself a substance, it makes something one per accidens.

27 It is to be noted second, concerning the nature of the abstract terms of accidents, that as they are taken in the common way of conceiving and speaking, they signify the accidental nature as abstracted from the subject by Physical abstraction, and not by the Metaphysical abstraction by which universals are abstracted from particulars. Hence they signify it not by way of something inhering in a subject, but by way of something as it were subsisting per se, after the likeness of substances: as whiteness, which truly inheres in a subject, is signified by the name white by way of something inhering; but by the abstract name whiteness it is signified as abstracted Physically from the subject, and therefore not by way of something inhering, but by way of something complete subsisting per se, and therefore as something one per se.

From this whole doctrine I gather three conclusions by which our view is explained. The first is: the accidental concrete composed solely of the accidental nature and its proper mode of actual inherence is placed per se in the category. It is proved by this argument: a category is made out of beings that are per se and complete; but this concrete is something one per se and complete; therefore it pertains per se to the category. The minor is proved: out of a substantial potency and a substantial act something one per se is composed, as Aristotle teaches, On the Soul 2, text 2; but the accidental concrete composed of the accidental nature as terminable and of its proper mode of actual inherence terminating it is composed of that same nature, as in substantial potency to its term as to a substantial act, and of the term itself, as its substantial act; therefore it is something one per se and complete, since it contains the accidental nature complete through its proper mode.

[p. 270]

The second conclusion: the concrete taken in the second way, as it signifies a Physical composite of the subject and the accidental form, is not placed in the category. It is proved: because a category is made out of beings per se; but the accidental concrete taken in this way is a being per accidens; therefore it does not pertain to the category. I prove the minor: because a being per accidens is that which is composed of several beings in act, that is, already complete in their substantial being; but the concrete so taken is composed of the subject, already complete in its whole substantial being, and of the accidental nature, also complete through its proper mode of actual inherence; therefore of many beings in act.

The third conclusion: the Physical abstract terms of accidents, as they are signified in the common way of conceiving and speaking, pertain per se to the category, as whiteness, color, etc. It is proved: because they signify the accidental nature by way of something existing and subsisting per se; therefore as something one per se and categorial. But if from these abstract terms, abstracted by Physical abstraction (which rather have the mode of substantial concretes), other Metaphysical abstract terms are taken, as from whiteness whiteness-ness, and from color color-ness, these abstract terms do not pertain per se to the category, just as neither do the abstract terms of substances, because they signify the nature in an incomplete mode, that is, not as a genus or species, but as principles of the genus and of the species.

29 To the testimony of Aristotle for the first opinion: it is to be granted that he enumerated the categories in both ways, in the concrete and in the abstract, because both the concrete per se and the abstract per se pertain to the categories, and only the concrete per accidens is excluded.

To the first argument the major is to be distinguished: because we can speak of things in two ways. Either according to themselves, and in this way the abstract terms of substances are more perfect than those of accidents; or as they are abstracted in such a way by the intellect, and so taken the abstract terms of accidents are more perfect, in the common way of conceiving and speaking, because they signify the nature, although accidental, as abstracted by Physical abstraction, and therefore by way of natures subsisting per se and complete; whereas the abstract terms of substances signify the nature, although substantial, yet abstracted by Metaphysical abstraction, and therefore in a certain incomplete mode, as the principle of the genus and of the species. Wherefore the former pertain per se to the category, the latter do not; but the abstract terms of accidents that are taken Metaphysically are also excluded from the category.

30 To the other point, which is said about concretes in the same argument, I reply: the concrete, as composed of the subject and the accident, is something one

[p. 271]

per accidens, although it is composed of potency and act: because the potency

and act are not the substantial ones out of which Aristotle affirms that some‐

thing one per se is made, but the accidental potency of the substance and the

accidental act of the form, out of which something one per accidens is made.

To the testimony of Aristotle for the second opinion it is replied that, if he

is speaking of genus for category, he takes just for the accidental concrete; and

taken in this way it is true that it is not in a genus, that is, in a category, as has

been explained.

And in the same way it is replied to the argument that the concrete, as it

signifies something composed of things of different categories, cannot pertain

to one determinate category, indeed not to any category; but it can, as it signi‐

fies something composed solely of the nature and its proper mode of actual in‐

herence, which is something one per se.

But if someone should argue thus against our view: accidents in the con‐

crete are defined by a single definition, as white, that it is what disperses sight;

and they are defined as they signify the subject and the accidental form, in

such a way that the subject is the material definitum, as denominated by the

form, and the form is the formal definitum, as denominating the subject;

therefore they are something one per se even as they include the subject, and

therefore they will pertain to the category, against our second conclusion: I re‐

ply that the concrete includes the subject in two ways, as is manifest from our

doctrine. First, as connoted per se and not signified; and then the concrete is

something one per se, because it signifies only the nature complete through its

proper mode of actual inherence, while it connotes the subject per se. In the

second way it includes the subject as signified per se, and in this way it is

something one per accidens. When, therefore, it is defined in the concrete, it

is taken in the first way and is something one per se, including the nature, and

the subject as connoted per se, not as components of something one but as or‐

dered; because, since the subject is connoted per se, it is ordered per se with

the complete nature that connotes it; therefore it makes something one per

se, not in entity but in order, which can be explained by one definition.

## QUESTION III

Whether it is necessary that the categories be distinguished really, or from the nature of

the thing, or whether it suffices that they be distinguished by reason. 31

T   he first opinion affirms that a real distinction must necessarily be posited be‐

tween the categories. So Paul of Venice, bk. 3 of his Metaph., ch. 31; Nifo,

Metaph. 4, q. 4, and bk. 5, 12; whom Cajetan seems to follow, 1 p., q. 28, a. 1.

They prove it first: because the division of being into ten categories

[p. 272]

is real; therefore being is divided into diverse real entities; but diverse real entities are really distinct, because things that are distinguished by reason alone are the same real entity; therefore it is necessary that the categories be distinguished really. The first consequence is proved: because just as animal is divided into diverse animals, and color into diverse colors, so being into diverse entities.

Second: the categories are primarily diverse; therefore they do not agree univocally in entity; but if they were not distinguished really, they would agree in some one entity common to many; therefore just as such agreement is repugnant to them, so real identity is repugnant to them, but not distinction; it is necessary, therefore, that they be distinguished really.

32 The second opinion does not posit a real distinction between all the categories, but a real or formal one, at least prior to the operation of the intellect, so that it is necessary that they have formal rationes distinct of themselves and without dependence on the intellect. And because they are accustomed to call this formal distinction “from the nature of the thing,” they say it is necessary that the categories be distinguished really or from the nature of the thing, so that it is not possible that they be distinguished only by the intellect. So John of Jandun, whom Fonseca cites, Metaph. 5, ch. 7, q. 6, sect. 1; and although he seems to refute him in sect. 2, concl. 2, yet in sect. 3, at the end, he seems to follow his opinion, affirming that the distinction of the categories does not depend on the intellect, but that they are all distinguished before its operation.

33 And it is proved by this argument: the categories contain diverse modes of being; therefore diverse formal rationes, distinct before the operation of the intellect, which is not to be distinguished by reason alone, but as it were from the nature of the thing. The consequence is proved: because the mode of being of things does not depend on the intellect; therefore neither will it depend on its operation whether they are diverse or not, but they will be distinct from their own nature.

The third opinion is now almost common in the school: that the categories are not necessarily distinguished really, nor from the nature of the thing, but that it is enough that they be distinguished by some distinction of reason, with a foundation in the thing. So St. Thomas, Metaph. bk. 11, lect. 7; q. 2, ad 18; Soto, ch. on quantity, q. 1; Toledo, q. 5 on the categories in common; and many among the moderns.

34 And that a real distinction between the categories is not necessary is evidently gathered from two passages of Aristotle. For in this book of the Categories he distinguishes two categories, of action and of passion. And in Phys. 3, text 19, he asserts and proves that action and passion are not distinguished really, but that the same real motion is action as it proceeds from the agent, and passion as it is received in the patient: as that the same heating, by which fire heats wood,

is

[p. 273]

is action as it proceeds from the same fire, and passion as it is received in the wood; therefore it follows evidently from both testimonies that a real distinction is not necessarily to be posited between the categories.

35 The second point is proved, that a distinction from the nature of the thing is not necessarily to be posited, but that one of reason suffices. First, because between the diverse essential grades of the same thing a distinction from the nature of the thing is not necessarily to be posited, but it suffices that they be distinguished by the intellect, as we proved in the chapter on difference; but the categories can agree in the same entity, in which the ratio of both is found, and their rationes are not distinguished by diverse essential grades, but only by diverse modes of being, as substance from the accidents by the mode of being per se, and the accidents among themselves by diverse modes of inhering in substance; therefore it is not necessary that they be distinguished from the nature of the thing, but it suffices that they be distinguished by the intellect. The consequence is proved: because modes differ less than essential grades.

It is proved second: because a distinction from the nature of the thing is not to be posited where a distinction by the intellect suffices; but a distinction of reason made by the intellect between the categories suffices; therefore a formal distinction, or one from the nature of the thing, is not to be posited. I prove the minor: because whenever some things are distinct from the nature of the thing, they cannot be found in the same thing except through real composition, since they are many, out of which something one results, which cannot come about except through composition; but action and passion, which are distinguished in this way, are in the same motion without composition, and in many other things several formal rationes are found without real composition, as in the divine attributes of justice and mercy; therefore they ought not to be posited as distinct from the nature of the thing, or before the intellect, but it is enough that they be distinguished by the intellect.

36 But such a distinction, made by the intellect between some categories which are not really distinct, must necessarily be with a foundation in the thing, and therefore a distinction of reasoned reason. For since they are primarily diverse formal rationes, they cannot be separated by the intellect in the same thing unless they are virtually contained in it. And this virtual containment is the foundation by which the intellect can separate and distinguish both, conceiving one without the other. For example, in Peter there is no foundation for distinguishing him from himself, because it is repugnant that he differ formally from himself; and therefore he cannot be distinguished by a distinction of reasoned reason, but only of reasoning reason, that is, by the sole work of the intellect. But action and passion, which are found in the same motion, are as it were virtually distinct before the intellect,

S

[p. 274]

because truly, before its operation, it is found in the motion that it proceeds from the agent and is received in the patient; and therefore they give a foundation to the same intellect to conceive the motion as proceeding from the agent, not conceiving it as received in the patient by the same concept, but by another, and indeed a different one: because it is true that to proceed from the agent, so conceived, is not to be received in the patient. And this is for those things which on the side of the thing were only virtually distinct to be distinct by the intellect actually and formally; but to be virtually distinct is nothing other than to be able to be formally distinguished. And this distinction of reasoned reason we say suffices between some categories, although others are distinguished really; but that none are formally distinct before the operation of the intellect, because we do not admit such a formal distinction.

37 To the first argument: the antecedent is to be distinguished, because a division can be understood to be real in two ways. First, in such a way that both the thing divided and the members are real and not beings of reason; in which sense we admit that the division of being into ten categories is real. Second, it can be understood to be real in such a way that the members are really distinct; and in this sense we deny that it is real. And we can give an example in the division of good into the honest, the useful, and the pleasant, which all grant to be real in the first sense and deny in the second, because it often happens that the members are not distinct really or from the nature of the thing, but by reason alone. And, this distinction being supposed, the consequence must also be denied, that the division of being is into diverse real entities, if by diverse real entities are understood ones really distinct.

To the second, I reply by distinguishing the antecedent, that the categories are primarily diverse; for this can be understood in two ways. First, according to their formal rationes; and in this sense it is true, but it is to be understood thus: that they do not agree univocally in any grade of a superior nature, nor are they distinguished by other, inferior grades of essential perfection, as species are distinguished by grades of essential perfection diverse from the genus; but that the categories are distinct through diverse intrinsic modes of being, included in the same ratio of entity in which they agree analogically. And so it is true that they are diverse through their very entities, and not through other grades of perfection, and therefore diverse by themselves, which truly and properly is to be primarily diverse, and does not belong to species, which are said to differ through differences. In the second way it can be understood that they are primarily diverse according to real entities, so that several cannot be in the same real entity

[p. 275]

agree; and in this way it is plainly false, as we have shown of action and pas‐

sion, whose formal rationes are found in the same real motion; but none‐

theless, so found and distinguished by the intellect, they are primarily di‐

verse in the way already explained.

Q U E S T I O N I V.

Whether the categories are ten, so that there can be neither more nor fewer.

38

S    ome, whom Plotinus cites, Ennead 6, bk. 1, multiplied the categories so

far that they posited infinitely many. But their opinion is proved false by

this argument: because if it is true of all things made by God that they were

made by him in number, weight, and measure, as Sacred Scripture teaches,

how much more of the genera and species in which the essences of things are

contained; but the categories are made out of these; therefore they will be

finite.

But among those who hold for certain that they are finite, there are three

different opinions. The first is that of those who posited more than ten,

whom Simplicius cites in his commentary on the Categories; and it can be

proved by this argument: for the efficient cause the category of action is

posited, and for the material cause receptive of the same action the category

of passion is posited; therefore for the other two causes, formal and final,

two other categories ought to be posited, because there is no greater reason

why they should be multiplied for the former than for the latter.

The second opinion was that of those who posited fewer than ten; but

they were divided. For Plato, in the dialogues on being and the one, which

are called by other names the Sophist or Parmenides, seems to posit only one

category, the most universal one of being, which he calls the supreme genus

of all things, under which the particular genera and species are placed.

39 This is proved by the argument: being is the most universal genus of

being; therefore all genera and species can be ordered under it; but one or‐

dering under one first genus is one category; therefore only one category is

to be posited, and not more. The major is proved: because if being were not

a genus, it would be chiefly because it is transcendent, and on account of its

transcendence is included in all the differences, against the proper condition

of a genus, which must be outside the ratio of the differences; but this reason

is not sufficient: for although being taken universally, as it is common both to

incomplete and to complete beings, has this, yet if it is taken for complete

beings alone, it is not included

S ij

[p. 276]

in the differences, because the differences are not complete beings, and for the same reason neither in the intrinsic modes; and therefore it could be the most universal genus of all complete things, out of which the category is made. But even if being could not be the genus of all things, accident at least would seem to be the genus of all accidents, and therefore one category alone of all accidents would have to be posited, and another of substance, and so only two. And this was the opinion of Xenocrates and Andronicus, whom Simplicius cites in the place above.

40 But other, more ancient Philosophers, whom Plotinus cites, Ennead bk. 1, ch. 29, posited four, namely substance, quality, relation, and the mode of the thing. And it can be proved from the doctrine of Aristotle, who in Topics bk. 1, ch. 7, posited four predicates; but a category is nothing other than an ordering of predicates; therefore out of four predicates no more than four categories can be made. Plotinus, however, in bk. 2 of Ennead 6, ch. 18, posited five, namely motion, rest, identity, diversity, and being.

Scaliger, however, in exercitation 65, posited nine, because he reduces the category of where, or the category of when, to quantity.

The third opinion is that of those who posit only ten categories, so that there are neither more nor fewer. Archytas of Tarentum, the disciple of Pythagoras, seems to have been the first to suggest it, and afterwards Aristotle introduced it into the schools. And this is now common and to be held; St. Augustine followed it, bk. 10 of the Categories, ch. 8; and St. Thomas not only follows it but proves it, Phys. 3, lect. 9, and Metaph. 5, lect. 5.

41 Now the argument of St. Thomas is this. First substance, which is the individual of substance, as Peter or John, is the foundation of all essential predicates; therefore the number of the categories must be taken according to the diverse modes of being and of being predicated of it; but a predicate can stand in one of three ways with respect to it. For either it pertains to its quiddity, or it is outside it; and if it pertains to its quiddity, it is the category of substance; but if it is outside it, either it is taken from something formally inhering in it, and from this three categories are distinguished: because a predicate taken from something inhering belongs to the first substance either in an absolute mode or with a respect to another; if in an absolute mode, then either by reason of matter, and it is the category of quantity, or by reason of form, and it is the category of quality; but if it belongs with a respect to another, it is the category of relation. Or it is taken from something

[p. 277]

extrinsic, that is, not inhering in the first substance; and from this six other categories are distinguished. Because either it is taken from that which is an extrinsic measure, as it were by way of a container, which is called place, and it will be the category of where; for where, at least naturally, is said to be in place, or to be circumscribed by place; or from such a disposition as a body has in place, because it stands or sits, and it is the category of position. Or from that which is a successive extrinsic measure, such as time is, and it is the category of when, which seems to be nothing other than to be fitted to time and measured by it. But if the predicate is taken from something extrinsic which is not a measure, but is properly said to be had, as to have a garment or arms, which is to be clothed or armed, the category of habit is produced. And if it is taken from something extrinsic from which it proceeds efficiently, it is the category of action. And from something extrinsic on which the action or effect is impressed, it is the category of passion. It follows, therefore, that there are only ten categories, and that more are not to be multiplied, because all created beings can easily be reduced to these ten heads.

42 To the argument of the first opinion St. Thomas replies, Phys. 3, lect. 5, after the middle, by denying the consequence that for the formal and final causes two other categories are to be posited: because the formal cause, together with the material, are intrinsic parts of the substance, of which it is composed, and therefore they are reduced to the category of the same substance; but the final cause does not have a special categorial mode, as the efficient cause does, but only moves the will, attracting it to love of itself; and this motion is a certain extrinsic ratio, not at all categorial; wherefore a category is not to be multiplied for it, as for the efficient cause, from which action issues according to a special mode constituting a category.

To the arguments proposed concerning being and accident, in favor of Plato and the other Philosophers who posit only one or two categories, it is replied that being is not the genus of all beings, nor accident of all accidents, for this reason: because a genus must be univocal; but being and accident are not univocal but analogous, as we proved above; therefore they are not genera.

To the argument of those who posited four categories on account of the four Dialectical predicates which Aristotle posited, I reply that the Dialectical predicates are taken in a different way from the categories: namely, by their order to a common subject with which they can constitute a Dialectical proposition; but the categories by the diverse most universal modes of being; and therefore a greater

S iij

[p. 278]

extension they have, and they make up a greater number, than the predicates, as we proved in q. 5 on Universals.

To the argument, finally, for the opinion of Scaliger, about the reduction of the category of where to place, or of the category of when to quantity: we reply that where and when have a formal ratio different from place, and also from quantity (as will be proved in their own places), and therefore they cannot be reduced to the category of quantity, but constitute categories distinct from it. Wherefore neither fewer categories than ten are to be posited, nor more.

C H A P T E R V.

Containing the category of substance.

TEXT OF ARISTOTLE. Substance, moreover, which is said properly, principally, and most of all, is that which nei‐

ther is in any subject nor is said of any subject, etc.

E X P O S I T I O N O F T H E T E X T.

he intent of Aristotle is to explain the nature of substance, which is

T           the first category. And the chapter is divided into three parts. In the

first, presupposing the division of substance into first and second sub‐

stance, he explains what first substance is and what second substance is. In the second part he compares first and second substance with each other, and also the second substances among themselves, and teaches which is more perfect than the other. In the third he enumerates six properties of substance. The definition of first substance is contained in these words: Substance which is said properly, principally, and most of all is that which neither is said of any subject nor is in any subject. And those three phrases, which is said properly, principally, and most of all, pertain to the definitum, not to the definition. And their sense is: substance, not under the common ratio and taken improperly for the essence of a thing, whether substantial or accidental, but properly for being per se; and which by reason of itself, that is, by its own power, stands under, or sustains, both the accidents and the second substances, and is therefore most of all called substance, is that which neither is said of any subject, that is, of a quidditatively inferior one, nor is in any subject through real inherence. As Peter is properly substance, since he is a being per se, and by his own power stands under, or sustains, not only whiteness and the other accidents, but also the second substances, which are the superior universal predicates, as man, animal, living, and substance.

[p. 279]

And he is not said of a subject, because he has nothing quidditatively inferior to himself of which he might be said; nor is he in a subject, because he does not inhere in anything.

2 He next defines second substance, and says in the plural: Second substances are the species and genera in which the first substances are: as man and animal are second substances, in which the first substances, as Peter and John, are, that is, under which they are contained as subjects under predicates. For the second substances are in the first as superior predicates in quidditatively inferior subjects, and therefore actually and formally; but the first are in the second as subjects of which they are predicated, and therefore not actually and formally, but as it were under their potency, in almost the same way in which the species are said to be in the genus.

In the second part he compares the first substances with the second, and then the second among themselves. And between first and second substance he asserts that the first is more perfect, and proves it: because substance is that which stands under others, or which sustains others; but first substance by its own power sustains and stands under all things, that is, not only the accidents but the second substances themselves, whereas second substance does not stand under by reason of itself, but by reason of the first, in which and by which it is sustained, nor does it stand under the first substances; therefore first substance is more substance than second. As Peter is more substance than man, because by reason of himself he stands under whiteness and the other accidents, and also under man itself; whereas man is said to sustain the accidents not by reason of itself but by reason of Peter, in whom it is sustained, nor does it sustain Peter himself, but is sustained by him.

He then compares the second substances, and says that if the species is compared with the genus, it is more substance than the genus; but if with another species, the ratio of substance is equal in both. He proves the first by a twofold argument. First, because that is more perfect in any order of things which approaches more closely to the most perfect of the same order: as among the species of animal that one will be more perfect which approaches more closely to the human, which is the most perfect species of such a genus. But the species approaches more closely than the genus to first substance, which is the most perfect, as man approaches Peter more closely than animal does; therefore it will be more perfect substance than the genus. Second, among substances that one is the most perfect which stands under all things; therefore of the others that one will be more perfect than another which stands under more; but the species stands under more than the genus; therefore it will be more perfect than it. The minor is proved: because it stands under all the things under which the genus stands, that is, the same accidents and the same superior predicates, and besides it stands under the genus itself; but the genus does not stand under the species. For example, man stands under all the accidents

S iiij

[p. 280]

and all the superior predicates under which animal stands, and also under animal itself; but animal does not stand under man, but is sustained in it.

3 But if the species are compared among themselves, as man with lion, neither is said to be more substance than the other. He proves it: because one does not stand under more things than the other, but stands under exactly the same accidents and superior predicates; and one does not stand under the other, because neither is in the other.

In the last part of the chapter he enumerates six properties of substance, of which the first is not to be in a subject. And of first substance he says that it is evident, because Peter is in no subject, but subsists in himself and per se. But that it belongs to the second substances he proves by a twofold argument. First, because if they were in anything as in a subject, it would be chiefly in first substance, in which all the accidents inhere; but they cannot be in it as in a subject; therefore in nothing. He proves the minor: because second substances are predicated of the first as of quidditatively inferior things; therefore they are not in them as in subjects. The consequence is proved: because to be in something as in a subject is to be in it through real inherence, as an accident is; but the second substances are of the quiddity of the first, as man and animal are of the quiddity of Peter; therefore they are not as in a subject.

4 The second argument is: things that are in something as in a subject, as accidents, are indeed predicated of their subjects in name, but they cannot be predicated in ratio, because the ratio is the definition, or quidditative concept; but the definition of white is not the definition of man; therefore it is not predicated of it in name and ratio, as univocals are predicated, but in name alone. But second substances are predicated of the first in name and ratio, as man of Peter, because the definition of man is the definition of Peter; therefore they cannot be in them as in a subject. And therefore this property, namely not to be in a subject, belongs not only to the first substances but also to the second.

5 The second property of Substance is to be predicated univocally, which is not understood of first substance. And therefore it is certain that this property belongs only to the second. But he says that it belongs not only to the genera and species, which are truly and properly second substances, but also to their differences: because of whatever the species is predicated univocally, its difference too must necessarily be predicated. And that it belongs to the second substances and to the differences Aristotle proves by this argument: Univocals are those whose name is common, and the ratio of substance the same; but the name of second substance is common to the first, of which it is predicated, and

[p. 281]

definition is the same: as the name man is common to Peter and John, and its definition is also the same and common to them, as is well known; therefore it is predicated of them univocally.

The third property is: To signify a this something. As for what he understands by this something: it is certain that he understands a singular substance, subsisting per se; and therefore he asserts that, although this property seems to belong to second substances, because man and animal seem to signify something subsisting per se, it nevertheless belongs only to first substances. Second substances, however, do not signify a this something, but rather a what-like [quale quid]. They signify a what-like, because they are as it were universal forms of first substances, and forms seem to bear a likeness to quality, one species of which is form and figure; but because they are substantial predicates, they are said to signify a what-like.

6 The fourth property of substance is: To have no contrary, as nothing can be contrary to Peter and John. And this property belongs both to first and to second substances, but not in the fourth mode (says Aristotle), because it is common to others also, as to quantity.

The fifth property is: Not to admit of more and less, in the way that qualities admit of them: for one hot thing is more hot than another, because it has more degrees of intension; but substance does not have these degrees, and therefore it is said not to admit of more and less.

The last property of substance is: That, remaining one in number, it can receive contraries: as Peter, remaining the same in number, can now be hot and afterwards cold. But this property does not seem to belong to second substances, but only to first ones, because only first substance is one in number, while second substance is one in species or in genus; therefore that, persevering one in number, it should receive contraries in itself can belong only to first substance.

7 But against this property Aristotle proposes an argument: because it seems to belong to something else, namely to a proposition, which, remaining one in number, from true becomes false and from false becomes true. As this proposition, Peter is sitting, is true while he sits, but false while he stands, and it remains the same; therefore it belongs to it that, remaining one in number, it receives contraries. And he replies in two ways. First, that although it receives contraries, it does not do so in the same way as substance, but in a different way: for substance receives contraries through a change of itself, because it receives them in itself formally, and therefore the thing receiving them is changed. But a proposition does so without a change of itself, and only through a change of something else extrinsic, namely of the thing about which something is enunciated. When, therefore, it is said that it is proper to substance

[p. 282]

to receive contraries, this is understood as through a change of itself, and in this way it belongs neither to a proposition nor to anything else. The second solution is almost the same: for he denies that a proposition receives contraries, because to receive contraries is for a subject to be moved from one to the other, losing the one and acquiring the other. But a proposition, while from true it becomes false, is not moved from truth to falsity, nor does it lose the one and acquire the other; rather, the change holds only on the side of the thing signified, and therefore the proposition is not said to receive contraries.

## QUESTION I
