Which is the supreme genus of the category of substance.

t seems that it has no supreme genus, which is proved thus: If it had

I         one, it would above all be substance; but this cannot be a genus; there‐

fore it will have none. I prove the minor: because if substance in common, as abstracted from all substances, were the supreme genus of this category, under which all substances would be comprehended, and therefore only one category were to be constituted for them, it would follow that accident in common also is the supreme genus of all accidents, and so constitutes one category, under which all accidents would be placed: wherefore there will be only two categories. The consequence is proved: because, just as substance taken universally, as it is common to complete and partial substances, is transcendent, and is included in the ultimate differences, and is not univocal with respect to all, but analogous, because it is said first of complete substances and afterwards of parts, and with an intrinsic dependence on the former, and therefore cannot be a genus, because a genus must be univocal and not transcendent, lest it be included in the ultimate differences, but must be outside their ratio; if, however, it is taken for substance in common, it will neither be transcendent, because it will not be included in the differences, nor analogous, but univocal, because it will be said equally of all, and therefore it will be able to be a genus. In the same way accident, although taken universally it is transcendent and analogous, and therefore cannot be a genus, yet if it is taken only for complete accident, it will not be transcendent, nor analogous, but univocal, because it will be said equally of all complete accidents, and therefore it will be able to be a genus.

For the solution of this question it should be noted that there are five acceptations of substance, as is gathered from the doctrine of Aristotle in the present chapter,

[p. 283]

and Metaph. 5, ch. 8, text 15, and also from St. Thomas in his Commentaries on the same place, and On Power, q. 9, a. 1, ad 4 and 5.

First, it is taken for the Essence of a thing. And this acceptation is common to accidents, in which an essence is also found, and therefore it is not proper, nor univocal, but analogous: because nothing real can be given that is common and univocal to substance and accidents.

Second, substance is taken for Being per se, in which two things are included: one negative, which is not to be in another; the other positive, which is to be an entity so perfect that existence and subsistence per se are due to it, so that it is sustained without the support of another. Hence this acceptation includes two. The first, which in order will be the second, in which substance is taken for a being that does not inhere in another, or, as is commonly said, as it is distinguished against accident, which is established to inhere. And this acceptation too is common and analogous, and therefore improper, because under it it comprehends not only complete substances but also incomplete or partial ones, of which it is true that they do not inhere. For although they are in the whole, yet they are not so by real inherence, but by composing it substantially. And substance is said of complete and incomplete substances not univocally but analogically.

The third acceptation in order is for that positive element which the particle per se includes, namely for a complete entity to which existence and subsistence per se are due. But this acceptation is still common and analogous, and therefore not so proper, because it comprehends finite and infinite, created and uncreated substance, to which nothing univocal can be common: for created substance implies an intrinsic dependence on and attribution to uncreated substance, which is God. Wherefore complete substance, to which existence and subsistence per se are due, will be analogous with respect to both.

10 In a fourth way it is taken for complete and finite substance in common, that is, abstracted from particular complete and finite substances. And taken in this way it is the supreme genus of the category of substance, which is divided into corporeal and incorporeal by the first division, from which there results the second genus, body, which is divided into living and non-living; and again living into sensible and insensible; and finally sensible, which is animal, into man, horse, and lion. From these divisions there results the category of substance, consisting of these predicates: substance, body, living thing, animal, man, down to Peter.

The last acceptation is for complete substance according to a certain property of it, which is to stand under accidents, or also under superior quidditative predicates. But to stand under [substare] signifies the same

[p. 284]

as to sustain them. And substance taken in this way Aristotle divided, at the be‐

ginning of this chapter, into first and second. But in this acceptation it cannot

constitute a category, because it is not taken essentially.

From these things this conclusion is gathered, by which the question is an‐

swered: The category of substance has a determinate supreme genus, and this is

complete and finite substance considered in common. This is proved by an argu‐

ment: The supreme genus of a category is that from which the genera and

species of the same category are derived, and which itself is not derived from an‐

other; but complete and finite substance has these conditions; therefore it is the

supreme genus of the category of substance. The minor is proved: because this is

not derived from another superior univocal predicate, but is immediately con‐

tained under analogous being, and from it are derived the genera and species out

of which the straight line of the category is made, as has been proved by

examples.

11 To the argument the reply is by denying the consequence, because the ra‐

tio of substance and of accident is different in two respects: In the first, indeed,

because substance implies a particular and determinate mode of being, whereas

accident implies several modes of being, determining none, but with a confused

ratio. Second, accident, however much it is abstracted, or taken for incomplete

accident alone, is analogous, on account of its intrinsic attribution to substance,

together with which it signifies all accidents, and therefore it cannot be a genus,

nor the determinate genus of one category. But substance, taken for complete

and finite substance, implies a univocal and common ratio with respect to all

complete substances, out of which the category is made, and therefore it can be

the supreme genus of a determinate category.

## QUESTION II

Whether God is placed in the category of substance.

12

A    lthough from what we said in the preceding question, namely that com‐

plete and finite substance is the supreme genus of the category of sub‐

stance, it could be gathered that God, who is infinite substance, does not pertain

to this category, yet many affirm that he is in the category, and therefore it calls

for a special disputation.

The first opinion, then, holds that God is in the category of substance. So Gregory

of Rimini and Gabriel on 1, d. 8, q. 3; Holcot, q. 6; and John Baconthorpe, d. 9, q.

1; and it is proved by the testimony of Aristotle, Topics 4, ch. 2, place 17, where he

says that God is in the genus of animal

[p. 285]

and is separated from man by the proper difference immortal, in these words: If he has assigned the difference as the genus, as if immortal were the genus of God: for immortal is a difference of animal. And in the second place of the same chapter: If he has placed the difference in the species, as that immortal is that very thing which God is, etc.

Next it is proved by reason. First, because if anything stood in the way of God’s being in the category, it would above all be that he is infinite substance; but this does not stand in the way; therefore nothing does. I prove the minor: because to be something infinite does not prevent a thing from being in the other categories: as, if an infinite line were given, it would be in the category of quantity; and if a heat infinitely perfect according to intension were given, it would be in the category of quality; therefore even if God is infinite substance, he will be able to be in the category of substance.

13 Second, through the mystery of the incarnation God was made man univocally with us; therefore he is truly and properly in the human species as an individual of this nature, and also under the genus of animal; but what is under a genus and a species is also in the category, which is made of genera and species; therefore God is truly and properly in the category of substance through the human nature which he assumed.

The second opinion denies that God, as God, is placed in the category. And this is the common and true opinion, which among the Philosophers was held by Hermes Trismegistus in the Pimander, ch. 1; Averroes, disputation 7, and against Algazel, the last chapter; Avicenna, Metaph. 8, ch. 4; and with these all the interpreters of Aristotle. Among the holy Fathers, Augustine in the book On the Knowledge of the True Life, ch. 3; Anselm in the Monologion, ch. 26; and with them Boethius, On the Trinity bk. 1, ch. 6. And among the scholastics, all except those Nominalists cited for the opposite opinion. So the Master on 1, d. 8, and in the same place Albert the Great, Scotus, Bonaventure, Richard, Durandus, Giles of Rome; St. Thomas, Contra Gentiles bk. 1, ch. 24 and 25, and there the Ferrariensis; and 1 p., q. 3, a. 5, and there Cajetan; Alexander of Hales, 1 p., q. 48, memb. 5, a. 2 and 3.

And it is proved by a twofold argument. First, because God is pure act in such a way that his actual being is as essential to him as his essence; therefore there is nothing potential in God that could be conceived after the manner of something contractible. Wherefore it is repugnant that there be a genus in God. The last consequence is proved: because a genus is essentially contractible; but what is not in a genus is not in a category; therefore it is repugnant that God be in a category.

Second, because if God were in a category, some genus would be given common to God and creatures; but no genus can be given common to them; therefore God will not be in a category. The

[p. 286]

minor I prove: because a genus must be univocal; but nothing univocal can be given common to God and creatures, on account of the intrinsic dependence and attribution of creatures to God, without which they cannot be understood; therefore neither can a common genus be given.

To the testimony of Aristotle the reply is that by the name of gods he does not mean true gods, since it was certain for him that there is only one, but certain superior substances having most subtle bodies, which many philosophers said were rational, more perfect indeed than man, because immortal, yet agreeing with him under the genus of rational animal, and distinguished by the differences mortal and immortal; and of these he asserts that they are to be placed in the category, if it is true that they are given.

14 To the first argument: granting the major, the minor is to be distinguished: because to be something infinite can be understood in two ways: either according to essence, or according to some accidental ratio of extension or of intension. And what is infinite in the first way cannot be in any category; and therefore God is excluded from the category, because he is a being infinite according to essence. What is infinite in the second way can pertain to a category: because although it is infinite according to an accidental ratio, yet it is finite according to essence, by reason of which it must be placed in the category, and not by reason of the accident. And such would be an infinite line, if it were given, or a heat infinite according to intension: for the line would have the finite essence of continuous quantity, and the heat too the finite essence of quality, although the former would have an infinite accidental extension of length, and the heat an infinite gradual intension; and these infinite accidents would not prevent them from being placed in their categories. And the reason of this is that the categories are constituted from the essences of things, not from their accidents.

15 To the second argument I reply that Christ is truly and properly in a genus and a species, and also in the category, by reason of his human nature; and consequently the divine Word, to which the human nature is united in person, is placed through it in the category of substance. But from this it does not follow that the divine Word is placed in the category by reason of the divine nature or of the divine person. Thus, then, one must speak in this matter, so that we say absolutely: First, that Christ is in the category of substance, because simply and absolutely he is a man, and this man. Second, that God too is absolutely in the category of substance, because it is absolutely true that God is a man; but because he has this by reason of the human nature, and not by reason of the divine nature or the divine person, it must be denied that God as God

[p. 287]

is, or as he is a divine person, in the category. And in this way is understood the

common and true opinion which we follow, which is no less true now than it was

before God became man: because the things that belong to God after the incar‐

nation, pertaining to the human nature, do not belong to him by reason of him‐

self but by reason of that same human nature, and therefore they posit nothing in

God, as he is God, which he did not always have. But someone will ask whether, al‐

though God is not per se in a category, he can at least be placed reductively in some category.

To which Fonseca replies that he can indeed be in those categories which contain

an extrinsic denomination, as in the category of where, in the category of action,

and of having. But I do not admit that he is in a category even reductively, be‐

cause so holds St. Thomas, 1 p., q. 3, a. 5, and with him Richard on 1, d. 8, a. 4, q.

1. And he proves it by this argument: That thing is said to pertain to some catego‐

ry reductively which falls short of the perfect and complete ratio of such a cate‐

gory, as parts and modes; for so the point pertains to the category of quantity, and

the arm to the category of substance; but God rather exceeds all the categorial ra‐

tiones infinitely; therefore he is not reductively in any category. Which St.

Augustine taught in these words, On the Trinity bk. 5, ch. 1: Thus let us understand

God (if we can) as good without quality, great without quantity, a creator without need,

present without position, containing all things without having, whole everywhere without

place, everlasting without time, making changeable things without any change of himself,

and undergoing nothing.

Thus Augustine; from which it is understood that even the extrinsic denomi‐

nations of some categories belong to God not properly but improperly, and there‐

fore not for the same reason, nor univocally, do they belong to him and to crea‐

tures in common; and consequently that on account of them he does not pertain

even reductively to any category.

## QUESTION III

Whether angels and the heavenly bodies are in the category of substance.

16

C    oncerning the heavenly bodies and the angels, in relation to the categorial

constitution, the first opinion was that of the Commentator, Metaph. 10, last

chapter, comment 16, which excludes both kinds of substance from the category. This

opinion was followed by John of Jandun, Metaph. 18, q. 22; Niphus in the same

place, q. 9, and that as regards the angels alone; Plotinus, Enneads 6, bk. 1; Giles of

Rome in his commentaries on this category, and

[p. 288]

Quodlibet 1, q. 8; Albert the Great on the Categories, treatise on substance, ch. 12.

And concerning the heavenly bodies they prove it by this argument: The corruptible and the incorruptible differ in genus; therefore they differ in category; but the heavenly bodies are incorruptible substances; therefore they differ in category from corruptible substances. The antecedent is proved from Aristotle, Metaph., last chapter, where he teaches it expressly. Next, corruptible substances are placed in this category; therefore the heavenly bodies are not in the same one, nor in another either, since they are not in any category of accidents; wherefore they will not be in a category at all.

Concerning the angels, it is proved by the testimony of Aristotle, Metaph. 10, text 30, where, besides the first principle, which is God, he posits certain other substances, which he calls intelligences, for moving the heavenly bodies. And these he says have no matter, but are pure and everlasting acts; but a substance that is pure act has nothing of potency; therefore it has no genus. The consequence is proved: because a genus is a potential whole. Next, those things that have no genus cannot have a species, nor a category, because a species is composed of genus and difference, and a category is made of genera and species; therefore, in the opinion of Aristotle, the intelligences, which we call angels, are not in a category, who also called them simple substances, Metaph. bk. 9, text 22, as having no composition; from which it also follows that they do not have a category, because the things that are in a category must be composite, at least of genus and difference.

Hence it follows evidently that the opinion of Durandus on 2, d. 3, q. 1, no. 12, and of Marsilius on 1, q. 2, is false and implies a contradiction; for though they place the angel in this category, they nevertheless deny that it has any composition whatever, even of genus and difference.

It is proved next by reason: because angels are simple substances, in which there is no composition of matter and form; therefore neither is there a real composition of potency and act; but the composition of genus and difference, which is of metaphysical potency and act, is founded on a real composition of potency and act; therefore neither is there in them a composition of genus and difference, and consequently they are not in a category.

The second opinion holds that not only the heavenly bodies but also the angels are placed in this category. And this is the common and true opinion, which as regards the heavenly bodies all the interpreters of Aristotle follow in the present chapter; and as regards the angels not only they, but all the scholastics except those cited for the opposite opinion

together

[p. 289]

together with the Master on 1, d. 8, and St. Thomas, 1 p., q. 50, a. 2, ad 1 and 3, and q. 88, a. 2, ad 4. And it is proved first of all concerning the heavenly bodies by the testimony of Aristotle, Metaph. 5, text 15; Metaph. 7, text 5; and bk. 8, text 1, in which places he teaches expressly that they are composite, not only of matter and form, but also of integral parts, in the way in which our body is composed of head, arm, and the other members. Therefore, in his mind too, they will be composed of genus and difference. The consequence is proved: because this composition is less than the others, and is founded on the composition of matter and form.

18 It is proved also by reason: because the heavenly bodies, besides the physical compositions of matter and form and of integral parts, have another, also physical, of material subject and accident: for they both have quantity and receive light from the sun; therefore they have all possible physical compositions, because besides the aforesaid no others can be thought of; therefore they must be composed of genus and difference. The consequence is proved: because where there is real potency and real act, the intellect will be able to form a potential concept under the ratio of something contractible, which is the generic concept, and also an actual and contracting concept, which is the differential concept, and to compose the species from both. But what has a genus and a species is placed in a category; therefore it is evident that the heavenly bodies are placed in the category of substance.

Concerning the angels, all the doctors cited, and especially St. Thomas, assert three things. First, that there is in them a true and real composition of act and potency, or of being and essence. Second, that they are truly composed of genus and difference. Third, that they are placed per se in the category of substance. And all are true and necessary.

19 But each must be proved. And in order that St. Thomas, in the place above, may prove the first, namely that there is in the angels a real composition of act and potency, he presupposes that in material things a twofold real composition is found. The first, of matter and form, of which their nature is composed, as human nature of body and soul. But a nature so composed is still not complete, but looks to a real act by which it is completed, and this act is called its being, by which the supposit or person is constituted: therefore the nature is a real potency with respect to its own being, by which it is completed, and being is its real act, and from both is made one thing, namely the supposit or person, which cannot be done except through a real composition; because a real composition is that through which one thing is made from two things distinct from the nature of the thing; therefore, besides the composition of matter

T

[p. 290]

and form, there is found in these things a real composition of essence and being, or of the nature and its proper act, by which it is completed.

20 This supposed, he proves that, although the first composition is not found in the angels, because they lack matter, the second must nevertheless necessarily be posited in them. Because this is the difference between divine and created being: that divine being is not received from another, but is had essentially, because it is an essential predicate of God, as to be good or wise; but created being is outside the essence of the created thing, and therefore the essence does not have it unless it is communicated by God, and this is to be being received from God; therefore the created essence is truly and really in potency to receive being from God, and the being received from God is its real act. Hence it follows that within the substance of the angel there is found a real potency and a real act, and since from these one thing is made, namely its complete substance, this cannot be done except through a real composition. And so the first has been proved.

From which the second can be proved, namely that there is in them a composition of genus and difference, by this argument: The intellect knows the nature of the angel as a real potency determinable by the act of being; therefore it can form in the same nature a perfectible and determinable concept, and a perfecting and determining concept; but these are the generic and the differential concepts, of which the species is composed; therefore in the angel there is a composition of the species from genus and difference.

From which the third is evidently proved, that the angel is in a category. Because a category is made of genera and species essentially ordered; but the angel has a genus and a species; therefore it will be orderable in a category.

21 To the argument of the first opinion concerning the heavenly bodies, St. Thomas replies, 1 p., q. 66, a. 2, ad 2, and q. 88, a. 2, ad 4, by distinguishing the major: because genus is twofold, Physical and Logical, or Metaphysical. The physical genus is matter, because real potency is found first in it, which is the first root and foundation of the metaphysical genus in material things. But the logical or metaphysical genus is a nature abstracted from species and differences, as substance from corporeal and incorporeal. To the form of the argument, then: where it is said in the major that the corruptible and the incorruptible differ in genus, one must distinguish between the physical and the logical genus, and grant it of the former, because incorruptible bodies consist of matter of a different species from the matter of corruptible bodies, and therefore they are said to differ in physical genus, which is matter.

22 And in this way is to be understood the testimony of Aristotle, in which

[p. 291]

that proposition is contained. But of the logical genus it is not true, nor does Aristotle speak of it: because corruptible and incorruptible body have a common genus, namely body abstracted from both, and under it they are placed in the category of substance. It does not follow, therefore: they differ in physical genus, therefore they differ in category; because the physical genus, which is matter, is not a categorial genus; but it would follow well if they differed in logical genus.

Although one could also reply, second, that Aristotle speaks of the logical or metaphysical genus. But in another way the same major would have to be distinguished, where it is said that the corruptible and the incorruptible differ in genus. For the categorial genus is twofold, supreme and intermediate; and it must be granted that they differ in intermediate genus, not in supreme genus: because body is divided into corruptible and incorruptible body as into two intermediate genera, and under one are contained the heavenly bodies, under the other the corruptible ones; and so they differ in intermediate genus, but not in supreme genus, because they are contained under the same genus of body and of substance, and agree in it. Hence neither do they differ in category, because only those things are said to differ in category which are contained under different supreme genera, as animal and science: for the former is contained under the supreme genus of substance, but science under the supreme genus of quality.

23 To the testimonies of Aristotle in which he speaks of the intelligences, I reply that they are everlasting and lack matter, and therefore do not have a potency to not being, because they do not have a principle of corruption as the substances of corruptible things do, which by reason of matter have in themselves a principle of not being. And therefore they are called by Aristotle acts, yet not pure acts: because, since they necessarily have a threefold composition, namely of being and essence; of subject and accident (for they have intellect and will, which are true accidents superadded to their substance); and besides, of genus and difference, they must also have a threefold potency, because every composition in its own way is of act and potency. Wherefore, just as he does not exclude them from these potencies, so neither could he exclude them from the category.

24 To the argument: the antecedent must be denied, that angels are simple substances in such a way that there is in them no real composition of potency and act, and so too of genus and difference. For it does not follow: they do not have a composition of matter and form, therefore not of act and potency either; because the composition of act and potency is more universal

T ij

[p. 292]

than the composition of matter and form, and common to material and imma‐

terial substances, because it is not necessarily founded on matter, but is found in

the nature itself from the fact that it is created and has its being received from

another. And since such is the nature of the angels (although spiritual), it neces‐

sarily includes this composition within its own substance, and consequently the

composition of genus and difference, which is proximately founded on it, al‐

though in material things it is radically and remotely founded on matter.

Q U E S T I O N I V.

Of what kind the division of substance into first and second is: univocal or analogous.

25

I    n order that the question may be better understood, it should be noted that

both the thing divided and the members of this division can be taken in four

ways. In the first way they are taken so that the thing divided is real and the

members are second intentions. But then the thing divided, according to its real

being, can be taken in two ways: either for real substance according to its es‐

sence, or according to the property of standing under. And if it is taken in the

first way, the sense of the division will be: Of real substance, one is universal, an‐

other particular; or one is subject, another predicate. And it will be a division of

a real subject into different accidents of reason. But if in the second way, the

sense will be different, namely: Of real substance, as standing under, one is the

first subject in a proposition, another the second. And it will be a division as it

were of a real accident into different accidents of reason.

26 In the second way it can be taken conversely, so that the thing divided is

a being of reason and the members are real, namely first and second substance

according to their real being; and the sense will be: Of the subject in a proposi‐

tion, one is first real substance, another second real substance. And it will be a

division of an accident of reason into different real subjects.

In the third way it is taken so that both the thing divided and the members

are beings of reason, and the sense is: Of the subject of a proposition, one is

first, another second, or one is particular, another common; and since these dif‐

ferent subjects are as it were species of subject abstracted from the common

and the particular, the division so taken will be of a genus into species. Lastly,

both the thing divided and the members can be taken for real substance accord‐

ing to the real property of standing under, and the sense will be: Of substance

really standing under accidents and superior predicates, one is first, which

stands under by its own power; another second, which stands under by the pow‐

er of the first. And the division will be

[p. 293]

of an analogous term into its analogates, because second substance is not said to stand under except through attribution to first substance, since it stands under by its power.

27 Of these four ways of taking this division, the second must be excluded, because there is no one who takes the division so, and it is truly beside the mind of Aristotle and irrelevant to his purpose: because, since the thing divided is ordered to the cognition of the members, if it is taken for a being of reason it will not be able to serve for knowing them. This way, then, being passed over, according to the other three there are four different opinions.

The first asserts that it is a division of a subject into accidents, because it considers it in the first way. So Canterus at the beginning of this chapter. He proves it from a sufficient division: because this division is not of an equivocal term into its equivocates, since something besides the name is divided. Nor is it a division of a whole into parts, because the thing divided is predicated of the members, indeed one member of the other: for it is true that first substance is substance; and since second substance is universal, it is true also that it is predicated of first substance, which is singular; and yet neither is the whole predicated of the parts, nor one part of another; therefore substance is not divided by this division as a whole into its parts. Nor is it a division of a genus into species, because one species is not predicated of another, but second substance is predicated of first. And besides, if the division were generic, a genus would be given superior to the most general genus of this category, which, since it is second substance, will be the other member of this division, and therefore inferior to the thing divided, as a species under a genus. Nor, finally, is it analogous: first, because if real substance is divided in the ratio of standing under, since to stand under is not the essence of substance but its property, it would not be substance that is divided, but a certain proper attribute of it. Next, the thing divided would not belong to second substance: because the thing divided is substance under the ratio of standing under, since to stand under is to be a subject; and second substance, since it cannot be a subject but a predicate, could not have it belong to it.

28 The second opinion takes the thing divided in the same way for real substance, and the members for second intentions, yet not for real substance according to its essence, but according to the real property of standing under. And it affirms that it is a division of a real accidental into accidents of reason: because the proper attribute of standing under is a real accident, while the members are accidents of reason, namely universal and particular substance. For this opinion the Louvain commentators and Toledo are cited, but I have been unable to find anything of the kind in them.

29 The third opinion, taking the whole division for second intentions, asserts that it is of a genus into species: which is followed

T iij

[p. 294]

by many moderns. And they prove it by this argument: The thing divided, which is subject in common, is participated equally by first and second substance, and by the one without dependence on the other; therefore it is a univocal and generic division. The antecedent is proved: because when in a proposition the copula is absolved from time, its truth does not depend on singulars, as in this one, Man is risible; therefore man, which is second substance, does not stand under the predicate risible with dependence on first substance. And in contingent singular propositions the truth does not depend on second substances, but only on first ones, to which accidents belong without dependence on second substances.

The last opinion holds that the division is of an analogous term into its analogates. But those who follow it do not take it in the same way: some take the thing divided for real substance and the members for second intentions, according to the first way, and so real substance is divided into different second intentions, Universal and Singular, or of Subject and Predicate. So Soto, q. 1, ad 1, and Cajetan on the present chapter also. But many others affirm that it is analogous, taking both the thing divided and the members really. So Albert the Great on the Categories, tract. 2, on substance, ch. 3; Javelli, Metaph. 5, q. 7; Toledo, q. 1; and expressly St. Thomas, On Power, q. 9, a. 1, ad 6. And this seems to me more probable.

30 But two things must be proved, in order that its greater probability may become manifest. First, that both the thing divided and the members are taken really, and not for second intentions. Second, that so taken it is a division of an analogous term into its analogates. The first is proved from Aristotle, who did not posit this division expressly, but we understand that he posited it from the fact that he defined each member. Therefore the members of the division are such as they are defined. But they are defined according to their real being; therefore they make a real division. The minor is proved: because the first is defined thus: Substance which is said properly, principally, and most of all, etc. But these excellences do not belong to it by reason of a second intention, but on account of its most perfect real nature; therefore it is defined really, and not by a second intention. Second substances too are defined as being the genera and species in which the first are, that is, under which they are placed in the category; therefore they are defined as they are placed in the category; but they are not placed in the category as they are denominated by second intentions, but as they are metaphysical and real genera and species; therefore they are defined really.

31 Besides, comparing the two members of the division, Aristotle says that first substance is more substance than second, because it stands under accidents by its own power; but to stand under is

[p. 295]

a real act, since it is really to sustain accidents; therefore they are compared according to real being and not intentional being, and therefore they make a real division.

It is proved finally: because Aristotle divided into first and second the same substance whose properties he afterwards enumerates; but the properties are real, as is manifest; therefore substance is really divided into first and second.

It is proved next by reason. First, because it is repugnant that the thing divided and the members be taken for second intentions, as the other opinions posit; therefore all of them are false. The antecedent is proved concerning the thing divided: for the members of the division are the second intentions of subject and predicate, as is gathered from the definitions of each, understood in the second, intentional, way; but no second intention is given common to subject and predicate except the universal ratio of being of reason; therefore this will be the thing divided. And the sense of the division will be: Of being of reason, one is subject, another predicate; which is plainly absurd, since being of reason considered in common denominates nothing, and if it did denominate, it would not denominate substance more than accidents. From which it is understood that neither can the thing divided in this division be subject in common: because it does not denominate substance more than accident, since either can indifferently be the subject of a proposition. It is proved also concerning the members, that they are not taken for second intentions: for the members are subject and predicate, as the first opinion asserts; but the predicate is nobler than the subject, since it is the form of the proposition; therefore second substance, as it is a member of the division, will be nobler than first, which is expressly against Aristotle, who often teaches in the text that first substance is nobler than second.

32 This supposed, the second must be proved, that the division is of an analogous term into its analogates. But in order that it may be proved, it should be noted that substance can be considered in three ways: according to its essence; according to its ultimate substantial act, which is subsistence; or according to the property of sustaining accidents. The essence of substance is to be a certain grade of perfect real entity, that is, independent of another, and to which subsistence per se is due; and although it cannot be in the nature of things except as actually existing, nor complete except through subsistence, yet neither pertains to its essence, but is outside it. Nor, however, are they accidents, but certain substantial acts of it, such that through existence it is in the nature of things, and through subsistence it is ultimately completed and constituted in a person or supposit. But the property of standing under follows substance already completed, or already

T iiij

[p. 296]

subsisting. These three, then, are related thus: to be a perfect entity, independent of itself, is the essence of substance, from which the two others proceed in this order: that subsistence is first, and then, by means of it, standing under proceeds; the former as a substantial mode, standing under as a property, but both outside the essence of the same nature, which is placed in the category according to its essence. But because this is not easily known by us, Aristotle wished to make it manifest through the intimate property of sustaining accidents; and therefore he divided substance according to the property of standing under, as the definition of first substance evidently shows. Hence the sense of the division is: Of substance, which is a complete and perfect being, to which subsistence per se is due, by reason of which it is as it were sustentative of other things, one is first, another second; that is, it has being first and per se in the singular, and as it were secondarily in the universal.

33 From this doctrine is gathered this argument, by which it is proved that the division taken really is of an analogous term into its analogates. An analogous term is a name that belongs to its significates in such a way that it belongs to one per se, first, and simply, but to the others only with an intrinsic dependence on and attribution to it: as being belongs to substance and accident. But substance taken really in the ratio of standing under (as it has been proved to be taken in this division) belongs to first substance first and per se, but to second substance only with an intrinsic dependence on and attribution to the first; therefore it stands as analogous with respect to both, and as such it is divided into them as into its analogates. The minor is proved: because to stand under, or to sustain other things by its own power, belongs to first substance, and by participation of it belongs to second substances.

To the argument of the first opinion, which contended to prove that the division is not analogous on account of two things. First, because the thing divided is substance in the ratio of standing under; therefore it is not substance that is divided, but a certain proper attribute of it. And we reply by granting that substance is not divided according to its essence, but inasmuch as there belongs to it the proper attribute of standing under, through which its essence is made manifest, just as animal could be divided inasmuch as it is sensible. The second was that if substance is divided in the ratio of standing under, it will not be able to belong to second substance, because to stand under is to be a subject, and second substance is a predicate. The reply is that second substances have both rationes, of subject and of predicate; and they pertain to this division rather as subjects, which really stand under accidents, than as predicates. But it was more fitting to divide substance through that real property

[p. 297]

of standing under than through second intentions, so that its categorial ratio

might become manifest, and it might also be established how it can be the

foundation of a second intention.

Q U E S T I O N V.

What the formal definitum of the definition of first substance is.

35

T      he first opinion is that of Soto, which many moderns follow: that the

formal definitum of this definition is the second intention of first substance

in common, which is abstracted from the particular second intentions denomi‐

nating Peter and John and the other first substances. And the material defini‐

tum is the real ratio of first substance, in which all first substances agree, not as it is

real, but as it is denominated by the second intention; and from both is made

one total and complete definitum. Just as in the definition of genus we said

that the formal definitum is the second intention of genus, and the material

definitum the generic nature in common, denominated by it.

It is proved from the definition of first substance given by Aristotle,

which runs thus: First substance is that which is neither said of any subject nor is in

any subject; and it contains a negation of predication and a negation of the foundation.

For first substance is not predicated of a subject because it is not in a sub‐

ject; therefore the definitum will be real first substance as the foundation

and as it were as the material element, and the second intention, or its nega‐

tion, as the formal element.

Next it is proved by reason: because first substances, as Peter and John,

can be considered in two ways: either according to the real being of singular

substance, or as they are denominated by the second intention; and if they

are considered in the first way, they can have nothing real common and uni‐

vocal; therefore neither can anything real common to them be the definitum.

The antecedent is proved: because singulars, as singulars, are primarily di‐

verse, just as they are ultimately distinct; therefore they cannot have a univo‐

cal agreement: for if they had it, they would have to be separated from it by

other differences, and so one would proceed to infinity. From which it fol‐

lows that first substance can be defined only as denominated by the second

intention.

36 Third, if something real and common were the definitum, two absur‐

dities would follow. First, that the definition would not belong to the defini‐

tum. Which I prove thus: The definitum is something real, common to all

first substances; therefore it is predicated of them and is in them; but the de‐

finition asserts that first substance is not

[p. 298]

said of a subject nor is in a subject; therefore it cannot belong to it. The second absurdity that follows is that the definitum is not first substance but second. The consequence is proved: because first substance is not a common predicate but a singular subject, whereas second substance is a common predicate, which is predicated of first substances; but that is a real common predicate which is predicated of first substances; therefore it is second substance. Wherefore it cannot be the definitum in the definition of first substance.

37 The second opinion is that of Cajetan on the present chapter, where he asserts that individuals, or first substances, as Peter and John, can be considered in two ways: either as they participate the human nature, or as they have a particular mode of subsisting. And in both ways they have a univocal agreement, but the first is an agreement of nature, the second of mode; and therefore the former is called specific, the latter modal: for the subsistence in which they agree is a mode of the nature. And the first agreement is signified by this name (man), the second by this name (first substance): because first substance signifies substance subsisting per se, abstracted from this and that first substance, as from Peter and John. The definitum of this definition, then, as it were the material one, is all first substances; but the formal one is that common ratio of subsisting particularly, and adequate to these first substances, as they agree in the same modal ratio. This is the express opinion of St. Thomas, 1 p., q. 29, a. 1, ad 1, where he says thus: Although this or that singular cannot be defined, yet that which pertains to the common ratio of singularity can be defined. And thus the Philosopher defines first substance; and in this way Boethius defines person. And q. 30, a. 4, ad 2: although a person is incommunicable, yet the very mode of existing incommunicably can be common to many. And this seems to me more probable and to be held.

38 It is proved by the testimony of Aristotle and by reason. For Aristotle, wishing to define first substance, explained it in these words: Substance which is said properly, principally, and most of all, etc. By which it is evident that the proper excellences of first substance are signified, which cannot belong to it in relation to the second intention, but according to its own real nature, subsisting per se; therefore it is defined according to that nature, and not as denominated by the second intention. And so it had to be defined rather than through the second intention, because unless its real nature is known, the mode by which it is the foundation of the second intention cannot be understood.

But the same opinion is proved by reason. First, because first

[p. 299]

substance extends to any substantial nature whatever, whereas person extends only to rational and intellectual nature; but Boethius defined person according to the real mode of subsisting, in the book On the Two Natures, at the beginning, saying: A person is an individual substance of a rational nature. For so the school of the Theologians understood this definition; therefore first substance could be defined by Aristotle in the same way. And that it was so defined, the testimony cited proves.

39 Second, because first substance is defined according to the ratio by which it is placed in the category, as the real foundation of the whole category; but it is evident that it is not placed in the category as it is denominated by the second intention, because so it is not a real foundation, but according to its real nature, subsisting per se and sustaining all things; therefore it is defined according to that nature, and not as it is denominated by the second intention of subject.

To the testimony of Aristotle for the first opinion, the reply is that first substance, through its proper real mode of subsisting, also has the real negations of inhering in a subject and of being predicated of it; and therefore the definition is to be understood according to these real negations, and not according to intentional negations.

To the first argument the reply is by denying the minor, that Peter and John, as they are singular men, do not agree: because from the mode of singularity of each a common concept of the mode of singularity can be abstracted. And in the same way first substances agree in the mode of subsisting per se; from which agreement it is not necessary that they be separated by other differences, but they are sufficiently separated by the same subsistences as determinate and distinct, and therefore there will be no process to infinity.

40 To the second, we deny that those two absurdities follow if something common to first substances is defined: for that common thing is not something to which the definition does not belong, but the ratio under which it belongs to first substances; wherefore it neither is in a subject nor is said of a subject, but is the common ratio of those things which neither are in a subject nor are said of a subject.

Nor does the second follow either, that the definition belongs to second substances: because second substance is not whatever is predicated of first substance, but what is predicated of it as a generic or specific nature; which is proved from the definition of second substances, which runs thus: Second substances are the genera and species in which first substances are. But that common ratio under which first substances are defined is not of the nature, and therefore it is neither generic nor differential, but only modal.

[p. 300]

F I R S T D O U B T, C O N C E R N I N G T H E

## COMPARISONS OF FIRST AND SECOND

## SUBSTANCES

41

T     wo things remain to be explained concerning the text of Aristotle. The

first pertains to the comparisons which he made between first and sec‐

ond substances; the second to the properties of the same substance. These,

for brevity’s sake, will be explained in certain doubts. And the first is about

the comparisons, whether they are true. Now they are four. For first he com‐

pares first substances with second ones, and asserts that first substance is more

substance than second. Second, he compares second substances among them‐

selves in two ways, namely genus with species, and species among them‐

selves; and he affirms that the species is more substance than the genus, but that

among species one is not more substance than another. Lastly he compares

first substances among themselves, affirming also that one is not more substance

than another.

But against these comparisons three arguments are proposed. The first

against all of them: because they seem to contradict a certain property of the

same substance, by which it is said that substance does not admit of more

and less; and if this is so, it will be false that one substance is more substance

than another, whether it be first or second.

The second argument is against the first comparison, in which it is said

that first substance is more substance than second: for second substance is

the species, as man, and first substance is the individual, as Peter; but the

species is more perfect than the individual; therefore second substance will

be more perfect than first, and therefore it will be more substance than it.

The minor is proved: because the perfection of an essential thing is taken

from the essential predicates; but the essential predicates belong first to the

species, and by participation of it to the individual; therefore the species will

be more perfect.

42 The third is against the comparison of second substances, and of first

ones, among themselves, in which Aristotle says that one species is not more sub‐

stance than another. Which I prove to be false: for that one is more substance

than another which stands under more things; but one species stands under

more things than another; therefore it will be more substance. The minor is

proved: because crow stands under more predicates than man: because it

stands under all those under which man stands, and under two others, name‐

ly brute and bird, which are genera inferior to animal; and among first sub‐

stances too, one

[p. 301]

stands under more things than another: for this singular crow stands under the same genera under which, just as man does not stand, so neither does Peter; therefore it will be more a substance than Peter.

For the solution of the first argument, it should be noted that More and Less can be taken in two ways, Properly and Improperly. They are taken Properly for the gradual intension of a quality: according to which Hot as four is properly called more hot than Hot as two, because it has more degrees of intension of the same heat. But improperly more and less are taken for more and less perfect, under any consideration whatever, whether essential or accidental, whether intensive or extensive: in which acceptation man is said to be more a substance than a horse, that is, more perfect essentially. When, therefore, Aristotle says at the beginning of the chapter that the first substance is more a substance than the second, and among the second substances the species is more a substance than the genus, he takes those words More and Less in the second signification; but when he asserts at the end of the chapter that substance does not admit of more and less, he takes them in the first way; and therefore he does not contradict himself.

For the solution of the second argument, it should be noted that Substance can be taken in two ways. First, as to the essence abstracting from actual existence and subsistence; and therefore as it regards only the essential predicates. Second, it is taken for the essence in order to the actual entity which it has outside its causes through actual existence, and complete entity through subsistence; and upon substance taken in this way there follows the property of standing under accidents and superior predicates: for from the fact that substance subsists per se, it can sustain all things. Now, then, if substance is taken in the first way, it belongs more perfectly to the second substance than to the first; and this is what the argument proves. But it is not so taken by Aristotle, but in the second acceptation, and insofar as the property of standing under belongs to it; and in this way it is true that the first substance is more perfect than the second, because it stands under by its own power, but the second only by the power of the first.

43 The third argument is to be solved by another distinction: for to stand under is taken in two ways, Intensively and Extensively. Intensively it is taken in order to the power of standing under, and in this way that is said to stand under more which stands under by its own power, and that less which does so by the power of another. But Extensively, in order to the more or fewer things under which something stands. And from this it is replied to the argument that when Aristotle says that the first substance is more a substance than the second, in both

[p. 302]

he understands this comparison both intensively and extensively. And in both ways it is true: because the first substance stands under more things than the second, and also stands under by its own power, while the second does so only by the power of the first. But the other comparisons are understood intensively, not extensively: and therefore it is true that among species there is none that stands under by the power of another. The argument, however, proves only that one stands under more extensively, that is, that it stands under more things. And in the same way it is true that among first substances one does not stand under more than another intensively: because one does not stand under by the power of another, but each by its own power. But the species is said to be more a substance than the genus in both ways: extensively indeed, for it stands under more things, since it stands under the genus itself and the rest. And also intensively, because, although it does not stand under by its own power, any more than the genus does, yet it comes nearer to that which stands under by its own power, namely to the first substance; and this suffices for it to be said to stand under more intensively.

## SECOND DOUBT CONCERNING THE THIRD

P RO P E RT Y O F S U B S TA N C E .

Whether it is true, and in what sense, that Second substances signify Quale quid.

T     hat second substances do not signify Quale quid, as Aristotle teaches, I prove

by two arguments. First, because only two things can be considered in any name from which it may be understood to signify Quid or Quale quid: namely, the thing signified, whether it is Substance or quality; and the mode of signifying it. The names of second substances, on the part of both, signify Quid, that is, Substance, and not Quale quid; therefore it is false that they signify Quale quid. The minor is proved: because on the part of the thing signified they signify substance, and also on the part of the mode, since they are substantive names, signifying the thing by way of something subsisting.

Second: the mode of predicating is taken from the mode of signifying; therefore if second substances, which are genera and species, signify Quale quid, it follows that they are predicated of the first in Quale quid. The consequent is false; therefore so is the antecedent. I prove the minor by authority and by reason: for Porphyry, in the chapter on genus and species, expressly taught that Genus and species are predicated in Quid. And reason itself joins with this: because to a question asked about the species by Quid, we reply by the genus; and to a question asked about the individual, by the species: as if you ask what is

Peter

[p. 303]

man, we reply that it is an animal; and if you ask what Peter is, that he is a man: therefore each second substance is predicated in Quid, and not in Quale quid.

Concerning the sense of this property, authors speak in different ways. And the first way of speaking is that of Albert the Great, Categories, tract. 7, ch. 8, where he says: Genera and species, which are second substances, by reason of the generic nature signify Quid; but on account of the difference, which the species contains in act and the genus in potency, they signify Quale, and therefore by reason of both, Quale quid; and that this was the sense of Aristotle.

This way of speaking, however, is proved false by this argument: If genus and Species, by reason of each essential part, signify Quale quid, then they are predicated in Quale quid, against the opinion of Porphyry, who, knowing that the species contains genus and difference, and the genus difference, expressly taught that each is predicated in Quid, and not in Quale quid; and it is against reason: because if they were predicated in Quale quid, they would not be distinguished from the predicable difference. Therefore Cajetan rightly refuted this opinion, in the present chapter.

Cajetan himself proposes a second way of speaking, distinguishing two things in genus and species: namely, the generic or specific nature, which is denominated genus; and the second intention, by which they are denominated. And on account of the generic and specific nature, which are substance, they signify something; but on account of the second intention, which is an accident and has the mode of a quality, as whiteness and color, they signify Quale; and therefore on account of both they signify Quale quid.

But this way of speaking is no less false than the first, which I prove thus: Second substances signify Quale by reason of the second intention, which is an accident; therefore they signify an accidental Quale, just as white signifies Quale by reason of whiteness, and therefore an accidental Quale. From which it follows that they are predicated of first substances in an accidental Quale, and therefore by the predication of the fifth predicable, which is absurd. And if someone should reply for Cajetan that they signify an accidental Quale, but concerning substance, since the natures of genus and species which are denominated are substantial: the solution does not satisfy, because white also signifies a quality concerning substance, since the subject in which whiteness inheres is a substance; therefore they signify Quale in the same way as white or colored; but these are predicated in an accidental Quale; therefore so too are second substances predicated of the first.

For the solution, then, of this doubt and of the arguments, it should be noted that Quale quid can be taken in two ways, in a Proper and in a Common sense. And since in both ways it is taken by similitude

[p. 304]

to true quality, which is an accidental form of the fourth category, each mode is to be understood from a proper and a common similitude to it. For Quality has two things. The first is to inhere in a subject, from which it can be absent, and to surround it, and to determine it in such a way that to a question asked about it by Quale we properly reply by means of the quality. And this is its proper ratio, to which the difference is likened, which is compared to the genus as to a potency, outside whose ratio it is, and to which it can be present and from which it can be absent; and therefore, as determining the genus for the constitution of the species, by way of something adjacent, signified by an adjectival name, it is predicated of the species: and this is to be likened to quality according to its proper ratio. Quality has another thing, common with the other accidents: that it is determined by the subject as to its actual inherence, and in some way at least as to individuation. And second substances are likened to quality, considered according to this common and improper ratio: because they are as it were common concepts and common forms, which are determined, as to subsistence and individuation, by the first substances in which they subsist. And on account of this similitude Aristotle taught that they do not signify This something, that is, singular and subsisting substance, against Plato, who posited substances separated from singulars and subsisting outside them; but that they signify Quale, since they are as it were forms abstracted from singulars by the intellect alone, and determinable by those same singulars as to subsistence and individuation, after the manner of accidental forms; and, because they are truly substances, that they signify Quale quid. Next, since the substantial ratio belongs to them properly, but the ratio of quality only by similitude, in the common and improper ratio of quality, they are signified by substantive names, they are called quidditative predicates, and they are said to be predicated in Quid, not in Quale quid, as difference is: because difference has a proper similitude with quality, whereas second substances are likened to it according to the common and improper ratio; and therefore they are not predicated in Quale quid, because the special mode of predicating must be taken from the proper ratio, not from the common. And this is the reason for which Aristotle taught that Second substances signify Quale quid, and are not predicated in Quale quid.

51 To the first argument posited at the beginning: all that it assumes is to be granted; but the consequent is to be distinguished, when it is inferred that they do not signify Quale quid: for if the proper Quale quid is understood, it is true; if the improper, false. Therefore

rightly

[p. 305]

it is rightly consistent that they signify Quid simply, on account of the thing

signified, which is substance, and on account of the mode of signifying of sub‐

stantive names, and that they also signify an improper Quale, on account of a

certain similitude with quality; and therefore in a certain way Quale quid.

To the second, the major is to be distinguished: for the mode of predicating

is taken from the proper mode of signifying, not from the improper; and be‐

cause second substances properly signify Quid, and by a certain common and

improper ratio Quale quid, they are predicated rather in Quid than in Quale

quid.

## THIRD DOUBT CONCERNING THE

F O U RT H P RO P E RT Y O F S U B S TA N C E .

Whether it is true that substance has no contrary. 52

I   n this property of substance Aristotle seems to contradict himself, which I

prove thus: for in Phys. 1, text 50, he asserts that the principles from which sub‐

stance is generated and composed are contraries; indeed, that they are the first contraries;

and that in each genus or category there is one contrariety; and therefore that in sub‐

stance, which is one genus, one contrariety is found. It is false, then, what he teaches

in the present chapter, that it is proper to substance to have no contrary.

And it is proved by argument that substance has a contrary: for the ele‐

ments are contraries, as fire and water, air and earth, and yet they are certain

substances. And if you reply that the elements are contraries not as they are

substances, but by reason of the first qualities, which are their accidents, as by

reason of heat and cold, moistness and dryness: against this is the fact that

these qualities proceed from the very substance of the elements; therefore

they receive their contrariety from it. Wherefore it will be first in substance,

and by participation from it in the accidents.

For the solution of this doubt it should be noted that there are four genera of

opposition, as Aristotle teaches in this book, in the chapter on opposites, and in

Metaph. 5, ch. One is privative opposition, between form and privation, as be‐

tween light and darkness. Another is contradictory, between affirmation and

negation, as between man and not-man, or between an affirmative and a nega‐

tive proposition. The third is relative, as between father and son. The fourth,

finally, is contrary, as between hot and cold; and this is to be explained, since

the doubt concerns it, whether it is found in substance.

Contrariety is taken in two ways. First, under a Common and improper ra‐

tio, for any opposition whatever. In which

V

[p. 306]

acceptation we call contraries things opposed in any way whatever. Second, Properly, for the last genus of opposition only, of the four enumerated, whose definition is gathered from Aristotle in the places cited: Contraries are those which under the same genus are most distant, and mutually expel each other from the same subject. As hot and cold under the genus of quality are most distant, that is, they are as it were extremes; and when one inheres in a body, the other is expelled, as heat is expelled from water, in which there is coldness. Contraries, then, must have two conditions necessary to the purpose. The first, that they be positive forms, because they are species of the same genus. The second, that they regard the same subject, in which each can inhere and expel the other from it.

53 From which it is understood, First, that of the four genera of opposition three are found in substance: namely, Privative, because substance, when it is generated, comes to be from its own privation, as man from not-man, that is, from matter, in which there is the privation of the rational soul; Contradictory, as between man and not-man; Relative, as between Peter and John, insofar as they are of the same species. Contrary opposition alone is repugnant to it, on account of the perfection of its nature: because, since substance is of so perfect a nature that subsistence per se is owed to it, it is repugnant to it to be a form inhering in a subject; and therefore that it should expel another form from it, as is said in the definition of contraries. Nor can such an imperfection be found in the whole latitude of its category. And this is the chief foundation of this property which Aristotle attributes to it.

54 Second, it is understood in what way it is to be granted that substance has a contrary, and also in what way it is to be denied: for of improper contrariety, taken for any opposition whatever, it is to be granted; but of proper contrariety, taken for the last genus of opposition only, posited above, it is to be denied. And because the fourth property is understood by Aristotle only of proper contrariety, his opinion is most true: That nothing is contrary to substance.

55 For the solution of the arguments it should be noted that among the oppositions the first, and as it were the foundation of the rest, is the privative, which is found in any genus and category whatever: for of the two opposed differences by which a genus is divided, one is related to the other as a privation, because it is more imperfect than the other, and therefore is as it were deprived of the perfection of the other; as is plain in the differences by which living is divided into sensible and insensible, and animal into rational and irrational: for insensible is understood as it were as a privation of sense, and irrational as lacking rationality. But that it is the foundation of the others

[p. 307]

is proved: because substance is the foundation of the other things among which the other oppositions are found; but privative opposition is found in the first generation of substance itself, because every substance is generated from its own privation in matter, as man from not-man; and consequently whatever other things are generated or come to be are understood to come to be from their own privation, as hot from not-hot, that is, from the privation of heat in the subject in which and from which it comes to be. From which it follows that, just as privative opposition is the first, the foundation of the others, so substance, in which it is first found, is as it were the root from which all oppositions proceed; which are therefore first found in it: privative, contradictory and relative formally; but contrary not formally, but only virtually, because formal contrariety is repugnant to its perfection.

From this doctrine the arguments are easily solved: for the testimonies of Aristotle speak of contrariety under its common and improper ratio, taken for any genus of opposition whatever, but chiefly for privative opposition; of which it is understood that the principles of the generation of substance are contraries, and that the first contrariety is found in substance, that is, the first opposition, which is the privative. But when he asserts that substance in this category has no contrary, he speaks of proper contrariety, as has been explained.

56 To the argument it is replied by distinguishing the antecedent: for the elements, by reason of substance, are not formally nor properly contraries, but by reason of their qualities. And when it is said that the Qualities proceed from substance, it is to be granted; but the consequent is to be distinguished, that true contrariety is first found in substance: for it is found there virtually, as in the first root from which it proceeds, not formally. But when Aristotle denies in this fourth property that substance has a contrary, he understands it of formal contrariety, not of virtual: because the latter does not imply an imperfection repugnant to the substantial nature, whereas the former conflicts with its perfection.

F O U RT H D O U B T C O N C E R N I N G T H E

L A S T P RO P E RT Y O F S U B S TA N C E . Whether it belongs to first substances alone to be receptive of contraries, or also to sec‐

ond substances and to accidents.

T    he last property of substance, Aristotle said, is That, being one in number,

it can receive contraries in itself.

V ij

[p. 308]

And since the first substance alone is one in number, while second substances have only specific and generic unity, it seems to be attributed by Aristotle to it alone, so that it does not belong to second substances, and much less to accidents, but to first substance in the fourth mode, that is, to every one, to it alone, and always.

57 But it seems that it belongs neither to all first substances, nor to them alone, but also to accidents: for a proposition is an accident, and yet, remaining the same, it is now true, if the thing is as it is enunciated through it, and afterwards false, if the thing changes: therefore it receives contraries. The consequence is proved: because truth and falsity are contraries. Nor does the solution which Aristotle gives to this argument seem to satisfy, saying: To receive contraries is the same as to be changed from one to the other; but what is changed receives the change itself in itself, and also the term of that change, as what is changed when it becomes hot from cold receives both in itself; but the proposition is not changed when it becomes true from false, but only the thing is changed, and from its change the proposition becomes true or false; and therefore it is not said to receive contraries. This solution, I say, does not satisfy the argument, which I prove thus: Truth and falsity, as complex, are not formally in things, but only virtually, as in a cause, because they cause them in the intellect; but in the intellect they are found formally, as enunciating or judging; nor are they found there except by means of the mental proposition through which it enunciates; therefore in the mental proposition, or in the intellect enunciating through it, truth and falsity are found as in a subject, which is formally changed when the proposition becomes false from true. Wherefore it is necessary to grant that it receives contraries, since it receives them through a true change of itself. But the intellect and the mental proposition are accidents; therefore it belongs to accidents to receive contraries, and not to first substances alone. Which is also true of quantity: for bodily accidents that are truly contraries are received in quantity before they are received in substance, as heat and cold; therefore quantity also, since it is one in number, will be receptive of contraries.

58 Now, that it does not belong to all first substances is proved: because a spiritual substance, as an Angel, does not receive any contraries in itself; indeed, neither does an incorruptible bodily substance, such as the heavens; therefore not every first substance is receptive of contraries. The antecedent is proved: because contraries dispose the subject in which they are toward corruption, as heat and cold; but Angels and celestial bodies are incorruptible substances; therefore they are not capable of contraries. The antecedent is proved: because contrary qualities dispose the subject

[p. 309]

to different substantial forms, as heat to the form of fire, and cold to the form of water; but different substantial forms cannot be at the same time in the same matter or subject, nor can one be expelled from it except through the corruption of the composite; therefore contraries are ordered to its corruption, wherefore they cannot be in an incorruptible subject.

59 In order that this doubt may be fully resolved, three things are to be determined. First: Whether this property belongs to substances alone, or also to accidents. Second: Whether, granted that it belongs to substances alone, it belongs not only to first substances but also to second. Third: Whether, if it belongs to first substances alone, it belongs only to some, or to all. And from the determination of these three it can be gathered Whether this is a property of substance, belonging to it in the fourth mode.

For the solution of the first, it should be noted that the First substance has two things by reason of which this property belongs to it. The first is that it is this something (to use Aristotle’s words), that is, a singular substance, subsisting per se, and therefore independent of others. The second, that it is the first subject of all accidents. And by reason of the first it belongs to it to be one in number, remaining under different accidents; by reason of the second, that it is receptive of contraries: for things contrarily opposed are accidents. And therefore by reason of both the entire property belongs to it, namely that, being one in number, it receives contraries in itself. But since neither belongs to accidents (as is known), neither can the same property belong to them.

60 But to the argument about the proposition, it is replied by this distinction: A proposition is twofold: One vocal or written, and the other mental. And of the vocal and written it is evident that they do not receive formal truth or falsity in themselves, but truth is in them only as in a sign, that is, by extrinsic denomination alone. Whence, although it passes from truth to falsity, this does not happen through a change of itself, because they do not receive these accidents in themselves formally, but only through the change of the thing; whence neither do they receive contraries in themselves. But of the mental proposition it cannot be denied that it contains formal truth or falsity in itself, since it formally represents the thing as it is or as it is not; nor can it be denied either that truth is formally in the judging intellect. But even so, the mental proposition, or the judging intellect, is not said to receive contraries, because it is not the principal subject of truth or falsity, but the means through which these are received in the soul; and moreover, not even so are they, as a means, receiving contraries by reason of themselves or by their own power: and from the con

V iij

[p. 310]

sequence, nor do they have them simply, but by the power of the substance whose accidents they are; and therefore it is substance alone that, as the chief subject and by its own power, receives contraries, not accidents.

61 Concerning the second, Whether this property belongs to second substances, Cajetan, in the present chapter, says that this particle (one in number) must be distinguished: for it is placed either on the part of the subject or on the part of the predicate. And placed on the part of the subject it makes this sense: It is proper to substance which is one in number to be receptive of contraries; in which sense it is evident that it belongs to first substance alone, because it alone is one in number. But if it is placed on the part of the predicate, the sense will be this: It is proper to substance that, numerical unity being preserved, it can receive contraries; and the property understood in this way, it is also evident, belongs to second substances: because, the numerical unity which they have in first substances being preserved, they can receive contraries; as man, the numerical unity which he has in Peter being preserved, can receive color and cold. In this way too this property is understood by other expositors, as Albert the Great, Simplicius and Villalpando; and they say that Aristotle spoke thus, so as to make this property common to all substances.

But others deny that it can be accommodated to second substances, as Ammonius and Cant., in their expositions of this chapter.

62 But our view is that one must reply with this distinction. We can speak of this property of substance in two ways. First, in the sense in which Aristotle spoke.
