Second, without any limitation of the words. And if we are to speak in the first way, this property belongs to first substances alone, and to second substances in no way. This is proved against Cajetan. First, Aristotle asserts that It is most proper to substance that, being one in number, it can receive contraries; therefore this property cannot belong to a substance unless it is one in number; but second substance has numerical unity neither in itself nor in first substance; therefore it belongs to it in no way. The minor is proved. Second substance is considered in itself as it is abstracted from the first; but as abstracted from the first it is not one in number, since it is common to all first substances, but one only in genus or in species; therefore this property does not belong to it. But as it is contracted to the first, it is indeed one in number, yet it is not second substance but first: because man, as contracted to Peter really and formally, is this man; but this man formally is a singular man; therefore formally first substance, and in no way second. Wherefore it is the same to say that sec

[p. 311]

ond substances have this property as they have numerical unity in first substances, and to say that it belongs to first substances alone.

Second, it is proved from the definition of second substances, which runs thus: Second substances are the genera and species in which first substances are. But they are not genera and species as they are contracted to the first, or as they have subsistence in it, but insofar as they are considered as abstracted from it; and under this consideration it is repugnant that it belong to them, since they do not have numerical unity; therefore this property, as assigned by Aristotle, cannot be accommodated to second substances as they are second substances. But to say It is proper to substance that, being one in number, it can receive contraries, was the same as to exclude second substances from this property.

63 But if the same property is taken in the second way, without any limitation of the words, namely so that we say that it is most proper to substance to receive contraries, it belongs to every substance in the same way as the property of standing under, but analogically: that is, to first substances per se primarily and by reason of themselves, but to second substances only with dependence on and attribution to the first.

Concerning the third, Whether this property belongs to all first substances, not all agree. But the first way of speaking is that it belongs to bodily and corruptible first substances alone, on account of the argument we made at the beginning: so Porphyry and Ammonius, in their explanation of this property.

64 The second way of speaking, common to all the other Interpreters, is That it belongs to all first substances. And so it is to be held. But two things are briefly to be noted in order that it may be understood. The first, That Aristotle does not speak only of contraries taken strictly, such as the first and second qualities are: for truth and falsity, of which he speaks in the text, denying that the proposition is said to receive them, are not properly contraries; but he speaks of contraries more universally. Second, it should be noted That for this property to belong to some substance, it is not necessary that it receive all contraries, but it suffices that it can receive some, according to what befits its nature. Whence it is enough, for the Celestial bodies to be receptive of contraries, that they can receive contrary motions, one from East to West, the other from West to East; or the motion of increase and decrease in light, which it is certain the Moon receives from the Sun. It also suffices that Angels can receive truth and falsity by means of the intellect, and moral goodness and malice by means of the will and its acts, for them to be called first substances receptive of contraries.

V iiij

[p. 312]

## 65 But to the argument, the antecedent is to be distinguished: because

contraries are of two kinds. Some proper, as the first and second qualities,

which are wont to dispose toward the corruption of the subject; others less

proper, not regarding the corruption of the subject. And although Angels and

celestial bodies cannot receive those former and proper contraries, because

they cannot be corrupted either, yet they are receptive of other contraries;

and this suffices for this property to belong to them, because it is not under‐

stood by Aristotle of the first contraries alone, but of these or others.

From what has been said it follows that this last property of substance be‐

longs to first substances in the fourth mode, because it belongs to every first

substance, to it alone, and always. And therefore Aristotle said, It is most prop‐

er to substance that, being one in number, it can receive contraries: to signify that the

other properties do not belong to it in the fourth mode, but are common to

accidents; this one to first substances alone, with which it is convertible.

## CHAPTER VI

Containing the category of quantity.

## TEXT OF ARISTOTLE

Of quantity, however, one kind is discrete, another continuous.

B R I E F E X P O S I T I O N O F T H E T E X T.

1

A      fter substance, Aristotle immediately disputes about quantity, because

among the bodily accidents it is the first, most immediately following

the nature of substance itself, and the medium by which the rest inhere in it.

And his intention is to explain the nature of quantity. This chapter is divided

into three parts. In the first, he divides quantity by three divisions, from

which he gathers the number of the species of quantity. In the second, he ex‐

plains the single species. In the third, he enumerates three properties of the

same quantity.

The first division of quantity is not assigned expressly by Aristotle, but is

presupposed and insinuated: for by the very fact that he treats of quantity

per se, he presupposes its division into Quantity per se and Per accidens. A

Quantity per se is that which has parts of extension of itself, as a line or a

surface. A Quantity per accidens is that which does not have extension of it‐

self, but is extended by another: as white is called a quantity per accidens, be‐

cause whiteness does not have extended parts of itself, but receives them

from the surface of the body in which it is extended.

[p. 313]

The second division is (although it is placed in the third place by Aristotle): Of Quantity, one kind is Continuous, another Discrete. The Continuous is that whose parts are joined by a common term, as the parts of a line are joined by points. But the Discrete is that whose parts are not joined by a common term: as number is a discrete quantity, because its units are not joined by any term, but remain separate.

2 The third division: Of Quantity, one kind has Position of parts in the continuum, another does not have such position. Now position in the continuum is twofold. One, which the parts of quantity have in order to place, by reason of which something is said to sit, to lie, or to stand. And this Position of parts does not pertain to this category, but to the category of Situation. The other is the Position which the parts have, not in order to place, but among themselves, according to which one is called prior, another posterior, one right, another left, one up, another down. And this is proper to this category; according to it is understood the division which says that this belongs to some quantities and not to others. For two conditions are necessary for some quantity to be said to have position in the continuum. The first, that it be continuous. The second, that it be permanent. Through defect of the first condition, no species of discrete quantity has such position. Through defect of the second, among the continuous quantities time does not have position; but the remaining four have it, as line, surface, body and place, because they have both conditions.

3 The species of continuous quantity are five: Line, Surface, Body, Time and Place. But the species of Discrete quantity are two only, namely Number and Speech. But it is proved of each that they are species of quantity; or, if this is known of some, Aristotle at least proves that they are continuous or discrete quantities. And he begins from Number, of which he does not prove that it is a quantity, because that is known per se, but that it is a discrete quantity he proves by this argument: A discrete quantity is that whose parts are not joined by a common term; but the parts of number, which are units, are not joined by any common term, but remain separate; therefore number is a discrete quantity.

But of Speech he proves both, that it is a quantity and that it is discrete, because neither is manifest per se. He proves that it is a quantity by this argument: Long and short are attributes of quantity; but speech is measured by the long and short syllable (for he speaks of vocal speech alone, because this alone can be a species of quantity); therefore it is a quantity. But that it is a dis

[p. 314]

crete quantity he proves as he had proved of number: because the parts of speech, which are syllables, are not joined by a common term, but remain separate.

4 Of the continuous species also he proves it in the same way. And first of Line, Surface and Body, that they are continuous quantities, presupposing as manifest that they are quantities, by this argument: A continuous quantity is that whose parts are joined by a common term; but the parts of these three species are joined by a common term; therefore they are continuous quantities. He proves the minor thus: A Line is length without breadth, whose parts are joined by points; a Surface is length and breadth without depth, whose parts are joined by lines; and a Body is length, breadth and depth, whose parts are joined by surfaces; therefore the parts of these three species are joined by a common term.

But of Time and Place he supposes as manifest that they are quantities, and proves that they are continuous: of Time, indeed, by this argument: The parts of time, which are present, past and future, are joined in the instant, by reason of which they become one time; therefore time is a continuous quantity. But of Place in this way: Place so contains the located body, as water contains a tree, that the parts of the place correspond to the parts of the located thing; but the parts of the located thing, since it is a body, are joined by a common term; therefore so are the parts of the place; and thus place will be a continuous quantity, just as the located body is.

The first property of quantity is To have no contrary: as two cubits long or three cubits long, which are quantities, have no contrary. And this property is common to quantity with substance, as Aristotle taught in the preceding chapter.

The second property is Not to receive degrees of intension or remission, or, as is said in other words, not to receive more and less, as heat receives them, which we call intense according to two or three degrees: for one time is not more time than another, because it does not have more degrees of perfection either; and so of the other species of quantity. This too is a property common to quantity with substance and the others; and therefore it does not belong to quantity in the fourth mode, just as the first does not.

The third property of quantity is That according to it things are called equal and unequal: as two bodies, which are truly substances, if they have the same length, are called equal, but by reason of quantity, because length is a quantity. And this property belongs to quantity in the fourth mode, since it belongs to all its species, to them alone, and always.

[p. 315]

## QUESTION I

In what the essential ratio of quantity is to be placed.

6

T      he first opinion places the essential Ratio of quantity in measure, that is, in

the fact that every quantity is measurable by another, or at least is mea‐

sured by its own parts, and is also the measure of other things. And it can be

proved by the testimony of Aristotle, who in Phys. 4, treating of time, which

is one species of quantity, defines it, saying that it is the number or measure of

motion according to before and after.

It is proved also by argument: because the species of quantity must be dis‐

tinguished by essential rationes; but there are some which cannot be distin‐

guished except by the ratio of measure; therefore this will be the essential ra‐

tio of quantity. The minor is proved: In place and surface, which are not dis‐

tinguished except by the fact that the surface is the extrinsic measure of the

containing body in which it is, as of air or water; and place is the extrinsic

surface of the contained body, for considered in this way it has the ratio of

place. This opinion is attributed to St. Thomas, opusc. 55, On the Nature of

Place, at the end.

The second opinion is that of Scotus, on the Categories, q. 17, and Metaph.

5, q. 9, where he asserts that the Essence of quantity is divisibility into its own inte‐

gral parts: so too Antonius Andreas, Metaph. 5, q. 10; Capreolus, in 2, d. 3, q. 1;

Soncinas, Metaph. 5, q. 12; Javelli, q. 10; and St. Thomas seems to hold the

same, lect. 15 of the same book, and in 1, d. 39, q. 1, a. 1, ad 1. Scotus proves it

by the testimony of Aristotle and by argument. For Aristotle, Metaph. 5, ch.

23, defines Quantity: That which is divisible into those things which are in it, that

is, into its own integral parts, of which it is composed; but that definition ex‐

plains the essence of quantity; therefore this will be the ratio, namely of

divisibility.

7 And by argument: because all distinguish the species of quantity by di‐

visibility, saying that what is divisible according to one dimension, of length,

is a line; according to two dimensions, of length and breadth, a surface; and

according to three dimensions, of length, breadth and depth, a body; and so

of the rest, according to their own rationes of divisibility. But the specific

distinction must be essential; therefore they are distinguished essentially by

divisibility; wherefore this will be the essential ratio of quantity.

The third opinion denies that the Essence of quantity is measure or divisibility,

but places it in the extension of parts, which is for one part to be outside another.

So Durandus, in 1, d. 34, q. 1, no. 26; Nifo, Metaph. 5, q. 9; Soto and Toledo, q.

1

[p. 316]

of this category; Canterus, in his exposition of the text; Fonseca, Metaph. 5, ch. 13, q. 1, sect. 5. And this is the more probable opinion.

But it is not explained in the same way by all. For its understanding, however, there should be noted the first distinction of quantity, which St. Thomas gives, 1 p., q. 42, a. 1, ad 1, taken from St. Augustine, On the Trinity 6, ch. 8, about the middle: One Quantity is of Bulk, another of Power. The Quantity of Bulk is that which, inhering in a bodily substance, so makes its parts extended as to give them bulk or magnitude. The Quantity of Power is the essential perfection of any thing whatever, according to which it is called great or small, that is, constituted in a greater or lesser degree of perfection: as an Angel is called greater than man, and man greater than a lion, because essentially more perfect. Now this quantity of power, or of perfection, pertains to all the categories; therefore we are not treating of it now, but only of the quantity of bulk, which constitutes this category. And Aristotle defines it, Metaph. 5, ch. 15, in these words: A quantity is that which is divisible into those things which are in it, each of which, whether both or each one, is apt to be some one thing and a this something.

8 Now the definition is to be explained thus: it is called Divisible to distinguish Quantity from points and other indivisibles. And it is said to be divisible into those things which are in it, that is, into the integral parts of which it is composed, which are therefore formally in it, and not only virtually, as the elements are said to be in a mixed body only from the fact that their powers, as heat, cold, moistness and dryness, are in mixed bodies, but not the elements themselves according to their substantial forms; and therefore they are not said to be in them formally. Each of which, both, if it has two parts, or certainly two halves, into which any continuum is wont to be divided; or each one, if more. But it is divided into them in such a way that after the division each can exist separated from it, per se. For example: A piece of wood a palm long is divisible into two halves in such a way that each of them, once the division is made, now exists per se and independently of the whole: in which the continuum is distinguished from the Physical whole, which is composed of matter and form as of parts, and from the Metaphysical whole, which is composed of genus and difference; yet in such a way that it could not be divided into these parts, able to exist separated per se naturally, because neither can the material form exist materially without matter, nor matter without form. The definition, then, is understood of integral parts, when it is said: Quantity is that which is divisible into those things which are in it.

9 Second, it should be noted that integral parts are of two different kinds. Some are substantial or entitative, which are rather called parts of entity than of extension; and these they call

[p. 317]

several, which substance and the bodily accidents have of themselves and do not receive from quantity. Others are parts of bulk or of magnitude, which are called parts of extension, because by their own nature they are occupative of place; and just as each is distinct from another, so to each a distinct part of place is owed, so that several cannot occupy the same part of place, nor be in it at the same time with another body or a part of it. For example: The two halves of a finger are different parts of extension, because each is apt by nature to occupy a distinct part of place, so that it cannot naturally occupy the same part of place at the same time with the other, nor with another body or a part of it. And this extension of parts we call bulk or magnitude, which quantity alone has, and gives to substance and the other bodily accidents; and in the extension of bulk we say the essence of quantity consists. This is wont to be explained in other words thus, namely that the extension of quantity is to have part outside part, or one part outside another, not according to entity (for in this way substance and the other accidents also have part outside part), but according to bulk: so that to each is owed the distinct part of place which it is apt by nature to occupy. But the integral parts of substance and of the other accidents (which we call entitative) are not occupative of place, but all can be in the same part of place; indeed, in the same indivisible place.

11 Third, it should be noted That from this extension of parts according to bulk, which is the essence of quantity, its proper attributes proceed. Of which the first is Divisibility into the same parts of extension, which can be called the aptitude or potency to be divided. For as soon as we understand that quantity has part outside part, in which the extension essential to it consists, we consequently conceive that it is divisible into the same parts.

The second property is Measure, that is, that quantity itself is measurable by another, or by its own parts.

The third: That it is finite or infinite.

The fourth: That it is the foundation of equality and inequality.

The fifth is: The extension of the same parts in order to place, which is nothing else than for it so to fill place that to its single parts there correspond single and distinct parts of place. This extension is to be so separated from the essential extension, from which it proceeds, that we understand it to be one thing that the parts are extended among themselves, another that they are extended in order to place. To be extended among themselves is to have distinct magnitude and bulk, which we explain a posteriori by that which is to be

[p. 318]

occupative of a distinct part of place; but for the parts to be extended in order to place is to occupy or fill distinct parts of place: which are very different things. For even if quantity does not occupy place, nor are its parts extended in it, they will nevertheless have distinct bulk, and by reason of it they will be parts occupative of place, although they do not occupy it in act. The distinction of each extension becomes manifest in the body of Christ existing in the Eucharist: whose quantity has parts extended among themselves and occupative of distinct parts of place, but does not have extension in order to place: because neither the whole body itself nor its parts occupy place, but they have an indivisible mode of being in order to place; and therefore the whole body is under the whole Host, and also whole under every least part of it. Whence it has the essential extension, in which we say the essence of quantity consists; but it does not have the other extension in order to place, which we say is a proper attribute of the same quantity; but by miracle there is the essence without the proper attribute.

13 The last property is That one quantity cannot penetrate itself with another in the same place. Now to penetrate is nothing else than to occupy the same place, or the same part of it: so that if Peter and John were in the same place, they would be said to penetrate each other; but the penetration of bodies is not naturally possible. And so we can explain this property in one word, if we call it formal impenetrability.

14 These things explained: the Essence of quantity is understood and explained in two ways by those who say that it is placed in the extension of parts. For certain moderns say that it consists in this, That quantity is the root of impenetrability, in the manner explained; but all the others cited, in this, That quantity has part outside part.

But we regard both of these as the same, and judge that they differ in name alone. For since the extension of parts is the root of impenetrability, as of the other attributes, it is the same to say that the essence of quantity consists in the extension of parts, and in the fact that quantity is the root of impenetrability. But we say that the extension is more clearly explained by that which is to have one part outside another according to bulk, or magnitude occupative of a different part of place, as already declared by us.

15 The conclusion, then, of our view, and the common one, is that the essence of quantity does not consist in divisibility and measure, but in the extension of parts. This is proved by an argument taken from the doctrine delivered. The essence of a thing ought to consist in that which we first conceive of it, not in the other things which we understand to follow from it; but

[p. 319]

the first thing that we conceive of quantity is the extension of parts, from which we understand divisibility and measure to follow; therefore extension will be the essence of quantity rather than divisibility or measure. I prove the minor: because it is prior to have parts than to be divisible into them or measurable by them; therefore it is prior to have extended parts than to be divisible into extended parts or measurable by them, and these follow from that; and therefore that will be the essence of quantity, but divisibility and measure its proper attributes.

16 To the testimony of Aristotle for the first opinion, I reply that when he said that Time is the number of motion, by number he did not understand measure, but the discreteness or distinction of the parts of motion according to before and after; for this is what number properly signifies, as is found explained in our Commentaries on the fourth book of the Physics.

To the argument of the same opinion, the major is to be granted, but the minor denied: Because if place is a species distinct from surface, it cannot be distinguished by the ratio of measure alone, but must first be distinguished by extension, by reason of which measure belongs to it.

17 To the testimony of Aristotle for the opinion of Scotus: We grant that Aristotle defined quantity by divisibility; but the minor is to be denied, that the definition is essential; rather it is to be judged descriptive, because it is given through the proper attribute of divisibility. And Aristotle wished to describe quantity through an attribute because divisibility is better known to us than the extension of parts, and so through it extension becomes manifest to us. Or, second, we reply that Divisibility can be taken in two ways. First, for the formal aptitude to division. Second, for its root, which we can call radical divisibility; and this is altogether the same as the extension of parts, from which we said formal divisibility proceeds as from its essence. This supposed, we can grant the same minor of the argument, that the definition is essential; but by the divisibility placed in it is understood not formal but radical divisibility, which is the same as extension. Wherefore it is also the same for quantity to be defined by divisibility so taken as by extension, in which the essence of quantity consists rather than in formal divisibility.

To the second, we grant that the species of quantity are distinguished by many through divisibility, as through a proper attribute better known to us, from which we come to know the essential distinction which it has through extension. Or, second, we say that they distinguish them through divisibility taken radically, which is the same as extension; and then the distinction is essential.

[p. 320]

## QUESTION II

Whether Line, Surface and body are three distinct species of continuous quantity.

18

I     n order that the ratio of these species may be understood, it should be noted,

from St. Thomas, opusc. 48, tract. 5, ch. 3, That although the point is not really sep‐

arated from the line, nor the line from the surface, nor the surface from the body, yet by the

intellect we can apprehend the point, which is altogether indivisible, as really sep‐

arated from the line, and imagine that it is drawn across a plane; and then from its

drawing there will remain a trace that is long, but neither broad nor deep. Which

trace, if it is extended sideways, will leave another, not only long but also broad;

and finally, if this is raised or lowered, it will leave a third trace, long, broad and

deep, that is, having thickness.

19 The first trace, then, is continuous and divisible according to length, and is

called a line; and since it is a trace left from the drawing of a point, it is continued

by points. Now to be continued is for any two of its parts to be joined by an indi‐

visible point, and thus it makes one continuum. The second trace is long and

broad, but lacks depth, because it does not have thickness (so to speak); and there‐

fore it is divisible according to length and breadth, but lacks depth, and therefore

is indivisible according to depth; and since it is a trace left from the extension of

the line, it is continued by lines, and is called a surface. The third trace is long,

broad and deep; and since it is left from the raising or lowering of the surface, its

parts are continued by surfaces, and it is divisible according to length, breadth and

depth, which are called the dimensions of quantity, because we can as it were mea‐

sure continuous quantity in these three ways, that is, according to length, breadth

and depth; and because there are no more dimensions, body is said to be divisible

according to every dimension.

20 Of these three, then, line, surface and body, two things could be disputed.

The first: Whether they are distinguished really or from the nature of the thing,

and whether they can be separated really. But this question is a Philosophical one,

and therefore does not pertain to our purpose. For now it is to be supposed, as the

common opinion, that they are distinguished really or from the nature of the

thing, without dependence on the intellect; and that, naturally at least, none of

them can be separated really from the others. The second thing that can be dis‐

puted is Whether they

are

[p. 321]

are distinguished in species, and are therefore distinct species of continuous quantity: and this is what the title of the question asks.

On this the first opinion is that of Durandus, in 2, d. 2, q. 4, who asserts that line and surface are not true species of quantity, but only certain negations of dimensions: line, the negation of breadth; surface, the negation of depth. He proves it by this argument: The difference that constitutes and distinguishes a species must be positive, since it stands as a form; but line and surface do not have a positive difference by which they are constituted and distinguished; therefore they are not true species of quantity. The minor is proved: because a line is distinguished from a surface only in that it lacks breadth, and a surface from a body in that it lacks depth; therefore they are only certain negations of breadth and of depth, and not true species.

21 The second opinion holds that line and surface are positive entities, and not mere negations, but that they are not distinguished in species. It proves this by the following reasoning. If line and surface were distinguished in species from each other and from body, they would be distinguished above all by length and breadth; but they are not distinguished by these; therefore in no way. The minor is proved: because a surface includes length and breadth; therefore a line is not distinguished from it by length. Next, a body includes length, breadth, and depth; therefore line and surface are not distinguished from it by length and breadth.

The third opinion is the common and true one: that line, surface, and body are true species of continuous quantity, and distinct ones. It is expressly found in Aristotle, not only in the present chapter but in Metaph. 5, ch. 13, where he explains each of these species by its own description; and all his interpreters follow it in their Commentaries on both passages.

Moreover, it is proved by reason, first, that they are true species of quantity: because extension of parts is the intrinsic ratio of quantity, and divisibility into parts its proper attribute; but each ratio belongs formally to line and to surface: to the former according to length, to the latter according to breadth, and to body according to depth, the dimensions according to which their parts are extended; therefore they are true species of quantity.

22 It is proved next that they are distinct species. First, because many things are demonstrated in Mathematics about these species as about distinct ones: for the geometer treats of the line alone as of his proper object, considering nothing of breadth or surface; and the student of perspective of the visual line: therefore it is a species distinct from surface and body. Second, because the formal

X

[p. 322]

ratios, when diverse, distinguish diverse species; but length, which line expresses, is a formal ratio diverse from breadth, which surface expresses, and from depth, which body expresses, as is plain of itself; therefore it is distinguished in species from them; and the same can be proved of surface and body.

23 But the whole difficulty of distinguishing these species consists in this: that the later ones seem to include the earlier, as body includes surface and line, and surface includes line. In order, then, that it may become manifest that this inclusion does not remove the specific difference, it should be noted, first, that line and surface can be taken in two ways. First, as they are indivisible: line according to breadth, and surface according to depth; and in this way they are not species of quantity, just as the point is not a species of quantity but what terminates and continues the parts of the line. Both are proved: because quantity is essentially divisible; therefore line and surface, as they are indivisible, cannot be species of quantity, but are what terminates and continues another species: the line what continues the parts of the surface, and the surface what continues the parts of the body. In the second way they are taken as they are divisible according to their proper dimensions: the line according to length, and the surface according to breadth; and they have their own indivisibles, by which their parts are continued and terminated: the line is terminated and continued by points, while the surface is continued by lines, as by indivisibles according to breadth. And in this way they are distinct species of quantity, and belong per se and directly to the category; but according to the first consideration they belong only reductively to that species whose parts they join, as the line to the species of surface, and this to the species of body. But when we say that the line is indivisible according to breadth, and the surface according to depth, by indivisibility we must not understand a pure negation of dimension, but a positive mode which is explained through the negation of divisibility; just as by the altogether indivisible point we do not understand a pure negation, but the positive mode by which the parts of the line are joined. The reason for this is that the office of joining parts is real and positive; therefore it cannot be performed by a pure negation, but by a positive entity. It should be noted, second, from the doctrine of St. Thomas in the place cited above, that these two species, surface and body, are so related that each of them expresses only one dimension formally, namely the last, but the other or others materially and as it were presuppositively: as surface formally expresses only breadth,

[p. 323]

but length materially; and body formally depth, but length and breadth as it were materially. And the reason for this is that, since depth is a continuous dimension, its parts must be joined by indivisibles according to depth; and such are surfaces, which, since they have the dimension of breadth, body must necessarily have it; and because a surface must be joined by indivisibles according to breadth, which are lines having length, therefore the surface must necessarily have length. But from this it becomes manifest that it does not have them formally, but only materially and as it were per accidens: because the proper indivisibles which they include per se are at the same time divisible according to those same dimensions. Whence, because the indivisibles of the line, which are points, are not divisible according to another dimension, neither does the line, materially or per accidens, import any other dimension besides length.

24 It should be noted, lastly, that genus and difference are to be taken in these species in such a way that we can assign their definitions: so that their common and proximate genus is continuous quantity, under which they are placed; but the difference is to be taken in relation to the proper dimensions of each; and so the definition of line will be this: A line is a continuous quantity extended according to the formal dimension of length. A surface is a continuous quantity extended according to the formal dimension of breadth. A body is a continuous quantity extended according to the formal dimension of depth. For length is not placed in the definition of surface, nor breadth in the definition of body, because, although they necessarily include these dimensions too, yet they do not do so formally but only materially; nay, not even per se but per accidens. This is proved by the following reasoning: One species is neither composed formally of another, nor can it be included in it; but line, surface, and body are diverse species of quantity; therefore none can include another or others formally.

25 From this whole doctrine it is understood in what way line, surface, and body are distinguished: not indeed, as some think, by the negation of some dimension, as line from surface by the negation of breadth, and surface from body by the negation of depth; but they are distinguished by positive extension according to their proper dimension: so that the line is distinguished from the surface by the positive extension of its parts according to length; and the surface from the body by the positive extension of breadth; and the body from both by positive extension according to the dimension of depth.

X ij

[p. 324]

But if it is said that Aristotle, Metaph. 5, ch. 13, defined these species in another way, namely: A line is a magnitude continuous in one, that is, according to the one dimension of length; a surface, in two, that is, according to two dimensions, of length and breadth; and a body, in three, that is, according to three dimensions, of length, breadth, and depth: I reply that he did so define them; but these definitions are not distinct from ours, rather they are the same as them; and they seem to differ because Aristotle placed not only the formal dimensions by which they are constituted and distinguished, but also the material ones, in which surface and body agree. We, however, define them only by the formal ones, not caring about the material ones, which we presuppose that they necessarily include.

26 To the argument of the first opinion, the minor must be denied, namely that line and surface are distinguished only by the negation of some dimension. For they are not distinguished except by positive extension according to the proper ratio of extension; although the one expresses the negation of a dimension which the other includes; which is common to all the species of any genus whatever: for man, by the very fact that he is rational, expresses the negation of every irrational species.

To the argument of the second opinion, granting the major, the minor must be denied, namely that line and surface are not distinguished by length and breadth: because, although surface includes length, yet not formally, as the line does, but only materially; and although body includes breadth, it does so not formally but materially; and since distinction must be through something formal, these species are distinguished by the several dimensions which they include formally, and which the others do not include formally, as has been explained. And if someone wished to say that the surface expresses another length, distinct from the length of the line, and the body another length, distinct from the length of the line and of the surface, and another breadth, distinct from the breadth of the surface; and so that it is distinguished from surface and line not only by one formal dimension but by three, all formal and proper to itself; and the surface from line and body by two formal ones proper to itself, of length and breadth (which would become manifest if these species were separated really, at least by the absolute power of God: for then the body would have a threefold dimension and be long, broad, and deep, and the surface long and broad, but the line only long): the reply is that this way of distinguishing these species can be devised by the imagination alone, but that according to reason it implies a contradiction.

[p. 325]

This is proved: because from it it would follow that the body has three distinct lengths, distinct by number alone, and includes them formally; and in the same way two breadths; nay, even a threefold set of points, by which the diverse lengths are continued: and both are impossible.

27 The first indeed, because all lengths are of the same species, since they have the same mode of extension of parts, the same mode of continuation through points, and the same formal effect in the subject; but it is repugnant that something should include formally and essentially three predicates of the same species. The second is proved to be impossible: because it is repugnant that many accidents that are purely absolute and of the same species, such as dimensions are, should be at the same time in the same subject, from which they in some way receive their individuation. But this would follow if surface and body had so many lengths and breadths, all of which they would impart to the subject in which they inhered.

But what is said, that these species can be separated really by the absolute power of God, is false, because it implies a manifest contradiction. I prove it thus: If a body were separated from the surface, it would be a continuous quantity divisible according to length, breadth, and depth; therefore its length would be continued by points, and so it would be a line (a line is nothing else but length continued by points); its breadth also would be continued by lines, and so it would be a surface; wherefore it would not be separated from line and surface, as is supposed: therefore it implies a contradiction that it be separated. And this can be proved in the same way of the surface, as is plain to one who understands.

28 But the fundamental reason why it is repugnant that these species be separated in any way is this: because no substance can be given, nay none can even be understood, in which quantity can inhere, except a corporeal one; and this, by its nature and essence, cannot receive any quantity except of threefold dimension, namely of length, breadth, and depth: wherefore no quantity can be given which does not have all of them.

## QUESTION III

Whether time is a true species of continuous quantity.

A     ristotle himself gave occasion to this question: for in the present chap‐

ter he enumerated time among the species of continuous quantity. But in Metaph. 5, ch. 13, he taught that time, together with motion, is quantified per accidens, so that from the mobile and the space, or another form,

[p. 326]

with which it is concerned, motion receives its continuation and extension, just as whiteness receives it from the body in which it inheres. Hence the opinions are diverse.

The first holds that time is not a species of quantity, nor has extension per se, but per accidens, like motion. So Father Francisco Suárez, vol. 2 of his Metaphysics, disp. 40, lect. 9, no. 8, and with him many of the more recent authors. And this opinion has, besides the testimony of Aristotle, several arguments, but these three are the strongest and difficult. The first: The species of quantity must be real beings, because quantity is a real category. But time is not a real being; therefore it is not a species of quantity. The minor is proved: for a real being that is a whole must have real parts; but time, since it is a whole comprehending under itself past, present, and future time, does not have real parts; therefore it is not real. I prove the minor again: because that is real which is in the nature of things; but no part of time is in the nature of things, for past time no longer is, future time is not yet, while the present can only be an instant, or indivisible moment, because, since time is successive, it can have no part present except the indivisible: therefore it will have none present, and so none really existing.

29 Second, it is proved because time, as Aristotle defines it, Phys. 4, ch. 11, text 100, is the number of motion according to before and after; but it is not a discrete number, which would be a species of discrete quantity, since it is truly continuous; nor does it have another extension distinct from the extension of motion, with which it is really identified; therefore, just as motion is not quantified per se but per accidens, so neither is time. The minor is proved: because time is nothing other than the duration of motion; therefore it cannot have another extension of parts distinct from the extension of the parts of motion, of which Aristotle affirms, and almost all his expositors, that it is quantified per accidens.

Third: It is impossible that the species of some genus should belong to some category without its genus and the other species belonging to the same category: as, if man belongs to the category of substance, animal must necessarily be placed in the same category of substance. But duration is a genus to the duration of angels, which is called aeviternity, to the duration of corporeal substance, and to the duration of motion, which is called time; therefore all are placed in the same category. But the durations of substances are not placed in this category, since they are indivisible, having no extension; therefore neither can time be placed in it.

[p. 327]

30 The second opinion distinguishes a twofold consideration of time, and says: If time is considered under the ratio of extension of parts and of divisibility into them, it is not quantified per se but per accidens; whence neither is it a species of quantity. But if it is considered under the ratio of measure, that is, insofar as it is the measure of motion, then it is quantified per se and is a species of continuous quantity. And Aristotle speaks of it in Metaph. 5 under the first consideration, and on that account numbers it among things quantified per accidens; but in the present chapter under the second, and therefore he says it is a species of continuous quantity per se. The ancient interpreters of Aristotle, such as the Commentator, St. Thomas, and others, seem to have devised this opinion under this distinction of time in order to reconcile the diverse passages of Aristotle cited; and Soncinas follows them, Metaph. 5, q. 8.

The third opinion affirms that time is a species of quantity per se, distinct from the others not only in the ratio of measure but of extension. So Fonseca, Metaph. 5, ch. 13, q. 10; Toledo, q. 1 of this chapter; and other interpreters of Aristotle; and Aristotle himself in the present chapter. And this seems to us the more probable and is to be held. It is proved chiefly by this argument, hinted at by St. Thomas, opusc. 42, ch. 2: The essential ratio of quantity is extension of parts; but time has an extension of parts distinct from motion; therefore it does not receive extension from it, but has it per se. The minor is proved: for it can happen that a motion has a small extension and the time a great one, and conversely the time a small one and the motion a great one; therefore they are distinct extensions, and the one is not received from the other. I prove the antecedent: because a motion made through the very same space of the same length has no greater extension whether it be slow or swift, and yet its duration is more extended. For if it is swift, it will last half an hour; but if slow, a whole hour: therefore it has a greater extension, and one distinct from the motion.

31 The moderns reply to this argument that if the duration of the slower motion is compared to extrinsic time, which is the duration of the motion of the first mobile, or to imaginary time, it will be called greater; but if to the intrinsic duration of the same motion, it will not be greater or more extended than the motion itself; rather, in the swifter motion its parts are as it were compressed, just as the parts of the motion are compressed by reason of the swiftness; whence it does not follow that the intrinsic duration has an extension distinct from its motion, which it follows, although the extrinsic duration of the first mobile has an extension distinct from it; and this too will not be distinct from that motion of its own, of the first mobile, which it follows; so that it is always true that no duration has an extension distinct from its motion, but receives what it has from it.

X iiij

[p. 328]

Against this solution, however, I argue thus: Not only the extrinsic duration of the celestial motion has a greater extension than that swift motion, but also its proper duration; therefore the solution is false. The antecedent is proved: because the proper duration is equivalent to an hour and coexists with it by a formal coexistence, since each duration is formally successive; but the hour is the extrinsic duration of celestial time; therefore they are formally equal; but the extrinsic duration of the slower motion is more extended; therefore the intrinsic and proper duration too will be more extended: wherefore it will not be received from it.

32 Whence it follows that what is said in the same solution is no less false, namely that the intrinsic parts of duration are compressed like the parts of motion: because the parts of motion are compressed by reason of swiftness, which is a certain mode of them, just as condensation is the mode by which the parts of water or of another body are compressed; but time is not capable of swiftness or slowness, as Aristotle teaches and proves, Phys. 4, text 96, in these words: Change indeed is in every case swifter or slower, but time is not: for slow and swift are defined by time; for that is swift which is moved much in a little time, and that slow which is moved little in much; but time is not defined by time, etc. Therefore it is repugnant that the parts of duration be compressed; and so it is false that the duration itself of the slower motion is not greater or more extended.

Second, it is proved in the time which is the duration of the motion of the first mobile. For if one revolution of the heavens, by which the sun is moved from East to West, which is now made in the space of 12 hours, were made in the space of 24 hours, it would be evident that the duration consumed in such a motion would be twice as great as that which is now consumed, and so would have an extension twice as great as that which it now has; but the revolution itself would not have a greater extension than it has now; therefore the extension of the duration is distinct from the extension of the motion. The minor is proved: because the extension of motion is taken from the extension of the space, or of the local presence which is acquired through the motion; but the space is the same, and consequently the local presence in it is of the same extension; therefore the motion made through it, whether slow or swift, will be of the same extension and not greater, while it is evident that its duration has an extension twice as great.

33 But in order that our opinion, which is the common one, may be better understood, it should be noted that time was defined thus by Aristotle, Phys. 4: Time is the number of motion according to before and after. In which definition two things are said concerning motion. The first, that it is the duration of the prior and posterior of motion; from which another follows, namely

[p. 329]

that it is the number of its parts. But number expresses discreteness, or separation, which is taken in two ways. First, according to quantity: and thus it is a species of discrete quantity, as three bodies, which are really discrete or separate, but with a certain order of numerability among themselves according to before and after, because the second unit is posterior to the first and prior to the third. In another way discreteness, or separation, is taken not according to quantity but according to quality: so that, although the parts are continuous according to quantity, yet they have diverse qualities, by reason of which they are called discrete or separate. When, therefore, it is said that time is the number of motion, this is understood not of quantitative number but according to quality: because the prior part has a quality distinct from the posterior; and this quality is understood to be the very mode of priority and posteriority. Hence time is not a species of quantity insofar as it is called number, but insofar as it is the continuous duration of motion, having prior and posterior parts joined by a common term, which is the instant.

34 It should be noted, second, that it is not certain in what way time is distinguished from motion. Some say that it is distinguished from the nature of the thing and prior to the intellect, which I judge to be the more probable, as is shown in our Commentaries on the fourth book of the Physics; but others hold that it is distinguished only by reason, yet by reasoned reason, that is, reason having a foundation in the thing itself, as action and passion are distinguished in the same motion. But whether this or that be said, it is enough for us to be able to understand that time has a real or formal extension distinct from motion, which is the extension of duration.

It should be noted, third, that motion has a twofold extension: one insofar as it is a way between two terms, the From-which and the To-which; the other insofar as it lasts, and this is called the extension of duration. And it has neither from itself, but the first from the mobile and the space, or the To-which term; the second from time, which, properly speaking, is the extension of duration. From which it is understood that in both ways and in every respect it is quantified per accidens. Time, however, has its extension in neither way from motion, or from the mobile or the space, but has it as its own and from itself; and it is called the extension of prior and posterior according to duration, distinct from the nature of the thing from motion, from the mobile, and from the space; and therefore it is called intrinsic. But it has it as dependent on the cause efficient of motion, by which the same time is produced according to its being by means of the motion, not as by a cause, but as by a causation; which plainly does not prevent it from having it per se and from within; for all the other

[p. 330]

species of quantity have their extensions, as they also have their entities, from the efficient cause by which they are produced.

35 It should be noted, fourth, that since time is the duration of motion, and motion is twofold, duration too is twofold. One is the duration of the first motion, that is, the celestial one; since that is the first body, its motion is called the first; and since this first motion is most regular, that is, always behaving in the same way as regards swiftness, and the other motions of the lower bodies depend on it, all are also measured by it; and therefore it is called the measure of all, because a measure must be most certain, and for that reason always behaving in the same way. And this is the reason why, in the common way of speaking, this duration alone is called time: because time seems to be the common measure of all motions; yet it is an extrinsic measure, since it is distinct from the other motions measured by it. The others are the durations of particular and lower motions: because to each motion there corresponds its own particular and intrinsic duration, just as each has its own prior and posterior parts, which necessarily imply particular and proper durations. But because these do not follow from regular motions, but now from swifter, now from slower ones, therefore they are not properly called times; but time, absolutely, is said to be one, for that first duration of the first motion.

36 From these things, I believe, the nature of time will be understood in some way, and from it what sense Aristotle held when he enumerated time among things quantified per accidens, in Metaph. 5: namely, that it does not have an altogether absolute extension, like the other species of quantity, but one with an order to something else, namely to motion; and therefore that it is as it were quantified through another, yet not per accidens, like motion, which does not have its own extension but one which it receives from the space and the subject. Time, however, does indeed have its own, not altogether absolute, but with an order to something else; therefore it is not so much quantified per se as the other species. But the first argument calls for that distinction of permanent and successive things, which also have parts of a diverse ratio: for permanent things have parts which exist at the same time, as wood or stone; but successive things do not have parts existing at the same time, but in succession and passage, as motion, whose parts do not exist at the same time, but some are future, others past; and the future ones first become present, then past; yet not even the present ones are present after the manner of something permanent or existing at the same time, but after the manner of something passing successively. Finally, the future parts as well as the present and the past are joined

[p. 331]

by indivisible instants, themselves also flowing, and they become one time and one continuous and successive quantity. Wherefore, although no part of time is present, or existing permanently, or whole at once, yet it has both after the manner of succession and flux.

But to the form of the first argument, the minor must be denied, namely that time is not a real being, or does not have real parts actually existing: because, although they do not exist after the manner of something permanent, yet they exist after the manner of something successive, that is, continually flowing; and so future time becomes present and past. And although future time is not yet, and past time is no longer, yet there is present time, not only by reason of the instant but also as it is time; yet it does not have a permanent presence, but a flowing one; and it becomes one continuous time with the past and the future by reason of the instant through which it is joined with them.

37 Whence it follows that the dependence on the intellect which some place in time is false and not necessary for the real entity of time: they say that time receives the complement of its essence from the intellect, so that before the operation of the intellect it is not complete; because, since it is the number of motion, and number is completed by the intellect, therefore time too will be so completed. I say that this is false: because from it it follows that time is formally a being of reason, and is not given before the operation of the intellect. The consequence is proved: because nothing real can be received from the intellect; if, therefore, it receives its essential complement, then this complement is a being of reason, and so the essence of time will be a being of reason, since it is completed by it. Wherefore it will not be given before the operation of the intellect, which is certainly false, since before the operation of the intellect there is given the duration of the first motion, which is true time. That such a complement is not necessary is proved: because without it time has true and real parts, consisting in a real flux according to the nature of successive being, no less than motion, of which it is evident that it does not depend on the intellect; just as we shall see that number does not depend on it.

To the second, the minor must be granted, namely that time is not a number really discrete by quantitative discreteness, nor a species of quantity from the fact that it is a number, but from the fact that it is the continuous duration of motion; from which it must be denied that it is not really distinguished; and although it is distinguished only by a formal ratio, this suffices for it to be a complete being and extended per se, although motion is incomplete and extended per accidens: for action and passion are really identified with motion, yet a distinction of reason suffices for action and passion to be complete and categorial beings:

[p. 332]

although motion has neither.

## 38 To the last, granting the major, the minor must be denied, namely that du‐

ration in general is a genus to the durations of substances and to time; rather it is

analogous. This is especially true, and necessary, according to those same mod‐

erns who assert that duration is distinguished only by reason from the existence

of the enduring thing. On this supposition, the duration of substances will be

the same as their existence, and the duration of accidents the same as their actu‐

al inherence; but nothing univocal is given common to substance and accident;

therefore neither to their durations. And even if duration is distinguished from

the nature of the thing from the existence of the enduring thing, since it follows

upon it naturally, yet duration in general cannot be univocal with respect to

both: because, just as an accident has being in a qualified sense, so the duration

following upon its nature will be such in a qualified sense, by attribution to the

duration of substance; nor will they be able to have a univocal ratio of duration.

Wherefore neither does it follow that the duration of motion is not a species of

quantity because the durations of substances are not in this category.

Q U E S T I O N I V.

Whether place is a species of continuous quantity distinct from surface.

39

A     ristotle gave occasion to this question: because, although in the present

chapter he enumerated place among the species of quantity, yet in Metaph.

5, ch. 13, where he treats of the same category expressly and enumerated the oth‐

er species of quantity, he made no mention of place. Hence the first opinion as‐

serts that place is a species of quantity distinct from surface: not indeed in the ratio of

the essential extension of quantity, but only in the ratio of measure. It proves

both: because those things are distinguished in species in the ratio of extension

which have a distinct extension; but place and surface do not have a distinct ex‐

tension, but the same; therefore they are not distinguished in the ratio of exten‐

sion. The minor is proved: because place is a certain surface; therefore it is ex‐

tended according to length and breadth; but it adds the containing of the located

thing, by reason of which it does not have any new dimension, but only a new

correspondence to the located thing; therefore it does not have a new or distinct

extension; but it does indeed have a new ratio of measure: because, from the fact

that it contains the located thing, it is its extrinsic measure; whereas the surface

is not the extrinsic measure of the located thing, but the intrinsic measure of the

locating body in which it inheres. Hence Aristotle

[p. 333]

in the present chapter, where he chiefly considered the ratio of measure, numbered place within quantity as a species distinct from surface; but in Metaph. 5, where he treated of quantity chiefly according to the essential ratio of extension, he made no mention of place, because under this consideration it is not distinguished from surface. Whence, in enumerating surface, he sufficiently enumerated place. So thinks Soto, on this chapter, and Masius, disp. on quantity, sect. 3, q. 4.

40 The second opinion holds that place is a species distinct from surface even under the essential ratio of extension: not indeed really, but only formally. This is followed by Albert the Great, tract. 8 on the categories, ch. 5; Javelli, tract. 5; Canter., in the extension of the text; and Toledo, q. 2 of this chapter. It is proved by the testimony of Aristotle in this chapter, where he not only taught but proved that place is a species of continuous quantity distinct from the others.

Next, by reason. First: because a distinct formal mode of extension suffices to distinguish the formal and specific ratio of two quantities; but place has a distinct formal mode of extension; therefore it is distinguished formally, and in species, from surface. The minor is proved: because surface, as surface, has extension only according to length and breadth; but as place, it adds a new mode of extension corresponding to the located thing which it circumscribes, insofar as its parts correspond to the parts of the located thing, and points to points; and from such correspondence it has a new mode of divisibility, because it is divisible upon the division of the located thing; therefore it has a distinct quantitative ratio, which suffices for it to be a species distinct from surface, although it is not distinguished from it really.

Second, because the chief property of quantity is the equal and the unequal; but place, as place, is equal to the located thing, as Aristotle teaches, Phys. 4, text 15; therefore, as such, the essence of quantity belongs to it, through which it will be a species distinct from surface; to which, just as equality with the located thing does not belong, so neither will the formal and proper ratio of the extension of place belong.

41 The third opinion asserts two things. The first, that place is a true species of quantity. The second, that it is not a species distinct from surface, neither in the ratio of extension nor in the ratio of measure, but is distinguished from it only by a certain accidental and extrinsic ratio, which is the containing or circumscription of the located thing. This is expressly the view of St. Thomas, Metaph. 5, lect. 15, and in 2, d. 12, single q., a. 5, ad 2; and it is followed by Soncinas, Metaph. 5, q. 40; Albert of Saxony, Phys. 4, q. 1; Paul of Venice on the present chapter; Vallés,

[p. 334]

controversy 13, for beginners; Fonseca, Metaph. 5, ch. 13, q. 5; Father Francisco Suárez, vol. 2 of his Metaphysics, disp. 51, sect. 2, no. 9; and many of the moderns. And this seems to me the more probable.

But in order that we may prove it, it should be noted that place is considered in two ways. First, mathematically, only for the surface containing another body. Second, physically, as it adds a certain immobility, by reason of which it regards local motion, or also the conserving power of the located thing. And Aristotle explained both its ratios, Phys. 4, text 36, defining it thus: Place is the ultimate immobile surface of the containing body. But in the present chapter he considers place only according to the first ratio, as it is the ultimate surface containing a body; but he refers immobility to the books of the Physics; and according to that first ratio he asserted that it is a species of quantity. And this is the first thing which our opinion affirms.

42 The second is proved, namely that it is not a species distinct from surface. First, because species are distinguished by differences contained under the same genus: therefore, if species of continuous quantity are distinguished, it is by differences of the same genus which add some grade of perfection above it. In order, then, that surface insofar as it is place may be a species distinct from surface as surface, it must add a new formal ratio of extension or of measure above it; but it adds none; therefore it is not a distinct species.

The minor is proved: because either we consider the surface as actually containing the located thing, or only as apt to contain it, which it will have if the place which is now filled by a body should remain empty; for there is no other ratio of considering it as place. But considered in neither way does it add a new ratio of extension or of measure; therefore it is in no way a species distinct from itself as surface. I prove the minor again: because as actually containing it adds nothing intrinsic, but to contain or circumscribe another is merely an extrinsic denomination in the circumscribing thing, as is plain; and the aptitude for containing must be such as the actual containing is, since potency takes its species from act; therefore it will only be a potency of denominating another as extrinsically contained or surrounded, just as is the aptitude in a garment of denominating the body as clothed. But a merely extrinsic denomination, or a mere aptitude for it, cannot be a new grade of perfection under the genus of quantitative extension, which of itself expresses something intrinsic and formal, since it is a purely absolute accident; therefore place cannot be distinguished in species from surface.

43 And it can be confirmed: because if containing the located thing actively, although extrinsically, added a new mode of extension, a distinct

[p. 335]

one from surface as such, and therefore made a distinct species of quantity, it follows that the body’s being passively contained by the place adds a new mode above the dimensions of that same contained body; and so for passive containing another species would have to be distinguished, which nobody grants.

Second, it is proved: because extrinsically containing the located thing, or the surface’s being apt to contain it, or also that correspondence of parts or points with the parts and points of the located thing, cannot be understood to be anything other than a relation; but a relation alone cannot distinguish species of quantity, because the difference of quantity must be absolute, as the genus is; therefore place is not distinguished in species from surface under the genus of quantity by the containing of the located thing; nor is it understood to add anything else by which it might be distinguished under the same genus.

To the argument of the first opinion, the minor must be distinguished, in the part which says that place adds a new ratio of measure: for measure is twofold, as will be explained below, Active and Passive; and the former is only an extrinsic ratio of quantity, while the passive, which is called measurability, is an intrinsic and proper attribute of it. By the former, therefore, the species of quantity cannot be distinguished, because it is extrinsic; but neither by the latter, because it is common to all, although intrinsic to all, as a common attribute.

To the first argument of the second opinion, granting the major, the minor must be denied: because the active containing of the located thing, or the correspondence according to parts and points, is not a new mode of extension, but only an extrinsic denomination in the surface, and perhaps a new relation to the contained body; and these cannot distinguish place from surface under the genus of continuous quantity.

44 To the second, the antecedent must be denied, namely that it is proper to quantity to be equal or unequal to another; rather this is a common accident. But its property is that according to it all things are called equal or unequal; and this property is common to all the species, and therefore cannot distinguish them. Whence that the containing surface is equal to the located thing is an accident of it, just as it is an accident that one body or one line is equal to another; wherefore it cannot on this account be distinguished from surface, just as neither can the surface of the located thing be distinguished in species from the surface of the place on the ground that it is equal to it.

To Aristotle, the reply is that he numbered place in the present chapter as a species distinct from surface because he had not yet determined what place was, until the fourth

[p. 336]

book of the Physics; and that according to various opinions it can be distinguished

or not distinguished from surface; meanwhile, however, on account of the extrin‐

sic containing, it is distinguished, not essentially but accidentally, so that from this

distinction it might be understood to be related in a somewhat diverse manner to

predications. But in the Metaphysics, where it was already established that it is the

ultimate containing surface, he made no mention of it; but he understood that,

surface having been enumerated, from which it is not distinguished in species, it

was sufficiently enumerated.

Q U E S T I O N V.

Whether motion is a species of continuous quantity. 45

T  he first opinion affirms that it is a species distinct from the others. It is held by

Fonseca, Metaph. 5, ch. 33, q. 8, sect. 1, 2 and 3, and with him by the Coimbra

commentators, Phys. 3, ch. 2, q. 2, a. 3, at the end, where they assert that motion

can be considered in six ways. First, as it proceeds from the agent; and thus it belongs

to the category of action. Second, as it is received in the patient; and it belongs to the

category of passion. Third, as a quasi-imperfect form tending to perfection. Fourth, as it

is the acquisition of a perfect form. Fifth, as it is successive; and in these three ways it be‐

longs per se to no category, because it is something essentially incomplete. But it

can be considered in a sixth way, as it is continuous; and in this way it belongs to this

category, like time; but it is a species distinct from time, because the parts of time

are joined by indivisible instants, while the parts of motion are joined by mutata

esse, also indivisible, which are very diverse from each other; and therefore they ar‐

gue that they are distinct species of quantity.

46 It is proved by the testimony of Aristotle, Phys. 3, at the beginning, where

he says that motion is of the genus of continuous things; but the genus of continuous

things is not found except in this category; therefore he thinks that it is placed un‐

der the genus of continuous quantity, which is to be a species of it.

It is proved next by reason: because the continuous is a genus of quantity;

therefore whatever has continuity per se will be a species of it, and a distinct

species if it has a distinct continuity; but motion has both; therefore it is a species

of continuous quantity distinct from the others. The minor is proved: because the

continuity of motion is distinct from the continuity of the space or of the term

which is made through it, and also from the continuity of the subject, the mobile,

in which it inheres, and finally from the continuity of time; therefore it does not

receive it from any of these, but has it from itself; and therefore it will be per se

quantified and continuous. The minor is proved: because the continuity of the

mobile, of the space, or of the term which is made through motion, whether it be

quality or quantity,

[p. 337]

or anything else, is permanent; but the continuity of motion is successive, like motion itself; therefore it is distinct from their continuity, and also from the successive continuity of time: because, when the motion is slow, its continuity is short, if the space which the mobile traverses is short, while the continuity of the time is long; therefore the one is diverse from the other. This is also gathered from the continuatives, which in time are instants, but in motion mutata esse, which are very diverse.

The second opinion denies that motion is quantified per se, and consequently that it is a species of quantity; and it is the common and true one. Aristotle expressly holds it, not only in the present chapter but also in Metaph. 5, ch. 13, in which places he teaches in express words that motion is quantified per accidens, like the white. And with him almost all the expositors: St. Thomas, Metaph. 5, lect. 15; Albert the Great, tract. 8 on quantity, ch. 4; Soncinas, Metaph. 5, q. 24; the Louvain commentators, Cajetan, Javelli, Soto, Toledo, Mercado, in their Commentaries on this chapter; Father Pereira, bk. 13, ch.; Father Francisco Suárez, vol. 2 of his Metaphysics, d. 40, sect. 8. And it is proved by a twofold argument. First, because motion is continuous because it is successive: for if it were made in an instant, it could have no succession. But it does not have succession per se, but by reason of the term which is made through it; therefore neither does it have continuity per se, but from the term.

47 I prove the minor: because the motion of heating is successive for this reason, that the heat made through it has a certain gradual latitude, contrary to the coldness existing in the same subject; and because a natural, finite agent cannot overcome this coldness all at once and in a moment, but little by little, it is overcome successively; and therefore heat is produced successively. Whence, if an agent of infinite power be given, such as God is, able to overcome in a moment the whole resistance of the coldness, heat will also be produced in a moment and without succession, and the heating will have no succession, nor continuation. It is therefore an evident sign that it has both from the term, and not per se; wherefore neither will it be continuous per se, but per accidens.

Second, because motion is essentially a way, a flux, and a tending between two terms, the From-which and the To-which, and is the very becoming of the term; therefore according to its proper entity and essence it is something incomplete, by which the mobile is not constituted in being simply, but on the way to it; and therefore it is excluded by Aristotle and his interpreters from all the categories, and is placed among the postpredicaments, which are certain incomplete modes of things. Whether, then, continuity pertains to its essence or is a proper attribute, it too will be something formally incomplete; wherefore

Y

[p. 338]

it will not belong to the category per se, nor will motion itself by reason of it. It is

false, therefore, that by reason of continuity motion is a species of continuous

quantity per se.

48 To the testimony of Aristotle, the reply is that his words are general, and

make this sense: Motion must be numbered among continuous things; from which

it does not follow that it is continuous per se, but that it has continuity, essential

or accidental: just as, if someone said that wood is of the genus of heavy bodies, he

would not by that very fact be forced to admit that heaviness is essential to it, but

it would be enough, for the truth of the general statement, that it belong to it in

an accidental manner.

And in almost the same way the reply is made to the argument: granting the

minor, that motion has a continuity distinct from the space and the term, but

denying the consequence, that it has it per se. For it is one thing to have a distinct

one, another to have it per se: because to have it per se means to have it from its

own intrinsic ratio, whereas to have a distinct one is common with respect to hav‐

ing it per se and having it from another, or per accidens; since it is evident that it

can have one that is distinct and communicated by another, as may be made mani‐

fest by this example. Whiteness has an extension which it participates from the

surface of the body in which it is extended, and by that very fact one distinct from

the extension of that same surface, because it is repugnant that the same exten‐

sion should be in something from itself and from another; and nevertheless the ex‐

tension of whiteness is not per se but per accidens. Wherefore, although motion

has an extension distinct from the mobile, the space, and the term, it does not fol‐

low that it has it per se; but it has it communicated by them, and therefore has it

per accidens, although it also has it distinct from the extension of time.

## QUESTION VI

Whether number is a species of discrete quantity. 49

H     aving examined the species of continuous quantity, we must come to dis‐

crete quantity, which has two species, Number and Speech. And first we ask

about number, whether it is a true species of discrete quantity. And the difficulty

consists in this: whether number is one per se; for if it is so, it will not be difficult

to understand whether or not it is a species of discrete quantity; but if it is only

one per accidens, it is certain that it does not belong to the category.

The first opinion holds that number is one per accidens, and therefore does not be‐

long to the category, nor is a species of quantity, but is one only by aggregation,

like a heap of stones or of other bodies; and that Aristotle enumerated it among

[p. 339]

the species of quantity because it has a certain discrete extension, similar to quantitative extension, and a certain mode of unity founded on the common way of speaking, by which we say that the ternary is one particular number and the quaternary another, distinct one.
