The third, a certain vicious circle: for one relative is defined through the other, and this same one through that; which is nothing other than to define the same thing through itself: for if father is defined through son, and in turn son through father, from first to last father will be defined through himself. Which Aristotle reproved, Metaph. 5, ch. 15, in these words: But the understanding is not toward that of which it is the understanding: for indeed the same thing would have been said twice. And in Posterior Analytics 1, ch. 3, he reproved the same circle in demonstrations.

64 The third opinion, midway between these extremes, affirms that non-mutual relations are terminated formally at something absolute, but mutual ones formally at a relative; and therefore relation in common, or relation as it is relation to a term, abstracts from the absolute and the relative. So Ferrara on Contra Gentiles 2, ch. 11; Nifo, Metaph. 5, d. 14; Deza of Seville, in 1, d. 3, q. 1, note 3; and several of the moderns. And I consider this to be certain in the doctrine of Aristotle and St. Thomas, and more probable than the others. Which we have effectively proved, as regards non-mutual relations, such as of the measurable and the measure, of the creature and the creator, against the first opinion, of Cajetan.

It is proved also against the second opinion, that mutual relations are terminated formally at a relative, by express testimonies of Aristotle, Porphyry, and St. Thomas. For Aristotle, in the present chapter, treating of the term of relation and teaching what it ought to be, says thus: Further, if that to which it is said is suitably assigned, when all the other things that are accidents have been taken away and that alone left to which it was suitably assigned, it will always be said toward it; as, if the master is assigned, all the things that are accidents to the master being set aside, such as being two-footed, or capable of science, or a man, and that alone left, that he is master, the slave will always be said toward him: for the slave is called the master’s slave. But if that to which it is said is not suitably assigned, all the other things being set aside and that alone left to which it was assigned, it will not be said toward it. Let the slave be assigned to man, or to something, and let being master be set aside from the man: the slave will no longer be said toward the man; for when there is no master, neither is there a slave. In which words he expressly teaches that the slave is terminated formally at the master as he is master, and the master at the slave as he is slave: because, if the relations of mastership and servitude are taken away, neither can terminate the relation of the other; and if the relations are posited, even if all other things are taken away, through them each sufficiently terminates the relation of the other.

65 Porphyry also, in the chapter on species, holds the same no less expressly: for he asserts that he defined genus through species, and in turn species through genus, because they are relatives, and one relative must be defined through the other, as through the term of its relation.

[p. 396]

Which St. Thomas teaches no less expressly, 1 p., q. 40, a. 2, ad 4, where, explaining the definition of relatives handed down by Aristotle and teaching how it belongs to mutual relatives, he says: When it is said that the being of a relative is to be disposed toward another, by “toward another” is understood the correlative, which is not prior but simultaneous in nature.

It is proved next by a twofold reason. The first, deduced from the intrinsic ratio of relatives. Relative opposition is found between relatives as they are formally relatives; therefore mutual relation essentially includes mutual relative opposition; but mutual relative opposition essentially includes both rationes, of referring and of terminating; therefore relatives exercise both offices through their relations, and not through their absolute foundations. All of this is evidently plain except the minor, which I prove no less evidently. Mutual opposition consists in this, that the relatives regard each other mutually, and the relations are the rationes of their regarding each other mutually; but to regard each other mutually is for each to regard the other and to be regarded by it; and to be regarded by it is to terminate its relation; therefore it is evident that in mutual opposition both offices, of referring and of terminating, are essentially included; and consequently that relatives exercise both through their relations, and not through their foundations: because it is through the relations, and not through the foundations, that they have formal opposition.

66 The second reason is taken from the Divine relations, in which it seems to be evidently proved that one relative cannot terminate the other through something absolute, but through the relation. Now this reason presupposes two things as certain. The first is that a real relation cannot exist except between extremes really distinct: because nothing can be referred to itself by a real relation. The second, that in Divine things one cannot be really distinguished from another through something absolute, but only through opposed relations. These being supposed, the reason proceeds thus: the Father is referred to the Son, and the Son to the Father, as they are really distinguished; therefore each terminates the relation of the other as really distinct from it: because, just as a real relation cannot be of the same thing to itself really, so neither can it be terminated at itself; but the father and the son are not really distinguished except through the opposed relations alone; therefore neither is one referred to the other, nor does he terminate the relation of the other, except through the relation: therefore as a relative, and not as something absolute. But the reason is the same concerning Divine and created relations as regards the ratio of referring and terminating; therefore created relations too are terminated at a relative, and not at something absolute.

67 To this argument the moderns try to reply in two ways,

[p. 397]

First, that although in the divine persons nothing distinguishes really except relation, and therefore it is the relative that terminates according to itself, yet, as the Divine Persons are conceived by us, the foundation of the relation can be distinguished from the relation itself and conceived by way of something absolute; and through it, so conceived, one person will terminate the relation of the other: as in the son we can consider passive generation, from which he is called begotten, by way of something absolute, as the foundation of filiation; and through it the son will terminate the relation of paternity, not through filiation; and so too the father, through active generation considered by way of something absolute.

This solution, however, is neither true nor does it solve the argument. I prove the first: because in the Divine persons not only paternity and filiation are relations, but also active and passive generation, which are called active and passive origin, say relation formally; otherwise they could not be distinguished really, as it is certain that they are distinguished. Next, by us, who know that nothing is distinguished in Divine things except through relations, they are conceived as relative; therefore, if through them one person terminates the relation of the other, it will terminate it as formally relative. I prove the second, that the solution does not solve the argument: because, although by us, who understand imperfectly, active and passive generation should be conceived by way of something absolute, since nevertheless they are relative, they have nothing absolute according to themselves; therefore, since relations are terminated according to themselves, and not only as they are imperfectly conceived by us, it evidently follows that according to themselves they are terminated formally at a relative and not at something absolute; and also as they are understood by God and by the blessed, who know them as they are in themselves.

Therefore the same moderns, seeing that the aforesaid solution was insufficient, handed down another, granting that the Divine relations are terminated formally at a relative, but not created ones; and that the difference consists in this, that the Divine relations are subsistent, or substantial, and therefore do not have another foundation besides themselves through which one relative could terminate the relation of the other; but created relations are accidental, and therefore presuppose another absolute accident as a foundation, by means of which they arise; and through such a foundation one relative can terminate the other.

But neither is this difference worth anything, which I prove thus: for a relation to be subsistent or inhering, or substantial or accidental, does not pertain to the formal ratio of relation or of relative, but is something material; but relations

[p. 398]

or mutual relatives, from the formal ratio of such relations and relatives, have mutual opposition, formally including both rationes, of referring and of terminating; which is the same in Divine and in created things; therefore the ratio of terminating will be the same in both, just as the ratio of referring is the same; wherefore, if the Divine relations are terminated formally at a relative and not at something absolute, created ones too will be so terminated.

69 The arguments of the first opinion are not against ours, and therefore it is not necessary to reply to them. But to the first argument of the second opinion: the major being granted, the minor too must be granted according to that part which asserts that relation, as it is relation, is not terminated formally at a relative; but it must be denied as regards the other part, that as it is mutual relation it does not require a relative term: because relation as relation is considered as a genus, abstracted from mutual and non-mutual; but as mutual relation it is considered in species; and it is certain that many things belong to a thing by reason of its difference, or species, which do not belong to it by reason of its genus; and therefore to be terminated at a relative can belong to relation as mutual, although it does not belong to it under the common ratio of relation; but just as in this way it abstracts from mutual and non-mutual, so it requires a term abstracting from the absolute and the relative. And in order that the other point adduced in the same argument may be solved, concerning mutual relations that sometimes lack the relation in one extreme, as is the relation of the creature to the creator, and the relation of maternity of the Blessed Virgin to Christ the Lord, according to St. Thomas, it should be noted, first, that relatives can be considered in two ways: Materially, when they are taken for the subjects or foundations: as when it is said that this white man is referred to another white man, or the one generating to the one generated; in which way also they are called relatives only accidentally, because This one generating is a father or The white thing is like is accidental. In another way they are taken Formally, as they are signified by relative names, of father or of like; and as relatives, so too terms are taken in the same ways: as when we say that the like is referred to the white, or the father to the one generated; but formally, if we say that the father is referred to the son.

70 It should be noted, second, that mutual relations are perfect, because they include relative opposition; but not so non-mutual ones, which are as it were maimed and imperfect, in which only one extreme of relative opposition is found; whence they are understood to have only material terms, not formal ones. As the relation of the measurable to the measure is said to be terminated only materially; and the same of mutual relations, if in the other extreme they were suspended

[p. 399]

through a possible or impossible case: as if, when a relation of similarity

arose in one white thing, the relation in the other were suspended (if this be

possible, which we are not discussing); for then the relation of the other

would remain terminated only materially.

From these things the reply is that the relations adduced in the argument

are not mutual: because mutual relations are found only between extremes of

the same order; but God and the creature are of diverse orders, and there‐

fore do not have mutual relations; and for this reason they are also terminat‐

ed only materially, and this is to be terminated at something absolute. But

mutual relations essentially say relative opposition, by reason of which each

is the ratio of referring to the other and at the same time the ratio of termi‐

nating: because opposition cannot be understood without both rationes; and

therefore mutual relatives, as such, are terminated formally at a relative.

Whether one relative can and must be defined through the other. 71

T     he second argument asks whether one relative can and must be defined

through the other. And concerning this doubt there is a twofold opinion.

The first denies that it must be so defined: which all those hold who main‐

tain that relation is terminated not at a relative but at something absolute;

and they prove it from the inconveniences which follow from such a way of

defining, adduced in the same argument.

The second opinion is that of those who follow our view, that one relative

must be defined through the other; and this is most certain in Aristotle and St.

Thomas, as their testimonies adduced in confirmation of our view prove. It

is also express in Porphyry, chapter on species, where he asserts that he

treated of species immediately after genus because they are relatives, and

therefore it is necessary to know and define one through the other. To this

testimony, however, the moderns reply that Porphyry did not posit species in

the definition of genus as it is referred to genus, but as it is referred to indi‐

viduals, and therefore he did not define one relative through the other for‐

mally. But I truly wonder that they devised a solution so openly false: be‐

cause it is clearer than daylight that he defined genus through species as

through the subject of which it is predicated; but the subject of which genus

is predicated is not species as it regards individuals, but as it regards the

genus itself, as is plain of itself; therefore he defined genus itself through it as

the relative of the genus. But in reasons it is more probable, and (unless I am

mistaken) it is evidently concluded from the Divine relations, in which they

admit that, although by our imperfect mode of understanding we can under‐

stand that they are terminated at the foundation, conceived by us by way of

something absolute, yet if they are taken as they are in themselves, or as by

God himself or by the blessed

[p. 400]

know them, they cannot in any way be terminated at something absolute: because, since they are subsistent and substantial, they have no other foundation besides themselves; and therefore they must terminate through themselves.

72 From this I deduce an evident argument in this way: the Divine relations, as they are in themselves and as they are known by God and the blessed, are terminated formally at a relative; therefore the formal term of one relative, as of the father, will be the other relative, namely the son as son; but a relative cannot be defined except through its term; therefore it cannot be defined except through the other relative. If, then, one of the blessed were to explain by some explanation what the Eternal Father is, he could not do so in any other way than by saying: The Eternal Father is he who has a son of the same nature. Then, therefore, either those inconveniences follow from such a definition, namely a vicious circle, by defining the same thing through itself, the unknown through the unknown, and also nugation, or useless repetition, or they do not. If they do not follow, therefore neither do they follow from the way of defining one created relative through the other; and if they do follow, it will not be true that the Divine relations are terminated at a relative. The parity of reasoning is evidently proved: because both in divine and in human things it will be true that in place of a name posited in a definition it is permissible to put its definition, from which those inconveniences follow; or in both it will be false, and not to be admitted in relatives.

73 To the argument, then: the consequence of the first enthymeme must be granted. But when it is said that in place of a name posited in a definition it is permissible to put its definition, a distinction must be made: because either that which is posited in the definition is posited as an intrinsic part of the definition, and then indeed it will be permissible; or it is posited only as an extrinsic addition, and then it will not be permissible. And because one relative is posited in the definition of the other not as a part of the definition but as an extrinsic addition, in order to which the difference of the relation is taken, therefore it is not permissible to put its definition in its place. And the reason for this difference is that a part of the definition is an essential part of the thing defined, composing it according to its proper nature; whence it is the same whether the part itself is posited or its definition, containing its proper nature. But what is posited as an addition is not a part of the definition or of the thing defined, nor does it compose it, but only extrinsically terminates or regards it; which it cannot accomplish through its definition, but through itself: because it is regarded by the other through itself, and is relatively opposed to it through itself, just as one contrary is opposed to the other through itself, and expels it from the subject, and not through its proper definition. Which

considering

[p. 401]

considering which, Aristotle, Topics 6, ch. 2, teaches that a relative, as placed in

the definition of another, is different from itself outside the definition, or taken according

to itself: for in the definition it is not placed according to itself, but only as an

extrinsic addition. Moreover, in the definition it is not placed as a relative but

as a term; therefore it is not permitted to put its definition as of a relative; but

as a term it has only an extrinsic denomination, as that in which the relation

of the other is terminated.

74 To the testimony of Aristotle, I reply that he is not speaking of the defi‐

nition of one relative through another, but only asserts that a potency is not

referred to its subject, in which it is, by the special relation of a potency, but

only to its proper object: as the intellect not to man but to the intelligible, and

sight to the visible. For if it were said, he says, relatively to man, the same

thing as the same would be said twice: that is, to two terms and through two

relations, which is plainly impossible. Thus, as a potency, it is said relatively

only to its object, that is, to the intelligible; but to its subject it is not said as a

potency, but under another, common ratio of accident. So the Commentator,

St. Thomas, and Alexander expound Aristotle’s words in their Commentaries

on those words; and therefore this must be believed to be their genuine sense.

75 To the other point made in the argument, that the unknown is defined

through the more unknown if one relative is defined through the other: this

must be denied; rather it is defined through something extrinsic, equally un‐

known, and without which it cannot be explained through better-known

things; and this makes no difference, because it is not required that whatever

is placed in the definition, taken by itself, be better known than the definitum;

but it is enough if it be equally known or unknown, provided that from it and

from other better-known things there results an entire definition, better

known absolutely than the definitum. And the definition of a relative has this,

although the term placed in it as an extrinsic addition is equally unknown if it

is taken as the definitum.

## QUESTION VIII

Whether one relative is ordered to two terms of the same species through the same rela‐

tion or through different relations.

76

W       hat pertains to the specific unity and distinction of relation has al‐

ready been explained in what precedes; therefore in this eighth ques‐

tion we inquire about numerical unity: whether, when one relative regards sev‐

eral terms of the same

Cc

[p. 402]

species, as a father several sons, or a similar thing several similar things, it regards each of them through single paternities or similitudes, numerically distinct, or through one and the same in number, extended to all. But it happens in two ways that one relative regards several terms. First, so that each is as it were partial and inadequate, and out of many one total and adequate term is constituted, which is also necessary for terminating the relation: and in this way the species regards the individuals, and the whole its several parts. And in this way it is certain that the relative regards several terms through the same relation in number, and not through several. In the second way it happens that one relative regards several adequate and total terms, so that each one alone and by itself could sufficiently terminate the relation: and in this way the question proceeds, whether, when these terms are multiplied, the relations are multiplied, so that a father is referred to several sons through several relations; or they are not multiplied, but he is referred to all through the same paternity in number.

77 And the first opinion holds that a relative is not referred to several terms by the same relation, but by many numerically different ones, so that it has as many relations as sons. So Scotus, in 3, d. 8, the single q., whom his disciples follow, and many moderns; and it is proved from the doctrine of Aristotle, who teaches in this chapter that relatives are simultaneous in nature and in cognition, so that when either of them exists in the nature of things the other is necessarily posited, and when one is taken away the other is also necessarily taken away, and when one is known the other is also necessarily known. But this property cannot belong to relatives if they are referred to several terms through one relation; therefore this is not possible. The minor is proved: because when the first term is posited the relation is posited; but one first term is always posited earlier in time than the others come to be; therefore the relative will not be simultaneous in time, nor in nature, with them, but only with the first; nor yet simultaneous in cognition, because the first is known before those others are known. Further, when all except the last, who has not perished, are taken away, the relative is not taken away.

78 It is proved, next, by reason. First: because if a father has one son, he will be ordered to him through one real relation; therefore, when he has a second, a new relation will arise in him. The consequence is proved: relation is an ordering to a term; therefore a new ordering will be a new relation; but he is ordered anew to a new son, since he was not ordered before; therefore there is in him a new ordering, and therefore a new relation; and thus relations will be multiplied when terms are multiplied.

Second: when the proximate foundation of the relation and the term are posited, the relation is necessarily posited, as when whiteness is posited in this

[p. 403]

wall, which is the foundation of similitude, and another white thing is posited, which is the term, similitude necessarily arises; therefore, when a new foundation and a new term are posited, a new relation arises. But when a new son is begotten, a new active generation is posited in the father, which is a new foundation of the relation; a new term is posited, which is the new son; therefore a new relation is posited. And it can be confirmed in this way: if the first son dies before the generation of the second, the relation of paternity ceases to be in the father, and through the generation of the second a new one arises, because there is a new foundation and a new term; therefore, even if the first did not die, a new relation would arise. The consequence is proved, because in the same way there is a new foundation and a new term.

79 And if you reply that while the first is living a new relation does not arise, because relation is an accident, and one paternity is an accident differing from another in number alone; but two accidents distinct in number alone cannot be in the same subject, because accidents are individuated by it; therefore neither can a new relation arise while the first remains. Thus a subject having one relation is incapable of another distinct in number alone, and therefore one relation prevents another from arising. Against this is the fact that, although purely absolute accidents are individuated by the subject, and therefore several distinct in number alone cannot be in the same subject, nevertheless respective accidents are not individuated by the subject alone, but together with the order to the term, or to something else which they regard. Hence several visible species (which they call intentional) are at once in the same eye when it sees two white things, or two other objects, at once. Therefore, since relation is a respective accident, it is not individuated by the subject alone, but together with the order to such a term; and if this is new, the subject will be capable of receiving a new relation, distinct in number alone, because there will be no impediment by reason of which relations should not be multiplied when terms are multiplied.

The second opinion denies that it is multiplied, but affirms that the first relation is extended to the new terms that supervene, and thus that the father is referred to all his sons through one relation in number. So St. Thomas in 3, d. 8, q. 1, and 3 p., q. 35, a. 5; Cajetan, ibid.; Ferrara, Contra Gentiles, bk. 1, ch. 4; Soncinas, Metaph. 5, q. 32, concl. 3; Toledo, q. 2 of this category.

80 The chief foundation of St. Thomas is the nature of accidents, which, just as they are essentially something of substance, so are apt to be individuated by it. Now accidents can be of two kinds: for either they are distinct in species or of the same species; and if they are distinct in species, they are thereby presupposed to be distinct in number, because

C c ij

[p. 404]

specific distinction, since it is greater, contains the lesser, which is numerical; and therefore no one has ever doubted that two accidents distinct in species are at once in the same subject, as is known by experience in the case of choler and heat existing at once in a man. But if they are of the same species, they are not presupposed to be distinct, but are apt to receive individuation and distinction from the subject; and on that account many cannot be at once in the same subject, whether they are purely absolute or respective. For since they are something of the substance in which they inhere and which they denominate, each is apt to be this one inasmuch as it is apt to make the substance this one in the species of such an accident, namely this white thing or this hot thing. But it is repugnant that the same subject in number should at the same time be diverse in number in the same accidental species, as that there should be two white or hot things in number; therefore it will be repugnant for it to have a double whiteness or heat. And from this it is inferred that the subject individuates accidents of the same species: because, even if it were admitted to have several at once, nevertheless it would be only one in number in their species, as one white thing in number, and not several; therefore it would draw them to its own individuation, so that they would become one in number; and this is to receive individuation from the subject. And since relations are ordered by their own nature to constituting a relative subject, and a double father in number, or a double similar thing in number, cannot be constituted, it will be repugnant for it to have at once two relations of the same species; but if the terms are multiplied, it will be ordered to all through the same relation in number. Those terms, however, since they are several subjects, will terminate through several relations the same relation existing in the father and extending itself to all. And so the opinion of St. Thomas, which we follow, is to be understood and explained.

81 It is proved, first: because this paternity is posited so that through it a man may be, and be formally denominated, this father in number; but through one paternity he becomes this father in number, and through several, even if they are multiplied, he does not become another father in number; therefore he is not capable of several relations; or, if several are posited, by that very fact they will all be made one in number, because through all of them he does not become another father in number, but the same. But if you reply that he becomes this father in number through this paternity in order to this son, and through another also the same father in order to another, and that this suffices for several to be able and obliged to be multiplied: against this I argue thus. In order to one son and to several sons he is the same father in number; therefore through one relative form in number, and not through several. The consequence is proved: because if each is distinct in number from another on account of a term distinct in number, therefore

[p. 405]

each is apt to make a father distinct in number; hence, if it does not make a distinct one, neither can it be distinct in number from another, even if it is ordered to a son distinct in number. Wherefore they cannot be multiplied in the same father; but just as he is the same father in number while regarding several sons, so he regards them through the same paternity in number.

82 It is proved, second: because real entities are not to be multiplied without urgent necessity; but if relations of the same species are multiplied through the multiplication of terms, almost infinite real entities are multiplied without urgent necessity; therefore they ought not to be multiplied. The minor is proved: because there are almost infinite white things of the same degree, to which one and the same thing is referred through the relation of similitude, and almost infinite men, to whom each is referred by the relation of specific identity; therefore each will have almost infinite real entities, distinct in number, if single relations are multiplied for single terms. That necessity does not urge is proved: because, according to the common opinion of the school, single habits of science are not multiplied in the same man for single conclusions of the same ratio, but the same habit in number extends itself to all, and could extend itself even if they were infinite; but it is equally easy for the same relation in number to extend itself to all the terms of the same ratio; therefore there is no necessity to multiply single relations for single terms.

To the testimony of Aristotle, I reply that the father’s being simultaneous in nature and in cognition with the son can be understood in two ways: either according to the substance of the relation, or according to its accidental extension to several; and in the first way he is simultaneous in nature only with the first son, in the second way with all and each of those that supervene. And in the same way we must speak of the conservation of the same relation: for since it regards each as an adequate term, it depends on one only in order to be conserved as to its substance, but on all and each in order to be conserved as to its extension. Wherefore, when any one of them ceases, it will not be conserved in the same extension, but in a lesser one.

To the first argument, the consequence of the first enthymeme must be denied; and when it is said that a new ordering is a new relation, this can be granted. But it must be denied that, when a new son comes, a new ordering arises in the father; rather there arises only a new extension of the same ordering, or of the same relation: just as when a new conclusion comes, a new habit is not multiplied, but only a new extension of the same is had anew.

C c iij

[p. 406]

To the second: granting the antecedent, the consequence must be denied; be‐

cause a new foundation induces a new relation if the subject is capable; but once

the first relation is had, the subject is not capable of another new relation dis‐

tinct in number (as has been proved); therefore the new foundation, which of it‐

self could induce a new relation, per accidens does not induce it, because the

subject was per accidens impeded by the relation already acquired. And an evi‐

dent instance is given in conclusions, each of which is productive of a habit, but

per accidens the habit is not produced by the others besides the first, because

they find it already produced and the subject impeded.

84 Second, I reply by granting the same consequence but denying the sub‐

suming minor, that through the generation of the second son a new foundation

is posited. For although a new generation is posited, this nevertheless is not the

foundation of the relation but only the ratio of founding; the foundation is the

potency of generating, as reduced to act through generation; and the potency is

not multiplied; therefore neither is a new foundation posited, nor, consequently,

a new relation. To the other point, finally, which is said about the individuation

of accidents: it could be denied that several intentional species are in the same

subject, that is, in the sense or the intellect, which cannot understand several

things at once except by way of one, that is, unless they are in some way ordered,

or are represented through one species if they are objects of the same species.

But it will perhaps be better said that the ratio is different for intentional acci‐

dents, which neither denominate the subject, nor are produced for its sake, nor

depend principally on it, but on the object, for the sake of which they are pro‐

duced, in order that it may be united to the power, and for real accidents, which

have physical being, and denominate according to it, and are produced for the

sake of the subject. These, accordingly, are individuated by the same subject; but

intentional ones rather by their own entity, together with the order to such an

action through which they are produced by the objects. But of this in its own

place.

## QUESTION IX

Whether there is a real relation of a real being to non-being, or to a being of reason.

85

T     he sense of the question is: whether it is necessary that the term of a real

relation be real, that is, actually existing; or whether, even if it is a being of

reason or a being in potency, a being actually existing is referred to it by a real

relation.

[p. 407]

86 Relation is threefold. The first, pertaining to the essence of something absolute, as transcendental relations and relations secundum dici, such as are the respects which accidents bear to their subjects, and sciences and powers to their objects; and concerning these it is certain among all that they can be real and be terminated to a being in potency, or a being of reason: for real is the aptitudinal respect of inherence which the quantity of the Eucharist bears to the substance of the bread in which it was, which no longer exists; real also is the respect which Dialectic bears to a being of reason as to its proper object. The other relation is one not pertaining to the essence of something absolute, but which befalls all things; and this is categorial. But it is twofold: one mutual, which is real on the part of both extremes, as similitude and equality. And concerning this also it is certain that it cannot obtain between a being in act and a being in potency, or between a real being and a being of reason. This argument proves it evidently: a mutual real relation must be real on the part of both extremes; but a being in potency, or a being of reason, is not capable of a real relation; therefore it cannot be referred to a being in act by a real relation; and consequently it is repugnant that a mutual real relation be given of a being in act to a being in potency or to a being of reason.

87 The difficulty of the question, therefore, is reduced to the non-mutual categorial relations alone, of which the third genus consists: whether they can be terminated to a being in potency, or to a being of reason; or whether it is necessary that they have a real and actually existing term, albeit an absolute one.

And the first opinion affirms that a real, non-mutual relation can be given of a being in act to a being in potency, or to non-being. So Gregory in 1, d. 28, q. 3; Soncinas, Metaph. 4, q. 7; and some of the moderns.

And it is proved by the testimony of Aristotle in the present chapter, where he says that the calefactive is referred to the calefactible, and the agent in act to the patient in potency, in the second genus of relations; therefore he holds that a real relation is given of a being in act to a being in potency.

It is proved, next, by reason. First: because relation does not take its real entity from the term but from the foundation; therefore, in order to be real, it has this not from the term but from the foundation. Wherefore it could be real even if the term is a being of reason or a being in potency. Dialectic proves this, which, though it is a real science and a real habit, has a being of reason for its object.

88 Second: powers, habits, and sciences are measurable by their objects; therefore they are referred to them by a real relation, of the measurable to the measure, placed in the third genus; yet they are not referred to them as actually existing, but it suffices that these be in potency; therefore this is a non-mutual relation, which can be given between a being in act and

C c iiij

[p. 408]

a being in potency. The minor is proved: because the visible does not say actual existence, but only potency; and when the rose does not exist, in winter, there is a true and real science of it. And it can be confirmed in this way: this is the difference between the office of referring and that of terminating, that the former says an intrinsic ordering of the relative to the term, and therefore requires a true relation inhering in the relative, and consequently the actual existence of the same relative; but terminating says only an extrinsic denomination, and an extrinsic denomination can belong to a thing that does not exist, because, since it posits nothing intrinsic in it, it does not necessarily presuppose its actual existence; therefore a being in potency can sufficiently terminate a non-mutual relation.

The second opinion denies that a non-mutual categorial relation can be given to a being of reason or to a being in potency, but asserts that relation necessarily requires a real, actually existing term. This is St. Thomas’s, Contra Gentiles 2, ch. 12, and 1 p., q. 13, whom Cajetan and Ferrara follow in the same places; Scotus in 1, d. 3, the single question; Capreolus, d. 31, q. 1; Soto, q. 1 of this chapter; Fonseca, Metaph. 5, ch. 15, q. 1, sect. 2; Father Francisco Suárez, vol. 2 of his Metaphysics; and almost all the moderns. And it seems to us more probable and to be followed.

89 But it must first be explained, then proved. For the explanation, the distinction should be noted between transcendental relations and relations secundum dici on the one hand, and categorial relations on the other: that the former belong to the essence of the absolute things whose essence they complete; therefore they are not said to have a foundation, nor to arise from any foundation, but they follow the nature of the absolute thing whose essence they complete; and if this is a categorial being, they will pertain reductively to its category and species. But categorial relations are outside the essence of all absolute things; nor are they intended per se or produced by nature or by any agent, but they follow upon the absolute thing intended and produced per se; nor do they follow it as it is in itself, but as it is commensurate or proportioned to another. For example: the relation of similitude is outside the essence of white or black, nor is it intended per se or produced by nature, but it follows upon whiteness or blackness intended and produced per se; nor does it follow it as it is in itself, but as it is commensurate to another whiteness: because if only one whiteness were produced in the nature of things, the relation of similitude would not follow upon it. And what we say of similitude is to be understood of the other relations.

90 It should be noted, second, that in powers, habits, and sciences there is a twofold relation: the first, through which the essence is completed

[p. 409]

of it; and this is not signified by the name of science, but is imbibed in its absolute ratio, which the name is imposed per se to signify. The other relation is one which does not pertain to the essence of science, nor follows it as it is in itself, but as it is commensurate and adequated to its object, so that it cannot be concerned with anything that is not contained under it, nor can it fail to be concerned with whatever is contained under it. And this is the relation of the measurable, through which science is referred to its object, not under the ratio of the knowable, but under the ratio of measure. Thus upon the nature of science, already completed through its respect to the object under the ratio of the knowable, there follows the relation of adequation or measurability. Hence the respect of science, as signified by the name of science, to the knowable is a relation secundum dici; but the respect of the same science as measurable is a relation secundum esse, and categorial, pertaining to the third genus of this category.

91 From this doctrine an efficacious argument is gathered for proving our opinion: because a categorial relation, since it is outside the essence of the absolute thing, is founded on its commensuration with another; and since it is real, it is founded on a real commensuration; but nothing can have a real commensuration or adequation with another unless that other too is real; therefore neither can a real relation arise in a real being toward a being of reason or toward a being in potency. The minor is proved: because real commensuration is a real and natural proportion of one thing with another, on which proportion the real relation is founded; therefore there cannot be such a commensuration or proportion with a being of reason, which has no being except through an operation of the intellect; nor yet with a being in potency, because a being in potency does not have real being in the nature of things; therefore a real being actually existing cannot be compared to it really and naturally either, but only through an operation of the intellect considering it as if it were in act. Wherefore neither can there be a real foundation in a real being from which a categorial relation may arise in respect of a being of reason or of a being in potency.

To the testimony of Aristotle for the first opinion, I reply that the relation of the motive to the mobile, and of the productive to the producible, is real if the extremes actually exist in the nature of things, so that it is true of them that one has a real active potency of producing or moving the other, for example the motive, while the mobile has a passive potency through which it is produced or moved by the other; but if both, or one of them, is only in potency, the relation will not be real, but of reason only.

92 To the first, the antecedent must be distinguished, because it can have a twofold sense. The first, material, namely: the relation

[p. 410]

takes its real entity from the material thing which is the foundation, as it is considered in itself; and in this sense it must be denied, because relation does not follow the thing on which it is founded as it is in itself, but as it is commensurate or naturally compared to another. The second sense is: relation takes its real entity from the foundation as commensurate to another; and this is true. But the consequence must be denied, that the relation can be real even if the term is a being of reason or a being in potency: because the thing that is the foundation cannot have a real and natural commensuration with these, and therefore cannot give entity to a real relation, nor, consequently, be its foundation.

To the second, the first enthymeme must be granted, but the minor must be distinguished; for science is taken in two ways, and likewise power and habit. Either according to their essentials, and in this way they regard their objects as knowable, and therefore not as actually existing. Or according to the real commensuration or adequation which they have with their objects, by reason of which the relation of real measurability to the objects follows upon them, taken not under the universal ratio of knowables but under the special ratio of measure; and in this way they regard their objects as actually existing: not so that actual existence is the objective ratio, but rather their nature, according to which they are attained by the same science; existence, however, is a necessary condition for the real relation of measurability, because unless they actually exist, the science cannot be really commensurated or compared to them; but the sciences will be called measurable only through a relation of reason of measurability, arising from the comparison by which the intellect compares them with the object as with their measure.

93 The reason for this difference between the two relations, that of science as science to the object as knowable, and the relation of the same science to the object as measure, is that, since the former relation is the complement of the science (which is an absolute quality, and therefore does not depend in its absolute entity on the entity of the object, but on the acts concerning it, through which it is produced), it can be real even if the object is a being of reason, or only a being in potency. The reason for this is that the intellect is no less concerned, through real acts, with a being of reason or a being in potency than with a real or actually existing object; nor does it produce a true and real habit any less through such real acts. But the real relation of the measurable befalls science from a real and natural commensuration and comparison with the object, not as knowable but as its measure; and it cannot have a real commensuration and comparison with it unless it actually exists

[p. 411]

and therefore neither can it have a real relation of the measurable, but only

one of reason, through the comparison of the intellect with it as existing in

potency. It does not follow, therefore, that if the relation secundum dici of sci‐

ence to the knowable is real in respect of an object in potency, or in respect of

a being of reason, the non-mutual categorial relation of the same science as

measurable to the same object as measure can also be real.

94 To the confirmation, the major must be granted, but the minor must be

distinguished: for although some extrinsic denomination can perhaps belong

to a being in potency, not, however, the extrinsic denomination of terminating

a real relation; because a real relation is founded on a real commensuration of

the relative with the term, and a real commensuration cannot exist except be‐

tween real beings actually existing.

## QUESTION X

Whether any categorial relation is founded proximately in substance.

95

H     aving explained the term of relation, we now treat of its foundation.

Three foundations of categorial relations Aristotle assigned in Metaph. 5, ch.

15. The first is unity, which he also called number, because it is the principle of

number. But unity is threefold: numerical, specific, and generic. And of numerical

unity he does not understand that it is a foundation of relation, because this is

repugnant to its nature: for a real categorial relation says a real opposition be‐

tween the extremes, and consequently a real distinction, because nothing is re‐

ally opposed to itself; but the individual, as it is one in number, is not one with

another individual by numerical unity, but only with itself; and it is not really

opposed to itself, because it is not really distinguished from itself; therefore it

cannot found the relation of unity. But specific and generic unity can, because

they are founded in different individuals or species, and therefore have really

distinct extremes: as human nature in distinct individuals, namely Peter and

John, and sensitive nature in distinct species, as man and lion.

96 The second foundation of relation, he says, is action and passion. As gen‐

eration, through which one man begets another, is an action; and passive gen‐

eration, through which one man is said to be begotten by another, is called

passion; and the former founds the relation of paternity, the latter the relation

of filiation.

[p. 412]

The third foundation is measure, that is, the adequation of one thing to another, which is found in powers, habits, sciences, and virtues with their objects, inasmuch as they extend to all the things contained under their proper objects, and to nothing else not contained under them; from which adequation the objects are called their measure, and they are called measurable by the same objects. And according to these three foundations Aristotle distinguished three genera of relations, calling the first that which is founded in unity, understanding under unity diversity also, because the ratio of opposites is the same. The second genus he calls that which is founded in action and passion. And the third, that which is founded in measure. And as far as pertains to this question, we suppose that relations of the second genus are not founded proximately in substance, but by means of these accidents, namely action, passion, and measure. Wherefore the question proceeds only about relations of the first genus, which are founded in unity: whether they are founded proximately in substance. And of numerical unity we have proved that it does not found a real relation; therefore the difficulty of the question is reduced to generic and specific unity, in which three species of relations are founded, as Aristotle teaches: for if specific unity is in substance, he says it founds the relation of specific identity, as the specific unity of Peter and John is the foundation of the relation of specific identity found between them. If it is in quality, he says it founds the relation of similitude, as between two white things. If it is in quantity, it founds the relation of equality, such as is that found between two bodies of the same length.

97 But in the foundations of these three species of relation two things are considered, namely the foundation and the ratio of founding. The foundation is the thing itself founding the relation, as substance, quality, and quantity. The ratio of founding is specific or generic unity or diversity, because by reason of it substance, quality, and quantity found the relation; so that unity is the ratio of founding the relation of identity, similitude, or equality, and diversity is the ratio of founding the relation of diversity, dissimilitude, and inequality. And this ratio of founding others call the proximate foundation, and the thing itself which founds, the remote one; as they call whiteness the remote foundation, and unity the proximate one.

Of these three species of relations, namely identity, similitude, and equality, it is certain that the two last are not founded proximately in substance, but in quality and quantity, through which two things are called similar or equal. The question, therefore, can only be about the relations of identity and diversity, generic

[p. 413]

or specific: whether their proximate foundation is substance.

And the first opinion asserts that they are not real relations, but of reason, as the relation of specific identity between Peter and John; and consequently it holds that no real relation is founded proximately in substance. So Fonseca, Metaph. bk. 4, ch. 2, q. 7, sect. 8, and bk. 5, ch. 1, q. 1, sect. 7.

He proves it, first: because specific or generic unity is the ratio of founding these relations; but these unities are not given on the part of the thing, but through an operation of the intellect abstracting the nature from its inferiors, or comparing it to them, as was said in q. 3 on Universals; therefore the relations which follow upon these unities will not be given on the part of the thing, but through the intellect; and therefore they will not be real, but of reason.

Second: relations which belong to things in the same way while they actually exist and while they are only in potency cannot be real, as is plain from the preceding question; but the relations of specific and generic identity and diversity are of this kind; therefore they are not real, but of reason. The minor is proved: because Peter and John are no less of the same species dead than alive; the horse and the lion are no less distinguished in species, whether they actually exist or only in potency; which is also certain of the rose, which is no less distinct in species from other flowers in winter than in springtime; therefore, being in either condition, they found relations of identity and diversity, which therefore cannot be real, but of reason.

The second opinion grants that such relations are real and belong proximately to substances, but denies that they are categorial, and holds that they are transcendental; and therefore that no categorial relation is founded proximately in substance. Soncinas cites this opinion, Metaph. 5, q. 31, and Mercado follows it in the present chapter, q. 1; and he proves it by the testimony of St. Thomas, Contra Gentiles 4, ch. 14, where he says: Relation presupposes not only the being of substance, but the being of other accidents, by which it is caused: as one in quantity causes equality, and one in quality similitude. Next, by this argument: one and distinct, or diverse, are attributes of being; therefore they are convertible with it; but being is transcendental; therefore they are too. Wherefore the relations following upon unity and diversity will also be transcendental, not categorial. This is also proved by this reason: because specific and generic unity is found in all the categories; therefore it is transcendental; and consequently the relation founded on it is such.

99 The third opinion asserts two things. First, that the relations of identity

[p. 414]

and diversity are real and categorial. Second, that they are founded proximately in substance. So Avicenna, Metaph. 3, ch. 10; Albert the Great, treatise on the category of relation, ch. 3; Cajetan, 1 p., q. 28, a. 1, ad 2; Ferrara, Contra Gentiles 4, ch. 1; Soncinas, Metaph. 5, q. 31; Soto, present chapter, q. 1; and it is the express opinion of Aristotle and St. Thomas, and not only probable but true. Of Aristotle, indeed, in Metaph. 5, ch. 15, where he assigns the foundation of relations of the first genus in these words: For all these are said according to one: for those things are the same whose substance is one; similar, those whose quality is one; and equal, those whose quantity is one. And of St. Thomas, opusc. 48, tract. 5, on the category of relation, ch. 4, who says: Nothing, however, prevents a relation from being able to be founded immediately in substance: for in one in substance identity is founded, in one in quantity equality, in one in quality similitude. And in 1 p., q. 28, a. 1, ad 2, he teaches that numerical identity is a relation of reason, but generic and specific identity real and categorial.

The same is proved by reason: because the specific unity of whiteness founds the real and categorial relation of similitude, and the specific unity of quantity the relation of equality; therefore the specific unity of substance founds the real and categorial relation of identity. The antecedent is evident, and is granted by the adversaries; but the consequence is no less evident, because all the conditions necessary for founding a real and categorial relation which are found between equal and similar things are found also between things that are of the same or of different species in substance; therefore they no less found the real and categorial relation of identity.

100 That substance is the proximate foundation of these relations is proved: because before substance is understood together with any accident, it is understood to be, and is, the same or diverse in species through its own genus and difference; therefore it is the proximate foundation of the relation of identity or diversity.

To the first argument of the first opinion, I reply from the doctrine delivered in q. 3 on Universals, by distinguishing the minor: for formal specific and generic unity is not given before the operation of the intellect; but virtual unity is given, which is the remote foundation of universality and a sufficient ratio for founding these real relations of identity.

To the second, the minor must be denied, that these relations of identity are found in the same way in extremes actually existing and not existing: because while Peter and

[p. 415]

Paul do not exist, they are not of the same species according to real specific entity, but only inasmuch as they can be apprehended by the intellect under the same essential predicates; and therefore they cannot found a real relation, but one of reason: because the foundation of a real relation must be a real entity, which is only one actually existing.

To the testimony of St. Thomas adduced for the second opinion, Ferrara replies in the same place that substance founds the relation of identity by means of unity as the ratio of founding; which unity, although it is truly substantial, nevertheless has an accidental mode, inasmuch as it is understood as something superadded to the extremes, as to Peter and John, to whom specific unity is understood as if superadded, in almost the same way as unity is understood to be superadded to whiteness. Thus it is universally true that substance founds a relation by means of a superadded accident, either a true one or one apprehended after the likeness of an accident. Or, second, we can reply that St. Thomas is speaking of relations for the greater part, because the greater part of them belong to substance by means of an accident, but not of all, since in the first place he expressly teaches that some are founded proximately in substance.

101 To the argument of the same opinion: the first antecedent must be distinguished, because unity is twofold: general, which follows upon entity; and special, which is called specific or generic; and the former is transcendental, and therefore cannot found a categorial relation; but the latter, because it is special, can. That it is found in all the categories is no obstacle, because, since its ratio is special, it is always deemed special; and according to its special and proper ratio it founds the relation of identity.

## QUESTION XI

Whether one real relation can be the foundation of another.

E    very relation has per se primarily to be the ratio of referring the relative

which it constitutes to the term opposed to it, as paternity has to be the ratio of referring the father to the son; it has also to be of the same genus or species as another relation, or of a different one, as paternity is of the same species as another paternity, and can also be called similar to it. We ask, therefore, whether it is referred per se to any other to which it is similar, or with which it is the same; or not per se, but through another relation of identity. For if it is referred per se, not needing another,

[p. 416]

relation, it will not be its foundation either; but if it is referred through another, as each individual of the same species is referred to another through a relation of identity superadded to it, it will without doubt be the foundation of such a relation.

The first opinion, denying in every way that one relation is the foundation of another, is held by Ferrara, Contra Gentiles bk. 4, ch. 4, and Soncinas, Metaph. 5, q. 29, ad 1. And it is proved from the doctrine of Aristotle, Metaph., ch. 15, where he posited only three foundations of relations, namely the unity of substance, quality, and quantity, for the first genus; action and passion, for the second; and for the third, measure; but relation is none of these, as is plain; therefore, according to Aristotle’s mind, it cannot be the foundation of a relation.

102 It is proved also by the testimony of St. Thomas, 1 p., q. 42, a. 1, ad 4, where he seems universally to deny that one relation is the foundation of another, in these words: One relation is not referred to another through some other relation: for when we say that paternity is opposed to filiation, the opposition is not a relation midway between paternity and filiation.

Next, it is proved by reason. First: because relation is essentially the ratio of referring one thing to another; therefore through itself, and not through another, it is referred to whatever it can be ordered to. Just as whiteness, because it is of itself the ratio of white, cannot become white through another whiteness. But if one relation founded another, it would be ordered to another through it, in the way in which the other things that found a relation are ordered; therefore it is impossible that a relation be the foundation of another.

Second: if one relation founded another, there would be a process to infinity in relations; but this is not to be admitted, because from it it follows that infinite relations in act are given; therefore neither is it to be admitted that one relation is the foundation of another. The antecedent is proved: because if paternity founds another relation, since that second one is a true relation, it will also be the foundation of another relation; and so of the third, up to infinitely many.

103 The second opinion grants that one relation is the foundation of another. Scotus holds it in 2, d. 1, q. 4 and 5, and in 4, d. 6, q. 10; and with him Lychetus and Mayronis in the same places, and Antonius Andreas, Metaph. 5, q. 13, and on the Book of Six Principles, q. 10.

He proves it, first, from Euclid, Geometry 5, at the beginning, where he defines proportionality, saying that it is the similitude of two proportions; which cannot be true unless similitude is founded on proportion; but proportion too is a relation, according to all; therefore one relation, according to Euclid’s mind, is the foundation of another.

Next

[p. 417]

Next, by reason: because just as two whitenesses are similar because they are of the same species, and are therefore foundations of the relation of similitude through which one is ordered to the other, so two paternities, or other relations of similitude, are similar; therefore they found other relations of similitude through which each is ordered to the other.

For the solution of this question, it should be noted that relation can be considered in two ways. First, per se, formally and essentially; and in this way it is the ratio of referring one extreme to the other opposed to it, as the relation of paternity is the ratio of referring the father to the son.

104 Second, it is considered materially and accidentally, inasmuch as it agrees with another relation in essence, or is different from it: as one paternity, or one similitude, inasmuch as it agrees with another paternity or another similitude, or differs from filiation and dissimilitude; and in this way it is not considered as the ratio of referring, but as that which is referred to another. And on that account it is called the material consideration of relation, because it is common to it with absolute things, which are referred to others, from which it is separated by the first, formal and essential, consideration. It is also called the accidental consideration, because just as it is accidental to Peter that he is the same in species with John, and to this whiteness that it is similar to another, by the same reasoning it is accidental to paternity that it is of the same species as another, or similar to it. The parity of reasoning is proved evidently: because, just as this predication, Peter is the same as John, or similar to him, is in the fifth predicable, so also is this one: this paternity is the same as that one, or similar to it.

This supposed, our opinion is explained in two conclusions, according to the sense of this distinction. The first is: relation considered formally and essentially, that is, as the ratio of referring the relative to the term opposed to it, cannot be the foundation of another relation. As paternity, inasmuch as it is the ratio of referring the father to the son, does not found another relation, but is the ratio of referring through itself, and not through another. This conclusion seems to me evident, and therefore would not need proof.

Nevertheless it is proved, first: that which founds a relation is referred through it to another, as whiteness founds the relation of similitude and through it is referred to another whiteness. But relation taken formally and essentially is not referred to another, but is the ratio of referring one thing to another; therefore it is not the foundation of another relation.

105 Second: one relation taken formally says a formal opposition with the other relation, of the term to which it orders the relative per se; therefore it is per se and essentially opposed to it,

Dd

[p. 418]

and not through another; wherefore it will be the ratio of referring through itself, and not through another, just as through itself, and not through another, it is opposed to the same relation; and therefore, taken in this way, it does not need another relation of which it would be the foundation.

The first consequence is proved: because if it were opposed to it through another relation, it would be opposed to it not essentially but accidentally. And in this way St. Thomas took relation in that testimony, when he denied that it could be the foundation of another, as the words cited show.

Second conclusion: relation considered materially and accidentally, as that which is referred to another, in which manner it is compared not to the relation opposed to it, but to another to which it is similar, or with which it is of the same species, is the foundation of another relation, through which it is referred to the same relation. As the relation of paternity, compared not to filiation but to another paternity, as that which is referred to it, inasmuch as it is of the same species with it, founds not another relation of paternity, but another relation of identity, in the first genus: just as Peter, inasmuch as he is of the same species with John. Father Francisco Suárez holds both our conclusions, vol. 1 of his Metaphysics, disp. 47, sect. 1, no. 5.

106 This one too is proved, first: one relation is ordered per se only to the opposite one, and to any other accidentally, as has been proved; therefore, although it is not ordered to the opposite one through another relation, but through itself, yet to another it cannot be ordered except through a relation superadded accidentally. The consequence is proved: because if it is ordered accidentally to another, it follows that such an ordering is accidental to it; but an ordering is a relation; therefore it is ordered through a relation accidental to it, which cannot be founded in anything other than the same relation.

Second: two paternities are of the same species, and each is that which is referred to the other under the ratio of specific identity, just as Peter is referred to John; therefore, taken thus, they pertain to the first genus of relation, and not as paternities, because as such they pertain to the second; therefore under the ratio of the same, that is, as they are extremes of specific identity; but specific identity per se founds a relation of the first genus; therefore two paternities under such a ratio will be the foundation of a relation of identity; and therefore it will necessarily have to be granted that one relation is the foundation of another, not of the same genus, but of a different one.

107 Which can be confirmed in this way: this predication is

[p. 419]

true of each paternity: this paternity is the same in species as that one; and identity is a relation of the first genus; therefore it is the same through a relation of the first genus; but the paternity itself, according to itself or essentially, does not pertain to the first genus, but to the second; therefore it pertains to the first accidentally; and therefore a relation of the first genus will be predicated of it accidentally. But it is impossible for a relation to be predicated accidentally except of that which is its foundation, as is plain in any relation; therefore the relation of identity will be predicated of the two paternities as of the things by which it is founded. It is proved, finally, in relations of reason, in which it is evident that one relation taken materially is the foundation of another. For the relation of genus constituting the first predicable is per se and essentially the ratio of predicating of the species; but taken materially, as it is that which is predicated of this and that second intention of genus, as of individuals, it pertains to the predicable of species, and founds its relation, by which it is denominated accidentally; therefore in real relations also one will found another when taken materially.

To the testimony of Aristotle, I reply that the foundations are not multiplied by this, since the one relation founds the other in the first genus. The testimony of St. Thomas has already been expounded through our first conclusion, whose sense it contains: for he speaks of relation taken formally and essentially; and in this way it is true that it cannot found another relation, but only when considered materially and accidentally.

To the first argument: the consequence of the first enthymeme must be distinguished. For one relation can be ordered to another in two ways. First, formally, and as the ratio of referring the relative to the term opposed to it; and in this way it is ordered by itself, and not by another relation; and the example of whiteness proves only this. Second, per accidens and materially, that is, as that which is accidentally referred, not to the relation opposed to it, but to another, with which it is the same in species; to which it is not referred as paternity or filiation, but as the same; indeed, not even by way of a relation, but of an absolute thing which is the same in species as another. Wherefore it cannot be referred by itself, but through another superadded to it, of which it must necessarily be the foundation.

108 To the second, some reply by granting a process to infinity in relations, and they assert that there is nothing unfitting in it, because they hold that relation is distinguished from its foundation by reason alone; on which supposition it follows only that relations distinguished by the intellect are given infinite in act, but not on the part of the thing, just as in the parts of the continuum there are to be granted relations

D d ij

[p. 420]

infinite in act. This solution, however, does not please me, because it is more prob‐

able that relations are distinguished from their foundations from the nature of the

thing, as will be proved below; and therefore infinite beings distinct on the part of

the thing will have to be granted, and complete ones at that, that is, categorial and

composed of genus and difference, which is unfitting. But the relations of the

parts of the continuum are incomplete and partial, from which as it were one total

relation is made; and therefore it is not unfitting to admit that they are infinite in

act.

I reply, therefore, by denying that there is a process to infinity in relations: for

it is one thing for there to be a process to infinity in some things, and another for

them to be able to be multiplied to infinity: for the former is for there to be an in‐

finite in act, the latter only in potency. But for there to be an infinite in potency is

nothing unfitting, but is necessary in the divisions of the continuum and in the in‐

dividuals of any species whatever; and only this is given in relations from the fact

that one founds another, not relations infinite in act. Which I show thus: for even

if two paternities found other relations of identity, it does not follow that such

founded relations of identity found others; but through them they are referred to

each other and to any others of the same species, just as through the same paterni‐

ties the fathers in whom they are are referred to these sons and to all the others

whom they will have. That they can be multiplied through other relations of diver‐

sity, to which these are referred through other relations, also of diversity, makes no

difference; because in the same way, through single relations of diversity, they will

be ordered to all the others of diverse species, and there will be no proceeding fur‐

ther in actual relations, nor are more multiplied from the fact that one relation is

the foundation of another. That others can always be multiplied, if relations come

to be anew in other things, is only for them to be able to be multiplied to infinity,

and for there to be an infinite in potency, as in the divisions of the continuum and

in any individuals of other species; and therefore there is nothing unfitting.

## CHAPTER XII

Whether relations of the second genus are founded in potency or in action.

109

T     hree different modes of relations Aristotle enumerated in this second genus,

Metaph. 5, ch. 15. And the first he said is founded in present action, as of the

calefacient to the heated thing, and universally of the agent in act to the patient in

act. The second, in future action, as of the calefactive to the calefactible. The third

[p. 421]

in past action, as father and son: for the former founds the relation of paternity because he begot, the latter the relation of filiation because he was begotten. Of these, moreover, some are relations according to being said only, or even relations of reason; but Aristotle enumerates them all as it were mixed together, because when all are known together the nature of categorial relations is better known. And of all these relations, everyone receives at least those as categorial which are founded in past action; and about these, and also about the other categorial relations of this second kind, we inquire: Whether they are founded in past, present, or future action, or in the potency from which the action proceeds: as, whether paternity and filiation are founded in the past action and passion which these names, to have begotten and to have been begotten, are wont to signify, or only in the active potency of generating of the father and in the passive potency of the son, through which he is said to be begotten?

110 Now potency can be taken in two ways. First, for the formal aptitude or power of acting, which is a certain accident superadded to corporeal substance for operating. Second, for the substance itself from which such a potency proceeds: and the former is called formal potency, the latter radical, because it is its root: as the formal potency for reasoning is the intellect, but the radical one the soul or rational nature.

These things being set forth, the first opinion holds: Relations of this kind are founded not in action but in formal potency: as paternity in the generative potency. So Scotus, Metaph. 5, ch. 13, and on 4, d. 6, q. 10, and d. 13, q. 1. It is proved by the testimony of Aristotle, Metaph. 5, ch. 15, where he speaks thus: But of those which are according to potency, some are also said to be relative according to times. In which words he says that potency is the foundation of these relations.

Next, by reason. First: Because what does not exist cannot be the foundation of a real relation; but past action no longer exists; therefore a real relation of this kind cannot be founded in it.

Second: Because it is not repugnant that God separate a relation from its subject; but if it were founded in past action, it would be altogether repugnant; therefore it is not founded in it. The minor is proved: because it is impossible that a past action should not have been; therefore it will also be impossible that he who has already begotten should not have begotten, and consequently that he should not have a relation to the begotten actually existing.

The second opinion is opposed to this one: Relations of this kind are founded not in potency but in action and passion. So Soto, Phys. 5, q. 2, a. 2, concl. 1. This is also proved by the testimony of Aristotle, Metaph. 5, ch. 15, speaking thus of the foundation of these relations: For thus the father too is called the father of the son, for the one has done, but the other has suffered something.

Dd iij

[p. 422]

111 And also by reason. First: Because that is the foundation of a relation which being posited, even if the other things are not posited, the relation is posited, and which being removed, even if the other things remain, the relation does not arise or does not remain; but such is past action; therefore it is the foundation of the relation. He proves the minor: because by the very fact that it is true that a man has begotten, it is true and necessary that he have the relation of paternity to the son; and as long as generation is not posited, even if there be potency and anything else whatever, the relation does not arise, as is manifest of itself.

Second: The relation of the agent in act and of the patient in act is founded not in potency but in present action; therefore neither will the relation of paternity be founded in potency, but in past action. The consequence is evident, because Aristotle speaks of both relations in the same way, and the ratio is entirely the same. The antecedent is proved: because an agent is not called such from potency, since we see that it is possessed by someone for a long time and he is not called an agent in act until the action proceeds from him; from this, therefore, he is denominated, and in this is founded the relation which he has to the patient, and not in potency.

The third opinion: It says that neither action nor active or passive formal potency is the foundation of these relations, but radical potency, taken for the substantial form or the very essence of the thing, from which the formal potency proceeds. Certain moderns follow this on account of this argument: A relation cannot be given in a subject without its foundation, by which, just as it receives its entity, so it is conserved in it: as without whiteness there cannot be given likeness, or without quantity equality; but if the relation of paternity were founded in the generative potency, it could be given in the subject without it; therefore it would be given without its proper foundation.
