The second opinion is held by Fonseca, Metaph. 5, ch. 14, q. 2, sect. 5: that they are not distinguished essentially but only accidentally, and therefore are not different species, but one. And this is more in the mind of Aristotle, and to be held as more probable.

But that each may become manifest, three things are to be presupposed as certain and received by all. First, that impotency is not taken by Aristotle for a pure negation or privation of potency. This is proved evidently: because he says it is a quality; but quality is a positive entity, while negation and privation are not positive entities, as is self-evident: therefore they are not qualities, nor are they understood by Aristotle by natural impotency; but by impotency he understands a positive quality, bestowed on substance by nature, for doing something or for resisting contraries, but each with difficulty. And so substance through this natural quality can do something, or can resist contraries, yet hardly and with difficulty: whence it is a principle of some operation or resistance, but a weak and as it were infirm one; and therefore it is called not so much a potency as an impotency, so that its defect and imperfection may be made manifest.

24 Second: it is certain that natural impotency is taken by Aristotle not only in relation to resisting with difficulty, but also to acting with difficulty: for he explained both in express words in the text. Third, it is certain that natural potency and impotency, when they are ordered to different operations, or one to acting and the other to resisting, are distinguished in species. As dullness of wit, which is ordered to understanding with difficulty, is distinguished in species from the visual power, ordered to seeing. This is proved efficaciously: because potencies are distinguished in species through the acts to which they are ordered; but seeing and understanding are acts

Ff ij

[p. 452]

distinct in species: therefore the potencies ordered to them are distinguished in species. Nor is it less evidently proved of a potency for acting and an impotency for resisting: because to act and to resist contraries are different things: as the nutritive power is distinct from the softness of wax, which is an impotency for resisting division with difficulty.

25 The difficulty of the question, then, lies in this: Whether a natural potency for doing something, and a natural impotency for doing the same thing hardly or with difficulty, are distinguished in species; and in the same way, whether a natural potency for resisting division strongly and a natural impotency for resisting it hardly are distinguished in species: as, whether the hardness of iron, by which it strongly resists division, is distinguished from the softness of wax, by which it resists the same division in a certain weak manner; for this seems to be as it were a certain imperfect hardness. And the first opinion teaches that they are distinguished in species; ours denies such a distinction.

And it is proved by the testimony of Aristotle in the present chapter, where he calls natural potency a quality through which substance can simply do something or resist a contrary; and impotency a certain weak and as it were infirm quality for accomplishing the same things, but in a certain weak manner and with difficulty, which is to accomplish them imperfectly. But to do the same thing, or to resist the same contrary, perfectly and imperfectly, are not distinguished essentially: therefore neither are natural potency and impotency, for doing the same thing or resisting the same thing, distinguished essentially, in the mind of Aristotle. The consequence is proved: because to effect the same operation perfectly or imperfectly can be only an accidental difference.

26 It is proved next by reason: Because potencies are distinguished in species through their acts and objects; but potency and impotency are certain natural faculties or potencies: therefore, if they are ordered to the same act, they will be of the same species. The consequence is proved: because they differ only as perfect and imperfect principle of the same act or of the same resistance, which plainly is only an accidental difference.

To the argument of the first opinion, the antecedent must be denied, that natural potency and impotency imply truly opposite formal rationes: for although the names themselves, of potency and impotency, seem opposed by reason of the negation which impotency seems to signify, yet in truth neither are the rationes signified opposed, nor the names: because impotency does not imply a pure negation, but a positive quality, yet a weak and imperfect one; and this imperfection is as it were a negation of the perfection which potency implies; and on account of this negation the name seems to signify

[p. 453]

impotency. But because a perfect and an imperfect faculty or potency, with re‐

spect to the same act, cannot be distinguished in species nor be truly opposed,

therefore neither are their formal rationes opposed, nor do the names signify

truly opposed rationes; but they stand as these two names, perfect and imper‐

fect: which also seem to signify opposed rationes, different in species, although

they are always of the same species, if they are distinguished only according to

the ratio of perfect and imperfect. And the same is to be understood of soft‐

ness and hardness, as ordered to resisting strongly and weakly: which, al‐

though they seem to differ in species, nevertheless do not differ; because soft‐

ness, considered in this way, is as it were a certain imperfect hardness.

Q U E S T I O N I V.

On the things that pertain to passion and passible quality.

our things are to be disputed concerning passion and passible 27

F         quality. First, whether they are true species of quality. Second, whether

they are distinct species, or only one, and so are distinguished only acci‐

dentally. Third, whether the passions of the soul, such as anger, joy, and the like,

pertain to this species. Fourth, whether the objects of all the external senses are also

placed in it. Therefore, four doubts having been proposed and solved, for the

sake of greater distinction and clarity, the question will be solved.

F I R S T D O U B T.

Whether passion and passible quality are true species of quality.

P    assion, to begin from the signification of the name, is taken in four ways.

First, for any affection whatever, whether of a thing disagreeing or harmful, or of

one agreeing and perfecting: in which acceptation the reception of a visible

species, or of vision, in the eye is no less called passion than the reception of

heat in water; whence this acceptation of passion is the most common and

improper.

It is taken, therefore, in a second way, for the sole reception of a contrary or dis‐

agreeing quality, through which the receiving subject is disposed toward cor‐

ruption; and this reception is properly called passion.

But it is taken, third, for an operation of the sensitive soul, accompanied

Ff iij

[p. 454]

by some bodily passion in the second acceptation: in which acceptation anger, joy, pain, and sadness are called passions, because by their own nature they come about with some bodily alteration, that is, with heating or cooling or something similar. Whence these passions include two things, namely the sensible operation of the sensitive appetite, and the natural alteration of the body, namely heating or chilling: the former formally, the latter as it were materially, and antecedently or concomitantly. From which it has come about that they are defined in two ways, by a material definition and by a formal or final one. Materially they are defined by the real alteration; formally, by the sensitive operation.

28 As anger is defined materially as the kindling of the blood around the heart; formally, as the appetite for revenge. And this third acceptation includes the first and the second. For the act of the sensitive appetite is not disagreeing, nor does it dispose the sensitive appetite in which it is received toward corruption, but rather perfects it; and therefore its reception is properly called passion according to the first acceptation, as the reception of a visible species, or of vision, in the eye; but on the side of the real alteration with which it comes about, it is properly called passion according to the second acceptation; and therefore the third acceptation can be called as it were mixed of the first and the second.

In the fourth way passion is taken for a quality which is the effect of passion taken in the third way: as the redness which appears in the face from shame, and the pallor from fear, are called passions; and passion in this acceptation is the third species of quality.

And it is distinguished from passible quality: because it not only is an effect of passion, but also has its mode, passing quickly; whereas passible quality, although it is an effect of passion, nevertheless remains in the subject, as the red color shows which certain men have permanently. And from this difference, of passing quickly and of remaining, there arises another, which Aristotle assigned in the text, between passion and passible quality: that passion does not denominate the subject simply qualified, but passible quality does denominate it. For a man is not called red or pale from that red color appearing in the face from shame or from fear, but is said to have suffered redness or pallor; but from the same color possessed from birth he is called red, or pale, simply.

29 From this doctrine this argument is taken, as a reason for doubting, to prove that passion and passible quality are not true species of quality, but certain analogates of it: because passion is not quality simply, but in a certain respect; but

[p. 455]

passible quality is quality simply: therefore quality in common, which is the supreme genus of this category, is predicated of both not univocally but analogically; and therefore not as a genus of its species, but as an analogous term of its analogates. The antecedent is proved: because quality, as Aristotle defines it, is that by which we are denominated qualified; but from passion we are not denominated qualified simply, though we are from passible quality, as was proved from the same Aristotle and from the common manner of speaking: therefore passible quality alone will be quality simply, but passion only in a certain respect.

It is replied nonetheless to the proposed doubt that passion and passible quality agree univocally in the ratio of quality in common; and this is predicated of them as a genus of its species, or of its species.

30 But that this may be explained and at the same time proved, it is to be noted that passion can be considered in two ways: namely, according to its entity or essence, or according to its mode of inhering in the subject. Its entity or essence is to be a quality produced through passion: which is to be an effect of passion (as we have seen). But its mode of inhering is by way of something passing quickly, which it has from the same passion, by which it is caused, itself also passing quickly; but this mode is accidental, because it is accidental to redness that it be produced by a permanent or by a quickly passing cause. Whence it follows that passion considered according to its essence is quality simply, but according to its accidental mode of inhering is quality in a certain respect. And since denomination is taken from the mode of inhering, it is not said to denominate the subject simply; whereas passible quality denominates the subject simply such, because it has the mode of something permanent; but if denomination were taken from the essence alone, it would denominate simply, just as passible quality does.

From this doctrine, then, an argument is gathered to prove that quality is said univocally of passion and of passible quality, and therefore as a genus: because that is univocal whose essence is participated simply and equally by its inferiors; but the essence of quality is participated equally and simply by passion and by passible quality: therefore it is predicated of them univocally and as a genus. The minor is proved: because to determine and qualify the subject pertains to the essence of quality; but that it be by way of something permanent, or of something passing quickly, is accidental, taken from a short or a long time; but passion determines and qualifies the subject simply, although it lasts little in it: therefore it is quality simply, and therefore univocally and as a genus

Ff iiij

[p. 456]

quality in common is predicated of it and of passible quality.

## 31 But to the argument brought to the contrary: the antecedent must be

denied. And when it is said that quality is that by which we are denominated

qualified, it is replied that by denomination Aristotle signifies not so much

the imposition of the name as the formal effect of quality. Whence the sense

of the definition is: Quality is that by which we are formally qualified; but

denomination is sometimes taken from the essence, sometimes from the ac‐

cidental mode of inhering. Whence the fact that we are not denominated

qualified simply from passion does not prevent it from being quality simply,

because it formally makes us qualified, as has been proved. We can adduce an

example in whiteness, of which it is plain that it is quality simply, and of the

same species as the whiteness of a wall, because it has the essence of white‐

ness and the formal effect in the subject, just as that one does; but it does

not denominate an Ethiopian white simply, because the mode of inhering in

the whole body or only in one part, from which the denomination is taken,

and which it is plain is accidental, is different on account of the greater or

lesser extension; yet no one has said that whiteness is not predicated univo‐

cally, as a species of its individuals, of the whiteness of the Ethiopian and of

the wall: so, then, must one judge of passion and passible quality.

S E C O N D D O U B T.

Whether passion and passible quality are different species, or only one. 32

T    he first opinion holds that passion and passible quality are distinct species, no

less than habit and disposition: which Soto judges probable, in the single

question on this category, in the solution to the confirmation of the fourth

argument; and some of the moderns follow it.

And it is proved by this argument: Habit and disposition are distinguished

in species because the former is not easily removable from the subject, from

the nature of its cause, while disposition is easily removed; but passion and

passible quality are so related: therefore they too will be distinguished in

species. The minor is proved: because passion, in the opinion of Aristotle,

passes quickly; passible quality remains in the subject; and each has this from the

nature of its cause: for the quality which is passion passes quickly for this

reason, that it is the effect of a quickly passing passion, as redness caused by

shame; but redness which is had from birth has permanent causes, and there‐

fore is permanent by its own nature, and is called passible quality. And this

difference is made manifest by the denomination,

[p. 457]

for passion, because by its nature it does not remain, does not denominate the subject simply; which passible quality nevertheless does, on account of its permanence: therefore they are distinguished in species no less than habit and disposition.

33 The second opinion, the opposite one, is that passion and passible quality are not distinct species, but one and the same, and are distinguished only accidentally. It is followed by Soto in the place cited above, by Fonseca, Metaph. 5, ch. 14, q. 2, sect. 3, and by many moderns. And it seems to us more probable.

And it is proved by reason: Because the intrinsic condition of each quality is that it be a cause or an effect of passion; but the ratio of passing quickly or of remaining long is accidental; yet they agree in that first essential ratio: therefore they are distinguished only accidentally. The minor is proved: because redness caused by shame is a passion; but if it is had from birth, it is a passible quality; but these rednesses are of the same species and are distinguished only accidentally: therefore passion and passible quality will be so related. I prove the minor: Because the essence of a quality is evidently gathered from the formal effect which it has in the subject; but these rednesses have the same formal effect, which is to constitute a man red, and differ only in that one lasts a short time and the other a long time, by reason of a permanent or a passing cause; which is plainly an accidental difference with respect to being formally red, since a man is no less formally red for that brief time than another who has the same quality from birth: therefore they cannot be distinguished essentially, nor be different species. And this can be confirmed and at the same time declared: because it is per accidens to the essential ratio of redness that it be produced by this or that efficient cause, that is, a permanent or a passing one, just as to the ratio of heat: therefore on this side different rednesses are not distinguished in species; but they have no other essential difference, but agree in the genus of quality: therefore they are not distinguished essentially.

34 But to the argument of the contrary opinion, the minor must be denied, that passion and passible quality are so related as habit and disposition. And the reason of the difference is gathered from the same Aristotle, Metaph. 5, ch. 20, text 25, where he teaches that permanence pertains to the ratio of habit: because habit of itself means to have or possess, as it were from custom and with long duration: therefore, for a quality to be a habit, it must be lasting; and if it has this from its own nature, it will have it essentially; but if from some extrinsic or accidental cause, it will have it only accidentally; and if from within it has the opposite condition, so that it is easily removable from the subject, necessarily

[p. 458]

it will be distinguished essentially from habit. And so disposition and habit are related, as we showed above in science and opinion. And so these two qualities are distinguished not on account of the denomination alone, or the signification of the name, but because by their own nature they imply different rationes, of being easily and not easily removable from the subject. But passion and passible quality differ only on the side of denomination, which, however, is not taken from their essential ratio but from the mode of inhering in the subject, which it is plain is accidental: for from it redness is called passion, and from it it does not denominate the subject simply red, because it inheres by way of something passing.

35 And that this is accidental to it has been proved, since it does not vary its formal effect: therefore passion and passible quality differ only accidentally: because to their essence there pertains only to be a cause or an effect of passion, in which they are distinguished from the other species of quality; but to pass quickly or to remain long, from which the denomination is taken, is an accidental ratio; whereas natural permanence in the subject pertains to the formal ratio of habit. And from this the difference of the two species is known with sufficient probability, and the solution of the argument is understood.

T H I R D D O U B T.

Whether the passions of the soul pertain to this species of quality.

T      he passions of the soul are anger, joy, sadness, delight, and the like: of

which we said above that they have two things. One as formal, which is to be operations of the sensitive appetite; the other as material, namely the bodily alteration with which they come about, as the heating or chilling of the body or of some part of it. The doubt therefore asks, whether they are placed in this species.

And the first opinion asserts that these passions do not pertain to this category as they are operations of the sensitive appetite, but only as, on the material side, they imply real qualities received in the body through a true alteration: so many moderns.

36 It is proved by the testimony of Aristotle, who placed sadness and delight in the category of action, for no other reason than that they are actions of the sensitive appetite: therefore, taken in this way, they cannot pertain to this category. The consequence is proved: because it is impossible for the same thing, according to the same formal ratio, to pertain to two categories.

It is proved also by reason: Because sadness and delight proceed from the sensitive appetite, by which to be saddened or delighted

[p. 459]

is said of man, just as through sight he is said to see and through hearing to hear: therefore they are immanent actions, which proceed from the same power as agent and are received in the same as in a subject; and as received in it they are called passions, because action, as received in the patient, is called passion. But action and passion, as such, have nothing of quality, but are placed in their own categories, of action and of passion: therefore these passions, as they proceed from the sensitive appetite and are received in it, do not pertain to this category; but by reason of the material quality, namely of the heat or cold which, at the same time as they come about, is impressed on the subject or on some part of it through a real alteration, they can pertain to it.

37 The second opinion is the opposite: that these passions pertain to this species not only by reason of the material, but by reason of the formal: which many moderns hold, and which seems to me necessarily to be held in the doctrine of Aristotle. I prove it thus: Aristotle in the present chapter asserts that anger, madness, and the other passions, if they are permanent, as when they are had from birth, denominate a man simply mad or irascible, and are passible qualities; but if they pass quickly, they do not denominate a man irascible or mad, but he is only said by reason of them to have suffered anger or madness, and then they are passions: therefore he thinks that they are placed in some way in this category as they proceed from the sensitive appetite. For what the authors of the first opinion assert, that Aristotle speaks of them only under the ratio of the material alteration with which they come about, and not under the formal ratio by which they proceed from the sensitive appetite, is frivolous and evidently false. I prove it thus: These passions do not denominate men irascible or mad by reason of the heat or heating with which they come about, but as they proceed from the sensitive appetite, disturbing or taking away the use of reason; but Aristotle teaches that they pertain to this category as they denominate a man irascible or mad: therefore he understands them to be qualities of this species not only according to the material heat or cold which is impressed in the body while they come about, but as they proceed from the sensitive appetite.

38 But the whole difficulty of this matter consists in finding the ratio of quality which these passions have as they are actions of the sensitive appetite, and also in distinguishing the same ratio of quality found in them from the rationes of action and passion. And both must be gathered from the doctrine of St. Thomas, 1-2, q. 21, a. 1 and 3, where he distinguishes the sensitive appetite from the rational, which is the will: that the rational is not a corporeal power, nor existing in a corporeal organ, but, since it is spiritual, inheres immediately in the soul, and through the soul is communicated to the body;

[p. 460]

but the sensitive appetite is a corporeal power, like sight and hearing, and therefore is in a corporeal organ as in its proximate and adequate subject. Whence there follows another difference: that the operation of the will proceeds immediately from the will, and not by means of a corporeal organ; but the operation of the sensitive appetite proceeds immediately from the composite, that is, from that part of the body in which this power is as in a subject, as sight from the eye; and therefore it comes about by means of a corporeal organ, as sight by means of the eye.

39 And this is the cause why it comes about with a bodily alteration of the same organ, or of the part in which it resides; and the more vehement the acts of the appetite are, the greater the commotion and alteration of the body they excite. And this alteration either is contrary to the complexion of the body or not: if it is not contrary, it nevertheless always has an excess, by reason of which it is disagreeable to it; much more if it is contrary. Whence it comes about that it always disposes in some way the body in which it is received toward corruption; and on that account it is properly called passion: from which the acts of the appetite that come about with it are called passions of the soul, because they always have this passion conjoined.

There are, then, two really distinct actions in any passion of the soul, as in anger and joy: one of the appetite, received in the same appetite; the other the bodily alteration, received in the body; and each has a term produced by it. And the term of the alteration is known by sense, as redness in shame is known by sight. But the term produced by the action of the appetite is not known by sense, because it is produced and remains within: for we do not know anger except through redness, or unless it is manifested by some other sign or by a word. And it is a certain corporeal quality, just as the act of the appetite itself is a corporeal action; but it has no proper name by which it is signified, but is wont to be signified by the name of the same action: just as the act of love proceeding from the will has its own produced term, since it is a true action, but has no proper name; and therefore we call it actual love; and it is a certain quality produced by way of an actual impression.

40 So, then, we call the term of the action of the appetite by the name of the action, and say that it is actual anger, or actual sadness; and it is a quality which the appetite itself impresses on itself through its action: just as the intellect impresses on itself, through its own proper vital action, an impressed species, which is a certain quality by way of an act, through which it understands the thing represented by it. These terms of the actions of the appetite, then, we also call passions, attributing to them the names of the same actions; and if by

[p. 461]

are produced by quickly passing actions, are called passions: as the interior quality produced by an action of the appetite which is called shame; but if it is produced by an action that is as it were permanent, as is irascibility, or madness had from birth itself, it is called a passible quality.

41 From this there is now plain, first, the truth of Aristotle’s opinion, which we follow: for there are four things in these passions. The first is material, namely the bodily alteration. The second, its term, which is the bodily quality with which they come about, as color, or heating, or cooling. The third is formal, and it is the action of the appetite, having its own term, which is a certain quality that the appetite impresses on itself through the same action: and this is a quality. The fourth is also called a passion, just as the action of the appetite is called a passion, because it comes about with a bodily passion. Of these four, two are actions, namely the bodily alteration and the act of the appetite; and two are their terms, which are truly qualities, namely the heat or cold produced by the alteration, and the actual anger or madness produced by the action of the appetite, which is called anger. Now concerning the actions it is certain that they do not belong to this category by reason of themselves, because they are not qualities, but to the category of action; and, as they are received in the subject, to the category of passion. The terms, however, properly belong to this category, and by reason of them the actions themselves: although the terms take the name of passion and of passible quality from the same actions; for if they are produced by quickly passing actions they are called passions, but if by lasting ones, passible qualities.

42 Second, there is plain the falsity of the first opinion, which asserts that the passions of the appetite belong to this category, and to this species of it, solely by reason of the material alteration with which they come about, and not by reason of the act of the appetite itself. And it is plain from the doctrine given that the actions of the appetite too, by reason of their term, belong properly and formally to this Category. This is proved by the following argument: passion and passible quality are so called because they are effects of a passion that passes quickly or remains for a long time; but the interior qualities produced in the appetite by its actions, which are called anger or madness, or are named by other names, are effects of those same actions which are called passions: therefore they will truly and properly be called passions of this species too, if they pass quickly, or passible qualities, if they remain for a long time.

43 To the testimony of Aristotle for the first opinion, the reply is that Aristotle placed the passions of the appetite in the category of action taking them for the actions of the same appetite; but in this category, and in this species, for their terms

[p. 462]

of the same action, which are truly and properly qualities, as has been ex‐

plained. And this same distinction solves the argument of the same opinion.

F O U R T H D O U B T.

Whether the objects of all the external senses, as they are their objects, belong to this

species of quality.

43

T      he object of sight is color, and also light; the object of hearing, sound; of

smell, odors; the object of taste is flavors; and the object of touch is the

four primary qualities, which are therefore commonly called tangible quali‐

ties, such as heat, cold, moisture, and dryness. And concerning all these ob‐

jects of the senses it is certain, first, that they are true qualities and belong to

this category. It is certain, second, that they belong to this species inasmuch

as they are effects of a passion: because either they are produced through

some real alteration, and therefore their impression is properly called a pas‐

sion or a passible quality of this species; or they are generated from the com‐

mon mixture, or action, of the primary qualities among themselves: and in

this way too they are called passible qualities if they are permanent, or pas‐

sions if they pass quickly. The doubt, then, can only be: Whether under the for‐

mal objective ratio through which they cause sensation in the senses, such as vision and

hearing, they are passible qualities of this species.

And the reason for doubting, on the one side, is: because the sensation

which they cause in the sense proceeds from them, concurring together with

the sensitive power, and is received in that same power; and inasmuch as it is

received, it is called a passion: therefore they are the cause of a passion in the

sense; but Aristotle calls a passible quality that which causes a passion in the

sense: therefore the objects of all the senses, as such, will be passible qualities

of this species.

44 On the other side, however, we have an express testimony of Aristotle

in the present chapter, where he concedes that the objects of taste and touch

alone are passible qualities because they cause a passion in the sense; but of

colors, which are the objects of sight, he denies that they are passible quali‐

ties for this reason, and concedes only that they have this inasmuch as they

are effects of some passion through which they are produced.

The first opinion is that of certain moderns, who assert that all the objects

of the senses, as such, are passible qualities, because they cause a passion in the

sense; but that Aristotle, because this was manifest in the senses of taste and

touch, therefore conceded it expressly only

[p. 463]

of their objects; yet he did not deny it of the objects of the other senses, but, because the matter was not so clear in them, he taught of them, by another reason, that they are passible qualities, namely because they are effects of a passion.

45 This opinion cannot be defended in the doctrine of Aristotle, because in express words he denies that the objects of sight are passible qualities because they cause a passion in the sense. But neither is it to be held, considering the nature of this species, which I prove thus: a quality is called a passible quality of this species only inasmuch as it is the effect of a passion, as is that which is the effect of a true passion, or of an action of its own which comes about with a true passion; whence the expressed species, which is produced through intellection, or which is produced in the internal senses from the sensations of the external senses, are not called passible qualities, because the operation of the intellect neither is a true passion (but a most improper one), nor comes about with a true passion: therefore neither will any quality be called passible inasmuch as it is the cause of a passion, unless it is the cause of a true and proper passion; but colors do not cause a true passion in sight, because vision neither is a true passion, as received in sight, but a most common one, nor does it come about with a true passion: therefore they are not passible qualities because they cause a passion in the sense. The true mind of Aristotle, therefore, and the true opinion, and the one to be held, is That only the objects of taste, smell, and touch are passible qualities because they cause a passion in the sense; but the objects of sight and hearing not for this reason, but only because they are effects of some passion.

46 To explain and at the same time prove this, the difference must be noted between the objects of taste, smell, and touch on the one side, and the objects of sight and hearing on the other: that the former by their nature move the senses, so as to be perceived by them, with a real alteration of the organ, namely with moistening, or heating, or some other similar quality; and these, as they are received in the organs, are properly called passions, since in some way they dispose the subject in which they are received toward corruption. Whence the sensations of these senses are properly called passions: because, although in themselves they would not be such proper passions, nevertheless they are so called because they come about with a true passion, as was said of the passions of the appetite. But the objects of sight and hearing neither are properly called passions in themselves, nor do they of themselves come about with a true passion, although sometimes it may perhaps happen per accidens that they come about with a true passion.

47 From this difference it follows that what Aristotle asserts is true: that only the objects of three senses are passible qualities because they cause a passion in the sense; but the objects of sight and hearing not for this reason, but only because they are effects of a passion. And this is proved

[p. 464]

by this argument. A passible quality is called that which causes a passion in the

sense; therefore, of whatever kind the passion caused is, of such kind will be the

denomination of the passible quality; but only the objects of three senses cause a

passion properly so called in the senses, since they move the senses with a true

and real alteration, which is properly called a passion; the others cause only a most

improper passion: therefore those alone will be passible qualities, properly speak‐

ing, because they cause a passion in the sense; but these not, but for another

reason.

To the argument proposed for the reason for doubting, the minor is to be dis‐

tinguished: for Aristotle does not define a passible quality by its causing any pas‐

sion whatever in the sense, but a passion properly so called; but the object of sight

and hearing is only the cause of a common and improper passion; and therefore

they are passible qualities, not inasmuch as a passible quality causes a passion in

the sense, but by another title or reason, because they are effects of a passion. And

the testimony of Aristotle confirms our opinion, as we have seen.

Q U E S T I O N V.

What Aristotle understands by Form and Figure, and whether they are diverse species of

quality, or the same.

48

C    oncerning the first, there are various acceptations of Form. For first, it is tak‐

en for the beauty of a thing, which results from the due ordering of its parts.

Second, for the substantial form, from which a thing receives its being, as man from

the soul. Third, for the exterior figure of things, not only natural but also artificial: as

what is artful in a chair we call its form.

And according to these diverse acceptations, form and figure are taken by the

expositors in diverse ways: for some understand by figure that which is found in

non-living things, and by form that which is found in living things. So Ammonius,

on the present chapter. This exposition, however, is not to be held, because there

seems to be no difference in the figures of these things on account of which one

should be, or be called, form, and the other figure.

Therefore Boethius and Simplicius, in the same place, assert that Aristotle calls

form the beauty resulting from the due adjustment and distinction of the members; but fig‐

ure, that which results from quantity alone, as triangular and quadrangular. But neither

can this exposition be according to the mind of Aristotle, who in this chapter

placed beauty in the species of habit.

Albert

[p. 465]

Albert the Great, treatise on the category of quality, ch. 8, says that figure is so called with respect to quantity alone, because it does not seem to be anything other than the termination of quantity: for the angles of which the triangular and quadrangular figure consists do not seem to be anything besides lines, which are the terms of quantity; but form, by order to substance: for just as the substantial form contains the whole perfection of the species, so the quality of this species manifests its whole perfection; whence things of diverse species, on account of their diverse substantial forms, have diverse figures.

49 The opinion of St. Thomas is more probable, which almost all modern Interpreters now follow; and he explains it in these words, Phys. 7, lect. 7: It should be considered that form and figure differ from each other in this, that figure implies the termination of quantity: for figure is that which is comprehended by a term or terms; but that is called form which gives specific being to the thing made by art: for the forms of artificial things are accidents. By these words he clearly teaches that figure is the bare termination of quantity, but that form expresses an order to the artificial composite. And a sign of this truth is that figure is found in Mathematical quantities, which abstract from sensible matter, as Aristotle teaches in Metaph. 5, ch. 14, where he calls mathematical things immobile, that is, abstracting from motion, figures. And this is found not only in continuous quantities but also in numbers: not indeed in simple ones, but in composite ones; for the number two does not express any figure, but the number six, which is composed of two threes, has, besides the units themselves which are quantities, a certain figure resulting from the composition itself, as Aristotle expressly teaches in Metaph. 5, ch. 14.

50 But this ought to be noted concerning this exposition: that when figure is called the term or termination of quantity, it can be understood in two ways. First, of the proper and intrinsic term of quantity, as of the points of a line, and of the lines of a surface, and of the surfaces of a body; in which sense it is not true, because these terms are essential to quantity, whereas figure is an accident of it, belonging to the category of quality. Second, of an accidental and as it were extrinsic term, which follows upon the intrinsic terms and the intrinsic termination; and such a term or termination, properly speaking, has the ratio of figure. And the reason for this is: because the three angles of which the triangular figure is constituted presuppose three lines already terminated by their points; and from these, already terminated and complete in their species, the triangular figure comes about. From which it is understood that, for the sake of clarity and propriety, it should rather be said that figure results

Gg

[p. 466]

from the terms or from the termination of quantity, than that it is the term or termination of quantity: for the term of quantity, or its termination, is something incomplete, since it is indivisible or made of indivisibles; therefore it has no other species or category than the quantities themselves; but figure is something complete, composed of genus and difference, and has of itself a species and a category.

Concerning the second, whether form and figure are distinguished in species: some interpreters make them diverse species, distinguished by the fact that figure abstracts from sensible matter, whereas form expresses an order to sensible matter, giving species to artificial things and making manifest the species of natural things, as is plain in the form of a statue and in the exterior of a man.

It must be held, however, that form and figure are not diverse species of quality, but one and the same, and are distinguished only accidentally. This is proved by the following argument: the same thing, according as it is considered as more or less abstracted from matter, is not distinguished in species, but only accidentally, inasmuch as it expresses a diverse order to matter: as man considered physically, according as he is composed of matter and form and has in himself a principle of motion, is not distinguished in species from himself according as he is composed of genus and difference, in which way he does not express an order to sensible matter; but form and figure are distinguished only by the fact that figure abstracts from sensible matter, whereas form regards it: therefore they are not distinguished in species, but only accidentally. The consequence is proved: because the order to sensible matter, or the abstraction from it, is accidental to it; for although a thing belongs to diverse sciences according as it is abstracted from matter in a diverse way, yet to belong to the same or to a diverse science, and thus to be abstractable from matter in one way or another, is accidental to it; although such a mode of abstracting from matter is essential to the science.

## CHAPTER IX

On the Category of Action and Passion.

our things are to be explained concerning these two categories of ac‐

F         tion and passion. The first is, What is signified by the name of action and of

passion. The second: What each is. The third, Which are the supreme genera

of each category, and into what species they are divided (for from these the categorial ordering is made). The fourth, How many and which are the properties of action and passion.

[p. 467]

Concerning the first, there are diverse acceptations of action and passion: for first, action is taken in the Grammatical manner, for the significate of any active verb, whether it is properly an action or is signified by way of an action. But leaving this acceptation aside, because it is not real but nominal, action is taken really in three ways. First, for the free act of the will alone; and in this way it is taken by Aristotle, Great Ethics 2, ch. 2. In the second way it is taken more universally, for any immanent action whatever, under which are comprehended not only the actions of the intellect and will but also those of the sensitive appetite and of the external and internal senses: this acceptation Aristotle uses in Ethics 6, ch. 4. The last acceptation is still more universal, yet proper: for any action whatever of any agent whatever, free or necessary, immanent or transient. And in this way Aristotle took action in the present chapter, which his examples evidently prove, both in immanent actions, as in pain and sadness, and in transient ones, as in heating and cooling, assigned by him. In this universal acceptation, too, action is the supreme genus of the category of action, and passion the supreme genus of the category of passion: for what has been said of action is to be understood in the same way of passion, since passion is nothing other than action itself as received in the subject.

What Action and Passion are.

G      ilbert de la Porrée (who is therefore called the author of the Six

Principles, because he wrote a certain little book on the six last categories) defines action thus: Action is that according to which we are said to act upon that which is subjected. This definition, however, is limited, because it comprehends only transient actions: for by these alone are we said to act upon something else subjected to us, whereas immanent ones are not concerned with something else but remain in the same agent. Nor does it comprehend the actions which have no presupposed subject, and are therefore not changes, if any such are nevertheless found, which is still placed in opinion. Another, more universal definition must therefore by all means be assigned, which comprehends all of them, and it could be this: Action is that by means of which, as by a way, the effect receives its being, or its conservation, from the agent. And passion will be that by which something is said to undergo, through the impression of the effect by the agent. And although the mode by which action and passion are distinguished does not belong to the present consideration but to the Physical one, of which Aristotle treats in Phys. 3, yet according to his mind and the common opinion of the school, not

Gg ij

[p. 468]

are they distinguished really, but by a distinction of reasoned reason: that is,

through the intellect, a foundation in the thing being supposed; for in the

same entity proceeding from the agent, the intellect considers the ratio of

going forth from it and of reception in the patient: and this is to distinguish

their formal rationes, which constitute diverse categories; for, as we proved

above, a real distinction, or one from the nature of the thing, is not required

between the categories, but a distinction of reasoned reason suffices.

How many and which genera and species action and passion have.

B     y the first division, action is divided into that which is concerned with a

presupposed subject, and this is called the eduction of a form from the po‐

tency of matter, or its union with matter: it is also called generation; and into

another, which is not concerned with a presupposed subject, but through it a thing

is produced from nothing: and such is creation, if indeed it is a true action

and not merely a relation of dependence of the creature on God, which is

still placed in opinion.

By the second division it is divided into Substantial and Accidental action:

the former is that through which a substance is produced or conserved, the

latter that through which an accident is produced; and under each are com‐

prehended several species.

The third division of action is into Immanent and Transient. Immanent ac‐

tion is that which is not concerned with some subject outside the agent

cause, nor produces any effect outside it, but itself, together with its pro‐

duced term, remains in the same agent: as vision, hearing, and the vital ac‐

tion of the intellect, by which the word of the mind is produced for under‐

standing. Transient action is that which does not remain in the agent, but is

concerned with a subject outside it, or produces an effect wholly outside it:

as the generation of a man and the heating of water.

Fourth, it is divided into Successive and Instantaneous action. Successive is

heating and nutrition; instantaneous is the generation of a man. And each of

these members has its species down to the lowest; and from all these genera

and species under the supreme genus the categorial ordering of action is con‐

stituted. And in the same way the category of passion is to be constituted,

because passion is divided by the same divisions.

How many and which are the properties of action and passion. 5

F   our properties of action and passion are customarily enumerated, of

which Aristotle assigned two in the text. The first is To have a contrary.

The second, To admit of more and less; but

[p. 469]

neither belongs to every action and passion, but only to those which are con‐

cerned with terms having a contrary, such as the action of heating and of cool‐

ing, and the like; nor do these properties belong to these actions by reason of

themselves, but only by reason of the terms, between which contrariety is

found.

Gilbert posited two others. The first, and third in order, that it is proper to

action and passion always to be with motion or change; but of this too it is not cer‐

tain that it belongs to every action, because many posit actions without pre‐

supposed subjects, of which it is therefore certain that they are not motions or

changes.

The second property, and last in order, is That action infers passion, and is to‐

gether with it; of which it is certain that it belongs to action in the fourth mode:

because, since action and passion are the same entity, and moreover it is neces‐

sary that action, since it is an accident, be received in something, and as re‐

ceived it is passion, it necessarily infers passion and is always with it.

## CHAPTER X

On the Remaining Categories.

The Category When.

1

T     hree things must be explained in order that the nature of this category

may be understood. The first, what When is, or in what its formal ratio

consists. The second, How many and which species it has, from which its categori‐

al ordering is made. The third, How many and which are its properties.

It is explained in what the formal ratio of the category When consists.

A     ristotle did not define When, nor did he teach in what its formal ratio con‐

sists; but Gilbert defined it, although with a quite obscure definition, say‐

ing: When is that which is left over from the adjacency of time. By adjacency he seems

to signify that it is a certain denomination coming to things from time, or from

the fact that they are in time.

This definition of Gilbert, however, is explained in diverse ways, and St.

Thomas posited two explanations of it, collected from diverse authors, in

Opusculum 48, treatise on the six last categories, ch. 1 and 2. The first asserts

that time is considered in two ways. First, as

Gg iij

[p. 470]

it is a successive and continuous measure. Second, as it is applied to measure substance and motion, or its operation; from which application it comes about that the thing measured is denominated by time with a certain extrinsic denomination, and things are said to be, to have been, or to be going to be, and an action is said to be yesterday’s or today’s. This extrinsic denomination, then, is that which is left over from the adjacency of time: that is, from the fact that time stands around substance and its operations; and to stand around is nothing other than to pertain to them by an intrinsic ratio, and not by inherence.

2 The second is not very different: for it asserts that that which is left over from time is that substance and its operations are said to be subject to time, inasmuch as they do not have their whole being at once, but receive as it were augmentation, or extension, or intension from time; and in this they are said to grow, to grow old, and finally to be consumed by it: and this is the category When, namely to be subject to time.

These two explanations agree in this: that each posits that the category When consists in an extrinsic denomination alone from time; and therefore it is false, which I prove thus: the categorial ordering (if it is true) must be made from true genera and species, albeit imperfect and diminished ones; but from an extrinsic denomination alone neither a genus nor a species can be taken: therefore a category cannot consist of it alone. The minor is proved: because genus and species express some nature and real entity; but an extrinsic denomination is neither any nature nor any real entity in the things to which this category can belong, as is plain: therefore a category cannot be constituted from it alone.

3 Second: if they posit something intrinsic, it cannot be absolute, because no absolute entity results in things, or in time itself, from its adjacency, but at most some relation, which, if it is real, will belong to the category Relative, and if it is of reason, to none: therefore from such an adjacency of time a real category cannot be constituted, or at least not one distinct from the category Relative.

Therefore certain moderns assert that three things are to be considered in this category, as in the others: namely, the Form denominating the subject, and this they say is Duration; and the subject denominated by it, and this is Motion, or another enduring thing; and the formal effect. But the formal effect, they say, is nothing other than to endure in being; therefore the concrete is Enduring, as such. But those who hold this opinion are divided: for some, from this category

[p. 471]

exclude not only eternity, which is infinite duration, but also time, because, since it belongs to the category of quantity, it cannot be placed in this one. Whence they assert that the abstract of this category is created indivisible duration, under which are placed the aevum of the Angels and the duration of corporeal substance, as subalternate genera; each of which durations, they say, is divided into diverse durations of the same genus but of diverse species, according to the specific diversity of the Angels and of corporeal substances.

4 This opinion, however, is first against Aristotle in this book of the Categories, ch. 4, where, having enumerated the categories and come to this one, he says thus: But When, as yesterday, last year, etc. Which words expressly signify time, as is plain.

Next, it is against reason: because either the aevum and the other duration of corporeal substance belong to this category because they are created durations, or because they are indivisible; not on account of the second, because the ratio of divisible or indivisible is impertinent to this category, since it is not quantity but When: therefore they belong because they are created durations; but time is a true created duration: therefore it cannot be excluded from this category.

Our view therefore is that When in the abstract signifies created duration in common, as it comprehends the aevum, the indivisible duration of corporeal substance, and the successive duration of motion, which is time; but in the concrete, the thing enduring by created duration. So hold many moderns.

5 And it is proved from a sufficient division: because When expresses in some way duration, as is manifest; yet it does not comprehend the infinite duration of God, because this does not belong to a category: therefore it expresses created duration, comprehending successive and momentary duration, whether it be Angelic or any other created duration. The consequence is proved: because successive duration cannot be excluded, as has been proved; nor momentary or indivisible duration either, because such a duration, since it is a created and complete accident, must per se belong to some category; but it can belong to none besides this one: therefore it will be placed per se in it. And so the supreme genus will be created duration, as it comprehends both; or the enduring thing, as it comprehends the things which endure by either duration. The minor is proved: because it is certain that indivisible duration does not belong to the category of quantity, whose proper ratio is extension, and divisibility its proper attribute; but that it does not

Gg iiij

[p. 472]

belong to the other categories is shown by their rationes, which are most di‐

verse from duration.

6 But the argument of the other opinion, by which it is proved that time

is to be excluded from this category because it belongs to the category of

quantity, proves nothing against those who assert that time is a quantity per

accidens and therefore does not belong to the category of quantity; accord‐

ing to whom it will be able to belong to this category. But it has the greatest

difficulty for us, who hold that it is a quantity per se, and a species of quantity. It

is solved, however, by this distinction. Two things can be considered in time,

namely that it is a successive duration, and that it is continuous; in the former re‐

spect it abstracts from extension and divisibility per se and per accidens.

This is proved: for it is evident to all that time is a successive duration, and

yet it is not evident that it is extended per se, but fairly probable that it is ex‐

tended per accidens: therefore the ratio of successive duration abstracts

from extension per se and per accidens. We, therefore, who hold that time is

extended per se, can place it by this ratio in the category of Quantity, but by

the ratio of successive duration in the category When; and by this distinction

the argument is solved.

How many and which genera and species this category has. 7

T     he supreme genus of this category, which is created Duration, or the creat‐

ed Enduring thing, is divided into Permanent and Successive duration, as

into two subalternate species; and again, permanent Duration into the Aevum,

which is the duration of the Angels, and into the Duration of corporeal sub‐

stance; but successive Duration into the duration of the first heavenly motion,

which by antonomasia is called time, and into the duration of the lower mo‐

tion. And further, each subalternate species of permanent duration has other

lowest species, according to the specific distinction of the Angels and of cor‐

poreal substances; and from these genera and species the ordering of the cat‐

egory When is made.

How many and which properties this category has.

8

G     ilbert attributes three properties to this category, but all of them seem

to be common to the others as well. The first is Not to have a contrary;

the second, Not to admit of more and less: of which it is manifest that they be‐

long to the others. The third

[p. 473]

he says is that created duration belongs only to those things which begin to be, or are apt

by nature to begin to be; of which too it is proved that it belongs to others: be‐

cause there are other accidents too which belong only to those things that are

apt by nature to begin, such as change and motion and others of this kind. This

category, therefore, has no property known to us; but without doubt it will

have some, which we do not know: for since it is of a most feeble nature, it is

no wonder if we do not know its inmost properties.

T H E C AT E G O RY W H E R E . 1

C     oncerning the category Where, four things are likewise to be explained.

The first, What is signified by the name Where. The second, In what its formal

ratio consists. The third, How many and which genera and species it has, from which

its categorial ordering is made. The fourth, How many and which are its properties.

Concerning the first, the name Where is taken in one way only, for real pres‐

ence, through which something is said to be present to a place, or to the space

of a place: for even if a body were in a vacuum it would have real presence,

since it is certain, and conceded by all, that it can be moved in a vacuum; in

which, just as it would have a true and real motion, so it would acquire a true

term of motion; and Where is the proper term of local motion: wherefore it

would have a true Where, and a true and real presence.

What Where is, or in what its formal ratio consists.

W         here is defined thus by Gilbert: Where is the circumscription of a body, pro‐

ceeding from the circumscription of place: by which words he intimates a

twofold circumscription. The first is the Circumscription of the located by the place,

and this can be called active. The second is passive: that the located is said to be

circumscribed by the place; and this he says is of the ratio of Where: for the other

rather pertains to place, and can be reduced to the category of quantity, in

which place is posited; but in the passive circumscription Gilbert virtually in‐

cludes local presence, because a body cannot be circumscribed by a place unless

it is present to it. Nevertheless this definition is limited and not altogether

complete, because it comprehends Where only for local presence, although a

body could have a true Where without it.

Thus, then, Where is to be defined, by an adequate definition comprehend‐

ing every Where: Where is the real presence which a body has in a place, or in the space

of a place.

[p. 474]

From this definition we understand that Where has four conditions. The

first is: To be something real; because something cannot be present to another

except through something real; and since Where is the term of a real motion,

it must also be something real: otherwise nothing real would be acquired

through a real motion, from which, as from its term, it would have a real

species.

It has, second, that it is something really inhering in the subject: because, since

through motion the mobile tends to acquire some term for itself, and the

motion is real, it must acquire not only a real term but one remaining in it‐

self. The consequence is proved: because the motion and the term must be

received in the same subject, as can be proved by a manifest induction in all

motions. Where has, third, that it is a real entity, distinct from the nature of the

thing from the subject in which it is.

5 This is proved from the new acquisition and from the separation from

the subject: for that which is really separated from another must be distin‐

guished from it without the operation of the intellect, since it is separated

before that operation; but this Where ceases to be in the body, and another

new one is acquired: therefore each is separated from the body before the

operation of the intellect; and therefore it is distinguished before it, and

from the nature of the thing.

The fourth which Where has is not to be a pure relation, but including some‐

thing absolute, and also a respect, as it is said, to the place by which the body is circum‐

scribed, or to the space of the place. This is proved by the following argument: be‐

cause a relation alone cannot per se terminate motion, as Aristotle expressly

teaches in Phys. 5; but Where terminates local motion per se, as he asserts in

the same place: therefore it does not express a relation alone, but a certain

real absolute mode, which we explain through a respect to something extrin‐

sic. And this absolute mode is nothing other than the accommodation of the

present thing to the place, or to the space of the place; so that if it is a body,

it so accommodates itself to it that the whole body corresponds to the whole

place or space, and the single parts also to the single parts of the place; but if

it is an indivisible thing, the whole corresponds to the whole place or space,

and the whole also to the single parts. But that, together with this absolute

mode, it includes a real respect to the extrinsic place or space ought to be

certain: because such an accommodation expresses an intrinsic correspon‐

dence: therefore also an intrinsic respect.

How many and which genera and species Where has.

4

W        here can be divided into Circumscriptive and Definitive.

Circumscriptive is that which a quantified body has, which so

[p. 475]

is present to the space in such a way that the whole body corresponds to the

whole space, and the parts correspond to the parts; and a spiritual thing can

have this in its own way, so accommodating itself to the place that the whole

of it corresponds to the single parts of the place, and the whole also to the

whole place. Definitive Where can be called simple presence, through which

a thing can be said to be present to something without commensuration or

accommodation to it; and in this way perhaps the Angels will be present in

the empyrean Heaven, in which they are not as in a place, according to the

opinion of St. Thomas more common in the school; although it is still placed

in opinion Whether the Angels are moved by a real motion inhering in them, and

consequently Whether they acquire a true Where, or only by an extrinsic de‐

nomination from the body which they move.

By the second division, Where is divided by Aristotle, Phys. 7 and 8, into

the Where Up and Down, as into diverse species, through which, as through

their proper terms, the species of local motion, up and down, are distin‐

guished; although many moderns do not admit this specific distinction of

Where and of local motions; but we, following Aristotle, prove that it is to

be admitted, Phys. 5, in our Commentaries.

How many and which properties it has.

5

G       ilbert concedes two properties to it, namely, Not to have a contrary, and

Not to admit of more and less: which plainly belong not to it alone but to

many others. And the first property, if it is true, must be understood of the

most proper contrariety, which is in qualities alone that expel each other

from the same subject: for Aristotle concedes another, not so proper, to cre‐

ated places. Others also attribute two other properties to Where: namely, To

be immobile, since it is plain that it cannot be moved with the body in which

it is, but that when the body is moved it at once ceases to be in it; and there‐

fore they say that another property of it is That it can be corrupted. Each prop‐

erty, however, is common to it with others: for Aristotle also concedes immo‐

bility to place, Phys. 4, and many other things are corruptible. I, however,

would concede to it a fifth property, because it can belong to no other, but

belongs to it in the fourth mode, because it is convertible with it: and this is,

To be acquirable, or producible, per se through local motion.

T H E C AT E G O RY P O S I T I O N . 6

F   our other things are to be declared concerning Position. The first, What

is understood by the Position that constitutes this category.

[p. 476]

The second, in what its formal ratio consists. The third, Into how many and

which genera and species it is divided. The fourth, How many and which properties are

attributed to it.

Concerning the first, Position is taken in various ways. First, for the place, or

the where, in which a thing is situated; but this is too improper. Therefore it is tak‐

en, second, for a certain relation of order which a thing has in place, through which

it is said to be up or down, to have a prior or posterior place; but this pertains

not to Position but to Where, and therefore it is too improper with respect to

position. Wherefore according to these two acceptations it cannot constitute a

special category, or one distinct from the others.

The third and proper acceptation, therefore, is gathered from Aristotle,

Metaph. 5, ch. 19, where he says: Disposition is called the order of that which has

parts, according to place. Which words all the Interpreters understand of the cate‐

gory of Position, which he wished to explain under the name of disposition.

In what the formal ratio of this category consists. 2

T     he definition of Position, according to this last conception, is to be gath‐

ered from Aristotle; and it will be this: Position is the disposition of the parts in

place, according to which someone is said to sit, to stand, or to lie.

But it is difficult to distinguish position from the category Where: because

to be something extended, and to be extended in such a way, belong to the

same category: therefore to be something in place, and to be in place in such a

way, will belong to the same category; but position is nothing other than to be

in place in such a way, that is, with such a disposition of the parts: therefore it

will not make a category distinct from the category Where, which is to be in

place. The minor is proved: for to stand or to sit is nothing other than to be in

place in such a way. Therefore Fonseca held, Metaph. 5, ch. 7, q. 2, sect. 4, that

although position and where are commonly said to make diverse categories, yet

according to Philosophical unity position is not distinguished from the catego‐

ry where.

3 This opinion, however, is first of all expressly contrary to Aristotle and to

the whole Peripatetic school, which receives ten categories, and among them

position: for if it is not distinguished from the category where, there will be

only nine. It is also against reason: because position has at least a formal ratio

distinct from the category where, as we shall show at once.

But in what this ratio consists is not certain among all. And so the second

opinion holds that it consists in an extrinsic denomination alone from place. Which is

also proved false. First: because an extrinsic

[p. 477]

denomination does not suffice to constitute a category, as we have proved. Second: because he who sits or stands in a place will stand and sit in the same way if the place in which he is is corrupted and he remains in a vacuum: therefore he will have position in the same way, just as it is certain that he has a where; but then he would not be denominated extrinsically by the place, since he is not in a place: therefore the category of position will be nothing.

Therefore the third opinion asserts that it is not an extrinsic denomination alone, but the relation of the body and of its parts to the place, or to the space of the place. But neither can this opinion be defended. Because if it expresses a relation alone, either it is a relation according to being, and so position would not be distinguished from the category relative; or it is a relation according to being said, and this not: because a relation according to being said is of the essence of the absolute, as we proved in the category relative: therefore the category of position cannot be constituted by a relation according to being said alone; but it must have something absolute in which the respect according to being said is included.

4 Therefore the last opinion, which almost all the Interpreters of Aristotle follow on the present chapter and on Metaph. 5, ch. 19, asserts that position expresses something absolute: namely, a special mode of being disposed of the whole body and of its parts in place, or in the space of place; in which absolute mode is included a respect according to being said to the place and its parts: whence the adequate ratio of this category consists of the absolute and the respective, as does the category where as well. Which ratio Aristotle explained in the place cited above by the name of the disposition of the parts in place. But position is not distinguished from the category where really, but only by reasoned reason, as action from passion. For it presupposes where, as something prior according to reason, and adds over it that special mode of disposition of the parts in place: for we understand a body to be present to a place, or to the space of a place, before we understand it to have such a disposition of the parts in it; but this disposition of the parts is not another real entity from the entity of where, but another formal ratio: since it is certain that where expresses only presence in place, or in the space of place, and nothing else; and presence in place is understood without such a disposition, and therefore without the ratio of position. And this is to distinguish, by the intellect, a twofold categorial ratio in the same real entity: just as in the same entity of real motion we distinguish the category of action and of passion.

5 To the argument of the first opinion, the major is to be distinguished: because to be, and to be in such a way, happens in two ways. First, so that such a mode of being is comprehended under the same being; and then it is true that it belongs to the same category. In another way, so that it is outside the

[p. 478]

ratio of it; and then it will belong not to the same but to another category.

Which is plain in the same example of quantity: for to be extended consti‐

tutes the category of quantity; but for a body to be extended in such a way

that it is equally extended with another is not comprehended under exten‐

sion; and therefore it belongs no longer to the category of quantity but to

the category relative. And so position stands in order to where, which ex‐

presses simply being in place, not comprehending per se, nor through its

species, the special modes or dispositions of being disposed in place; and

therefore position expresses a special mode of being disposed in place which

is not comprehended in the formal ratio of where: wherefore it can consti‐

tute another category.

How many and which are the genera and species of Position.

6

T     he genera and species of this category are gathered thus by Albert the

Great, book on the Six Principles, treatise on position, ch. 1, and by St.

Thomas, Opusculum 48, ch. 2: that the supreme genus, which is the disposi‐

tion of the parts in place, or in the space of place, is divided into that which

is To be placed upright, or bent, as into two subalternate genera laid down; un‐

der which are contained To sit, To stand, To lie, To recline, and other things

of this kind, as species into which the same genera are divided; and from all

of them the categorial ordering is made.

How many and which are the properties of this category. 7

A     lbert the Great and St. Thomas, in the places cited above, attribute two

properties to it: namely, To lack a contrary, and To admit of more and less,

which also belong to many others; to which Gilbert adds a third, namely, To

stand by substance most closely; which also belongs to the category where, and

more immediately, since it is prior according to reason, as we have proved;

but since they are the same really, it belongs to both immediately, really at

some time. But it is not to be understood thus, that position stands by sub‐

stance in such a way that it is disposed toward it altogether extrinsically: for

it truly inheres in it, as its mode; but it is said to stand by because it depends

on something extrinsic.

T H E C AT E G O RY H AV I N G . 1

T    he same things that have been explained concerning the other cate‐

gories are, concerning having, or habit, which is the last category,

[p. 479]

to be declared. The first, What is to be understood by having? The second, What

having is, or in what its formal ratio consists. The third, How many genera and

species it has. The fourth, How many and which are its properties.

2 Concerning the first, having is taken in many ways, as Aristotle teaches

in Metaph. 5, ch. 10, text 25; but there are three principal acceptations of it.

The first is universal, such that between the one having and the thing had there is

only a distinction of reason: as man is said to have substance and the other es‐

sential predicates. The second acceptation is less universal: such that there is a

real respect, and consequently a real distinction, between the one having and the thing

had. In which signification to have something is the same as to regard it: as a

father is said to have a son. But each of these acceptations is improper, and

according to it having does not constitute a special category. Wherefore,

third, it is taken for that which is to have something, not in any way whatever, but

so that the one having is accommodated, by a special ratio, or commensurated to the

thing had, with a real respect to it: not as to a term, but as to something to which the

one having is adapted in a special mode. And according to the diverse mode of

this adaptation or accommodation to it, it will be said to have it in a diverse

way, and will constitute a diverse category. To have a place or a space is the

category where; to have duration, the category when; to have a position of

the parts in place, the category position; to have clothes or arms, the catego‐

ry Having: because there is a special accommodation of the body to clothes

and arms; whence the general name having is attributed to it specially.

And according to this acceptation it is defined by Gilbert with this defini‐

tion: Habit is the adjacency of bodies and of the things which are about the body. As

if it were said that clothes surround or cover the body through a special ac‐

commodation of the same body to them, as to something extrinsic not in‐

hering in it. And so the formal ratio of this category consists in the special

mode by which the body accommodates itself to clothes or arms; which mode is di‐

verse from the others by which it accommodates itself to place or to dura‐

tion; and therefore it constitutes a special category, which in the Concrete is

called Having, or Habit; but the Abstract has no name, but its abstract is called

the ratio of habit, or the ratio of having.

How many and which are the genera and species of Having. 3

H      aving is divided, as a supreme genus, into diverse modes of having, dis‐

tinguished by the diverse things had, to which

[p. 480]

the body accommodates itself in diverse modes: as To have clothes is one genus, and another To have arms; and each of these is divided into other species, such as are To be tunicked, To be cuirassed, and others like them; and from these genera and species, down to the individuals, which are Peter or John being shod, tunicked, or cuirassed, the categorial ordering is constituted.

How many and which are the properties of this category.

T     he first property of Having is: That it admits of more and less; for the

horseman is more armed than the foot soldier, and he is said to be more shod who is furnished with greaves and shoes together than he who is furnished with shoes alone. The second property is: Not to have a contrary. For to be shod and to be cuirassed are not opposites. But each of these properties is common to other things; concerning which St. Thomas well notes, Opusculum 48, treatise on the six last categories, ch. 3, that they are not repugnant to each other: because, although to admit of more and less, taken properly, proceeds from a greater or lesser admixture of the contrary, and therefore nothing can admit them unless it has a contrary, yet more and less are not attributed to this category taken properly, but improperly: that is, according to a certain extension, because the body is adorned with more or fewer clothes or arms; therefore, taken well in this way, more and less can belong to this category, although it does not have a contrary.
