Its last property is That it necessarily expresses adjacency between several things, so that one is actually in the other: for unless the clothes or arms are on the man, he will not be called clothed or armed, nor be said to have them according to the special signification of this category (although by another title, of possession, he can have them); which in the others is not necessary: for a body can have a where and a position even if it is not actually circumscribed by a place. Therefore this property seems to belong to this category in the fourth mode.

SINGLE QUESTION. Whether having is something intrinsic and inhering, or consists in an extrinsic denomi‐

nation alone.

C     oncerning this question, there must first of all be rejected the opinion

of certain moderns who, finding nothing intrinsic in that which is having, said that it is not a special category. But this is against the common consensus of the whole school, which

with

[p. 481]

with Aristotle holds that there are ten categories, and that Having is one of them: if it is excluded, there will be only nine. And it is also against reason, by which it will be proved that it has a special and categorial ratio, although an imperfect and diminished one.

5 This opinion, then, being refuted, there is another of certain moderns, who say that this category consists in an extrinsic denomination alone, from clothes or arms, beyond which it signifies nothing intrinsic or inhering. They prove it first: Because to have is nothing other than to be clothed or armed: therefore the form by which the body is denominated is the clothes or the arms; but these do not inhere in it, but lie extrinsically beside it, surrounding it: therefore it does not signify something intrinsic or inhering, but only an extrinsic denomination from them.

Second: From the fact that a man has clothes or arms, no real and intrinsic mode can come to him, besides the relation of proximity or of contact with them; but it is certain that this respect is general, and therefore does not pertain to this category: therefore it signifies nothing special and intrinsic, but only an extrinsic denomination from the clothes or arms. A sign of which is that even if a clothed or armed man is stripped of his clothes or arms, he loses nothing real and intrinsic, or inhering in him: therefore neither does he acquire anything inhering in him while he is dressed in clothes or arms, but he acquires and admits only an extrinsic denomination from them; wherefore the formal ratio of this category consists in this alone. This opinion, however, will be proved false in the following question, where I shall show that an extrinsic denomination alone cannot make a special category.

6 Our view, then, is the opposite, namely that having, besides the extrinsic denomination from clothes or arms, contains some mode formally inhering in the body; and that this mode is an absolute real entity, which nevertheless includes a respect secundum dici to the clothes or arms: so that the formal ratio of this category consists of the absolute together with the respect.

But what this mode inhering in the body is must be gathered from the doctrine of Aristotle, who in Metaph. 5, ch. 10, speaks thus of this category: Having is said as a certain act of the one having and of the thing had, as a certain action or motion: for when the one makes and the other is made, the making is in between; thus too between the one having clothing and the clothing had there is a habit in between: this habit, then, it is manifest, cannot be had; for it would proceed to infinity, if there were a having of the habit had. In which words he expressly teaches two things. First, that between the clothing and the clothed man there is something in between, just as between the agent and the effect the action is in between: and this

Hh

[p. 482]

in between, between the clothing and the man, he calls the act of having, or “habitation” (if one may speak so to explain these matters). He teaches second that this middle act is not had through another middle habit, lest there be a process to infinity: because it is not that which is had, but the ratio of having; whence it belongs to the clothed or armed man by itself, and not through another medium.

And from both I gather this argument to prove our view. If between the body and the clothing by which the clothes are said to be had there is something in between, this medium holds itself on the side of the body: therefore it is something real in it; and indeed accidental, since it can be present and absent while the man is dressed in and stripped of his clothes: wherefore it must formally inhere in that same man. Moreover, if this medium is not had through another medium but by itself, because it is the ratio of having, it follows that it is not extrinsic to the man, as the clothes are: for if it were extrinsic, it would be had through another medium, as the clothes are had: therefore it is something intrinsic, inhering in him.

7 But what this intrinsic medium is, in which the formal ratio of this category consists, must be gathered from the doctrine of the same Aristotle, On the Parts of Animals 3, ch. 1, where he asserts that nature gave the animals clothing with which to be covered, such as skin, hair, wool, or something similar, and arms with which they might defend themselves from others, and also attack them if need be; but that it brought forth man naked, while giving him intellect, by which through his own industry he might seek clothes and arms for himself, and make them from other things.

From this two things are gathered that are very much to be noted, in which man differs from the other animals. The first is that their clothing and arms are integral parts of their bodies: whence they are not said to have them properly, but by a most common and most improper ratio, not pertaining to this category, just as they are said to have feet or a head; but the clothes and arms of man alone are certain other bodies extrinsic to him, which are properly said to lie beside him: and therefore he is properly said to have them, and by a special and most proper ratio is said to be clothed and armed: wherefore the category Having belongs properly to him alone. We do indeed clothe monkeys and arm horses, yet they are not said to be clothed or armed properly, but by a certain analogy and likeness to man: wherefore neither are they said properly to have clothes and arms according to the formal ratio of this category.

8 The second thing that is gathered is that in place of clothes and arms nature gave man a natural aptitude, and an accommodation

[p. 483]

for putting them on, by which aptitude he might in a special manner fit and accommodate himself to them while he was dressed in them: and by reason of this accommodation, clothes and arms give him a special and as it were natural adornment; but to the other animals, which have their clothing and arms as integral parts of their bodies, nature neither gave, nor was it necessary to give, such an aptitude and accommodation to extrinsic clothes and arms: whence these do not give them an adornment as it were natural, as they do to man, but as it were artificial, and excessively improper.

From which I infer that while a man is naked he has only a natural aptitude, and an as it were aptitudinal accommodation and coaptation, to clothes and arms; but while he is dressed in them, such an aptitude goes out into act: not indeed into the act which is an action, but into the act which is the formal mode of actual accommodation and coaptation produced in him, in some way similar to action and passion, inasmuch as clothes and arms are said to clothe and arm a man, and the man himself is said to get clothed and armed, and to be clothed and armed.

9 And this mode of actual accommodation and coaptation is called habit, or “habition,” which Aristotle taught is the medium between the clothes and the man, and is not had through another mode, but inheres in the man by itself, as the medium of having clothes and arms. In this absolute mode, then, which nevertheless includes a respect secundum dici to the clothes and arms, and also extrinsic denominations from them, the formal ratio of this category consists: which St. Thomas and other older Interpreters sometimes call extrinsic, on account of the same extrinsic denominations which it includes; not, certainly, wishing to exclude an intrinsic and inhering mode.

To the first argument of the other opinion: The first consequence must be denied, that the man would be denominated clothed and armed by the clothes and arms alone: rather he is denominated first and formally by the actual mode of accommodation and coaptation inhering in him, and then by the clothes and arms with an extrinsic denomination; in which the ratio of this category does not principally consist, but in the other, formal denomination.

To the second: The first antecedent must be denied, that no real mode arises in the man from the fact that he is dressed in clothes: for there arises an actual inhering mode of accommodation, as has been explained; which mode he loses while he is stripped of his clothes and arms, and acquires another anew if he is dressed again. By reason, then, of this formal and intrinsic mode, this category also has an intrinsic and formal concrete.

Hh ij

[p. 484]

## GENERAL QUESTION FOR ALL THE LAST

S I X C AT E G O R I E S .

Whether their formal ratio consists in something intrinsic and formally inhering, or in

an extrinsic denomination alone.

10

B     efore we bring forward the probable opinions, that of those who held

the following is to be excluded as improbable: Of the ten categories, only

the first four, namely substance, quantity, relation, and quality, are proper categories;

while the remaining six are only certain complications or aggregations of cer‐

tain less imperfect predicates, from which neither genera nor species, nor

even categorial orderings, can be constituted, except through a certain like‐

ness and analogy to those four: and therefore, they say, Aristotle distin‐

guished their genera and species in very few words and quite perfunctorily.

But this altogether lacks probability; since Aristotle, in the chapter on in‐

complexes, enumerated ten categories without distinction, and afterwards,

having set out those four, enumerated action and passion with the rest; and

since it has been proved of each in its own place that they have proper cate‐

gorial rationes, and also genera and species, although most imperfect ones,

and of which the use in the sciences is not so frequent: and therefore they

were explained by Aristotle in few words.

11 This false opinion, then, being excluded, the first opinion is that of

Scotus, in 3, d. 1, q. 1; in 4, d. 13, q. 1; and Quodlibet 11, q. 4; in which places he

devised this distinction of relations: Some relations (he says) come intrinsically,

which, once the foundation and the extremes are posited, necessarily arise in

them, such as paternity and filiation. Others are extrinsically coming, which

even when the foundation and the extremes are posited do not necessarily

arise: and therefore they do not come from the nature of the extremes, but

from something extrinsic. Such are the relation of union between matter and

form, and the relation between the located thing and the place: of which it is

certain that while the extremes exist, namely matter and form (as when the

soul is separated from the body), and also the located thing and the place

that carries it away, the relation of union or of location between them does

not follow, unless they are united again by some efficient, and consequently

extrinsic, cause.

And in these extrinsically coming relations, he says, the rationes of these

six categories consist. According to Scotus, then, the category of Action will

be the relation to the principle, or efficient cause, from which the effect pro‐

ceeds; and Passion, the relation

[p. 485]

to the same, as impressing the effect on the patient; Where, the relation of the body to the place or space; When, the relation of the thing to its proper duration; Position, the relation of the body, according to its parts, to the place; and Having, the relation of the same body to the clothes or arms. And he says these six categories are sufficiently distinguished.

12 Scotus proves it with this argument: Peter’s being in a place, or having where, is not Peter himself, nor the place surrounding him: therefore, since it is something, it will be only his relation to the place. The consequence is proved: because, since the surface containing Peter does not inhere in him, he acquires nothing else when he begins to be in a place besides the relation to the place; nor does he lose anything else when he withdraws from the place besides the same relation: therefore Where will be nothing besides a relation. And so of the other five categories, to which the same argument can be applied. Almost the same opinion as Scotus is followed by Capreolus, in 2, d. 2, q. 1, and Soncinas, Metaph. 5, q. 6, ad 4: for although they do not admit that distinction of relations, they nevertheless assert that the last six categories do not consist in something absolute, nor in the absolute together with a respect, but include certain pure respects alone.

This opinion, however, contains two falsehoods. For first, it is false that there are such relations as Scotus calls extrinsically coming. Second, it is also false that, if there were, the formal ratio of these categories would be placed in them alone.

13 Now the first is proved, that there are none. Scotus calls an extrinsically coming relation that which, once the foundation and the extremes are posited, does not follow or does not arise; but it is impossible that, once the extremes are posited with the foundation, the relation should not arise in them: therefore such relations are impossible. The minor is proved: because all the extremes of a relation are such through the foundation, whether the relation comes to them from something extrinsic or from something intrinsic: therefore it is repugnant that the foundation be posited in them without the relation following. For example: two white things are the extremes of likeness through the whiteness posited in each; two men are the extremes of paternity and filiation through active and passive generation: and therefore it is naturally repugnant that, once the foundation and the extremes are posited, the relation should not follow in them. Which is no less evident in Scotus’s own examples: for the relation of union between matter and form is founded on the action by which they are united by the agent (which they call “unition”); and the relation of the place to the located thing, and of the located thing to the place (if it is real on the part of both), is founded on the approximation or commensuration of the located thing to the place, or the circumscription of the place to the located thing; but it is naturally impossible that the located thing be approximated

Hh iij

[p. 486]

or commensurated to the place, or that the place circumscribe the located thing, and such a relation not follow: therefore such relations are impossible.

14 And Scotus’s deception becomes manifest: because in his examples he posits only the extremes and not their foundation, namely matter and form, making no mention of the unition, which is the foundation; and also the located thing and the place, without the circumscription or approximation: which is to posit the extremes bare, or taken materially, not formally, as they are extremes of the relation, which they are through the foundation: wherefore it is no wonder if, when they are posited in this way, the relation does not follow, whereas when they are posited with the foundation it is impossible that it not follow. Which is found also in the other relations: for although you posit two men, unless you posit that one proceeds from the other by generation, which is the foundation of the relation, the relation of paternity and filiation does not follow in them; but once this is posited, it necessarily follows. And so it is plain how frivolous and without foundation the Scotist distinction of relations is.

15 Likewise the second is proved, that even if there were such relations, the formal ratio of these categories could not consist in them alone. And to prove it I take the categories of action and passion, and argue in this way: Action and passion are the same as motion, so that action is nothing other than motion as it proceeds from the agent, and passion motion as received in the patient; but motion as it proceeds from the agent signifies the absolute entity of the way, besides the respect to the agent; and passion signifies the same entity as received, besides the respect to the patient: therefore it is evidently proved of these two categories that they cannot consist in a respect alone. And in the same way it can be proved of the others, although in these two it is more manifest.

16 It is proved second: Because if these categories consist in relations alone and pure, it is impossible that they be distinguished from the category of relation: therefore, since it is certain, and is granted by Scotus, that they are distinguished from it, they cannot consist in relation alone. The antecedent is proved from the definition of the category of relation. Relatives of the category of relation are those whose whole being is to be referred to another; but the whole being of these categories is to be referred to another: therefore they are relatives of that category. The minor is proved: because if they consist in relation alone and pure, since relation signifies nothing absolute, but only the ratio of referring to another, the whole being of these will be relation, and consequently the whole will be to be referred to another.

The second opinion is the opposite, asserting that these last categories

[p. 487]

consist in a purely absolute ratio: not indeed an intrinsic or inhering one, but a purely extrinsic one, which a respect to something extrinsic follows, not pertaining, however, to their formal or essential ratio, but as it were accidental: as the category of where is nothing other than the place, as extrinsically denominating the located thing; and so of the rest. So Hervaeus, Quodlibet 1, q. 9; Javelli, Metaph. 5, last q.; Soto, sole q. on the last six categories; Fonseca, Metaph. 5, ch. 15, q. 7, sect. 3.

17 It is proved by a sufficient enumeration of the parts: for these categories do not signify a bare relation, as has been proved against Scotus; nor the absolute together with a respect, because this is an aggregate per accidens out of things of diverse categories. Nor again do they signify a purely absolute ratio, intrinsic or inhering; because Aristotle, and with him the whole school, calls these categories adjacent and extrinsic; and rightly, since where is nothing other than to be extrinsically circumscribed by a place, and to be clothed, to be extrinsically circumscribed by clothes; and so of the others: therefore it is necessary to posit their formal ratio as absolute and altogether extrinsic.

This opinion too is proved false by a twofold argument. First: Because a category signifies an ordering constituted of genera and species; but genera and species cannot consist of, or be made from, an extrinsic denomination alone, since they signify a real and intrinsic nature: therefore neither can a category consist of an extrinsic denomination alone. Moreover, an extrinsic denomination posits nothing in the thing denominated: and therefore all admit a new extrinsic denomination in God, as that He is creator in time, a denomination which He did not have from eternity: therefore, if an extrinsic denomination alone suffices to constitute these six categories, God could be placed in them without any imperfection or limitation of Himself: which we proved above to be false.

Second: Because of two categories at least it is evidently proved that they do not consist in an extrinsic denomination alone, namely of the category of passion and of where. For the proper and formal ratio of passion consists in the reception of motion or action in the patient: therefore it formally signifies an inhering ratio, and not only an extrinsic one. Where, too, is the proper term of local motion: therefore it must be received in the same mobile in which the motion is received; but motion formally inheres in the mobile, since it is the act of the mobile insofar as it is mobile, as Aristotle defines it at the beginning of Phys. 3: therefore Where too will inhere in the mobile, and will not be an extrinsic denomination alone.

Hh iiij

[p. 488]

The last opinion, which all the other interpreters of Aristotle hold, not only in the present chapter but also in Metaph. 5, ch. 15, asserts that the formal ratio of these categories consists in some absolute mode, inhering in the subject, which at the same time includes a respect secundum dici to something extrinsic, and also an extrinsic denomination from it: as that the category Where includes real presence in the place, or in the space of the place; and that this presence is an absolute mode inhering in the body, with a respect secundum dici to the place or space; and that besides this it includes also the denomination from the place itself, if the presence is local. This is the more probable opinion, and to be held.

And it is proved from the refutation of the other opinions, in this way: These categories do not signify a respect alone, as we proved against Scotus; nor an extrinsic denomination alone: therefore they signify some absolute and intrinsic ratio, because the respect must be included in something absolute, so as not to pertain to the category of relation.

19 And that the absolute with the respect is not one per accidens was proved in the category of relation: for since the respect is included essentially in the absolute ratio, they do not concur to constitute one thing by way of composition; and therefore they do not make one thing per accidens: but the absolute, essentially including the respect, is one per se, to whose category the respect itself pertains, and not to the category of relation: which we proved must necessarily be granted in powers, habits, and sciences. Nor are these respects transcendental: because they are not common to all the categories, nor to several, but are reduced to the sole category of the absolute in which they are included and whose essence they complete.

To the argument of Scotus: The consequence must be denied, that Where is a relation to the place alone; rather it is a real presence, consisting in an absolute mode inhering in the located thing, and including a respect to the place, or an extrinsic denomination from it.

20 To the argument of the second opinion: The second part of the antecedent must be denied, that these categories do not signify the absolute with a respect; it must also be denied that such an absolute with a respect is a being per accidens: because, since the respect itself does not pertain to the category of relation, nor concur together with the absolute to constitute one third thing by way of composition, but is included in it as an essential complement of that same absolute, and is reduced to the very same category, the absolute with the respect is one per se, and can constitute one categorial ratio, although an imperfect one.

[p. 489]

## GORIES, WHICH THEY CALL

## THE POSTPREDICAMENTS

## CHAPTER XI, ON OPPOSITES

TEXT OF ARISTOTLE. Now concerning opposites, in how many ways things are wont to be opposed, we must speak.

B R I E F E X P O S I T I O N O F T H E T E X T.

fter the explanation of the categories, Aristotle proposes certain

A          things to be declared, which are as it were certain modes, or incom‐

plete rationes, common to many categories: which he excludes from

the categories for both reasons, namely on account of the transcendent ratio and the incomplete one. And there are five: Opposition, Prior and Posterior, Simultaneous, Motion, and the diverse modes of Having: therefore through the five following chapters, up to the fifteenth, he completes their explanation and the whole book.

The intent of Aristotle in this eleventh chapter is to explain the nature of Opposition and its species; and it is divided into two parts. In the first he divides opposition into four genera, and explains the single members. In the second he enumerates the special conditions of contrary opposition. Opposition, says Aristotle, is fourfold: Relative, Contrary, Contradictory, and Privative.

Relatively opposed are said to be those whose whole being is to be ordered to another: as father and son, a like thing and another like it, are opposed relatively. Contrarily opposed, he says, are those which, though they are not ordered to each other, are nevertheless repugnant to each other: as heat and cold. And to be repugnant to each other is the same as to be forms repugnant to each other with respect to the same subject: and by this they are distinguished from things opposed contradictorily and privatively, and by the first particle from things opposed relatively.

Privative opposition is that of things which are apt by nature to come to be with respect to the same subject, as blindness and sight, or blind and seeing; that is, with respect to a subject apt to have both: as blindness and sight with respect to a stone, in which there is no aptitude for sight; therefore a man is properly called blind, while a stone is only called not seeing.

[p. 490]

The last opposition, and the greater or more perfect than all, is the

Contradictory, which has no middle, although the others have a middle. Nor

does it belong to things except as they are conceived by us and signified by

words: and therefore Aristotle defines it through affirmation and negation, say‐

ing: Those things are opposed contradictorily which are repugnant as affirmation and

negation; that is, which are judged to be repugnant through affirmation and nega‐

tion, as Peter sits and does not sit.

In the second part of the chapter he explains the conditions of contraries, of

which the first is that to good evil is necessarily contrary, but to evil not only good

but also another evil. The second condition is that one can exist in the nature of

things without the other, as white without black: in which they are distinguished

from relatives, of which it is repugnant that one exist without the other. The

third condition: Contraries cannot be at the same time in the same subject, as the same

body cannot be at the same time white and black. The fourth condition:

Contraries cannot come to be with respect to a subject the same in genus or in species, as

white and black with respect to Peter and John, who are of the same species, and

also with respect to man and horse, who are of the same genus. The last condi‐

tion is that contraries are under the same proximate genus, or under diverse ones, as white

and black under the same proximate genus of color, virtue and vice under diverse

ones; which, however, must be understood thus: that they are always and neces‐

sarily under the same genus, proximate or remote, intermediate or supreme; as

virtue and vice are under the same remote genus of Habit, and under the same

supreme genus of Quality.

## CHAPTER XII

On the Modes of Prior.

## TEXT OF ARISTOTLE

One thing is said to be prior to another in four ways: first, indeed, and most properly.

B R I E F E X P O S I T I O N O F T H E T E X T.

he intent of this chapter is to explain the modes of Priority; and it 1

T         needs no division, because in it Aristotle only explains the four modes

of priority which were current in the school in his time, to which he

himself adds a fifth found by himself. The first mode of priority is

that according to which one thing is said to be prior in time to another: as he who is

born today is said to be prior in time to him who is born tomorrow. Second,

[p. 491]

in the mode in which that is said to be prior to another from which the consequence of sub‐

sisting does not hold: for which reason one is said to be prior to two, and any superior

predicate prior to the inferior: because the consequence holds, There are two, there‐

fore there is one; but this does not hold, There is one, therefore there are two. It is a man,

therefore it is an animal; but it does not follow, It is an animal, therefore it is a man. The

third mode of priority is not in the ratio of essence, but of order, and is found among

those things which are so ordered, or orderable, that in such an ordering one is

prior, the other posterior: as in speech the elements, or letters, are prior to sylla‐

bles, and syllables prior to words; and in the number three the first and second

unit are prior to the third. In the fourth mode the worthier or more honorable are said

to be prior to the less worthy. In which signification some are wont to call prior in

their esteem those whom they love more, or for some other reason value more.

But Aristotle says this mode of priority is improper, because it is not founded on

the being of things or on their natural orderability, but only on the apprehension

of men. To these four modes Aristotle adds a fifth, by which one thing is said to be

prior with respect to another because it is its cause, although it is simultaneous in

time with it: as man is said to be prior to risible, because it is its cause; and univer‐

sally every cause is prior to its effect in this genus of priority. Of these five modes,

the second, the third, and the fifth are called priorities of nature; but all are real

priorities, to which we can add priority according to reason, by which that is said

to be prior to another which, although it is not in reality prior to it, is so neverthe‐

less according to our mode of understanding: as is manifest in second intentions

and relations of reason. Everything that has been said of the mode of prior is un‐

derstood of the mode of posterior, according to the same proportion.

## CHAPTER XIII

On the Modes of Simultaneous.

## TEXT OF ARISTOTLE

Those things are called simultaneous simply, and most properly, whose generation is at the

same time.

B R I E F E X P O S I T I O N O F T H E T E X T.

he intent of Aristotle is to explain the modes in which one thing is said 1

T         to be simultaneous with another; nor does it need division, because in

it Aristotle only hands down three modes of simultaneity, of which the

first is that in which some things are said to be simultaneous in time, which

are generated or come to be in the nature of things at the same time.

[p. 492]

The second mode is that in which some things are said to be simultaneous by na‐

ture: and these are the things which are said to reciprocate, and neither is the

cause of the other: as father and son, a like thing and another like it, and uni‐

versally all the relatives of the category of relation: whose property, we said,

according to the mind of Aristotle, is that they are simultaneous by nature and

in cognition. For although, taken materially, father and son, that is, as genera‐

tor and generated, the former is prior by nature because he is the cause, and

the latter posterior because he is the effect, nevertheless under the formal rela‐

tive ratio of father and son they are simultaneous by nature.

The third mode of simultaneity concerns the differences dividing a genus equal‐

ly, and the species constituted by them; and to divide a genus equally is to divide it

equally proximately: as rational and irrational are said to be simultaneous by

nature; but not rational and creeping, or aquatic: because rational and creep‐

ing do not divide animal equally proximately, but creeping divides only animal

already contracted by irrational, whereas rational divides it immediately.

Therefore they are not simultaneous by nature. And what we say of the differ‐

ences must be understood also of the species constituted by them, according

to the same proportion.

C H A P T E R X I V.

On the Species of Motion.

## TEXT OF ARISTOTLE

The species of motion, moreover, are six.

Generation, Corruption, Augmentation, Diminution, Alteration, and Change according

to place, etc.

B R I E F E X P O S I T I O N O F T H E T E X T.

he intent of Aristotle is to explain the nature of the species of mo1

T          tion; and this chapter is divided into two parts. In the first he enu‐

merates six species of motion. In the second, how many and which

things are contrary to motion and to its species. Now Aristotle

takes motion universally, for every physical change: in which way he defined it in

Phys. 3: That it is the act of a being in potency, according as it is in potency; nor does he

call

[p. 493]

those which he enumerates species of motion because he understands them to be true species, or motion to be a true genus. For since motion and its species are incomplete beings, and therefore not categorial, neither is motion itself a true genus, nor are those true species; but they are called species in a certain manner, that is, essentially diverse modes of the same motion. In this sense, then, he asserts that the species of motion are six. The first is Generation, by which a substance is produced, as a man. The second, Corruption, by which a substance ceases to be, as the death or ceasing of a man. The third is Augmentation, by which a thing acquires a greater quantity than it has, and therefore is said to be augmented. The fourth, Diminution, by which it loses some quantity out of that which it had before, and on that account becomes smaller. The fifth is Alteration, by which a thing acquires a quality which it did not have before, or one contrary to that which it had before; or finally an intension or extension in the same quality which it already had: as when hot water becomes hotter because it acquires more degrees in the same hot parts, or the heat is extended to new parts not yet heated. Local motion, finally, is the sixth, by which a body acquires where, or real presence.

2 And so it is not called local because its proper term is place, but because the where which it acquires is always a local presence: that is, commensurated to the place by which it is circumscribed; although supernaturally it can acquire a where without a place.

In the second part of the chapter Aristotle teaches that motion considered in common has one contrary, namely rest; but he asserts that any special motion has two opposites, one under the common ratio of motion, the other under the special ratio, as it is such a motion. For example, Generation, as it is a motion, has rest in common as its contrary; but as it is a motion to substance, it has as its contrary rest in substance; and the same is to be understood of the other species of motion. But when Aristotle asserts that motion in common has as its contrary rest in common, and motion in particular rest in common and in particular, he is not speaking of proper contrariety, but of a common and improper contrariety, for any genus of opposition whatever: because motion and rest, or such a motion and such a rest, are not opposed contrarily but privatively.

[p. 494]

C H A P T E R X V.

On the Modes of Having.

TEXT OF ARISTOTLE. To have is said according to several modes: for either as a habit and disposition, or some

other quality.

B R I E F E X P O S I T I O N O F T H E T E X T.

he intent of Aristotle is to hand down all the modes or accepta‐

T            tions in which we are said to have something. The chapter needs no

division, because in it Aristotle only enumerates seven modes of

having, of which the First is that according to which we are said to have a quality: as intellect, virtues, and sciences. The second mode is to have quantity, as a body is said to have a magnitude of two cubits or three cubits. The third is to have not things that inhere in the body, but things that surround it, or are extrinsic to it, as to have clothing or arms. In the fourth mode something is said to have another thing, not in the whole body, but in some part of it, by reason of which the whole body is said to have it: as to have a hooked nose, or a ring on the hand, or a hat on the head. The fifth mode is to have the part itself: as a head or a hand. In the sixth mode one thing is said to have another because it contains it: as a jar is said to have wine. The last mode of having is by possession: as a husband is said to have a wife, a wife a husband, and also a man to have money. Aristotle enumerates many other modes of having in Metaph. 5, ch. 23, text 18; but he says these are more in use, and therefore suffice for the use and capacity of Dialecticians. And we too say that it suffices to have noted these things on the book of the Categories, to the greater glory of God and the benefit of students.

The End.

[p. 495]

## COMMENTARIES ON THE WHOLE DIALECTIC

## OF ARISTOTLE, TOGETHER WITH THE DOUBTS

## and Questions customarily debated

in this age.

S E C O N D PA R T,

C O N TA I N I N G T H E B O O K S O N I N T E R P R E TAT I O N ,

ON PRIOR AND POSTERIOR RESOLUTION, T H E B O O K S O F T H E T O P I C S , A N D O F T H E S O P H I S T I C A L R E F U TAT I O N S .

Book 1 of Aristotle, περὶ ἑρμηνείας, or On Interpretation.

P RO E M O F T H E W H O L E WO R K .

his work now pertains to the second operation of the intellect, which

T           is called Composition and division: and therefore it is entitled by Aristotle

περὶ ἑρμηνείας, or On Interpretation: because he alone is said to interpret something who sets forth the truth or falsity contained in something; and therefore interpretation is properly said only of a speech containing truth or falsity (which is the enunciation), as St. Thomas rightly asserts in the first lecture of these commentaries: but simple things, such as the noun and the verb, are rather called parts of interpretation; so too certain other things by which natural affections are expressed, such as sighs and groans, are quite improperly called interpretations. Whence it follows that it is the same for this work to be called On Interpretation as On Enunciation.

What the object of this work is.

F    rom the title now explained it is understood that the enunciation is the adequate

object of this work, in which all the interpreters of Aristotle agree: because this is what is principally treated in it, and whose parts are explained, which are the noun and the verb; this is also the one whose attributes are proved, and to which the other things that are disputed are ordered as to their end: which are the proper conditions of an object.

[p. 496]

But the enunciation is twofold: one Simple, which they call Categorical, and the other Composite, which is called Hypothetical: and therefore it can be taken either for the simple alone, as for the principal part, when we say that it is the object, or in common, as it abstracts from both and comprehends them. And the first opinion holds that the simple enunciation alone is the object: so Boethius, Ammonius, and the Louvain commentators in the proem of this work, and certain others among the moderns; and St. Thomas seems to think the same, since he says that Aristotle determinately treats of the simple alone.

And it is proved, first, by reason: Because in this work Aristotle treats only of the parts of the simple or categorical enunciation, not of the parts of the hypothetical: therefore that alone is the object.

Second: Because this work is ordered proximately to the treatise on the syllogism; but the syllogism is composed only of categorical propositions: therefore it treats of this alone, as of its proper object.

The second opinion asserts: The enunciation in common, as it comprehends the simple and the composite, is the object. So Villalpando and Toledo, in the same proem. And this seems to us more probable. It is proved by the testimony of Aristotle: because in ch. 4 of this first book, where he speaks expressly of the enunciation, he divides it into simple and composite as into proper species, and explains each by its proper definition: therefore he disputes of both per se, and both are comprehended per se under the adequate object.

It is proved also by reason: Because the composite enunciation pertains per se to Dialectic, and to no other part than to this one: therefore it is considered per se in it, and therefore is comprehended per se under its object. I prove the minor: because it does not pertain to the preceding parts, in which only simple things are treated, nor to the following ones, in which the syllogism and its species are treated per se: therefore it is considered per se only in this work.

To the first argument of the opposite opinion: It must be denied that Aristotle treats only of the parts of the simple enunciation. For although he disputes principally of the simple enunciation and its parts, as of the principal species of the enunciation considered in common, it must nevertheless not be denied that he also treats of the hypothetical, since he defines it, and also of its parts, which are simple enunciations. But he hands down very few things about it, because its use in Dialectic is not so frequent: and this is what St. Thomas meant when he said that Aristotle determinately treats only of the simple, not, however, that he excludes it from the object of this work.

2 To the second: The minor must be denied, that the syllogism is composed only of categorical enunciations; for the syllogism is twofold

the

[p. 497]

the categorical and the hypothetical, as Aristotle expressly teaches in Prior

Analytics 1, where he treats of each per se, although principally of the categori‐

cal, as of its more perfect species: and so also in this work he treats of both

enunciations, of the one as of the principal species: both therefore pertain per

se to the object, just as each syllogism pertains to the object of the Prior

Analytics.

On the place which this work holds among the other parts of Dialectic, and on its

division.

T   his work holds the second place among the parts of Dialectic, because it

treats of the second operation of the intellect: therefore it is placed im‐

mediately after the book of the Categories, which treats of the first, and before

the books of the Prior Analytics and the others, in which the third is treated.

The division, however, is not the same among all the interpreters: for the

Greeks include the whole work under one and the same book, while the Latins,

whom we follow, divide it into two books: in the first of which the enunciation

and its parts are treated, namely the noun, the verb, affirmation, and negation;

and in the second, the various modes of enunciations: which is the same as of

modal enunciations.

The first book has six chapters. The first, as it were the proem of the whole

work, in which Aristotle proposes the matter he is going to treat. In the second

he treats of the noun. In the third of the verb. In the fourth of the enunciation.

In the fifth of the opposition of enunciations. In the last, of particular enunciations

(which he calls about future contingents), explaining the mode in which truth

and falsity are found in them.

## CHAPTER I

## TEXT OF ARISTOTLE

First it is necessary to establish what a noun is, and what a verb, etc.

B R I E F E X P O S I T I O N O F T H E T E X T.

he intent of Aristotle in the present chapter is to explain the mode 1

T           of signifying of concepts, words, and writings. And the chapter is di‐

vided into two parts. The first, as it were the proem of the whole work,

in which he proposes the things he is going to treat. In the second he

treats of concepts, words, and writings, explaining the mode of signifying of all of

them.

Ii

[p. 498]

The things to be treated in this work, he says, are six, namely the Noun, the Verb, Affirmation, Negation, the Enunciation, and Speech; and each is to be explained by its proper definitions.

In the second part he says that the signification of concepts, words, and writings is to be treated. Among which the order is this: that from the things themselves, as from objects, intelligible species are impressed on the intellect, informed by which it operates; and through its proper operation it produces another species, which is called expressed, and also the concept, or word of the mind, representing the thing as actually or expressly understood: but since the thing represented through the concept must be signified to others, therefore words and writings were invented, so that it might be signified through words to those present, through writings to those absent. From which Aristotle gathers that concepts signify things immediately; words signify the same things by means of the concepts; writings, finally, signify words: all of which he teaches in these words: Those things, therefore, which are in the voice are signs of the passions which are in the soul; and those which are written, of those which are in the voice. By passions of the soul he means concepts, according to all the expositions: because, since they are received in the same intellect by which they are produced, and the reception is as it were a certain passion, they are rightly called passions; of which he says words are the marks, that is, signs.

And so Concepts signify things; Words, things and concepts; and Writings, words immediately, and concepts and things remotely. Yet by a diverse ratio: for concepts, he says, signify naturally; but words and writings only by convention. He proves both by this argument: Nature always behaves in the same way among all nations: therefore things which behave in the same way among all are natural, and things which are not the same among all are not natural, but vary according to the diverse convention of men: but the concept of any thing whatever is the same among all, whereas words and writings are diverse among diverse nations: therefore concepts signify naturally, but words and writings by convention. The minor is proved: because the Greeks as well as the Latins form the same concept of man, but signify it with diverse words, according to the diversity of the language.

Further, he teaches that simple and composite concepts, words, and writings stand in a diverse way in order to truth and falsity: for the simple contain nothing true or false unless is or is not is added to them; but the composite, with that same verb, already signify the true and the false. He proves the first by this reason: because if simple or incomplex things signified the true or the false per se, composite nouns would have this most of all, as centimanus [hundred-handed]; but he who uttered this noun would not say something true or false,

[p. 499]

because he would not lie, nor would he speak the truth, unless is or is not were

added: therefore in simple words or concepts there is no truth. That composite

ones, with the verb is or is not, contain truth or falsity, he leaves as known per se.

## SOLE QUESTION

Whether words signify concepts and things; and whether writings signify words by conven‐

tion, but concepts signify things naturally.

4

C    oncerning this question certain things are certain among all. First, that con‐

cepts signify things naturally: on account of Aristotle’s reason, because all form

the same concept of the same thing if they conceive the same ratio of it, and a di‐

verse one if a diverse one: therefore concepts are always the same among all, and

consequently signify things naturally. The antecedent is proved: because all form

the same concept of being if they consider only entity in it; and likewise if they

consider its univocation with respect to substance and accident, or also its analo‐

gy: for although those who think it is univocal form a diverse concept of it from

those who think it is analogous, this nevertheless is because they consider a di‐

verse ratio in it, namely univocation and analogy; nonetheless all who consider uni‐

vocation form the same concept of it, and so too those who consider analogy; and

those who consider the latter always form a diverse one from those who consider

the former. So Aristotle is understood when he says that concepts signify things

naturally, because they are the same among all if they are of the same thing, or of

the same formal ratio of it; but if of a diverse thing, or of a diverse ratio of the

same thing, the concepts are diverse. From which it is shown also that concepts

signify naturally: because it is no less natural that what is diverse by its own nature

be diverse among all, than that what is the same by its own nature be the same.

It is certain, second, that writing signifies the word by convention: which is proved

evidently, because writings were invented by men, and diverse ones are applied by

the same men at will to signify diverse words: therefore they signify words by the

free imposition of men.

The difficulty of the question therefore consists in the signification of words

and in their mode of signifying. In the signification, indeed: Whether words signify

not only things, but also the concepts which we form of the same things. In the mode of sig‐

nifying, also: Whether they signify things naturally or by convention.

Ii ij

[p. 500]

And the first opinion is that of certain moderns, which asserts that words signify only things; concepts, however, they do not signify, but express. Which they prove thus: A word signifies that for which it supposits in a proposition; but words do not supposit for concepts, but for things: therefore they do not signify concepts, but things. The minor is proved, first, from Aristotle, Sophistical Refutations 1, ch. 1, where he asserts: Since we cannot bring the things about which we dispute into the schools, we use words in place of things; just as those who play use counters in place of money: therefore Aristotle understands that words supposit for things alone. It is proved, second: because in this proposition, Man disputes, the word man does not supposit for the concept of man, but for man himself, of whom disputing is verified, and not of the concept.

Now, that words express concepts they explain thus: words were invented not only so that they might be put in a proposition in place of things, but also so that through them we might manifest to others our internal concepts, which cannot become known to them by themselves: therefore words are as it were manifestative and declarative of concepts; but to declare and to express are the same: and therefore, although words do not signify concepts, they are nevertheless properly said to express them.

5 The second opinion holds that words signify not only things, but also concepts: so St. Thomas expressly, On Power, q. 8, a. 1, and 1 p., q. 27, a. 1, whom almost all the interpreters of Aristotle follow on the present chapter; and Aristotle himself expressly teaches it in these words: Those things, therefore, which are in the voice are signs of the passions which are in the soul, etc.; by passion of the soul meaning the concepts themselves, and not the things conceived, as the moderns would have it: because passions of the soul signify its acts remaining in it, which are the concepts, not the things understood: for the things are nothing of the soul itself, nor do they remain in it, but are only objects of its act, existing outside it: and he asserts that words are marks of them, that is, signs: therefore he holds that they signify them. And so it is to be held.

But in order that we may explain and prove it at the same time, it should be noted that the sign is divided by four divisions.

The first division is: One sign is Proper, another improper. The proper sign has two conditions. The first, that it make us come into the cognition of some thing distinct from itself, which it is said to signify. The second, that it be instituted, by nature itself or by the will of men, to signify such a thing. Sighs and groans have both conditions, and therefore they are proper natural signs of some internal affection. But for lack of the first condition, words that signify no thing outside themselves are not proper signs, but quite improper ones: as blictri,

[p. 501]

and the like. But for want of the second condition, laughter is not a sign of rationality, although rationality is known by us through it: because it is not instituted by nature to signify rationality, although rationality can be known demonstratively by us through it.

By the second division the proper sign, the improper being left aside, is divided into the sign Natural, By Convention, and From Custom. Natural is that which is instituted by nature to signify some thing, as groaning. By convention: that which is instituted by the will of men, as the word man to signify man. From custom, that which custom brings about, so that through one thing we understand another which it is commonly ordered to signify: as napkins laid out are signs of a meal.

The third division of the sign is into Internal and External. Internal is that which remains within our soul, as a concept; external, that which is perceived through the external senses, such as sight and hearing: and such signs are words and writings. This sign alone St. Augustine described in the book On Christian Doctrine, ch. 1, in these words: A sign is a thing which, besides the species that it impresses on the senses, makes something other than itself come into cognition.

The fourth division of the sign is: one sign is Manifestative only, another Manifestative and Suppositive at once. Manifestative only is that which signifies or represents some thing distinct from itself, for which it is not substituted, or does not supposit, in a proposition: as the sound of the bell is a sign of the lecture to come, but is not put for it in a proposition. Manifestative and suppositive at once is that which not only signifies a thing but is put for it: as this word man is put in a proposition for the man whom it signifies.

6 Second, it should be noted that the significate can be twofold, Quo and Quod. The significate Quod is the name given to that thing which the sign is ordered to signify. The significate Quo is the name given to the medium by which it signifies it. Moreover, one significate is Proximate, another Remote and as it were ultimate. And according to this doctrine it is to be understood in what way words signify things and concepts. For they signify concepts immediately indeed, not as quod, but only as quo: because by means of the concepts which we form of things we signify those things through words; but things they signify also immediately as quod, yet as it were remotely and ultimately, compared with the significate quo, namely the concept. Moreover, words are signs of concepts that are significative only, not suppositive; but of things they are significative and suppositive at once: because in a proposition they supposit for things, and not for concepts.

These things supposed, the opinion of Aristotle, of St. Thomas, and our own is set out in two conclusions.

I i iij

[p. 502]

The first is: Words signify concepts immediately, and as quo, and therefore less principally; but things immediately indeed, as Quod, and therefore principally, but with respect to the concepts as it were remotely and ultimately; and both concepts and things by convention.

The first part is proved by this argument: Many words have been imposed to signify universal natures, as man and animal; but things are not universal as they exist outside, but as abstracted and known by us through common concepts: therefore they are not signified by words except by means of the common concepts which we form of them. And consequently, words signify concepts immediately, as quo, and therefore less principally; and by means of these, things ultimately and principally. This last consequence is proved: because concepts are nothing but certain media by which the things are signified which they are ordered to signify.

The second part, that words signify things and concepts by convention, is evident: because they do not have their signification from nature, but are certain sounds, improperly signifying nothing besides themselves and the speaker; but they have been ordered by men to signify other things by means of concepts: therefore they signify by convention. This is gathered from the words of sacred Scripture, Gen. 2: Therefore the Lord God, having formed out of the ground all the living creatures of the earth and all the birds of the air, brought them to Adam to see what he would call them: for whatever Adam called a living creature, that is its name.

But what we say of words is to be understood only of those which are articulate, that is, formed by the tongue, teeth, and palate: for only these do men use to signify concepts and things, and therefore they are said to signify by convention. But inarticulate ones, such as the sounds of brute animals, and also our groans and sighs, signify some internal affection naturally, unless perhaps we express it by an articulate word: for then it would at once be signified by that word by convention, because different nations sometimes use different articulate words for this purpose of signifying an internal affection.

To the argument of the other opinion: The major is to be distinguished. For a sign that is significative only, and not suppositive, does not signify that for which it supposits, but that for which it does not supposit; whereas a sign that is significative and suppositive at once signifies only that for which it supposits. And therefore it is not universally true that words signify only that for which they supposit: because, although with respect to things they are signs significative and suppositive at once, yet with respect to concepts they are only significative: whence they can signify concepts although they do not supposit

[p. 503]

for them in a proposition. And in this sense is to be understood the testimony of Aristotle, who speaks of words as they are signs of things significative and suppositive at once: this, however, does not exclude that they can also signify concepts, as media, although they do not supposit for them.

## CHAPTER II

On the Noun.

TEXT OF ARISTOTLE. A noun, then, is a word significative by convention, without time, no part of which is

significative when separated.

B R I E F E X P O S I T I O N O F T H E T E X T.

he intent of this chapter is to explain the nature of the noun,

T         which Aristotle treats as an actual part of the enunciation, and

before the verb, as being simpler: for the verb signifies not only some thing but also action with time, whereas the noun signifies only a thing; or because the noun is as it were the matter of the proposition, and therefore its first foundation, while the verb is as it were its form. This chapter, moreover, needs no division, because Aristotle does nothing else in it than assign the definition of the noun and explain each of its particles.

The definition of the noun runs thus: A noun is a word significative by convention, without time, no part of which is significative when separated. Word is put in this definition in place of the genus, and is taken only for the articulate word uttered by the human instruments, namely the tongue, teeth, palate, and the rest; which the same Aristotle defined thus in On the Soul 2, text 90: A word is a sound uttered from the mouth of an animal with a certain imagination. Hence by word are excluded the inarticulate sounds of brute animals, and also the sounds of instruments, which are called voices in another, rather imperfect way. It is also called significative, so that human words which are articulate but nevertheless signify nothing, such as blictri, may be excluded. By convention, so that all natural signs may be excluded. Without time, so that the verb, which signifies with time, may be excluded. What it is to signify without time, however, will be clear from the following chapter, in which it is explained what it is to signify with time. No part of which is significative when separated: in distinction from speech, whose parts signify per se when separated: as the parts

I i iiij

[p. 504]

of this speech, white man. He proves this particle, finally, by this argument: If the parts of any noun signified when separated, most of all would the parts of a composite noun, as the parts of this noun equiferus [wild horse]: but its parts, when separated, signify nothing: therefore neither will the separated parts of any noun signify. The major is evident, because, since a composite noun often contains several simple nouns as parts, there was greater reason in it for its parts to signify when separated than in a simple noun, whose parts are nothing but syllables and letters. The minor he proves: because the parts of this noun equiferus, separated from it, if they are taken as its parts, retain no signification: since equiferus does not signify a fierce horse, but another animal different from it. Finally, by the ratio of noun he excludes infinite nouns, as non-man, non-lion: because they do not have a determinate signification, but are said of all things except the thing signified by the noun on which the negation falls, as Non-man is said of all things except man. But a true noun must signify something determinate. He also excludes the oblique cases, as hominis [of a man] and hominem [man, accusative]: because they are judged not so much nouns as certain derivations from the direct noun itself.

## QUESTION I

Whether the noun is rightly defined through word.

T     he reason for doubting is: because the noun and the verb are parts of

the proposition; but in the mind and in writing there are propositions no less than in words: therefore there will also be nouns and verbs there: if, then, the noun is defined through word, the definition will be deficient, not comprehending all nouns.

On the manner of understanding this definition, the first opinion is that of the Louvain commentators on the present chapter, who assert that it can be accommodated to mental and written nouns, a few things being changed: to mental ones, indeed, by changing two particles, namely word and by convention; to written ones, by changing word alone; and that it is therefore not deficient, because, although it does not comprehend all nouns as it stands, it can nevertheless comprehend them all by accommodation.

This opinion, however, cannot be sustained: because, since the definition is as it were an indivisible term of the definitum, under which its whole essence must be contained, if any particle whatever is changed or added the whole definition is changed: therefore, if this definition cannot fit all nouns unless some particles are taken away, it follows

[p. 505]

that it cannot fit them, but is deficient. The consequence is proved: because, when those particles are taken away, it is not the same definition, but another: therefore it is impossible that this definition should fit all nouns; whence it will be judged deficient if it can fit them only with the removal of those particles.

Our view, therefore, is that true nouns are found, simply speaking, only in words; but in the mind there are only the concepts of the things signified by the nouns, which are rather called mental terms, and of which the mental proposition is composed. In writings, on the other hand, nouns are found only by derivation from words, of which they are as it were supplements, so that we may deal with those who are absent. Whence it follows that the noun was rightly defined by Aristotle through word.

This is proved by the testimony of Aristotle, ch. 2 of the Antepredicaments, where, defining equivocals, he says: They are those whose name is common, but the ratio of the substance accommodated to the name is different. But by the ratio of the substance, according to the common exposition of all, the concept is understood: therefore Aristotle holds that the name is distinguished from the concept, and that therefore the concept is not a name, but that names are found in words alone. The consequence is proved: because where the name is common, he asserts that the concept is different.

It is proved also by reason: Because before Adam imposed names on things, they were held to be nameless, even if he had proper concepts of them; and as soon as he imposed names on them, God said: Whatever Adam called a living creature, that is its name. As if to say that names then first began. And we too, as long as we do not have a proper word imposed to signify some thing, say that such a thing is nameless, although we have its proper concept in the mind. From which it follows that in the mind there are not nouns but concepts, which are called mental terms, of which the mental composition is composed; and that the ratio of term is more universal than noun and verb, of which alone the vocal proposition is properly and simply composed; but in writing nouns and verbs are found only through a certain analogy to the word signified by it: for writings are as it were nouns and verbs depicted. It is not necessary, therefore, to take particles away from Aristotle’s definition in order that it be accommodated to concepts and writings, because it cannot properly fit them either; and therefore he rightly defined the noun through word.

To the argument proposed for the reason for doubting: Granting the major and the minor, the consequence is to be denied: because the proposition in common is not composed of noun and verb, but of terms

[p. 506]

whose ratio is more universal; but only the vocal proposition is composed of noun and verb. Whence it does not follow that true nouns and verbs are found wherever a proposition is found, but only that terms are found of which it is composed: which in the mental proposition are the concepts of the extremes and of the copula, and in the written one nouns and verbs depicted; and therefore not such simply, but in a certain respect.

## QUESTION II

Whether the noun is defined through word as through a true genus.

W        ord can be considered in two ways. First, Materially, as it denotes

only an articulate sound made by the human instruments. Second, Formally, as significative, from which it has it that it is a noun or a verb. And considered in the first way, it stands as the subject of that same signification, common to the noun and the verb: just as wood is a common subject with respect to a chair and a door, able to receive the artificial form of both. But if it is considered as significative, it is a true genus with respect to the noun and the verb. The question, then, is whether the noun is defined through word taken materially, as through a subject, as a statue is defined through wood; or rather through word taken formally, as significative, as through a true genus: so that significative word is the genus of this definition, and the remaining particles are differences.

And the first opinion holds that the noun is not defined through word as through a subject, but through significative word, as through a true genus common to the noun and the verb. So Nifo, Lemosius, and Psellus, on the present chapter; and it is proved: Because any thing whatever is to be defined by a quidditative definition, if that can be done, since this is the best mode of defining; but if significative is posited as a true genus, the definition of the noun will be quidditative, whereas if word alone is posited as a subject it will not be quidditative, since the subject is not the genus of an accident but outside its quiddity: therefore the noun as defined by Aristotle ought to be understood in the first way rather than in the second.

The second opinion is that of St. Thomas and Ammonius, on the present chapter: that the noun is not defined by Aristotle through significative word as through a true genus, but through word alone, as through a subject, put in the place of the genus. And this is the more probable; its chief foundation is gathered from Aristotle, Metaph. 8, text 6, where

[p. 507]

he says that the proper mode of defining artificial things is through the subject in

place of the genus, and through the artificial form in place of the difference: as, if you wish

to define a house, you will say that it is stones and timbers so put together. And

St. Thomas, in the opuscule On Being and Essence, ch. 7, says that not only artificial

things but also all accidents are better defined through the subject in place of the genus

than through a true genus. And the reason for this is manifest: because the essence

of an accident and its mode of being are taken from its order to the subject:

therefore both become better known through the subject; and since the defini‐

tion is handed down for this end, that through it we may know the nature of the

definitum, the better mode of defining accidents will be through the subject, put

in place of the genus, rather than through the true genus, which becomes known

through that same subject. But the noun and the verb are certain artificial acci‐

dents, made by the intellect and signified in the concrete: therefore they are bet‐

ter defined through word, as through a subject, than through significative word,

as through a true genus; and so they are to be judged to have been defined by

Aristotle.

To the argument of the other opinion: The major is to be distinguished. For if

the thing that is defined is a substance, it is to be defined quidditatively through

genus and difference, if that can be done; but if it is an accident, especially an ar‐

tificial one and signified in the concrete, the more natural mode, and that

through which its essence will be more clearly explained, will be to define it

through the subject in place of the genus: because its true genus and its true dif‐

ference are to be known through the subject with respect to which they are tak‐

en, rather than through themselves; and consequently so are its quiddity and es‐

sence, for the knowing of which a definition is per se ordered.

## QUESTION III

Whether the noun truly signifies by convention, as is said in the definition.

10

C     oncerning the mode of signifying of Words, St. Thomas reports three opin‐

ions in the commentary on this chapter. The first was that of those who

held that they are natural signs of things, as we say of concepts: which Dexippus, bk.

1 of the Questions on the Categories, ch. 6, attributes to Pythagoras and his disci‐

ples; and it seems also to have been that of Heraclitus and Cratylus. And it is

proved by this argument: Because to those to whom nature has given a faculty, or

power, for exercising some act, it consequently gives natural instruments by

which they can exercise it: as it gave man the faculty of walking, and therefore

gave him feet so fashioned that he can walk with them; but the faculty of speak‐

ing is natural: therefore nature gave man, together with

[p. 508]

it, natural instruments through which he might speak; but these instruments are words, not bare ones (otherwise brute animals too could speak), but articulate and significative ones, just as to brute animals nature gave sounds signifying naturally, by which they might manifest their internal affections: therefore significative words were given by nature to men, by which they might manifest to others the internal concepts of the mind. From which it evidently follows that their signification is natural, and not from the imposition of men: because whatever is granted by nature is natural.

The second opinion is diametrically opposed, asserting that the signification of words not only is not from nature, but proceeds from the good pleasure of men in such a way that anyone may at his discretion use these names already imposed, or devise other new ones and impose them for signifying, and use them in speaking as he pleases, and afterward, leaving these, impose other new ones. This seems to have been held by a certain Hermogenes, a Philosopher older than Plato and Aristotle, as Plato himself testifies in the dialogue Cratylus.

The reason for this view is: because, if the signification of words depends on the free will of men, it can be changed at discretion; so that words imposed today for signifying may tomorrow signify nothing any longer, or be changed from their first signification and be imposed anew to signify other different things, and therefore be said to fall away from their signification; from which no inconvenience follows.

The third opinion is midway between these extremes, granting that words do not signify naturally, but from the imposition of men; yet that this imposition is not so free that anyone may at his discretion use these or those words and impose them anew for signifying, but is congruent with the natures of the things they are imposed to signify: so that to each thing, according to its proper nature, such names are accommodated. And so the free imposition of men had a certain discerning consideration accompanying or preceding it, through which the imposer, knowing the natures of things, accommodated to them proper names by which they might be congruently signified; and such an imposition lasts perpetually, and has been so inviolably received by all that no one may change it at his discretion or introduce new impositions of words. This view has been followed by the weightiest Philosophers: Plato in the place cited above; Aristotle in these chapters; Cicero, bk. 1 of the Academic Questions; Quintilian, bk. 8 of the Institutes, ch. 6; St. Thomas; Albert the Great, with the other expositors of this chapter. And this is true and to be held.

[p. 509]

11 In order to explain and prove it at the same time, it should be noted that things are of two different kinds. For some are Natural, to which it is certain that names were accommodated, at God’s direction, by our first parent, endowed with divine wisdom, through which he perfectly knew the nature of each thing, as these words of Gen. 2 show: Therefore the Lord God, having formed out of the ground all the living creatures of the earth and all the birds of the air, brought them to Adam to see what he would call them: for whatever Adam called a living creature, that is its name. As if God were saying that this universal imposition, made by his commission, is perpetual in such a way that it is never altogether, or anywhere, to be changed by anyone, although names are different according to the diversity of nations and languages; in which also it is evident that no one has ever been permitted to change the imposition at his discretion. Others are Artificial things, to which also names have been accommodated by men endowed with art, who through it perfectly know their condition, names agreeing with that condition: that is, such that their signification is taken either from the way in which they are made, or from some property of theirs, or from the use to which they are ordered by art.

This is to be understood as true for the most part: for it sometimes happens that no such likeness, at least none known to us, is preserved in the imposition of a name. And this doctrine at once explains and proves the truth of the common view, which we follow.

But to the argument of the first opinion: Granting the major, the minor is to be denied, namely that words are the instruments of the natural faculty of speaking; rather, the instruments of this faculty are the tongue, teeth, and palate, by which those same words are formed; and once formed they are imposed for signifying, so that they may be media by which a man may express his own concepts to others. Wherefore, although on the part of the sound words are natural, yet on the part of the signification they come about through art or science: just as a chair is natural on the part of the wood, but artificial on the part of the form, made through art, and therefore is called simply artificial; so too nouns and verbs are to be called artificial.

But the argument of the second opinion is solved by the doctrine handed down: because, although the imposition of words for signifying is free, it is nevertheless conformed to the natures of things, and therefore not made by just anyone, but by wise men who, perfectly knowing their natures, accommodated to them such names as were congruent with them; whence neither can the signification of names be varied at discretion, nor can names fall away from it.

[p. 510]

Q U E S T I O N I V.

Whether it is true that the parts of a noun, when separated, are not significative.

A      ristotle proved this particle of the definition from a composite noun, whose

parts when separated, he says, are not significative as they are its parts, even though they are whole nouns: therefore much less will the parts of a simple noun be significative when separated, since they are not whole nouns but syllables and letters. But this reasoning is worth nothing: therefore it is not proved by it that the parts of a noun when separated are not significative; nor will this be true. The antecedent is proved: Because the parts of a composite noun are whole nouns, or a whole noun and a verb, as is plain in this noun agricola [farmer]; and when separated they retain the same signification through which they composed the noun: therefore the parts of a composite noun when separated are significative even as its parts, or according to the signification of the whole. The minor is proved: for this noun ager [field] and this verb colo [I till] composed the noun agricola through their proper significations, namely, ager signifying a field and colo the action of tilling: whence agricola signifies one tilling a field; and they retain this same signification when separated from the composition, as is well known: therefore they truly signify according to the earlier signification, or as they are its parts. Wherefore neither does Aristotle’s reasoning prove that the parts of a noun do not signify when separated, nor can it be true, at least in a composite noun.

It is proved second: Because if simple nouns fell away from their proper signification and were imposed to signify different things, the composite noun too would fall away from its signification: therefore its signification depends on the proper significations of the parts; but the parts when separated retain their proper significations: therefore when separated they will signify according to the signification of the whole. For the solution of this question it should be noted that a composite noun is composed of whole nouns, or of a noun and a verb, in such a way that from their several and different significations there results a certain third, indivisible signification of that composite noun; which signification cannot be preserved in those same parts once separated. In which respect the composite noun is like a natural living composite made of soul and body, not any body whatever but a heterogeneous one, that is, one having parts of different ratio, as the arm, the head, and the feet: for no noun is composed of many nouns signifying the same thing, as from gladius [sword],

[p. 511]

and ensis [sword], but of nouns signifying different things: wherefore from these different significations there results a third signification of the whole, different from the parts.
