this most certain presupposition it will not be difficult to understand that

both of Aristotle’s assertions are true. The first, indeed, that the universal

negative de contingenti is not converted simply. For example: It is contin‐

gent that no man is white is not converted into this, It is contingent that

nothing white is a man; because it includes these two propositions de possi‐

bili: That no man is white is possible, and It is possible that every man is

white; but this second is not converted simply, as is manifest of itself; there‐

fore neither can the universal negative that includes it be converted simply.

That the second rule, on the conversion of the particular negative, is true

is proved in this way: The particular negative proposition, on account of the

signification of the mode, infers the affirmative, as we proved; therefore this

is a good consequence: It is contingent that some man is not white; therefore

it is contingent that some man is white. From this there follows, by the sim‐

ple conversion already handed down: therefore it is contingent that some‐

thing white is a man; and from this there follows also, on account of the sig‐

nification of the mode, the negative, namely, It is contingent that something

white is not a man, which is the converse of the particular negative taken at

the beginning; therefore it is evidently proved that it is to be converted sim‐

ply. But in order that this rule may be true, the propositions have to be taken

with the existence of the extremes supposed, as we said in the case of propo‐

sitions de possibili and de necesse; otherwise the antecedent will be true

[p. 571]

and the consequent false, as in this example: It is contingent that a man is not laughing; therefore it is contingent that something laughing is not a man; and also: It is contingent that a man is not a grammarian; therefore it is contingent that a grammarian is not a man. But supposing the existence of the extremes, namely of laughter and of man, or of grammar and of man, just as the consequent is false, so is the antecedent; for when man and grammar exist, it is not contingent that a grammarian is a man, but necessary by supposition: for if grammar is in the nature of things, it cannot be except in a man, or cannot not be in a man; therefore it is necessary that it be in a man; wherefore it will be false that it is contingent that a grammarian is a man.

18 But against this conversion of the particular negative there is a rather difficult argument. For Aristotle said that the particular negative de inesse is not converted simply for this reason, that the antecedent is true and the consequent false; and this because the argument is made from a term not distributed to a term distributed, on the part of the subject of the proposition to be converted, as is plain in this: Some animal is not a man; therefore some man is not an animal. For animal is not distributed in the antecedent, and yet it is distributed in the consequent, by reason of the negation falling upon it. But the same defect occurs in the conversion of the particular negative de contingenti; therefore it will be false that it is converted. And this rule will be contrary to the one that denies that the particular negative de inesse is converted. The minor is proved: because when we proceed thus, It is contingent that some man is not white; therefore it is contingent that something white is not a man, man, which is the subject in the antecedent, is not distributed, but is only affected by a particular sign; and yet it is distributed in the consequent, by reason of the negation falling upon it; therefore on its part such a conversion will be an argument from a term not distributed to a term distributed, like the conversion of the particular negative de inesse; and consequently it will be faulty and null, as that one is.

The reply is by distinguishing the minor: that in the conversion of the negative de contingenti an argument is made from the non-distributed to the distributed, because it is made in a different way than in the proposition de inesse; for in the latter it is made on the part of the whole and entire extreme, but in the modal de contingenti only on the part of a partial extreme, while on the other side the extreme nevertheless remains without distribution; for the extreme of a modal proposition is the dictum; and since a negative proposition of the contingent mode also contains the affirmative, its dictum has two parts;

[p. 572]

one negated and the other affirmed, and therefore one distributed and the other without distribution. For example, when we proceed thus, in the same argument adduced as an example: It is contingent that some man is not white; therefore it is contingent that something white is not a man: this negative consequent also contains the affirmative, namely, It is contingent that something white is a man, in which it is plain that man is not distributed, although it is distributed in the other, negative part of the same dictum; and from the affirmative there follows in turn the other, negative part, namely, It is contingent that something white is not a man, which is the converse of that same particular negative. Whence it follows that argumentation from the non-distributed to the distributed, on the part of a partial extreme that remains without distribution in the other, affirmative part of the same, does not impede conversion nor render it faulty.

But against this solution there is a still more difficult argument: Because from it it follows that the universal negative of the same contingent mode is converted simply, against the other rule denying its conversion. That this follows is proved: because the universal negative cannot be converted simply only for this reason, that it includes the universal affirmative, which is not convertible simply; but the universal affirmative cannot be converted simply only for this reason, that such a conversion would be an argument from the non-distributed to the distributed on the part of its predicate, which, since it is not distributed in it, is distributed in the converse, as is plain when we proceed thus: It is contingent that every man is white; therefore it is contingent that everything white is a man. But it is certain that the universal affirmative is only part of the dictum of the universal negative that includes it, and therefore only its partial extreme; therefore, if it does not render the conversion faulty that an argument is made in it from the non-distributed to the distributed on the part of a partial extreme, as was said in the conversion of the particular negative, then neither is the conversion of the universal negative rendered faulty. The reply is that the reason is different in the universal negative, which includes the universal affirmative, and in the particular negative: for in the conversion of the latter there are two things. First, that the same term which is not distributed in the subject of the antecedent is not distributed in both parts of the consequent, but in one only, while in the other it remains without distribution, since it is a particular affirmative.

The second is that the same affirmative part is converted simply, and through such a conversion the particular negative is evidently gathered from it, which is the converse of the particular negative assumed at the beginning for conversion; and therefore from

[p. 573]

first to last it follows evidently that the particular negative is converted. But in the universal affirmative, included in the universal negative, neither of these is found. Not the first: because when we convert it, the argument is made from the non-distributed to the distributed in such a way that the term which is not distributed in the antecedent is always distributed in the consequent; that is, both in the converse affirmative, as is plain, since it is universal, and in the universal negative which it includes, all of whose terms are plainly distributed. Therefore the argumentation is in every respect from the non-distributed to the distributed, and more is inferred in the consequent than is contained in the antecedent. But neither is the second found: because the universal affirmative into which it is converted does not include a convertible proposition from which the converse of the universal negative could be deduced, but only the universal negative, which is not convertible, or about which the dispute is whether it is converted; wherefore we cannot use its conversion in the same argumentation, as we can use the conversion of the particular affirmative included in the other, particular negative; and therefore we can never gather, from the conversion of the universal affirmative which it includes, the universal negative that would be the converse of the other universal negative whose conversion is in question. From these two differences, then, as from an evident sign, we gather that the particular negative proposition virtually contains its converse, since it is deduced from it through evident consequences, and therefore that it can be converted, as Aristotle taught; but that the universal negative in no way contains its converse, since it cannot be deduced from it, but only the universal affirmative, which is an impediment to it, so that it cannot be converted simply.

And if, finally, it is said that it follows from this that the universal negative can at least be converted into part, since the universal affirmative which it includes, and on account of which alone it cannot be converted, is converted into a particular (which nevertheless seems to be against the rule of Aristotle denying that it is converted in any way), I reply: It must necessarily be granted that the universal negative is converted into a particular, because the argument convinces of it; because Aristotle never denied this; because there is no foundation on account of which it could be denied. He denied only that it is converted as its own nature demands, that is, by simple conversion, as it is converted in the other modes and in propositions de inesse. And this concerning the conversion of propositions of the contingent mode.

[p. 574]

Single Note.

On the Conversion of Propositions de Possibili and de Impossibili.

12

L     astly, it should be noted that, concerning the conversion of propositions de possibili

and de impossibili, Aristotle did not speak expressly and in particular of them,

because they are converted in the same modes, according to sense and equipol‐

lence, as propositions de necesse, although they sometimes appear different from

them, especially propositions de impossibili. And as for propositions de possibili,

the matter is manifest, since they are of the contingent improperly taken, of which

we said above that they can be converted in the same way as propositions de

necesse. But as for propositions de impossibili, it will be easily understood if we

consider that propositions of an affirmed de impossibili are equipollent to propo‐

sitions de necesse having the opposite dictum: as this proposition, It is impossible

that some man is a horse, is equipollent to this, It is necessary that no man be a

horse; wherefore it is to be converted as that one is; and so of the others of the af‐

firmed de impossibili mode, for of these alone Aristotle speaks in these conver‐

sions, as we said. It need only be repeated in this part that this is always under‐

stood with the existence of the extremes supposed.

## CHAPTER IIII

## TEXT OF ARISTOTLE

These things having been determined, let us now say through what things, and when, and

how every syllogism comes about, etc.

B R I E F E X P O S I T I O N O F T H E T E X T.

he intent of Aristotle in the present chapter is to explain the na22

T            ture and ratio of the first figure. And it is divided into two parts. In the

first he explains the universal moods in which syllogisms can be made,

and from them he rejects all the other, useless ones that seem similar to

them. In the second he explains two other, particular useful moods, and from

them he likewise rejects as useless all the others that can be made in a similar

disposition.

He explains the universal moods in these words: When three terms are so related

that the last is in the whole middle, and the middle is or is not in the whole first, there must be

a syllogism of the extremes, etc. By the middle term he understands the one that is tak‐

en twice in the premises. By the last term, the minor extreme

[p. 575]

and by the first, the major extreme. The sense of his words, then, is this: When three terms are so disposed that the middle is subjected universally to the major extreme in the first proposition, and in the second the minor extreme is subjected universally to the middle, there comes about, affirmatively, a syllogism in the first mood, which is called Barbara, because it consists of three affirmative propositions; and it is this: Every animal is a substance; every man is an animal; therefore every man is a substance. Negatively, in the second mood, which is called Celarent, because it consists of an affirmative minor and of a negative major and conclusion; and it is constructed thus: No animal is a stone; every man is an animal; therefore no man is a stone. But however else the middle and the extremes are disposed in universal propositions, they produce useless and faulty moods, in which universal propositions, affirmative as well as negative, follow indifferently; or, as others say, terms are given in which “all” follows and also terms in which “none” follows; and the consequences are proved to be faulty, for example by two contradictories being given true at the same time. And so from the universal disposition of the terms only the two moods produced result as useful, in which perfect syllogisms are made. This is proved evidently: because in the first, said of all holds, that is, the predicate of the major, which is said universally of the subject in the major, is necessarily said of something contained and taken under it in the conclusion. In the second, said of none holds: for the predicate of the major is denied universally of its subject, and therefore it is also necessarily denied of the subject of the minor in the conclusion.

In the second part of the chapter he explains two other useful moods of the same figure, which he calls particular, because one of the premises is particular and the other universal. If, then, he says, each premise is particular, all the moods become useless. But if one is particular and the other universal: either the major is universal, in which the major extreme is said universally of the middle, and the minor particular, in which the middle is said of the minor extreme in a particular mode, and there comes about the third mood of perfect syllogism, which is called Darij, because it consists of a universal affirmative major and of a minor and conclusion that are particular and also affirmative. And this mood is such: Every rational animal is risible; some man is a rational animal; therefore some man is risible. Or if the major is a universal negative, in which the major extreme is denied universally of the middle, and the minor a particular affirmative, in which the middle is said of

[p. 576]

the minor extreme in a particular mode, there comes about the fourth useful mood of the first figure, which is called Ferio; and it is this: No animal is a stone; some man is an animal; therefore some man is not a stone. That these two syllogisms are perfect is evident from the two other, prior ones, from which they differ only on the part of the minor proposition, which in those is universal and in these particular; and consequently their conclusions are particular. Since, then, their particular propositions are contained under the universals of the others, if those are evident and in them said of all and said of none hold, these will have altogether the same. But the other moods in which a universal and a particular premise can be disposed are useless, and in them terms are given in which “all” follows and in which “none” follows. Thus far Aristotle.

What a figure is, and how many kinds, and what a mood is, is explained.

T    he figure of syllogisms is nothing other than the due disposition of three terms, that is,

of the middle and the extremes, according to the due mode of predication and subjection. It is so called by metaphor, from its likeness to a geometrical figure: for just as the latter results from lines terminated by points and so disposed, in the same way the syllogistic figure results from propositions, which are as it were lines terminated by extreme points, that is, by the subject and the predicate, which are called the terms of propositions because they are their extremes.

The figure is threefold: because the middle and the extremes can be disposed in only three ways. For either the middle is the subject in the first and the predicate in the second, and this is called the first figure, for three reasons. First, because the middle in this disposition not only has the ratio of a middle, in that the extremes are conjoined through it, but also the proper position due to a middle, since it is placed between the extremes, so as to be the subject of one and the predicate of the other. Second, because in this figure every kind of proposition is concluded, namely the universal affirmative, the universal negative, the particular affirmative, and the particular negative. Third, because the others are derived from this figure: for either the middle is the predicate of both premises, and so it is the second figure; or it is the subject of both, and so it is the third. The reason for this order is quite fitting: because the predicate is nobler than the subject, and therefore the middle has a nobler ratio and place, and consequently the disposition itself in which it is always the predicate is nobler than that in which it is always the subject; and

therefore

[p. 577]

therefore that disposition rightly constitutes the Second figure, and this one the Third.

A mood is the due disposition of the premises according to due quality and quantity, that is, according to the ratio of universal and particular, in which the quantity of a proposition consists, and according to affirmation and negation, in which its quality consists.

25 Of the first, then, only four moods have been enumerated, namely two universal and two particular, because only in these four moods can the premises be disposed in the due manner so that the conclusion is evidently inferred from them; but all the other moods are useless, as has been said.

S E C O N D D O U B T.

Whether, besides the three figures enumerated by Aristotle, a fourth is to be added.

T     he first opinion holds that a fourth is to be added; they attribute it to

Galen, the prince of physicians. And it is proved by this argument: A figure is the due disposition of the middle and the extremes according to due subjection and predication; but besides the three modes in which they are disposed by Aristotle, they can be disposed in a fourth mode different from them; therefore from such a disposition a different figure will be produced, which is the fourth. The minor is proved: because the disposition of the first figure is that in which the middle is the subject of the major and the predicate of the minor; the disposition of the second, that in which the middle is the predicate of each premise; and the disposition of the third, that in which the middle is the subject of each; but they can also be disposed in a fourth mode, so that the middle is the predicate of the major and the subject of the minor, namely in such a way that from such a disposition the conclusion follows no less evidently than from the three prior ones; therefore from such a disposition there will result a fourth figure, distinct from the three. The minor is proved by this example: Everything risible is a man; every man is a rational animal; therefore every rational animal is risible.

26 The common consensus of the whole school, however, posits only three figures with Aristotle. And so we must hold; and it is proved by this reason: Because a figure, properly speaking, is as it were the form of the syllogism, in which the propositions are formally disposed, that is, according to the natural mode and that due to their form. But the due mode consists in this, that what stands as form be the predicate, and what stands as matter be the subject; but only in three modes can propositions be disposed

Oo

[p. 578]

in this way; therefore there will be only the three figures enumerated by Aristotle.

The minor I prove thus: They cannot be disposed in that fourth mode unless in

the major that which truly stands as matter is predicated, and that which stands as

form is subjected; but this disposition is against the nature and form of the propo‐

sition, as the same example assigned proves; therefore no proper figure can result

from that disposition; wherefore we rarely or never use such a disposition of syllo‐

gisms in disputations. Such a disposition, then, if it can have anything like a figure,

is something imperfect, and in a certain way akin to the disposition of the first fig‐

ure, to which it ought to be reduced. To the argument: the minor must be distin‐

guished, because they can be disposed, but not in the due manner for producing a

figure, as has been proved; and therefore such a disposition does not produce a

distinct figure, but on account of a certain likeness it is reduced to the first.

27 And if someone objects from the opposite side that the first alone suffices,

since every kind of proposition is inferred through it, and therefore that the sec‐

ond and third ought not to have been added, I reply that the second and third are

necessary: because, although every kind of proposition can be concluded in the

first, we cannot nevertheless always use it in disputations, because a consequence

cannot always be constructed so manifest that it appears evident to all; but it is

necessary often to use others, less evident, so that through them we may arrive at

the more evident ones of the first figure. Moreover, they are necessary so that we

may have an abundance of syllogisms for conducting disputations, which we

should not have through the first figure alone.

C H A P T E R V.

## TEXT OF ARISTOTLE

But when the same belongs to all of one and to none of the other, or to all of each, or to none,

such a figure I call the second.

B R I E F E X P O S I T I O N O F T H E T E X T.

he intent of Aristotle in the present chapter is to explain the na28

T          ture of the second figure. And it is divided into two parts. In the first he

explains the disposition of the second figure; in the second he reviews

all the useful moods of syllogizing in it, the useless ones having been

refuted.

The second figure is produced (says Aristotle) when they are so disposed

[p. 579]

the premises, that the middle is a universal predicate of the extremes in each, so that it is affirmed in one and denied in the other; indifferently, indeed, because whether the major is negative or the minor, provided that both are not affirmative or negative, the disposition is good, as is shown by these two examples: No stone is an animal; every man is an animal; therefore no man is a stone; and again: Every man is a living thing; no stone is a living thing; therefore no stone is a man. Therefore the middle in this figure, says Aristotle, is that which belongs to all or to none of the extremes; and the extremes are those to which the middle belongs. And to distinguish the two, he asserts that the major extreme is the one placed next to the middle; and he says it is placed next to the middle because, just as the middle is the predicate in the premises, so is the major extreme in the conclusion; therefore it is similar to the middle. The minor extreme, however, he says stands farther from the middle, because, since the middle is always the predicate, the minor extreme is always the subject. Whence (he says) it follows that the middle is placed as it were outside, or beyond, in respect of the extremes, because it is always predicated and never subjected; and also that it is first in position, because, since it is always the predicate, it holds the principal place in this figure, while each extreme is subjected in the premises. He says that no perfect syllogism is made in this figure: because a perfect syllogism is that which needs nothing in order to appear necessary; but all the syllogisms of this figure need reduction to syllogisms of the first; therefore none of them is perfect.

29 In the second part of the chapter he enumerates the useful moods of this figure and rejects the useless ones. He says, then: When the middle belongs to all of the one and to none of the other, there comes about the first useful mood, which is called Cesare, in this way: No stone is an animal; every man is an animal; therefore no man is a stone. And it is reduced to the second mood of the first figure by the simple conversion of the major alone, in this way: No animal is a stone; every man is an animal; therefore no man is a stone.

But if, on the contrary, the middle belongs to none of the one and to all of the other, that is, if in the major it is denied universally of the major extreme and in the minor is affirmed universally of the minor extreme, there comes about the second mood, which is called Camestres, as is shown by this example: Every man is an animal; no stone is an animal; therefore no stone is a man. It is reduced to the second mood of the first figure by converting the minor simply and transposing the premises, so that the converted minor becomes the major and the major becomes the minor, in this way: No animal is a stone;

Oo ij

[p. 580]

Every man is an animal; therefore no man is a stone.

The third mood comes about, he says, if the middle belongs to none of the one, that is, is denied universally of the major extreme in the major, but belongs to some of the other, that is, is said of some of the minor extreme in the minor: there comes about the third mood, which is called Festino. And both of these come about if the major is a universal negative and the minor a particular affirmative, in this way: No stone is an animal; some man is an animal; therefore some man is not a stone. And it is reduced to the fourth mood of the first figure by the simple conversion of the major alone, in this way: No animal is a stone; some man is an animal; therefore some man is not a stone.

30 The fourth mood, finally, he says comes about when the middle belongs to all of the one but does not belong to some of the other; that is, when the major is a universal affirmative, in which it is predicated universally of the major extreme, and the minor a particular negative, in which it is denied of that extreme taken in particular, there results this mood, which is called Baroco; and it is this: Every man is an animal; some stone is not an animal; therefore some stone is not a man. But this mood cannot be reduced to the first figure ostensively, as is manifest of itself; therefore Aristotle reduces it through the impossible to the first mood, in this way: so that from the major and the contradictory of the conclusion, taken as minor, there is inferred the contradictory of the minor of the same syllogism, true at the same time with it. As if we say thus: The syllogism in Baroco, you say, is not a good consequence; therefore in it the antecedent can be true and the consequent false. Let, then, that antecedent be true, for the major and the minor, and let the conclusion be false; its contradictory must then certainly be true, namely, Every stone is a man. This I take thus as a minor, and with the major of the same syllogism I make this syllogism: Every man is an animal; every stone is a man; therefore every stone is an animal; which is the contradictory of the minor of that syllogism, namely, Some stone is not an animal; and both are true: the latter because it was part of the antecedent of the bad consequence, the former because it was the contradictory of the false consequent of the same bad consequence. Whence it follows either that the syllogism of the fourth mood of this figure is good, or that two contradictories are true at the same time. But the other moods of this disposition are useless, and such can be proved by terms in which “all” follows and in which “none” follows.

[p. 581]

## CHAPTER VI

TEXT OF ARISTOTLE. But if the same term belongs to all of the one and to none of the other, or to all of both,

or to none of either, such a figure I call the third.

B R I E F E X P O S I T I O N O F T H E T E X T.

he intent of this chapter is to explain the nature of the third fig‐

T          ure. It is divided into two parts. In the first he defines and ex‐

plains the third figure: the middle and the extremes, how they are disposed in it. In the second he enumerates the useful moods that can be made in it, the useless being excluded.

In the first part he says: The third figure is made when three terms are so disposed that the middle is the subject in each premise: but the major extreme is the predicate of the major, and the minor the predicate of the minor; but it is necessary that the major proposition always be universal, and the conclusion always particular. Therefore he defines the middle thus: But the middle in this figure I call that of which both are predicated. That is, that of which both extremes are predicated. The extremes, he says, are those which are predicated, both in the premises and in the conclusion; but the middle is always subjected, and so they have as it were dissimilar and opposite rationes; and for this reason this extreme is said to be farther from the middle. But the minor extreme (he says) is the one which is nearer, that is, which comes closer to the middle, since at least in the conclusion it is the subject, just as the middle is in each premise. He teaches that no perfect syllogism is made in this figure, because all need reduction to the first, in order that they may appear necessary.

31 In the second part of the chapter he enumerates the useful moods that can be produced in this figure, the useless ones being excluded. The first mood, then, is produced when each premise is universal affirmative: as if we say, Every man is living; Every man is an animal; therefore Some animal is living. And this mood is called Darapti. It is reduced to the third mood of the first figure by the sole conversion of the minor in part, in this way: Every man is living; Some animal is a man; therefore Some animal is living.

The second mood is made when the major is universal negative, and the minor universal affirmative; and it is called Felapton, and is as follows: No animal is a stone; Every animal is living; therefore

Oo iij

[p. 582]

some living thing is not a stone. It is reduced to the fourth mood of the first figure by the sole conversion of the minor in part, in this way: No animal is a stone; Some living thing is an animal; therefore some living thing is not a stone.

The third mood is made when the major proposition is particular affirmative, and the minor universal affirmative; and it is called Disamis. As if we say, Some animal is a body; Every animal is living; therefore some living thing is a body. It is reduced to the third mood of the first figure by conversion of the major and transposition of the premises, so that the converted major becomes the minor, and this through simple conversion of the conclusion, and the minor becomes the major, in this way: Every animal is living; some body is an animal; therefore some body is living. The fourth mood is made when the major is universal affirmative, and the minor particular, also affirmative; as if we say: Every animal is living; Some animal is a body; therefore some body is living; and it is called Datisi. It is reduced to the third mood of the first figure by the sole simple conversion of the minor, in this way: Every animal is living; Some body is an animal; therefore some body is living. The fifth mood is made when the major is particular negative, and the minor universal affirmative; as if we say: Some animal is not a stone; Every animal is living; therefore some living thing is not a stone. And it is called Bocardo, which cannot be brought back to the moods of the first figure ostensively, as the others can, but only through the impossible, according to the rules of this reduction, in this way: Every living thing is a stone; Every animal is living; therefore Every animal is a stone.

The sixth mood is made when the major is universal negative and the minor particular affirmative, as in this example: No animal is a stone; some animal is living; therefore some living thing is not a stone; and it is called Ferison, which is reduced to the fourth mood of the first figure by the sole simple conversion of the minor, in this way: No animal is a stone; some living thing is an animal; therefore some living thing is not a stone. And through these reductions to the moods of the first figure it is evidently proved that all the syllogisms of the second and third figures are useful and good. We have, however, used only ostensive reduction, because it is brief. Reduction through the impossible, as being longer, we judge should be referred to the Summulae, where the young are frequently exercised in it; and for this reason it is not necessary to repeat it in this place. From the three figures there result only fourteen useful moods, signified by the following words, each of which signifies its own mood; and the first four signify

[p. 583]

the four moods of the first figure; the four following signify four others of the second figure; and the last six, six others of the third figure. The words are these: Barbara, Celarent, Darii, Ferio, Cesare, Camestres, Festino, Baroco, Darapti, Felapton, Disamis, Datisi, Bocardo, Ferison. For the five other, imperfect moods of the first figure were not established by Aristotle, but were added after him by others.

The art of finding the middle is delivered, for constructing syllogisms and proving any

kind of proposition.

O      f this art Aristotle treats in ch. 29 of this first book, where what is ob‐

scure of itself he made much more obscure, using elements, or letters signifying nothing, for finding middles. We, however, shall explain it briefly in significant terms familiar to us, and also in words that are not at all obscure, presupposing as a foundation the proper office of the middle in a syllogism: which is nothing other than to unite or to disjoin the extremes; to unite them in an affirmative or predicative syllogism, which is composed of affirmative propositions, but to disjoin them in a negative syllogism, that is, one consisting of some negative proposition. And the reason for this distinction is manifest: because through an affirmative syllogism an affirmative proposition is to be proved, in which some predicate is united to some subject; and the middle must come in to unite the terms. But in a negative syllogism a negative proposition is to be proved, in which the predicate is denied of the subject, which is to be separated from it; and a middle for separating some things must be such that it disjoins them, not that it unites them. Both offices, therefore, belong to the middle, with respect to diverse syllogisms and diverse propositions to be proved.

From which follow two universal rules. The first: To prove any affirmative proposition whatever, a middle must be sought by which its extremes, that is, the predicate and the subject, are united. But to prove any negative whatever, a middle must rather be sought that disjoins them. But in order that we may understand the particular rules which Aristotle delivers, another foundation must be presupposed: namely, that the middle, compared to the extremes which it must unite or separate, is threefold: Antecedent, Consequent, and Extraneous. The antecedent middle is said to be that from which one or both extremes follow: as man, with respect to risible. The consequent middle, that which follows from one or from both extremes. The extraneous middle, finally, that which is repugnant to one or both extremes: as stone with respect to animal and also to living.

Oo iij

[p. 584]

From which it is inferred, first, that to prove any affirmative proposition whatever, an antecedent or consequent middle must be sought, with respect to one or both extremes; but to prove a negative proposition, one must seek neither an antecedent nor a consequent middle, but an extraneous one.

It follows, second, that to prove any proposition offered, one must consider in what way its predicate and subject are related: for if the one belongs to the other, it is to be proved through an antecedent or consequent middle; but if it is repugnant to it, through an extraneous middle. We suppose, moreover, that the proposition to be proved must be true, or probable, or thought to be such: for to prove false propositions as such, neither can a middle be given, nor any art of finding it.

These things supposed, Aristotle delivers four rules in the place cited above for concluding the four kinds of propositions under which all others are comprehended. The first rule is: To infer a universal affirmation, such a middle must be sought as is consequent with respect to the subject and antecedent with respect to the predicate. For example, to infer this proposition, Every man is a substance, animal will have to be assumed, which is consequent to man and antecedent with respect to substance; and the syllogism will be made in this way in Barbara: Every animal is a substance; Every man is an animal; therefore Every man is a substance.

The second rule: To infer a particular affirmative, a middle must be assumed which is antecedent with respect to the subject and to the predicate, which are the extremes: as, to infer this, Some animal is a substance, man must be assumed, from which both follow; and it will be done in this way in Darapti: Every man is a substance; Every man is an animal; therefore Some animal is a substance.

The third rule: To infer a universal negative, a middle must be assumed which is consequent with respect to the subject and extraneous with respect to the predicate: as, to prove this, No man is a stone, animal must be assumed; and thus it will be proved in Cesare: No stone is an animal; Every man is an animal; therefore No man is a stone.

The fourth rule: To conclude a particular negative, a middle must be assumed which is antecedent to the subject and extraneous with respect to the predicate: as, to conclude this, Some animal is not a stone, Man must be assumed; and so it will be concluded in Festino: No man is a stone; Some man is an animal; therefore Some animal is not a stone.

End of this work.

[p. 585]

## COMMENTARIES ON THE TWO BOOKS OF ARISTOTLE

## T H E S TAG I R I T E , O N T H E P O S T E R I O R

Analysis, or Resolution, together with the doubts

and questions customarily debated

in this age.

P RO E M O F T H E W H O L E WO R K .

ince the office of Dialectic is to direct the operations of reason,

S        that is, to dispose and order them into divisions, definitions, propo‐

sitions, syllogisms, and the other argumentations, according to the threefold operation of the intellect to be directed, this science is divided by all in such a way that its first part is considered to be the one that orders the first operation, namely simple apprehension, explaining its nature so that we may know how to apprehend things as is fitting for effecting composition: which pertains to the second operation of the intellect, to be so directed that through it we may know how to construct a composition out of simples already apprehended, namely division, definition, and argumentation; for through the due construction of these instruments the operation is considered directed and ordered. The third, however, Logic directs when out of these same compositions it constructs argumentation. For in an argumentation constructed according to the rules of Dialectic the third operation of the intellect, whose office is to gather one thing from another, is considered ordered. The first part of Dialectic, therefore, is the categories, constituted out of ordered simples. The predicables, however, are considered not so much to constitute the first part as to be a certain preamble to the first part, that of the categories.

2 The second part of Dialectic is the work On Interpretation, in which the rules are delivered for constructing a proposition or enunciation. To the third part belong the books of the Prior Analytics, in which the syllogism in general is treated; the books of the Posterior Analytics, the Topics, and the Sophistical Refutations, in which syllogisms in particular are treated, namely the demonstrative, the topical or probable, and the sophistical. And in this way we have this whole science

[p. 586]

divided into three parts, through which the three operations of the intellect are directed, ordered, and perfected. That these two books, on the Posterior Analysis or Resolution, which we now undertake to interpret, belong to its last part is made manifest from the same division. This supposed, let us come to set before our eyes the scope of this work (which they call its subject or object).

Which is the subject or object of this work?

B    y the subject, whose cognition a science delivers by demonstrating its

properties or attributes, and by the object, about which its consideration is concerned as about a scope, the same thing is now understood. We ask, therefore, first: Which is the subject or object of this posterioristic part. The conditions of the object, delivered by us in Proemial Question 6, are to be presupposed.

3 The first opinion holds: That it is the mode of knowing, as it comprehends not only demonstration but also definition; indeed, the latter principally. So the Commentator, Alexander, and Theophrastus, in the proem of this work; whom some of the moderns follow.

And it is proved by this argument: Because definition is the principal instrument of science; therefore it pertains per se to Dialectic, which teaches how to make all the instruments of knowing. But in no other part does Aristotle teach the mode of producing a definition except in these books; therefore it pertains per se to them to treat of definition, wherefore it will pertain to their object together with demonstration. The minor is proved: because in the books of the Topics, and in any other part of Dialectic, if there is one, in which something is treated concerning definition, it is not the mode of producing it that is treated, but, supposing it already constituted in these books, it is examined.

4 The second opinion is the common and true one: that demonstration alone, and not the mode of knowing common to demonstration and to definition, is the object of this work. So St. Thomas, Albert the Great, Cajetan, Soto, Toledo, Mercado, and almost all the modern interpreters. It is proved by the testimony of Aristotle, who at the very beginning of the first chapter teaches and proves that all doctrine and all discipline comes about from pre-existing cognition: which is the chief foundation of the whole demonstrative art. From this we know that the assent to the conclusion is generated from the cognition of the principles; which is to understand the nature of demonstration.

[p. 587]

It is proved next by reason: Because that is the object of some work whose es‐

sential parts are delivered in it, whose nature is explained, and whose attrib‐

utes are proved; but all these things are performed in these books concerning

demonstration alone, and not concerning the common mode of knowing, as

is manifest in the course of them: therefore. For if definition is treated

(which we concede), it is treated not as another mode of knowing distinct

from demonstration, but as an essential part of it, because it is its chief prin‐

ciple: therefore demonstration alone is the object, and not something else

common to demonstration and definition.

And from this the argument of the contrary opinion is solved; everything

in it is to be conceded, but from conceding it one has only this: that in these

books definition is treated per se as an essential part of demonstration, but

not as another, distinct mode of knowing. Hence whoever asserts that

demonstration alone is the object does not exclude definition, but compre‐

hends it: not as under some common predicate, but as a part is comprehend‐

ed under the whole, and consequently under its consideration.

This part of Dialectic is shown to be more worthy than all the others.

5

S   ince it is known that a science takes its dignity from its object, it is gath‐

ered that this work is more worthy and more perfect than the other

parts of Dialectic; which I prove thus: The cognition of simples, of which

the first part of Dialectic treats, is ordered to composition, as to its end,

which is treated in the second part; and composition is ordered in the same

way to the syllogism: therefore, just so, the syllogism will be more perfect

than composition and than these same simples. But among syllogisms the

most perfect is demonstration, to which whatever is treated in this science is

ordered as to the chief instrument through which science is generated:

therefore this work is as it were the end of the other parts of Dialectic, and

for this reason it will be more worthy than all the others.

6 But against this there is a difficult argument: Because the books on the

Prior Resolution treat of the form of the syllogism, that is, of the figure and

mood in which it must be constructed; but the other books, of its matter:

namely, the books on the Posterior Resolution, of the necessary matter of

which demonstration consists; the books of the Topics, of the probable mat‐

ter out of which the Dialectical syllogism is made; the books of the

Sophistical Refutations, of the apparent matter out of which is made the

syllogism

[p. 588]

that is pseudographic or deceptive. But form, since it is act, is more perfect than matter, which is potency: therefore the books of the Prior Analytics are a nobler part of Dialectic than the books of the Posterior Analytics, the Topics, and the Sophistical Refutations. The consequence is proved: because just as a total science takes its dignity from the dignity of its total object, so each part of a science takes it from the partial object proper to it. Hence it follows that what we say is false, that these books of the Posterior Analytics are the nobler part of the whole of Dialectic.

7 This argument is conclusive against the many who hold that this work treats only of the necessary matter of the syllogism, and is distinguished by this from the books of the Prior Analytics, which treat of syllogistic form, and from the books of the Topics and the Sophistical Refutations, which treat of probable and apparent matter. Therefore it must be said that this work treats not only of the matter of the syllogism but also of its form. But the form of the syllogism is twofold, generic and specific. The generic form is the disposition in mood and figure. The specific form, however, is taken from the special mode of concluding one thing from another. Which I prove thus: The generic form of the syllogism is taken from the mode of inferring the conclusion from premises disposed in mood and figure: therefore the special mode of inferring the conclusion from the premises will be the special form of the syllogism. But demonstration, which is treated in this work as its proper object, contains not only the disposition in mood and figure, but also a special mode of inferring the conclusion from the premises: namely, as an effect from its per se and proper cause, or as a cause from its proper and per se effect: therefore it contains the special and most perfect form of the syllogism.

8 It is proved second: Because demonstration generates science, but the probable syllogism opinion; and these two effects are distinct in species: therefore these two syllogisms, namely the demonstrative and the probable, which are the per se causes of these effects, are distinguished in species. And specific distinction is not through matter, but through form: therefore they are distinguished through form. Not, surely, through the common form, which is the disposition in mood and figure, since this is generic and common to both: therefore through a special form, and not only through matter.

It must be held, therefore, that besides the common and generic form of the syllogism, taken from mood and figure, there is given a twofold special form, taken from the special mode of concluding, through which demonstration and the Dialectical or probable syllogism are distinguished in species. The special form of demonstration is the mode of concluding evidently an effect per se from its cause, or a cause per se from its effect; but the mode of concluding of the probable syllogism is not evident

[p. 589]

but probable. Thus they agree in mood and figure, but they are distinguished

in the special mode of inferring the conclusion from the premises disposed

in mood and figure: because the mode of concluding of demonstration is evi‐

dent and necessary, whereas the mode of concluding of the Dialectical syllo‐

gism is not evident or necessary, but probable; and since the former mode is

the most perfect, demonstration will be the most perfect species of syllo‐

gism. These two syllogisms can serve as an example: Every animal loves its like;

but Every man is an animal like another man; therefore every man loves another man.

And: Every rational animal is risible; Every man is a rational animal; therefore

Every man is risible. For although each is constructed in the first mood of the

first figure, the second concludes evidently, because its conclusion follows

from the premises as a proper and per se effect from its cause. For risibility is

a proper, necessary, and per se effect of rationality, with which it is convert‐

ible. Nevertheless the first syllogism does not conclude evidently, but only

probably, because its conclusion does not follow from the premises as a nec‐

essary or per se effect, but as a quasi-contingent effect. For although likeness

inclines to love, yet not as to a necessary effect, but to a free one, and one

which is often impeded by other reasons. The Sophistical syllogism, however,

is distinguished in species from both, because it sins in form: for it does not

have the due disposition in mood and figure, although it seems to have it;

wherefore it does not have a true form, but only an apparent one.

9 To the argument, then: the antecedent must be denied, namely that this

work treats only of the matter of the syllogism; for it treats also of form, not

the common or generic form, of which the books of the Prior Analytics treat,

but the specific form, and indeed the most perfect, inasmuch as it is taken

from the most perfect mode of concluding evidently; and from this it has it

that it is the noblest part of the whole of Dialectic, to which all the others

are ordered as to their end. But the deception of those who falsely think that

it treats of matter alone took its occasion from this: that this most perfect

mode of evidently inferring the conclusion from the premises is not found

except in propositions constituted in necessary matter. Hence it is true that

this work treats of the necessary matter of the syllogism, but false that it

treats of matter alone; rather it treats chiefly of the special and most perfect

form.

The end of this work, and its title or inscription, is explained. 10

T    he end of this work is most noble: because it perfects the natural desire of

man as he is rational. For from rational nature

[p. 590]

of man there proceeds the natural desire of knowing, that is, of cognizing effects through causes or causes through effects, as Aristotle expressly taught at the beginning of Metaph. 1, saying: all men by nature desire to know. And to fulfill this desire this work is ordered, which treats of the nature of demonstration, which is the chief instrument of knowing, as is plain from its definition, delivered by Aristotle in ch. 2 of this first book in this way: Demonstration is a syllogism that makes one know. It is inscribed, however, On the Posterior Resolution.

11 In order that we may understand this title, each of its particles must be explained: namely, Resolution and Posterior. Now the resolution of anything is twofold, Physical or real, and Logical or rational. Physical resolution is the real dissolution or destruction of a thing: as when a horse dies, it is said to be resolved into matter; and when a house is destroyed, we say it is dissolved or resolved into the wood, stones, and earth out of which it was constructed. Logical or rational resolution, however, is not the destruction but the perfection of a thing. For it consists in a certain examination of the single parts of which the thing is constituted, by which examination it is shown that its single parts are such as they ought to be according to the precepts of that art through which it was constructed. As when we examine the parts of a definition according to the rules of defining delivered by Dialectic, showing that it consists of its proper genus and proper difference, we are said to resolve the definition. Which is plainly the same as to show that it is perfect. To resolve a demonstration, therefore, will be nothing other than to examine its parts, that is, its principles or premises: namely, when they are shown to be not true in just any way, but also necessary, per se, and immediate, so that once the terms are known the intellect assents to them without any argument by which they are proved; or at least that they are reduced through evident demonstrations back to first principles evident from the sole cognition of the terms. For unless someone knows in one way or the other that they are per se evident, he will have neither a true demonstration nor science of the conclusion, but a Dialectical syllogism and opinion. As Aristotle teaches in ch. 2 of this first book in these words: But from first indemonstrable premises, since he who does not have a demonstration of them will not know.

12 Let the matter be made manifest by this demonstration: Every rational animal is risible; Every man is a rational animal; therefore Every man is risible. Its minor is a proposition known per se, or immediate, since in it the definition is predicated of its definitum without any middle or proving argument, and it belongs per se and immediately to the definitum alone, so that as soon as the intellect cognizes the signification of the terms it judges it to be true. This

[p. 591]

is what it is to be an immediate principle, or one known per se. But the major is not known per se, because risibility does not belong to man immediately, but by means of another, prior attribute, namely wonder. It must therefore be demonstrated, so that the intellect may know certainly and evidently that it is true. And it is demonstrated through wonder, assumed as the middle, in this way: Everything capable of wonder is risible; Every man is capable of wonder; therefore Every man is risible. But this demonstration still does not suffice: because although the major premise is immediate, in which one immediate attribute is predicated of another, namely risibility of wonder, which follows from it without any middle, yet the minor, in which wonder is predicated of man, is not immediate: because wonder does not follow from rationality per se immediately, but by means of another, prior attribute, namely capacity for learning.

Wherefore, in order that the intellect may know that it is certain and evident, it must know how to demonstrate it through capacity for learning taken as the middle, in this way: Whatever is capable of learning is capable of wonder; Every man is capable of learning; therefore Every man is capable of wonder. Now this demonstration is most perfect, because it consists of premises that are immediate, or evident per se, and indemonstrable. For such is the major, in which one immediate attribute is predicated of another, namely wonder of capacity for learning, by means of which it follows from rationality. Such also is the minor, in which the first attribute, which immediately follows the essence, is predicated of the definition that explains that same essence. And to this demonstration the first is reduced, which would not be a true demonstration unless it were reduced to it through true demonstrations. But if someone does not know how to reduce it thus, there will not be a true demonstration in his intellect, but a probable syllogism; nor will he have through it science of the conclusion, but opinion. And this reduction is logical and rational resolution, because through it the parts of the demonstration are examined and are evidently proved to be such as they ought to be according to the rules of this art: that is, according to the definition of that same demonstration, to be delivered in ch. 2 of this book, which is the first rule of the whole art and science. And finally, because in this work this mode of resolving demonstration through the reduction of the premises back to first principles known per se, or indemonstrable, is taught, it is therefore inscribed On Resolution.

14 But since demonstration consists of a twofold form (as we have already said), the common or generic, taken from mood and figure, and the special, taken from the mode of concluding, it is resolved in two ways

[p. 592]

namely, according to the common form, which is examined and proved through those principles, said of all and said of none; and also according to the special form, which resolution we have just shown. And resolution according to the generic form is prior to resolution according to the specific form, because more universal things are prior, and the genus is prior to the species. Therefore the books that treat of the syllogism in general are called On the Prior Resolution, that is, on resolving the syllogism according to the generic form, which is prior. But this work, which teaches how to resolve the syllogism according to the special form, which is posterior, is inscribed On the Posterior Resolution.

But against this there is an argument: Because in these books Aristotle teaches not only how to resolve demonstration back to first principles, but also how to compose it out of such premises and parts; and it is prior to compose a demonstration than to resolve it, because resolution is as it were an examination of the composition: therefore they ought rather to be named from composition, as from what is first, than from resolution.

15 I reply, other solutions being omitted: the antecedent is conceded, but the consequence denied. Because although composition is treated per se, and is prior, resolution is nevertheless more perfect: because it is as it were the form and soul of the composition, through which it is evidently established that it has been made according to the rules of the art, and is therefore good; and that the demonstration composed is exact, firm, and stable, and generative of science.

From which it follows that the resolution of reason is not to be distinguished into Logical and Mathematical, as Toledo distinguishes it in the proem of this work, q. 2: because if the resolution is to be certain, it must be made through true demonstrations. But every resolution made through demonstrations is logical, because it pertains to Logic alone to teach it. Wherefore it can be called Mathematical only insofar as it is applied to that science, just as it can also be called Physical or Metaphysical as it is applied to those sciences. For although every science resolves its conclusions and demonstrations back to first principles, yet it receives the mode of resolving through true demonstrations from Dialectic, to which it properly belongs to teach it.

It is explained what place this work ought to hold among the other parts of Dialectic.

S  ome (as Villalpando, in the proem to the book on the Prior Resolution) assert

that one and the same treatise is composed of the books of the Prior and the Posterior Analytics; and therefore that the same place must be granted

to

[p. 593]

to these books and to those. Others, however, as John Philoponus and Avicenna, say that it is a distinct treatise, yet they place the books of the Topics immediately after the books of the Prior Analytics, and this work immediately after the books of the Topics.

But the common opinion asserts two things. First: That this work is distinct from the books of the Prior Analytics. Because in it the syllogism is treated according to the special form, but in the books of the Prior Analytics the same is treated according to the common form; and these considerations are diverse, and therefore they belong to distinct treatises. Second: That these books are to be placed immediately after the books of the Prior Analytics, and before the books of the Topics and the Sophistical Refutations. So St. Thomas in the proem of this work; Albert the Great, Posterior Analytics 1, tract. 1; Cajetan, Soto, the Louvain commentators, Toledo, Marc., and all the moderns, in this proem. And the reason is manifest: Because in the books of the Prior Analytics the syllogism is treated in general, under which consideration it is prior to its being treated according to its species, which are treated in the other books: therefore the first place, with respect to the others in which the syllogism is treated, is owed to the books of the Prior Analytics. But among the species of syllogism the most perfect is demonstration (of which this work treats), and consequently the first: therefore it ought to be placed immediately after the books of the Prior Analytics.

Why this posterioristic part is called judicative, but the topical part inventive.

B    ut finally it is customarily asked in this proem: Why this part of Dialectic is

called Judicative? To which, other opinions being omitted, I reply, from the doctrine of St. Thomas set down in this proem, that the reason of the matter is this: because the judgment of the intellect made about the truth of a thing is a certain sentence; and a perfect judgment is not any sentence whatever pronounced by the intellect, but a firm and certain one. But the intellect cannot pass a firm and certain sentence unless it adheres firmly and certainly to one part of a contradiction. And this it attains through demonstration, of which not only the premises but also the conclusion deduced from them is certain and evident, as Aristotle taught in bk. 2, ch. 1, saying: He who knows simply must be immovable from belief. Rightly, therefore, is this posterioristic part called judicative: because in it is taught the mode of passing certain judgment on the truth of propositions, which is something most perfect. But the Topical part is not called judicative, because through the Topical syllogism certain judgment is not passed on the conclusion, but only probable judgment. It is called inventive, however, because for invention (as St. Thomas well says) certitude is not required: although the places themselves, once found, by certain

Pp

[p. 594]

demonstration, are proved in the Topical part insofar as it is a part of logica do‐

cens. Through the Topics, too, the same Logic teaches how to find places in the

other sciences for drawing out probable arguments. Thus each part of Dialectic

has something of invention and also something of judgment. But to judge be‐

longs as it were by antonomasia to this posterioristic work, and to the others by

participation in it; and to find the places of probable arguments belongs in the

same way to the Topical part, and to the others by participation in it. Therefore

the posterioristic part is called Judicative, but the Topical Inventive: because the

name is determined from that which is principal, or belongs more principally.

The mode of proceeding, and the division of the whole work.

19

C     oncerning the mode of proceeding, whether Aristotle proceeds by defining and

dividing, or also by demonstrating, not all agree. But Paul of Venice, in ch. 1 of

this work, affirms that in the course of this work Aristotle uses divisions and def‐

initions, not demonstrations; which can be proved by the testimony of Aristotle,

who in ch. 2 of bk. 1 defines demonstration with a twofold definition. And also

by this argument: Aristotle in this work treats of demonstration; therefore he

does not proceed by demonstrating. The consequence is proved: because if he

proceeded through demonstrations, there would be a process to infinity, and the

same thing would be proved through itself. The consequence is proved: because

if the nature of demonstration were proved through demonstration, then the na‐

ture of that demonstration which he would use would have to be proved through

another demonstration, and so to infinity. And if the nature of demonstration is

proved through demonstration, that same demonstration through which it

would be proved would prove itself, since it is a true demonstration; or the un‐

known would be proved through the more unknown, since before the demon‐

stration through which the nature of demonstration is proved, that demonstra‐

tion is not known.

20 Two things, however, must be said on this matter. First: That every science,

or every part of a science, for the most part proceeds by defining. Because it is necessary

to define the proper object at the beginning, so that its definition can be as‐

sumed as the middle for proving attributes of it; and therefore in this work

Aristotle does not so proceed by demonstrating that he does not also proceed by

defining. Second, it must be said: That the proper mode of proceeding of this work is

through demonstration, as is shown in chs. 2 and 10 and in many others, in which

Aristotle uses demonstrations to show the nature of demonstration and its prop‐

erties; and concerning this

[p. 595]

no one can doubt. To the argument, however: it must be denied that those inconveniences follow. For once the definition of demonstration has first been assigned, the nature of any demonstration whatever is already known through it, even of that which is afterwards adduced to prove something about demonstration. Nor yet does the demonstration that is adduced need another through which it is proved; rather it proves itself under a diverse ratio: because insofar as it agrees with the other demonstrations in the common nature of demonstration, explained through the definition, it is that of which something is proved; and insofar as it is the middle through which something is proved, it is that by which something is proved of that same common nature, but not that of which it is proved. And to be, under a diverse ratio, that of which something is proved and that by which that same thing is proved is not inconvenient: because the definition through which the common nature of definition is explained explains itself under a diverse ratio, as is well known.

The general division of the whole work is into two books. In the First of these Aristotle treats of the nature of demonstration and its parts. In the Second: Of the mode of constituting a definition, which is the chief middle of that same demonstration. The particular division of each book will be indicated in its own place.

## CHAPTER I

## TEXT OF ARISTOTLE

All doctrine and all intellective discipline comes about from pre-existing cognition, etc.

B R I E F E X P O S I T I O N O F T H E T E X T.

his first book, on the Posterior Resolution, is divided into three

T          parts. In the first Aristotle teaches That demonstration exists. In the sec‐

ond: What demonstration is, and of what parts it consists. In the third: Of what sort it is, that is, what attributes or properties it has.

The intent of this chapter is: That actual cognition of things, and science, truly exists in us, and is generated from another, prior cognition. It has two parts: in the first of which Aristotle delivers a certain universal proposition containing the aforesaid truth, and proves it in every kind of intellectual cognition. In the second, how many and which are the precognitions, and about what they are had.

Pp ij

[p. 596]

Two errors were current in the schools in Aristotle’s time concerning the acquisition of science. The first was that of Heraclitus and Cratylus, ancient Philosophers, who, not distinguishing intellective cognition from sensitive, and not thinking that anything universal exists in things, but only sensible singulars, which are in continual motion and flux, consequently asserted that there neither is science of things nor can there be, because science, if it were possible, would have to be of universal and perpetual things.

2 The second error was that of Plato, as the same Aristotle testifies in Metaph. 1 and 7, who granted science, yet not newly acquired, but possessed from the beginning, in this way: that when the matter out of which a man is generated is disposed by the natural agent, immediately, through the impression and power of the separated idea of man, a soul is infused full of the species of all things, through which it could know all things; only that it does not go out into the act of cognizing, on account of the impediment of the body and as it were the binding of the senses, until such impediment is removed by exercise; and once this is removed, the soul begins to cognize, not the things of which it was previously ignorant, but those which it had cognized from the beginning, though it had been impeded from the actual consideration of them; and therefore it was as if it had consigned to oblivion what it had previously cognized. Hence Plato inferred that our knowing is as it were a certain reminiscence of the things which we previously cognized. Which he proved by this argument in a certain dialogue on science and virtue which is called Meno, from a certain person of the same name, Meno, introduced in it. When a man wishes to know something, either he wishes to know what he already knew, or what he did not know. The first is impossible, because no one wishes to know the things he already cognizes. Nor is the second less impossible, that he should wish to know what he is ignorant of: for just as someone would seek in vain a man whom he did not know, because even if he found him he could not recognize him, so someone would seek in vain the science of what he has not cognized, because he will not be able to cognize it even if it offers itself to him. It must be said, therefore, that we wish to know the things which we previously cognized but have as it were consigned to oblivion; and therefore we cognize it now not anew, but as it were through a certain reminiscence.

3 Against these two errors Aristotle proposes this universal proposition: All doctrine and all intellective discipline comes about from pre-existing cognition. Whose sense is: Every judgment of the intellect that is had not from the sole cognition of the terms, but is acquired by some middle or reasoning, whether by one’s own industry or labor, so that it is called doctrine, or received from a master, and therefore called discipline, comes about, that is, is truly given

[p. 597]

(against Heraclitus) and comes about anew, so that the thing cognized through it was not cognized before but was simply unknown (against Plato). This universal truth Aristotle proves in a threefold kind of cognition. In scientific cognition, indeed the most certain, such as is that which is had through the Mathematical disciplines, in which it is evident that the judgment and cognition of the conclusion comes about from the cognition of the premises previously had. And in the same way in the other Arts, not only the liberal but also the mechanical, in which one thing is always cognized from the cognition of another previously had, until one arrives at the first principle of that art, known not through another but through itself, that is, from the sole cognition of the terms. He proves it next in probable cognition, which is had through the Dialectical syllogism, whose conclusion is cognized from the probable or evident cognition of the premises through a probable consequence, or through induction, in which from the cognition of singulars there comes about experience, which is a universal judgment. He proves it finally in the Rhetorical argumentations, which are the Enthymeme and the example: for the Enthymeme is as it were a truncated syllogism, which lacks the major or the minor, which is nevertheless understood by the one arguing; and the judgment of the conclusion comes about from the judgment of the other premise previously had. The example, however, proceeds from one singular to another through likeness, and therefore the cognition of the one is had from the cognition of the other previously had.

4 In the second part of the chapter Aristotle treats of the things to be precognized and the things precognized. For if the cognition of the conclusion must come about from pre-existing cognition, it is necessary to explain what and how many are the things to be precognized, and about what, so that from them the cognition of the conclusion can be had. He says that two things are to be precognized, or that two precognitions are necessary for the cognition of the conclusion: Whether it is, and What it is. But that there are three things about which precognitions are to be had, namely the Subject, the Attribute, and the Principle; and these are called the things precognized. The subject is that of which there is science, or the scientific conclusion. The principles are the premises of the demonstration, from which the conclusion is inferred. The attribute is what is demonstrated of the subject in the conclusion. Aristotle gives examples in the Mathematical disciplines, but we shall bring them forward in things better known to us, in this way: In order that we may have evident cognition of this conclusion, Every man is risible, it is necessary that we precognize two things, Whether it is and What it is; and about three things, namely about the subject concerning which the conclusion is occupied, which is man; about the principles, which are those premises through which it is demonstrated, namely, Every rational animal is risible, and every man is a rational animal; and about the attribute demonstrated of it, which is risibility,

Pp iij

[p. 598]

Yet both precognitions are not to be had of each one, but only of the subject; of

the principles, the first, namely whether they are, that is, whether they are true;

of the attribute, the second, namely what it is, that is, what the name signifies:

for that it is is proved in the conclusion, that is, that it inheres in the subject;

because, since it is an accident, it has no other being than to inhere in the

subject.

5 These things explained, Aristotle replies at the end of the chapter to the

argument of Plato by distinguishing the major. For when it is asked whether he

who wishes to know something wishes to know what he knew before or what he

was ignorant of, he says it must be replied that he does not wish to know what

he knew simply, nor what he was altogether ignorant of, but what he was igno‐

rant of formally and simply, yet knew virtually and in a certain respect, that is,

not in itself, but in another thing previously cognized, in which it is virtually

contained. For example, when I wish to know whether man is capable of learn‐

ing, I wish to know what I did not know actually and formally, but only virtually,

in those two premises previously cognized: Every rational animal is capable of

learning, and every man is a rational animal, in which its cognition is virtually con‐

tained; and therefore, when it is inferred in them, it can be cognized: because it

was not altogether unknown, but was at least virtually cognized; and through

the inference it is cognized formally.

## QUESTION I

Whether Aristotle’s universal proposition is understood of all and only intellective

cognition.

6

B     efore we propose the various opinions, Aristotle’s proposition must be ex‐

plained in a few words. In it, by doctrine and discipline the same intellectual assent

is signified, which, as it is acquired by one’s own industry or as it proceeds from a

master, is called doctrine, but as received by the disciple, discipline. Next, by in‐

tellective cognition not just any judgment of the intellect is signified, but only

that which is had through some middle or reasoning: for if it is had from the

sole cognition of the terms, it is certain that it does not come about from an‐

other judgment of the intellect, although it comes about from the apprehensive

cognition of the terms and of their signification. Otherwise, if it came about

from another judgment, there would be a process to infinity. The sense of the

proposition, therefore, is: Every judgment of the intellect had through some

middle or reasoning comes about from another, also had

[p. 599]

through reasoning, or from the sole cognition of the terms, so that it is finally reduced to another known per se, or had without a middle. This is the sense of the proposition about which it is inquired whether it is to be taken of all and only intellective cognition, and whether it is true.

And the first opinion holds that it is true and is understood not only of the sciences, but also of opinion and human faith, and consequently of every judgment of the intellect had through a middle. So Soto, q. 1 of this chapter, in the solution to the first confirmation of the 2nd argument. He proves it: Because both are generated from some evident principle through a probable or inevident consequence: opinion, indeed, when we argue thus: A spherical, or perfectly round, body touches another perfectly plane body at a point; therefore there is an indivisible point. Human faith also, when we say: A man worthy of faith is to be believed; therefore the things said by this man, worthy of faith, are true.

The second opinion asserts that it extends not only to the human sciences but also to the science of the angels, and that it is true in it. So certain moderns, who prove this view thus: Because an angel cognizes the effect through the cause, as that man is risible because he is rational; and the cognition of the cause is prior to the cognition of the effect, just as the cause is prior to the effect: therefore the cognition of the effect comes about in him from pre-existing cognition of the cause. Moreover, inferior angels are illuminated by superior ones; and illumination does not seem to be anything other than the manifestation of a truth which the superior cognizes and the inferior is ignorant of: therefore the cognition of the inferior angel comes about from the pre-existing cognition of the superior.

8 Our view, and the common view of almost all the expositors of Aristotle on this chapter, is explained by these conclusions. First: Aristotle’s proposition is not understood of the science of the angels, nor can it have truth in it.
