In order to explain and at the same time prove this, it should be noted: That it is one thing to cognize how one thing is from another, or out of another, or on account of another; and another thing to have cognition of one thing from the cognition of another. For the first does not imply a distinct cognition of each, nor any imperfection on the part of the one cognizing, but through one and the same cognition both can be cognized, with that order or dependence which they have according to themselves: and thus any cause and effect whatever are cognized by God and by the angels, so that through one simple cognition they cognize both, and how the one has being from the other; so too they cognize any essence and all the attributes proceeding from it. But to have cognition of one thing from the cognition of another implies a distinction of cognitions, and causality, not only between the objects cognized,

Pp iiij

[p. 600]

but also between the cognitions themselves, so that the one is the cause of the other in some genus; and this is the greatest imperfection, which is found only in our discursive cognition, through which we cognize several things successively, and the cognition of one follows after another and comes about from another; and this is to come about from pre-existing cognition, as Aristotle’s proposition asserts.

9 From this most true doctrine, then, it is proved that no judgment of the divine or angelic intellect comes about from pre-existing cognition. Which I prove thus: For a judgment of the intellect to come about from pre-existing cognition implies a distinction of cognitions, because the same cognition is not said to come about from itself; but God and the angels do not cognize the effect and the cause by distinct cognitions: therefore the cognition of the effect in them does not come about from pre-existing cognition of the cause.

As for what is said, that an angel cognizes the effect through the cause, a distinction must be made: for on the part of the thing cognized it is true, because the angel truly cognizes that the effect has being from the cause and is on account of it; but on the part of the cognition it is not true: because, since the cognition of the cause and of the effect is the same, it is not true that the cognition of the one comes about from the cognition of the other; for this implies a distinction of cognitions, which is not found in God, nor in the angels, with respect to cause and effect. And what we say of the science of the angels is to be understood in the same way of the infused science of our first Parent, which he had from the beginning, in which he was made by God.

10 As to illumination, however, we concede that the cognition of the inferior angel comes about from the pre-existing cognition of the superior; yet Aristotle’s proposition is understood in the same intellect, not in diverse ones.

Second conclusion: In opinions it is not always true that one cognition comes about from another, as the first opinion asserts, but only in those which are had through discursive reasoning. This conclusion is proved: Because opinion is not had only through discursive reasoning from an evident proposition, but there are also opinions known per se, that is, probable per se, just as the principles of the sciences are evident per se; and in them one cognition is not had from another, but from the sole cognition of the terms: as this proposition, A mother loves her son, is probable per se; and not because it is gathered from another, but, once the signification of the terms alone is had, the intellect necessarily judges it to be probable: therefore in these opinions cognition does not come about from another, pre-existing cognition. But this very point will be explained expressly in ch. 26 of this book.

11 Third conclusion: The assent of human faith does not come about from pre-existing cognition. This too is proved, against Soto: Because the formal and proximate reason for assenting in faith is the testimony of one worthy of faith

[p. 601]

by which ratio it is distinguished from opinion. For the assent of the latter is

either had from the cognition of the terms alone, or gathered from another ev‐

ident assent through a probable consequence; therefore the assent of faith does

not come about from another, nor through discursive reasoning, but is had

from testimony alone, without discourse: wherefore it does not come about

from preexisting cognition. And what we say of human faith is to be under‐

stood in the same way of divine faith and of the revelations of the Prophets.

But to the argument of the first opinion I reply that the assent of opinion

had through that discursive reasoning comes about from preexisting cognition,

but that not every assent of opinion is had by discursive reasoning, as we have

proved; and therefore it does not always come about from preexisting cogni‐

tion. But that the assent of human faith comes about through that discursive

reasoning we deny. For it is had immediately from the testimony of one worthy

of credence: otherwise, if it came about through that discursive reasoning, it

would be opinion, not human faith.

From these three conclusions it follows that Aristotle’s proposition is uni‐

versally true in every science acquired in the human manner, and in opinion

which is had through discursive reasoning only. And therefore its sense is this:

Every judgment of the intellect had through discursive reasoning, whether it be evident

or probable, comes about from some preexisting judgment of the intellect had from the cog‐

nition of the terms alone; or also had through discursive reasoning, but reducible

to another judgment to be had from the cognition of the terms alone.

## QUESTION II

Whether actual existence is to be presupposed of the subject.

11

T    wo precognitions were assigned by Aristotle, namely Whether the thing is

and What it is, and he taught that both are to be had of the subject or ob‐

ject with which the science is concerned; and the reason for this is manifest:

because if the subject does not have being, neither will it have an essence or

quiddity, and therefore not proper attributes either, to be proved of it in the

science. Nor, finally, will it have a quidditative definition through which they

might be proved: wherefore, if it is not, it will not be able to be the subject of a

science. Now being, as we are speaking now, is nothing other than existence in

the nature of things. But this is had in two ways: In act, while the thing exists

outside its causes; or In potency, while it is not outside them but in the power of

those by which it can be produced. Concerning the possible existence of the

subject, no one doubts that it must necessarily be presupposed: because if it

could not have it in any way, it would be reputed an impossible being, like a

Chimera; wherefore there could not be science of it. Therefore we inquire only

[p. 602]

about actual existence: Whether it is necessary to know beforehand of the subject that it is in act in the nature of things, in order that science may be had of it, or whether it suffices to presuppose that it can have it.

13 And the first opinion affirms that it is necessary that actual existence be presupposed of the subject: not that it always have it, but at least at the times established by nature; as of the rose, though it does not actually exist, science is had in winter, because we know beforehand that it will have it in the time of spring. But if it were not going to have it in its own time, science could not be had of it. So Cajetan on the present chapter, and Toledo, the single question, ad 5.

And it is proved by the testimony of Aristotle, who expressly asserts it in bk. 1 of this work, text 8, in these words: But to ask What it is when one does not have That it is, is to ask nothing. As if to say that the definition of that which does not have existence is not to be sought, because it cannot be found; and therefore neither will it be able to be the object of a science.

It is proved also by reason: because a proposition is said to be true or false from the fact that the thing is or is not, that is, from the fact that it actually exists or does not exist; therefore the actual existence of the subject, at least at the times at which it can receive it from natural causes, is the foundation of all the truths that can be known of it in a science: wherefore it will necessarily have to be known beforehand of it.

14 The second opinion is the opposite: That the actual existence of the subject need not necessarily be known beforehand, even at the times established by nature; but that, although it never has it nor ever will have it, science can be had of it if it is known beforehand that it can have it. So Soto, q. 1 on the precognitions, where he teaches that when Aristotle says that it must be known beforehand of the subject Whether it is, this has the sense, that is, Whether it is a true being, having at least possible being in its causes.

The reason for this opinion is: because it suffices for the subject to have possible being in its causes in order that it may have a true definition and true attributes which can be proved of it in a science; therefore it suffices to know this of it beforehand.

Our view is explained by two conclusions. The first is: The intrinsic ratio of science does not require the actual existence of the subject; therefore it need not necessarily be known beforehand of it, but it suffices to know beforehand its possible existence. This is proved by an argument. Science by its own nature is perpetual, and must be concerned with a necessary and perpetual object; but actual existence belongs to the subject neither always nor necessarily, but in a certain contingent manner, since things everywhere lose it when they are corrupted: therefore science is not had of the subject as actually existing, even at the established times

[p. 603]

Nor will its actual existence necessarily have to be known beforehand, but it

will suffice to know beforehand its possible existence. This is against Cajetan.

15 The second conclusion: In order that science may be had of some subject by us

who know imperfectly, it is necessary that it have had actual existence at some time; not

at every time established by nature, but at least once. This is in part against both

opinions. And it is proved by this reason: our imperfect cognition is had

through the senses; therefore we cannot have science of any object unless we

perceive it through some sense; but the senses perceive only things actually ex‐

isting; therefore it is necessary that the object have at some time had actual ex‐

istence, in order that the scientific cognition of it may reach the intellect by

means of the senses. But that it should have it at the times established by na‐

ture is not necessary, since it can be known by us in a scientific manner through

that existence which it once had. Both our conclusions are held by Ferrara, bk.

1 Contra Gentiles, ch. 66.

16 But the testimony of Aristotle adduced for Cajetan’s opinion is to be un‐

derstood of possible being, which suffices in order that its quiddity may be

found. Or, if it is understood of actual being, Aristotle speaks in that passage of

the mode in which science is acquired by us, not of science according to its in‐

trinsic ratio.

To the argument of the same opinion, the antecedent must be distinguished.

For it is from the fact that the thing is or is not, that is, from its possible exis‐

tence, that the truth of a scientific proposition is taken, not from its actual ex‐

istence; and that possible existence is a sufficient foundation for the truths of

the whole science.

But the argument for Soto’s opinion is to be granted: because it proves only

that it suffices to know beforehand the possible existence of the subject for the

intrinsic ratio of science, as our first conclusion asserts; but for the imperfect

mode in which we commonly acquire it, it is necessary that it have had exis‐

tence at some time, and that it have at some time been known beforehand of

it, as the second conclusion proves.

## QUESTION III

Whether what the thing is, or only what the name is, must be known beforehand of the

subject. 17

D     efinition is twofold. One is that through which the essence of a thing is

explained; and this is called the definition of the thing, or what the thing is, as

rational animal. The other is the definition, or rather the explanation, of the

word, as

[p. 604]

when we say: magnanimous is having a great soul; or infinite, that which has no end. And this is called the definition of the name, or what the name is, because the quiddity of a name seems to be its signification explained through it. And there is no doubt that this must necessarily be known beforehand of the subject of a science: for if we do not know what this word man signifies, we shall not be able to have any true cognition of him, nor science. But the question proceeds concerning the definition of what the thing is, or the quidditative definition of the subject: whether it must necessarily be known beforehand.

And the first opinion asserts that it need not necessarily be known beforehand, but that without cognition of it science can be had of the thing. So Toledo in the place cited above, who proves it in this way: because in order to demonstrate an effect through its cause it is not required to know beforehand what the Cause is and what the effect is, but only that the effect proceeds per se from the cause; therefore the precognition of what it is is not required. Hence Astrologers demonstrate that the moon is eclipsed through its cause, though they are ignorant of the definition of the moon and of the heavens; Mathematicians demonstrate many things about figures and numbers, though ignorant of their definitions.

18 But in order that we may decide what is to be held in this question, it should be noted that demonstration is twofold, Quia and Propter quid. Demonstration propter quid is that through which we demonstrate an effect through its cause; such is this: Every rational animal is risible; every man is a rational animal; therefore every man is risible. Demonstration quia is that through which, conversely, we demonstrate the cause through the effect, as if you say: Everything risible is capable of wonder; every man is risible; therefore every man is capable of wonder. Moreover, demonstration propter quid is in turn twofold: One, through which a proper attribute is demonstrated of the subject; and such is the first that we adduced; such also are many in the particular sciences, which demonstrate attributes of the subject, as Metaphysics and both Philosophies, Natural and Moral. The other is that in which an effect is demonstrated through a cause of which it is not the proper attribute; and such is the second demonstration adduced; such also are almost all the Mathematical demonstrations. For these sciences do not so much demonstrate attributes of the subject as certain rationes of figures and proportions of numbers, the posterior through the prior.

19 These things supposed, our view is explained by three conclusions. The first is: The precognitions, and the order in which those things called precognita are to be had of the subject, the attribute, and the principles, have no place in demonstration Quia, but only in demonstration propter quid. It is proved by the testimony of Aristotle in ch. 2 of this bk. 1, who asserts of

[p. 605]

the mode of knowing a posteriori, that is, through demonstration Quia, that he had not yet spoken, and would not speak of it until the tenth chapter, where he distinguishes the two demonstrations. Therefore the rules of the second chapter on precognitions and precognita are understood only of the process of demonstration Propter quid, as all the examples adduced by Aristotle also show.

It is proved also by reason: because through demonstration Quia the definition or essence of a thing is often demonstrated through its proper attribute, as this demonstration shows: Everything risible is a rational animal; every man is risible; therefore every man is a rational animal. Sometimes, too, it is customarily proved that the subject is, when this is not so manifest. But that which is demonstrated cannot be presupposed or known beforehand; therefore in demonstration Quia it need not be known beforehand of the subject whether it is, nor what it is, but it will suffice to know beforehand what the name is.

The second conclusion: Also in demonstrations Propter quid in which a proper attribute is not demonstrated of the subject, but an effect from its cause, it is not necessary to know beforehand what the thing is of the subject; but it suffices to know beforehand the proper concept of the cause, and the dependence of the effect on it, or the ratio through which the effect is demonstrated. It is proved: because in these definitions the definition of the subject is not taken as the middle of demonstrating, but only the per se dependence of the effect on the cause; therefore the precognition of the former is not required, but that of the latter will suffice.

The third conclusion: In demonstrations that prove an attribute of the subject, the definition of what the thing is must necessarily be known beforehand. This too is manifest: because in these demonstrations the definition of what the thing is is assumed as the middle; therefore it is one of the premises; but the premises are known beforehand in order to infer the conclusion; therefore it is necessary to know beforehand what the subject is. And it is in these demonstrations that Aristotle’s precept about knowing beforehand what the subject is is understood, as St. Thomas expressly teaches, 1 p., q. 1, a. 7, ad 1; from which all three of our conclusions are taken, which Cajetan also holds on the present chapter. From these it is understood that Aristotle’s rules on precognitions and precognita are to be understood proportionally in the different demonstrations; so that of the subject what the thing is, and also what the name is, must be known beforehand in those demonstrations which prove an attribute of the subject; but in the others, in which a posterior ratio, as an effect, is proved through a prior ratio or cause, only the concept of the cause and its dependence on the effect

[p. 606]

is to be known beforehand; but what the name is, in all.

But Toledo’s argument proves only that it is not necessary to know beforehand

what the subject is in demonstrations that prove effects through causes, or poste‐

rior rationes through prior ones: which our second conclusion grants; therefore it

achieves nothing against the third.

## QUESTION IIII

Whether the precognitions of the subject, the attribute, and the principle must be had before

the demonstration, or also in the demonstration itself.

n order that the title of the question may be understood, it must be ex21

I       plained what it is to know something beforehand of something, and with what

necessity these precognitions of the three precognita must be had. To

know something beforehand of something is, before one thing is disputed or proved of

it, to know or presuppose another distinct thing, which is not proved but is pre‐

supposed as certain. For example: if we wish to demonstrate of man that he is ca‐

pable of wonder, or risible, before the intellect assents to the conclusion it must

understand that man is, and also what he is, and what the name risible signifies. For

unless these are known, the intellect will not be able to assent to the premises, nor

infer the conclusion from them. And this is the necessity of knowing beforehand.

But whether these things are to be known beforehand before the demonstration is

formed, or whether it is enough to know them beforehand while the premises are

being disposed and the intellect assents to them, this is the question.

22 On this the first opinion holds that they must necessarily be known beforehand

before the whole demonstration, and that it does not suffice in the demonstration it‐

self. So Toledo, who proves it by the testimony of Aristotle, who gave as examples

that most universal principle, Anything whatever either is or is not; and unity, which is

the principle of number, for the subject; and the triangle for the attribute: of

which it is evident that they are known before the whole demonstration; therefore

Aristotle meant that the precognitions are to be had before the demonstration,

and not in the demonstration itself.

He proves it also by reason: because the precognitions and precognita are pre‐

supposed to the science to be acquired; but the whole demonstration pertains to

the acquisition of science, since science is acquired through it; therefore before

the demonstration

[p. 607]

the precognitions must necessarily be had. For the solution of the question it should be noted that the precognitions and precognita can be considered in two ways: In common, and in particular; or in exercise, or in universal apprehension. As if we say that the principle is The whole is greater than its part; the subject, unity; and the common attribute, the triangle of a figure. For these hardly ever, or never, enter a demonstration, but are brought forward as most common examples and as it were speculative ones. But the subject, the attribute, and the principle are taken in particular for those things which enter a demonstration and pertain to the particular sciences: as the subject in the science of man is man; the attributes which are proved of him are wonder and risibility; the principle through which they are proved is his definition.

23 This supposed, our view asserts two things. The first is that the precognitions and precognita, considered under a universal ratio, are had before the demonstration. The second, that if they are considered in particular, that is, those which pertain to the particular sciences, they can indeed be had before the demonstration, and commonly are had before it; yet this is not necessary for the assent of the conclusion, nor for the acquisition of science, but they can be had in the demonstration itself, at the same time as the intellect disposes the premises and assents to them. This is the common opinion, which is held by Themistius in his Paraphrase on Posterior Analytics 1, chs. 1 and 2; St. Thomas, Cajetan, Paul of Venice, Soto, and the others on the present chapter. And there is no need to prove the first, since the opposite opinion grants it; but the second is proved by this reason: that is said to be known beforehand which is not proved through the demonstration but is presupposed before the assent of the conclusion. But the things that are known in the premises of the demonstration, and not before the integral demonstration, are not proved through the demonstration, but are presupposed before the assent of the conclusion; therefore they are truly and properly said to be known beforehand; and it suffices for the assent of the conclusion and the acquisition of science that they be known beforehand within the demonstration. But that they are commonly presupposed to the demonstration is manifest: because it is established by experience that we almost always know them before we form the demonstrative syllogism; but it could happen that one or another of them is not known to us, and then it suffices to perceive it while disposing the premises.

24 The testimony of Aristotle for the first opinion proves nothing against ours: because Aristotle, in the most common precognita,

[p. 608]

gave examples which, since they hardly ever or never enter a demonstration,

have to be precognized before it. But to the argument, the antecedent must be

distinguished: for by the acquisition of science we can understand the constitu‐

tion of the whole demonstration, and then it must be denied that the precogni‐

tions must necessarily be had before the acquisition of science. Or we under‐

stand only the assent of the conclusion, in which the acquisition of science

more properly consists (for the premises are rather the principles of the acquisi‐

tion than the acquisition); and in this more proper sense the antecedent is to be

granted, that they must be had before the acquisition of science; but from this

it does not follow that they must be had before the demonstration, as is mani‐

fest of itself.

Q U E S T I O N V.

Whether the assent of the conclusion comes about from the assent of the premises or princi‐

ples in the genus of efficient cause, or only of material cause.

his question has its foundation in the universal proposition of 25

T           Aristotle, who asserts that Doctrine or discipline, which is the judgment of

the conclusion, comes about from a preexisting judgment of the premises or

principles. Now that one thing comes about from another denotes

some genus of cause. And it can denote the material cause, as when we say that

a house comes about from wood and stones; or that intellective cognition

comes about from sensitive cognition: for this too denotes material causality,

because sensitive cognition concurs toward intellective cognition by determin‐

ing the matter, or the object, with which it must be concerned. And it can also

denote the efficient cause, as when we say that heat comes about from fire, or by

fire. Therefore we ask whether the assent of the conclusion comes about from the assent

of the principles in the genus of efficient cause, or of material cause only. And that it

comes about from it materially is most certain: because the conclusion is com‐

posed of the terms of the premises, namely of the major and minor extreme;

and moreover it is determined by the assent of the principles, because from

such principles the intellect can deduce such conclusions, and not other, differ‐

ent ones. And it is manifest that these things pertain to the genus of material

cause. But whether beyond the genus of material cause the efficient is also found in them,

so that the assents of the premises are efficient causes of the assent of the con‐

clusion, this is the question.

On this there is the first opinion, of Durandus, who denies them efficiency, in 2,

d. 2, q. 2, ad 4, on account of these two arguments. First: because an efficient

cause acts insofar as it is in act in the nature of things; for what is not can effect

nothing; but

when

[p. 606]

when the intellect assents to the conclusion, the assents of the principles no longer exist; therefore they cannot be its efficient cause. He proves the minor: because the intellect cannot have several acts or assents at the same time, but one after another; therefore when it has the assent of the conclusion, the assent of the premises has already passed: wherefore it will not be able to be its efficient cause. And, speaking universally, one act cannot have effective power over another.

Second: the assent of the principles, since it is had through the cognition of the terms alone, is distinguished in species from the assent of the conclusion, which is had through the middle of the demonstration; therefore if the former is the efficient cause of the latter, it will be an equivocal cause, distinct in species from its effect; but it cannot be an equivocal cause; therefore neither will it be efficient. The minor is proved: because an equivocal cause is universal and remote, as the heavens or the Sun; but the assent of the principles is the particular and proximate cause of the conclusion, as is manifest of itself; therefore it is not equivocal.

27 The second opinion is the opposite: That the assents of the principles are not only the material cause of the conclusion, but also the efficient cause. This is expressly held by St. Thomas on the present chapter, lect. 3, where he asserts that it is the opinion of Aristotle, Phys. 2; and Contra Gentiles 1, ch. 57, reason 4, where Ferrara expounds and follows him; and also by Gabriel, q. 8 of the prologue, doubt 2; Soto, q. 1 on this chapter, ad 2; Toledo in the exposition of the first text, note 3. And this is true and to be held.

It is proved by a twofold argument. First: because that which constitutes a power in first act concurs efficiently with it toward second act: as the species of a color, as the power of that same color, which is the object of sight, constitutes the visive power in first act for seeing, and therefore concurs efficiently with it toward the vision, which is second act; but through the species of the principles and the assent to them the intellect is constituted in first act for assenting to the conclusion; therefore the assent to them concurs efficiently toward the assent of the conclusion. I prove the minor: because the bare intellect is not a sufficient nor a complete cause of the assent of the conclusion unless it is informed by the assent of the principles; therefore this assent concurs by way of a form determining the intellect and constituting it in first act for the assent of the conclusion; but a form determining and constituting in first act is an efficient cause of the operation; therefore the assent of the principles concurs effectively toward the assent of the conclusion.

28 Second: the formal objective ratio is an efficient cause of the act, as is plain in the act of seeing, whose formal objective ratio

Qq

[p. 610]

is the visibility of that same color, and therefore it is an efficient cause. Likewise in human faith, whose formal objective ratio is the testimony of one worthy of credence, and therefore it is efficient of the act of believing; but the formal objective ratio on account of which the intellect assents to the conclusion is the assent of the principles, as Aristotle expressly teaches in the following chapter. And an evident reason proves it: because it is on account of the principles that the intellect assents to the conclusion; therefore it will be the efficient cause of the assent of the conclusion.

To the first argument of Durandus: the minor must be denied, namely that while the intellect assents to the conclusion the assents of the principles do not remain. And when it is said that the intellect cannot have several assents at the same time, a distinction must be made: because several assents can be related in two ways, either by way of many, when they are not ordered among themselves, or by way of one, when they are ordered. The intellect, then, cannot have several assents by way of many, but it can indeed by way of one; and so are related the assents of the principles and of the conclusion, which are ordered, since the former is the formal ratio of assenting to the latter. While, then, the intellect assents to the conclusion, it can persevere, and does persevere, in the assents of the principles, as it were continuing them; and therefore they can be the efficient cause of the assent of the conclusion. But that one act of the intellect cannot be the cause of another must be denied: for at least it can be a cause Quo [by which], although it is not a cause Quod [which], that is, the formal ratio of causing, although it is not that which causes. And so the assent of the principles is the formal ratio of assenting, although it is not the cause which effects the assent of the conclusion; but the intellect alone has this, by reason of that same assent of the principles; and therefore this assent is efficient Quo of the assent of the conclusion, not efficient Quod: as the truth of a thing is the efficient cause of the understanding of it as a cause Quo, not as a cause Quod.

29 To the second: the first consequence is to be granted, namely that the assent of the principles is an equivocal cause of the assent of the conclusion, because it is distinct in species from it; but the minor is to be denied, namely that only a universal and remote cause is equivocal: for every cause, whether universal or particular, proximate or remote, is truly equivocal, because the ratio of an equivocal cause does not consist in its being particular or universal, proximate or remote, but only in its being distinct in species from its effect: which is plain, because by the very fact that it is of the same species, it is univocal.

[p. 611]

## QUESTION VI

Whether the assent of the principles is formally included in the assent of the conclusion.

30

I   t is certain that the intellect assents by a different and prior act to the

premises, and then to the conclusion; and by one different indeed in

number and in species: because it assents to the principles on account of

themselves, that is, without any middle, but having only the signification of

the terms; but to the conclusion not on account of itself, but on account of

the principles, the assent to which is presupposed to the assent of the con‐

clusion. The question, then, is whether, after the intellect has had the assent

of the principles and comes to assent to the conclusion, it assents to it on ac‐

count of the principles in such a way that it repeats the assent to them again;

or whether it is enough, for it to be said to assent to the conclusion on ac‐

count of the principles, that it has had the assent to them immediately be‐

fore, without its repetition: for if it comes about in the first way, the assent

of the principles will be formally included in the assent of the conclusion;

but if in the second way, it will not be included formally, but only presupposi‐

tively: which is truly not to be included formally, but to be presupposed.

And the first opinion, which certain moderns follow, holds that it is indeed

necessarily presupposed, but that, since it is prior, and really and in species dis‐

tinct from the assent of the conclusion, it cannot be formally included in it.

It proves this by the testimony of Aristotle and by a twofold argument. For

Aristotle, in the books of the Prior Analytics, treating of the form of the syllo‐

gism, asserts that the middle is to be taken twice in the premises, and therefore is

not to be repeated in the conclusion, but in it one extreme is to be predicat‐

ed of the other. The syllogism would therefore sin in form if the middle en‐

tered the conclusion; but this must necessarily be granted if the assent of the

principles is formally included in the conclusion; therefore it cannot be in‐

cluded. I prove the minor thus: the premises are composed of the middle

and the extremes; therefore if they are repeated in the assent of the conclu‐

sion, the middle will necessarily have to be repeated in the conclusion; but it

cannot be included formally unless it is repeated, as is manifest of itself;

therefore it is false that it is formally included. Aristotle also asserts in the

present chapter, treating of the mode of demonstrating, that the cognition

of the conclusion comes about from the preexisting cognition of the princi‐

ples: if, then, the assent of the principles is preexisting with respect to the

assent of the conclusion, it will be presupposed, and consequently not for‐

mally included in it: for if it were formally included, it would be had at the

same time, and not before.

Q q ij

[p. 612]

31 The first argument of the same opinion is: because if the principles are formally included in the conclusion, then by the same act by which the intellect assents to the conclusion it assents also to the principles; but the assent of the conclusion is scientific, proceeding from the habit of science; therefore we would assent to the principles through an act and habit of science; but the consequent is false, because the assent of the conclusion is a discursive cognition, whereas the assent of the principles is intuitive and without discursive reasoning; therefore the latter cannot be formally included in the former. This is also proved to be impossible: because the assent of the principles is distinct in number and in species from the assent of the conclusion; therefore it cannot be formally included in it. The consequence is proved: because things that are thus distinct cannot formally include one another.

It is proved second: because in an evident syllogism a true conclusion is sometimes inferred from false premises, as is plain in this one: Every tree is an animal; every man is a tree; therefore every man is an animal. If, then, the premises are formally included in the conclusion, the false will be formally included in the true: which is repugnant. It can also be confirmed by experience: because in the conclusion only one extreme is joined with the other, no mention being made there of the middle; it is joined, therefore, on account of the middle as presupposed, not as formally included, but at most virtually. The consequence is proved: because formal inclusion is impossible without formal mention or repetition.

The second opinion affirms that the assent of the principles is not only presupposed to the assent of the conclusion, but formally included in it. So St. Thomas, 1-2, q. 8, a. 3, in these words: First someone understands the principles themselves according to themselves; but afterwards he understands them in the conclusions themselves, inasmuch as he assents to the conclusions on account of the principles. He holds the same also in q. 12, a. 4. St. Thomas is followed by Capreolus in 1, d. 2, q. 1, in the solution to the arguments against the 4th conclusion; Ferrara, Contra Gentiles 1, ch. 57; Soncinas, Metaph. 6, q. 10; Durandus in 2, d. 38, q. 3, ad 3; who all teach that the intellect is borne by the same act to the conclusion and to the principles, since it assents to it on account of the principles: which cannot come about otherwise unless the assent of the principles is formally included in the assent of the conclusion.

32 Next, this is proved by a quite efficacious argument: any power is borne by the same act to its object and to its formal ratio, as sight is borne by the same act to color and to the ratio of visibility; or to color and light, if light stands on the side of the object in the vision of color. And the reason for this is evident: because from the object which is perceived and from the formal ratio of perceiving it there is constituted one total and complete object, as

[p. 613]

from a Quo and a Quod; but the assent of the principles is the formal objective ratio of assenting to the conclusion; therefore the intellect is borne by the same act to the conclusion, which is the object to which it assents, and to the principles, which are the rationes of assenting; but it cannot be borne to the principles by the same act unless they are formally included in the object of that same act; therefore it is necessary that they be formally included; especially since the assent of the conclusion is distinguished in species from human faith and from opinion solely on account of the different formal ratio of assenting: which in opinion is a probable reason, in human faith the testimony of one worthy of credence, in scientific assent principles evident per se.

34 It is proved second by induction in the acts of the intellect and of the will: for in the act of faith the testimony of one worthy of credence is formally included, because it is the formal ratio of believing; as in the act of the will by which we will the means the willing of the end is included, as the ratio of willing the means; as in the act by which we will to take a potion for the sake of health the act of intention by which we will health is formally included; but the assent of the principles is the formal and actual ratio on account of which we assent to the conclusion; therefore it is actually and formally included in the assent of the conclusion.

But in order that the truth of our view may be understood, and the opposing arguments better solved, it should be noted that the principles and the conclusion, and the assent of each, can be considered in two ways. First, insofar as the intellect assents to the principles per se and from the cognition of the terms alone, and to the conclusion as to another, distinct object, not considering that it assents to it on account of the principles: since it is established that it can assent to it on account of another reason, as on account of the testimony of one worthy of credence, or on account of a probable argument. And in this way neither are the premises included in the conclusion, nor the assent to them. In the second way they are considered insofar as they have order and dependence among themselves: namely the conclusion, as the intellect assents to it on account of the principles; and the principles, as they are the cause of the conclusion, as the formal ratio of assenting; and this dependence and this order is essential to the assent of the conclusion, just as the order and dependence of the assent of faith on testimony is intrinsic to it. It is evident, then, that the assent of the conclusion essentially includes the order of dependence on the assent of the principles, as on the formal objective ratio.

35 But where an order is formally contained, that at which the order itself terminates is consequently contained; therefore in the assent of the conclusion the assent of the principles is also consequently contained, as the term of the essential dependence which it has

Q q iij

[p. 614]

on it, the assent of the conclusion. Thus the assent is not contained formally or essentially in the assent, since they are distinguished in species and in number; but the order of dependence of the one on the other is contained formally, and consequently the assent itself on which it essentially depends. Hence the order of dependence is included as something intrinsic and formal; but the assent as something extrinsic, on which it depends, and without which that same essential order of dependence can neither be nor be understood. It is, however, actually included, because the order is actual; nor is it included as Quod, but only as Quo, because only as the ratio of assenting. We can adduce an example of this in the vision of color, supposing that light is necessary on the side of the object for seeing: for then sight is borne by the same act to the color and to the light; not in such a way that the light is that which is seen, but the formal ratio of seeing; nor is the light itself included in the color itself which is seen, nor indeed in the object of the act of seeing as something intrinsic; but because color, as the object of sight, has an essential order of dependence on light, since it can neither be nor be understood without it, therefore light too is actually included in the object of vision, through which the color is seen, as the term of the actual objective dependence. Thus, then, it is to be understood that the principles and the assent to them are included in the conclusion and in the assent to it: because the order of dependence on them is essential to the assent of the conclusion; and because this order is actually, formally, and essentially included in the assent of the conclusion, it is necessary that the principles too, and the assent to them, be actually and formally included: not as intrinsic to it, but as that without which the essential order itself can neither be nor be understood.

36 From this doctrine, then, the reply is made to the testimonies of Aristotle. To the first, indeed: by granting that the middle ought not to enter the conclusion; nor does it follow from our view that it enters formally: because the principles do not enter as Quod, that is, as that to which the intellect assents, but only as Quo. Therefore they are not to be formally expressed or repeated in the conclusion; but it suffices to express or repeat the extremes formally, and to join them with an actual dependence on the principles, and consequently on the middle, so that they are formally included although they are not expressed: just as in the act of faith we do not express the testimony by saying that we believe on account of the testimony of one worthy of credence, but only that which is believed is expressed; yet by reason of the actual dependence on that same testimony the testimony is deemed included, although it is not expressed. To the second

[p. 615]

testimony, we reply: the cognition of the conclusion comes about from the preexisting cognition of the principles, presupposed indeed as Quod, but included in it as Quo; that is, as the ratio of assenting to that same conclusion.

To the first argument: everything it assumes and concludes is to be granted except the last consequence, which it infers in this way: therefore the intellect would assent to the principles through an act and habit of science. For this is to be denied: because the principles, or the assent to them, are not included in the assent of the conclusion as that to which the intellect assents, but as the ratio of assenting; whence it follows only that the intellect assents to the conclusion through an act and habit of science on account of the principles.

But as for what is said, that the assent of the principles is distinguished in species and in number from the assent of the conclusion: it is true; but from this it follows only that it cannot be included in it as something intrinsic to it, but as something extrinsic, without which the essential order of dependence on it, which the assent of the conclusion includes, can neither be nor be understood. For numerical or specific difference does not take away this mode of inclusion, as is manifest of itself.

To the second: the antecedent is to be granted, and the consequence denied, namely that the false is included in the true: because a true conclusion does not follow from the premises as false, but as so disposed in syllogistic form; wherefore it is inferred only that they, as so disposed, are included in the assent of the conclusion as Quo, in the manner already explained.

To the confirmation: the antecedent is to be granted, that in the conclusion only the extremes are joined, no mention being made of the middle; but because they are joined through the middle, that is, with an actual and formal dependence on it, it is necessary that the middle be formally included in such a conjunction, which is the very assent of the conclusion; nevertheless, because it is not included as Quod, that is, as that to which the intellect assents through the assent of the conclusion, but as Quo, that is, as the formal and actual ratio by which it assents to that same conclusion, therefore it is not expressed, nor is express mention made of it; nor indeed can it be expressed without a sin against syllogistic form.

QUESTION VII. Whether, once the assent of the premises is had, the intellect assents to the conclusion in

the same instant.

I   f the premises are disposed in the due order which the syllogistic and

demonstrative form requires of them, it is certain that the assent of the major,

Q q iiij

[p. 616]

can be had prior in time to the assent of the minor and of the conclusion. Because it is the universal proposition, under which the minor is to be subsumed as a particular, and from both of which the conclusion is to be inferred, therefore it does not depend on the assent of the minor and of the conclusion.

38 It is certain also that if the order of disposing the premises is not observed, the assent of the minor too can be had prior in time to the assent of the major and of the conclusion: because while the minor is not subordinated to the major, it can be without it; and if it is had in this way, it is not necessary that the conclusion be immediately inferred from it. For example: the intellect can have this assent of the major, Every rational animal is risible, prior in time to having the assent of the minor, Man is a rational animal, and this assent of the conclusion, Every man is risible. It can also, no order being observed, have the second prior in time to the first and the third: about these, then, there can be no doubt.

But only whether, the assents of the major and minor being had, disposed and ordered, it is necessary to have the assent of the conclusion at the same time; or whether those can be had prior to the having of this one. And with respect to priority of nature it is certain that those are had first, because they are the cause of the assent of the conclusion, and a cause is prior by nature to its effect. The question therefore proceeds concerning priority of time: whether the intellect can have the assent of the major and minor, disposed in this instant, and not have the assent of the conclusion in the same instant; or whether it is necessary that it follow from them in the same instant and be had simultaneously in time with them.

And it seems that it is not necessary that it be had in the same instant: because the intellect cannot understand many things at the same time, as Aristotle teaches in Topics 2, ch. 3, place 33, in these words: For it happens that one knows many things, but does not think of them, understanding by thinking actual cognition; but the premises and the conclusion are many; therefore it will not be able to understand them at the same time, that is, in the same instant. And if you say that they are indeed many, but have the mode of one, inasmuch as they are ordered in the same syllogism: there is still a twofold further impediment.

39 The first: because it can have an error contrary to the conclusion, too deeply rooted in the subject through many acts; then, therefore, it will not be able to expel it immediately through the assent of the conclusion, and therefore not to assent to it immediately either. The second: because the capacity of the intellect, by which it can understand many things at the same time, is finite; therefore if the number of the things it can actually consider is filled by the assents of the premises, it will not be able to have the assent of the conclusion at the same time until it lets another go.

[p. 617]

The true opinion, however, is that the assent of the conclusion follows in the

same instant from the assents of the premises. The reason for this is: because, as

Aristotle taught in the present chapter, it comes about from their terms and

is contained in them virtually, as in a cause, or as a tree in its seed; therefore

there can be no impediment to its following from them immediately.

To the testimony of Aristotle the reply is that it is to be understood of

many things as they are many, that is, diverse, and in no way ordered among

themselves or to a third: for things that are understood by way of one are not

said to be many simply, but one; but the assents of the premises and the con‐

clusions are related by way of one, because they are ordered in the same syl‐

logism; therefore they can be had by the intellect at the same time. Nor does

the impediment of error stand in the way of this: for since demonstration is

the stronger cause, it immediately overcomes and expels it; and even if it is

too deeply rooted, it will not impede the assent of the conclusion, nor the

habit of science, which is produced through that demonstration in the same

instant; but it will remain together with it until it is altogether expelled by

multiplied demonstrations. For it is not repugnant that contrary habits, re‐

miss, should remain together in the same subject, just as neither are contrary

qualities, remiss, such as heat and cold. The other impediment, finally, con‐

cerning the finite capacity of the intellect (about which Soto spends many

words on the present chapter), is without difficulty: for although the intellect

can understand only two or four different things at the same time, and actu‐

ally considers one or three, when it comes to constitute a demonstration it

will be able to have the assents of the premises and of the conclusion at the

same time, since they have the mode of one, although they are three.

## QUESTION VIII

Whether, once the assents of the premises are had, the intellect is free to assent to the

conclusion, or whether it is necessary to have the assent to it in the same instant.

he freedom of the will is twofold, of Contrariety and of 40

T           Contradiction: and the former is also called freedom as to specifica‐

tion, the latter freedom as to exercise. Freedom of contrariety is that

the will can have a good and a bad act, or the intellect assent or

dissent. And it is called of contrariety because a good and a bad act are con‐

traries, and so too are the assent and dissent of the intellect. But of specifica‐

tion, because acts receive their species from the object. Freedom of contradic‐

tion is that the will or the intellect can exercise an act, or

[p. 618]

suspend it: because to have an act and not to have it are contradictorily opposed. And to exercise an act or not to exercise it denotes the exercise of the power. Now the intellect, although it has a certain radical ratio of freedom, inasmuch as the formal freedom of the will has its origin from the fact that the intellect can propose several objects to it, and therefore the will is able to operate about one or the other as it pleases, nevertheless the will alone has formal freedom, which consists in this, that it wills to apply itself to operating or wills not to operate: from which the intellect participates it, inasmuch as it can be applied to understanding, not by itself but by the will, and can also be diverted or removed from understanding.

Which supposed, we ask: Whether, the evident assents of the major and minor being had, the intellect can, through dependence on the will, suspend the assent of the conclusion, so that in the same instant it either does not operate, or is diverted by the will to operating about another object different from the assent of the conclusion; or whether it is altogether necessitated to assent to that same conclusion.

41 Now it is certain that it is necessitated as far as pertains to specification, so that it is not free for it to assent or dissent; but if it operates about the proposed object, it must assent to the conclusion, and can in no way dissent: because from true and necessary assents of the principles nothing but a true and necessary assent can proceed; therefore if any proceeds, it must be assent; dissent cannot be. For just as the will cannot pursue the good, as good represented to it, with hatred, so the intellect cannot dissent from the true and necessary as proposed to it as such. The question, then, is: whether it can not assent to the conclusion, or, what is the same, suspend the assent, by ceasing altogether from operation or by operating about something else.

And the first opinion is that of certain moderns, who assert that the intellect can in no way suspend the assent of the conclusion, but necessarily elicits it. They prove it first: because the assents of the principles are per se evident and necessary, and contain virtually the assent of the conclusion, and indeed by a natural containment, as a seed virtually contains a tree and a tree its fruit; therefore the intellect is convinced by them naturally to assent to the conclusion; but natural necessity is not subject to the freedom of the will, as is plain in the act of the nutritive power, which the will cannot suspend so as to keep it from converting the food applied to it into the substance of the living thing; therefore the will will not be able to suspend the act of the intellect so as to keep it from assenting immediately to the conclusion.

[p. 619]

Second: because as the intention of the end is related in the will to the choice of the means, so the assent of the principles is related in the intellect to the assent of the conclusion, as St. Thomas teaches, 1-2, q. 8, a. 3, and with him the whole school; but it is certain among all that, given an efficacious intention of the end and the will persevering in it, it cannot suspend the act of choice, but is altogether necessitated to choose some means for attaining it; therefore, the assent of the principles being had and the intellect persevering in it, it cannot in any way suspend the act of the conclusion.

The second opinion is the opposite: that even given the assents of the premises, the intellect can suspend the assent of the conclusion, so that it is diverted by the will to operating about another object. This is now followed by the greater part of the moderns, and it is contained in the doctrine of St. Thomas, and therefore is to be held by us.

But in order that we may explain it and prove it at the same time, two things are to be noted from the doctrine of St. Thomas, now received by all. The first is that the intellect is subject to the will as to the exercise of its act, that is, as to its application to operating, or its removal from this or that operation: so St. Thomas teaches, 1-2, q. 9, a. 1, ad 3, in these words: The will moves the intellect as to the exercise of its act: because the true itself, which is the perfection of the intellect, is contained under the universal good, as a certain particular good.

43 From which this distinction is deduced: Just as the good is twofold, the Highest and most perfect, in which every ratio of good is contained, such as God is, and the Particular and limited, such as is any created good; in the same way the true is twofold, the Highest and most perfect, containing every ratio of the true, as God likewise is, and the Particular and limited, such as is any created truth, whether it be an evident principle or a conclusion deduced from it. Moreover, just as the will is free about any particular good whatever, whether it be an end or a means, so that it can operate or not operate about it, but about the highest good perfectly known, such as is God clearly seen by the blessed, it has no freedom, but is altogether necessitated to love it: in the same way the intellect is free about any particular truth through its dependence on the will, so that it can be applied by the will to operating about it and diverted from operation; but about the highest truth clearly shown to it, it has no freedom, nor can it be diverted by the will from operating about it. And St. Thomas gives the reason for this: because any particular truth, and the operation of the intellect about it, is also a particular good; but about any particular good whatever,

[p. 620]

the will is not necessitated, but can will it and not will it; therefore the will is free to will to apply the intellect to operating about any particular truth whatever, or to divert it from operating about it: not, however, about the universal and most perfect truth clearly shown to it, such as God is in the fatherland. Because every power is naturally determined to operate about that which most perfectly contains every ratio of its object, so that while it is offered to it, it cannot suspend its operation; but God clearly seen most perfectly contains every ratio of the true; therefore neither can the will suspend the act proposed to it by the intellect about him, nor the intellect its act about him clearly shown to it. Because, just as he is the universal good, so to operate about him is the universal good of the power; and therefore for the intellect to see him clearly is its highest good, and the highest good of the will; and so neither can the will fail to love him, nor divert the intellect from the clear vision of him.

45 From this whole doctrine is gathered this reason, which efficaciously proves our view: the will is not necessitated to operate about any particular good; therefore neither is the intellect about a particular truth. The consequence is proved, supposing that the intellect is subject to the will as to application, or the exercise of operating: because for the intellect to operate about a particular truth is its particular good, and also a particular good of the will; therefore it does not necessitate the will to apply the intellect so that it operates about it, but the will is free to apply it or divert it. But the conclusion of a demonstration is a certain particular truth; therefore, even when the assent of the principles is had, the will is not necessitated to apply the intellect so that it assents to the conclusion, but it can divert it from assenting.

46 Second, it should be noted from the doctrine of the same St. Thomas, 1-2, q. 50, a. 1 and 3, deduced from Aristotle and also received by all, that a power is not capable of a habit except in order to an object about which it can operate freely: whence a wholly natural power, having no freedom in its operations, at least by participation in the will, is not capable of a habit, nor can it acquire one, however frequently it operates: as is plain in the visive power, which is not capable of a habit for seeing, nor can it acquire one through frequent acts of vision. But the intellect acquires through the assents of the principles a habit, which is called understanding; and, the assents of the principles being had, it also acquires the habit of science through the assent of the conclusion,

[p. 621]

according to the common opinion of the whole School. Therefore it has some freedom in the assent to the principles, and, having had that, in the assent to the conclusion. But the least freedom is to be able to assent and to suspend assent; therefore it cannot be denied that it has this.

47 To the first argument of the opposite opinion: The antecedent is to be granted together with the consequence, but the consequent is to be distinguished, namely that the intellect is compelled by the assent to the principles to assent to the conclusion. For although it is compelled as to the specification of the act (because, if it operates about the conclusion, it is not free to elicit an act of dissent, but it must necessarily assent to it), yet as to the exercise it is not compelled: because the intellect is not a purely natural power, as sight is, nor does it operate altogether from determination to one, as that does; but it is subject to the command of the will, about any particular truth whatever, as to application or exercise. And so it can be applied by the will to assenting to the principles and to the conclusion (which are particular truths), and diverted from assent to them.

To the second: The antecedent is to be distinguished: because the assent to the principles stands in the intellect, with respect to the assent to the conclusion, as the intention of the end stands in the will with respect to the election of the means, as to one thing, but as to another it stands in a different manner.

48 For they agree in this: that just as the will per se primarily tends to the end, and from the intention of the end is moved to the means, so the intellect per se primarily is moved to the assent to the principles, and from the assent to the principles is moved to the assent to the conclusion. They differ, however, in that the will does not elect the means on account of the end regarded in any way whatever, but on account of attaining it; and from this it comes about that, if it wishes to persevere in the intention of the end, it cannot suspend the act of election, but, although it is free for it to elect one means or another, it cannot fail to elect some one. But in the intellect this is not found, because the assent to the conclusion is not ordered to the attainment of some end, but has only the necessity of the consequence: because it is virtually contained in the principles, from which it proceeds through an evident consequence. But to proceed or not to proceed depends on the application of the will to eliciting the assent; which application is free, as we have proved, since it is about some particular truth, distinct from the principles themselves. Whence the will is free to apply the intellect or to divert it from assenting.

[p. 622]

## CHAPTER II

## TEXT OF ARISTOTLE

We think, moreover, that we know each thing simply, and not in the sophistical manner, etc.

B R I E F E X P O S I T I O N O F T H E T E X T.

n the preceding chapter Aristotle taught that science exists, and is acquired 1

I        anew through demonstration, from preexisting cognition of the principles. In this

second chapter, however, he intends to teach what science is and what

demonstration is. And it is divided into three parts. In the first he hands down one

definition of science and a twofold one of demonstration. In the second he defines princi‐

ple, and divides it by a twofold division. And in the third he teaches and proves that

the principles, or premises, are better known than the conclusion.

He defines to know, that is, science in the concrete, in many words, from

which these few are to be taken, by which a brief definition is assigned: To know

is to cognize the cause of the thing, and that it is the cause of that, and that it cannot be oth‐

erwise. By which Aristotle defines only the most perfect science, which he calls

science Propter quid (for he promises to treat of science Quia, which is less per‐

fect, in ch. 10 of this book), for having which he affirms that a threefold condi‐

tion is required. The first is that we cognize the cause of the conclusion. The second,

that we cognize such a cause to be the cause not only according to our cognition but also ac‐

cording to the thing: for when we prove that man is rational because he is risible,

risible is prior in our intellect, and therefore it is the cause of cognizing rational,

but it is not the cause of its being; rather it is its effect. And therefore we do not

have science Propter quid of rational, but only Quia. The third condition is that

we cognize it to be not only a cause of being, but a necessary cause, so that, it being posit‐

ed, the effect necessarily follows: for this is signified by those words, And that it

cannot be otherwise. Aristotle explains the whole definition most briefly, saying: To

know is to understand through demonstration; because, if the demonstration is truly

Propter quid, those three conditions are found in the premises with respect to

the conclusion.

2 Next he defines demonstration by a twofold definition, the first of which

runs thus: Demonstration is a scientific syllogism, or a syllogism producing knowl‐

edge; and it is a final definition, because the end of demonstration is to generate

science; and this science generated through demonstration is the assent to its

conclusion, generated from the premises.

[p. 623]

3 The second definition is material. For just as from the end for the sake of which a house is made, namely that it may defend us from rains and other injuries of the weather, we gather of what material parts it ought to consist, namely of timbers, stones, and other parts disposed in such a way: so Aristotle, from the end of demonstration, gathers of what parts, disposed and ordered, demonstration ought to consist, as if arguing thus: Demonstration is ordered to generating science as to its end; therefore it ought to be such that it proceeds from things true, first, immediate, better known, prior, and causes of the conclusion. He proves the single parts of the definition; and first, that demonstration proceeds from things true, in this way: The object of science ought to have being; therefore what is not is not known; but the false is nothing; therefore there cannot be science of it. Therefore the conclusion of a demonstration, whose assent is science, must be true; therefore it ought to proceed from true premises as from a cause. The consequence is proved: because the false, since it is nothing, cannot be the cause of the true. That demonstration proceeds from first things he proves second: because unless the premises are principles evident per se formally, that is, such that, once the signification of the terms is cognized, the intellect at once assents to them, or at least virtually, if he who makes the demonstration knows how to reduce them to principles known per se through other demonstrations, he will not have science of the conclusion, nor consequently a true demonstration, but only a Dialectical syllogism and an assent of opinion concerning the conclusion. He proves finally, third, that it proceeds from things better known, prior, and causes of the conclusion. Because to know is to cognize a thing through its cause; therefore the premises ought to be the true cause of the conclusion; but a cause is prior to and better known than its effect; therefore they ought to be prior and better known: not only as regards us, in which way that is prior which is better known to us, although according to nature it is posterior, as an effect is better known to us than the cause, and therefore prior as regards our cognition; but the premises ought to be prior to and better known than the conclusion from the nature of the thing, which they will be if according to the thing they are its causes, as has been explained.

4 In the second part of ch. 2: Because he had said that demonstration ought to proceed from first things, that is, from premises which are indemonstrable principles, he defines indemonstrable principle in this way: A principle is an immediate proposition of demonstration. And he explains what it is to be a proposition of demonstration, or demonstrative, and what it is to be immediate. A proposition, he says, is one part of an enunciation, stating one thing. For an enunciation is divided into affirmative and negative. Therefore to be a proposition

[p. 624]

of demonstration is the same as to be an affirmative or negative enunciation which is posited in the demonstration as a premise, for inferring the conclusion; and therefore it ought to be true and necessary, so that it may be distinguished from a Dialectical proposition, which is only probable and therefore can be false. But an immediate proposition is one to which there is no other prior; that is, which does not have another through which it could be demonstrated, but to which the intellect assents from the cognition of the terms alone.

5 Next he divides principle into two members, namely into dignity and position. A dignity, or ἀξίωμα, is an immediate and indemonstrable proposition so universal and manifest that its truth is plain to all; and perhaps it is called a dignity for this reason, because it is worthy that all should assent to it. And for this cause also Aristotle says that all who wish to acquire any science ought to cognize the dignities before they approach to learning it. Such are: Anything whatever is or is not; The whole is greater than its part; and the like. But a position, or θέσις, is a proposition known per se and indemonstrable, but neither so universal as an ἀξίωμα, nor one whose truth is manifest to all; and therefore it is not necessary that he who begins to learn some science should cognize it beforehand, but he can then receive it by himself or from a master. And such are all the principles of the particular sciences, such as definitions. And there is another difference between dignity and position: that dignities scarcely or never enter a demonstration, but are presupposed by all sciences, whereas positions are the premises of a demonstration; and therefore they are called positions, because they are posited in the demonstration for inferring the conclusion.

He divides position again into that which contains the true or the false; and this is the proposition which they call a supposition, because it is posited under such a disposition in the demonstration for inferring the conclusion. And into that which contains neither the true nor the false, but from which a supposition can be made; and he says it is a definition: as rational animal is a principle which is called a definition, from which another principle can be made which is a supposition: as if we say, Man is a rational animal, it is a supposition, because it contains the true or the false.

6 In the third part he teaches that the principles, or premises of a demonstration, ought to be more evident and more certain than the conclusion of the same demonstration. Which he proves from that common axiom: That on account of which each thing is such is itself more so. As, if I love Peter on account of John, I love John more than Peter. But to the conclusion of the demonstration

the

[p. 629]

On Book 1 of the Posterior Analytics, Chap. 2, Quest. 1.  625 the intellect assents on account of the premises; therefore it assents more strongly and more certainly to the premises; wherefore they ought to be more certain and better known than the conclusion.

## QUESTION I

Whether the second definition of demonstration is good.

T     his question is proposed not so much to discuss the difficulty of the matter

as to elucidate Aristotle’s definition and to show that it is exact. In order that this may be done, we shall propose two arguments against it, from the solution of which this will become manifest. The first is: Because a definition ought to be given through genus and difference, or through something which is posited in place of the genus or difference; but nothing is posited for the genus in this definition, as its words show, by which it is distinguished from other argumentations, while in none of them does it agree with them; therefore it altogether lacks a genus, and therefore it is not entire or complete.

9 The second: Because a good definition ought not to have even one superfluous word; but this one has many such; therefore it is not good. The minor is proved: because for demonstration to proceed from first things and from prior things is the same, for first and prior signify altogether the same thing; therefore one of them is redundant. Moreover, a cause is prior to and better known than its effect; therefore he who says that demonstration proceeds from causes says that it ought to proceed from things prior and better known; it would therefore suffice to posit in the definition the phrase from causes, and thus the two others, namely from things prior and better known, seem superfluous and make the whole definition faulty. And finally, that it proceeds from first things and from immediate or indemonstrable things is the same, since it is the same for the principles of a demonstration to be first and to be immediate or indemonstrable; therefore some one of these words is superfluous.

Nevertheless I prove that this definition is good thus: A definition is good through which the nature of the definitum is sufficiently explained and distinguished from the rest; but this definition of demonstration performs these two things, explaining the nature of demonstration and distinguishing it from the other argumentations; therefore it is to be judged exact. The minor is proved: because this definition explains the parts of which demonstration ought to consist, namely true and necessary premises, which are true and per se causes of the conclusion, and which are so disposed that the conclusion is evidently inferred from them. And a demonstration constituted of these is essentially distinguished from the other species of argumentation, with which it agrees in the remote genus of argumentation, and with the dialectical syllogism in the genus

Rr

[p. 626]

proximate genus of syllogism. Which genus is without doubt understood by Aristotle, nor was it necessary to posit it expressly in the definition: because in the books of the Prior Analytics, immediately preceding, he had defined the syllogism; and in the first definition of the same demonstration, handed down in the present chapter, he expressly posited the same syllogism as the genus, saying: Demonstration is a scientific syllogism, or one producing knowledge. Wherefore the second definition ought to be assigned in these words: Demonstration is a syllogism proceeding from things true, first, immediate, better known, and prior, and causes of the conclusion: so that through syllogism it agrees in the immediate genus with the dialectical syllogism; and through the same particle the other argumentations are judged separated from it, and also the sophistical syllogism, which, since it sins in form, is not a syllogism simply but in a certain respect, and therefore does not agree with demonstration in syllogism as in a genus, but only analogically; and for that reason it is thus judged separated. But by the other particles of the definition demonstration is distinguished from the Dialectical syllogism, which proceeds from very different things, as will be said in the Topics. And from these things the definition of demonstration remains explained, and the first argument solved.

9 To the second: The minor is to be denied, namely that in this definition some word is superfluous: because, although certain of them signify the same thing, yet each signifies a different ratio of the same thing, which is enough for none to be superfluous. Thus, for the principles to be first and to be immediate or indemonstrable denote different rationes of the principles. For a principle is called first in order to the conclusion, which is not first, but derived from the first; but immediate or indemonstrable with respect to another prior middle through which it could be demonstrated, which it lacks. The principles are also called first on account of their dignity, and prior on account of their causality. Finally, a cause has a twofold dignity with respect to its effect: both that it is prior by nature to it, and that it is better known; and although the one follows from the other, they are nevertheless distinguished in ratio. Wherefore there is no word in the definition which does not signify some ratio or dignity of the principles distinct from that which another signifies, which is enough for none to be superfluous. Indeed, it was necessary to posit all those words in the definition, so that all the rationes of the principles might be expressed, and the ratio and dignity of demonstration might be handed down more explicitly. One thing, however, is to be noted: that when demonstration is said to proceed from causes, by causes are understood not only those from which the effect really proceeds, but those which

[p. 617]

rationes are prior to others. For of being its properties or attributes are demonstrated in Metaphysics, as that it is one, true, and good; and of God we demonstrate that he is eternal because he is immutable, and this through true demonstrations; and yet there cannot be true causality between the one and the other, since there is not even a distinction from the nature of the thing; but the priority of reason which our intellect posits between them suffices for a true demonstration.

QUESTION II. In how many ways a proposition is known per se, and whether every immediate proposition

is to be called known per se.

C     oncerning the definition and division of a proposition known per se, St.

Thomas and Soto do not seem to think in the same way, and consequently neither do the followers of each. For St. Thomas, On Truth q. 10, a. 12, Contra Gentiles bk. 1, ch. 10 and 11, and 1 p., q. 2, a. 1, thus defines a proposition known per se: A proposition known per se is one whose predicate is included in the intrinsic ratio of the subject: as Man is an animal. Next he first divides the proposition known per se into that which is known per se according to its own nature, and not as regards us; and into that which is known per se also as regards us.

10 Known per se by its nature and not as regards us is that whose predicate is truly intrinsic with respect to the subject, but we are ignorant of it; and such will be that in which a definition unknown to us is predicated of its definitum.
