And such a conjunction of the middle with the extremities of which the principle of the subalternate science to be demonstrated is composed is the continuation of the inferior science with the superior; and in this continuation consists the formal ratio of subalternation. All of which is made manifest by this example. A principle of the subalternate science (namely of perspective), which it neither knows nor can demonstrate within its own limits, is this: A thing far off is seen under a smaller, or more acute, angle. And it is demonstrated thus by the subalternating science, namely by geometry: A thing which is seen under a more protracted angle is seen under a smaller angle (for a more protracted angle is more acute, and therefore smaller); but a thing seen from far off is seen through a more protracted, or longer, angle, as is manifest; therefore it is seen under a smaller angle. Behold the geometrical middle, namely that a more protracted angle is smaller, which could not demonstrate that principle of perspective unless it were joined with the extremities of which it is composed, namely with the thing seen from far off and with the smaller angle; and unless, so joined with them, it produced each premise of the same demonstration through which that same principle would be demonstrated, as a conclusion composed of the same extremities,

[p. 684]

And behold the subalternate science continued with the subalternating science in the same demonstration, through such conjunctions. And that which effects the continuation is the middle of the subalternating science, as joined in the premises with the extremities of which the principle of the subalternate science, demonstrated through it, is composed.

And this continuation does not take away the distinction of the two sciences, as will be proved presently.

42 From these things it is understood, first, how it is possible that the subalternating science should prove the principles of the subalternate science by demonstration a priori, even though it abstracts from sensible matter and the principles to be proved regard that matter: for it does this through the union of its own middle with the extremities of the principle to be proved, with which it is joined in the premises; and through that conjunction it descends, as it were, and is contracted through them to sensible matter; and through such contraction it is continued with it.

43 Now, therefore, the arguments of the opposite opinion are easily solved. To the first: we grant the antecedent, that the subalternate science renders the proximate cause of its conclusion; but we deny the consequence, that it demonstrates them within its own limits. For to a true demonstration it is not enough to render the cause; rather it is required to render all the causes up to the first: otherwise it will not have a certain assent to the premises, since it does not know how to reduce them up to principles known per se and indemonstrable; and therefore it will have neither true science of the conclusion nor a true demonstration of it.

But to the other point which is added in the same argument, namely that the Arithmetician alone would be a musician, and the geometer alone a perspectivist, if these alone are said to demonstrate a priori the conclusions of music and of perspective, it must be denied: because the principles of any science, through which its conclusions are demonstrated, do not pertain to the habit of such a science, but to another distinct habit, which is called the habit of principles; and therefore they do not receive the denomination of the science, nor do they have a denomination from the sciences. But the principles of the subalternate science, which are demonstrated by the subalternating science, are related to its principles, through which they are demonstrated, as their conclusions; and therefore they do not pertain to it, but to another, inferior habit, which is the subalternate science.

44 Wherefore neither is the Geometer denominated a perspectivist, nor the Arithmetician denominated a musician; just as neither are the conclusions of music called geometry; although it is true that one is not denominated a musician truly knowing unless he is at the same time an Arithmetician, nor a perspectivist knowing unless he is at the same time a geometer,

[p. 685]

To the second, we grant the first and the second consequence, namely that the principles of the subalternate science are conclusions of the subalternating science; we deny, however, that they cannot be joined to them in the same demonstration. For although the principles of the subalternating science abstract from sensible matter, they can nevertheless be determined, and as it were contracted, through the principles of the subalternate science, so as to construct the same demonstration, as has been explained. And through this union of the principles of the one with the principles of the other, as their conclusions, the distinction of the two sciences is not taken away; just as, through the union of the principles of any science with its conclusions in the same demonstrations, the distinction of the habit of science from the habit of principles is not taken away. Especially since the subalternate and the subalternating science always have diverse objects, abstracting from matter in a diverse manner, from which the distinction of the habits is plainly gathered. And if anyone should ask what, then, or in what manner it must be said that the subalternate science demonstrates within its own limits, or how one must speak of it, I reply: if within its own limits is taken precisely, it can have no demonstration propter quid, nor even quia, nor can it demonstrate any conclusion. Whence, taken in this way, it is not a science either: because, taken under this precision, it does not know how to demonstrate its own principles, which are truly demonstrable; therefore it will not have a certain assent to them; and therefore it will not be able to infer a certain or scientific conclusion. As for demonstration quia, it is certain that it does not have it under the formal ratio of subalternate science, because as such it does not proceed from the effect but from the cause. It demonstrates its conclusions, therefore, only by demonstration propter quid, with the help of the subalternating science, as it is continued with it; wherefore only in this manner is it a true subalternate science.

## CHAPTER XXVI

## TEXT OF ARISTOTLE

But the knowable and science differ from the opinable and opinion, since science is

universal.

B R I E F E X P O S I T I O N O F T H E T E X T.

he intention of Aristotle in this chapter is to distinguish science from

T         opinion, after he has distinguished the sciences from one another in

these intermediate chapters, from the tenth up to this twenty-sixth.

And it is divided into two parts. In the first, he asserts and proves that science and the knowable are distinguished from opinion

[p. 686]

and the opinable. In the second, he proposes two doubts to be solved in the contrary sense.

Aristotle’s conclusion is this: Science and the knowable, on the one side, differ from opinion and the opinable, on the other. Which he proves by this argument: Science is concerned with the universal and necessary: therefore the knowable is universal and necessary; but opinion is concerned with the contingent, and often with the particular, or even the singular: therefore the opinable is contingent and particular: therefore science is diverse from opinion, and the knowable from the opinable. He proves the antecedent, on the side of science, because, as was said in ch. 2, science is of things which cannot be otherwise: therefore it is of necessary things, because the necessary is that which cannot be otherwise. Moreover, science is of things which are said of all, per se, and universally, or according as it is itself: therefore it is of universals. Next he proves the same antecedent on the side of opinion and the opinable. For certain things, he says, are true in estimation which in reality can be true or false: of these there is no science, nor understanding, which is the cognition of principles: therefore of these there will be opinion; and since they can be otherwise, which is to be contingent, it will be of the contingent; and therefore the opinable will be contingent.

2 The antecedent is proved, namely that of things which can be otherwise there is neither science nor understanding: because science is of things which cannot be otherwise; and understanding is as it were a certain immediate science, and can be defined thus: Understanding is the certain cognition of an immediate proposition; that is, it is a certain cognition had from the sole signification of the terms. But a certain cognition had from the terms cannot be of a contingent thing, but only of necessary things: therefore it is repugnant that understanding and science be of a contingent thing. And the consequence, namely that opinion is of a contingent thing, he proves because, if a certain cognition cannot be had of a contingent thing, there will be an uncertain and fallible one. This is such that, although it is thought to be true, nevertheless it is not repugnant to it that falsity underlie it.

Whence he infers that opinion should be defined thus: Opinion is the acceptance, or estimation, or assent of an immediate and non-necessary proposition. And by the first particle, of an immediate proposition, opinion is distinguished from science, which is the cognition of a mediate proposition, and it agrees with understanding. But by the second, namely non-necessary, it is distinguished from both, that is, from understanding and from science, because both are of necessary things, as has been proved.

3 But this definition of opinion is not delivered by Aristotle of every opinion, but only of the immediate one. For there is also a mediate

[p. 687]

opinion, which is inferred from an immediate opinion through an evident or probable consequence, or from an evident proposition through a non-necessary consequence, as Aristotle teaches in this same chapter. But he wished to define only the immediate one, so that, since it is known that a mediate opinion is given, he might show by the definition itself that immediate opinions are also given, to which the intellect assents probably from the sole cognition of the terms; just as there are necessary propositions to which it assents from the sole cognition of the terms with a certain and necessary assent.

But against the difference proved between the knowable and science, and the opinable and opinion, he proposes two doubts in the second part of the chapter. The first is for proving that the knowable and the opinable do not differ: because it often happens that what one man knows, another opines: therefore the same thing will be knowable and opinable. He replies that of the same simple or incomplex thing there can be science and opinion, as of man; not, however, of the same complex thing, as of a proposition. For of man there can be science and opinion, but not of a proposition: as of this one, That the diagonal is commensurable, or equal to the side, there could perhaps be opinion, not science.

4 The second doubt is: because just as science proceeds from immediate principles to a mediate conclusion, so opinion can proceed from an immediate probable proposition to a mediate one, which it infers from it. Moreover, just as demonstration, if it proceeds from the cause, will be propter quid, and if from the effect, will be quia, by the same reasoning opinion, if it proceeds from an immediate proposition containing the cause of the conclusion, is called propter quid; but if from one which contains the effect, it is called quia: therefore science and opinion agree in these two things; wherefore they will not be distinguished. He replies that the antecedent is true, but that the consequence must be denied, because the mode of proceeding of each is diverse. For science proceeds through a necessary middle, that is, from necessary principles and through a necessary consequence; but opinion through a contingent middle, that is, either from non-necessary principles, or through a consequence that is not necessary but probable: and this is to be distinguished essentially, through diverse middles of assenting. Whence it follows that falsity cannot underlie science, but that opinion can be false.

T R E AT I S E I .

On the Habit of Principles.

O     f three things Aristotle treats in the present chapter: of Understanding,

which is the cognition of principles; of Science, which is the cognition

[p. 688]

of conclusions, which are demonstrated from principles; and of Opinion, which he

teaches differs from these. Of which we must treat in the same order, and we insti‐

tute a separate treatise on each: in which we explain very briefly the things that

are necessary for understanding their nature and ratio, so that in this way we may

better understand the difference which Aristotle posited among them. And first,

concerning the habit of principles four things will be explained. First, whether it ex‐

ists: that is, whether, besides the intellective power and the intelligible species

through which we apprehend principles, that is, immediate propositions, a habit

must be posited through which the intellect may easily judge of their truth and

give them its assent. Second, what this habit is. Third, whether it is natural, so that

the soul received it together with the intellective power when it was created by

God; or whether it is acquired through its own acts. Fourth, whether it is one in

species for the principles of all the sciences, or diverse for diverse principles.

Whether, besides the intellect and the intelligible species, there is a habit of principles.

6

F    irst, it must be presupposed, as certain in the doctrine of Aristotle and in the

Peripatetic school, that in the intellect and the will there are habits of the moral and

of the intellectual virtues.

Second, it must be presupposed that these habits are to be posited in the intellect as

distinct from the intelligible species. Which the office of the former and of the latter

effectively proves. For the office of the intelligible species is only to unite the ob‐

ject to be understood with the intellective power, from which union follows the

apprehension of it, which is the first operation of the intellect; or the union itself

is the apprehension. Whence it follows that intelligible species serve proximately

only for apprehending objects. But since after apprehension there follows the

judgment of the truth or falsity of propositions, in which the second operation of

the intellect principally consists, and in which there can be some indifference, or

even difficulty, in judging, another habit is added by Aristotle and by all (the

Nominalists alone excepted), who say that the intelligible species themselves are

habits, and therefore posit nothing besides them for judging.

These things supposed, the first doubt is: whether, besides the intelligible species

through which we apprehend principles, a habit of principles is necessary for judging of their

truth, which is to assent to them. And the first opinion is that of Durandus, in 3, d.

33, q. 1, toward the end, and of Soto, On Justice and Right bk. 1, q. 4, a. 2, who, al‐

though they posit habits of the sciences in the intellect, besides the intelligible

species, for assent to

conclusions

[p. 689]

conclusions, nevertheless assert that no habit is to be posited for assenting to principles; rather, they say, the natural light suffices, which is the intellective power itself.

7 They prove it by this argument. For natural operations, in which there is no indifference or liberty, habits are not posited: as in the visual power; nay, not even in the will with respect to the ultimate end, to which it tends naturally through love. But the intellect assents naturally to principles, since they are immediate and necessary truths, so that, once they are proposed, it cannot fail to assent to them; for it is related to them as the will is to the ultimate end, or sight to colors: therefore it needs no habit in order to assent to them.

The opposite opinion holds that, besides the intellect and the species intelligible, a habit is to be posited for assenting to the first indemonstrable principles. This is express in Aristotle, Ethics bk. 6, ch., where among the intellectual virtues, which are habits superadded to the powers, he enumerates understanding, which is the habit of principles. And St. Thomas, in his Commentary on the same passage, declaring that Aristotle speaks of understanding not as a power but as a habit superadded to the power, in these words: But understanding is taken here not for the intellective power itself, but for a certain habit by which man, by virtue of the light of the agent intellect, naturally knows indemonstrable principles. And in 1-2, q. 94, a. 1, he says: Indemonstrable principles in speculative matters are not the habit of principles itself, but are the principles of which there is the habit. This opinion is followed by Henry of Ghent, Quodlibet 5, 28; Cajetan, 1-2, q. 51, a. 1, and Conrad in the same place; Ferrara, Contra Gentiles bk. 1, ch. 94; Medina, 1-2, q. 49; and all the moderns. And it seems to us true and to be held.

8 It is proved, first: the necessity of positing a habit in a power with respect to some object is its indifference to operating well or badly with respect to it, so that, since it can operate in either way, it may be determined to operating well through the habit. For a habit, as we saw in Aristotle in the category of quality, is a disposition of the subject by which it is well or badly disposed in order to its proper nature or operation. But the intellect can operate well or badly with respect to the first principles, since it can err about them: therefore it needs a habit for operating well; and therefore it is necessary to posit it.

Second: because if the intellect does not need a habit for assenting to principles, because they are evident and move it naturally, it follows that neither does it need a habit for assenting to conclusions. The consequence is proved: because, once assent to the principles is had, the conclusion contained in them contains evident truth, and also moves the intellect naturally; but the opposite

Xx

[p. 690]

opinion posits a habit for conclusions: therefore it must necessarily posit one

with respect to principles.

9 And to its argument: the minor must be distinguished, namely that the

intellect assents naturally to the first principles. For as regards specification,

it is true: because, given the due apprehension of them, if it passes judgment

on them, it cannot be a judgment of dissent, but must be one of assent. But

as regards exercise, it has liberty with respect to them, dependently on the

will; and therefore it can suspend its assent, as we proved above. Which lib‐

erty the senses do not have, nor the will with respect to the good in general:

therefore they are not capable of a habit.

What the habit of principles is. 10

T      he nature and essence of a habit are to be understood from its proper act and from

the object with respect to which it is apt to operate. For from these powers

and habits take their species, as Aristotle teaches in On the Soul bk. 2, ch. 4. It

is necessary, therefore, to explain what the proper object of this habit is, and what

act it has with respect to it. The proper object of the habit is evident and imme‐

diate truth, whether it be universal or particular. Its proper mode of tending

to its object, from which the formal and ultimate ratio of the habit is taken,

is through an immediate comparison to the evident truth itself, which it re‐

gards without any middle. Whence, just as the other habits of the intellect

are constituted and distinguished in species through this or that middle of

assenting (as science through a demonstrative middle, opinion through a

probable middle, and faith through testimony), so the habit of principles,

which is called understanding, is such in its proper species, and is distin‐

guished from the other habits, because it is compared per se and immediate‐

ly to the evidence of truth. Whence its proper act is to assent to it without any

middle, just as the act of science is to assent through a demonstrative middle.

Its definition, therefore, will be this: The habit of principles is an intellectual

virtue through which the intellective power is determined to the assent to principles

evident per se, and to eliciting that assent easily. And in what this facility consists

we shall say below.

Whether the habit of principles is natural, or acquired by the intellect through its own

acts. 11

H      aving now explained that the habit of understanding exists, and what it

is, there follows the third thing to be explained: in what manner it is gen‐

erated, or comes to be in us; namely, whether the soul receives it together with its

own nature and intellect when it is created by God, or whether, just as

[p. 691]

in its very creation it receives the intellect without any intelligible species, but as a blank tablet in which nothing is painted, as Aristotle asserted, it receives it in the same manner, without any habit of principles. For concerning the other habits, of the sciences and of the virtues, it is certain that the intellect has no such habits from the beginning; and thus, just as it acquires these in the course of time through its own acts, by parity of reasoning it would acquire the habit of principles. For if the soul receives it together with the intellect, it will be called natural, that is, implanted by nature; but if it acquires it through acts, it will be called not natural but acquired, like the others.

The first opinion affirms that it is natural and not acquired. So Conrad, 1-2, q. 94, a. 1, and Báñez, 1 p., q. 1, a. 6, notable 3, etc.; and it seems to be express in St. Thomas, 1-2, q. 49, a. 1, ad 3, where he says: 12 A child cannot use the habit of the understanding of principles, or even the natural law, which is in him habitually, on account of the defect of age. In which words he posits the habit of principles in a child who does not yet have the use of reason, and adds that he cannot use it on account of the defect of age: therefore he thinks that it is in him from nature, and is not acquired through acts. And in 2, d. 24, q. 2, a. 3, ad 3, he calls it natural, in these words: A natural habit is never lost, as is plain of the habit of principles.

And it is proved by reason: because acquired habits are certain facilities, and therefore they are posited for overcoming the difficulty which the power has in operating with respect to such an object. But the intellect has no difficulty in assenting to the first principles, especially the most universal ones, such as these: Anything whatever either is or is not; The whole is greater than its part: therefore it does not acquire any facility in the frequent assent to them; nay, it does not even need one. The consequence is proved: because facility is opposed to difficulty, and is ordered to overcoming it; whence it follows either that such a habit is not to be posited, or that it is natural and not acquired. And the common manner of speaking calls it such, founded perhaps on the very name: because it is called understanding, like the power itself in which it is received, because it is natural to it.

13 The second opinion is that of Cajetan, 1-2, q. 51, a. 1, d. 1, where he denies that it is acquired; but he teaches that it is natural in such a way that the soul does not receive it from the beginning together with the intellect itself; rather, just as the intellect receives no intelligible species when the soul is created and infused into the body, so it receives no habit; but once the species of the first principles have been acquired through the abstraction of the agent intellect, the habit of principles, he says, immediately flows forth naturally from the very nature of the passive intellect, to which it is attributed

X x ij

[p. 692]

so that through it the intellect immediately assents to the same principles, once they are apprehended through the species. And in this way, he says, it is to be called natural.

The third opinion asserts that the habit of principles neither comes with nature, nor flows from that same nature of the intellect by the very fact that it has the species of the principles through which it apprehends them; but that it is acquired through the very acts by which the intellect assents to the principles, just as the habits of the sciences and of the virtues are acquired through their own acts. So Ferrara, Contra Gentiles 2, ch. 78; and it is the common opinion of the moderns, and seems to us true and to be held. It is proved, first, by the express testimony of Aristotle in the last chapter of this book 1, where, explaining the manner in which this habit is generated in us, he speaks thus: Therefore the determinate habits are neither innate in us, nor do they come to be from other, better-known habits, but from assent. In which words he teaches that it is not in us from nature, nor does it come to be from other, better-known cognitions, as the habit of science does, but through the immediate assent to truth known per se. Which is to be acquired through its own acts.

It is proved next by reason: because nature does not grant to things anything but what is necessary for being and for operating simply; but the things which serve for operating better or more easily it leaves to be acquired by their own industry and labor, granting them principles by which they can operate and, by operating, acquire them. And for this reason it did not grant to men the habits of the virtues: because they are not required for doing good works simply, but for doing them better, that is, for operating with facility and promptness. But the habit of principles is not necessary for assenting to the first principles simply, but only for assenting with facility: therefore it is not given to us by nature, but acquired by our own industry and labor. The minor is proved: because the assent to principles does not exceed the faculty of the intellect; rather, informed by the intelligible species through which it apprehends the terms of which the principles are made, while it knows their signification, it can by its own power judge of their truth, which is to assent to them: therefore for assenting simply it does not need a habit. The antecedent is proved: because principles are certain natural truths, evident per se: therefore they are proportioned to the natural light of the same intellect; wherefore by its own power it can operate with respect to them through assent.

15 But in order that this view of ours may be better understood, and that the testimonies of St. Thomas may be explained according to his mind, it should be noted that, although the habit of principles is not given to us by nature, it nevertheless has its greatest principle in nature itself, by reason of which it can also in some manner be called natural. Which the other habits do not have. For, as we were saying above, the proper ratio of this

[p. 693]

habit is taken from its immediate comparison to truth itself evident per se, which it neither regards nor attains through any middle, but needs only the cognition of the terms; which, again, it has through the species of the terms of which the principles themselves are composed. And these species are produced by the agent intellect and impressed on the passive intellect, by means of the sensible species of the objects, which are called phantasms. Now the operation of the senses, and of the same agent intellect, through which the species are produced, is natural, and is performed without a habit. And the patient intellect, informed through these species of the principles, and having understood through them the signification of the terms, assents to the principles without any art or industry, without any middle or discursive reasoning; and through such assent the habit of principles is generated, which is afterwards intensified and perfected through frequent repetition of the same assent. And therefore, both on the side of the species, which are produced naturally, and on the side of the assent to the principles, this habit is called natural; although the assent is free, and consequently the habit is freely produced through it. And finally, because the assent to principles and the habit itself are produced without a middle, without discursive reasoning, without art, solely through the natural light of the same intellect, therefore no other name has been given to it, but it is signified by the name of the same intellect, when we say that it is the understanding of principles.

16 But the other intellectual habits do not have these features, as the habit of science. For besides the operation of the agent intellect, and besides the species of the conclusion, which it impresses on the patient intellect, it prerequires art, through which the principles are disposed; it prerequires the assent to them, as the formal middle by which the intellect assents to the conclusion; and through such assent it is generated. And therefore neither the habit of science nor other similar habits are called natural.

From which it is understood that the habit of principles has both features: both that it is natural and that it is acquired through its own acts; not, however, as the other habits are acquired, but without any middle, without any art or industry, solely through the natural power of both intellects, the agent and the patient, and of the senses, whose natural operations are presupposed. And it is in this sense that St. Thomas speaks when he calls this habit natural, or when he says that it is had from nature; not denying, by these ways of speaking, that it is acquired through its own acts, because each sense is true and neither contradicts the other. And that this is his sense is evidently gathered from the proper place where St. Thomas treats expressly of this habit, inquiring whether it is natural,

X x iij

[p. 694]

namely in 1-2, q. 1, a. 1; and he asserts that it is natural according to its inchoation, which the other habits do not have; and nevertheless that it is acquired, through the operation of the agent intellect and of the senses, presupposed to the assent of the passive intellect, through which it is proximately acquired. In which sense also Aristotle said that this habit is had from the senses and not from nature.

17 In the same sense, too, is understood the testimony of St. Thomas about the child, whom he says has this habit but does not use it on account of the defect of age. For he understands that he has it according to its inchoation, because in this manner it is natural; yet he does not have it formally, until it is generated in him through the first assent to principles and perfected through the subsequent ones.

Concerning the solution of the first argument, certain moderns assert that a habit is not to be posited for the assent to the most universal principles, which are called axioms: because, since they are most known to us, we assent to them without any difficulty; and therefore through frequent assent to them we do not acquire a habit. But they say it is to be posited only for the particular principles of the sciences, to which the intellect does not easily assent, since they are not so known to us; therefore we need for them an acquired facility, which is called a habit. And this opinion seems to me sufficiently probable; although it is also probable that in assenting to these principles the intellect has some difficulty, though far less than in assenting to particular principles; and this is enough for it to need a habit for assenting, and to acquire a new facility through frequent repetition of the assents.

18 And from this doctrine the reply is given to the argument: the major being granted, the minor is denied, namely that the intellect has no difficulty in the assent to the first principles, and therefore acquires no facility through repetition of the assent. For experience teaches the opposite: both that the intellect has some difficulty, which it overcomes by exercise, and consequently that it acquires a new facility.

But what this facility is, or in what it consists, is explained in diverse ways by the authors. Leaving these aside, it must be said that facility is nothing else than a certain mode by which the power is rendered ready and prompt for operating, and apt to operate with delight, which it does not have of itself or from nature; and the habit gives it this mode, the more perfect the more it is intensified and perfected through the repetition of acts.

[p. 695]

Whether the habit of principles is the same in species for all principles, or diverse for di‐

verse ones.

C     oncerning the specific distinction of this habit nothing is found in the

authors; therefore we must proceed by reason alone. And it seems that one habit is to be posited for all, which I prove thus: Habits are distinguished through diverse acts, as we have often said; but the habit of principles has an act of the same species with respect to all principles: therefore it is the same in species for all.

19 The minor is proved: because the act of this habit is the assent to principles; and assents are of the same or of diverse species through the same or a diverse ratio of assenting, which is as it were their formal object; but the formal ratio of assenting to the first principles is always the same: therefore all the assents are of the same species, and therefore the habit too will be the same in species. The minor is proved: because the intellect always assents to the first principles without a middle, having only the signification of the terms: therefore always in the same manner.

Our view, however, is explained by two conclusions, in this manner. The first is: The habits of practical and of speculative principles are distinguished in species. Which St. Thomas holds, 1 p., q. 79, a. 12. And an evident reason proves it: because acts and habits are distinguished in species through diverse objects; but practical truth, which practical principles contain, and with which the habit is concerned as with its proper object, is diverse in species from speculative truth, since the former by its own nature is ordered to operating, but the latter is not: therefore these habits are distinguished in species. Practical principles are these and the like: Good is to be pursued, and Evil is to be fled; Virtue is to be embraced, and Vice is to be rejected; which, it is plain per se, are ordered to operating. Speculative ones are: The whole is greater than its part; Man is a rational animal; and the like, of which it is manifest that they say no order to operating.

20 The second conclusion: The habits of speculative principles, too, are distinguished in species, according as they are found in diverse matters; in this manner, that the habit of the principles of one science is distinguished in species from the habit of the principles of another. And if a habit is to be posited for the most universal principles, for diverse ones too a habit distinct in species is to be posited; so that the habit through which we assent to this principle, Anything whatever either is or is not, is another from that through which we assent to that one, The whole is greater than its part. This conclusion I prove thus: habits are distinguished through diverse acts, and acts are

XX iiij

[p. 696]

diverse through diverse objects; but the assent to the principles of one science is distinguished in species from the assent to the principles of another; and the assent to one most universal principle is also distinguished in species from the assent to another: therefore the habits too will be distinct in species. The minor is proved: because diverse principles contain diverse truth, which the assents regard as their proper object; as this principle, Man is a rational animal, contains a truth diverse in species from that one, Nature is the principle of motion and of rest of that in which it is: therefore they produce assents distinct in species in the intellect, and diverse assents will produce diverse habits too. And the same example can be adduced in diverse most universal principles.

21 And if you say that the assents are distinguished in species, but nevertheless pertain to the same habit, because they are inadequate acts with respect to it, since it extends itself to all principles and to all the assents to them: against this is the fact that, if they are distinguished in species, though inadequate, they must necessarily generate partial habits distinct in species. Because any cause whatever produces an effect according to its own species (though an inadequate one): therefore from causes distinct in species (though inadequate) effects diverse in species (though inadequate) must proceed. Wherefore there will now be diverse habits, at least partial ones, distinct in species. But that they must be distinguished by a total species is proved: because the habit of principles does not have so great an extension as the intellect, so that one and the same habit can extend itself to all truths; nor does it have a greater extension than the habit of science, to which it is proportioned and by which it is necessarily presupposed. But the habits of science are distinguished in species through diverse formal objects: therefore the habits of principles, which correspond to them, must also be distinguished in species through the diverse truths of the principles with which they are concerned as with their proper objects.

To the argument of the opposite opinion: the minor must be denied, namely that the habit of principles has an assent of the same species with respect to all principles. For although the intellect assents to all of them without a middle, once the signification of the terms is understood, this mode of assenting and formal ratio is generic; just as in the sciences, too, to assent to conclusions through a demonstrative middle is generic. Just as, therefore, in the sciences the ratio of assenting is distinct in species according to the distinct ratio of the principles through which the intellect assents to the conclusions of this or that science, and just as the habits of science are distinguished in species through this distinct specific ratio, so in the assent to principles the specific ratio of assenting is distinct according to the specific distinction of the diverse truths which the diverse principles contain. For the ratio

[p. 697]

of assenting to a principle is the very truth of the principles, through itself

and not through another middle; since, therefore, the immediate truth is di‐

verse, the ratio of assenting will also be diverse, and will produce an assent

diverse in species; and assents diverse in species will generate diverse habits

of principles.

T R E AT I S E I I .

On the Habit of Science.

oncerning the habit of science, these things are to be explained:

C          whether it exists, and what it is, and whether it is of singulars and con‐

tingents, and of beings per accidens.

Whether, besides the habit of principles, another, distinct habit, which is called science,

is to be posited for conclusions.

23

T     he first opinion is that of certain moderns, who, although they do not posit

a habit of principles for the most universal principles, but only for the partic‐

ular principles of this or that science, nevertheless assert that such a habit of

principles, after it has the assent to them, the cognition of the terms being

had, extends itself to the assents to all the conclusions of the same science;

and thus that, besides the habit of principles, no habit of science distinct

from it is to be posited.

They prove it by the testimony of Aristotle, Ethics bk. 6, ch. 3, where, enu‐

merating the intellectual habits, he asserts of wisdom, which is one habit of

the intellect, that it is science and understanding together, of the things that

are most honorable: therefore he thinks that the same habit suffices for prin‐

ciples and conclusions; wherefore it is not necessary to multiply another.

22 They prove it next by reason: because assents of which one depends

on the other cannot generate distinct habits, because diverse habits must be

independent; but the assent to conclusions presupposes the assent to princi‐

ples, on which it has an intrinsic dependence, as is plain of itself: therefore it

does not generate a habit distinct from it, but the very same habit which is

of the principles extends itself to the conclusions. They prove the major by

the example of the more universal sciences, such as Dialectic and Philosophy,

which, although they have diverse conclusions, nevertheless do not on that

account have posited in them a single and diverse habit for each conclusion,

but one which extends itself to all, on account of the intrinsic dependence

[p. 698]

of one conclusion on another, by which it is necessarily presupposed, or which it presupposes, as we asserted and proved in Proemial q. 3: therefore, since the conclusions of the same science have a more intrinsic dependence on the principles of the same science than the conclusions themselves can have among themselves, it follows that no habit distinct from the habit of principles is to be posited for the conclusions, but that this one extends itself to all.

This opinion, however, is manifestly contrary to the same Aristotle in the same place, ch. 6, where he teaches expressly that not only is the habit of principles, which is called understanding, distinct from the habit of science and from the others, but that it cannot coincide with any of them, in these words: Understanding is neither science, nor art, nor prudence. Not science, because the knowable itself is demonstrable; not art and prudence, because they are concerned with things that can be otherwise. But neither is it wisdom: for it belongs to the wise man to have demonstration of certain things. If, then, the things by which we speak the truth, and never falsehood, about things which either can or cannot be otherwise (and these are science, prudence, wisdom, understanding), and of these three habits none can be it (and I call the three prudence, science, wisdom), it remains that understanding is of principles.

25 It is also contrary to reason, which I prove thus. Habits are distinguished through acts, which in intellectual matters are the assents themselves; but the assents to the principles of the same science and to its conclusions are distinguished in species: therefore they must pertain to habits distinct in species, which they generate. The minor is proved: because assents are distinguished in species through diverse formal ratios of assenting; but the assent to conclusions has a ratio diverse from the assent to principles, as is manifest of itself, since the intellect assents to principles without a middle, on account of the truth itself, evident per se, but to conclusions on account of the principles disposed in a demonstration: therefore the assents themselves will be distinguished in species. And if you say that they are distinguished in species as inadequate acts of the same habit: against this is the fact that, if the assents are inadequate, there will be given some ratio of assenting more universal than both, under which they are comprehended, and which is adequate to the habit that is posited for both. But such a ratio is impossible: therefore it is impossible that it be the same habit. I prove the minor again: because such a ratio, common to both assents, would be that of a necessary or evident assent, abstracting from both; which cannot be one except by a generic unity, comprehending under itself assents diverse in species. Moreover, even if we granted that the assents to principles and to conclusions are inadequate, since they are distinct in species it is necessary that distinct habits, at least partial and inadequate

[p. 699]

generate; and thus a distinct habit, at least by a partial species, will now have

to be posited for the conclusions.

The testimony of Aristotle for the opposite opinion St. Thomas explained

excellently, not only in his Commentaries on the same passage, but also in 1-

2, q. 57, a. 1, ad 2, where he says that wisdom properly taken, of which Aristotle

speaks there, is a certain habit, truly a scientific one, but the most universal, which

is concerned with conclusions, also the most universal ones, proper to itself;

and at the same time judges in a certain manner of the principles and conclu‐

sions of the particular sciences, as of inferiors: because it considers the high‐

est causes, to which the inferior ones are reduced and on which they depend;

and also the most universal rationes of being, such as essence, whole, part,

and the like, on which the particular conclusions of all the sciences depend,

and which it sometimes demonstrates through universal extrinsic reasons, or

reasons leading to the impossible.

26 And on account of these excellences it is related in a certain manner

to the other sciences as understanding, which is the habit of principles; and

at the same time it is also the habit of science with respect to its own conclu‐

sions; yet it is not the same habit as that which is posited for its principles,

but a diverse one. And a universal science of this kind is none other than

Metaphysics, to which the aforesaid excellences belong.

To the argument of the same opinion the reply is that the major is false

absolutely: which the subalternating and the subalternate science prove. For

the object of the latter is contained under the object of the former, and its

conclusions have an intrinsic dependence on the conclusions of the other,

through which they are proved, as through principles; and nevertheless they

are habits and sciences distinct in species, according to Aristotle and all. And

much better will the habits of science and of principles be distinguished, al‐

though the assent to conclusions has an intrinsic dependence on the assent

to principles, since they have diverse formal ratios, as has been proved. But

in the more universal sciences the reasoning is different: because the conclu‐

sions not only presuppose one another and have an intrinsic dependence on

the principles, which presuppose and depend in the same manner, but all the

conclusions also have the same formal ratio of assenting, through a demon‐

strative middle; and nevertheless even in these sciences a distinct habit is

posited for principles and for conclusions, according to Aristotle and all.

Whether evidence pertains to the essence of science. 27

T    his is the second thing to be explained concerning science, pertaining

to its essence: namely, whether evidence is essential to it. And

[p. 700]

because the essential predicates of anything whatever are established from its definition, it is necessary to bring forward the definition of science and to explain it, so that from its explanation it may be established whether evidence ought to be numbered among its essential predicates: because if it is not to be numbered among them, it will not be judged essential to it either.

Aristotle, in ch. 2 of this book, defined science in the concrete, saying: To know is to know a thing through its cause, and that it is the cause of that thing, and that it is impossible for it to be otherwise. Which definition, if we apply it to science in the abstract, can be assigned under the form of a quidditative definition in this manner: Science is the true and certain cognition of a necessary thing through its proper cause. In which cognition has the ratio of genus, because in it science agrees with the other acts of the intellect. Now cognition can be taken for actual or habitual cognition, or for both; and in this way both sciences, actual and habitual, are defined. Actual science is the assent to the conclusion; habitual science the habit generated through it. But in the common manner of speaking it is taken rather for habitual science. The remaining particles are posited in place of the difference, so that through them it may be distinguished from the other habits of the intellect. For a cognition is called true so that it may be distinguished from error; certain, so that it may be distinguished from opinion and the other cognitions to which it is not repugnant that falsity underlie them; by of a necessary thing it is separated from prudence and art, which are concerned with contingent things. Finally, the particle through its cause distinguishes science from the habit of principles, which does not proceed through a middle, but assents immediately to the truth, once the cognition of the terms is had.

28 It is distinguished also from the science which is had a posteriori and through the effect, which Aristotle does not comprehend under this definition, but only perfect science, which is called propter quid. But we can designate a definition common to both, and as it were generic, comprehending both, by changing only the last particle, through its cause, and putting in its place the particle through demonstration; and it will be this: Science is the true cognition of a necessary thing through demonstration.

But whether these definitions are complete, or whether they lack the particle evident, which must at least be understood: of this is the present question. For its better understanding, these three terms must be explained and distinguished: Certitude, Necessity, and Evidence. Certitude is the firm adhesion of the intellect to some object, without doubt or fear. So the Scholastic Doctors define it, in 3, d. 26, especially St. Thomas, q. 2, a. 4; Bonaventure, q. 4; Durandus, in 4, d. 37, q. 8. But the firm adhesion of the intellect is twofold, Apparent and True. It is apparent when the intellect, from some probable reason and from an efficacious application of the will, tenaciously

[p. 701]

adheres to some object; and it is of this apparent adhesion that the axiom laid down by Aristotle, Ethics bk. 7, ch. 3, is understood: Some adhere as firmly to their false opinions or errors as others adhere to the sciences. But the definition is not understood of this firm adhesion, but of the True one, by which the intellect, on account of the truth of the thing itself, or of a solid and firm reason, or of an infallible authority, adheres to some object. Certitude, then, explained in this way, has those three degrees which we explained above.

But Necessity, taken in order to a proposition (of which we are not speaking), is the determination of the intellect to truth; and a proposition will be necessary which is true in such a way that it is repugnant for it to be false; which Aristotle expressed by that phrase, impossible to be otherwise. And necessity has the same degrees as certitude.

Finally, Evidence adds over firm adhesion the manifestation of the truth under the clarity of some light, so that an object is called evident as being clear and perspicuous, or manifest. This evidence or clarity principles have of themselves, but science has it as participated from the principles. And of certitude and necessity no one can doubt that they are essential to science, since both are expressly set down in Aristotle’s definition. Concerning evidence alone, therefore, since it is not expressed, there can be a question: Whether it is essential to it? and therefore whether it must be understood, or declared, in the definition.

And the first opinion denies that it is essential. So Diego Mas, on the present chapter, q. 3, conclusions 1 and 2. He proves it, first: Because subalternate science is true science, and yet it is not evident; therefore evidence is not of the ratio of science. He proves the minor: because it can happen that it exists without the subalternating science and has only principles accepted through the testimony of him who has the subalternating science; and then it is plain that it is not evident. And even if it is together with the subalternating science, still within its own limits it does not know how to reduce its principles all the way to the first and indemonstrable ones; therefore it does not have evidence of them, and consequently neither of the conclusions which it deduces from them. Nevertheless in both ways it is true science, since it is of a necessary thing through an evident consequence.

Second, he proves it: Because Theology, which is deduced from the principles of divine faith through true demonstrations, is not evident, since from the obscure principles of faith an evident conclusion cannot be gathered; and yet it is true science, as is manifest; therefore evidence does not pertain to the essence of science.

This opinion, however, asserts two false things. First, that subalternate science, existing without the subalternating science, and having principles

[p. 702]

accepted only through the testimony of him who has the subalternating science, is true science. For if the principles are held only through the testimony of that man, the assent to them will be only human faith, under which falsehood can lie; therefore they cannot be the cause of a certain or scientific conclusion; otherwise the effect would be more perfect than its proper cause.

31 The second thing it asserts is that subalternate science, even when it exists together with the subalternating science in the same man, is science within its own limits, but is not evident, because it does not know how to reduce its conclusions all the way to the indemonstrable principles. But these two things contain a manifest repugnance: because if it does not know how to reduce its principles, then it will not be science. The consequence is evidently proved from these words of Aristotle, which are found in ch. 2 of this book: He does not know who does not have the demonstration of these, etc., that is, of the premises of which the demonstration consists; and if he does not know how to reduce them, they will not be certain to him; therefore neither will he be able in any way to deduce a certain conclusion from them.

Subalternate science, then, existing together with the subalternating science, is considered in two ways. First, precisely within its own limits: that is, without considering the continuation or union which it has with the subalternating science; and in this way it is neither science, as we proved in chapter 10, nor is it evident, but it will be a kind of opinion. Second, it is considered as continued or united with the subalternating science, in which continuation subalternation formally consists; and therefore only as taken in this way is it formally subalternate; and in this way it is true science, and evident, because through such a continuation, by the help of the subalternating science, it reduces its principles all the way to the first indemonstrable ones.

32 And if you say: It is not it that reduces its principles, but the subalternating science; I reply: the subalternating science reduces them as the subalternate science is continued with it, and in no other way; and this is the same as the subalternate science reducing them as it is continued with the subalternating science. For thus it comes about that he who has both has evidence of the principles of the subalternate science by reason of the continuation; and therefore the subalternate science is in him true science, and evident.

In order, then, to explain our view, it should be noted that Science can be taken in two ways. First, insofar as it can be had through the natural light of the intellect; and Aristotle defined only this, because only this could he know. In the second way it can be considered more universally, as it says only the assent to a conclusion had through demonstration from premises known whether by natural light or by any other whatever, of which, however, it has a certain assent,

[p. 603]

whether by reduction to the first indemonstrable principles, or in another way.

33 This distinction supposed, our view is contained in two conclusions. The first is: To the essence of science considered in the first way evidence pertains. This is proved: Because if someone demonstrates a conclusion through a cause or an effect known by the natural light of the intellect, he must have evidence of the premises, since they are manifest to him under the clarity of the natural light; and the consequence also is evident there in the same way; therefore the conclusion deduced from them is also evident. The consequence is proved: because from a per se cause evident in every respect an evident effect too must follow; but from such an evident assent to the conclusion the habit of science is generated; therefore it too will be evident essentially. But although evidence is an essential predicate of science, Aristotle did not express it in the definition, because it was sufficiently manifest that it was contained in the words of that same definition. But if someone wishes to express it, he will say thus: Science is a true, certain, and evident cognition of a necessary thing through its cause. And if he wishes to define all science, both quia and propter quid, he will say thus: Science is a true, certain, and evident cognition of a necessary thing through demonstration.

Second conclusion: To the essence of science taken in that more universal acceptation evidence does not pertain; but it can be defined thus: Science is a certain cognition of a thing through demonstration. This is proved: Because Theology, which is had from the principles of divine faith, is a certain cognition of a thing through true demonstration; therefore in some way it is science. The consequence is proved: because it is not opinion, nor human faith, since it is certain; nor is it divine faith, because faith does not rest on demonstration nor on any other argumentation, but only on divine testimony; whereas a Theological conclusion does not rest immediately on testimony but on demonstration, although one of the premises, or both, rests on divine testimony, and so is an assent of faith.

But neither does the same Theological conclusion pertain to understanding, which is the habit of principles, since it is deduced through demonstration; therefore it pertains to the habit of science. I prove the consequence again: because there is not, nor can there be, any other habit to which it could pertain. If, then, Theology is science, though imperfect because it is not evident, it must agree in some way with science taken in the first way; and therefore some ratio of science common to both can be abstracted, to whose essence evidence does not pertain. And this is the one which, considered under this common ratio, has been defined by us.

[p. 704]

Whether there is science of singulars, of contingents, and of beings per accidens.

oncerning these three we shall say very briefly and separately what is to

C           be held. And first, concerning singulars, a distinction must be made: for

some are singulars which are at the same time species, or contain the specific perfection eminently and most perfectly, as God and the angels; and, as many hold, in the angels the specific difference is not distinguished from the individual one. And concerning these singulars it is certain among all that the most perfect science can be had. Others are singulars in which the individual difference is distinguished from the specific one and is outside its ratio, as are corruptible things; and perhaps the angels too have this, for it is very probable that they can be multiplied under the same species; and concerning these there can be a doubt whether they can be objects of science, or whether science can be only of universals.

35 Next, science must be distinguished, because it can be taken in three ways. First, for a certain and evident cognition of a thing, had through discursive reasoning or without it, by simple intuition; and concerning science taken in this way it is certain that it is concerned with any singulars whatever. For God and the angels, through intuitive cognition, without discursive reasoning, know all singulars most perfectly; and such intuitive cognition of theirs has the most perfect ratio of science. We too can have science of God and the angels; and by means of the senses we have intuitive cognition of sensible singulars, which according to this acceptation can be called science. In the second way science is taken for that only which is discursive, had through an evident consequence, whether it be a true demonstration or not. In the third way it is taken for discursive science, but had through a true demonstration. The doubt, then, proceeds concerning science taken in these two ways: whether it can be had of corruptible singulars.

But these singulars are further considered in two ways. First, as they participate in the specific nature in which they agree, namely the human nature or another. Second, as they are distinct through their own individual differences; and this is to consider them as they are singulars formally and reduplicatively. And if they are considered in the first way, it is certain that there can also be science of them in some way. For since there can be science per se, primarily and immediately, of the species, there will also be science of the singulars through participation and application of that same science of the species to them: because, if it is proved of man through demonstration that he is risible, it

can

[p. 705]

can be proved of Peter or John, by applying the same demonstration to him and proving through it that he is risible.

36 And in this way, in the science of Theology, some things are demonstrated of Christ our Lord as man, from principles of faith and propositions that are at the same time evident: for instance, that he is risible because he is a man, through this demonstration applied to him: Every man is risible; Christ is a man; therefore Christ is risible.

The whole difficulty, then, concerns these same singulars as they are singulars and distinct through their own individual differences: whether there can be discursive science of them, taken in the second or the third way. And some say that there can, while others say that it is altogether repugnant. Meanwhile our view is explained in two conclusions. The first is: Discursive science had through true demonstration cannot in any way be of singulars taken in this way. This is proved evidently: because a true demonstration is a true syllogism, disposed in mood and figure, and proceeding from universal indemonstrable principles, whose middle is a true definition composed of genus and difference; but this cannot be made from singular terms; therefore neither can it be had of singulars.

37 For disposition in mood and figure cannot be found in singular terms except improperly, as in the expository syllogism, which is a syllogism very improperly, through a certain likeness to the one that is made in universal terms.

Second: Because of a singular, as it is singular, nothing can be proved except a singular property, belonging to it alone; but through universal principles nothing can be proved except a universal or common property, since it belongs equally to all the singulars, that is, no more to one than to another; therefore such science cannot in any way be of singulars as they are singulars. And since discursive science is said properly and absolutely only of this kind, it must also be said absolutely that there cannot be discursive science of singulars. Therefore Aristotle, in many places of his doctrine, expressly and without any distinction denies that there can be science of singulars, and the common manner of speaking of the whole School holds the same.

38 Second conclusion: Speaking naturally, there cannot be science of singulars as they are singulars even through an evident consequence which is not a demonstration. This is proved by this argument: To have science of something is to prove some property of it through an evident consequence; but of a singular as such we cannot naturally prove any property through an evident consequence; therefore neither have true science

Yy

[p. 706]

of it. I prove the minor: because the property of a singular as singular is that which follows from its own individual difference, or from the singular as constituted through it; but we know with certainty no determinate individual difference, nor any such property, nor can it be known with certainty by us naturally, as is manifest to all; therefore neither can we prove it of the singular itself through an evident consequence, nor in this way have science of it, even improper science.

Whether there can be science of being per accidens.

B     eing per accidens is the name given to that which is composed of several

beings in act, as white or musician; concerning which we ask: Whether there can be science of it had through true demonstration?

39 And some distinguish a twofold being per accidens. One, which results from two beings in act concurring by chance or fortuitously, as a musician or a builder, or also the finding of a treasure. And of this they deny that there can be science, because it is not only a being per accidens according to its being, but neither can it fall per se under the consideration of the intellect; but just as the things of which it consists are joined by chance, so they stand altogether per accidens in relation to the consideration of the intellect. The other is the being per accidens which results from two things concurring naturally and united, as White, Quantified, etc.; and of this they say there can be science, because although it is a being per accidens according to its being, yet it can be considered per se by the intellect, be defined per se, and attributes can be demonstrated per se of it. For we define white as that which is disgregative of sight; and quantified, as a body having extended parts.

Our view, however, is that there can be science of no being per accidens as it is a being per accidens; and concerning being per accidens resulting from two things concurring by chance or rarely, Aristotle expressly holds this, Metaph. bk. 6, texts 5, 6, and 7. But in order that we may prove it of any other also, it should be noted that it can be considered in two ways. First, as it is composed of two beings in act by way of aggregation, that is, with no order considered in them: such is a heap, such is white and musician, as we consider in them only one aggregate of many actual things. Second, it can be considered as consisting of two things ordered, namely one as determinable, the other as determining. And considered in the first way it is called one per accidens in every way. Wherefore there cannot be science of it.

40 This is proved: Because it has in no way one nature, nor one ratio; wherefore it cannot be explained by one definition,

[p. 707]

nor have determinate attributes which can be demonstrated of it. Therefore

Aristotle’s doctrine, in the place cited, extends to every being per accidens. But

if it is considered in the second way, although it is one per accidens in entity, it

is nevertheless one per se in order; and therefore it can be defined by one defi‐

nition, in the way in which white and quantified are defined by those defini‐

tions which we adduced. It can also have determinate attributes which are

proved of it. And music and perspective treat of sonorous number, taken in this

way, and of the visual line, as of their proper objects, as we saw in ch. 10, and

these are true sciences.

Whether there is science of things by chance and by fortune. 41

T   hat is called Chance which consists of two things concurring by chance: as

that summertime is cold and rainy. But Fortuitous, that which comes about

from two things concurring by fortune (as it is said): as the finding of a treasure

with the digging of the earth. Now these can be considered in two ways. First,

in common, as they are called chance or fortuitous things. In another way, in par‐

ticular, as it is this one or that. And of them considered in the first way there

can be science, because the ratio of the chance or fortuitous, considered in

common, is per se one and per se considerable. Therefore Aristotle treats of

chance and fortune, so considered, in Phys. bk. 2. But of the same considered in

particular no science can be had, because they have no ratio per se consider‐

able, but are utterly contingent and per accidens. Wherefore they can neither

be defined per se, nor have any attribute demonstrable of them.

T R E AT I S E I I I .

On Opinion and Human Faith.

What opinion is, and what human faith is.

hree things are to be explained concerning opinion and human faith. 42

T           First: What each is. Second: How they are distinguished. Third: Whether

opinion, and consequently human faith, can exist together with science.

Opinion we can define thus: Opinion is the assent to some non-necessary

proposition, through a probable middle, or without one. In assent it agrees with sci‐

ence and the other intellectual cognitions; and by the same particle there is un‐

derstood to be excluded from the ratio of opinion any thought whatever, or es‐

timation, or suspicion, or doubt, by which the intellect, not determined

Y y ij

[p. 708]

to either part of a contradiction, does not assent to it, but either thinks lightly, or as it were hesitates or hangs between the two parts. For assent says its determination to one part or the other, which it reckons true, or at least probable. And it is called Probable in order that it may be distinguished from science and understanding, which are evident assents. But it is distinguished from human faith by those particles, Through a probable middle, or without one: because human faith is not had through a probable middle, nor without one, but through the testimony of one worthy of belief.

Through a probable middle, or without one, is said also so that we may understand that opinion is twofold. One, which is had without a middle, through simple intuition alone of the probable truth itself, which Aristotle defined thus in the present chapter, saying: Opinion is the acceptance of an immediate and non-necessary proposition. The other is that which is had through a probable middle. For it is gathered either from an immediate opinion, through an evident or a probable consequence; or from an evident proposition, through a merely probable consequence; and in both ways it is said to be had through a probable middle, because it is merely probable either on the part of the proposition from which it is gathered, or on the part of the consequence. Thus, just as certain and evident assent is twofold, namely either evident per se, which the intellect has once the signification of the terms is known, and it is called Understanding; or evident through a demonstrative middle, and it is called Science: in the same way probable assent is twofold. One, which is had without a middle, once the signification of the terms is known: as when the intellect, having known the signification of the terms of this proposition, Every mother loves her son, at once, awaiting no reason, assents to it probably; and it can be called Understanding of opinion. The other probable assent is the one which is had through a probable middle, as has been set out. And thus opinion is twofold, distinct without doubt in species through the diverse mode of assenting, from the cognition of the terms alone, or through a middle; and the definition assigned comprehends both.

Human faith, on the other hand, can be defined thus: Human faith is a probable assent had on account of the testimony of one worthy of belief. So that through Probable assent it agrees with opinion and is distinguished from the other cognitions or assents of the intellect, as we said of opinion; but through Testimony it is distinguished from opinion. And so much for the first point.

Whether fear is of the intrinsic ratio of opinion and of human faith.

T    his too pertains to the explanation of the quiddity of opinion and hu‐

man faith. In order that it may be understood, it must be explained

[p. 709]

first of all: What is signified by fear. And it is nothing other than an apprehension lest the part to which the intellect assents be false, or the opposite true. For opinion, as we said, is a probable assent under which it is not repugnant that falsehood lie: that is, it is a certain weak assent, of whose truth one rightly fears, or can fear, because the intellect adheres to it in such a way that the foundation on account of which it adheres to it (which is the truth itself, probable per se, or the reason through which it deduced the conclusion from the premises) is not altogether solid nor firm, but such as can fail by its own nature, and be otherwise. The doubt, then, is whether this fear, which they call apprehension, pertains to the essence of opinion or of human faith.

44 The first opinion distinguishes a twofold opinion, Perfect and Imperfect. It calls perfect opinion the one which rests on the testimony of one worthy of belief; but imperfect, the one which rests on probable reasons. And it asserts that fear in no way pertains to the essence of the former, because it says not only the determinate assent to one part, but a firm and certain one: not on account of the firmness of the testimony, but on account of the efficacious determination of the will, by reason of which the intellect adheres to the same part not only firmly but also tenaciously, as we adduced above from Aristotle. But imperfect opinion has fear essentially annexed, without which it neither is found nor can in any way be found. So Durandus, in 1, q. of the prologue; Diego Mas, on the present chapter, who says that Capreolus and Cajetan, whom he himself cites, hold so; and, what is more, St. Thomas in many places of his doctrine, especially 1-2, q. 67, a. 3, where he says thus: It is of the ratio of opinion that one part is accepted with fear of the other opposite, etc.

It proves it also by reason. For he who opines judges that the opinion which he follows can be false; therefore by the very ratio of opining he fears lest it be false; wherefore this fear or apprehension is intrinsic to opinion.

For the solution of this question a twofold fear must be distinguished. For one is Actual, which is an actual fear; the other Virtual, or radical, which does not consist in any actual fear or doubting, but only in this: that the assent of opinion is such, on the part of the object or of the middle of assenting, that it is not repugnant to it that falsehood lie under it. And from this root there is sometimes born an actual fear or apprehension lest the opposite part be true, or that part false to which the intellect assents; and therefore it is called virtual or radical fear.

45 This distinction supposed, our view is that virtual or radical fear pertains to the essence of opinion, or of human faith

Y y iij

[p. 710]

but that actual fear is altogether accidental to it, so that it is often found without it. This is the common opinion of almost all the expositors of Aristotle on the present chapter. And it is proved by the express testimony of Aristotle, Ethics bk. 7, ch. 3, where he speaks thus of opinion: For whether it be true opinion and not science by which men act incontinently, it makes no difference to the argument, since some of those who opine do not doubt, but think they know with certainty.

And it is proved by evident experience: Because there are many opinions, not only in Dialectic but also in Philosophy and Theology, approved by the common consent of almost the whole School and confirmed by efficacious arguments, which we follow without any actual fear or apprehension. And sometimes we see some men deduce from evident principles some conclusion through a syllogism which they think evident, but which is in truth only probable, and such men judge the conclusion to be certain, although in them it is truly only opinion; therefore it is repugnant that they should at the same time have fear lest it be false, or the opposite true. Wherefore it is evident that actual apprehension is not intrinsic to opinion, since it is often found without it. Virtual or radical fear, however, is intrinsic even to these opinions, since on the part of the middle of assenting it is not repugnant that falsehood lie under them.

The testimony of St. Thomas, moreover, is understood of this virtual fear, not of the actual.

To the argument: granting the antecedent with the consequence, the consequent must be distinguished. For if it is understood of actual fear or apprehension, it is false; but if of virtual or radical fear, true; and therefore the argument proves that only this is intrinsic to opinion, not the other.

Whether opinion can exist together with science concerning the same proposition and in

the same intellect.

I   t is certain that opinion can exist together with science concerning the same thing.

For of the line the Geometer has science, and the Dialectician or Metaphysician has opinion whether it is really distinguished from substance. Nor is it certain only that they can exist at the same time concerning the same thing in diverse men or intellects, but also in the same intellect. For the same geometer has science of the line, and can at the same time have opinion about its distinction from substance. Therefore the title of the question does not ask whether they can exist at the same time in the same intellect concerning the same simple thing, but whether concerning the same proposition. Of which it is certain also that in diverse

[p. 711]

intellects there can be science and opinion.

47 For it can happen that someone has the assent to some conclusion through a true demonstration which another deduces from the same or other principles through a probable syllogism, and therefore has only opinion. The difficulty, then, is whether the same man can at the same time have science and opinion concerning the same proposition.

But a further distinction must be made concerning science and opinion, because it can be conceived in four ways that they exist at the same time. First, according to habit: so that the same man has at the same time the habit of science and of opinion concerning the same conclusion. Second, so that he has at the same time the assent of each. Third, that he has at the same time the habit of science and the assent of opinion. Fourth, that he has at the same time the habit of opinion and the assent of science. And the present question seems to proceed according to all the comparisons.

On it the first opinion is the negative one, of Scotus, in 3, d. 24, single q., § Contra haec 1; of Cajetan and Soto on the present chapter; and of Diego Mas, in the same place, q. 5. They prove it by the testimony of Aristotle in this chapter, where he proposed almost the same question, whether the same object can be known and opined by the same man. To which he answered that it cannot. And he proves it by this argument: The knowable is that which cannot be otherwise; but the opinable, that which can be otherwise, as it is opinable. But it is repugnant that the same thing can be otherwise and cannot be otherwise, since these are contradictories; therefore it will be repugnant that something be at the same time knowable and opinable, or known and opined.
