But these are the proper objects of science and opinion; therefore it will also be repugnant, according to the mind of Aristotle, that both exist at the same time in the same intellect concerning the same proposition.

48 It is proved next by reason. First, concerning the acts or assents; then concerning the habits. Concerning the acts, indeed: Because it is impossible that the same man judge at the same time that the same thing can be otherwise and cannot be otherwise, since these are contradictory judgments. But the assent of science is an actual judgment concerning the conclusion, that it cannot be otherwise; and the assent of opinion is a judgment concerning the same, that it can be otherwise; therefore they contain an actual repugnance; wherefore they cannot exist at the same time in the same intellect. And, what is more, these assents are repugnant as the evident and the inevident: because evidence is of the intrinsic ratio of the one, while the other is inevident by its own nature, since it is contingent, either on the part of the principle from which it is deduced or on the part of the probable middle through which it is deduced. But the evident and the inevident are opposed privatively, like light and darkness, because evidence is the manifestation of an object under the clarity of a light; therefore it is repugnant that they exist at the same time in the same intellect, just as it is repugnant

Y y iiij

[p. 712]

that light and darkness exist at the same time in the same part of the air.

49 Concerning the habits, they prove it second: Because acts and habits are concerned with the same object and through the same middle; and a habit is an inclination to an act concerning such an object and through such a middle; therefore they have altogether the same repugnance as the acts; wherefore neither can they exist at the same time.

The second opinion is that of Durandus, in 1, q. of the prologue, no. 20, where he distinguishes opinion: for, he says, it can be had in two ways. First, from probable premises, or from evident ones, through a probable middle, and one known as such by the one who opines. Second, from necessary premises, and evident ones, and through a middle that is truly probable, but reckoned evident by the one who opines. And if it is had in the first way, it is repugnant that it exist at the same time with science, both according to act and according to habit, as the first opinion asserts, with which it agrees in this. But if it is had in the second way, they can exist at the same time, both according to the acts and according to the habits; in which it contradicts the same opinion.

Therefore he proves this second point by such an argument. The whole repugnance of the assent of opinion and of science comes from this: that by the one it is judged that the conclusion cannot be otherwise, but by the other that it can be otherwise. But when opinion is had through a middle thought to be evident, and from evident premises, it is judged that the conclusion cannot be otherwise, just as by the assent of science; therefore there remains in them no repugnance or opposition on account of which they could not exist at the same time. On the contrary, they are altogether in conformity, because by both the conclusion is judged necessary, and therefore such that it cannot be otherwise. But two conformable causes can well concur to the same effect; and if the assents are not repugnant in this way, it will be evident that the habits are not repugnant, which can be repugnant only on account of the assents.

50 The third opinion is that of certain moderns, altogether opposed to these two, because it affirms that science and opinion can exist at the same time concerning the same proposition, in the same intellect, both according to act and according to habit, and whether the opinion is had through a probable middle reckoned as such by the one who opines, or reckoned necessary. Only concerning the proposition of which each assent is, does it distinguish in this way: for it can be considered in two ways. First, as it is a certain proposition about which each habit or assent is concerned. Second, as it is the conclusion of a demonstration, or of a probable syllogism. And the first consideration, it says, is as it were material, the second as it were formal: because there is one and the same proposition about which they are concerned; but that same proposition is the conclusion of each syllogism, and since these are distinguished in species,

[p. 713]

the same proposition is as it were a twofold conclusion, formally and specifically distinct; whence it comes about that each assent and habit is indeed of the same proposition, but not of the same conclusion, rather of conclusions formally diverse. And they say this is the opinion of Alexander of Hales, 3 p., q. 79, memb. 3; St. Bonaventure, in 3, d. 24, q. 2, a. 3; Durandus, q. 1 of the prologue, and in 3, d. 31, q. 4; William of Auxerre, Summa bk. 3, tit. 3, q. 4 and 5; Richard of Middleton, in 3, d. 15, q. 1; and Villalpando on the present chapter; and also St. Thomas, 1-2, q. 67, a. 3, where he grants that the same proposition can be known through diverse middles, an evident and a probable one, as through a perfect and an imperfect middle, which are not altogether repugnant; which he repeats in 3 p., q. 9, a. 3, ad 2, where Father Francisco Suárez follows the same opinion.

51 They prove it first: Because the whole repugnance on account of which the assents of opinion and science concerning the same proposition cannot exist at the same time is that it is repugnant that it be judged at the same time that it can be otherwise and cannot, since these two judgments are contradictory. But this would be so if each were to be judged through the same middle. But since this is done through diverse middles, it would contain no repugnance or contradiction: because it is in no way repugnant that the intellect judge that a proposition cannot be otherwise, as it is the conclusion of a demonstration, and that it can be otherwise, as it is the conclusion of a probable syllogism; nor are these two judgments, compared to diverse middles, opposed contradictorily. Which is especially true since actual fear is not intrinsic to opinion, nor is it necessary that the one who opines actually judge that the conclusion can be otherwise; indeed he can judge the contrary, as Durandus noted.

Second: Because together with a demonstration a probable reason can be, and usually is, adduced to prove the same conclusion, just as together with divine faith, for believing the same truth; therefore the intellect assents at the same time on account of both middles; and therefore each will have its own effect, which is the probable and the scientific assent, and they will exist at the same time; otherwise each middle would be adduced in vain.

52 Our view is as it were a middle one, and is explained in one conclusion: Science and opinion according to habit can exist at the same time in the same intellect concerning the same proposition, but not according to assent or act. By the first part the first opinion is excluded, and in part the second. By the second part, the second is also excluded in part, and the third as well. Moreover, those authors whom the last opinion cites for itself hold our view, as will be plain to one who reads them; for he will see (unless I am mistaken

[p. 714]

) that they grant concerning the habits alone that they can exist at the same time, not concerning the assents. And this is the sense of St. Thomas, especially in the last place, if his words are attentively considered.

But in order that we may at once explain and prove it, it should be noted that science and opinion, while they affirm the truth of the same proposition, are not opposed contradictorily, nor privatively, indeed not by any kind of opposition: Because things of which each affirms cannot be opposed contradictorily; nor is it necessary that the judgments of the two be opposed contradictorily, so that by the judgment of science it is said that the proposition cannot be otherwise, but by the opinative judgment that it can be otherwise. For, as the second and third opinions prove well, it is not necessary that such a judgment be found in the one who opines; rather it is often not found, and sometimes the contrary is found. Further, neither are they opposed privatively: because the assent of opinion does not lack evidence, nor is it properly deprived of it, but it says a certain negation of it, just as any species says the negation of another; and yet they are not on that account said to be opposed privatively or contradictorily, but to be disparate. And so science and opinion stand.

53 And yet they are not altogether disparate or diverse, but very similar, since they are ordered to the same end, which is to make truth firm in the intellect; except that science effects this altogether, but opinion in some part, not fully or perfectly. Therefore they are distinguished only as the perfect and the imperfect, as St. Thomas says excellently in the last place: because science is as it were a perfect form, but opinion as it were a disposition to it; and they have these rationes of perfect and imperfect from their own nature and essence. But the perfect and the imperfect are repugnant in two ways, or in respect of two things. First, in respect of the same form: because it is repugnant that the same form be by its own nature a habit and a disposition; and thus it is repugnant that the same quality or habit be at the same time science and opinion. Second, it is repugnant in order to the same subject: because it is impossible that the same body be at the same time perfectly and imperfectly hot, or the same part of the air perfectly and imperfectly illuminated. And this repugnance science and opinion without doubt have in respect of the same subject, concerning the same proposition. Because opinion does not altogether, or not fully, determine the intellect to its truth, nor make it firm or stable; but it determines it indeed in a certain infirm and weak manner, and leaves it as it were undetermined in some part; and every opinion whatever has this from its nature and essence,

[p. 715]

however it is had, even through a probable middle reckoned necessary. But science fully, perfectly, and altogether determines the intellect to the truth of the demonstrated proposition, and also renders it altogether firm and stable.

54 From which each part of our view can be efficaciously proved. First, indeed, that science and opinion cannot exist at the same time according to the acts or assents, against the second and third opinions, by this argument: It is impossible that something be at the same time fully and altogether determined, and not fully and altogether determined, concerning the same thing, since these are opposed contradictorily. But by the scientific assent the intellect is fully and altogether determined to the truth of the demonstrated proposition, and is rendered firm and stable in it; and by the assent of opinion it is neither altogether determined, nor made firm and stable; therefore it is repugnant that these two exist at the same time in the intellect concerning the same truth. But you will say, for the third opinion, that this argument concludes that it is repugnant for the intellect to be in both ways at the same time in respect of the same middle, but not by reason of diverse middles. It is therefore proved efficaciously that it is repugnant even through diverse middles: because for the intellect to be at the same time convinced and not convinced concerning the same truth, from whatever source this comes, whether through the same or a diverse middle, is plainly repugnant, since these are to be and not to be at the same time in respect of the same thing; therefore it does not remove the difficulty of the argument that this happens through diverse middles. And if it can happen through diverse middles, it follows that a scientific assent and an erroneous one can exist at the same time concerning the same proposition, so that the intellect judges at the same time that it is true and false: true indeed through demonstration, but false through a probable syllogism. For then the opposition will cease, because it is said to be only in respect of the same middle, not in respect of diverse middles; which things, however, are absurd.

Concerning the habits, however, it can easily be proved, because they do not say an actual determination of the intellect to the truth, but as it were a potential and habitual one. And it is not repugnant that the intellect be imperfectly determined in act and be able to be fully determined, although full actual determination is repugnant to the non-full. Whence that there be in the same intellect at diverse times a full and a non-full determination contains no repugnance; but that this should happen at the same time is supremely repugnant.

55 To the argument of Scotus, by which he proved the repugnance of the habits, the consequence must be denied: because although act and habit are concerned

[p. 716]

with the same object and are had through the same middle, they nevertheless have far diverse rationes: because a habit is as it were an inclination, and as it were a potency to the act, whereas the act comes about through an actual attaining of the object. But it is not repugnant that someone have at the same time inclinations to repugnant acts, which he can exercise at diverse times, although it is repugnant to exercise both at the same time. Whence, although it is repugnant that the acts or assents of opinion and of science exist at the same time, it is nevertheless not repugnant that the habits exist at the same time.

56 To the argument of Durandus: granting the major and the minor, the consequence must be denied. Because the repugnance of the assents of opinion and of science does not consist in the opposition of the judgments, of which it is well proved that it is not necessary that they be had at the same time; but in this: that the ratio of opinion is essentially imperfect, not altogether determining the intellect to the truth, nor making it firm in it; whereas the ratio of science is essentially perfect concerning the same thing, since it fully and altogether determines the intellect and makes it firm in the same truth. But for the intellect to be firm and stable in the same truth, and at the same time infirm and weak, is repugnant; and likewise to be at the same time altogether determined and undetermined. And this follows whether it happens through the same or through a diverse middle; and therefore it is repugnant that opinion and science exist at the same time concerning the same proposition in the same intellect. Thus, although actual fear is not intrinsic to opinion, and although it can be had through a middle that is truly probable but thought necessary (which things are to be granted), nevertheless the assent of opinion has from its own intrinsic ratio that it does not altogether determine the intellect, nor make it firm in the truth. And therefore it cannot exist at the same time with the assent of science, which fully determines and makes it firm; but when this comes, and with it the full determination of the intellect, the former ceases: because all indetermination ceases, and some indetermination pertains to its essence; and therefore when all ceases, some ceases; and consequently there ceases the assent that is in some part undetermined and infirm: just as weakness of the limbs ceases when strength comes, and sickness ceases when health comes. And from these things it is plain that the arguments of the last opinion are solved. And let it suffice to have noted these things concerning the work of the Posterior Resolution.

The end of this work.

[p. 717]

## SOME SELECTIONS FROM

THE BOOKS OF ARISTOTLE’S TOPICS,

BY WHICH STUDENTS OF THE LIBERAL

Arts of this most flourishing Academy of Alcalá

may satisfy the customary questions of the

Masters in the examination

to be undergone for the degree

of Bachelor.

On the end and division of these books.

he end which Aristotle intends in these eight books of the Topics 1

T          is to hand down a Method of disputing probably on any theme whatever,

or proposed problem. And since the universal and principal instru‐

ment of Topical disputation is Dialectical reasoning, which we call the

Topical syllogism, he does two things in the whole work, so that we may pro‐

pose its universal division. First, he explains the nature of the dialectical syl‐

logism, and the parts of which it is composed. Second, because this syllogism

is called Topical, that is, local, he copiously hands down and explains all the

places from which we can draw an abundance of probable arguments, so that

the Dialectician, thus instructed, may be able to set up any disputation what‐

ever concerning probable matters. We, therefore, desiring to hand down in a

certain brief summary the things which are necessary for understanding the

Topical art and for instructing students of the liberal arts, so that they may

satisfy the customary questions of the examination to be undergone, shall

carry out two other things in the same order. First, we shall explain what the

Dialectical syllogism is, and what and how many are the parts of which it

must be composed, both simple ones, such as the Topical predicates, and

also composite ones, such as the Dialectical problem and the Dialectical

proposition, of which Aristotle treats through the first eight chapters of

book 1. Then we shall summarily collect, enumerate, and explain the places

from which probable arguments are to be drawn.

What the object of this work is, and its order with the other parts of Dialectic, is

explained. 2

F   rom these things it can easily be understood what the object of this

work is. For if all the things which are treated in it are either

[p. 718]

parts of the Dialectical syllogism, or places from which an abundance of

probable arguments can be drawn, which are also ordered to the composi‐

tion of the same syllogism, then the aim of the whole work, whose nature

and properties Aristotle intends to explain in it, will be that same syllogism,

and consequently its proper subject or object. For these are the principal

conditions of an object. Nor will it be difficult to understand the order which

the books of the Topics keep among the other parts of Logic, and the place

due to them among the others; for they follow immediately the books on the

Posterior Resolution recently explained by us. The reason for this is: Because

among the species of syllogisms, after demonstration, explained in the books

of the Posterior Analytics, the dialectical syllogism is worthier than the others;

therefore this treatise, dealing with it as with its proper object, must be

placed immediately after those same books.

What a Dialectical predicate is. 3

T    he simple things of which the Dialectical problem and proposition are

proximately composed, and the Dialectical syllogism remotely, are the

Topical or Dialectical predicates (which is the same thing), of which Aristotle

treats in ch. 4 of the first book, where he enumerates them and explains each

by its proper definition. The Topical predicate we can define in general thus: It

is the principal part of which the Dialectical problem and proposition are composed.

We call it the principal part to distinguish it from the subject, of which the

same Dialectical proposition is composed. For we do not wish now to call

the copula of the proposition a part so much as the connection of each part,

by which, when coupled, they compose the proposition.

How manifold the Dialectical predicate is. 4

O      n the one hand the Dialectical predicates seem to be five, on account of this

argument: Because a predicate is distinguished from a predicable as act

from potency; but act and potency must be numbered in the same way, be‐

cause potency takes its unity and distinction from act; therefore there will be

as many predicates as predicables. But it is established from Porphyry that

the predicables are five; therefore the predicates too must be five.

But on the other hand they seem to be ten, on account of a second argument:

Because a category is nothing other than a series and ordering of predicates;

therefore the number of predicates and of categories will be the same. But it

is established that there are ten categories

[p. 719]

from Aristotle; therefore ten predicates must be posited.

5 These things notwithstanding, our view is that there are only four Topical predicates, as Aristotle expressly teaches, bk. 1, ch. 4, which are: Definition, Genus, Property, and Accident, so that neither are more to be added nor any of these to be taken away. But the whole difficulty of this matter consists in assigning the reason on account of which Aristotle posited these four predicates. For whose explanation it should be noted that the end of this topical art, as we said, is to hand down a method of disputing probably on any thing proposed. But a disputation consists of three parts, ordered thus. First, of the Question, or interrogation, which we usually call the title of the disputation, saying thus: Whether the heavens are incorruptible, or not? or something similar. Next, of the Places from which probable arguments are to be drawn, by which means we may render the question doubtful; and in the third place, of the Arguments themselves, which are Dialectical syllogisms composed of Dialectical propositions. Now the Dialectical proposition (as will be said afterward) is one part of the problem. And problems, and consequently Dialectical propositions, are made of predicates: because a problem is nothing other than a question or interrogation whether some predicate belongs to such a subject: as when we say, Whether the heavens are incorruptible, or not? it is the same as if we asked whether this predicate, incorruptible, belongs to the heavens, or not. Whence it follows that a topical predicate is nothing other than that which can be asked about some thing. There will therefore be as many predicates as there can be questions made about some thing, and as many questions as predicates. And since a question is the same as a problem, the number of predicates and of problems will be the same. And finally, since a proposition and a problem differ only in the form of the interrogation (because a problem is an interrogation of both parts of a contradiction: as if you say, Whether the heavens are incorruptible or not, you make a problem; whereas a proposition is an interrogation of one of the two parts, as Do you think the heavens are incorruptible?), there are as many Dialectical propositions as problems. And thus it is understood that the Dialectical predicate is the first thing from which the number of problems must be taken; then from the number of problems, the number of Dialectical propositions. And thus the number of predicates is taken from the order to the problems and propositions to be constituted. And this discourse is drawn from ch. 4 of bk. 1.

6 This supposed, it is proved by Aristotle by this argument that there are only four predicates. A predicate is that which can be asked about some thing for setting up a Dialectical disputation; but four

[p. 710]

only can be asked; therefore there are only four predicates. He proves the minor: For either we ask about something its definition, in order that we may understand its nature; or its genus, in order that we may understand in which category it is; or its properties, or its common accidents. And nothing else can be asked which is not reduced to these; therefore there are four predicates, so that there are neither more nor fewer. And these are definition, genus, property, and accident, which he explains by their definitions thus in ch. 4 of bk. 1. Definition is an expression signifying what it was to be. He says it is an expression because it is not a proposition, since it contains neither truth nor falsehood, as rational animal. He also calls the definition a term, taking the metaphor from the boundaries of fields. For to any field there belongs alone and wholly that which is enclosed within its boundaries, so that nothing of it is outside, but the whole that it has is comprehended within its boundaries. So the definition contains whatever pertains to the essence of the thing, so that nothing of it is outside, nor is there anything of it that is not comprehended within it; and therefore it is called a term by Aristotle. Genus, he says, is that which is predicated of many things differing in species, in quid, as animal. Property, that which does not indicate what the being of the thing is, but belongs to it alone and is predicated convertibly, as risible in respect of man. Accident is that which is neither definition, nor genus, nor property, but belongs to the thing; or also: Accident is that which can belong to the same thing, as whiteness in respect of a wall.

7 But if you say: Beyond these four questions, or interrogations, or problems, which seem to be general, many special ones can be asked about a thing: as whether it is a man, whether it is a lion, whether it is a substance, and innumerable others; therefore more than four, indeed innumerable predicates must be granted. And besides, the general predicates are still more: because just as we ask about the genus of some thing, as whether Animal is the genus of man or not, so we can ask about its difference, namely whether Rational is the difference of man; and also about the species, as whether Man is the species of Peter or John, or even whether it is a species of animal; therefore two other general predicates must be added, namely Species and Difference.

8 Concerning the first part of the argument, about the special interrogations, Rudolph Agricola, On Dialectical Invention bk. 1, ch. 3, asserts that Aristotle erred in assigning the number of predicates: because, just as there are many kinds of particular problems, so more predicates than four must be established. But this author seems to me to have erred more in reproving Aristotle, because the true solution is to be gathered from the doctrine of the same Aristotle, Topics bk. 1, ch. 4, and bk. 5, last chapter, toward the end. In which places

two

[p. 721]

he asserts two things. The first: Since problems are ordered to dialectical disputation, whose end is the determination of the same problem about which the dispute is held, so that, after probable arguments have been set out for each side, it may finally be decided which of them is the more probable, it follows that all problems which are determined by the same arguments and in the same way belong to the same genus of problem; and that all their predicates are comprised under one of the four designated. And therefore in this first place he asserts that difference, if it is general, that is, if it is predicated of several species as a genus is, must be counted together with genus, and that no other predicate is to be added for it. The second is what he teaches in the second place: that a question of accident is settled, or determined, solely from someone’s proving that it belongs to the subject. From this doctrine we deduce that all special problems, whatever they may be, are reduced to the problem of accident, and all their predicates to the predicate of accident. And the reason for this deduction is that in every special problem it is asked: Does this predicate belong to such a subject, or is it in it, or not? which plainly has the mode of interrogation, or of problem, of accident, in which we ask only whether an accident belongs to, or is in, the subject. And they are settled, or determined, by exactly the same arguments: because if you ask whether animal belongs to man or not, or whether man belongs to Peter or not, it is sufficiently determined, and the disputation about it will be finished, if we prove that it is in it in any way whatever, even though it is not proved to be of its essence, or to be convertible with it, or to belong to it in any other special way. Therefore they are reduced to the form of an accidental problem, and their predicates are comprised under the predicate of accident, and there is no need to multiply others.

From the same doctrine we can reply to the other part of the same argument, concerning species and difference: that if the difference is subaltern, it is reduced to the predicate of genus; but if it is lowest, to the predicate of definition. Species, however, is reduced to the predicate of genus. And the reason for all of these is that a question of genus and of subaltern difference is settled by the same arguments, since each is predicated of several things differing in species, in quid. For by the same arguments we prove that animal is the genus of man, and that sensible is its subaltern difference; and also that man is the species of Peter and John, because just as genus is predicated in quid of species, so species is predicated of individuals. By the same arguments we also prove that rational animal is the definition of man, and that rational is its atomic difference. As to what concerns species, a quite probable reply is also given by Albert

Zz

[p. 722]

the Great, Topics tract. 2, ch. 8, at the end, and Soto, q. 5 on universals, ad 1:

that it is not to be enumerated among the predicates: because predicates are

taken by relation to a common subject, which species does not regard, but

singulars. And the reason for this is that predicates, as we were saying, are or‐

dered by their proper ratio to constituting problems and dialectical proposi‐

tions, and each of these to constituting the dialectical syllogism, which is not

constituted per se out of singular propositions, but out of those consisting of

a common subject, in which alone the syllogistic form, consisting of mood

and figure, can be found, as is manifest per se.

11 To the first argument, concerning the predicables: the antecedent

must be distinguished. For predicate taken universally is distinguished from

predicable as act from potency, and therefore it is numbered in the same way

as predicable. But predicate taken specially, for the Topical one, does not re‐

gard the predicable as a potency, but is taken only for the actual one, and in‐

deed in a special mode, distinct from the general predicate, that is, in order

to setting up a question, or problem. Hence predicates are also numbered in

another, different way, and are allotted a number different from the predica‐

bles, and also from the categories, which belong to the ordering of predicates

as they are considered under a general ratio, not under a special and Topical

one, ordered also to the special end already explained. Wherefore it does not

follow from the fact that the categories are ten that the Topical predicates

must be as many. And this is the solution of the second argument.

What a dialectical problem is, and how many kinds there are.

12

A     ristotle, bk. 1, ch. 3, defines the dialectical problem, saying that it is an

interrogation, or question, of either part of a contradiction: as if you say,

Whether walking two-footed animal is the definition of man, or not? And there are

four genera of problems, as the same Aristotle asserts in ch. 3 and 4, just as

there are four predicates. Thus the Problem of definition, such as the one as‐

signed from the definition of man. The Problem of genus, as if you say, Whether

animal is the genus of man, or not? The Problem of property, as when we say,

Whether risible is a property of man, or not? And finally the Problem of accident:

Whether whiteness is an accident of the wall, or not? In ch. 9 of the same book,

too, Aristotle divides the dialectical problem universally, saying that one is

Practical: that which pertains to choice or avoidance, or to something to be

pursued

[p. 723]

or avoided. For this, he says, is ordered to practice, or operation, and there‐

fore it is called practical. Such is this: Whether pleasure is to be chosen, or not.

Another, however, is Speculative: that which contains nothing about some‐

thing to be pursued or avoided, nor is ordered to operation, but only to the

cognition of truth: as if you say, Whether the heavens are incorruptible, or not?

The problem can also be divided by another division, according to the mat‐

ters of the diverse sciences in which it is found; for which reason we say that

one is a Physical problem, as, Whether the principle of motion and rest of that in

which it is, is the definition of nature, or not? Another Metaphysical, as if you

should say, Whether being is univocal with respect to substance and accident, or not?

Nevertheless, the formal consideration of all problems, according to which

they are reduced to those four, taken from the diverse predicates, is proper

to the dialectician: because it pertains to the dialectician alone to teach all

how a disputation is to be set up, and what instruments are to be used in it

for attaining cognition of the truth about which the dispute is held.

What a dialectical proposition is, and how many kinds there are; and how it is distin‐

guished from a problem. 14

T     hree things Aristotle delivers in bk. 1, ch. 3, at the end. In the first place

he defines the dialectical proposition as being, as it were, the proposition

of the other part of a contradiction: as if you say, Do you think that rational animal is

the definition of man? And he says that it differs from the problem not in reali‐

ty but in mode: because the Proposition, as the etymology of the word shows,

proposes something to another, so that he may reply to the thing proposed,

explaining what he judges or thinks about it. The Problem, however, has the

mode of a question, and proposes both parts to be debated by way of a ques‐

tion: as if you say, Whether rational animal is the definition of man, or not? Thus

the dialectical proposition interrogates by way of a simple proposition, not

by way of a question, and takes up only one part; whereas the problem takes

up both, and interrogates by way of a question. This is customarily put for‐

ward in two ways: either by interrogating both parts formally, as in the exam‐

ple assigned; or one formally and the other virtually, as if you should say only,

Whether rational animal is the definition of man? And in this way problems are

put forward in the common usage of the schools whenever some question to

be disputed is proposed: which is done, no doubt, for the sake of brevity, be‐

cause the other part too is now understood by all to be interrogated, from

the very mode of the problematic interrogation.

Z z ij

[p. 724]

15 Here we must notice that Aristotle, Prior Analytics 1, ch. 1, did not distinguish the dialectical proposition from the problem, nor indeed from the probable proposition: since he said that it is an interrogation of a contradiction, which is proper to the problem; and again, that the dialectical proposition is, for the one who questions, an interrogation of a contradiction, but for the one who reasons, the taking of something apparent and probable. Therefore he referred the distinction of these three to ch. 3 of Topics 1, which he cited, saying: as was said in the Topics. For there was the proper place to distinguish these things, in the way in which they have been distinguished by us. The dialectical proposition is fourfold, as we said of the problem. Of Definition is this: Do you think rational animal is the definition of man? Of Property: Do you think risible is a proper attribute of man? Of Genus: Do you think animal is the genus of man? Of Accident: Do you think whiteness is an accident of man?

16 But it should be carefully noted in this matter that Proposition, taken under this general ratio, signifies only an enunciation as it is proposed in a syllogism for inferring the conclusion. If it is proposed in the first place, it is called Proposition simply, or Proposition, or major premise, or the First part of the antecedent. If in the second place, it is called Assumption, because it is assumed under the major proposition, under which it is contained; it is also called Minor proposition, or Minor premise, and the Second, or posterior, part of the antecedent. And if it is proposed in a demonstrative syllogism, it is called a Principle; if in a dialectical syllogism, a Probable proposition; and an Apparent proposition, if in a sophistical syllogism. But the dialectical Proposition adds to the enunciation the mode of a proposition, as it were by way of one who doubts; and the problem the mode of one who interrogates, as has been explained.

From which it is understood that the Dialectical proposition, as well as the problem, and also the probable proposition, serve for setting up a disputation, but in a different ratio: for the dialectical problem serves by way of a question proposed for disputing, and therefore it holds the first place and is called, as it were, the head of the whole disputation.

17 The dialectical Proposition, however, serves as it were for an interrogation made to the respondent, so that by means of it the respondent may put forward another, through which he explains what he thinks of the thing proposed; and from the reply given the interrogator may take occasion to dispute for one or the other part of the proposed question. The probable proposition, in turn, serves now for constituting the syllogism by which what is intended may be proved, and the question terminated or settled. Thus the problem and the dialectical proposition, under

[p. 725]

their proper formal ratios, pertain to setting up a disputation, yet not to the

dialectical syllogism, except only antecedently and as it were presuppositive‐

ly. The probable proposition alone pertains to the same disputation as a part

of the dialectical syllogism. Here we must notice that Aristotle in this place

distinguishes the proposition from the problem, saying that the problem in‐

terrogates both parts.

What a probable proposition is, and how many kinds there are. 18

A     ristotle, bk. 1, ch. 1, defines the probable in these words: Probable things

are those which seem so to all, or to most, or to the wise; and to these, either to all,

or to most, or to the most familiar and approved. Which is understood either on

account of the thing itself, which of itself appears true, or on account of

some verisimilar reason. Thus the probable is not the same as the true, nor

yet as the necessary or certain, but is that which appears true to all, or to

most, or to the wise. For propositions are of three different kinds. For some are

evidently true, and their truth is evidently known. Others evidently false, and

their falsity too is evidently known. Others, however, hold the middle: because

they are true or false, but their truth or falsity is not evidently known, be‐

cause their cause is either unknown or not fully known; and therefore they

appear true to many, while to others it happens that they appear false, since

there is usually a verisimilar reason for each side. And these are called proba‐

ble. It is plain, then, how the probable proposition is distinguished from the

proposition that is True, Certain, Necessary, and false. For it can happen that

in reality it is necessary, having necessary truth, or that in reality it is neces‐

sarily false, having a necessary cause of its falsity, and yet it seems probable

on account of the verisimilitude, the appearance of truth, which it has, or on

account of a verisimilar reason by which it can be proved. So that it may be

understood that the formal ratio of the probable proposition consists not so

much in the thing itself as in the appearance, or in an apparent reason, with

respect to many, or to the wise, as Aristotle taught.

From which it follows that, although it is repugnant that two contradicto‐

ries be true at the same time, it is nevertheless not repugnant that they be

probable at the same time: because it often happens that each has on its side

learned men, to whom it appears true, and also verisimilar reasons by which

it is proved. But in the thing itself one of them must be false. It is not, how‐

ever, necessary (as some mistakenly think) that if one proposition is proba‐

ble, by that very fact its contradictory is also probable, since it is manifest

that it can happen

Z z iij

[p. 726]

that the one appears true to learned men and has verisimilar reasons on its side, while the other appears true to no one, nor has any verisimilar reason been found by which it may be proved.

The probable proposition is twofold: one per se, the other on account of another, from which it is deduced. That is called per se probable whose probability is evident from the cognition of the terms alone, without any other reasoning by which it is proved, so that the intellect cannot but judge that it is probable. Such is this: Every mother loves her son; or, Every friend is to be loved. And this per se probable proposition Aristotle defined in Posterior Analytics 1, saying: Opinion is the acceptance of an immediate and non-necessary proposition, understanding by the name of opinion the assent of such an immediate proposition, that is, of one which is judged probable without a middle, from the cognition of the terms alone. And the assent of this per se probable proposition can be called understanding within the genus of the probable proposition, just as within the genus of the evident the assent of a necessary proposition which is had without a middle, once the signification of the terms alone is known, is called understanding. The other is the Proposition not per se probable, but which is gathered from another that is per se probable through an evident or probable consequence, or from another evident one through a consequence that is only probable. And this is similar to a scientific conclusion, which we gather from evident premises and through an evident syllogism. Nevertheless, from either probable proposition a dialectical syllogism can be made, as is manifest per se.

What a Topical or dialectical syllogism is.

O     nce the single parts of the dialectical syllogism have been explained, it

will not be difficult to understand its definition, which Aristotle assigned in Topics 1, ch. 1, in these words: But the dialectical syllogism is one which is gathered from probable things; that is, one which, proceeding from probable propositions, gathers a conclusion that is also probable. This is to be understood thus: that it must proceed from both premises probable, or at least from one of them; for it often happens that it is made from one evident and the other probable. For such is this one: Every animal loves its like; Every man is an animal; therefore Every man loves his like. And it agrees with the demonstrative syllogism in the common and generic ratio of disposition in Mood and figure; but it is distinguished from it in species by the mode of concluding: for demonstration concludes through a necessary middle, that is, through a necessary cause or effect; whereas the probable syllogism concludes through a probable middle, because it neither renders

[p. 727]

a necessary cause nor a necessary effect of the conclusion, but only a proba‐

ble one, that is, such as appear so to many or to the wise, as has been ex‐

plained. Thus they are not distinguished by matter alone, as we proved in the

Posterior Analytics, but also by a special form, taken from the special mode of

concluding, since they agree in the generic form of syllogistic disposition.

From the sophistical syllogism, however, it is distinguished by true or appar‐

ent form, and also by probable or apparent propositions. For the dialectical

proceeds from the former, but the sophistical from the latter. But to proceed

from probable things and from apparent ones is something different: for al‐

though a probable proposition is one which appears true, even though per‐

haps it is not true, yet it does not appear so to anyone whatever, but only to

the wise, and this on account of the foundation of a verisimilar reason, or on

account of the verisimilitude of that same truth. But the apparent things

from which the sophistical syllogism proceeds are not called such with re‐

spect to the wise, nor do they appear true with the foundation of a probable

reason, or with the verisimilitude of that same truth, but to anyone whatev‐

er, and without these foundations. Hence they have only the bare appearance

of truth, and are therefore properly called deceptive; and the syllogism itself,

proceeding from things so apparent, is also called deceptive.

Enumeration and explanation of the places from which probable arguments are de‐

duced for entering upon a disputation. 22

T     his alone remained to be explained among the things that pertain to

setting up a dialectical disputation: namely the Places from which prob‐

able arguments, or syllogisms, are to be taken. For once places of this kind

have been explained and known, it will be easy for anyone to find probable

arguments which he can use in disputations. And although the use of the

places pertains to any science whatever, according to their application to its

proper matter, their explanation nevertheless belongs to Dialectic alone,

whose proper office is to furnish all the sciences and disciplines with a

method for setting up a disputation.

23 The Place, then, from which arguments are drawn out, is divided into

the Intrinsic and the Extrinsic. The Intrinsic place is called that which pertains

to the substance of the thing, or accompanies its substance. Those that per‐

tain to the substance are these: Definition, Genus, Difference, or some Part

of the thing, such as Matter and Form; or the integral Parts, such as the

Head, the Hand, or the Arm. That which accompanies the substance, on the

other hand, is either the Whole (which is said to accompany the substance of

the thing because it includes the parts),

Z z iiij

[p. 728]

or the Description of the thing itself, or the Property of the thing, or an

Accident, or its subject. Hence there are only nine intrinsic places: Definition,

Genus, Difference, Parts, Whole, Description, Property, Accident, and

Subject.

The extrinsic place is said to be that which is not in the thing itself, nor

proceeds from it, but is taken from something extrinsic. And the extrinsic

place is divided into That which has some affinity with the thing itself, and

That which has some repugnance to it. The extrinsic places having affinity are

Conjugates, Similars, extrinsic Causes, namely the Efficient and the Final, ex‐

trinsic Effects, the Greater, the Lesser, Authority Divine or human. The re‐

pugnant extrinsic places, on the other hand, are Contraries, Disparates, and

Dissimilars. Hence the extrinsic places are eleven; and if we join them with

the nine intrinsic ones, we shall find that all the places, intrinsic as well as ex‐

trinsic, are only twenty. These we shall explain one by one, though very

briefly, so that the ratio of each may be understood and their use made easy.

The first place, from Definition. 24

F    requent is the use of this place from Definition in disputations, because

the definition contains the essence and is convertible with it. Hence it

happens that several universal propositions can be deduced from it, which

are called Maxims, and as it were heads under which several particular ones

are taken for setting up dialectical syllogisms. And if the proposed question

about which the dispute is held is Absolute, we can take up in the argumen‐

tation the definition of the subject, or of the predicate, or of both; from

which are deduced Maxims, Affirmative and Negative. The affirmative are:

Whatever belongs to the definition belongs to the defined; and Whatever can belong to

the definition can belong to the defined; and others like them. The negative: What

does not belong to the definition does not belong to the defined; and What cannot belong

to the definition cannot belong to the defined. For example: if the proposed q. to be

disputed is, Whether dialectic is necessary for acquiring the other sciences, the

Subject of this question is Dialectic, and the Predicate is necessary. We can

therefore use the definition of Dialectic, arguing thus: A science teaching how

to construct arguments is necessary for acquiring the other sciences; but dialectic is a sci‐

ence teaching how to construct arguments; therefore it is necessary for acquiring the

other sciences. And according to the same proportion we can use the definition

of necessary, which is the predicate of the question, and also the definition of

subject and predicate together.

[p. 629]

But if the question is Comparative, namely, Whether necessity for acquiring

the other sciences belongs more to dialectic than to the other arts, we can use the defi‐

nition of the subject, and also of the predicate, or of both, deducing from

them certain Maxims similar to the ones above, with these adverbs more and

less. As if we say: To that to which the definition belongs more, the defined belongs

more; and To that to which the definition belongs less, the defined belongs less; and so

of the rest.

The second place, from Genus. 25

I   n almost the same ways we can use the place from genus. For on account of

the necessary connection which it has with the species, several Maxims

are deduced from this place, from which we can set up arguments: such as

these, Whatever belongs essentially to the genus also belongs essentially to the species;

and, What is repugnant to the genus is also repugnant to the species; and so of the

others, according to the modes of arguing explained for definition. And to

this place of genus is reduced the place of Species, because it has a similar

connection with the individuals; and therefore no other place from species is

added, but almost the same Maxims can be deduced as from genus, and they

must be applied in the same way to forming arguments from species.

The third place, from Difference.

V     ery similar to the two preceding places, from definition and from

genus, is the place from Difference. For difference is twofold, Subaltern

and Atomic. And if it is subaltern, it is predicated of the same species as the

genus is, and has the same intrinsic connection with them. Wherefore the

same Maxims can be deduced from it as from genus. But if it is Atomic, it

agrees with definition in two things. First, in that it is intrinsic to the

species. Second, because it is convertible with it. Hence similar Maxims too

can be deduced from it as are deduced from definition, and they must be ap‐

plied in the same ways to constructing dialectical syllogisms.

The fourth place, from the parts.

P    arts are of three different kinds: Subjective, as species with respect to

genus; Essential, as matter and form, or genus and difference; and

Integral, as head, hand, and arm. And of these, some are necessary for the con‐

sistence of the whole, without which it cannot be, such as the head, the

heart, and the like. Others are not necessary, but it can be without them, such

as the hand, the finger, the foot. And from the first an argument can be de‐

duced; from the second it cannot be deduced, because neither

[p. 730]

do they infer the consistence of the whole, nor do they remove it. From the

## parts several Maxims can be deduced, on account of the necessary connec‐

tion which they have with the whole, and the whole with them: such as

these, What necessarily accompanies the part must necessarily also accompany the

whole; and, What is repugnant to the part is also repugnant to the whole. And these

are taken on the side of the subject of the proposed q. Others, however, can be

taken on the side of the predicate, according to proportion.

The fifth place, from the Whole. 27

T     he Whole is twofold. One is universal, which is a universal predicate with

respect to its inferiors, which are its subjective parts: as genus with re‐

spect to the species, and a term distributed by a universal sign, as every man,

with respect to the particulars which are contained under it. And from this

whole to its parts are taken all the arguments that are made from superior to

inferior negatively; and these are manifest in the Summulae. The other is the

Essential or integral whole, as man, horse, house. And from this whole several

Maxims can be deduced, and from them several syllogisms constructed: as,

When the whole is posited, all the necessary parts must be posited. Hence the argu‐

ment holds from the positing of the whole to the positing of any necessary

part whatever. And also, When the whole is taken away, some necessary part must

be taken away. Hence the argument holds from the negation of the whole to

the negation of some necessary part, under a disjunction: as, if the house is

lacking, either the foundation does not exist, or the roof does not exist, or

some other necessary part does not exist.

The sixth place, from Description. 28

D     escription is a definition which they usually call descriptive, because it

does not explain the essence of the thing, nor is it delivered through

genus and difference, but through a proper attribute, which is nevertheless

convertible with the thing described: as animal apt to laugh with man. And

therefore all the Maxims which are deduced from definition can be deduced

from description, and applied in the same way to constituting syllogisms.

And what is said of description ought to be understood of the definition of

what the name means, since it too is convertible with the thing; but not of

the etymology of the name: because it often happens that that from which

the name is imposed and that which it signifies are different; wherefore a

firm argument cannot be drawn from the etymology to the thing signified.

The seventh place, from Property.

P   roperty is that which does not indicate what it is to be for the thing, but is in it

alone, and is predicated convertibly, as Aristotle defines it, ch. 4, bk. 1: as if

[p. 731]

to say that a proper attribute does not pertain to what the thing is, or to its

essence, yet is convertible with it, just as the definition is convertible with

the defined. And therefore in almost the same ways almost the same argu‐

ments can be deduced from property as from definition: because, To whatever

the definition belongs, the proper attribute belongs; and, To whatever the proper at‐

tribute does not belong, neither does the definition belong. And just as it is rightly

gathered that a thing is more perfect the more perfect the definition it has,

so also the more perfect the attribute it has, since the latter proceeds from

the essence as from its proper cause.

The 8th place, from Accident. 29

A     n accident is that which is present to and absent from the subject without its cor‐

ruption, as Aristotle defines it in the same place. But this definition

seems to belong only to truly inhering accidents, which are therefore called

intrinsic; nevertheless, the others too, which seem to signify only an extrinsic

denomination, ought in this place to be understood under the name of acci‐

dent: as for a wall to be right or left, or to be seen or understood; because in

the mode of denominating they are similar to intrinsic accidents. From acci‐

dent several Maxims can be deduced, and from these several arguments. As,

If the accidents of the predicate do not belong to the subject, the predicate will not co‐

here with the subject: which argument blessed Peter seems to have used, Acts 2,

proving that the disciples were not drunk because that time, the third hour

of the day, was not suited to drunkenness, and therefore not to the disciples

either, since drunkenness was imputed to them at that same hour. And it is

well proved that someone did not kill another if it is proved that at the time

when he was killed he was not in the same place as the killing, but elsewhere.

Place 9, from the Subject.

T     his place is understood of the subject of inherence, in which accidents in‐

here, not of the subject of predication, to which a predicate can belong

essentially; and therefore it is rightly numbered among the intrinsic places.

From the subject these Maxims and the like can be deduced: To whatever the

accidents are repugnant, the subject too is repugnant: as, if intellect is repugnant to

something, so also is the soul; and if corporeal accidents are repugnant to it,

the body too will be repugnant to it. Where the subject is, there the accidents must

be; and Where the accidents are not, neither is the subject; and All things move with

our motion that are in us, that is, the accidents. And from these and other

Maxims many arguments can be made from the place of the subject. And

these are all the intrinsic places. The extrinsic ones follow.

[p. 732]

The tenth place, and the first among the Extrinsic ones, from Conjugates.

30

C     onjugates are said to be words which under different endings signify and partici‐

pate in the same form; and for this reason they seem as it were to draw the

same yoke, as just, justice, and justly; and all the cases by which the same noun

and verb are varied. To these are reduced others which signify the same

form, although they are altogether different words: as just and virtuous, which

are related, as regards the thing signified, as justice and just are. From these

are deduced these maxims and the like: What is said of one of the conjugates is

said also of the other in its own way, and with due variation: as, if the Philosopher

is knowing, Philosophy will be knowledge; and, Of whatever one of the conju‐

gates is said, the other too is said in its own way. And from these and similar

propositions many arguments can be made from conjugates.

Place 11, from the Similar.

S    imilar things are those which participate in the same form: as all white things.

To these are reduced those which have the same proportion: as the char‐

ioteer and the general, because the general ought to have in the army a care

similar to that which the charioteer has in his chariot. To similars are also re‐

duced equals; and from them several Maxims are deduced for setting up ar‐

guments, similar to this: The swan disperses the sight; therefore the white wall does

too. But in these the argument must always be made from the formal ratio of

similitude, and not from other material features which similar things can

have: for it is not a good argument if we say, The swan is a bird; therefore the

white wall too is a bird.

Place 12, from Cause. 31

C     ause is fourfold: Final, Efficient, Material, and Formal. But this place, since it

is extrinsic, embraces only the Final and the Efficient, not the Material

and the Formal, which, since they are intrinsic parts of the thing, will rather

pertain to the place of the parts. The final cause is that for the sake of which

the efficient operates and produces the effect; the efficient cause, that from

which the effect proceeds. The Maxims which can be deduced from them are

similar to these: When the cause is posited, the effect is necessarily posited, which is

understood of an actual and sufficient cause; and When the effect is not posited,

the cause is not posited. The things which pertain to the property of these caus‐

es are explained by us in Phys. bk. 2.

[p. 733]

Place 13, from the Effect.

V      ery similar to the preceding is this place, because the same Maxims are

deduced from cause and from effect: the mode of arguing in them is the

same, as from the positing of the effect to the positing of the cause: e.g., If it is day, the

sun is in our hemisphere. When the effect is taken away, the cause is taken away: as, It

is not day; therefore neither is the sun in our hemisphere. But these and others like

them are understood of necessary and sufficient causes.

Place 14, from the Greater, and 15, from the Lesser. 32

V      ery similar are these two places, from the greater and the lesser, and

therefore we must speak of them together. From the greater this Maxim

is taken: What can effect the greater can effect the lesser; and from the lesser this

one: What cannot effect the lesser cannot effect the greater either. But each must be

understood of a greater and a lesser of the same condition. For if they are of a

different ratio, the argument will not hold: e.g., An angel can understand, which

is greater; therefore he can walk, which is lesser; because understanding and walk‐

ing are of different conditions. Likewise, He cannot walk; therefore neither can he

understand.

Place 16 and 17, from Authority, Divine and human.

T     he testimony of one worthy of belief, on which faith rests, is very extrinsic to the

things testified or believed, as is manifest of itself. Hence the place from the

authority of one worthy of belief is supremely extrinsic. But if it is from

Divine authority, it attributes infallible truth to the thing: because, since God

is the highest and first truth, he cannot be deceived; and since he is the high‐

est goodness, he cannot deceive. Hence the things which G o d testifies have

infallible truth; and such are the things of our faith, which we believe on ac‐

count of the Divine authority; and Theological arguments are deduced chiefly

from this place.

33 From human authority or testimony, however, so firm an argument cannot be de‐

duced. But it is of very great value for explaining the things of divine faith. For

although the sacred Doctors were men, nevertheless an exposition of sacred

Scripture which all, or most of them, put forward (even if one, or another,

dissents) produces the greatest belief: because it is not to be believed that

God has permitted those to be deceived in this matter to whom it pertains to

expound Scripture and to hand it on, expounded, to others. It is also of great

value in matters which depend on the free will of men, as for the imposition

and signification of names: because names are to be used as most

[p. 734]

use them. Moreover, in things which are evidently known through the senses, and also in those which pertain to history, which must rest on some evidence, had for the most part through assents, from which others believe that things happened thus. But it is not of value in those things which are known through discursive reasoning, in which reason holds the chief place, although even in these the common consent of all is still of much value. A probable argument, therefore, is always drawn from human authority; and the more there are who testify to something, the more efficacious the argument that is deduced. Negatively, however, one must not argue from human authority, as if it were proved that a thing is not so because it is related by no one: because it is not necessary that all things have been written.

Place 18 and 19, from Opposites, and from Repugnants or Disparates.

T    hese two places, from Opposites and from Repugnants, or Disparates, do not differ

much, because almost the same arguments are deduced from both. Opposition is fourfold, as we said in the Postpredicaments: Contrary, which is between White and Black; Contradictory, between white and Not-white; Privative, between blind and seeing; and Relative, between Father and Son. And in contradictory opposites this Maxim is always true: What belongs to one cannot belong to the other; and, To whatever one does not belong, the other necessarily belongs: because their opposition is immediate. And the same holds in privative opposites, not indeed absolutely, but concerning an apt subject: as, To whatever blindness belongs, sight cannot at the same time belong; nor, To whatever sight belongs can blindness at the same time belong. And if sight does not belong, blindness must belong; and, If blindness does not belong, sight must belong. In contraries, however, the argument holds from the affirmation of one to the negation of the other: as, It is white; therefore it is not black. But it does not hold from the negation of one to the negation of the other: as, It is not white; therefore it is black; because contrary opposition is not immediate. And similar arguments can be deduced from repugnants, or disparates, whose examples are manifest enough.

Place 20, from the Dissimilar.

T    hose things are called Dissimilar which have a different form or nature: as

whiteness and sweetness, white and black, man and lion. To these are reduced those which, although they have the same form, yet have it not in the same degree but in a different one: such as hot as one and hot as eight. And from both, arguments can be taken: because what belongs to one cannot belong to the other. But they must always be taken formally, that

[p. 735]

is, inasmuch as they are dissimilar in nature or degree, and not according to other

material ratios, in which it is manifest that they can agree. And let it suffice to

have noted these things concerning the book of the Topics.

F O R T H E B O O K S O F T H E S O P H I S T I C A L R E F U TAT I O N S . T R E AT I S E

## ON THE SOPHISTICAL SYLLOGISM

hat Aristotle does in the two books of the Sophistical Refutations we 1

W              comprehend, so as to embrace this whole work in a universal divi‐

sion. He explains the nature of the Sophistical syllogism, and of the parts of

which it is composed, as of his proper object. Then he enumerates all the places from

which fallacious arguments are deduced, or take their occasion: which are the Fallacies

both in Speech and outside Speech. We, however, referring the things that pertain

to the fallacies to the Summulae, in which they are copiously explained, shall say

something about the nature of the sophistical syllogism; once this is understood,

whatever Aristotle delivers about it in the present work can be grasped, at least in

some measure.

What a Sophistical syllogism is, and how many kinds there are; and whether it is a true syllo‐

gism, or not? 2

T     he sophistical syllogism, if we follow the etymology of the name, signifies the

same as the syllogism of a wise man, since σοφός [sophos] is “wise”; yet by the

philosophical usage of the school it has come about that by it is now understood

not the syllogism of a wise man, but of one who deceives, or wishes to deceive.

Because by a sophist all now understand not a truly wise man, but one who wishes

to seem wise. Aristotle delivers the definition and division of the sophistical syllo‐

gism in Topics 1, ch. 1. But in order that the three things which can be considered

about it may be explained more conveniently, we must begin from the division.

Aristotle, then, divides the sophistical syllogism into three members, and de‐

fines the first thus: But the contentious is a syllogism from things which seem probable but

are not. The second in these words: And that which is from probable things, or from

things which seem probable, is apparent. And a little below, speaking of each in particu‐

lar, he asserts that the First is a true syllogism, the Second not true but apparent.

The last member he calls a paralogism; and he says that it is one because it takes

up propositions proper to some science, which, as they are taken up by that sci‐

ence, are necessary, but as they are taken up by him, only appear necessary, and are

false. And such is this syllogism: Lines drawn from the same point to the same point are

equal; the chord and the arc are drawn from the same point; therefore they are equal. This

syllogism is constituted in matter

[p. 736]

of geometry, but geometry takes the major proposition thus: All straight lines drawn from the same point to the same point are equal. And thus it is true and necessary; but since it is taken in that syllogism without the word straight, it appears indeed necessary, because it appears the same, but it is false and very different, as is evident; and therefore it proceeds from propositions of that science which appear necessary, yet are not truly necessary, but false.

3 Of these three syllogisms, then, the first, which is called Contentious, and the third, which is called Paralogism, agree in this, that each preserves the syllogistic form, since it is constituted in Figure and Mood; hence on this side it does not sin; but they differ in the things from which they proceed. For the former proceeds from things which appear probable but are not probable; whereas the paralogism proceeds from things necessary and proper to some science, but which are neither necessary nor pertain to that science, but are false. The second, however, which is also called contentious, differs from the other two in both respects. For in the first place it does not preserve the form of the syllogism, but sins in it; and therefore Aristotle said of it that it is a contentious syllogism, but not truly a syllogism, that is, that it does not have the true form of a syllogism, but only an apparent one.

And from these things it is understood, first, that the First and the third have the true form of a syllogism, and are therefore true syllogisms. For to proceed from apparent, or even from false, things does not take away the true form of a syllogism. But the Second is not a true syllogism, but an apparent one; and such are all those which do not preserve the rules of syllogisms, but proceed either from an equivocal middle, or from one not distributed, or from negative premises, or suffer other defects concerning form.

4 It is understood, second, that these three syllogisms are essentially diverse: because they differ either by reason of the syllogistic form or on the side of the premises. On the side of form, the second differs from the first and the third; and since a difference on the side of form is essential, it is evident that it differs essentially from them. Finally, the first and the third, although they agree in the syllogistic and as it were generic form, nevertheless differ in the special form, taken from the mode of concluding.

For the first proceeds and concludes from things which only appear probable; the third, however, from things which appear necessary. Therefore the first and the third differ as true species of syllogism. The second, however, does not differ from them as a true species, because, since it does not have the true form of a syllogism, neither can it be a true species of it, but only according to appearance. Hence

those

[p. 737]

those two are syllogisms simply, but this one is not, except in a certain respect: because it has only the appearance of a syllogism, in the way in which a painted man has only the appearance of a man. It differs from them, therefore, analogically.

Wherefore it is understood, third, that the division of the sophistical syllogism into these three members is a division of an analogous term into its Analogates; but with respect to two members, namely the first and the third, it is a division of a genus into its species. And therefore Aristotle did not define them all by one definition, but by different ones, at once dividing the sophistical syllogism into these three members and defining each by its proper definitions.

It is understood, fourth, that the general division of the syllogism into Demonstrative, Dialectical, and Sophistical is a division of a genus into its species, if sophistical is taken only for that which does not sin in form, in which way it comprehends only the first and the third. For taken in this way alone it is a true species of syllogism, though a subaltern one, since it is divided into two other species. The second syllogism, however, is not a true species of syllogism, since it lacks the form, but only according to appearance. Hence, if sophistical is taken as it comprehends all three, the same general division will, on its side, be analogous, since it comprehends one member which is not a syllogism except in a certain respect.

6 Besides this division of the syllogism into those three members, which is essential, it is divided by an accidental division into members according to the two different effects, or ends, which the sophist can intend through it. The first end is to display knowledge and to hunt for glory; and then it is called a sophistical syllogism only, or contentious: because through it the sophist intends not so much to set up a disputation as a quarrel or strife, and to overcome the respondent with fallacious words, and thus to be held wise in the opinion of the crowd. The second end is to make trial, or to take a test, of the knowledge of another; and then it is called a Tentative syllogism.

Next it is also divided accidentally into five other members, according to the five absurdities to which the sophist intends to lead the respondent. And these absurdities are customarily called goals, or terms: because it is as it were to them, as to the goal, mark, or end of his disputation, that he intends to lead the other. The first is the goal of Refutation: when the respondent is compelled, by the force of an apparent syllogism, to deny what he had previously granted, or to grant what he had denied.

7 The second is the goal of the false: when he is compelled to grant something openly false, as that he himself is not a man, by this syllogism: What I am, you are not; I am a man; therefore, You are not

AA a

[p. 738]

a man. The third is the goal of the unbelievable, or Paradox: when he is compelled to grant something unbelievable to the wise, or unheard of in the opinion of the crowd, although perhaps it is not false. The fourth, the goal of Solecism: when he is compelled to grant some incongruous expression. The fifth is called the goal of Babbling: when he is compelled to a useless and less ornate expression, by which he seems to babble. As if he is compelled to say that a nose is a curved or snub nose. And let it suffice to have noted these things on the sophistical syllogism: from which we shall know its nature, and also how many species and members it has, and how many of its members are true syllogisms, and how many not true, but only apparent. All the fallacies, however, which are as it were the places from which various fallacious syllogisms can be deduced, have been sufficiently explained in the Summulae; and therefore we do not think that the enumeration and explanation of each is to be repeated in this part.

These things, finally, we have noted in our Commentaries concerning the whole Logic of Aristotle, rendering it, I think, clear enough and brief, so that it may easily, and in a short time, be explained to the students of the liberal Arts of this most flourishing Academy by their Masters in the Schools, and be grasped by them. May G o d , Best and Greatest, grant that this labor of ours, undertaken for their sake, may redound to his glory and that of the most holy Mother of God, and of St. Thomas, and to the greatest benefit of those same students (as we hope). THE END OF THE WHOLE LOGIC.
